Tattha [M 0.0003][V 0.0003] abhidhammassa mātikāti ettha kenaṭṭhena abhidhammo? Dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena. Atirekavisesatthadīpako hi ettha abhi-saddo “bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti (saṃ. ni. 4.87; 5.195, 1022; ma. ni. 3.384, 389), abhikkantavaṇṇā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.1; khu. pā. 5.1; su. ni. maṅgalasutta; vi. va. 857) viya, tasmā yathā samussitesu bahūsu chattesu ceva dhajesu ca yaṃ atirekappamāṇaṃ, visesavaṇṇasaṇṭhānañca chattaṃ, taṃ aticchattaṃ, yo atirekappamāṇo, visesavaṇṇasaṇṭhāno ca dhajo, so atiddhajoti ca vuccati, evameva ayampi dhammo dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena “abhidhammo”ti vuccati. Bhagavatā hi suttantaṃ patvā khandhāyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaccayākārādayo dhammā ekadesena vibhattā, na nippadesena, abhidhammaṃ patvā pana anekehi nayavisesehi nippadesatova vibhattā. Evaṃ dhammātirekadhammavisesaṭṭhena “abhidhammo”ti veditabbo.

Here, regarding 'the matrix of the Abhidhamma,' in what sense is it Abhidhamma? In the sense of the Dhamma's superiority and distinctiveness. For here, the prefix 'abhi-' indicates superiority and distinctiveness, just as in such examples as 'Strong painful feelings advance in me, they do not recede' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.87; 5.195, 1022; Ma. Ni. 3.384, 389), or 'of surpassing beauty' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.1; Khu. Pā. 5.1; Su. Ni. Maṅgalasutta; Vi. Va. 857). Therefore, just as among many raised umbrellas and flags, that umbrella which is of surpassing size and has a distinguished color and shape is called a 'superior umbrella,' and that flag which is of surpassing size and has a distinguished color and shape is called a 'superior flag,' just so, this Dhamma, in the sense of the Dhamma's superiority and distinctiveness, is called 'Abhidhamma.' For in the Suttanta, the Blessed One has explained the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so on, partially, not exhaustively. But in the Abhidhamma, they are exhaustively analyzed by various special methods. Thus, 'Abhidhamma' should be understood in the sense of the Dhamma's superiority and distinctiveness.

Kenaṭṭhena mātikā? Mātusamaṭṭhena. Mātā viyāti hi mātikā yathā padumikaṃ mukhanti. Yathā hi mātā nānāvidhe putte pasavati, te pāleti, poseti ca, evamayampi nānāvidhe dhamme, atthe ca pasavati, te ca avinassamāne pāleti, poseti ca, tasmā “mātikā”ti vuccati. Mātikaṃ hi nissāya dhammasaṅgaṇīādisattappakaraṇavasena vitthāriyamānā anantāparimāṇā dhammā, atthā ca tāya pasutā, pālitā, positā viya ca honti. Tathā hi dhammasaṅgaṇippakaraṇe catasso vibhattiyo cittavibhatti rūpavibhatti nikkheparāsi atthuddhāroti[V 0.0004]. Tattha nānānayehi ekūnanavuticittavibhāvinī [M 0.0004] cittavibhatti vitthāriyamānā anantāparimāṇabhāṇavārā hoti, tadanantaraṃ ekavidhādinā rūpavibhāvinī rūpavibhatti vitthāriyamānā anantāparimāṇabhāṇavārā hoti, tadanantaraṃ mūlakhandhadvārādīni nikkhipitvā desito nikkheparāsi vitthāriyamāno anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāro hoti, tadanantaraṃ tepiṭakassa buddhavacanassa aṭṭhakathābhūto atthuddhāro vitthāriyamāno anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāro hoti. Evamidaṃ dhammasaṅgaṇippakaraṇaṃ vācanāmaggato atirekaterasamattabhāṇavārampi samānaṃ vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

In what sense is it a matrix (mātikā)? In the sense of being like a mother. For 'mātikā' is 'like a mother', just as in the expression 'padumikaṃ mukhaṃ' (a face like a lotus). Just as a mother gives birth to various kinds of children, protects them, and nourishes them, in the same way, this matrix gives birth to various kinds of dhammas and meanings, protects them without letting them perish, and nourishes them. Therefore, it is called a 'matrix.' For, based on the matrix, the immeasurable and boundless dhammas and meanings, elaborated through the seven treatises beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, are as if born, protected, and nourished by it. Indeed, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, there are four divisions: the analysis of consciousness (cittavibhatti), the analysis of matter (rūpavibhatti), the summary of categories (nikkheparāsi), and the extraction of meaning (atthuddhāro). Therein, the analysis of consciousness, which distinguishes the eighty-nine types of consciousness through various methods, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition. Following that, the analysis of matter, which distinguishes matter through the single type and so on, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition. After that, the summary of categories, which is taught after setting aside the root aggregates, doors, and so forth, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition. Then, the extraction of meaning, which serves as the commentary to the Buddha’s words in the three baskets, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition. Thus, this Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, even though the recited text amounts to over thirteen bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Tathā vibhaṅgappakaraṇe khandhavibhaṅgo āyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaappamaññāsikkhāpadapaṭisambhidāñāṇakhuddakavatthudhammahadayavibhaṅgāti aṭṭhārasa vibhaṅgā vibhattā, te suttantabhājanīyaabhidhammabhājanīyādinānānayehi vitthāriyamānā paccekaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavārā honti. Evamidaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ vācanāmaggato pañcatiṃsamattabhāṇavārampi samānaṃ vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

Similarly, in the Vibhaṅga treatise, the Vibhaṅga on aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, right exertions, bases of psychic power, enlightenment factors, path factors, jhānas, immeasurables, training rules, analytical knowledges, knowledge, minor topics, and the heart of the Dhamma—these eighteen Vibhaṅgas are distinguished. They are detailed in various ways, such as according to the Suttanta exposition and the Abhidhamma exposition, each becoming an immeasurable and boundless exposition. Thus, this Vibhaṅga treatise, even though the recited text amounts to thirty-five bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Tathā dhātukathāpakaraṇaṃ “saṅgaho asaṅgaho”tiādinā cuddasavidhena vibhattaṃ vācanāmaggato atirekachabhāṇavāramattampi samānaṃ vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

Similarly, the Dhātukathā treatise, analyzed in fourteen ways, beginning with 'inclusion and non-inclusion,' etc., even though the recited text amounts to just over six bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Tathā puggalapaññattippakaraṇaṃ khandhapaññatti āyatanadhātusaccaindriyapuggalapaññattīti chabbidhena vibhattaṃ vācanāmaggato atirekapañcabhāṇavāramattampi vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

Similarly, the Puggalapaññatti treatise, classified in six ways—the Designation of Aggregates, the Designation of Sense-Bases, the Designation of Elements, the Designation of Truths, the Designation of Faculties, and the Designation of Individuals—even though the recited text amounts to just over five bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Tathā [M 0.0005] kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ sakavāde pañca suttasatāni, paravāde pañca suttasatānīti suttasahassaṃ samodhānetvā vibhattaṃ vācanāmaggato saṅgītiāropitanayena dīghanikāyappamāṇampi vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

Similarly, the Kathāvatthu treatise, analyzed by combining a thousand suttas—five hundred suttas on one's own side and five hundred suttas on the other side—although by way of recitation it is the size of the Dīgha Nikāya according to the method established at the Saṅgīti, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Tathā yamakappakaraṇaṃ mūlayamakaṃ khandhāyatanadhātusaccasaṅkhāraanusayacittadhammaindriyayamakanti dasavidhena vibhattaṃ vācanāmaggato vīsabhāṇavārasatampi vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti.

Similarly, the Yamaka treatise, classified into ten types—the Root Yamaka, the Aggregates Yamaka, the Sense-Bases Yamaka, the Elements Yamaka, the Truths Yamaka, the Formations Yamaka, the Latent Tendencies Yamaka, the Mind Yamaka, the Phenomena Yamaka, and the Faculties Yamaka—even though the recited text amounts to one hundred and twenty bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition.

Paṭṭhānappakaraṇaṃ [V 0.0005] hetupaccayaārammaṇapaccayādicatuvīsatipaccaye gahetvā tikapaṭṭhānādicatuvīsatividhena vibhattaṃ paccekaṃ katipayabhāṇavārampi vitthāriyamānaṃ anantāparimāṇabhāṇavāraṃ hoti. Evaṃ anantāparimāṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ, atthānañca pasavanato, pālanato, posanato ca “mātā viyāti mātikā”ti vuccati. Pālanaposanañcettha sammuṭṭhānaṃ, viraddhānañca pāḷiatthānaṃ mātikānusārena sallakkhetvā samānayanato, rakkhaṇato ca veditabbaṃ. Sā panāyaṃ paricchedato dhammasaṅgaṇīmātikā vibhaṅgamātikā dhātukathāmātikā puggalapaññattimātikā kathāvatthumātikā yamakamātikā paṭṭhānamātikāti sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ ādimhi ṭhapitā sattavidhā hoti.

The Paṭṭhāna treatise, taking the twenty-four conditions such as root condition and object condition, is analyzed in twenty-four ways through the Tikapaṭṭhāna and others, and even though each amounts to a few bhāṇavāras, when elaborated, it becomes an immeasurable and boundless exposition. Thus, because it generates, protects, and nourishes immeasurable and boundless dhammas and meanings, it is called 'mātikā,' like a mother. Here, 'protection' and 'nourishment' are to be understood as the discerning and bringing together, according to the matrix, of Pāli texts and their meanings which are forgotten or corrupted, and also as their preservation. This matrix, in terms of its divisions, is established at the beginning of seven treatises: the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix, the Vibhaṅga matrix, the Dhātukathā matrix, the Puggalapaññatti matrix, the Kathāvatthu matrix, the Yamaka matrix, and the Paṭṭhāna matrix—thus being sevenfold.

Tattha dhammasaṅgaṇīmātikā ādi, sāpi tikamātikā dukamātikāti duvidhā. Tattha dvāvīsati tikā tikamātikā nāma. Dvecattālīsasatadukā dukamātikā nāma, sā puna āhaccabhāsitā sāvakabhāsitāti duvidhā. Tattha dvāvīsati tikā ceva, “hetū dhammā na hetū dhammā…pe… saraṇā dhammā araṇā dhammā”ti ime ca sataṃ [M 0.0006] dukāti ayaṃ āhaccabhāsitā sammāsambuddhadesitā sattannaṃ pakaraṇānaṃ mātikā nāma, tadanantarā “vijjābhāgino dhammā avijjābhāgino dhammā…pe… khayeñāṇaṃ anuppādeñāṇa”nti ime dvācattālīsa suttantikadukā dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherena ṭhapitattā sāvakabhāsitā nāma. Ime ṭhapento pana thero na sāmukkaṃsikena attano ñāṇena ṭhapesi, ekuttariyaṃ pana ekakanipātadukanipātasaṅgītisuttadasuttarasuttehi samodhānetvā ābhidhammikattherānaṃ suttantaṃ patvā akilamanatthaṃ ṭhapesi.

Among these, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix is primary, and it is of two kinds: the Triadic Matrix (Tikamātikā) and the Dyadic Matrix (Dukamātikā). Among them, the twenty-two Triads are called the Triadic Matrix. The one hundred and forty-two Dyads are called the Dyadic Matrix, which is further divided into two: the Directly Expounded (Āhaccabhāsitā) and the Disciple-Expounded (Sāvakabhāsitā). Here, the twenty-two Triads and the one hundred Dyads—such as 'root states, non-root states… states that are refuges, states that are not refuges'—are called the Directly Expounded, the matrix taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One for the seven treatises. Immediately following these, the forty-two Suttanta Dyads—such as 'states pertaining to knowledge, states pertaining to ignorance… knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising'—are called the Disciple-Expounded, as they were established by the Elder Sāriputta, General of the Dhamma. However, when establishing these, the Elder did not establish them solely on his own independent knowledge. Instead, he correlated them with the Ekuttara, Ekaka Nipāta, Duka Nipāta, Saṅgīti Sutta, and Dasuttara Sutta, and established them for the Abhidhamma experts, so that they would not become weary in regard to the Suttanta.

Sā puna sappadesanippadesavasena dve koṭṭhāsā honti. Ettha hi nava tikā, ekasattati ca dukā sappadesānaṃ sāvasesānaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ pariggahitattā sappadesā nāma, avasesā terasa tikā, ekasattati ca dukā nippadesānaṃ niravasesānaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ gahitattā nippadesā nāma. Tesaṃ vibhāgo tattha tattheva āvi bhavissati. Tathā nāmalābhavasena dvidhā. Sabbeva hi ete tikadukā ādipadavasena, sabbapadavasena cāti dvidhā nāmaṃ labhanti. Tattha “kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā”ti ayaṃ tāva ādipadavasena laddhanāmo kusalattiko nāma. “Sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā…pe… dhammā”ti ayaṃ sabbapadavasena laddhanāmo vedanāttiko nāma. Evaṃ sabbesampi tikadukānaṃ nāmaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, they are of two sections based on having a remainder (sappadesa) and having no remainder (nippadesa). Here, the nine triads and seventy-one dyads are called 'with remainder' because they encompass name-and-form with remainder. The remaining thirteen triads and seventy-one dyads are called 'without remainder' because they encompass name-and-form without remainder. Their classification will become evident in their respective places. Similarly, they are twofold based on how they receive their names. All these triads and dyads receive a name in two ways: either by the first term or by all the terms. For instance, the triad 'wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states' is called the 'wholesome triad' by the first term. The triad 'states associated with pleasant feeling… states' is called the 'feeling triad' by all the terms. In this way, the names of all triads and dyads should be understood.

Sā panesā pañcadasahi paricchedehi vavatthitā. Tikānaṃ hi eko paricchedo, dukānaṃ cuddasa[V 0.0006]. “Hetū dhammā nahetū dhammā”tiādayo hi cha dukā ganthato ca atthato ca aññamaññasambandhena kaṇṇikā viya, ghaṭā viya ca hutvā ṭhitattā “hetugocchako”ti vuccati. Tato apare “sappaccayā dhammā”tiādayo satta dukā aññamaññaṃ asambandhā [M 0.0007] kevalaṃ dukasāmaññena uccinitvā gocchakantare ṭhapitattā, aññehi ca antaradukehi cūḷakattā “cūḷantaradukā”ti veditabbā. Tato paraṃ āsavadukādīnaṃ channaṃ dukānaṃ vasena āsavagocchako nāma. Tato saṃyojanadukādīnaṃ channaṃ vasena saṃyojanagocchako nāma. Tathā ganthaoghayoganīvaraṇadukādīnaṃ channaṃ channaṃ vasena ganthaoghayoganīvaraṇagocchakā nāma. Parāmāsadukādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vasena parāmāsagocchako nāma. Tato paraṃ sārammaṇadukādayo catuddasa dukā mahantaradukā nāma. Tato paraṃ upādānadukādayo cha dukā upādānagocchako nāma. Tato kilesadukādayo aṭṭhadukā kilesagocchako nāma. Tato paraṃ dassanenapahātabbadukādayo aṭṭhārasa dukā abhidhammamātikāya pariyosāne ṭhapitattā piṭṭhidukā nāma. Vijjābhāgiyadukādayo pana dvācattālīsa dukā suttantikadukā nāma. Evametissā pañcadasahi paricchedehi vavatthitāya tāva ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā bhavissati.

It is arranged into fifteen sections. Of these, one section belongs to the triads, and fourteen to the dyads. The six dyads beginning with “states that are roots, states that are not roots” are called the “Root Cluster” because they stand connected to each other in terms of text and meaning, like the hub of a wheel or a pot. Then, the other seven dyads, beginning with “states with conditions,” are to be understood as the “Minor Intermediate Dyads” because they are unrelated to each other, merely picked out by their common characteristic as dyads, placed between the clusters, and are minor compared to other intermediate dyads. Following that, the six dyads beginning with the “taints” form the “Taints Cluster.” Then, the six dyads beginning with the “fetters” form the “Fetters Cluster.” Similarly, the six dyads each beginning with the “ties,” “floods,” “yokes,” and “hindrances” form the “Ties Cluster,” “Floods Cluster,” “Yokes Cluster,” and “Hindrances Cluster” respectively. The five dyads beginning with “misconception” form the “Misconception Cluster.” After that, the fourteen dyads beginning with “states with an object” are called the “Major Intermediate Dyads.” Then, the six dyads beginning with “grasping” form the “Grasping Cluster.” Next, the eight dyads beginning with “defilements” form the “Defilements Cluster.” After that, the eighteen dyads beginning with “states to be abandoned by seeing” are called the “Rear Dyads” because they are placed at the end of the Abhidhamma matrix. However, the forty-two dyads beginning with “states pertaining to knowledge” are called the “Suttanta Dyads.” Thus, this exposition of meaning will now proceed according to its arrangement into these fifteen sections.

Kusalattikavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Wholesome Triad

Yasmā panettha tikamātikā ādi, tatthāpi kusalattiko ādi, tasmā kusalattikassa tāva –

Since here the matrix of triads is primary, and among them the wholesome triad is primary, therefore, first of all, concerning the wholesome triad—

Atthato bhūmibhedā ca, paccekaṃ sampayogato;

Uddesato ca dhammānaṃ, lakkhaṇādivibhāgato.

By way of meaning, by way of distinctions of planes, and by way of individual association; by way of enumeration of phenomena, and by way of divisions of characteristics and so on.

Saṅgahā suññato ceva, visayādippabhedato;

Yathānurūpaṃ sabbattha, veditabbo vinicchayo.

By way of comprehension, by way of emptiness, and by way of distinctions of object and so on; the analysis should be understood everywhere accordingly.

Tattha atthato tāva kusalā dhammāti ettha kusalasaddo ārogyānavajjachekasukhavipākesu dissati. Ayaṃ hi [M 0.0008] “kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmaya”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.15.246; 2.20.129) ārogye dissati. “Katamo pana, bhante, kāyasamācāro kusalo[V 0.0007]? Yo kho, mahārāja, kāyasamācāro anavajjo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.361) anavajje. “Kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgāna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.87) cheke. “Kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 431) sukhavipāke. Svāyamidha ārogyepi anavajjepi sukhavipākepi vattati. Yatheva hi rūpakāye nibyādhitāya ārogyaṭṭhena kusalaṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ arūpadhammepi kilesabyādhino abhāvena ārogyaṭṭhena kusalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kilesavajjassa pana abhāvā anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ.

Here, first, as to the meaning: in the phrase “wholesome states” (kusalā dhammā), the word “kusala” is found in the senses of health, blamelessness, skill, and pleasant result. Indeed, it is found in the sense of health in passages such as, “I hope you are well, sir, I hope you are free from illness” (Jā 1.15.246; 2.20.129). It is found in the sense of blamelessness in passages such as, “But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That bodily conduct, great king, which is blameless” (MN 88). It is found in the sense of skill in passages such as, “You are skilled in the parts and accessories of the chariot” (MN 151). And it is found in the sense of pleasant result in passages such as, “Because of having done and accumulated wholesome kamma” (Dhs §431). Here, it applies in the sense of health, blamelessness, and pleasant result. Just as in the case of the physical body, being free from disease is called wholesome in the sense of health, so too in the case of immaterial states, what is wholesome should be understood as being free from the disease of defilements in the sense of health. Moreover, because of the absence of the fault of defilements, it is wholesome in the sense of blamelessness.

Dhamma-saddo panāyaṃ pariyattihetuguṇanissattanijjīvatādīsu dissati. Ayaṃ hi “dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti suttaṃ geyya”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.102) pariyattiyaṃ dissati. “Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 720) hetumhi. “Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino”tiādīsu (theragā. 304) guṇe. “Dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373) nissattanijjīvatāyaṃ, svāyamidhāpi nissattanijjīvatāyameva vaṭṭati.

The word “dhamma,” however, is found in the senses of scripture, cause, quality, non-self, lifelessness, and so on. Indeed, it is found in the sense of scripture in passages such as, “He learns the Dhamma—discourses, verses…” (AN 4.102). It is found in the sense of cause in passages such as, “Knowledge of cause is the discrimination of phenomena” (Vibh §720). It is found in the sense of quality in passages such as, “For neither the Dhamma nor the non-Dhamma yield the same result” (Thag 6.11). It is found in the sense of non-self and lifelessness in passages such as, “He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena” (DN 22). Here too, it applies solely in the sense of non-self and lifelessness.

Vacanattho panettha – kucchite pāpadhamme salayanti calayanti kampenti viddhaṃsentīti kusalā. Kucchitena vā ākārena sayantīti kusā, te kuse lunanti chindantīti kusalā. Kucchitānaṃ vā sānato tanukaraṇato ñāṇaṃ kusaṃ nāma, tena kusena lātabbā parivattetabbāti kusalā. Atha vā kosallaṃ vuccati paññā, tato kosallato sambhūtattā kusalā. Idaṃ pana anantare vuttañcāti nibbacanadvayaṃ kiñcāpi nippariyāyato ñāṇasampayuttānameva [M 0.0009] yujjati, ruḷhīvasena pana taṃsadisatāya ñāṇavippayuttānampīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā vā kusā ubhayabhāgagataṃ hatthappadesaṃ lunanti, evamimepi uppannānuppannabhāvena ubhayabhāgagataṃ saṃkilesapakkhaṃ lunanti, tasmā kusā viya lunantīti kusalā. Attano pana sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhammā, dhārīyanti vā paccayehi, dhārīyanti vā yathāsabhāvato ādhārīyantītipi dhammā. Na kusalā akusalā, mittapaṭipakkhā amittā viya kusalapaṭipakkhāti attho. Na byākatāti abyākatā, kusalākusalabhāvena akathitāti attho. Tesu anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā kusalā, sāvajjadukkhavipākalakkhaṇā akusalā, avipākalakkhaṇā abyākatā.

Here, the etymological meaning is: they shake (salayanti), disturb (calayanti), agitate (kampenti), and destroy (viddhaṃsenti) despicable (kucchite) evil states—thus, they are “wholesome” (kusalā). Or, because they lie down (sayanti) in a despicable (kucchitena) manner, they are “kusa”; they cut (lunanti) and sever (chindanti) those “kusa”—thus, they are “kusalā.” Or, knowledge that weakens or reduces despicable things is called “kusa”; by means of that “kusa,” they should be grasped and transformed—thus, they are “kusalā.” Alternatively, skillfulness (kosallaṃ) is called wisdom (paññā); because they arise from that skillfulness, they are “kusalā.” Moreover, this twofold explanation, stated immediately before, applies strictly to those associated with knowledge; but conventionally, it should be understood to extend to those dissociated from knowledge, due to similarity. Just as blades of kusa grass cut the part of the hand that is on both sides, so too do these cut both sides—the arisen and unarisen—of the faction of defilements. Therefore, like blades of kusa grass that cut, they are called “kusalā.” Furthermore, they bear their own nature—thus, they are “dhammas.” Or, they are sustained by conditions; or, they are supported according to their own nature—thus, they are “dhammas.” “Unwholesome” (akusalā) means not wholesome. Just as enemies are the opposite of friends, so the unwholesome is the opposite of the wholesome—this is the meaning. “Undeclared” (abyākatā) means not declared as either wholesome or unwholesome—this is the meaning. Among these, the wholesome is characterized by blamelessness and pleasant results, the unwholesome by blameworthiness and painful results, and the undeclared by the absence of results.

Kiṃ panetāni kusalāti vā dhammāti vātiādīni ekatthāni, udāhu nānatthānīti? Kiñcettha [V 0.0008] yadi tāva ekatthāni, “kusalā dhammā”ti idaṃ “kusalā kusalā”ti vuttasadisaṃ hoti. Atha nānatthāni, tikadukānaṃ chakkacatukkabhāvo āpajjati, padānañca asambandho “kusalā rūpaṃ cakkhumā”tiādīnaṃ viya. Athāpi yadi etāni ekatthāni, kusalākusalābyākatapadānaṃ tiṇṇampi dhammānaṃ dhammasabhāvena ekattā kusalādīnampi ekattaṃ āpajjati. Atha “kusalapadato akusalādipadassa aññattaṃ siyā”ti vadatha, na etāni ekatthāni. Tadā dhammo nāma bhāvo. Bhāvato ca añño abhāvoti. Evaṃ aññoññāpekkhāya abhāvattamāpannehi dhammehi anaññe kusalādayopi abhāvā eva siyunti? Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ, kasmā? Yathānumativohārasiddhito, na hi “kusalā dhammā”tiādīni padāni yathā kusalā kusalāti, evaṃ atthavisesābhāvena paṇḍitehi [M 0.0010] anumatāni, nāpi kusalā rūpaṃ cakkhumā-saddā viya aññamaññaṃ anolokitatthabhāvena, atha kho anavajjaiṭṭhavipākattādisaṅkhātassa atthavisesassa, sabhāvasādhāraṇādiatthasāmaññassa ca jotakattena yathākkamaṃ anumatāni. Kusala-saddo hi dhamma-saddassa purato vuccamāno kusalākusalādisabbasādhāraṇasāmaññatthadīpakaṃ dhamma-saddaṃ akusalādito nivattetvā attano attano atthavisesavisiṭṭhatthadīpakaṃ karoti. Evaṃ paccekaṃ bhinnavisayānampi nesaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena pavattiyaṃ ekatthatāya paṇḍitānumatatāya yathāvuttadosāropane kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ tato paresupi sabbattha yathānurūpato ñātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva padatthato vinicchayo.

But are these terms, such as “wholesome” or “phenomena,” synonymous, or do they have distinct meanings? For if they were synonymous, then the phrase “wholesome phenomena” would be similar to saying “wholesome wholesome.” On the other hand, if they had distinct meanings, then the triads and dyads would become sixfold and fourfold, and the words would lack connection, as in phrases like “wholesome form, the eye,” and so on. Furthermore, if these terms were synonymous, then all three—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—would be unified by their intrinsic nature as phenomena, and likewise, the wholesome and other categories would also become one. But if you say that the term “wholesome” differs from “unwholesome” and other terms, then these are not synonymous. In that case, a phenomenon is an existent. And what is other than an existent is a non-existent. Thus, if phenomena, by mutual dependence, were to imply non-existence, then the wholesome and other categories would also be mere non-existents, would they not? All this is without reason—why? Because it is established by sanctioned convention. For terms like “wholesome phenomena” are not sanctioned by the wise as being without distinction in meaning, like saying “wholesome wholesome,” nor are they like the words “wholesome, form, eye,” etc., which have unrelated meanings; but rather, they are sanctioned respectively because they illuminate a specific meaning—such as being blameless, having desirable results, etc.—and a general meaning, due to their shared intrinsic nature. For the word “wholesome,” when placed before the word “phenomena,” turns the general meaning of the word “phenomena”—which applies to all, including the unwholesome—away from the unwholesome and illuminates its own specific meaning, qualified by that specific meaning. Thus, even though their objects are individually distinct, their functioning as qualifier and qualified is regarded by the wise as being a unity. Therefore, the reason given for attributing the aforementioned faults is without reason; all this is without reason. In this way, the same principle should be understood everywhere in subsequent cases accordingly. This, then, is the analysis from the perspective of word meanings.

Kusalapadattho

The Meaning of the Term 'Wholesome'

Bhūmibhedāti tesu kusalākusalābyākatesu dhammesu kusalā tāva dhammā bhūmibhedato catubbidhā honti – kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā arūpāvacarā lokuttarāti. Ayaṃ bhūmibhedato vinicchayo.

By way of the division of planes: Among those wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states, the wholesome states are fourfold by way of the division of planes—namely, the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, the formless-sphere, and the supramundane. This is the analysis by way of the division of planes.

Sampayogatoti evaṃ bhūmibhedato catubbidhānampi nesaṃ paccekaṃ sampayogato vinicchayo veditabbo. Tattha kāmāvacarā tāva sampayogato aṭṭhavidhā honti. Seyyathidaṃ? Somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ. Upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ. Somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ. Upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāranti. Tattha iṭṭhārammaṇatā, saddhābāhullatā, visuddhadiṭṭhitā, ānisaṃsadassāvitā ca ekādasa pītisambojjhaṅgakāraṇāni cāti [V 0.0009] imehi tāva kāraṇehi somanassasahagatabhāvo veditabbo. Ñāṇasampattiṃ pana [M 0.0011] patthetvā katakammato, brahmādiupapattito, paññādasakavasena indriyaparipākato, vikkhambhanena kilesadūribhāvato ca sattavidhadhammavicayasambojjhaṅgakāraṇato ca ñāṇasampayuttatā veditabbā. Attano vā paresaṃ vā vasena pavatto pubbapayogo saṅkhāro nāma.

By way of concomitance: Thus, the analysis of these four types, divided by way of planes, should be understood individually by way of their concomitance. Among these, the sense-sphere types are eightfold by way of concomitance, namely: accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted; similarly, prompted; accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, unprompted; similarly, prompted; accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; similarly, prompted; accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; similarly, prompted. Here, the state of being accompanied by joy should be understood due to such causes as a pleasing object, abundance of faith, purity of view, seeing the benefits, and the eleven factors that are causes for the joy enlightenment factor. Association with knowledge should be understood to arise from having performed a deed while aspiring for the attainment of knowledge, from rebirth as a Brahma or the like, from the maturity of faculties in fifteen ways, from the distancing of defilements through suppression, and from the seven factors that are causes for the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor. Prior effort, whether initiated by oneself or by others, is called 'prompting' (saṅkhāra).

Tena uppannaṃ sasaṅkhāraṃ, tadabhāvā asaṅkhārañca veditabbaṃ. Etesu hi yathāvuttasomanassañāṇahetuṃ āgamma pahaṭṭho “atthi dinna”nti ādinayappavattaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā asaṃsīdanto, parehi ca anussāhito dānādīni puññāni karoti, tadāssa somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana vuttanayena haṭṭhatuṭṭho sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā amuttacāgitādivasena saṃsīdamāno, attano paṭisaṅkhārena vā parehi vā ussāhito karoti, tadāssa tadeva sasaṅkhāraṃ dutiyaṃ kusalaṃ hoti. Yadā pana ñātijanādipaṭipattidassanena jātaparicayā bāladārakādayo bhikkhuādidassanena somanassajātā sahasā dānavandanādīni karonti, tadā ñāṇavippayuttaṃ tatiyaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana ñātiādīhi ussāhitā evaṃ paṭipajjanti, tadā tadeva catutthaṃ sasaṅkhāracittaṃ hoti. Yadā pana somanassahetuno abhāvena visuṃ catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitā honti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni kusalāni uppajjanti. Evaṃ paccekaṃ sampayogato vinicchayo veditabbo.

One should understand that which arises with prompting (sasaṅkhāra) and that which is unprompted (asaṅkhāra) due to its absence. For in these cases, when one is joyful, having relied on the cause of joy and knowledge as previously described, and with right view at the forefront, without wavering, thinking, 'There is giving,' and so forth, in that manner, and without being encouraged by others, performs meritorious deeds such as generosity—then the first wholesome state arises in him, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge. But when, being joyful and delighted in the manner described, with right view at the forefront, yet wavering due to lack of generosity or other reasons, he performs the act either through self-reflection or being urged by others—then the second wholesome state arises with prompting. When, upon seeing the conduct of relatives and others, children and the like, having become accustomed, or upon seeing monks and the like, spontaneously feel joy and perform acts such as giving or paying respects—then the third wholesome state arises, dissociated from knowledge. When relatives and others encourage them to act in this way, then that very fourth state of mind arises with prompting. But when there is no cause for joy, and in the four different cases they are devoid of joy, then the remaining four wholesome states of mind arise, accompanied by equanimity. Thus, the analysis should be understood individually in terms of their concomitants.

Uddesato ca dhammānanti evaṃ sampayogato aṭṭhavidhesu kusalesu paccekaṃ dhammānaṃ uddesatopi vinicchayo veditabbo. Tattha paṭhamakusale tāva pāḷiyā sarūpena āgatā tiṃsa dhammā, yevāpanakā navāti ekūnacattālīsa dhammā [M 0.0012] honti. Seyyathidaṃ – phasso vedanā saññā cetanā cittaṃ vitakko vicāro pīti vīriyaṃ cittekaggatā jīvitaṃ saddhā sati hirī ottappaṃ alobho adoso amoho kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi kāyalahutā cittalahutā kāyamudutā cittamudutā kāyakammaññatā cittakammaññatā kāyapāguññatā cittapāguññatā kāyujukatā cittujukatāti ime sarūpena āgatā tiṃsadhammā. Chando adhimokkho manasikāro tatramajjhattatā karuṇā muditā kāyaduccaritavirati vacīduccaritavirati micchājīvaviratīti ime yevāpanakā navāti.

And by way of the enumeration of states: Thus, the analysis of the states should be understood individually in terms of their enumeration within the eightfold wholesome states by way of concomitance. Here, in the first wholesome state, thirty states are presented in the Pāli text in their own form, and nine are included as occasion requires, making a total of thirty-nine states. Namely: contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, initial thought, sustained thought, joy, energy, mental one-pointedness, life faculty, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, rectitude of mind—these are the thirty states presented in their own form. Zeal, resolution, attention, neutrality, compassion, sympathetic joy, abstinence from bodily misconduct, abstinence from verbal misconduct, abstinence from wrong livelihood—these are the nine included as occasion requires.

Padabhājanīye [V 0.0010] pana –

In the Analysis of Terms, however:

“Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti…pe… tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti, vedanā…pe… saññā cetanā cittaṃ vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā saddhindriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ samādhindriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ manindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi saddhābalaṃ vīriyabalaṃ satibalaṃ samādhibalaṃ paññābalaṃ hiribalaṃ ottappabalaṃ alobho adoso amoho anabhijjhā abyāpādo sammādiṭṭhi hirī ottappaṃ kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi kāyalahutā cittalahutā kāyamudutā cittamudutā kāyakammaññatā cittakammaññatā kāyapāguññatā cittapāguññatā kāyujukatā cittujukatā sati sampajaññaṃ samatho vipassanā paggāho avikkhepo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) –

"When a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere arises... at that time there is contact, feeling... perception, volition, consciousness, initial thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, mental one-pointedness, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of mind, the faculty of joy, the faculty of life, right view, right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, non-covetousness, non-ill-will, right view, moral shame, moral dread, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, rectitude of mind, mindfulness, clear comprehension, serenity, insight, exertion, non-distraction." (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1)

Evaṃ sarūpato uddiṭṭhā chapaññāsa dhammā “ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā”ti [M 0.0013] (dha. sa. 1) evaṃ yevāpanakavasena sāmaññato uddiṭṭhā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ cassā tesu tesu suttappadesesu āgate gahetvā sarūpato niddiṭṭhā chandādayo navāti pañcasaṭṭhi dhammā āgatā. Yasmā pana tesu sarūpena āgatā jhānaṅgaindriyamaggaṅgabalamūlādīnaṃ vasena ekasseva bahukiccatādassanatthaṃ punappunaṃ gahetvā pariyāyena chapaññāsavidhena desitāpi agahitaggahaṇena yathāvuttā samatiṃseva dhammā honti, te pana savibhattikā avibhattikāti duvidhā. Tattha phassādayo aṭṭhārasa ekakattā avibhattikā. Vedanādayo dvādasa dhammā aṭṭhatiṃsappabhedena yathāyogaṃ vibhattattā savibhattikā, yevāpanakā pana avibhattikā eva. Tasmā te sabbepi nippariyāyena ekūnacattālīsa dhammāva honti. Honti cettha –

Thus, fifty-six states have been enumerated in their own form. "And whatever other dependently arisen, formless phenomena exist at that time" (Dhs. 1)—in this way, they have been enumerated generally by way of inclusion. In the commentary, however, taking those that appear in various sutta passages, nine such as desire and so on, specifically indicated, are added, totaling sixty-five states. But since among these, those that are presented in their own form—such as the jhāna factors, faculties, path factors, powers, and roots—are repeatedly taken up for the purpose of showing the multifunctionality of one thing, even though they are taught in fifty-six ways by way of variation, by not taking what has already been taken, they amount to only thirty states as stated. These, however, are of two kinds: those with divisions and those without. Among them, the eighteen beginning with contact are single-fold and without divisions. The twelve states beginning with feeling are divided into thirty-eight categories according to their respective appropriateness, hence they are with divisions. The inclusive ones, however, are without divisions. Therefore, all of them, without variation, amount to only thirty-nine states. Herein, there are—

Phassādipañcakaṃ pañcajhānaṅgānindriyaṭṭhakaṃ;

Maggaṅgapañcakaṃ sattabalaṃ mūlattikampi ca.

The group of five beginning with contact, the five jhāna factors, the eight faculties; The five path factors, the seven powers, and the three roots as well.

Kammapathattikañceva[V 0.0011], lokapāladukaṃ tathā;

Passaddhiādī cha dukā, tīṇi piṭṭhidukāniti.

And the group of three courses of action, and likewise the pair of world-protectors; The six pairs beginning with tranquility, and the three subsidiary pairs.

Sattarasahi rāsīhi, chapaññāseva pāḷiyaṃ;

Vuttā sabhāvato tiṃsa, dhammā agahitaggahe.

By seventeen groups, fifty-six in the Pāli text; Thirty states are said by nature, by not taking what has already been taken.

Phasso jīvitasaññā ca, cetanā cārapītiyo;

Cha dukā kāyapassaddhi-pamukhāṭṭhārasekakā.

Contact, life faculty, and perception; Volition, examination, and joy; The six pairs beginning with tranquility of body—these eighteen are single-fold.

Cittaṃ vitakko saddhā ca, hiriottappiyampi ca;

Alobho ca adoso ca, satta dvidhā vibhāvitā.

Consciousness, thought, and faith; Moral shame and moral dread as well; Non-greed and non-hatred—these seven are classified as twofold.

Vedanā tividhā vīriyaṃ, sati ca catudhā matā;

Chaddhā ekaggatā paññā, sattadhāva vibhāvitā.

Feeling is threefold; energy and mindfulness are considered fourfold; Mental one-pointedness is sixfold; wisdom, indeed, is analyzed sevenfold.

Viratī [M 0.0014] appamaññāyo, manakkāro chandamajjhattā;

Dhimokkho yevāpanakā, navete paṭhame mane.

The abstinences and the immeasurables, attention, desire and equanimity; Resolution—these nine from the inclusive category are in the first mind.

Pañcasaṭṭhividheneva, pariyāyena desitā;

Navādhikā ca tettiṃsa, dhammāva paramatthatoti.

Indeed, they are taught in sixty-five ways by way of variation; And thirty-nine states are indeed the ultimate reality.

Ettha ca sarūpena āgatā tiṃsa dhammā, yevāpanakesu cattāro cāti catuttiṃsa dhammā ekakkhaṇe niyatā labbhanti, sesā pana karuṇādayo pañca karuṇāpubbabhāgamuditāpubbabhāgavasena, kāyaduccaritavacīduccaritamicchājīvehi viramaṇavasena ca cittassa pavattikālesu eva uppajjitvā aññathānuppajjanato aniyatā. Te ca yasmā dukkhitasukhitasattavasena, kāyaduccaritādittayavasena ca paccekaṃ bhinnavisayattā ekato na uppajjanti, tasmā karuṇāpubbabhāgādivasena pavattesu pañcasu cittakkhaṇesu niyatā catuttiṃsa, karuṇādīsu [V 0.0012] ekanti pañcatiṃsa dhammā uppajjanti, kevalaṃ pana dānādivasena pavattiyaṃ niyatā catuttiṃseva uppajjantīti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ dhammuddesato vinicchayo.

Herein, thirty states presented in their own form, and four among the included ones—making thirty-four states—are found to be determined to arise in a single moment. The rest, however, namely the five beginning with compassion, are undetermined, since they arise only on occasions of compassion and sympathetic joy, or of abstaining from bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and wrong livelihood, and do not arise otherwise. And because they do not arise together due to having distinct individual objects—such as suffering and happy beings, or the three kinds of bodily misconduct—thus, in the five types of mind-moments occurring on occasions of compassion and so on, thirty-five states arise: the thirty-four determined states, and one from among compassion and the others. However, it should be understood that when occurring solely in connection with giving and the like, only the thirty-four determined states arise. This is the analysis in terms of the enumeration of states.

Lakkhaṇādivibhāgatoti evaṃ uddiṭṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇarasādito vinicchayo veditabbo. Phusatīti phasso. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno. Ayaṃ hi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe phusanākārena pavattatīti phusanalakkhaṇo, sā cassa phusanākārappavatti ambilādidassane kheḷuppādādinā ñātabbā. Ekadesena pana anallīyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhuṃ, saddo viya ca sotaṃ cittamārammaṇañca saṅghaṭṭetīti saṅghaṭṭanaraso. Tikasannipātasaṅkhātassa pana attano kāraṇassa vasena paveditattā sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, phalaṭṭhena paccupaṭṭhānena panesa vedanāpaccupaṭṭhāno nāma hoti. Tajjāsamannāhārena ceva [M 0.0015] indriyena ca parikkhate visaye anantarāyena uppajjanato āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhānoti vuccati. Vedanādhiṭṭhānabhāvato panesa niccammā gāvī viya daṭṭhabbo. Lakkhaṇādīsu ca tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo vā sāmaññaṃ vā lakkhaṇaṃ nāma, kiccaṃ vā sampatti vā raso nāma, upaṭṭhānākāro vā phalaṃ vā paccupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, āsannakāraṇaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Evaṃ uparipi sabbattha lakkhaṇādīnaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The analysis of characteristics, etc., is as follows: The characteristics, function, and so on of the phenomena thus enumerated should be understood. "Phusatīti phasso" means "contact is that which touches." Its characteristic is touching. Its function is impacting. Its manifestation is concurrence. Its proximate cause is the object that has entered the sensory range. Though this is a formless phenomenon, it operates by way of touching its object—thus, its characteristic is touching. This operation of touching can be understood through examples like the production of saliva when seeing something sour. Though not entirely clinging, like the eye to form or the ear to sound, it impacts the mind and its object—thus, its function is impacting. Because it is declared to arise dependent on its own cause, which is the concurrence of the three, its manifestation is concurrence. But in terms of its result, its manifestation is said to be feeling. It arises unimpeded in an object that has been prepared by appropriate attention and the faculty—thus, its proximate cause is the object that has entered the sensory range. Because it serves as the basis for feeling, it should be regarded like a flayed cow. Among the characteristics, etc., the intrinsic nature or generality of each phenomenon is called its characteristic. Its function or accomplishment is called its function. Its mode of appearance or result is called its manifestation. Its immediate cause is called its proximate cause. In this way, the diversity of characteristics, etc., should be understood in all cases above as well.

Vedayatīti vedanā, sā vedayitalakkhaṇā, sabhāvabhedato panesā pañcavidhā hoti – sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ somanassaṃ domanassaṃ upekkhāti. Tattha iṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ sukhaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ, kāyikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyindriyapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Aniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ milāpanarasaṃ, kāyikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyindriyapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ somanassaṃ, yathā tathā vā iṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ vā, cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, iṭṭhākāradassanapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, yathā tathā vā aniṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ milāpanarasaṃ vā, cetasikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ekantena hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ. Majjhattavedayitalakkhaṇā upekkhā, sampayuttānaṃ nātiupabrūhanamilāpanarasā, santabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, nippītikacittapadaṭṭhānā. Ettha ca sukhaṃ, dukkhañca ekantamabyākataṃ, domanassamekantamakusalaṃ, somanassupekkhā pana siyā kusalā, siyā akusalā, siyā abyākatā. Idha pana kusalā somanassavedanā adhippetā.

To feel is feeling; feeling has the characteristic of experiencing. But through distinctions of nature, it is fivefold: pleasant, painful, joyful, sorrowful, and neutral. Herein, pleasant feeling has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object, the function of invigorating associated states, manifestation as bodily enjoyment, and the body faculty as its proximate cause. Painful feeling has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object, the function of withering associated states, manifestation as bodily affliction, and the body faculty as its proximate cause. Joyful feeling has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object, the function of enjoying a desirable aspect in various ways, or the function of invigorating associated states, manifestation as mental enjoyment, and the sight of a desirable aspect as its proximate cause. Sorrowful feeling has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object, the function of experiencing an undesirable aspect in various ways, or the function of withering associated states, manifestation as mental affliction, and exclusively the heart-basis as its proximate cause. Neutral feeling has the characteristic of experiencing in a middling way, the function of neither greatly invigorating nor withering associated states, manifestation as peacefulness, and a mind without zest as its proximate cause. Herein, pleasant and painful feelings are exclusively indeterminate, sorrowful feeling is exclusively unwholesome, while joyful and neutral feelings may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Here, however, wholesome joyful feeling is intended.

Nīlādibhedaṃ [V 0.0013] ārammaṇaṃ sañjānātīti saññā. Sā sañjānanalakkhaṇā, paccābhiññāṇarasā, punasañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā vā dāruādīsu tacchakādayo viya, yathāgahitanimittavasena [M 0.0016] abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā hatthidassakaandhā viya, ārammaṇe anogāḷhavuttitāya aciraṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānā vā vijju viya, yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā tiṇapurisesu migapotakānaṃ purisāti uppannasaññā viya.

It perceives an object distinguished as blue, etc.; thus, it is perception. Its characteristic is perceiving; its function is recognition, or its function is making a sign as a condition for repeated perception, like carpenters with wood, etc. Its manifestation is clinging to the perceived sign, like the blind men and the elephant; or its manifestation is fleetingness like lightning, due to its non-entrenching nature on the object. Its proximate cause is the object as it appears, like the perception of a human arising in deer fawns at the sight of scarecrows.

Cetetīti cetanā, saddhiṃ attanā sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇe abhisandahatīti attho. Sā cetanābhāvalakkhaṇā, āyūhanarasā, sā ca kusalākusalesu eva hoti. Itaresu pana taṃsadisatāya saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānā sakiccaparakiccasādhakā jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakiādayo viya. Accāyikakammānussaraṇādīsu panāyaṃ sampayuttesu ussāhanabhāvena pavattamānā pākaṭā hoti.

To intend is volition (cetanā). It means coordinating mental states associated with itself toward an object. Its characteristic is the state of intending, and its function is accumulating (kamma); this function occurs only in wholesome and unwholesome states. In other states (i.e., resultant and functional), however, its manifestation is coordinating, like an experienced pupil or a master builder accomplishing their own and others’ tasks. However, in situations such as recollecting urgent past actions, it becomes evident through its nature of instigating the associated states.

Ārammaṇaṃ cintetīti cittaṃ, viññāṇaṃ. Vitthārato panassa vacanattho cittaduke āvi bhavissati. Tadetaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cittaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, nirantarappavattito sandhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

It thinks of an object, thus it is mind (citta); consciousness (viññāṇa). Its meaning in detail, however, will become clear in the Dyad on Mind. This mind has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being a forerunner, manifestation as connection due to its uninterrupted process, and name-and-form as its proximate cause.

Vitakketi ūheti, vitakkanamattameva vā soti vitakko. Svāyamārammaṇe cittassa abhiropanalakkhaṇo, āhananapariyāhananaraso, ārammaṇe cittassa ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

It thinks, it ponders, or it is merely the act of thinking—this is initial application (vitakka). Its characteristic is the directing of the mind onto an object; its function is striking and repeated striking; it manifests as leading the mind to the object.

Ārammaṇe tena cittaṃ vicarati, vicaraṇamattameva vā soti vicāro. Svāyamārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo, tattha sahajātānuyojanaraso, cittassa anuppabandhanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Abhiniropanānumajjanavasena panesaṃ yathākkamaṃ oḷārikasukhumatāya ghaṇṭābhighāto viya cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko, ghaṇṭānuravo viya anuppabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko ākāse uppatitukāmapakkhino pakkhavikkhepo viya, santavutti vicāro ākāse [M 0.0017] uppatitassa pakkhino pakkhapasāraṇaṃ viya. So pana nesaṃ viseso paṭhamadutiyajjhānesu pākaṭo hoti. Ubhopi panete sampayuttadhammapadaṭṭhānā.

By means of it the mind moves about on the object; or it is merely the act of moving about—this is sustained application (vicāra). Its characteristic is repeated attention to the object. Its function is yoking co-arisen states to that object. It manifests as the mind's continuous connection to the object. By way of directing and repeated attention, these two are, in their grossness and subtlety respectively, like the initial striking of a bell (initial application) and its subsequent reverberation (sustained application). Here, initial application is like the flapping of a bird's wings when it wishes to fly into the sky, while sustained application is like the spreading of its wings once aloft in the sky. The distinction between them becomes evident in the first and second jhānas. Both have associated states as their proximate cause.

Piṇayatīti pīti. Sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā, kāyacittapīṇanarasā, pharaṇarasā vā, odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā, somanassasahagatacittapadaṭṭhānā.

It gladdens, thus it is rapture (pīti). It has the characteristic of endearing, its function is to refresh body and mind, or its function is pervasion. It manifests as elation. Its proximate cause is a mind associated with gladness.

Vīrānaṃ [V 0.0014] bhāvo, kammaṃ vā vīriyaṃ, vividhena vā upāyena īrayitabbaṃ pavattayitabbanti vīriyaṃ. Tañca ussāhalakkhaṇaṃ, sahajātānaṃ upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, “saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti (a. ni. 4.113) vacanato saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Idaṃ pana kusalapakkhe padaṭṭhānaṃ, akusalādipakkhe pana sādhāraṇavasena yathā tathā vā dukkhavinodanakāmatāpadaṭṭhānaṃ, sampayuttadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Taṃ samāraddhaṃ sabbāsaṃ sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The state of heroes, or their action, is energy (vīriya); or it is that which should be stirred and set in motion by various means. It has the characteristic of striving. Its function is to support co-arisen states. It manifests as non-collapse. Its proximate cause is a sense of urgency, as in the saying, 'Being stirred, one strives wisely.' Or its proximate cause is the grounds for arousing energy. This is its proximate cause on the wholesome side. On the side of the unwholesome and so forth, in general, its proximate cause is the desire to dispel suffering in any way whatsoever, or it is associated states. It should be understood that when properly initiated, energy becomes the root of all attainments.

Eko aggo visayo assāti ekaggaṃ, cittaṃ, tassa bhāvo ekaggatā, cittassa ekaggatā cittekaggatā, samādhissetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sā avisāraṇalakkhaṇā, sahajātānaṃ sampiṇḍanarasā nahānīyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya, upasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, ñāṇapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, sukhapadaṭṭhānā, akusalādisādhāraṇavasena panetthāpi paccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni vuttanayena yojetvā ñātabbāni. Nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viya cetaso ṭhitīti daṭṭhabbā.

It has a single, chief object, thus it is one-pointed (ekagga); the mind's state of being so is one-pointedness (ekaggatā), one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). This is a name for concentration (samādhi). It has the characteristic of non-distraction. Its function is to bind together co-arisen states, like water with bath powder. It manifests as tranquility or as knowledge. Its proximate cause is happiness. However, in the case of the unwholesome and so forth, its manifestation and proximate cause should be understood in the way already stated. It should be understood as the steadiness of the mind, like the flame of a lamp in a windless place.

Ettha ca kiñcāpi ārammaṇaṃ bhinditvā anupavisantā viya kusalapakkhe cattāro dhammā ārammaṇaṃ ogāhanti saddhā sati ekaggatā paññāti, teneva saddhā “okappanā”ti vuttā, sati ca “apilāpanā”ti, ekaggatā “avaṭṭhitī”ti, paññā [M 0.0018] “pariyogāhanā”ti ca vuttā. Akusalapakkhe ca tayo taṇhā diṭṭhi avijjāti. Tena te eva “oghā”ti vuttā. Tathāpi nesaṃ lakkhaṇādito nānattampi siddhameva. Akusalapakkhe pana ekaggatā uddhaccasamāgatattā “ogāhanā”ti na vuttā. Akusaladhammā hi ekavisaye sampiṇḍanakiccena samādhinā yuttāpi udakasittarajuṭṭhānaṃ viya taṅkhaṇaññeva vikiraṇasabhāvā honti. Teneva hettha upacārappanāppatti na hoti, kusaladhammā pana yasmā udakaṃ āsiñcitvā āsiñcitvā ākoṭanamajjanādīni katvā upalittaṭṭhānaṃ viya sakalampi divasaṃ niccalapavattanasamatthāti upacārappanāppattāpi hoti, tasmā tattha ogāhanāti vuttāti gahetabbaṃ.

Here, on the wholesome side, four states—faith, mindfulness, one-pointedness, and wisdom—plunge into the object as if breaking into it and entering. For this reason, faith is called 'conviction,' mindfulness 'non-superficiality,' one-pointedness 'stability,' and wisdom 'thorough penetration.' On the unwholesome side, there are three: craving, wrong view, and ignorance. For this reason, they are called 'floods.' Nevertheless, their diversity in terms of characteristics and so on is indeed established. On the unwholesome side, however, one-pointedness is not called 'plunging' because it is associated with restlessness. For unwholesome states, even when conjoined with concentration through the function of binding to a single object, are by nature instantly scattered, like a heap of dust sprinkled with water. Therefore, in this case, there is no attainment of access or absorption concentration. But wholesome states, because they are capable of proceeding immovably for a whole day—like a place that has been plastered by repeatedly sprinkling water and then pounding and smoothing it—do attain access and absorption concentration. Therefore, it should be understood that in that context it is called 'plunging.'

Jīvanti tena, jīvanamattaṃ vā tanti jīvitaṃ, taṃ sahajātānupālanalakkhaṇaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaññeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Attano ṭhitikkhaṇe eva cetaṃ te dhamme anupāleti udakaṃ viya uppalādīni, na bhaṅgakkhaṇe. Sayaṃ bhijjamānattā sayaṃ pavattitadhammasambandheneva pavattati niyāmako viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

They live by it, or it is merely living, thus it is life (jīvita). It has the characteristic of maintaining co-arisen states. Its function is to make them occur. Its manifestation is their establishment. Its proximate cause is states that are to be maintained. It maintains those states only at their moment of presence, not at their moment of dissolution, just as water sustains lotuses and so on. Since it is itself perishing, it should be understood that it proceeds only through its connection with states that have arisen, like a regulator.

Saddahanti [V 0.0015] etāya, sayaṃ vā saddahati, saddahanamattaṃ vā esāti saddhā. Sā saddahanalakkhaṇā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā, pasādanarasā udakappasādakamaṇi viya, pakkhandanarasā vā oghuttārakavīrapuriso viya, akālusiyapaccupaṭṭhānā, adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā vā, saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā, saddhammasavanādisotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānā vā, hatthavittabījāni viya daṭṭhabbā.

One has faith by means of it, or one has faith oneself, or it is merely the act of having faith—this is faith (saddhā). It has the characteristic of faith, or the characteristic of conviction. Its function is to clarify, like a water-purifying gem; or its function is to leap forward, like a hero crossing a flood. It manifests as non-turbidity, or as resolution. Its proximate cause is an object of faith, or its proximate cause is hearing the good Dhamma and other factors of stream-entry. It should be seen as being like a hand, wealth, and a seed.

Saranti tāya, sayaṃ vā sarati, saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati. Sā apilāpanalakkhaṇā, asammosanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, visayābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā, kāyādisatipaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ārammaṇe [M 0.0019] daḷhapatiṭṭhitattā pana esikā viya, cakkhudvārādirakkhaṇato dovāriko viya ca daṭṭhabbā.

One remembers by means of it, or it remembers by itself, or it is merely the act of remembering—this is mindfulness (sati). It has the characteristic of not floating away; its function is non-confusion; its manifestation is guarding, or its manifestation is facing the object. Its proximate cause is firm perception, or its proximate cause is the foundations of mindfulness such as that of the body. Because it is firmly established on the object, it should be seen as like a pillar; and because it guards the sense doors such as the eye, it should be seen as like a doorkeeper.

Kāyaduccaritādīhi hirīyatīti hirī, lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehiyeva ottappatīti ottappaṃ, pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī, uttāsalakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ. Lajjanākārena pāpakānaṃ akaraṇarasā hirī, uttāsākārena ottappaṃ. Asucimakkhitassa, aggisantattassa ca ayoguḷassa gahetuṃ avisahanaṃ viya etesaṃ yathākkamaṃ jigucchanasantāsākārehi pāpākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttākāreneva ca pāpato saṃkocanapaccupaṭṭhānāni etāni, attaparagāravapadaṭṭhānāni kulavadhūvesiyā bhāvo viya, lokapālakāni cāti daṭṭhabbāni. Ubhinnampi panesaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ adhipati sabhāvo lakkhaṇena cāti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā yathākkamaṃ ajjhattabahiddhāsamuṭṭhānatā, attalokādhipatitā, lajjābhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitatā, sappatissavavajjabhayadassāvitālakkhaṇatā ca aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 balarāsivaṇṇanā) vitthārato vibhattā, atthikehi taṃ tattheva gahetabbaṃ.

One is ashamed of bodily misconduct and so on—this is moral shame (hiri); it is a synonym for shame. One is apprehensive of those same things—this is moral dread (ottappa); it is a synonym for dread of evil. Herein, moral shame has the characteristic of disgust toward evil, while moral dread has the characteristic of fear. Moral shame has the function of not doing evil out of a sense of shame; moral dread, out of a sense of fear. Their non-performance of evil out of disgust and fear, respectively, should be understood as being like the inability to grasp a filth-smeared or a red-hot iron ball. Their manifestation is shrinking away from evil in the manner described. Their proximate cause is respect for oneself and for others. They are to be seen as the guardians of the world. Moreover, their arising, predominance, intrinsic nature, and characteristics—leaving aside the matrix definition—are analyzed in detail in the Aṭṭhasālinī as, respectively: internal and external arising; self-regard and regard for the world as the dominant influence; being founded on the intrinsic nature of shame and fear; and being characterized by reverence and by seeing danger in what is blameworthy. Those who are interested should grasp it from that very source.

Na lubbhati etena, sayaṃ vā na lubbhati, alubbhanamattameva vā tanti alobho. Adosāmohesupi eseva nayo. Tesu alobho ārammaṇe cittassa agedhalakkhaṇo, alaggabhāvalakkhaṇo vā kamaladale jalabindu viya, apariggaharaso muttabhikkhu viya, anallīnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno asucimhi patitapuriso viya.

One is not greedy by means of it, or one is not greedy oneself, or it is merely non-greed—this is non-greed (alobha). The same method applies to non-hatred and non-delusion. Among these, non-greed has the characteristic of the mind's lack of greed for an object, or the characteristic of non-adherence, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Its function is non-appropriation, like a liberated monk. It manifests as detachment, like a person who has fallen into filth.

Adoso acaṇḍikkalakkhaṇo, avirodhalakkhaṇo vā anukūlamitto viya, āghātavinayanaraso, pariḷāhavinayanaraso vā candanaṃ viya, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno puṇṇacando viya.

Non-hatred has the characteristic of non-fierceness, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a favorable friend. Its function is to subdue resentment, or to subdue feverishness, like sandalwood. It is manifested as gentleness, like the full moon.

Amoho [M 0.0020][V 0.0016] yathāsabhāvappaṭivedhalakkhaṇo, akkhalitappaṭivedhalakkhaṇo vā kusalissāsakkhittausuppaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanaraso anuddhaṭo padīpo viya, asammohapaccupaṭṭhāno araññagatasudesako viya. Tayopi cete sabbakusalānaṃ mūlabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

Non-delusion has the characteristic of penetrating intrinsic nature, or the characteristic of penetrating without error, like the penetration of a well-aimed arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function is to illuminate the object, like a steady lamp. It is manifested as non-confusion, like a good guide for one who has gone into the forest. These three should be seen as the root of all wholesome qualities.

Apica alobho cettha dānahetu, adoso sīlahetu, amoho bhāvanāhetu. Tīhipi cetehi yathāpaṭipāṭiyā nekkhammasaññā abyāpādasaññā avihiṃsāsaññā honti, tathā adhikaūnaviparītaggahaṇānaṃ abhāvo, tathā piyavippayogaappiyasampayogaicchitālābhadukkhānaṃ, jātijarāmaraṇadukkhānaṃ, petanirayatiracchānagatidukkhānañca abhāvo, tathā bhogamittaattasampattipaccayabhāvo, tathā kāmasukhapariccāgaattakilamathapariccāgamajjhimapaṭipattīnaṃ sambhavo, tathā asubhaappamāṇadhātusaññānaṃ, aniccadukkhaanattasaññānaṃ, dibbabrahmaariyavihārānañca sambhavo hotīti evamādīhi nayehi tesaṃ vitthāro veditabbo.

Furthermore, non-greed here is the cause for generosity, non-hatred for virtue, and non-delusion for mental development. By these three, in their proper order, arise the perceptions of renunciation, non-ill-will, and non-harming. Thus, there is the absence of excessive, deficient, or distorted grasping. Similarly, there is the absence of suffering from separation from the beloved, union with the unloved, not getting what is desired, the suffering of birth, aging, and death, and the suffering in the realms of departed spirits, hell, and the animal kingdom. Also, they become conditions for wealth, friends, and personal well-being. Also, there is the possibility of the middle way—the giving up of sensual pleasure and the giving up of self-mortification. Also, there arises the possibility of the perceptions of unattractiveness, the immeasurables, and the elements; the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self; and the divine, Brahma, and noble abodes. Thus, their detailed exposition should be understood by these and similar methods.

Ettha ca amoho nāma paññā, sā pajānanalakkhaṇā. Viññāṇaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ. Saññā sañjānanalakkhaṇā. Kiṃ panetāsaṃ saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ nānattanti? Sañjānanavijānanapajānanameva. Etāsaṃ hi samānepi jānanabhāve saññāya “nīlaṃ pīta”ntiādinā puna saññuppādakamattena ākārena sañjānanamattameva hoti, ajātabuddhidārakassa viya cittavaṭṭādibhāvamattākārena kahāpaṇādidassanaṃ, na tato uddhaṃ. Viññāṇassa pana yathāvuttena ca tato visiṭṭhena ca aniccādinā ākārena jānanaṃ hoti, gāmikapurisassa viya yathāvuttena ceva upabhogārahatādinā ca ākārena kahāpaṇādidassanaṃ, na tato uddhaṃ. Paññāya pana tehi ca yathāvuttehi nānappakārehi ca [M 0.0021] maggapātubhāvādihetūhi sabbehi ākārehi pajānanaṃ hoti, heraññikassa viya yathāvuttehi ceva chekakūṭaaddhasārādisabbehi ākārehi ca kahāpaṇādidassanaṃ. Paññāya hi ajānitabbaṃ nāma natthi. Evaṃ sañjānanavijānanapajānanākārehi etāsaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca cakkhuviññāṇādīni vitakkavīriyādisahajātapaccayavirahato rūpādīsu saññākiccato adhikavijānanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti, balapariṇāyakāni viya senaṅgāni paññānuvattakāneva hontīti veditabbāni. Tenāha bhagavā “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”tiādi (vibha. 766).

Here, non-delusion is called wisdom; its characteristic is understanding. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Perception has the characteristic of perceiving. But what is the distinction among these—perception, consciousness, and wisdom? It is simply perceiving, cognizing, and understanding. For although they share the nature of knowing, perception is only the mere act of perceiving in a way that simply gives rise to a subsequent perception, such as 'blue' or 'yellow.' It is like a child whose intellect has not yet developed seeing a coin merely as a colored, round object, and nothing more. Consciousness, however, knows in the aforesaid manner and also in a more distinct way, like a villager who sees a coin and knows not only its appearance but also that it is suitable for use, but knows nothing further. Wisdom, on the other hand, understands through all these aspects and in various other ways, including the causes for the arising of the path. It is like a money-changer who examines a coin and knows it in all its aspects: whether it is genuine, counterfeit, of half-value, and so on. Indeed, for wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be known. Thus, the distinction among them should be understood through the modes of perceiving, cognizing, and understanding. Here, eye-consciousness and the like, due to the absence of co-arisen conditions such as applied thought and energy, cannot perform a function of cognizing that goes beyond the function of perception with regard to forms and other objects. They should be understood as merely following wisdom, like the divisions of an army that follow a powerful commander. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'With the five kinds of consciousness, one does not understand any phenomenon beyond mere impingement,' etc.

Kāyapassambhanaṃ [V 0.0017] kāyapassaddhi. Cittapassambhanaṃ cittapassaddhi. Kāyoti panettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Ubhopi panetā kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittadarathanimmaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ aparipphandasītibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānañca avūpasamakarauddhaccādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The calming of the body is bodily tranquility. The calming of the mind is mental tranquility. Here, 'body' refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Both of these have the characteristic of allaying the agitation of body and mind, the function of suppressing that agitation, the manifestation of the stilling and cooling of body and mind, and have body and mind as their proximate cause. And they should be seen as the opposites of defilements such as restlessness, which cause the non-allayment of body and mind.

Kāyalahubhāvo kāyalahutā. Cittalahubhāvo cittalahutā. Evaṃ uparipi padattho daṭṭhabbo. Kāyacittānaṃ garubhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā kāyalahutā, cittalahutā ca, tesaṃ garubhāvanimmaddanarasā, tesaṃ adandhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, tesaṃ garubhāvakarathinamiddhādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The lightness of the body is bodily lightness. The lightness of the mind is mental lightness. The meaning of the terms that follow should also be understood in this way. Bodily lightness and mental lightness have the characteristic of calming the heaviness of body and mind, their function is to subdue that heaviness, and their manifestation is unsluggishness. They should be seen as being opposed to defilements such as sloth and torpor, which cause heaviness in body and mind.

Kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā kāyamudutā, cittamudutā ca, tesaṃ thaddhabhāvanimmaddanarasā, appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā, tesaṃ thaddhabhāvakaradiṭṭhimānādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

Bodily malleability and mental malleability have the characteristic of quieting the rigidity of body and mind. Their function is crushing that rigidity. Their manifestation is non-resistance. Body and mind are their proximate cause. And they should be seen as opposing defilements such as wrong view and conceit, which cause rigidity in body and mind.

Kāyacittānaṃ [M 0.0022] akammaññabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā kāyakammaññatā, cittakammaññatā ca, tesaṃ akammaññabhāvanimmaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampattipaccupaṭṭhānā, tesaṃ akammaññabhāvakarāvasesanīvaraṇapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Pasādanīyavatthūsu pasādāvahā, hitakiriyāsu viniyogakkhamabhāvāvahā suvaṇṇavisuddhi viyāti daṭṭhabbā.

Bodily wieldiness and mental wieldiness have the characteristic of quieting the unwieldiness of body and mind. Their function is crushing that unwieldiness. Their manifestation is the successful taking up of an object by body and mind. And they should be seen as opposing the remaining hindrances that cause that unwieldiness. They should be understood as bringing confidence in regard to inspiring objects, and bringing fitness for application in beneficial actions, like the purity of gold.

Kāyacittānaṃ agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā kāyapāguññatā, cittapāguññatā ca, tesaṃ gelaññanimmaddanarasā, nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā, tesaṃ gelaññakaraassaddhiyādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Kāyacittānaṃ ajjavalakkhaṇā kāyujukatā, cittujukatā ca, tesaṃ kuṭilabhāvanimmaddanarasā, ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, tesaṃ kuṭilabhāvakaramāyāsāṭheyyādipaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Sabbepete passaddhiādayo dhammā kāyacittapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

Bodily proficiency and mental proficiency have the characteristic of absence of sickness in body and mind. Their function is crushing sickness. Their manifestation is blamelessness. And they should be seen as opposing defilements such as lack of faith, which cause sickness in body and mind. Bodily rectitude and mental rectitude have the characteristic of straightness in body and mind. Their function is crushing crookedness. Their manifestation is non-crookedness. And they should be seen as opposing defilements such as deceit and dishonesty, which cause crookedness in body and mind. All these states—tranquility and the rest—should be understood as having body and mind as their proximate cause.

Kiṃ panettha passaddhādayo dhammā uddhaccādiṃ vinodetuṃ na sakkonti, yena ime passaddhādayo dhammā na visuṃ vibhattāti? No na sakkonti, ime pana sahitā eva sakkonti, itarathā tesaṃ uppattiyā eva asambhavato. Yathā vā passaddhādīsu vijjamānesu mohāhirikādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhabhāvena [V 0.0018] amohahiriādayo honti, evametepi uddhaccādiujupaṭipakkhabhāvena icchitabbāti gahetabbā. Yasmā cettha dvīhi dvīhi eva yathāsakaṃ paṭipakkhā haritabbā, tasmā te ete eva dvidhā vibhattā, na amohādayoti ñātabbā.

But is it that states such as tranquility cannot dispel restlessness and so forth, for which reason these states such as tranquility are not classified separately? It is not that they cannot. But these can do so only when conjoined; otherwise, their very arising would be impossible. Just as when tranquility and so forth are present, non-delusion, moral shame, and so forth arise as direct opposites to delusion, shamelessness, and so forth, so too should these be understood as direct opposites to restlessness and so forth. Since here, their respective opposites must be eliminated two by two, therefore they are classified in this twofold manner, and not like non-delusion and so forth. This should be understood.

Yevāpanakesu chandoti kattukāmatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā so kattukāmatālakkhaṇo, ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, tadevassa [M 0.0023] padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ārammaṇaggahaṇe cāyaṃ cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo. Ayañca yasmā virajjitabbādīsupi nekkhammādinā saha lobhavisadisena kattukāmatākārena pavattati, tasmā asekhānampi uppajjati. Lobho pana subhasukhādivipallāsapubbakena abhisaṅgākāreneva pavattatīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Evaṃ mettākaruṇādīnampi lobhādīhi viseso yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbo.

Among the 'miscellaneous' factors, 'desire' (chanda) is a designation for the wish to act. Thus, it has the characteristic of wishing to act, the function of seeking an object, the manifestation of being desirous of an object, and that very object is its proximate cause. In grasping an object, it should be seen as the mind's extending forth like a hand. And because this, even in cases where one should become dispassionate, functions with renunciation and so forth, in the form of a wish to act that is dissimilar to greed, it arises even in Arahants. Greed, however, arises solely through the mode of clinging, preceded by the perversions of the beautiful, the pleasant, and so forth—this is the difference between them. Similarly, the differences between loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, and greed and so forth, should be understood as appropriate.

Adhimuccanaṃ adhimokkho. So sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo, asaṃsappanaraso, nicchayapaccupaṭṭhāno, sanniṭṭhātabbadhammapadaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena indakhīlo viya daṭṭhabbo. Nanu ca saddhāpi adhimokkhoti vuccati. Tathā hi adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti saddhindriyanti vuccatīti? Saccaṃ, sā ca kho sampasādanabhāvena adhimokkho, ayaṃ pana yathā tathā vā nicchayabhāvenāti na koci virodho.

Determination is adhimokkha. It has the characteristic of conviction, the function of not wavering, the manifestation of certainty, and its proximate cause is a matter to be decided upon. It should be regarded as being as unshakable on its object as a city-gate post. But is not faith also called determination? For is it not said that because it exercises control in the sense of determination, it is called the faculty of faith? True, but that faith is determination by way of confidence, whereas this is determination by way of making a firm decision; thus there is no contradiction.

Kiriyā kāro, manasmiṃ kāro manasikāro, purimamanato visadisaṃ manaṃ karotītipi manasikāro, svāyaṃ ārammaṇapaṭipādako vīthipaṭipādako javanapaṭipādakoti tippakāro, tattha ārammaṇapaṭipādako idha manasikāro. So sāraṇalakkhaṇo, sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇesu payojanaraso, ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇapadaṭṭhāno, saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno. Ārammaṇapaṭipādakattena sampayuttānaṃ sārathi viya daṭṭhabbo. Vīthipaṭipādakoti pana pañcadvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Javanapaṭipādakoti manodvārāvajjanassa, na te idha adhippetā. Ettha cāyaṃ manasikāro samannāhāramattākārena ārammaṇe sampayuttānaṃ payojako, cetanā cetokiriyābhāvena, vitakko pana saṅkappākārena, upanijjhāyanākārena ca abhiniropako. Teneva hettha padabhājanīye “takko [M 0.0024] saṅkappoti ca, jhānaṅga”nti ca vuccatīti ayametesaṃ viseso.

Doing is action; doing in the mind is manasikāra (attention). It is also manasikāra because it makes the mind different from the preceding mind. This is of three kinds: that which presents the object, that which produces the cognitive process, and that which produces the impulsion. Here, the manasikāra that presents the object is intended. It has the characteristic of directing, the function of yoking the associated states to the object, the manifestation of facing the object, and its proximate cause is the object; it is included in the aggregate of formations. Because it presents the object, it should be regarded as the charioteer of the associated states. 'That which produces the cognitive process' is a term for five-door adverting. 'That which produces the impulsion' is a term for mind-door adverting. These are not intended here. Here, this manasikāra yokes the associated states to the object in the manner of mere attending; volition does so by way of mental action; while applied thought applies them in the manner of conception and close examination. For this reason, in the Analysis of Terms, it is called 'thought and conception' and a 'factor of absorption.' This is the distinction between them.

Tesu [V 0.0019] tesu dhammesu majjhattatā tatramajjhattatā. Sā cittacetasikānaṃ samavāhitalakkhaṇā, ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā, pakkhapātupacchedanarasā vā, majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, samappavattasampayuttadhammapadaṭṭhānā. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhaṇena samappavattānaṃ ājānīyānaṃ ajjhupekkhakasārathi viya daṭṭhabbā.

Neutrality towards those various states is specific neutrality (tatramajjhattatā). It has the characteristic of conveying mind and mental factors evenly, the function of preventing deficiency and excess, or the function of cutting off partiality, the manifestation of neutrality, and its proximate cause is the associated states that proceed evenly. It should be regarded as being like a charioteer who looks on with equanimity at thoroughbreds proceeding evenly.

Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampanaṃ karotīti karuṇā, kirati vā paradukkhaṃ hiṃsati ca, kirīyati vā dukkhitesu pasārīyatīti karuṇā. Sā paradukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā, paradukkhāsahanarasā, avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā, dukkhābhibhūtānaṃ anāthabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Modanti tāya taṃsamaṅgino, sayaṃ vā modati, modanamattameva vā tanti muditā. Sā pamodalakkhaṇā, anissāyanarasā, arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ sampattidassanapadaṭṭhānā.

When there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble—this is compassion. Or, it scatters or destroys the suffering of others, or it is scattered or extended towards those in distress—this is compassion. Its characteristic is activity in the mode of removing the suffering of others, its function is the inability to bear the suffering of others, its manifestation is non-harming, and its proximate cause is seeing the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering. Those who possess it rejoice, or it rejoices itself, or there is merely rejoicing—this is sympathetic joy. Its characteristic is delight, its function is absence of envy, its manifestation is the removal of discontent, and its proximate cause is seeing the success of beings.

Kasmā panettha mettupekkhā na vuttāti? Pubbe gahitattā. Adoso eva hi sattesu hitapharaṇavasena pavattiyaṃ mettā. Tatramajjhattatā eva ca iṭṭhāniṭṭhasattesu majjhattākārena pavattiyaṃ upekkhā. Te ca dhammā niyatā, kevalaṃ pana nesaṃ sattesu mettupekkhābhāvena pavatti aniyatāti. Kāyaduccaritato virati kāyaduccaritavirati. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Lakkhaṇādito panetā tissopi kāyaduccaritādivatthūnaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇā, tato saṃkocanarasā, tesaṃ akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā, saddhāhirottappaappicchatādiguṇapadaṭṭhānā, pāpakiriyato cittassa vimukhabhāvabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā. Evaṃ lakkhaṇādito vinicchayo veditabbo.

Why are loving-kindness and equanimity not mentioned here? Because they have been included previously. For non-aversion itself, when it occurs by way of pervading beings with what is beneficial, is loving-kindness. And specific neutrality itself, when it occurs in the mode of impartiality towards agreeable and disagreeable beings, is equanimity.
