These mental states are fixed, but their occurrence as loving-kindness and equanimity towards beings is not fixed. Abstinence from bodily misconduct is abstinence from bodily misconduct. The same method applies to the other two terms. As to their characteristic, etc., all three have the characteristic of not transgressing against the objects of bodily misconduct, etc.; their function is to shrink away from them; their manifestation is the non-commission of them; their proximate cause is such qualities as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and fewness of desires; and they should be regarded as the mind's state of being turned away from evil action. Thus the analysis by way of characteristic, etc., should be understood.

Saṅgahāti [M 0.0025] evaṃ ye ime imasmiṃ kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vibhattā ekūnacattālīsa dhammā, sabbete khandhato catubbidhā honti – vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandhoti. Tattha rāsaṭṭhena somanassavedanā vedanākkhandho, tathā saññā saññākkhandho, cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, avasesā phassādayo chattiṃsa dhammā saṅkhārakkhandhoti veditabbā.

Inclusion: Thus these thirty-nine states that have been analyzed in this first wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere are all fourfold by way of the aggregates—the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and the consciousness aggregate. Therein, pleasant feeling is the feeling aggregate; likewise, perception is the perception aggregate; consciousness is the consciousness aggregate; and the remaining thirty-six states beginning with contact should be understood as the formations aggregate.

Nanu ca yadi rāsaṭṭhena khandho, phassādīnaṃ tāva anekattā saṅkhārakkhandhatā yuttā, kathaṃ pana vedanādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ khandhatāti? Upacārato. Paccekaṃ hi atītādibhedabhinnesu vedanāsaññāviññāṇesu niruḷhopi khandha-saddo tadekadesesu ekekavedanādīsupi samudāyopacārena [V 0.0020] voharīyatīti tadekadesepi tabbohāro, yathā rukkhassa sākhāya chijjamānāya “rukkho chijjatī”tiādīsu viyāti. Evaṃ khandhato catubbidhā honti.

But if an aggregate is so in the sense of a collection, then while it is proper for contact and the other states to be the formations aggregate due to their multiplicity, how can the three beginning with feeling have the status of an aggregate? By figurative usage. For although the word 'aggregate' is established for feelings, perceptions, and consciousnesses in their entirety as divided into past, future, and present, etc., it is also applied by a collective figure of speech to single instances of feeling, etc., which are but a part of that whole. Thus that term is used for a single part, just as when a branch of a tree is being cut, one says, 'The tree is being cut.' In this way, they are fourfold by way of aggregates.

Te puna āyatanato duvidhā honti – manāyatanaṃ dhammāyatananti. Sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena hettha cittaṃ manāyatanaṃ, sesā pana aṭṭhatiṃsa dhammā dhammāyatananti. Evaṃ āyatanato duvidhā honti. Te puna dhātuvasena duvidhā manoviññāṇadhātu dhammadhātūti. Nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena hettha cittaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu, sesā dhammadhātūti. Evaṃ dhātuvasena duvidhā.

Again, by way of bases, they are twofold: the mind base and the mental-object base. Here, consciousness is the mind base in the sense of being a place of origin and meeting, while the remaining thirty-eight states are the mental-object base. Thus, by way of bases, they are twofold. Again, by way of elements, they are twofold: the mind-consciousness element and the mental-object element. Here, consciousness is the mind-consciousness element in the sense of being without a being and without a soul, while the remaining states are the mental-object element. Thus, by way of elements, they are twofold.

Tathā āhārānāhāravasena. Tattha phasso cetanā cittanti ime tayo dhammā visesapaccayattena yathākkamaṃ “phassāhāro manosañcetanāhāro viññāṇāhāro”ti vuccanti, avasesā na āhārāti. Kiṃ panete paccayā na honti, ye na āhārāti vucceyyunti? No na honti, visesapaccayā pana na honti, phassādayo pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ visesapaccayā honti, visesato vedanādayo [M 0.0026] ca āharanti. Phassāhāro hi tisso vedanāyo āharati, manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave, viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ. Nanu ca so vipāko, idaṃ pana kusalaviññāṇanti? Kiñcāpi evaṃ, taṃsarikkhatāya pana viññāṇāhārotveva vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā ime “arūpino āhārā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.15) vacanato kabaḷīkārāhāro viya rūpakāyassa upatthambhakaṭṭhena nāmakāyassa āhārapaccayā honti, tasmā imeva “āhārā”ti vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ āhārānāhāravasena duvidhā.

Similarly, by way of nutriment and non-nutriment. Here, these three states—contact, volition, and consciousness—are, on account of being specific conditions, respectively called 'nutriment of contact,' 'nutriment of mental volition,' and 'nutriment of consciousness'; the remaining states are not nutriments. But are these others not conditions, that they are not called nutriments? It is not that they are not conditions, but they are not specific conditions. Contact and the others, however, are specific conditions for those states, and they specifically bring forth feeling and so on. For the nutriment of contact brings forth the three feelings; the nutriment of mental volition brings forth the three kinds of existence; and the nutriment of consciousness brings forth name-and-form at rebirth-linking. But is not that consciousness a resultant, while this is a wholesome consciousness? Even so, it is called the nutriment of consciousness because of its similarity to that. Or, because these 'immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated states and for material phenomena co-arisen with them by way of nutriment condition' (Paṭṭh. 1.1.15), they are conditions for the mental body by way of nutriment condition through their function of supporting it, just as physical food supports the physical body. Therefore, it should be understood that only these are called 'nutriments.' Thus, by way of nutriment and non-nutriment, they are twofold.

Tathā indriyānindriyato. Tattha saddhā vīriyaṃ sati ekaggatā amoho cittaṃ somanassavedanā jīvitanti ime aṭṭha dhammā adhipatiyaṭṭhena yathākkamaṃ “saddhindriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ samādhindriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ manindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ jīvitindriya”nti vuccanti, avasesā na “indriyānī”ti. Evaṃ indriyānindriyato duvidhā.

Similarly, by way of faculty and non-faculty. Here, these eight states—faith, energy, mindfulness, one-pointedness, non-delusion, consciousness, pleasant feeling, and life—are, on account of their exercising dominance, respectively called the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of mind, the faculty of pleasant feeling, and the faculty of life. The remaining states are not faculties. Thus, by way of faculty and non-faculty, they are twofold.

Tathā jhānaṅgājhānaṅgavasena. Tattha vitakko vicāro pīti somanassaṃ ekaggatāti ime pañca dhammā upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena “jhānaṅgānī”ti vuccanti, itare “ajhānaṅgānī”ti. Evaṃ jhānaṅgājhānaṅgavasena duvidhā.

Similarly, by way of jhāna factors and non-jhāna factors. Herein, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness—these five phenomena, due to their nature of close contemplation, are called "jhāna factors." The others are called "non-jhāna factors." Thus, it is twofold by way of jhāna factors and non-jhāna factors.

Tathā [V 0.0021] maggaṅgāmaggaṅgavasena. Tattha amoho vitakko viratittayaṃ vīriyaṃ sati ekaggatāti ime aṭṭha dhammā niyyānaṭṭhena, vimokkhaṭṭhena ca yathākkamaṃ “sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhī”ti nāmena “maggaṅgānī”ti vuccanti, itare “amaggaṅgānī”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana lokiyacitte viratīnaṃ [M 0.0027] aniyatattā, yevāpanakattā ca tā vajjetvā “pañcaṅgiko maggo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 58, 121) vuccati. Evaṃ maggaṅgāmaggaṅgavasena duvidhā.

Similarly, by way of path factors and non-path factors. Herein, non-delusion, applied thought, the three abstinences, energy, mindfulness, and one-pointedness—these eight phenomena, by way of their characteristic of leading out and of liberation, are respectively called by the names "right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration," and are thus termed "path factors"; the others are "non-path factors." However, in the Pāli Canon, because the abstinences in mundane consciousness are not fixed and are occasional, it is said, "the path is fivefold" (Dhs. 58, 121), excluding them. Thus, it is twofold by way of path factors and non-path factors.

Tathā balābalavasena. Tattha saddhāvīriyaṃ sati samādhi paññā hirī ottappanti ime satta dhammā akampiyaṭṭhena balānīti vuccanti, itare abalānīti. Evaṃ balābalavasena duvidhā.

Similarly, by way of strengths and non-strengths. Herein, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, moral shame, and moral dread—these seven phenomena are called strengths because of their unshakeable nature; the others are non-strengths. Thus, it is twofold by way of strengths and non-strengths.

Tathā hetunahetuvasena. Tattha alobho adoso amohoti ime tayo dhammā mūlaṭṭhena hetūti vuccanti, itare nahetūti. Evaṃ hetunahetuvasena duvidhā. Evaṃ phassāphassavedanāvedanā saññāsaññācittācittādivasenapi vuttanayānusārena yathāyogaṃ saṅgahavibhāgo veditabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana padabhājanīyasaṅgahavāre (dha. sa. 103 ādayo), tadaṭṭhakathāyañca (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 58-120) gahetabbo. Evaṃ saṅgahato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Similarly, by way of roots and non-roots. Herein, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—these three phenomena are called roots because they have the characteristic of a root; the others are non-roots. Thus, it is twofold by way of roots and non-roots. In this way, the classification and analysis should be understood appropriately according to the method stated, by way of contact and non-contact, feeling and non-feeling, perception and non-perception, consciousness and non-consciousness, and so on. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is to be taken from the section on the analysis of terms (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 103 ff.) and its commentary (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Aṭṭhakathā 58–120). Thus, the determination by way of inclusion should be understood.

Suññato cevāti evaṃ khandhādīhi saṅgahitesu tesu dhammesu tabbinimutto kārakavedakādisabhāvo attā vā sassato vā bhāvo na upalabbhati. Suññā te dhammā attena vā attaniyena vā, kevalaṃ paṭiccasamuppannā, salakkhaṇadhāraṇato dhammamattā, niccasukhādisāravirahato asārā, pavattakaniyāmakābhāvato apariṇāyakā aniccā, dukkhā, anattā, anattaniyā ca hutvā pavattantīti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana padabhājanīyasuññatavāre, tadaṭṭhakathāyañca gahetabboti. Evaṃ suññato vinicchayo veditabbo.

And by way of voidness: When these phenomena are classified by aggregates, etc., no self, or eternal being, or nature of an agent or experiencer, etc., free from these, is found therein. Those phenomena are void of self or what belongs to self; they are merely dependently arisen, mere phenomena by virtue of bearing their own characteristics, essenceless due to the absence of permanence, happiness, etc., as their core, without a director due to the absence of a mover or controller, impermanent, suffering, non-self, and not belonging to a self—thus they proceed. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is to be taken from the section on voidness in the Analysis of Terms and its commentary. Thus, the determination by way of voidness should be understood.

Niṭṭhitā paṭhamakusalassa atthavaṇṇanā.

Here ends the explanation of the meaning of the first wholesome consciousness.

Dutiyādīsupi [M 0.0028] paṭhamakusale vuttanayena dhammuddesādinā sabbo vinicchayo veditabbo. Na kevalañca ettheva, ito paresupi sabbattha heṭṭhā vuttasadisānaṃ padānaṃ, dhammānañca attho, sabbo ca vinicchayo [V 0.0022] ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ito paraṃ pana apubbameva vaṇṇayissāma. Dutiyacitte tāva sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva paṭhamacittato viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Dutiyakusalaṃ.

In the second and subsequent instances also, the entire determination is to be understood by the method stated for the first wholesome consciousness, such as the enumeration of phenomena, etc. Not only here, but henceforth also, the meaning of all terms and phenomena similar to those previously stated, and the entire determination, is to be understood by the method stated here. From now on, however, we will explain only what is unprecedented. In the second consciousness, the only difference from the first consciousness is just the state of being prompted; the rest is the same. The second wholesome consciousness.

Tatiyepi dhammuddese amohābhāvā indriyamaggaṅgabalamūlasaṅgahesu paññindriyasammādiṭṭhimaggaṅgapaññābalaamohamūlānaṃ parihāniyā saddhindriyādīnaṃ bhāvova viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Tathā catutthe sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva viseso. Tatiyacatutthāni.

In the third, in the enumeration of phenomena, due to the absence of non-delusion, the difference within the classifications of faculties, path factors, strengths, and roots is the absence of the wisdom faculty, the path factor of right view, the strength of wisdom, and the root of non-delusion, while the faculty of faith and so on remain; the rest is the same. Similarly, in the fourth, the only difference is just the state of being prompted. The third and fourth.

Pañcamachaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamesu pana sukhasomanassaṭṭhānesu upekkhābhāvo, pītiyā ca abhāvo. Teneva jhānaṅgasaṅgahavāre caturaṅgajjhānatāva viseso, sesaṃ paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthacittasadisameva. Upekkhāsahagatesu cettha catūsu karuṇāmuditā na uppajjantīti keci vadanti, parikammabhūtānaṃ panettha tāsaṃ uppattiyā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātattā upacārappattā pana uppajjanti, na itarāti gahetabbaṃ. Pañcamachaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamāni.

In the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth, however, in place of happiness and joy, there is equanimity, and also the absence of rapture. Thus, in the section on the inclusion of jhāna factors, the distinction lies only in the four-factored jhāna, while the rest is similar to the first, second, third, and fourth states of consciousness. Herein, in these four states accompanied by equanimity, some say that compassion and sympathetic joy do not arise. However, since their arising is permitted in the Great Commentary for those in the preliminary stage, it should be understood that they do arise when access is attained, but not otherwise. The fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth.

Visayādippabhedatoti evaṃ dhammuddesādinā vibhattāni aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalāni ārammaṇavibhāgato paccekaṃ chabbidhāni honti rūpārammaṇaṃ…pe… dhammārammaṇanti. Tattha nīlādibhedabhinnā, atītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattikabāhiraoḷārikasukhumādibhedabhinnā ca vaṇṇadhātu rūpārammaṇaṃ nāma. Evaṃ saddārammaṇādīsupi yathānurūpaṃ bhedo veditabbo.

And by way of the classification of objects, etc.: Thus, the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, distinguished by way of the enumeration of phenomena, etc., are each sixfold according to the division of objects: a form-object…up to a dhamma-object. Herein, the color element, distinguished by divisions such as blue, etc., and also distinguished by divisions such as past, future, present, internal, external, coarse, subtle, etc., is called a form-object. Similarly, the distinctions for sound-objects and the rest are to be understood accordingly.

Ettha [M 0.0029] ca phoṭṭhabbanti āpodhātuvajjitabhūtattayaṃ, dhammārammaṇanti pañcārammaṇāni vajjetvā avasesā rūpārūpapaññattiyo veditabbā, sesaṃ tādisameva. Keci panettha “cakkhuviññāṇādīnamāpāthagatāni etānārammaṇāni rūpārammaṇādivohāraṃ labhanti, anāpāthagatāni pana atītānāgatadūrasukhumādibhedabhinnāni dhammārammaṇānevā”ti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ dibbacakkhādīnaṃ rūpārammaṇatādivacanato.

Herein, tangible objects refer to the three great elements, excluding the water element. Mental objects are to be understood as the remaining things—forms, formless phenomena, and concepts—excluding the five sense objects. The rest is the same as before. However, some say here: 'These objects, visible forms, etc., which come within the range of eye-consciousness, etc., receive the designation of visible objects, etc., but those that do not come within range—such as past, future, distant, subtle, etc.—are mental objects.' This is incorrect, because of the statement that the divine eye, etc., has form as its object.

Anāpāthagatā eva hi tāni dibbacakkhuādīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, na ca tāni dhammārammaṇāni. Rūpādayo hi pañca paccekaṃ dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu ekasmiṃ khaṇe āpāthamāgantvā taṃtaṃdvārikajavanānaṃ, tadanantare manodvārikānañca aparabhāge ca diṭṭhasutādivasenānussarantassa suddhamanodvārikānañca ārammaṇāni honti. Tathā hi nānāvaṇṇavicittacetiyādidassanaṃ karontassa, dhammaṃ [V 0.0023] suṇantassa, bherisaddādīhi vā pūjādiṃ karontassa ca gandhamālādīni ghāyitvā, khādanīyabhojanīyādiñca sāyitvā, sukhasamphassāni attharaṇapāvuraṇādīni ca phusitvā manāpabhāvaṃ ñatvā tehi cetiyapūjaṃ karontassa, tattha tattha akusalaṃ vā uppādentassa, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe gayhamānāni rūpādipañcārammaṇāni sākhāya akkamanaṃ, pathaviyaṃ chāyāpharaṇañca ekakkhaṇe kurumānaṃ rukkhagge nilīyamānaṃ pakkhino sarīraṃ viya yathāsakaṃ pasādañca ghaṭṭetvā tasmiṃyeva khaṇe bhavaṅgacalanapaccayabhāvena manodvārepi āpāthamāgantvā tato bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā uppannānaṃ āvajjanādivoṭṭhabbanapariyosānānaṃ, vīthicittānaṃ, tadanantarānañca kusalākusalādijavanānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hutvā tadanantarāsu manodvāravīthīsu ca aparabhāge tathārūpaṃ paccayaṃ āgamma attanā pūjādikaraṇakālesu, diṭṭhasutaghāyitasāyitaphuṭṭhavasenānussarantassa, paccakkhato anubhuyyamānāni viya manodvāre ca ārammaṇāni honti.

Indeed, those objects that are not within the range of the ordinary senses are the objects of the divine eye, etc., and they are not mental objects. For the five objects beginning with forms, each individually, having come within range through its respective two doors in a single moment, become the objects of the javanas pertaining to those respective doors, and immediately afterwards, of the mind-door javanas. Later, when one recollects them as seen, heard, and so on, they become objects of purely mind-door processes. For example, for one who sees a multicolored and intricately adorned shrine, listens to the Dhamma, or performs acts of worship with drum sounds and the like; and for one who, having smelled fragrant garlands, tasted delicious food, or touched pleasant coverings and robes, knows their agreeable nature and performs shrine worship with them, or gives rise to unwholesome states in relation to them—at that very instant, the five sense objects, forms and so on, are grasped. Just as a bird's body perched on a treetop simultaneously causes a branch to bend and a shadow to spread on the ground, so each sense object strikes its corresponding sense faculty and, in that same moment, enters the cognitive range of the mind door, acting as a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum. Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, they become the objects of the process-consciousness that arises, beginning with adverting and culminating in determining, and of the wholesome, unwholesome, etc., javanas that immediately follow. And in the subsequent mind-door processes, later, having encountered a similar condition, when one recollects them during times of performing worship, etc., as seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched, they become objects at the mind door as if being directly experienced.

Athāpi [M 0.0030] pañcahi dvārehi agahitapubbāni buddharūpādīni, dibbarūpādīni ca pañcārammaṇāni savanavasena sallakkhetvā javanakkhaṇe vā aparabhāge sutavaseneva anussaritvā vā pasādaṃ, kammaphalasaddhādiṃ, lobhādiñca uppādentassāpi manodvāre āpāthamāgacchanti. Abhiññānaṃ pana suddhamanodvāre eva, tasmā evaṃ pañcadvāre, manodvāre, suddhamanodvāre ca āpāthagatāni atītādibhedabhinnāni sabbānipi pañcārammaṇāni kadācipi dhammārammaṇaṃ na honti, taditarā nāmarūpapaññattiyo dhammārammaṇanti gahetabbaṃ. Nanu cetāni iṭṭhakantamanāpāni ārammaṇāni lobhassa vatthu, kathamettha kusalaṃ uppajjatīti? Niyamādikāraṇato. Cittaṃ hi “kusalameva mayā kattabba”nti pubbe niyamitavasena sabbattha akusalappavattiṃ nivattetvā kusale pariṇāmanavasena ca abhiṇhaṃ āsevitakusalasamudācāravasena ca sappurisūpanissayādiupanissayavasena ca yonisoābhujitavasena cāti imehi kāraṇehi kusalaṃ hutvā uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Evamimesu chasu ārammaṇesu uppajjanato paccekaṃ chabbidhāni honti. Ārammaṇavavatthānakathā.

Moreover, the five sense objects, such as forms of the Buddha and divine forms, which were never before grasped by the five sense-doors, having been discerned by way of hearing, at the moment of impulsion or afterwards, having been recollected by way of hearing, come within range of the mind-door even for one who is arousing confidence, faith in karmic results, etc., or greed, etc. However, supernormal knowledge arises purely in the mind-door. Therefore, in this way, all five sense objects that appear at the five sense-doors, the mind-door, or purely in the mind-door—divided into past, etc.—at no time become mental objects. The others, namely name-and-form and concepts, are to be taken as mental objects. But are not these pleasing and delightful objects the basis for greed? How then does wholesome consciousness arise here? Due to causes such as determination. For the mind, having previously determined, 'I must do only what is wholesome,' by way of suppressing the occurrence of unwholesome states everywhere and turning towards the wholesome, and by way of repeatedly cultivated wholesome conduct, and by way of supporting conditions such as association with virtuous people, and by way of wise attention—for these reasons, it is to be understood that it arises as wholesome. Thus, since these wholesome consciousnesses arise in relation to these six kinds of objects, they are each of six kinds. Here ends the explanation on the classification of objects.

Evaṃ ārammaṇabhedabhinnesu rūpārammaṇaṃ tāva kusalaṃ dasapuññakiriyavatthuvasena dasavidhaṃ hoti. Tattha ekekaṃ pana kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammanti tividhaṃ. Tattha kāyadvāre pavattaṃ kāyakammaṃ, vacīdvāre pavattaṃ vacīkammaṃ, manodvāre pavattaṃ manokammaṃ. Tattha kāyadvāranti kāyaviññatti. Vacīdvāranti vacīviññatti. Tāsaṃ vibhāgo rūpavibhattiyaṃ āvi bhavissati. Manodvāranti [V 0.0024] sabbaṃ cetanāsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ vuccati, visesato kusalākusalaṃ. Taṃ hi sahajātānaṃ cetanānaṃ, kāyaṅgavācaṅgacopanaṃ asampāpuṇitvā pavattānaṃ suddhamanokammānaṃ pavattiokāsadānato dvāranti vuccati, imesu pana tīsu [M 0.0031] dvāresu pavattā cetanā kāyakammādayo nāma. Apica pāṇātipātādayo, pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādayo ca kāyakammaṃ nāma, musāvādādayo, musāvādāveramaṇiādayo ca vacīkammaṃ nāma, abhijjhādayo, anabhijjhādayo ca manokammaṃ nāma.

Thus, among the objects distinguished by their divisions, wholesome consciousness that has a form-object, for instance, is tenfold by way of the ten bases of meritorious action. Here, each is threefold as bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. Here, bodily action is that which occurs through the body-door; verbal action is that which occurs through the speech-door; mental action is that which occurs through the mind-door. Here, the body-door means bodily intimation; the speech-door means verbal intimation. Their classification will become clear in the analysis of form. The mind-door means all consciousness associated with volition, especially the wholesome and unwholesome. For it is called a door because it provides the opportunity for the occurrence of pure mental actions, which arise without the co-arising volitions reaching bodily and verbal expression. Moreover, the volitions occurring at these three doors are called bodily actions and so forth. Furthermore, killing living beings and the like, and abstaining from killing living beings and the like, are called bodily action; false speech and the like, and abstaining from false speech and the like, are called verbal action; covetousness and the like, and non-covetousness and the like, are called mental action.

Kusalapakkhe pana dānādidasapuññakiriyavatthūni ca yathārahaṃ kāyavacīmanokammāni honti. Evaṃ yebhuyyavuttito cesa kāyakammādibhāvo vutto pāṇātipātādīnampi vacīdvārādīsu pavattito kesañci purisānaṃ vanacarakādibhāvo viya, dvārānañca kāyakammadvārādibhāvo kesañci gāmānaṃ brāhmaṇagāmādibhāvo viya. Akusale tāva ettha pāṇātipātādikāyakammaṃ kāyadvāre, vacīdvāre ca yathārahaṃ samuṭṭhāti, no manodvāre. Tathā musāvādādivacīkammaṃ. Pāṇātipātādinipphādanatthaṃ hi manodvāre eva cintentassa cetanābyāpādādīsu kammapathappattesu vā kammapathaṃ appattesu vā manokammesu eva pavisanato kāyakammādibhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Nanu vijjāmayenāpi kevalaṃ manokammena pāṇātipātādiṃ karontīti? Na aloṇabhojanadabbhasayanamantaparijappanādikāyavacīpayogaṃ vinā tassāsijjhanato. Abhijjhādimanokammaṃ pana tīsupi dvāresu samuṭṭhāti. Abhijjhāya hi kāyena parabhaṇḍaggāhādīnaṃ, byāpādena daṇḍaparāmasanādīnaṃ, micchādiṭṭhiyā titthiyavandanādīnaṃ karaṇakāle, vācāya parasampattipatthanāya “haññantu bajjhantū”ti anatthapatthanāya ca titthiyatthutitadatthadīpanādīnañca yathākkamaṃ pavattikāle ca tassa manokammassa kāyavācāsu pavatti veditabbā.

On the wholesome side, the ten bases of meritorious action, such as giving and so forth, are bodily, verbal, and mental actions as appropriate. Thus, this classification as bodily action and so on is stated according to predominance, since killing living beings and the like also occurs through the speech-door and so on, just as some men have the status of forest-dwellers and the like. And the classification of the doors as the door of bodily action and so on is like the classification of some villages as a brahmin village and so on. In the unwholesome, here, the bodily action of killing living beings and so on arises through the bodily door, and through the verbal door as appropriate, but not through the mental door. Similarly with verbal actions such as lying and so on. For the volition of one who merely intends through the mind-door to produce killing living beings and so forth, since it enters only as mental actions, whether they have reached the level of a path of action or not, it does not attain the nature of bodily action and so forth. But do some not kill living beings and so forth through mere mental action, such as by knowledge alone? No, because that would not be accomplished without the application of bodily and verbal effort, such as eating unsalted food, lying on grass, reciting mantras, and so on. However, mental actions such as covetousness and so on arise through all three doors. For covetousness, when one seizes another’s goods with the body; for ill-will, when one raises a stick with the body; for wrong view, when one pays homage to sectarians with the body—at the time of performing such actions; and when speech arises—such as longing for another’s fortune, wishing harm like "May they be killed or bound," or praising sectarians and explaining their doctrines and so on—then the occurrence of that mental action in body and speech should be understood in due order.

Kāmāvacarakusalaṃ pana pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādikaṃ kāyavacīmanokammaṃ paccekaṃ dvārattayepi pavattati. Tattha pāṇātipātādīhi [M 0.0032] samphappalāpapariyosānehi sattahi viramantassa tāva hatthamuddāya, vacībhedena ca samādiyanakāle, manasā viramaṇakāle ca tesaṃ kāyavacīkammānaṃ tīsu dvāresu pavatti veditabbā. Anabhijjhādīhi sahagatena cetasā tajjassa kāyapayogassa, “paravittupakaraṇaṃ ciraṭṭhitikaṃ hotu, sabbe sattā averā hontu, so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādinā vacīpayogassa, kevalaṃ manopayogassa ca karaṇakāle manokammassa tīsupi dvāresu pavatti veditabbā. Ettha ca pañcadvāre uppannāni javanāni kāyavacīkammāni [V 0.0025] na honti, manokammāni eva. Tāni ca na kammapathappattāni, kevalaṃ kusalādīni honti. Manodvāre paṭutarappavattāni eva hi kammapathappattāni manokammāni honti, rūpārūpajavanāni pana ekantaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ manokammameva manodvāre eva ca pavattanti.

However, wholesome actions of the sense-sphere, such as abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, as individual bodily, verbal, and mental actions, occur through each of the three doors. Here, for one who abstains from the seven unwholesome actions beginning with killing living beings and ending with idle chatter, the occurrence of these bodily and verbal actions through the three doors should be understood: at the time of undertaking the vow by a gesture of the hand or by verbal declaration, and at the time of abstaining by means of the mind. When performing actions associated with a mind free from covetousness and so forth, the bodily effort concerning that object, the verbal effort, such as "May the possessions of others last long, may all beings be free from enmity, may that Blessed One be the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One," and the mere mental effort—the occurrence of that mental action through all three doors should be understood. Here, the impulsions that arise at the five sense-doors are not bodily or verbal actions, but only mental actions. And they are not classed as courses of action, but are merely wholesome and so forth. Only those mental actions that are very clearly manifest in the mind-door are classed as courses of action. But the impulsions pertaining to the form and formless realms are exclusively meditation-based mental actions and occur only in the mind-door.

Kiñcāpi abhiññāñāṇāni viññattidvayajanakāni, tathāpi kāyavacīkammavohāraṃ na labhanti, lokuttarakusalaṃ pana kāyavacīdvāresu anuppajjamānampi micchāvācākammantājīvānaṃ samucchedappahānakārīnaṃ viratīnaṃ vasena kāyavacīkammampi hoti, taditaramaggaṅgavasena manokammampīti ekakkhaṇe tīṇipi kammāni honti, tañca bhāvanāmayaṃ, dvāraṃ panassa manodvārameva. Yathā ca pāṇātipātāveramaṇiyādīnaṃ vasena kusalassa dvārattaye pavatti vuttā, evaṃ dasapuññakiriyavatthūnampi vasena vattabbā. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana na vicāritā, tathāpi nayato evaṃ veditabbā.

Even though the supernormal knowledges produce two kinds of intimation, they do not obtain the designation of bodily and verbal action. However, supramundane wholesome states, even though they do not arise through the doors of body and speech, still constitute bodily and verbal action by way of the abstinences that eradicate wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood. By way of the remaining path factors, they also constitute mental action. Thus, in a single moment, three kinds of action occur, and that is development-based. Its door, however, is only the mind-door. Just as the occurrence of wholesome states through the three doors was explained in the case of abstaining from killing living beings, etc., the same should be stated in the case of the ten bases of meritorious action as well. Although this is not discussed in the commentaries, it should be understood in this way by inference.

Tesu dānaṃ kāyakammameva, vacīkammampi vā. Pattānuppadānaṃ, abbhanumodanaṃ, desanā vacīkammameva. Sīlaṃ apacitisahagataṃ, veyyāvaccasahagatañca kāyakammampi atthi, vacīkammampi atthi. Tattha sīlassa kāyavacīkammabhāvo siddho eva. Apacitiyā pana [M 0.0033] pupphapūjādinā, vandanādinā vā pavattikāle kāyakammabhāvo, thutimayapūjādinā pavattikāle vacīkammabhāvo ca veditabbo. Veyyāvaccassāpi sahatthā karaṇakāle kāyakammabhāvo, gilānādīnaṃ catupaccayasamādāpanādivasena, garūhi āṇattasaddena ārocanapakkosanādivasena vacīkammabhāvo ca veditabbo. Bhāvanā, savanaṃ, diṭṭhijukammañca manokammameva, abbhanumodanampīti keci. Savanampi hi sotadvārānusārena manodvāre eva dhammatthasallakkhaṇavasena pavattikāle manokammameva.

Among these, giving is bodily action, or it may also be verbal action. Transference of merit, rejoicing in merit, and teaching are verbal action only. Morality accompanied by respect and service is both bodily action and verbal action. Herein, the state of morality as bodily and verbal action is indeed established. Regarding respect, when it occurs in the form of offering flowers and so forth, or paying homage and so forth, its state as bodily action should be understood; and when it occurs in the form of praiseful offerings and so forth, its state as verbal action should be understood. Regarding service also, when it is done with one's own hands, its state as bodily action should be understood; and its state as verbal action should be understood in ways such as arranging the four requisites for the sick and so forth, or by announcing or summoning with words at the command of elders. Meditation, listening, and straightening of views are mental action only—some include rejoicing in merit as well. For listening, too, following the ear-door, when it occurs in the mind-door by way of discerning the meaning of the Dhamma, it is mental action only.

Tattha dānaṃ apaciti veyyāvaccaṃ pattānuppadānaṃ desanāti imāni pañca kāyavacīdvāresu eva pavattanti, na manodvāre. Ettha ca pattānuppadānadesanānaṃ kāyavikārena pattiṃ dentassa, dhammaṃ desentassa ca kāyadvārepi pavatti veditabbā. Sīlaṃ bhāvanā abbhanumodanaṃ savanaṃ diṭṭhijukammanti imāni pana pañca tīsupi dvāresu pavattanti, “na punevaṃ karissāmī”ti cettha manasāva duccaritato viramantassa, abbhanumodantassa ca vasena sīlabbhanumodanānaṃ manodvārepi pavatti veditabbā. Yaṃ pana aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “dānamayaṃ kāyavacīmanokammavasena tividhaṃ [V 0.0026] hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ pubbacetanāvasena manodvāre pavattaṃ gahetvā pariyāyato vuttaṃ, nippariyāyato kāyavacīdvārappavattā sanniṭṭhānacetanāva. Teneva hi tattheva vuttaṃ “vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā hi ‘dassāmi karissāmī’ti vācā bhinnā hotīti. Iminā lakkhaṇena dānaṃ nāma hoti, abhidhammapariyāyaṃ patvā pana vijjamānakavatthuṃ ārabbha manasā cintitakālato paṭṭhāya kusalaṃ hoti. Aparabhāge kāyena vā vācāya vā kattabbaṃ karissatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1). Itarathā “dassāmī”ti cintitamattenāpi dānaṃ [M 0.0034] nāma bhaveyya, tathā ca tādisaṃ vatthuṃ yathācintitaniyāmena adentassa dhuranikkhepe adinnādānampi siyā. Evaṃ manasā pāṇātipātādayopi siyuṃ, tañca na yuttaṃ, tasmā vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Atha vā “sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ dinnaññeva haratū”ti pariccajanasambhavato dānassa manodvārepi pavatti veditabbā.

Here, giving, respect, service, transference of merit, and teaching—these five occur only through the doors of body and speech, not through the mind-door. In this context, the occurrence of transference of merit and teaching through the body-door should also be understood, in the case of one who gives merit or teaches the Dhamma by bodily gesture. Morality, meditation, rejoicing in merit, listening, and straightening one’s views—these five, however, occur through all three doors. Here, the occurrence of morality and rejoicing in merit through the mind-door should also be understood, in the case of one who mentally abstains from misconduct, thinking, "I will not do this again," and in the case of one who rejoices in merit. Now, what is stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī—"Merit from giving is threefold through bodily, verbal, and mental action, etc."—is said figuratively, taking into account the preliminary volition occurring through the mind-door. In the strict sense, it is the concluding volition that occurs through the doors of body and speech. For this reason, it is stated there: "According to the Vinaya method, when the words 'I will give, I will do' are uttered, by this characteristic, it is called giving. According to the Abhidhamma method, however, from the moment one mentally thinks about an existing object, it is wholesome, and later, what should be done is done through body or speech." Otherwise, merely thinking, "I will give," would constitute giving, and in such a case, if one does not give as intended, it would amount to theft by abandoning the undertaking. Similarly, mental acts like killing living beings would also be possible—but that is not correct. Therefore, it should be understood only in the way stated. Alternatively, the occurrence of giving through the mind-door should also be understood, due to the possibility of relinquishment when one thinks, "Let them take all my possessions as given."

Ettha ca dānasīlādikāyakammānaṃ kāyadvāre pavattiyaṃ kammaṃ kāyakammameva, dvārampi kāyadvārameva. Vacīdvāre pavattiyaṃ kammaṃ kāyakammameva, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ. Manodvāre pavattiyampi kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ, dvāraṃ pana manodvāraṃ. Desanābbhanumodanādīnaṃ vacīkammānaṃ vacīdvāre pavattiyaṃ kammampi vacīkammaṃ, dvārampi vacīdvārameva. Kāyadvāre pavattiyampi kammaṃ vacīkammameva, dvāraṃ pana kāyadvāraṃ. Manodvāre pavattiyampi kammaṃ vacīkammaṃ, dvāraṃ pana manodvāraṃ. Bhāvanādimanokammānaṃ manodvāre pavattiyaṃ kammampi manokammaṃ, dvārampi manodvārameva. Kāyadvāre pavattiyampi kammaṃ manokammameva, dvāraṃ pana kāyadvāraṃ. Vacīdvāre pavattiyampi kammaṃ manokammameva, dvāraṃ pana vacīdvāraṃ. Evaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ, pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādīnañca vuttānusārena kammavavatthānaṃ, dvāravavatthānañca yathānurūpaṃ yojetvā asaṅkarato ñātabbaṃ.

Here, in the case of bodily actions such as giving and morality, when occurring through the body-door, the action is a bodily action, and the door is the body-door itself. When occurring through the speech-door, the action is a bodily action, but the door is the speech-door. Even when occurring through the mind-door, the action is a bodily action, but the door is the mind-door. In the case of verbal actions such as teaching and rejoicing, when occurring through the speech-door, the action is a verbal action, and the door is the speech-door itself. Even when occurring through the body-door, the action is a verbal action, but the door is the body-door. Even when occurring through the mind-door, the action is a verbal action, but the door is the mind-door. In the case of mental actions such as meditation, when occurring through the mind-door, the action is a mental action, and the door is the mind-door itself. Even when occurring through the body-door, the action is a mental action, but the door is the body-door. Even when occurring through the speech-door, the action is a mental action, but the door is the speech-door. Thus, concerning actions such as killing living beings and abstaining from killing living beings, the classification of actions and the classification of doors should be understood without confusion by applying them appropriately according to what has been stated.

Dvārakammavavatthānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Classification of Doors and Actions is concluded.

Idāni yasmā dasavidhāni cetāni puññakiriyavatthūni tīsu evaṃ saṅgayhanti dānamaye sīlamaye bhāvanāmayeti. Pattānuppadānaṃ hi dānamaye saṅgayhati, “abbhanumodanampī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 156-159 puññakiriyavatthādikathā) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Apacitiveyyāvaccāni sīlamaye. Desanāsavanadiṭṭhijukammāni bhāvanāmaye, tasmā rūpārammaṇassa kusalassa [M 0.0035] dānasīlabhāvanāvasena dvārattayappavattiṃ yojetvā dassessāma. Tadanusāreneva itaresaṃ vasenāpi sakkā ñātunti. Kusalaṃ hi vaṇṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā uppajjamānaṃ dānasīlabhāvanāvaseneva tīsu dvāresu [V 0.0027] pavattati. Kathaṃ? Yadā hi nīlapītādivaṇṇavicittaṃ pupphavatthādideyyadhammaṃ labhitvā “vaṇṇadānaṃ me bhavissatī”ti vaṇṇavasena ābhujitvā cetiyādīsu sahatthena pūjeti, tadā rūpārammaṇaṃ dānamayaṃ kāyadvāre pavattati, tañca pubbacetanā sanniṭṭhānacetanā aparacetanāti tividhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ uparipi sabbavāresu tividhatā veditabbā. Yadā pana tadeva yathāvuttavatthuṃ vācāya āṇāpetvā puttadārādīhi dāpeti, tadārūpārammaṇaṃ dānamayaṃ vacīdvāre pavattati. Yadā pana tadeva vijjamānakavatthuṃ “dassāmī”ti cinteti, paccāsīsati, yathādhippāyaṃ nipphādessati, tadā pubbacetanāvasena pariyāyato dānamayaṃ manodvāre pavattati nāma. Evaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ dānamayaṃ dvāravasena tividhaṃ hoti.

Now, since these ten bases of meritorious action are included in the three categories of that which is based on giving, that which is based on morality, and that which is based on meditation, we shall explain accordingly. For transference of merit is included in that which is based on giving; and in the commentary it is said, 'rejoicing also.' Respect and service are included in that which is based on morality. Teaching, listening, and straightening one's views are included in that which is based on meditation. Therefore, we will explain how a wholesome consciousness with a visible object arises through giving, morality, and meditation via the three doors. Following this method, the rest can also be understood. A wholesome consciousness that arises with a visible object occurs through giving, morality, or meditation via the three doors. How? When someone obtains an offerable item of variegated color such as blue or yellow flowers or cloth and, reflecting on its appearance, thinks, "This will be my gift of beauty," then, with their own hands, they make an offering at a shrine or similar place. At that time, the merit based on giving with a visible object arises through the body-door. And that is threefold: preliminary volition, concluding volition, and subsequent volition. The same threefold division is to be understood in all cases hereafter. When, however, they instruct others verbally—such as their children or spouse—to give that same object as described, then the merit based on giving with a visible object arises through the speech-door. When they think, "I will give," regarding that same existing object, anticipate it, and resolve to fulfill their wish, then, through preliminary volition, the merit based on giving arises figuratively through the mind-door. Thus, the merit based on giving with a visible object is threefold according to the door.

Yadā pana vuttappakāravaṇṇaṃ deyyadhammaṃ labhitvā “evaṃ manāpavaṇṇānaṃ pariccajanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ kulavaṃsāgatavattameta”nti sahatthā pūjeti, tādisavaṇṇavantaṃ vā parapariggahitādibhogasampattiṃ pariccajitvā sīlaṃ rakkhati, tadā rūpārammaṇaṃ sīlaṃ kāyadvāre ca pavattati. Yadā pana vuttappakāravaṇṇaṃ deyyadhammaṃ kulavaṃsādivasena vācāya āṇāpetvā parehi dāpeti, tādisaṃ vā parapariggahitādiṃ vācāya apanetvā sīlaṃ rakkhati, tadā rūpārammaṇaṃ sīlaṃ vacīdvāre pavattati. Yadā pana tādisaṃ vijjamānakavatthuṃ kulavaṃsādivasena “dassāmī”ti, tādisaṃ parapariggahitādikaṃ anāmasitvā “sīlaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti vā cinteti, tadā rūpārammaṇaṃ sīlaṃ manodvāre pavattati. Evaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ sīlamayaṃ dvāravasena tividhaṃ hoti.

When one obtains an offerable item of the kind and appearance described and, thinking, "Giving up such pleasing appearances is indeed the tradition handed down in my family lineage," makes an offering with one's own hands, or when one gives up possessions of such an appearance that have been appropriated by others and thus maintains morality, then the merit based on morality with a visible object occurs through the body-door. When one instructs others by speech, citing family tradition, to give an offerable item of the kind and appearance described, or when one verbally renounces such possessions appropriated by others and thus maintains morality, then the merit based on morality with a visible object occurs through the speech-door. When one reflects, citing family tradition, "I will give" regarding such an existing object, or when one resolves, "I will maintain morality," without touching such possessions appropriated by others, then the merit based on morality with a visible object occurs through the mind-door. Thus, the merit based on morality with a visible object is threefold according to the doors.

Yadā [M 0.0036] pana vuttappakāraṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ datvā tadeva vaṇṇaṃ, sabbaṃ vā rūpāyatanaṃ caṅkamanto aniccādito vipassati, tadā rūpārammaṇaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ kāyadvāre pavattati. Tadeva vacībhedaṃ katvā sammasantassa rūpārammaṇaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ vacīdvāre pavattati. Tadeva kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ acopetvā sammasantassa rūpārammaṇaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ manodvāre pavattati. Evaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ dvāravasena tividhaṃ hoti. Iti rūpārammaṇassa kusalassa tividhapuññakiriyavatthuvasena navasu kammadvāresu pavattivibhāgo veditabbo. Imināva nayena rūpārammaṇassa kusalassa dasapuññakiriyavatthuvasenāpi tiṃsāya kammadvāresu pavattivibhāgo yojetvā ñātabbo. Yathā ca rūpārammaṇassa, evaṃ saddārammaṇādīnampi pañcannaṃ kusalānaṃ puññakiriyavatthudvārehi vibhāgo, yojanānayo ca yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbo.

When, after giving something possessing the described appearance, one contemplates that very appearance, or the entire visual base, while walking, as impermanent and so forth, then the mental development-based action with a visible object arises through the body door. When one makes a verbal analysis of that same object and contemplates it, the mental development-based action with a visible object arises through the speech door. When one contemplates that same object without agitating the body or speech, the mental development-based action with a visible object arises through the mind door. Thus, the mental development-based action with a visible object is threefold according to the doors. In this way, the division of the arising of the wholesome action with a visible object should be understood as occurring in nine doors of action, based on the threefold basis of meritorious action. By this same method, the division of the arising of the wholesome action with a visible object should also be connected and known to occur in thirty doors of action, based on the tenfold basis of meritorious action. Just as with the visible object, so too the division of the five wholesome states—with sound as object and the rest—according to the bases of meritorious action and the doors, and the method of application, should be known as is appropriate.

Apica [V 0.0028] saddaṃ nāma kandamūlaṃ viya hatthena gahetvā dātuṃ na sakkā. Yadā pana “saddadānaṃ me”ti ābhujitvā bheriāditūriye tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ deti, tehi upahāraṃ vā karoti, dhammakathikādīnaṃ sarabhesajjādiṃ deti, dhammassavanaṃ ghoseti, sarabhaññadhammakathādiṃ vā karoti, tadā kusalaṃ saddārammaṇaṃ hoti. Evaṃ gandhādivatthupariccāgepi gandhādiārammaṇaṃ. Dhammārammaṇaṃ pana ojājīvitindriyatadāyattānaṃ vasena ñātabbaṃ. Yadā hi ojavantāni annapānasappinavanītādīni “ojadānaṃ me bhavissatī”ti deti, gilānānaṃ bhesajjaṃ vā vejjaṃ vā upanetvā, pāṇoparodhakaṃ āvudhajālakuminādiṃ vināsetvā vā, vajjhappatte pāṇino mocetvā vā “jīvitadānaṃ me bhavissati jīvitāyattavuttitāya, pañcapasādasoḷasasukhumarūpacittacetasikānaṃ vasena pasādādidānaṃ me bhavissatī”ti ca manasi karoti, tadā kusalaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

Furthermore, sound cannot be grasped by the hand and given like a root or a tuber. But when one, reflecting, “This is my gift of sound,” offers drums and other musical instruments to the Triple Gem, or makes offerings with them, gives medicine for the voice and the like to preachers of the Dhamma, proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, or engages in recitation of the Dhamma with a pleasant voice and the like, then a wholesome state with sound as its object arises. Similarly, in the offering of objects such as scents, a wholesome state with scent as its object arises. A wholesome state with a mental object, however, should be understood in terms of nutritive essence, the life faculty, and what is dependent on them. For when one gives nutritious food, drink, ghee, fresh butter, and the like, thinking, “This will be my gift of nutritive essence”; or brings medicine or a physician to the sick; or destroys weapons, nets, fish-traps, and the like that harm life; or frees beings destined for slaughter, and reflects, “This will be my gift of life, and by reason of its being a condition for life, this will be my gift of the sense faculties and so forth, in terms of the five sense faculties, sixteen subtle material qualities, mind, and mental factors,” then a wholesome state with a mental object arises. The rest is similar.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0037] nānāvatthūsu ṭhitārammaṇānaṃ yojanā. Ekavatthusmimpi chārammaṇaṃ labbhateva. Piṇḍapātasmiṃ hi manāpo vaṇṇo, khādanakāle murumurāyanasaddo, gandho, raso, phoṭṭhabbaṃ, ojā, tadāyattā vā jīvitapasādādayo, tabbisayāni ca viññāṇādīnīti chārammaṇampi veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ cīvarādīsu ceva vatthādīsu ca yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Etthapi dānasīlabhāvanāmayatā, kāyavacīmanokammabhāvo ca vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Yathā ca kusalānaṃ, evaṃ akusalānampi ārammaṇakammadvāravavatthānaṃ, apuññakiriyavatthūsu yojanānayo ca vuttānusārena yathāyogaṃ ñātabbo.

This is the application of objects that exist in various bases. Even in a single base, six objects can indeed be found. For example, in almsfood: a pleasing appearance is the visible form, the crunching sound while eating is the sound, the smell, the taste, the tangible, the nutritive essence, or the life faculty and other factors dependent on it, and the consciousnesses and other factors pertaining to them—these six objects are to be understood. Similarly, in robes and other requisites, as well as in dwellings and other bases, the appropriate objects should be recognized. Here too, the nature of being made up of giving, virtue, and mental development, as well as the nature of bodily, verbal, and mental actions, should be understood in the same way as previously explained. Just as with wholesome states, so too with unwholesome ones—the classification of objects and doors of action, and the method of applying them to the bases of demeritorious action, should be understood according to the appropriate context, following what has been said.

Evaṃ ārammaṇato, puññakiriyavatthuto, kammato, dvārato ca anekasahassappabhedesu cetesu kusalesu upaḍḍhāni pana ñāṇasampayuttāni catunnaṃ adhipatīnaṃ vasena paccekaṃ catubbidhāni, ñāṇavippayuttāni pana upaḍḍhāni vīmaṃsādhipativajjitādhipatittayavasena paccekaṃ tividhāni, tadubhayāni puna hīnattikavasena paccekaṃ tividhāni, tāni puna aparimāṇesu pana cakkavāḷesu paccekaṃ aparimāṇesu sattesu ekekasmiṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaoḷārikasukhumatādīhi anantehi pakārehi uppajjanato anantāparimāṇāni honti. Tāni sabbāni sambuddho anantena buddhañāṇena mahātulāya tulayamāno viya, mahātumbe pakkhipitvā minayamāno viya sabbākārato paricchinditvā mahākaruṇāya kāmāvacaraṭṭhena sarikkhatāya ekattaṃ upanetvā, puna somanassupekkhāsahagataṭṭhena, ñāṇasampayuttavippayuttaṭṭhena, asaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikaṭṭhena [V 0.0029] ca koṭṭhāse katvā desesi, yathā taṃ lokavidū satthā devamanussānanti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana ādito paṭṭhāya dhammasaṅgaṇiyā (dha. sa. 1), tadaṭṭhakathāya ca aṭṭhasāliniyā (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1) sabbākārato [M 0.0038] ñātabboti. Evaṃ visayādippabhedato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus, from the standpoint of objects, bases of meritorious action, actions, and doors, among these wholesome states, which have thousands of divisions, half are associated with wisdom and are fourfold individually due to the four dominant conditions. The other half, not associated with wisdom, are threefold individually, due to the three dominant conditions which exclude investigation. Both these types are further threefold individually based on the classification of inferior, medium, and superior. Moreover, in immeasurable world-systems, they arise in each of the immeasurable beings in countless ways—past, future, and present, gross and subtle, etc.—and are thus infinite and immeasurable. The Fully Enlightened One, with his boundless Buddha-knowledge, as if weighing them on a great scale or measuring them by pouring them into a vast vessel, comprehended them in all aspects. Out of great compassion, he unified them by their similarity as sense-sphere states, then further classified them by way of being accompanied by joy or equanimity, associated or dissociated with wisdom, and unprompted or prompted, and taught them, just as the Teacher, knower of the worlds, did for gods and humans. This here is the summary. The detailed exposition, however, should be understood in all aspects from the beginning of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī (Dhs. 1) and its commentary, the Aṭṭhasālinī (DhsA. 1). Thus, the analysis should be understood in terms of distinctions such as objects and so on.

Kāmāvacarakusaladhammā niṭṭhitā.

The wholesome states of the sense sphere are concluded.

Rūpāvacaradhammā pana kusalā jhānaṅgasampayogabhedato pañcavidhā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ paṭhamajjhānikaṃ, tato vūpasantaṃ atikkantavitakkaṃ vicārapītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ dutiyajjhānikaṃ, tato vūpasantaṃ atikkantavicāraṃ pītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyajjhānikaṃ, tato vūpasantaṃ virattapītikaṃ sukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ, tato vūpasantaṃ atthaṅgatasukhaṃ upekkhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ pañcamajjhānikanti. Evaṃ sampayogabhedato vinicchayo veditabbo.

The wholesome states of the form sphere, however, are fivefold according to the distinction in their association with the jhāna factors. That is to say: associated with initial application, sustained application, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness—this is the first jhāna. Then, with that stilled, with initial application transcended, associated with sustained application, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness—this is the second jhāna. Then, with that stilled, with sustained application transcended, associated with joy, bliss, and one-pointedness—this is the third jhāna. Then, with that stilled, with joy faded away, associated with bliss and one-pointedness—this is the fourth jhāna. Then, with that stilled, with bliss set aside, associated with equanimity and one-pointedness—this is the fifth jhāna. Thus, the analysis should be understood according to the distinction in association.

Dhammuddesādito pana paṭhamajjhāne tāva kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vuttesu ṭhapetvā viratittayaṃ sesā chattiṃsa dhammā honti. Tattha chandādayo cattāro, karuṇā, muditā cāti cha yevāpanakā. Sesaṃ suññatavārapariyosānaṃ sabbaṃ kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vuttasadisameva. Kevalaṃ hi viratīnaṃ abhāvo, saṅgahavāre pañcamaggaṅgabhāvo, bhūmantaravasena rūpāvacarabhāvo ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Paṭhamajjhānaṃ.

Regarding the exposition of states, in the first jhāna, setting aside the three abstinences mentioned in the first wholesome sense-sphere state, the remaining thirty-six states are present. Herein, the four beginning with desire, along with compassion and sympathetic joy—these six are occasional. The rest, up to the end of the section on emptiness, is all just like what was stated in the first wholesome sense-sphere state. The only distinctions are the absence of the abstinences, the state of having five path factors in the compendium section, and its nature as form-sphere due to the difference in plane; the rest is similar. This is the first jhāna.

Tathā dutiyajjhānepi kevalaṃ dhammuddese vitakkābhāvo, saṅgahavāre catukkajjhānaṅgamaggaṅgabhāvo ca viseso, sesaṃ paṭhamasadisameva. Dutiyaṃ.

Similarly, in the second jhāna, the only distinctions are the absence of initial application in the exposition of states, and in the compendium section, the state of having four jhāna factors and path factors; the rest is similar to the first. This is the second jhāna.

Tathā tatiyajjhānepi kevalaṃ dhammuddese vicārābhāvo, saṅgahavāre tivaṅgikajjhānatā ca viseso, sesaṃ dutiyasadisameva. Tatiyaṃ.

Similarly, in the third jhāna, the only distinctions are the absence of sustained application in the exposition of states and, in the compendium section, its being a three-factored jhāna; the rest is similar to the second. This is the third jhāna.

Tathā [M 0.0039] catutthe kevalaṃ dhammuddese pītiyā abhāvo, koṭṭhāsavāre duvaṅgikajjhānabhāvo ca viseso, sesaṃ tatiyasadisameva. Catutthaṃ.

Similarly, in the fourth jhāna, the only distinctions are the absence of joy in the exposition of states and, in the section on constituents, its being a two-factored jhāna; the rest is similar to the third. This is the fourth jhāna.

Tathā [V 0.0030] pañcame kevalaṃ dhammuddese karuṇāmuditādīnaṃ abhāvo, somanassaṭṭhāne upekkhābhāvo, koṭṭhāsavāre jhānindriyesu upekkhājhānaṅgabhāvo, upekkhindriyabhāvo ca viseso, sesaṃ catutthasamameva. Pañcamaṃ.

Similarly, in the fifth jhāna, the only distinctions are the absence of compassion, sympathetic joy, and so on in the exposition of states; the presence of equanimity in place of mental pleasure; and, in the section on constituents, the state of equanimity being a jhāna factor among the jhāna faculties and its being the faculty of equanimity; the rest is similar to the fourth. This is the fifth jhāna.

Padabhājanīye pana vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā dutiyaṃ, pītiyā ca virāgā tatiyaṃ, somanassassa ca atthaṅgamā catutthanti catukkanayopi āgato, so tikkhapaññānaṃ ekappahāreneva vitakkavicārasamatikkamasambhavato vutto. Tattha dutiyādīnaṃ sabbaso pañcakanaye tatiyādisamattā tattha vuttanayeneva sabbo vinicchayo veditabbo tattheva antogadhabhāvo cāti. Catukkanayo.

In the section on analysis of terms, the second [jhāna] is due to the stilling of initial application and sustained application, the third due to the fading away of joy, and the fourth due to the disappearance of mental pleasure—thus, the fourfold method is also presented. This is stated because those of keen wisdom can transcend initial application and sustained application in a single stroke. Here, the second and so forth [jhānas] in the fourfold method are entirely similar to the third and so forth [jhānas] in the fivefold method. Therefore, the entire discernment should be understood according to the method stated there, and their inclusion therein. This is the fourfold method.

Visayādippabhedato pana vinicchayaṃ pañcakanayeneva vakkhāma, tadanusārato eva catukkanayavasenāpi sakkā ñātunti. Evaṃ upari lokuttarepi. Pañcavidhāpi cete rūpāvacarakusaladhammā kasiṇārammaṇabhedato paccekaṃ aṭṭhavidhā honti pathavīkasiṇaṃ āpotejovāyonīlapītalohitodātakasiṇañcāti, ālokākāsakasiṇehi saddhiṃ dasavidhā honti. Padabhājanīye (dha. sa. 202) pana ālokakasiṇassa odātakasiṇena saṅgahitattā aggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, ākāsakasiṇassa pana ugghāṭanāsambhavato anāruppajjhānikattā. Taṃ hi punappunaṃ ugghāṭiyamānampi ākāsameva hoti, tasmā tatthuppannaṃ rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānaṃ bhavavisesāya, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya ca saṃvattati, abhiññāya, vipassanāya ca pādakampi hoti, anāruppattā pana [M 0.0040] nirodhapādakaṃ na hoti. Sesāni pana nava kasiṇāni nirodhapādakānipīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Ānāpānajjhānassāpi panettha vāyokasiṇe saṅgaho daṭṭhabboti. Kasiṇakathā.

Regarding the discernment based on the distinction of objects and so forth, we will explain it according to the fivefold method; following that, it can also be understood through the fourfold method. Similarly, this applies also to the supramundane [states] above. These five types of wholesome states of the form sphere, according to the distinction of their kasiṇa objects, each become eightfold: namely, earth kasiṇa, water kasiṇa, fire kasiṇa, air kasiṇa, blue kasiṇa, yellow kasiṇa, red kasiṇa, and white kasiṇa. Together with the light kasiṇa and the space kasiṇa, they become tenfold. In the section on analysis of terms (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 202), however, the non-inclusion of the light kasiṇa should be understood, as it is included in the white kasiṇa; but the space kasiṇa is not included because it cannot be opened up, and because it is a jhāna that does not lead to the formless attainments. For even when repeatedly opened up, it remains simply space. Therefore, the fifth jhāna of the form sphere arising there conduces to a special state of existence, to the blissful abiding in this very life, and also serves as a foundation for direct knowledge and insight; however, because it is not an immaterial attainment, it does not serve as a foundation for cessation. The remaining nine kasiṇas, however, serve as foundations for cessation—this is their distinction. Here, the ānāpāna jhāna should also be understood as included in the air kasiṇa. This is the discussion on kasiṇas.

Evaṃ kasiṇavasena aṭṭhavidhā cete abhibhāyatanavasena pana paccekaṃ aṭṭhavidhā honti. Bhagavatā hi –

Thus, these are eightfold by way of kasiṇa, but by way of the bases of mastery, they are each eightfold. For the Blessed One has said:

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni, tāni abhibhuyya…pe… appamāṇāni. Tāni abhibhuyya [V 0.0031] …pe… parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni…pe… appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni suvisuddhaṃ nīlaṃ pītaṃ lohitaṃ odāta”nti (dha. sa. 211 ādayo) –

“Internally not perceiving form, one sees external forms that are limited. Having overcome them… immeasurable. Having overcome them… limited, well-favored and ill-favored… immeasurable, well-favored and ill-favored, very pure blue, yellow, red, white.” (Dhs. 211 ff.)

Aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni desitāni, tāni ca kasiṇesveva abhibhavitvā samāpajjanavasena jhānuppattivisesato, anārammaṇavisesato. Tattha hi ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti alābhitāya vā anatthikatāya vā ajjhattarūpe kasiṇavasena parikammasaññāvirahitova. Bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti bahiddhā aṭṭha kasiṇarūpāni parikammavasena ceva appanāvasena ca passati. Parittānīti khuddakaparimāṇāni, tāni abhibhuyya passanto ca sampannagahaṇiko kaṭacchumattaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā “kiṃ ettha bhuñjitabbaṃ atthī”ti saṅkaḍḍhitvā sabbaṃ ekakabaḷameva karoti, evameva ñāṇuttariko “kimettha parittake ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ atthi, nāyaṃ mama bhāro”ti tāni abhibhavitvā saha nimittuppādeneva appanaṃ nibbatteti, tasmā taṃ jhānaṃ “abhibhāyatana”nti vuccati. Appamāṇānīti mahantāni. Tāni abhibhuyyāti mahagghaso ekaṃ bhattapātiṃ labhitvā viya ñāṇuttaro appamāṇaṃ labhitvā “etaṃ vā hotu aññaṃ vā, kimettha samāpajjitabba”nti appanaṃ nibbatteti. Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇāni[M 0.0041]. Parisuddhāni hi nīlādīni, aparisuddhāni ca suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti idha adhippetāni, etānipi “suvaṇṇāni vā hontu dubbaṇṇāni vā, parittaappamāṇavaseneva abhibhāyatanānī”ti āgamaṭṭhakathāsu (dī. ni. aṭṭa. 2.173; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.249; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.65) vaṇṇitāni. Vaṇṇābhogassa hi atthitāya purimāni abhibhāyatanāni vaṇṇābhogarahitasahitatāya ettha kevalato visesasabbhāvā catudhā vuttāni, nīlādīni pana cattāri suvisuddhavaṇṇavasena sukhārohatāya ñāṇuttariko abhibhavitvā appanaṃ nibbatteti, tasmā ārammaṇavisesābhāvepi jhānuppattivisesato imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ vasena paccekaṃ aṭṭhavidhā hontīti veditabbā. Abhibhāyatanakathā.

The eight bases of mastery have been taught, and they are distinguished by the special arising of jhāna through overcoming the kasiṇas, and by the special object. Herein, “internally not perceiving form” means being without the preliminary perception by way of kasiṇa regarding internal forms, either because they are not obtained or because they are not desired. “Externally perceiving forms” means perceiving the eight external kasiṇa forms both through preliminary work and through absorption. “Limited forms” refers to forms of small measure. One who overcomes and perceives them, being one whose apprehension is complete, is like one who obtains a spoonful of food and, thinking, “Is there anything to eat here?” gathers it all into a single mouthful. Similarly, one endowed with superior knowledge thinks, “What is there to attain in these limited objects? This is no burden for me,” overcomes them, and generates absorption immediately upon the arising of the sign. Therefore, that jhāna is called a “base of mastery.” “Immeasurable forms” refers to forms of great measure. Overcoming them is like obtaining a large bowl of food—one endowed with superior knowledge, having obtained the immeasurable, thinks, “Let it be this or another; what is there to attain here?” and generates absorption. “Well-favored and ill-favored forms” refers to forms that are pure and impure in color. Here, the pure colors are blue, etc., while the impure colors are the well-favored and ill-favored forms. These too are described in the commentaries (Dī.A. II 173; M.A. II 249; A.A. III 8.65) as bases of mastery by way of being limited or immeasurable, whether well-favored or ill-favored. Because the first bases of mastery involve the presence of a color-object, here, due to the distinct nature of being entirely with or without a color-object, they are stated as fourfold. However, the four pure colors—blue, etc.—are easily ascended by one endowed with superior knowledge, who then overcomes them and generates absorption. Thus, even though there is no distinction in the object, due to the special arising of jhāna, these eight bases of mastery should be understood as each eightfold. This is the explanation of the bases of mastery.

Tāni puna yathā ca abhibhāyatanavasena, evaṃ vimokkhavasenāpi paccekaṃ tividhā honti. Bhagavatā hi “rūpī rūpāni passati, ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati, subhantveva adhimutto hotī”ti (dha. sa. 240 ādayo; dī. ni. 3.339, 358; a. ni. 8.66) tayo vimokkhā desitā. Te ca kasiṇesveva adhimuccanavasena jhānuppattivisesato, bhāvanārammaṇavisesato kimidaṃ adhimuccanaṃ nāma? Paccanīkadhammehi [V 0.0032] suṭṭhu vimuccanaṃ, ārammaṇesu ca suṭṭhu abhirati, pitu mātu aṅke vissaṭṭhaṅgapaccaṅgassa dārakassa sayanaṃ viya aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya ārammaṇe pavattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpīti ajjhattaṃ kesādīsu uppāditaṃ rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ nāma, tadassa atthīti rūpī. Ajjhattampi hi kesādīsu nīlaṃ, medādīsu pītaṃ, maṃsādīsu lohitaṃ, dantādīsu odātañca vaṇṇakasiṇavasena ābhujitvā parikammaṃ karontassa rūpajjhānāni, kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ca arūpajjhānāni uppajjanteva[M 0.0042]. Rūpāni passatīti bahiddhāpi nīlakasiṇādirūpāni jhānacakkhunā passati, iminā ajjhattabahiddhavatthukesu kasiṇesu jhānappaṭilābho dassito. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti attano kesādīsu anuppāditarūpāvacarajjhāno, iminā bahiddhā paṭiladdhajjhānatā dassitā. Subhantveva adhimutto hotīti iminā suvisuddhesu nīlādivaṇṇakasiṇesu “subha”nti adhimuttivasena paṭiladdhajjhānatā dassitā. Evaṃ ārammaṇavisesābhāvepi adhimuttivasena jhānuppattivisesato imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vimokkhānaṃ vasena paccekaṃ tividhā hontīti veditabbā. Vimokkhakathā.

Again, just as they are eightfold by way of the bases of mastery, so too are they each threefold by way of the liberations. For the Blessed One has taught three liberations: “Possessed of form, one sees forms; inwardly not perceiving form, one sees forms externally; one is resolved only on the beautiful.” These are distinguished by the special arising of jhāna through being resolved upon the kasiṇas, and by the special nature of the meditation object. But what is this “being resolved”? It is thorough liberation from opposing qualities, deep delight in the objects, and the undisturbed flow of the mind in the object, like a child lying carefree with limbs relaxed in its mother’s or father's lap, unconstrained and unhesitant. Here, “possessed of form” means that internally, one has the form jhāna produced based on the hair, etc., and that form exists for them. For even internally, when one does the preliminary work by focusing on the color kasiṇas—blue in the hair, yellow in the fat, red in the flesh, white in the teeth—form jhānas arise, and after dismantling the kasiṇa, formless jhānas also arise. “Sees forms” means that one also sees external blue kasiṇas, etc., with the jhāna-eye. This shows the attainment of jhāna based on internal and external objects in the kasiṇas. “Inwardly not perceiving form” means that one has not produced form-sphere jhāna internally based on the hair, etc. This shows the attainment of jhāna externally. “One is resolved only on the beautiful” shows the attainment of jhāna through being resolved upon the highly purified blue, etc., color kasiṇas as “beautiful.” Thus, even without a difference in the object, due to the difference in the arising of jhāna based on being resolved, it should be understood that they are individually threefold by way of these three liberations. This is the discussion on the liberations.

Yathā ca vimokkhato, evaṃ paṭipadābhedato paccekaṃ catubbidhā honti dukkhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, dukkhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññaṃ, sukhapaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, sukhapaṭipadaṃ khippābhiññanti. Tattha paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva upacāraṃ uppajjati, tāva pavattā jhānabhāvanā “paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Sā ekaccassa dukkhā nīvaraṇādipaccanīkadhammasamudācāragahanatāya asukhasevanā hoti, ekaccassa tadabhāvato sukhā. Upacārato pana paṭṭhāya yāva appanā, tāva pavattā paññā “abhiññā”ti vuccati. Sā ekaccassa dandhā asīghappavattinī, ekaccassa khippā. Asappāyasevino dukkhā paṭipadā hoti dandhā ca abhiññā, sappāyasevino sukhā paṭipadā hoti khippā ca abhiññā. Pubbāparakālesu sappāyāsappāyasevanavasena vomissatā ca veditabbā. Tathā palibodhupacchedādikaṃ pubbakiccaṃ asampādentassa paṭipadā dukkhā, sampādentassa sukhā paṭipadā. Appanākosallaṃ asampādentassa dandhābhiññā, sampādentassa khippā. Kilesindriyānaṃ vā tikkhamudutāya paṭhamā, vipariyāyena catutthā, vomissatāya majjhimā dveti veditabbā. Taṇhāvijjābhibhavanānabhibhavanavasena vā samathavipassanāsu katādhikārākatādhikāratāvasena vāpi [M 0.0043] etāsaṃ pabhedo veditabbo. Paṭhamajjhānādiāgamanavasenāpi dutiyādīnaṃ paṭipadābhiññābhedo hotiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipadāvasena paccekaṃ catubbidhā hontīti veditabbā. Paṭipadākathā.

Just as with respect to the liberations, so too with respect to the path, they are individually fourfold: painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Here, the development of jhāna that occurs from the initial application of mind up to access concentration is called 'the path.' For some, this is painful due to the density of the arising of opposing states such as the hindrances, making it an unpleasant practice. For others, due to their absence, it is pleasant. From access concentration up to absorption, the wisdom that arises is called 'direct knowledge.' For some, this is slow, not proceeding quickly, while for others, it is quick. For those who cultivate unsuitable things, the path is painful and direct knowledge is slow. For those who cultivate suitable things, the path is pleasant and direct knowledge is quick. A mixture should also be understood as due to cultivating suitable and unsuitable things at earlier and later times. Similarly, for one who does not fulfill preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments, the path is painful. For one who fulfills them, the path is pleasant. For one who does not attain skill in absorption, direct knowledge is slow. For one who attains it, direct knowledge is quick. Alternatively, the first should be understood as due to the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of defilement, the fourth as the opposite, and the middle two as a mixture. Or, the distinction among these should be understood based on the overcoming or non-overcoming of craving and ignorance, or based on whether or not one has previously made a foundation in serenity and insight. It should also be seen that the distinction in path and direct knowledge occurs for the second jhāna and so on, according to their mode of attainment. Thus, it should be understood that they are individually fourfold based on the path. The Discussion on the Path.

Yathā [V 0.0033] ca paṭipadāhi, evaṃ ārammaṇabhedatopi paccekaṃ catubbidhā honti parittaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, parittaṃ appamāṇārammaṇaṃ, appamāṇaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, appamāṇaṃ appamāṇārammaṇanti. Tattha yaṃ appaguṇaṃ, uparijjhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, idaṃ parittaṃ. Yaṃ pana avaḍḍhite ārammaṇe pavattaṃ, taṃ parittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assāti parittārammaṇaṃ. Vipariyāyato appamāṇaṃ appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Tadubhayavomissatāya majjhe itaradvayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ ārammaṇabhedato catubbidhā hontīti veditabbā. Ārammaṇakathā.

Just as with the paths, so also with respect to the distinction of the object, they are individually fourfold: limited with a limited object, limited with an immeasurable object, immeasurable with a limited object, and immeasurable with an immeasurable object. Here, that which is of little quality and cannot serve as a condition for higher jhānas is 'limited.' That which occurs with an undeveloped object is what has a 'limited object.' Conversely, the immeasurable has an immeasurable object. The other two in the middle should be understood as a mixture of these two. Thus, it should be understood that they are fourfold based on the distinction of the object. The Discussion on the Object.

Yathā ca paṭipadārammaṇehi, evaṃ adhipatīnaṃ vasena paccekaṃ catubbidhatā, hīnattikavasena puna tividhatā ca yojetvā veditabbā.

Just as with the path and object, so too by way of the dominant factors, they should be understood as being individually fourfold, and again as threefold by way of the triad of inferior, medium, and superior.

Dasakasiṇamūlavibhāgakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion on the Root Divisions of the Ten Kasiṇas is concluded.

Yathā kasiṇamūlesu, evaṃ brahmavihāramūlesupi yathāyogaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo – mettākaruṇāmuditāvasena hi ādito cattāri jhānāni paccekaṃ tividhā honti mettāsahagataṃ, karuṇāsahagataṃ, muditāsahagatanti. Pañcamajjhānaṃ pana upekkhābrahmavihāravasena ekavidhaṃ upekkhāsahagatanti. Purimesu hi tīsu pañcamajjhānaṃ nuppajjati. Kasmā? Somanassāvippayogato, somanassasamuṭṭhitānaṃ byāpādavihiṃsāratīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ nissaraṇattā, pacchime ca tikacatukkajjhānaṃ nuppajjati. Kasmā? Upekkhāvedanāsampayogato, tassā ca paṭighānunayanissaraṇato majjhattākārena pavattito, tāni puna paṭipadārammaṇādhipatihīnattikabhedehi pubbe [M 0.0044] vuttanayena yojetvā veditabbāni. Ettha ca appasattārammaṇavasena parittārammaṇatā, bahusattārammaṇavasena appamāṇārammaṇatā ca ekasmiṃ satte appanaṃ pāpetvā anukkamena ekāvāsaekavīthigāmādigatasattesu pāpanavasena vaḍḍhanā ca veditabbā. Dhammuddese panettha karuṇāsahagate muditāvirahitā pañcatiṃsa dhammā, tesu chandādayo cattāro, karuṇā cāti pañceva yevāpanakā, karuṇā ca niyatāti veditabbā. Evaṃ muditāsahagatepi. Kevalaṃ karuṇāvirahitā muditā niyatā pavattāti ayamettha viseso. Avasesabrahmavihāradvaye, pana kasiṇāsubhādīsu ca sabbattha karuṇāmuditāvirahitā ca catuttiṃsa dhammā, tattha ca chandādayo cattārova yevāpanakā veditabbāti. Brahmavihāramūlavibhāgakathā.

Just as in the case of the kasiṇa bases, so too in the case of the brahmavihāra bases, the classification should be understood as is appropriate. For initially, the first four jhānas are individually threefold by way of loving-kindness, compassion, and altruistic joy: namely, accompanied by loving-kindness, accompanied by compassion, and accompanied by altruistic joy. The fifth jhāna, however, is of one kind, accompanied by equanimity, as it pertains to the equanimity brahmavihāra. In the first three, the fifth jhāna does not arise. Why? Because of their non-separation from joy, and because they are the means of escape from ill will, cruelty, and discontent respectively. In the last, the third and fourth jhānas do not arise. Why? Because it is associated with equanimous feeling, and because that equanimity is the escape from aversion and approval, and proceeds with a neutral quality. These should be further understood by applying the previously stated method regarding the divisions by path, object, dominance, and the triad of inferior, etc. Here, the meditation has a limited object when it is directed toward a few beings, and an immeasurable object when directed toward many beings. It should be understood that absorption is first achieved in a single being and then gradually expanded to beings in a single dwelling, street, village, etc. In this exposition of the Dhamma, in the state accompanied by compassion, devoid of altruistic joy, there are thirty-five mental factors; among them, the four beginning with intention, and compassion—only these five are variable, and compassion is fixed. The same applies to the state accompanied by altruistic joy, but the distinction here is that, devoid of compassion, altruistic joy is fixed and arises. In the remaining two brahmavihāras, and also in all the kasiṇas, foulness meditations, etc., there are thirty-four mental factors, devoid of compassion and altruistic joy; and there, it should be understood, only the four beginning with intention are variable. The Discussion on the Root Divisions of the Brahmavihāras.

Asubhabhedato [V 0.0034] pana paṭhamajjhānamevekaṃ dasavidhaṃ hoti uddhumātakasaññāsahagataṃ vinīlakavipubbakavicchiddakavikkhāyitakavikkhittakahatavikkhittakalohitakapuḷavakaaṭṭhikasaññāsahagatanti, dasavidhepi cetasmiṃ asubhe paṭikūlattā, dubbalattā ca vitakkabaleneva jhānaṃ tiṭṭhati, na vinā vitakkena sīghasotāya nadiyā arittabaleneva nāvā viya, tasmā paṭhamajjhānamevettha uppajjati, samathavipassanādiānisaṃsadassāvitāya, panettha nīvaraṇappahānena ca pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati bahuvetanalābhadassanena pupphachaḍḍakassa gūtharāsimhi viya, upasantabyādhidukkhassa ca rogino vamanavirecanappavattiyaṃ viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ pana dasavidhampi paṭhamajjhānaṃ paṭipadārammaṇādhipatihīnattikavasena paccekaṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca asubhārammaṇassa avaḍḍhanīyatāya khuddake uddhumātakādiṭṭhāne uppannaṃ nimittaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ, mahante appamāṇārammaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etesu pana [M 0.0045] dasasu asubhesu sāmaññato dvattiṃsākāravasena, navasivathikapabbavasena ca pavattā kāyagatāsati saṅgahitā, vaṇṇakasiṇesu ca kesādīnaṃ koṭṭhāsānaṃ nīlādivaṇṇārammaṇā, catukkapañcakajjhānavasena uppannā kāyagatāsati ca saṅgahitā. Padabhājanīye visuṃ na vuttā, tasmā tesaṃ vasenāpi vibhāgo veditabbo. Asubhamūlavibhāgakathā.

Regarding the division by way of foulness, the first jhāna alone is tenfold: accompanied by the perception of a bloated corpse, a livid corpse, a festering corpse, a fissured corpse, a gnawed corpse, a scattered corpse, a hacked-and-scattered corpse, a bloody corpse, a worm-infested corpse, and a skeleton. In these ten kinds of foulness, due to the repulsiveness and the weakness of the object, the jhāna is maintained only by the strength of applied thought—not without it—just as a boat on a swiftly flowing river is maintained only by the strength of the rudder. Therefore, only the first jhāna arises here. And here, through the abandoning of the hindrances, joy and happiness arise, like a scavenger seeing a heap of dung as a great gain, and it should be seen as similar to a sick person finding relief from their illness through the act of vomiting and purging. This tenfold first jhāna should be understood by applying to it individually the divisions by way of path, object, dominance, and the triad of inferior, etc. And here, due to the un-extendable nature of the foul object, the sign that has arisen in a small place, such as a bloated corpse, is known as having a limited object, while one that has arisen in a large place is known as having an immeasurable object. Among these ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness of the body is included in general by way of the thirty-two aspects and the nine charnel ground contemplations. Similarly, mindfulness of the body is also included when it arises by way of the fourth and fifth jhānas with the colors of the body parts (hair, etc.) as object, as in the color kasiṇas. These are not separately mentioned in the Padabhājanīya; therefore, their division should also be understood accordingly. The Discussion on the Root Divisions of Foulness.

Evaṃ ārammaṇādibhedato ca bhinnānaṃ rūpāvacarakusaladhammānaṃ kāladesādibhedena anantatā, bhagavatā ca ekattaṃ upanetvā desitabhāvo, vitthāranayātideso ca kāmāvacarakusale vuttānusārena yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbo. Ito paraṃ arūpāvacarādīsupi visesamattameva vakkhāma. Evaṃ visayādippabhedato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus, the infinitude of wholesome states of the fine-material sphere, which are distinct due to differences in object, etc., and in time, place, etc.; the fact that they are brought to unity and taught by the Blessed One; and the application of the detailed method—all this should be understood as appropriate in accordance with what was said concerning sense-sphere wholesome states. From here on, we will speak only of the specific points regarding the immaterial sphere and so on. Thus, the analysis should be understood in terms of the divisions by way of object and so forth.

Rūpāvacarakusaladhammā niṭṭhitā.

The wholesome states of the fine-material sphere are finished.
