Arūpāvacarā pana kusaladhammā sampayogato na bhinnā, sabbepi upekkhekaggatāsampayuttāva, dhammuddesāditopi sabbaso rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānasadisā. Arūpāvacarabhāvo eva hettha viseso. Visayādippabhedatoti ettha pana ārammaṇato te catubbidhā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti. Tattha hi kasiṇugghāṭimākāse “ananto ākāso”ti pavattaṃ paṭhamaṃ, tasmiṃ paṭhamāruppaviññāṇe “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti pavattaṃ dutiyaṃ, tassa paṭhamāruppaviññāṇassa abhāve “natthi kiñcī”ti pavattaṃ [V 0.0035] tatiyaṃ, tasmiṃ tatiye “santametaṃ paṇītameta”nti pavattaṃ catutthaṃ. Purimapurimehi pacchimapacchimaṃ santasantatarasantatamanti ca veditabbaṃ.

However, the wholesome states of the immaterial sphere are not distinct in terms of association, for they are all associated with equanimity and one-pointedness. Also in terms of the enumeration of states, etc., they are in all respects similar to the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. The distinction here is simply their being of the immaterial sphere. But here, as to the division by way of object, etc., they are fourfold in terms of their object, namely: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. For here, the first is that which occurs as 'space is infinite' in the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed. The second is that which occurs as 'consciousness is infinite' with respect to the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment. The third is that which occurs as 'there is nothing' with respect to the absence of that first immaterial consciousness. The fourth is that which occurs as 'this is peaceful, this is sublime' with respect to that third attainment. And each succeeding attainment should be understood as progressively more peaceful than each preceding one.

Nanu [M 0.0046] rūpāvacaresu vitakkādiaṅgasamatikkamato uparūparijhānānaṃ santatarādibhāvo vutto, aṅgātikkamarahitesu pana āruppesu kathanti? Ārammaṇātikkamato. Etesu hi kasiṇarūpasamatikkamato paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānato santaṃ, tatopi kasiṇugghāṭimākāsātikkamato dutiyaṃ, tatopi ākāse pavattaviññāṇātikkamato tatiyaṃ, tatopi ākāse pavattaviññāṇassa samatikkamato catutthanti. Evaṃ aṅgasamattepi thūlathūlātikkamena sukhumasukhumārammaṇatāya uparūparijjhānānaṃ santatarādibhāvo veditabbo samāyāmavitthārānampi vatthānaṃ suttasukhumatarādibhāvo viya. Nanu abhāvārammaṇatāya tatiyāruppaṃ santapaṇītato manasi karontassa catutthāruppassa kathaṃ tattha nikantipariyādānaṃ, kathaṃ ca samatikkamo vā hotīti? Asamāpajjitukāmatāya, sā ca attano santapaṇītatāya. Yathā hi rājā dantakārādisippikānaṃ atisukhumamanāpasippaṃ disvā “chekā vatime ācariyā”ti tesaṃ chekatāya tussantopi na taṃ sippikabhāvaṃ pattheti, taṃ samatikkamma rājabhāve eva tiṭṭhati, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ ārammaṇabhedato catubbidhānampetesaṃ puna paṭipadārammaṇādhipatihīnattikabhedehi pubbe vuttanayeneva paccekaṃ bhedo veditabbo.

Is it not said that in the case of the fine-material sphere attainments, the higher jhānas are progressively more peaceful because of the transcending of the factors such as applied thought? How then is this so in the case of the immaterial attainments, which are without the transcending of factors? It is because of the transcending of the object. For in these, the first jhāna is more peaceful than the fifth jhāna of the fine-material sphere because it transcends the kasiṇa-form; the second is more peaceful than that because it transcends the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed; the third is more peaceful than that because it transcends the consciousness that occurred in space; and the fourth is more peaceful than that because it also transcends the consciousness that occurred in space. Thus, although the jhāna factors are the same, the progressive peacefulness of the higher jhānas should be understood as due to the progressive subtlety of the object by transcending what is progressively grosser, just as with fabrics of the same length and width, there is a progressive subtlety due to the fineness of the thread. But when one attends to the third immaterial attainment, which has absence as its object, as peaceful and sublime, how can one be overcome by delight in it, and how can there be its transcendence? Because of the wish not to enter into it, and this arises from its own peaceful and sublime nature. For just as a king, on seeing the extremely subtle and pleasing craft of ivory-workers, might think, 'How skilled these masters are!' and though pleased by their skill, he does not aspire to become a craftsman but transcends that and remains in his royal state; so too should this be seen. Thus, for these four, which are distinct by way of object, a further division for each should be understood according to the previously stated method based on the threefold distinctions of path of practice, object, and predominance.

Ettha ca rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānanikanti pariyādānadukkhatāya paṭhamāruppassa, paṭhamāruppādinikantipariyādānadukkhatāya dutiyāruppādīnañca dukkhapaṭipadatā, pariyādiṇṇanikantikassa tadappanāparivāsadandhatāya dandhābhiññatā, vipariyāyena itarā ca veditabbā. Parittakasiṇugghāṭimākāsamūlakānaṃ pana catunnaṃ parittārammaṇatā, vipariyāyānaṃ appamāṇārammaṇatā veditabbā. Rūpārūpāvacarā panettha adhipatisahitāva uppajjanti, na vinā adhipatīhi. Kāmāvacarā tu adhipatirahitāpi uppajjanti[M 0.0047], te ca ārammaṇādhipati sahajātādhipatīti dvepi labbhanti. Rūpārūpāvacarā pana sahajātādhipatimeva, netaraṃ. Tattha ca chandādhipatinā sahajātā dhammā chandādhipateyyā, chando pana adhipati eva, na chandādhipateyyo. Itare pana adhipateyyāva, nādhipatayo aññassa attanā sahajātassa chandassa, itaresañca adhipatiyatthassa abhāvā. Ekasmiṃ hi cittuppāde chandādīsu catūsupi vijjamānesu yathāpaccayaṃ sahajātādhipati [V 0.0036] ekova labbhati. Evaṃ vīriyādhipatiyādīsupi yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Evaṃ visayādippabhedato vinicchayo ñātabbo.

And here, for the first immaterial attainment, the path of practice is difficult because of the painfulness of being overcome by delight in the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere; for the second immaterial attainment and so on, the path of practice is difficult because of the painfulness of being overcome by delight in the first immaterial attainment and so on. For one who is overcome by delight, there is slow direct knowledge because of the slowness of the preliminary work for that absorption. The opposite should be understood in the contrary case. However, for the four attainments based on the space from which a limited kasiṇa has been removed, the object is limited; for the contrary cases, the object should be understood as immeasurable. Here, the fine-material and immaterial sphere states arise only with a predominance condition, not without predominance conditions. But sense-sphere states can arise even without a predominance condition, and they can obtain both object-predominance and conascence-predominance. The fine-material and immaterial sphere states, however, have only conascence-predominance, not the other. And therein, states conascent with desire as predominance are 'desire-predominated,' but desire itself is only a predominance, not 'desire-predominated.' The other factors, however, are only predominated, not predominances, because there is no other desire conascent with itself that could be predominated, and because the others lack the nature of predominance. For in a single mind-moment, even if all four—desire, etc.—are present, only one conascence-predominance is obtained in accordance with conditions. This should be understood as appropriate in the case of energy-predominance, etc. Thus the analysis should be understood in terms of the divisions by way of object, etc.

Arūpāvacarakusaladhammā niṭṭhitā.

The wholesome states of the immaterial sphere are concluded.

Lokuttarā pana kusalā maggasampayogabhedato catubbidhā. Seyyathidaṃ – sotāpattimaggasampayuttaṃ sakadāgāmimaggasampayuttaṃ anāgāmimaggasampayuttaṃ arahattamaggasampayuttanti. Nanu catūsupi cetesu maggasampayogo samāno aṭṭhannampi maggaṅgānaṃ sabbattha uppattito kathaṃ tattha bhedoti? Anusayappahānasaṅkhātassa maggakiccassa bhedato. Anusaye mārento gacchatīti hi maggo. Maggā hi yathāsakaṃ anusaye pajahanti eva, nimittā vuṭṭhahanti, pavattañca chindanti nāmāti vuccanti. Nimittanti ca pañcakkhandhā, pavattantipi te eva. Taṃ duvidhaṃ upādinnakaṃ, anupādinnakañca.

However, the supramundane wholesome states are fourfold by way of the distinction in their association with the path, that is: associated with the path of stream-entry, associated with the path of once-returning, associated with the path of non-returning, and associated with the path of arahantship. Now, since the association with the path is the same in all four of these, and since the eight path factors arise in every case, how is there a distinction among them? Because of the difference in the function of the path, which is designated the abandoning of the underlying tendencies. For 'path' (magga) is so called because it goes along destroying the underlying tendencies. Indeed, the paths are so called because they abandon their respective underlying tendencies, emerge from the sign, and cut off what is proceeding. The 'sign' is the five aggregates, and 'what is proceeding' is also those same aggregates. This is twofold: that which is clung to and that which is not clung to.

Tatthapi sotāpattimaggo diṭṭhānusayaṃ, vicikicchānusayaṃ, tadekaṭṭhe ca kilese, taṃsahajātāni diṭṭhisampayuttāni, vicikicchāsampayuttañcāti pañcākusalacittāni ca uppajjamānova samugghāteti, samugghātento ca apāyabhavato ceva sugatibhavato ca ṭhapetvā satta bhave tadavasesato vuṭṭhāti[M 0.0048]. Tattha yadetaṃ paṭhamamaggānuppattiyaṃ uppajjamānārahaṃ diṭṭhivicikicchāsampayuttapañcacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ rūpakkhandho, tāni pañca cittāni viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanādayo itare tayo khandhā. Ime anupādinnapañcakkhandhā anupādinnanimittaṃ, anupādinnappavattaṃ nāma. Tato paṭhamamaggo vuṭṭhāti, taṃ chindati nāma. Yadetaṃ apāyabhave, sugatiyañca ṭhapetvā satta bhave tadavasese ca paṭhamamaggānuppattiyaṃ āyatiṃ uppajjamānārahaṃ kammajakkhandhapañcakaṃ, taṃ upādinnanimittaṃ, upādinnappavattaṃ nāma. Tato paṭhamamaggo vuṭṭhāti, tañca chindati nāma. Tatova paṭhamamaggo anusayaṃ pajahantova nimittā vuṭṭhahati, pavattañca chindati nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ itaramaggesupi upādinnānupādinnanimittappavattaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ chindanaṃ yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ.

Herein, the path of stream-entry, as it arises, eradicates the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the defilements that share their object, and the five unwholesome consciousnesses that are conascent with them—those associated with views and the one associated with doubt. And in eradicating them, it emerges from the plane of misery and from all remaining existences apart from seven at most in the fortunate destinations. Herein, that material form originated by the five consciousnesses associated with views and doubt, which is fit to arise when the first path has not arisen, is the form aggregate; those five consciousnesses are the consciousness aggregate; the associated feeling, etc., are the other three aggregates. These five aggregates are called the 'sign not clung to' and 'what is proceeding not clung to.' The first path emerges from that; it is said to cut that off. That pentad of kamma-born aggregates fit to arise in the future when the first path has not arisen—in the plane of misery, and in the remaining existences apart from seven at most in the fortunate destination—is called the 'sign clung to' and 'what is proceeding clung to.' The first path emerges from that; it is said to cut that off too. Therefore it should be understood that the first path, by abandoning the underlying tendencies, emerges from the sign and cuts off what is proceeding. In the same way, the emerging from and cutting off of the sign and what is proceeding, whether clung to or not clung to, should be understood as appropriate in the case of the other paths as well.

Sakadāgāmimaggo pana oḷārikakāmarāgānusayaṃ, paṭighānusayaṃ, tadekaṭṭhe ca kilese, taṃsahajātāni ca tathā pavattāni cattāri diṭṭhivippayuttāni, dve ca domanassasahagatānīti cha akusalacittāni [V 0.0037] ca uppajjamānova samugghāteti, samugghātento ca kāmasugatito ṭhapetvā ekabhavaṃ tadavasesato vuṭṭhāti, patanubhūtāva taṃsamaṅgino kāmarāgabyāpādā adhimattā, te ca kadāci viraḷāva uppajjantīti veditabbā.

The path of the once-returner, however, as it arises, eradicates the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the defilements that share their object, and the six unwholesome consciousnesses that are conascent with them and arise in such a way, namely, the four disassociated from views and the two accompanied by displeasure. And in eradicating them, it emerges from the remaining existences in the fortunate sense-sphere destinations, apart from one. For one endowed with this path, gross sensual lust and ill will are attenuated, and it should be understood that they arise only rarely.

Anāgāmimaggopi tāneva tanusahagatakāmarāgappaṭighānusayavasena uppannāni cha cittāni uppajjamānova samugghāteti, samugghātento ca kāmabhavato vuṭṭhāti. Arahattamaggo pana rūparāgaarūparāgamānāvijjānusaye, uddhaccaṃ, tadekaṭṭhe sabbe kilese ca taṃsahajātāni cattāri diṭṭhivippayuttāni, uddhaccasahagatañcāti pañcākusalacittāni ca uppajjamānova samugghāteti, samugghātento ca rūpārūpato, sabbabhavatopi [M 0.0049] vuṭṭhāti. Sesaṃ paṭhamamagge vuttānusārato veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ anusayappahānasaṅkhātakiccabhedato catunnaṃ maggānaṃ bhedo veditabbo.

The path of the non-returner, as it arises, also eradicates those same six types of consciousness that arise by way of the attenuated underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion; and in eradicating them, it emerges from sense-sphere existence. The path of arahantship, however, as it arises, eradicates the underlying tendencies to lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, and ignorance, and also restlessness, all defilements that share their object, and the five unwholesome types of consciousness that are conascent with them—the four disassociated from views and the one accompanied by restlessness. And in eradicating them, it emerges from the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and from all existence. The rest should be understood in accordance with what was said about the first path. Thus the distinction between the four paths should be understood by way of the difference in their function, which is designated the abandoning of the underlying tendencies.

Tadevaṃ maggasampayogabhedato catubbidhaṃ, puna jhānaṅgasampayogabhedato paccekaṃ pañcavidhā honti. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamamaggasampayuttaṃ tāva vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ paṭhamajjhānikaṃ, vicārapītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ dutiyajjhānikaṃ, pītisukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ tatiyajjhānikaṃ, sukhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ, upekkhekaggatāsampayuttaṃ pañcamajjhānikañcāti pañcavidhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ dutiyamaggādisampayuttā cāti vīsatividhā honti, ettha ca catukkanayavasena soḷasavidhatāpi yojetabbā. Kiṃ panettha evaṃ jhānaṅgayogabhedassa niyāmakaṃ kāraṇanti? Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ hi vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanābhūte somanassasahagate ariyamaggā pañcamajjhānikā na uppajjanti, somanassasahagatā catukkajjhānikāva uppajjanti, upekkhāsahagate ca catukkajjhānikā na uppajjanti, upekkhāsahagatā pañcamajjhānikāva uppajjanti.

Thus, it is fourfold based on the distinction of its association with the paths. Further, based on the distinction of its association with the jhāna factors, each becomes fivefold. How? First, that which is associated with the first path is fivefold: pertaining to the first jhāna, associated with initial application, sustained application, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness; pertaining to the second jhāna, associated with sustained application, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness; pertaining to the third jhāna, associated with joy, bliss, and one-pointedness; pertaining to the fourth jhāna, associated with bliss and one-pointedness; and pertaining to the fifth jhāna, associated with equanimity and one-pointedness. In the same way, those associated with the second path and so forth also become twentyfold. Here, by way of the fourfold method, its being sixteenfold should also be applied. Now, what is the determining cause here for this distinction in the association with jhāna factors? It is the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations. For when that insight leading to emergence is accompanied by mental pleasure, the noble paths pertaining to the fifth jhāna do not arise; only the noble paths pertaining to the four jhānas, which are accompanied by mental pleasure, arise. And when it is accompanied by equanimity, the noble paths pertaining to the four jhānas do not arise; only the noble paths pertaining to the fifth jhāna, which are accompanied by equanimity, arise.

Nanu cettha saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ somanassupekkhāsahagatattā catukkapañcamajjhānikānaṃ somanassupekkhāsahagatabhāvassa niyāmakahetu, vitakkādiaṅgasamatikkamato pana nesaṃ dutiyādijjhānabhāvassa niyāmakena aññena bhavitabbaṃ. Na hi saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ vitakkādivikalaṃ uppajjati. Yena taṃ niyāmakaṃ bhaveyya, kiṃ taṃ niyāmakakāraṇanti? Pādakajjhānaṃ, sammasitajjhānaṃ vā. Rūpārūpāvacaresu hi yaṃ yaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tatuṭṭhāya ye keci pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā ye magge uppādeti, te sabbe taṃtaṃjhānasadisāva honti. Yaṃ [V 0.0038] yaṃ vā pana jhānaṃ, taṃsampayutte ca aniccādito vipassitvā ye [M 0.0050] ye magge uppādeti, te ca taṃtaṃjhānasadisāva honti bhūmivaṇṇasadisavaṇṇā godhā viya. Tattha ca sukkhavipassakassa uppannamaggāpi, samāpattilābhinā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ akatvā asammasitvāva uppāditamaggāpi paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā taṃ taṃ vā sammasitvā uppāditamaggāpi sabbe ekasadisā paṭhamajjhānikāva honti. Na hi lokuttaramaggo appanaṃ appatto nāma atthi. Dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni pādakāni katvā vā tattha gate dhamme sammasitvā vā uppāditamaggā yathākkamaṃ caturaṅgikā, tivaṅgikā, duvaṅgikā ca honti. Pañcamajjhānaṃ, pana āruppajjhānāni ca pādakaṃ katvā vā tattha gate dhamme sammasitvā vā uppāditamaggā upekkhekaggatāvasena duvaṅgikāva honti. Etesañca pañcannaṃ jhānikānampi pubbabhāge vipassanā somanassasahagatāpi hoti upekkhāsahagatāpi, vuṭṭhānagāminī pana vipassanā catukkajjhānikānaṃ somanassasahagatā hoti. Pañcamajjhānikānaṃ pana upekkhāsahagatāvāti tadeva pādakajjhānaṃ, sammasitajjhānaṃ vā niyāmakakāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sampayogato vinicchayo.

Is it not that here the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations, because it is accompanied by mental pleasure or equanimity, is the determining cause for the paths pertaining to the four jhānas and the fifth jhāna being accompanied by mental pleasure or equanimity? However, on account of the transcending of factors such as initial application, there must be another determining factor for their state of being the second jhāna and so on. For the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations does not arise deficient in initial application and so on, whereby it could be the determining factor. What then is that determining cause? It is either the foundational jhāna or the contemplated jhāna. For in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, whatever jhāna one attains, and having emerged from that, contemplates any miscellaneous formations and produces a path, all those paths are similar to that respective jhāna. Or whatever jhāna, and the states associated with it, one contemplates as impermanent and so on, and produces any path, those paths too are similar to that respective jhāna, like a lizard whose color is similar to the color of the ground. And in this regard, the paths that have arisen for a dry-insight meditator, the paths produced by one who has attained absorption without making a jhāna foundational or without contemplating it, and the paths produced by making the first jhāna foundational or by contemplating it—all are of one kind, similar, pertaining to the first jhāna. For there is no such thing as a supramundane path that has not reached absorption. The paths produced by making the second, third, and fourth jhānas foundational, or by contemplating the states pertaining to them, have respectively four, three, and two factors. But the paths produced by making the fifth jhāna or the formless jhānas foundational, or by contemplating the states pertaining to them, have only two factors, by way of equanimity and one-pointedness. For these five types of jhānic paths, in the preliminary stage, insight may be accompanied by mental pleasure or equanimity. However, the insight leading to emergence is accompanied by mental pleasure for the paths pertaining to the four jhānas, but for the paths pertaining to the fifth jhāna, it is accompanied by equanimity. Thus, it should be understood that the foundational jhāna or the contemplated jhāna is the determining cause. Thus is the analysis by way of association.

Dhammuddesādito pana paṭhamajjhānikesu tāva catūsu kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vuttadhammesu ṭhapetvā karuṇāmuditā sattatiṃsa dhammā honti. Viratiyo panettha niyatā, pāḷiyañca (dha. sa. 277) rūpena niddiṭṭhā, chandādayo ca cattāro yevāpanakāti veditabbā.

Now, beginning with the enumeration of states, first, in the paths pertaining to the first jhāna, among the states mentioned in relation to the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, excluding compassion and sympathetic joy, there are thirty-seven states. Here, the abstinences are fixed, and in the Pāli text (Dhammasaṅgaṇī §277), they are indicated by their own nature. And the four beginning with zeal should be understood as applicable as appropriate.

Saṅgahavāre pana bodhipakkhiyadhammesu pubbe saṅgahitāvasesānaṃ satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādabojjhaṅgānaṃ vasena atirekā cattāro saṅgahā veditabbā. Paṭhamajjhānikamaggasampayuttesu hi dhammesu sati upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena satipaṭṭhānaṃ, sā visayabhedena catubbidhā, itare assatipaṭṭhānāti sabbeva [M 0.0051] te dvidhā honti. Tathā vīriyaṃ padahanaṭṭhena sammappadhānaṃ, taṃ kiccabhedena catubbidhaṃ, itare asammappadhānāti. Tathā chando vīriyaṃ cittaṃ amohoti cattāro dhammā ijjhanakaṭṭhena yathākkamaṃ “chandiddhipādo vīriyacittavīmaṃsiddhipādo”ti nāmena “iddhipādā”ti vuccanti, itare “aniddhipādā”ti. Tathā sati amoho vīriyaṃ pīti passaddhi samādhi tatramajjhattatāti ime satta dhammā bujjhanaṭṭhena yathākkamaṃ “satisambojjhaṅgo dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo vīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgo”ti vuccanti, itare abojjhaṅgāti evaṃ cattāro saṅgahā.

In the section on inclusion, regarding the aids to enlightenment, four additional inclusions should be understood by way of the remaining factors not previously included: foundations of mindfulness, right strivings, bases of spiritual power, and enlightenment factors. For in the states associated with the first-jhāna path, mindfulness is the foundation of mindfulness by virtue of its establishing nature; it is fourfold by division of objects, while the others are not foundations of mindfulness—thus, all are twofold. Similarly, energy is right striving by virtue of exertion; it is fourfold by division of function, while the others are not right strivings. Likewise, zeal, energy, consciousness, and wisdom—these four phenomena, by their meaning of accomplishing, are called 'bases of spiritual power' in sequence by name as 'the base of spiritual power of zeal, the base of spiritual power of energy, the base of spiritual power of consciousness, and the base of spiritual power of investigation'; the others are not bases of spiritual power. Similarly, mindfulness, wisdom, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—these seven phenomena, by their meaning of awakening, are called 'enlightenment factors' in sequence as 'the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity'; the others are not enlightenment factors. Thus, there are four inclusions.

Sesaṃ sabbaṃ lakkhaṇādito paṭṭhāya suññatavārapariyosānaṃ kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vuttasadisameva[V 0.0039], kevalaṃ pana maggaṅgasaṅgahe “aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hotī”ti (dha. sa. 337) padabhājanīye sarūpeneva niddiṭṭhaṃ, indriyasaṅgahe paññindriyaṭṭhāne paṭhamamaggassa anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ gahetvā itaramaggānaṃ aññindriyaṃ gahetvāva aṭṭhindriyanti aṭṭhindriyatā, sabbattha lokuttaratā ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Paṭhamajjhānikā cattāro maggā.

All the rest, beginning from the characteristics up to the end of the section on emptiness, is just like what was said for the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. However, in the inclusion of path factors, it is specified in its own nature in the verbal analysis by the phrase 'the path is eightfold' (Dhs. §337). In the inclusion of faculties, in place of the wisdom faculty, the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' is taken for the first path, and the faculty of final knowledge is taken for the remaining paths—thus, there are eight faculties, and the state of having eight faculties. Their supramundane nature is the distinction everywhere; the rest is the same. The four paths pertaining to the first jhāna.

Tathā dutiyajjhānikesupi kevalaṃ dhammuddese vitakkābhāvo, saṅgahavāre caturaṅgajjhānatā, sattaṅgamaggatā ca viseso, sesaṃ paṭhamajjhānikasadisameva. Dutiyajjhānikamaggā.

Similarly, in the states pertaining to the second jhāna, the only distinction in the enumeration of states is the absence of initial application. In the section on inclusion, the distinction is the state of being a four-factored jhāna and a seven-factored path. The rest is similar to the states pertaining to the first jhāna. The paths pertaining to the second jhāna.

Tathā tatiyajjhānikesupi kevalaṃ dhammuddese vicārābhāvo, saṅgahavāre tivaṅgikajjhānatā ca viseso, sesaṃ dutiyajjhānikasadisameva. Tatiyajjhānikamaggā.

Similarly, in the states pertaining to the third jhāna, the only distinction in the enumeration of states is the absence of sustained application; and in the section on inclusion, the state of being a three-factored jhāna is a distinction. The rest is similar to the states pertaining to the second jhāna. The paths pertaining to the third jhāna.

Tathā catutthajjhānikesupi kevalaṃ dhammuddese pītiyā abhāvo, koṭṭhāsavāre duvaṅgikajjhānatā, chaḷaṅgikabojjhaṅgatā [M 0.0052] ca viseso, sesaṃ tatiyajjhānikasadisameva. Catutthajjhānikamaggā.

Similarly, in the states pertaining to the fourth jhāna, the only distinction in the enumeration of states is the absence of joy; in the section on divisions, the state of being a two-factored jhāna and the state of being six-factored enlightenment factors are the distinction; the rest is similar to the states pertaining to the third jhāna. The paths pertaining to the fourth jhāna.

Tathā pañcamajjhānikesupi kevalaṃ sabbattha vedanāparivattanameva viseso, sesaṃ catutthajjhānikasadisameva. Pañcamajjhānikamaggā. Evaṃ dhammuddesādito vinicchayo.

Similarly, in the fifth jhāna states, the only distinction is simply the transformation of feeling throughout. The rest is similar to the fourth jhāna. The paths pertaining to the fifth jhāna. Thus is the analysis from the enumeration of phenomena onward.

Visayādippabhedato pana sabbepi lokuttarakusalā ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇāva, tasmā na tato nesaṃ bhedo, paṭipadādibhedato pana pubbe vuttanayena paccekaṃ bhedo veditabbo. Ettha ca yo nāmarūpapariggahato paṭṭhāya kilamanto vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā dukkhena kasirena kilese vikkhambheti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Yo pana vikkhambhitakileso, so vipassanāparivāsaṃ vāsento cirena maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa dandhābhiññā hoti. Iminā nayena itarā tissopi paṭipadābhiññāyo veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭipadādibhedato, evaṃ vimokkhabhedatopi paccekaṃ dvidhā honti – suññatavimokkho appaṇihitavimokkhoti.

Moreover, all supramundane wholesome states, even though distinguished by differences in object, have Nibbāna alone as their object; therefore, there is no difference among them in that regard. However, distinctions should be understood individually based on differences in the path and so forth, in the manner previously stated. Here, one who, starting from the thorough grasping of name-and-form, strives and initiates insight meditation, suppressing the defilements with difficulty through suffering—for him, the path is painful. On the other hand, one whose defilements are already suppressed, dwelling in the cultivation of insight, attains the manifestation of the path only after a long time—for him, realization is slow. In this way, the other three kinds of practice and realization should also be understood. And just as they are distinguished by differences in the path and so forth, so too are they individually twofold based on differences in liberation—namely, the emptiness liberation and the desireless liberation.

Tattha suññatanti, appaṇihitanti ca lokuttaramaggassa nāmaṃ. So hi āgamanato saguṇato ārammaṇatoti tīhi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhati. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu vipassanākammaṭṭhāniko ādito paṭṭhāya “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tividhaṃ anupassanaṃ āropetvā [V 0.0040] sammasanto vicarati, sacassa vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā tebhūmake saṅkhāre anattato vipassati, ayaṃ attasuññatādassanaṭṭhena suññatā nāma hoti. Sace dukkhato vipassati, ayaṃ taṇhāpaṇidhirahitaṭṭhena appaṇihitā nāma hoti, tā ubhopi āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano attano maggassa yathākkamaṃ suññatamaggo [M 0.0053] appaṇihitamaggoti nāmaṃ denti. Evaṃ āgamanato nāmalābho veditabbo. Nanu suttantesu sace vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā aniccato passati, tassā vasena maggo animittavimokkho hotīti katvā tayo vimokkhā kathitāti? Saccaṃ, api ca kho pariyāyato kathitā, nippariyāyato pana sayampi sanimittā attano maggassa animittanāmaṃ dātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya dve eva vimokkhā hontīti. Tissopi hi vipassanā niccanimittaṃ, sukhanimittañca ugghāṭanena animittavohāraṃ labhanti, tissopi nimittabhūtesu khandhesu caraṇato sanimittāva, tasmā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano maggassa nippariyāyato animittanāmaṃ dātuṃ na sakkonti. Yasmā pana maggo sayaṃ rāgādīhi suñño, rāgādinimittapaṇidhirahito ca, tasmā saguṇeneva suññatanāmaṃ, appaṇihitanāmañca labhati. Evamassa saguṇato nāmalābho veditabbo. Yasmā pana nibbānaṃ rāgādīhi, saṅkhārehi ca suññattā, rāgādinimittapaṇidhirahitattā ca “suññataṃ, animittaṃ, appaṇihita”nti ca vuccati, tasmā taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannamaggopi “suññato, animitto, appaṇihito”ti ca nāmaṃ labhati. Evaṃ ārammaṇato nāmalābho veditabbo.

Here, "emptiness" and "desirelessness" are names for the supramundane path. That path obtains these names for three reasons: by way of approach, by way of its inherent qualities, and by way of its object. How? Here, a monk engaged in insight meditation, from the very beginning, undertakes contemplation by applying the threefold reflection: "impermanent, suffering, non-self," scrutinizing them. If, through insight leading to emergence, he sees the formations of the three realms as non-self, this is called "emptiness" in the sense of seeing the emptiness of self. If he sees them as suffering, this is called "desirelessness" in the sense of being free from the inclination of craving. Both, standing in the place of approach, give their respective names to their paths in due order: the emptiness path and the desireless path. Thus, the obtaining of the name by way of approach should be understood. Now, in the suttas, it is said that if insight leading to emergence sees impermanence, then by means of that, the path becomes the signless liberation; thus, three liberations are spoken of. True, but this is spoken of figuratively. Literally, however, since even it, being itself with signs, cannot give the name "signless" to its path, there are only two liberations. For even the three insights, by uprooting the signs of permanence and pleasure, obtain the designation "signless," yet because they operate on the aggregates, which are themselves signs, they are still "with signs." Therefore, even standing in the place of approach, they cannot literally give the name "signless" to their own path. But because the path itself is empty of lust and so on, and free from the inclination towards signs of lust and the like, it obtains the names "emptiness" and "desirelessness" by way of its inherent qualities. Thus, the obtaining of the name by way of its inherent qualities should be understood. And because Nibbāna is empty of lust and so on, and also of formations, and free from the inclination towards signs of lust and the like, it is called "emptiness, signlessness, desirelessness." Therefore, the path that arises taking it as its object also obtains the names "emptiness, signlessness, desirelessness." Thus, the obtaining of the name by way of its object should be understood.

Tesu idha āgamanatova maggo nāmaṃ labhati, na saguṇato, nāpi ārammaṇato, saguṇārammaṇato nāmalābhassa suttantesu pariyāyadesitattā. Teneva hettha maggānaṃ saguṇārammaṇatopi animittavimokkhataṃ aggahetvā suññataappaṇihitavimokkhatāva āgamanato vuttā, tañcāgamanaṃ duvidhaṃ vipassanāgamanaṃ, maggāgamanañca. Tattha vipassanāgamanato maggo ca suññatādināmaṃ labhati, maggāgamanato ca labhateva, idha pana maggassa adhippetattā [M 0.0054] vipassanāgamanatova veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ vimokkhabhedato paccekaṃ dvidhā honti. Evaṃ visayādippabhedato vinicchayo.

Here, the path obtains its name only from its approach, not from its qualities or its object, because the acquisition of the name from qualities and object is taught figuratively in the discourses. For that reason, here, not taking up the signless liberation of the paths from their qualities and object, their nature as the emptiness liberation and the desireless liberation is stated based on the approach. And that approach is twofold: the approach of insight and the approach of the path. Therein, from the approach of insight, the path obtains the name of emptiness, etc., and from the approach of the path, it also certainly obtains it. Here, however, since the path is what is intended, it should be understood as being only from the approach of insight. Thus, they are each twofold by way of the distinction of liberations. In this way, the analysis is made according to distinctions such as the object, etc.

Lokuttarakusaladhammā niṭṭhitā.

The supramundane wholesome states are concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca mohavicchedaniyā nāma

And concluded is the treatise called "The Cutting Off of Delusion."

Abhidhammamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanāya

Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix

“Kusalā dhammā”ti padassa atthavaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Term 'Wholesome States'.

Akusalapadattho

The Meaning of the Term 'Unwholesome'.

Lobhamūlavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Root of Greed.

Akusalā [V 0.0041] pana dhammā bhūmito ekavidhā kāmāvacarāva, sampayogato pana mūlavasena tividhā honti lobhamūlā dosamūlā mohamūlāti. Tattha lobhamūlā aṭṭhavidhā somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ, somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ, upekkhāsahagataṃ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāranti.

Unwholesome states, however, are of one kind by way of the plane—being solely of the sense-sphere—but are of three kinds by way of association, rooted in greed, hatred, and delusion. Herein, those rooted in greed are eightfold: accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted; likewise, prompted; accompanied by joy, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; likewise, prompted; accompanied by equanimity, associated with wrong view, unprompted; likewise, prompted; accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; likewise, prompted.

Tattha iṭṭhārammaṇe lobhabahulatādīhi kāraṇehi somanassasahagatatā, asaddhammasavanaakalyāṇamittatādīhi diṭṭhisampayuttatā ca veditabbā. Yadā hi “natthi kāmesu ādīnavo”tiādinā nayena micchādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho kāme vā paribhuñjati, diṭṭhamaṅgalādīni vā sārato pacceti sabhāvatikkheneva anussāhitena cittena, tadā paṭhamaṃ akusalacittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā mandena samussāhitena, tadā dutiyaṃ. Yadā micchādiṭṭhiṃ apurakkhatvā kevalaṃ haṭṭhatuṭṭho methunaṃ vā sevati, parasampattiṃ [M 0.0055] vā abhijjhāyati, parabhaṇḍaṃ vā harati sabhāvatikkhenānussāhitena, tadā tatiyaṃ. Yadā samussāhitena, tadā catutthaṃ. Yadā pana kāmānaṃ vā asampattiṃ āgamma, aññesaṃ vā somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvena catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitatā hoti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni uppajjantīti ayaṃ sampayogato vinicchayo.

Herein, in the case of a desirable object, it should be understood that the mind is accompanied by joy due to causes such as being dominated by greed, and is associated with wrong view due to causes such as listening to false teachings or having unwholesome friends. For when someone, influenced by wrong view such as "There is no danger in sensual pleasures," enjoys sensual pleasures with delight and excitement, or regards seen omens and other such superstitions as essential with a naturally keen and unprompted mind, then the first unwholesome consciousness arises. When it is with a sluggish and prompted mind, then the second arises. When, without being influenced by wrong view but merely out of delight and excitement, one engages in sexual intercourse, covets others' fortune, or steals others' belongings with a naturally keen and unprompted mind, then the third arises. When it is prompted, then the fourth arises. But when, due to the non-attainment of sensual pleasures or the absence of other causes of joy, joy is absent in all four variations, then the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity. This is the analysis in terms of association.

Dhammuddesato pana paṭhamākusale tāva niyatā pāḷiyaṃ sarūpenāgatā soḷasa, yevāpanakavasena cattāroti vīsati dhammā honti. Kathaṃ? Phasso vedanā saññā cetanā cittaṃ vitakko vicāro pīti vīriyaṃ ekaggatā jīvitaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ lobho moho micchādiṭṭhīti ime sarūpenāgatā soḷasa dhammā, chando adhimokkho manasikāro uddhaccanti ime yevāpanakā cattāroti. Padabhājanīye pana pubbe vuttanayeneva “phassapañcakaṃ jhānaṅgapañcakaṃ vīriyasamādhimanosomanassajīvitavasena indriyāni pañca, micchādiṭṭhisaṅkappavāyāmasamādhivasena maggaṅgāni cattāri, vīriyasamādhiahirikānottappavasena balāni cattāri, lobho mohoti dve mūlāni, abhijjhā micchādiṭṭhīti dve kammapathāni, ahirikaṃ anottappanti [V 0.0042] lokanāsadukaṃ, samatho paggāho avikkhepo cāti evaṃ sarūpenāgatānaṃ dvattiṃsadhammānaṃ soḷasasu eva samavarodho, savibhattikāvibhattikabhedo ca kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusale vuttānusārato ñātabbo. Ayaṃ dhammuddesato vinicchayo.

In the enumeration of the Dhamma, first, in the first unwholesome consciousness, there are sixteen dhammas that appear explicitly in the Pāḷi, and four by way of incidental mention, making a total of twenty. How? Contact, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, initial application, sustained application, joy, energy, one-pointedness, life, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, greed, delusion, and wrong view—these are the sixteen dhammas that appear explicitly. Desire, resolution, attention, and restlessness—these are the four by way of incidental mention. In the word analysis, however, as previously explained: 'the pentad of contact, the pentad of jhāna factors, the five faculties by way of energy, concentration, mind, joy, and life, the four path factors by way of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration, the four powers by way of energy, concentration, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread, the two roots as greed and delusion, the two courses of action as covetousness and wrong view, the pair of shamelessness and lack of moral dread as the destroyers of the world, and tranquility, exertion, and non-distraction'—thus, the thirty-two dhammas that appear explicitly are included within just those sixteen, and the distinction between those with and without inflections should be understood according to the explanation given for the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. This is the analysis in terms of the enumeration of the Dhamma.

Lakkhaṇādivibhāgato pana na hirīyatīti ahiriko, ahirikassa bhāvo ahirikkaṃ, na ottappaṃ anottappaṃ. Tesu ahirikkaṃ kāyaduccaritādīhi ajigucchanalakkhaṇaṃ, alajjālakkhaṇaṃ vā, anottappaṃ teheva asārajjanalakkhaṇaṃ, anuttāsalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0056] vā, sesaṃ hiriottappānaṃ vuttappaṭipakkhavasena veditabbaṃ.

Regarding the classification by characteristics and so on: one is not ashamed, thus 'shameless' (ahiriko); the state of being shameless is 'shamelessness' (ahirikkaṃ); not fearing wrongdoing is 'lack of moral dread' (anottappaṃ). Among these, shamelessness has the characteristic of not being disgusted by bodily misconduct and so on, or the characteristic of lacking shame. Lack of moral dread has the characteristic of not shrinking back from those same things, or the characteristic of not being alarmed. The remainder should be understood by way of opposition to what was stated for shame and moral dread.

Lubbhati tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti lobho. So ārammaṇagahaṇalakkhaṇo makkaṭālepo viya, abhisaṅgaraso tattakapāle khittamaṃsapesi viya, apariccāgapaccupaṭṭhāno telañjanarāgo viya, saññojanīyadhammesu assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno. Taṇhānadibhāvena vaḍḍhamāno sīghasotā nadī viya mahāsamuddaṃ apāyameva gahetvā gacchatīti daṭṭhabbo.

One is greedy by means of it, or one is greedy oneself, or it is merely the state of greed; thus, it is greed. It has the characteristic of seizing an object, like monkey-lime. Its function is clinging, like a piece of meat thrown on a hot pan. It manifests as non-relinquishment, like a stain from lampblack. Its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that are fetters. It should be regarded as a swift-flowing river which, growing by way of the river of craving, carries one to the great ocean that is the plane of misery.

Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho. So cittassa andhakāralakkhaṇo, aññāṇalakkhaṇo vā, asampaṭivedharaso, ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaraso vā, asammāpaṭipattipaccupaṭṭhāno, andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāno, sabbākusalānaṃ mūlanti daṭṭhabbo.

One is deluded by means of it, or one is deluded oneself, or it is merely the state of delusion; thus, it is delusion. It has the characteristic of mental darkness, or the characteristic of ignorance. Its function is non-penetration, or its function is concealing the intrinsic nature of the object. It manifests as wrong practice, or it manifests as darkness. Its proximate cause is unwise attention. It should be seen as the root of all unwholesome states.

Micchā passanti tāya, sayaṃ vā micchā passati, micchādassanamattameva vā esāti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā ayoniso abhinivesalakkhaṇā, parāmāsarasā, micchābhinivesapaccupaṭṭhānā, ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā, paramaṃ vajjanti daṭṭhabbā.

One sees wrongly by means of it, or one sees wrongly oneself, or it is merely the state of wrong seeing; thus, it is wrong view. It has the characteristic of unwise adherence, the function of misapprehension, manifests as wrong adherence, and has the desire not to see the noble ones as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as the supreme fault.

Uddhatabhāvo uddhaccaṃ. Taṃ avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ, anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ, bhantatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, cittavikkhepoti daṭṭhabbo. Seso panettha suññatavārapariyosāno sabbopi vinicchayo kusalādhikāre vuttānusārato veditabbo. Kevalaṃ saṅgahavāre pāḷiyaṃ āgatavasena [V 0.0043] pañcindriyatā, caturaṅgamaggatā, catubbidhabalatā, dvehetutā, sabbattha akusalabhāvo ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Paṭhamākusalaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The state of agitation is restlessness. It has the characteristic of non-subsidence, the function of instability, manifests as bewilderment, and has unwise attention as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as mental distraction. The rest of the analysis here, ending with the section on voidness, should all be understood according to what was said in the section on the wholesome. Only in the section on inclusion, because of the way it appears in the Pāḷi, are the five faculties, the four-factored path, the four kinds of power, the two roots, and its universally unwholesome nature the distinctions—the rest is just the same. The first unwholesome state is concluded.

Yathā [M 0.0057] ca paṭhame, evaṃ dutiyepi sasaṅkhāratā, yevāpanakesu thinamiddhānaṃ sambhavo, niyatatā ca viseso. Tattha thinanatā thinaṃ, middhanatā middhaṃ, anussāhanasaṃsīdanatā, sattivighāto cāti attho. Tattha thinaṃ anussāhalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyavinodanarasaṃ, saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Middhaṃ akammaññatālakkhaṇaṃ, onahanarasaṃ, līnatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, ubhayampi aratitandivijambhikādīsu ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

Just as in the first, so too in the second—promptedness, the arising of sloth and torpor among the incidental factors, and fixedness are the distinctions. Here, the nature of sloth is sloth, the nature of torpor is torpor—the meaning is sinking due to lack of encouragement and the destruction of power. Here, sloth has the characteristic of lack of encouragement, the function of removing energy, and manifests as sinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unworkability, the function of obstructing, and manifests as languor or as sleepy drowsiness; both have unwise attention regarding discontent, laziness, yawning, etc., as their proximate cause. The second.

Tatiye sabbopi vinicchayo paṭhamākusale vuttanayova. Kevalaṃ diṭṭhiyā abhāvo, yevāpanakesu mānassa sambhavo, aniyatatā ca, saṅgahavāre tivaṅgikamaggatā ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Tattha maññatīti māno. So uṇṇatilakkhaṇo, sampaggaharaso, ketukamyatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno, ummādo viya daṭṭhabbo. Tatiyaṃ.

In the third, the entire analysis is as stated for the first unwholesome consciousness. The only distinctions are the absence of view, the arising of conceit among the incidental factors, and its unfixed nature. In the section on inclusion, the threefold path is also a distinction; the rest is just the same. Here, 'one conceives,' thus it is conceit. It has the characteristic of haughtiness, the function of self-exaltation, manifests as a desire for prominence, and has greed disassociated from view as its proximate cause. It should be regarded as being like madness. The third.

Yathā ca tatiye, evaṃ catutthepi. Thinamiddhañcettha sasaṅkhāratā ca adhikā, sesaṃ tādisameva. Catutthaṃ.

Just as in the third, so also in the fourth. Here, sloth and torpor and promptedness are additional; the rest is just the same. The fourth.

Pañcamachaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamesu somanassaṭṭhāne upekkhāsambhavo, pītiyā ca abhāvo, tato eva saṅgahavāre caturaṅgajjhānatā ca viseso, sesaṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthacittasadisameva.

In the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, equanimity arises in place of joy, and there is an absence of rapture. Therefore, in the section on inclusion, the state of having four jhāna factors is a distinction; the rest is all the same as the first, second, third, and fourth consciousnesses, respectively.

Lobhamūlā niṭṭhitā.

The Greed-Rooted States are Concluded.

Dosamūlavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Root of Aversion

Dosamūlā pana dvidhā domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ, tathā sasaṅkhāraṃ. Evaṃ sampayogato. Dhammuddesādito pana paṭhame tāva paṭhamākusale vuttesu pītilobhadiṭṭhiyo vajjetvā dosaṃ[V 0.0044], yevāpanakesu aniyatāni [M 0.0058] issāmacchariyakukkuccāni, somanassaṭṭhāne domanassañca pakkhipitvā ekavīsati dhammā honti. Yevāpanakā cettha satta. Tattha dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā dussati, dussanamattameva vā tanti doso. So caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo pahaṭāsīviso viya, visappanaraso visanipāto viya, attano nissayadahanaraso vā dāvaggi viya, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno laddhokāso viya sapatto, āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno, visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo. Issāyanā issā. Sā parasampattīnaṃ usūyanalakkhaṇā, tattheva anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, parasampattipadaṭṭhānā, saññojananti daṭṭhabbā. Maccherabhāvo macchariyaṃ. Taṃ laddhānaṃ vā labhitabbānaṃ vā attano sampattīnaṃ nigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ, tāsaññeva parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaakkhamanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kaṭukañcukatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, attasampattipadaṭṭhānaṃ, cetaso virūpabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ, tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ, dāsabyamiva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saṅgahavāre dukkhena saddhiṃ caturaṅgajjhānatā, domanassena pañcindriyatā, tivaṅgikamaggatā, dosamohavasena dvihetukatā ca veditabbā. Seso pana sabbo vinicchayo paṭhamākusale vuttasadiso eva. Yathā ca paṭhame, evaṃ dutiyepi, sasaṅkhāratā pana thinamiddhehi saddhiṃ navayevāpanakatā ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

Consciousness rooted in aversion is twofold: accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion, unprompted; and similarly, prompted. Thus, by way of association. However, from the enumeration of states, in the first type, by excluding joy, greed, and wrong view from those mentioned in the first unwholesome consciousness, and including aversion, the non-fixed particulars of envy, avarice, and worry, and substituting displeasure for pleasure, there are twenty-one states. Here, the particulars are seven. Among these, `dosa` (aversion) is that by which one is corrupted, or one corrupts oneself, or it is merely the state of corruption. It has the characteristic of ferocity, like a struck venomous snake; the function of spreading, like a dose of poison, or the function of burning its own support, like a forest fire; it manifests as malevolence, like an enemy who has found an opportunity; its proximate cause is a ground for vexation. It should be seen as being like putrid urine mixed with poison. `Issā` (envy) is the act of envying. It has the characteristic of jealousy towards others' success; its function is not delighting therein; and it manifests as turning away from it. Its proximate cause is others' prosperity. It should be regarded as a fetter. `Macchariya` (avarice) is the state of being avaricious. It has the characteristic of concealing one's own attainments, whether acquired or to be acquired; the function of being unable to bear sharing them with others; and it manifests as shrinking, or as a state of constriction. Its proximate cause is one's own prosperity. It should be seen as a disfigurement of the mind. `Kukkucca` (worry) is what is badly done (`kukata`), and its state is `kukkucca`. It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; the function of sorrowing over what was done and not done; and it manifests as remorse. Its proximate cause is what was done and not done. It should be regarded as a state of servitude. In the summary section, it should be understood that with painful feeling, it has four jhāna factors; with displeasure, five faculties; a three-factored path; and it is two-rooted by way of aversion and delusion. The rest of the analysis is exactly as stated for the first unwholesome consciousness. And just as in the first, so too in the second; the distinction, however, is its prompted nature and its having nine particulars along with sloth and torpor. The rest is the same.

Dosamūlā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on States Rooted in Aversion is Concluded.

Mohamūlavaṇṇanā

Exposition of States Rooted in Delusion

Mohamūlāpi dvidhā upekkhāsahagataṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ, tathā uddhaccasampayuttanti. Tattha paṭhame dhammuddesato tāva phassapañcakaṃ vitakko vicāro vīriyaṃ ekaggatā jīvitaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ moho vicikicchāti sarūpenāgatā cuddasa[M 0.0059], uddhaccaṃ manasikāroti yevāpanakā dve cāti soḷasa dhammā honti, ekaggatā cettha cittaṭṭhitimattā, indriyamaggabalabhāvaṃ na sampāpuṇāti. Tato eva saṅgahavāre samādhiṃ vajjetvā upekkhāya saddhiṃ cattāri indriyāni, dve [V 0.0045] maggaṅgāni, tīṇi balāni honti. Moho panettha ekova hetu. Seso panettha sabbo vinicchayo vuttanayo eva.

States rooted in delusion are also twofold: accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt; and similarly, associated with restlessness. Here, in the first case, from the enumeration of states, there are fourteen factors that have arisen in their own nature: the pentad beginning with contact, applied thought, sustained thought, energy, one-pointedness, life faculty, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, delusion, and doubt. And with restlessness and attention as the two particulars, there are sixteen states. Here, one-pointedness is merely the stability of mind and does not attain the status of a faculty, path factor, or power. Therefore, in the summary section, excluding concentration, there are four faculties, two path factors, and three powers, along with equanimity. Here, delusion alone is the root. The rest of the analysis here is according to the method previously explained.

Tattha vigatā cikicchā etissāti vicikicchā. Sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, kampanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā, anekaṃsabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā, paṭipattiantarāyakarāti daṭṭhabbā. Yathā ca vicikicchāsampayutte, evaṃ uddhaccasampayuttepi. Kevalaṃ vicikicchāya abhāvo, adhimokkhassa ca bhāvo, tato eva balavatarasamādhitā, teneva saṅgahavāre samādhinā saddhiṃ pañcindriyatā, tivaṅgikamaggatā, catubbalatā ca hoti. Uddhaccañcettha sarūpeneva niddiṭṭhaṃ, adhimokkhamanasikārā dve yevāpanakavasenāti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva. Imāni pana dve cittāni nānāvisaye, ekavisaye ca asaṇṭhahanato pavaṭṭanakāni. Uddhaccasahagataṃ hi laddhādhimokkhatāya laddhapatiṭṭhaṃ ekārammaṇeyeva patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhāya pavaṭṭati caturassamaṇi viya, itaraṃ nānārammaṇesu vaṭṭamaṇi viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uddhaccasahagatañca ṭhapetvā sesā ekādasa paṭisandhiṃ janentīti veditabbaṃ.

Here, `vicikicchā` (doubt) is so called because inquiry (`cikicchā`) is departed from it. It has the characteristic of uncertainty; the function of wavering; and manifests as indecisiveness or as a state of being non-committal. Its proximate cause is unwise attention. It should be seen as an obstacle to practice. And just as with consciousness associated with doubt, so too with consciousness associated with restlessness. The only difference is that in the latter, there is an absence of doubt and a presence of resolution, and therefore a stronger concentration. For this reason, in the summary section, along with concentration, it has five faculties, a three-factored path, and four powers. Here, restlessness is specified in its own nature, while resolution and attention are by way of being two particulars. This is the distinction; the rest is the same. These two types of consciousness, however, arise from not being firmly established on various objects and on a single object respectively. Indeed, consciousness accompanied by restlessness, having gained resolution and stability, proceeds by repeatedly establishing itself on a single object, like a square gem. The other, however, should be seen as revolving among various objects, like a round gem. It should be understood that, except for consciousness accompanied by restlessness, the remaining eleven generate rebirth-linking.

Visayādippabhedato panete dvādasapi vatthārammaṇavasena tāva chabbidhā honti. Tesu lobhamohamūlā pana dasa pañcadvāre hadayavatthuṃ nissāyeva, manodvāre nissāya vā anissāya vā javanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā chabbidhā. Tathā dosamūlā nissāyeva pana pavattanti. Lobhamūlā pana [M 0.0060] adinnādānakāmamicchācāramusāvādapesuññasamphappalāpābhijjhāsaṅkhātānaṃ channaṃ kammapathānaṃ vasena chabbidhā. Diṭṭhisampayuttā panettha micchādiṭṭhivasenāpīti sattavidhā honti. Dosamūlā pana pāṇābhipātādinnādānamusāvādapesuññapharusasamphappalāpabyāpādavasena sattavidhā honti. Dasannampi panesaṃ dvārakammavasena ceva vīmaṃsāvajjitādhipatittayavasena ca kusale vuttanayena vibhāgo veditabbo. Ekantahīnattā hīnattikabhedo natthi. Ārammaṇādhipati panettha lobhamūlesu eva, na itaresu, mohamūlesu pana sahajātādhipatipi natthi, tathā kammapathabhedopi. Na hi pavaṭṭamānaṃ kañci adhipatiṃ karoti. Doso vā savisayaṃ, vicikicchācittañca paṭipattimantarāyakarattena duccaritahetubhūtampi pāṇātipātādīnaṃ dosalobhamūlacitteheva sanniṭṭhāpaniyato kammapathabhedaṃ na gacchati, pubbabhāge eva pana hetu hoti. Tenevassa apāyahetutā paṭhamamaggavajjhatāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atītādibhedato pana dvādasannaṃ paccekamanantatā, seso ca vinicchayo kusalādhikāre vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

However, regarding the classification by object and so on, these twelve types are first sixfold by way of base and object. Among these, the ten rooted in greed and delusion are sixfold, as they perform the function of impulsion at the five sense-doors dependent solely on the heart-base, and at the mind-door either dependent or not dependent on it. Similarly, those rooted in aversion arise dependent solely on it. However, those rooted in greed are sixfold by way of the six courses of action: taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, frivolous chatter, and covetousness. Here, those associated with wrong view are also sevenfold by way of wrong view. Those rooted in aversion are sevenfold by way of killing living beings, taking what is not given, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, and ill-will. For all ten of these, the classification by way of door and action, and by way of the threefold predominance excluding investigation, should be understood in the same way as explained for the wholesome states. There is no division into three grades due to their entirely base nature. Here, predominance based on the object applies only to those rooted in greed, not to the others. In those rooted in delusion, there is no predominance by co-nascence, nor is there a division by course of action, for it does not make any presently occurring thing predominant. Aversion is with its object, and the consciousness of doubt—though being a cause of misconduct by obstructing practice—does not fall into the classification of courses of action, since actions like killing are definitively established only by consciousness rooted in aversion or greed; however, it is a cause in the preliminary stage. Therefore, it should be seen that its being a cause for the lower realms is abandoned by the first path. However, regarding the classification by past, etc., the twelve are each individually infinite, and the remaining analysis should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the wholesome states.

Akusalā dhammā niṭṭhitā.

The Section on Unwholesome States is Concluded.

Abyākatapadattho

The Meaning of the Term 'Indeterminate'

Ahetukakusalavipākavaṇṇanā

Exposition of Rootless Wholesome Resultants

Abyākatā [V 0.0046] pana dhammā jātito catubbidhā vipākakiriyarūpanibbānavasena. Tattha vipākābyākatā dhammā jātito ca dvidhā honti kusalākusalavipākavasena. Tattha kusalavipākā bhūmito catubbidhā kāmarūpārūpāvacaralokuttaravipākavasena. Tattha kāmāvacaravipākā ahetukā sahetukāti duvidhā. Tattha alobhādisahajātahetuvirahitā ahetukā. Te sampayogavatthārammaṇādibhedato [M 0.0061] aṭṭhavidhā. Seyyathidaṃ – upekkhāsahagataṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tathā sotaghānajivhāviññāṇaṃ, sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagatā manodhātu, somanassasahagatā manoviññāṇadhātu, tathā upekkhāsahagatā cāti. Cakkhuviññāṇādīni hi cattāri cakkhupasādādīsu catūsu upādāyarūpesu upādāyarūpānaṃ ghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa picupiṇḍe picupiṇḍassevātidubbalatāya upekkhāvedanāsampayuttāneva honti. Kāyaviññāṇaṃ pana kāyindriye phoṭṭhabbabhūtattayaghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa adhikaraṇimatthake ṭhapitapicupiṇḍe kūṭapahārasseva balavatāya pasādanissayesupi bhūtesu paṭighātasambhavato sukhasahagataṃ hoti, manodhātu attano gahaṇadubbalatāya atiiṭṭhepi upekkhāsahagatāva, manoviññāṇadhātu pana atiiṭṭhe somanassasahagatā, iṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāsahagatāti ayaṃ sampayogato vinicchayo.

Indeterminate states, however, are fourfold by nature: as resultants, as functional, as material form, and as Nibbāna. Among these, indeterminate states that are resultants are twofold by nature: as wholesome resultants and unwholesome resultants. Among these, wholesome resultants are fourfold by plane: as sense-sphere resultants, form-sphere resultants, formless-sphere resultants, and supramundane resultants. Among these, sense-sphere resultants are twofold: unrooted and rooted. Among them, those devoid of concomitant roots such as non-greed are unrooted. They are eightfold by way of their association, basis, object, and so on. Namely: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity; similarly, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure; mind-element accompanied by equanimity; mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy; and similarly, that accompanied by equanimity. For the four kinds of consciousness—eye-consciousness and so on—arise in the four sensitive material phenomena (eye-sensitivity, etc.), which are derivative materiality. Due to the extreme weakness of the impact and friction of these derivative material phenomena, like that of a cotton ball upon a cotton ball, they are associated only with the feeling of equanimity. Body-consciousness, however, arises in the body faculty with the impact and friction of the three tangible primary elements. Because of the strength of this impact, like a hammer blow on a cotton ball placed on an anvil, and because resistance can occur in the primary elements that support the sensitivity, it is accompanied by pleasure. The mind-element, due to the weakness of its own apprehension, remains accompanied by equanimity even when the object is extremely desirable. The mind-consciousness element, however, is accompanied by joy when the object is extremely desirable and by equanimity when the object is moderately desirable. This is the analysis by way of association.

Dhammuddesādito pana cakkhuviññāṇe tāva phassapañcakaṃ, ekaggatā, jīvitanti sarūpenāgatā satta, yevāpanakavasena manasikāro eko cāti aṭṭha dhammā honti. Saṅgahato panettha khandhāyatanadhātuāhārindriyavasena pañcevasaṅgahā. Tattha cakkhuviññāṇadhātudhammadhātuvasena dhātusaṅgaho, mano upekkhājīvitindriyavasena indriyasaṅgaho ca veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ettha ca vijjamānāpi vedanā jhānaṅgataṃ na gacchati, indriyaṃ pana hoti. Ekaggatā indriyamaggaṅgabalabhāvampi na gacchati atidubbalattā. Vitakkapacchimakaṃ hi jhānaṃ, hetupacchimako maggo, balañca. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇesupi. Kevalaṃ pana saṅgahavāre sotaviññāṇadhātuādivasena dhātusaṅgaho, kāyaviññāṇe vedanāparivattanañca viseso. Yathā [M 0.0062] cettha, evaṃ manodhātuyāpi. Kevalaṃ pana vitakkavicārā dve yevāpanakā ca adhimokkhoti tayo dhammā adhikā. Saṅgahavāre manodhātudhammadhātuvasena dhātusaṅgaho, vitakkavicārupekkhekaggatāhi catūhi jhānaṅgasaṅgaho ca viseso. Pāḷiyaṃ panettha kiñcāpi jhānaṅgasaṅgaho [V 0.0047] na uddhaṭo, tathāpi savitakkesu niyamena jhānaṅgatāsambhavato gahetabbova. Yathā cettha, evaṃ manoviññāṇadhātudvayepi. Somanassasahagatatāya panettha pīti adhikā, saṅgahavāre ca pañcaṅgajjhānatā, vedanāparivattanaṃ, ubhayatthāpi manoviññāṇadhātudhammadhātuvasena dhātusaṅgaho ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

Regarding the exposition of phenomena, in eye-consciousness there are seven factors that arise by their own nature: the contact pentad, one-pointedness, and the life faculty. And attention, as an additionally included factor, is an eighth. Thus, there are eight phenomena. From the standpoint of inclusion, there are five modes of inclusion here: by way of aggregates, sense bases, elements, nutriments, and faculties. Here, the inclusion by way of elements is to be understood through the eye-consciousness element and the mind-object element, and the inclusion by way of faculties is to be understood through the mind, equanimity, and life faculties. The rest is as stated. Although feeling is present here, it does not qualify as a jhāna factor, but it is a faculty. One-pointedness, being too weak, does not qualify as a faculty, path factor, or power. For the minimum requirement for jhāna is initial thought, for the path it is a root, and similarly for a power. The same applies to ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. However, in the inclusion section, the inclusion by element is through the ear-consciousness element, etc., and in body-consciousness, the change in feeling is a distinction. Similarly, this applies to the mind-element. However, here there are three additional factors: initial thought and sustained thought, which are additionally included, and decision. In the inclusion section, the inclusion by element is through the mind-element and the mind-object element, while the inclusion by jhāna factor is through four factors—initial thought, sustained thought, equanimity, and one-pointedness—this is the distinction. Although the Pāli text does not explicitly state the inclusion of jhāna factors here, they should still be included, since jhāna factors are necessarily present in states accompanied by initial thought. The same applies to the two mind-consciousness elements. Here, due to being accompanied by joy, zest is an additional factor. In the inclusion section, the distinctions are the inclusion of the five jhāna factors, the change in feeling, and in both cases, the inclusion by element through the mind-consciousness element and the mind-object element. The rest is the same.

Visayādippabhedato pana cakkhuviññāṇādīni pañca yathākkamaṃ cakkhādiekekameva vatthuṃ nissāya paccuppanne, iṭṭhe ca rūpādiekekārammaṇe eva kiriyamanodhātuanantaraṃ ālokākāsavāyujalapathavīsahakārīni pasādakādīni dassanasavanaghāyanasāyanaphusanakiccāni sādhayamānāni cakkhudvārādīsu ekekasmiṃ eva vipaccanti. Evametesaṃ vatthudvārārammaṇakiccāni visuṃ niyatāni. Ṭhānaṃ pana tesaṃ pañcannampi ekameva, tena nesaṃ na bhedo. Manodhātu pana hadayavatthuṃ nissāyeva paccuppannesu rūpādīsu pañcasupi ārammaṇesu pañcaviññāṇānantaraṃ sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pañcasupi dvāresu pavattati, somanassasahagatā manoviññāṇadhātu pana hadayavatthuṃ nissāyeva atiiṭṭhe paccuppanne pañcārammaṇe vipākamanodhātuanantaraṃ santīraṇakiccaṃ, chasupi dvāresu chasu balavakāmāvacarārammaṇesu atītādīsu javanānantaraṃ tadārammaṇakiccañca sādhayamānā vipaccati. Evametissā dvārārammaṇakiccaṭṭhānāni anibaddhāni, tato tehi bhedo hoti, vatthu pana tattheva nibaddhaṃ, tato na bhedo, evamupekkhāsahagatāyapi. Kevalaṃ [M 0.0063] panesā dvāravinimuttāpi hutvā sugatiyaṃ jaccandhabadhirajaccummattakādīnaṃ paṭisandhikāle purimacuticittānantaraṃ kammabalenopaṭṭhitaṃ kammakammanimittagatinimittesu aññataraṃ atītādibhedaṃ chabbidhampi kāmāvacarārammaṇamārabbha paṭisandhikiccaṃ, tadanantarato paṭṭhāya yāvatāyukaṃ bhavaṅgakiccaṃ, ante cutikiccañca, vuttanayena santīraṇatadārammaṇakiccāni ca sādhayamānā imesu pañcasu ṭhānesu vipaccatīti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

By way of the division of objects and so forth, the five kinds of consciousness—eye-consciousness, etc.—each depending on a single basis (eye, etc.), arise in relation to a single, present, and desirable object (such as form, etc.). Following the functional mind-element, with the assistance of light, space, air, water, and earth, and the sensitive material phenomena, they accomplish the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, arising as resultants exclusively at their respective doors (eye-door, etc.). Thus, their basis, door, object, and function are distinctly determined. However, their location is the same for all five, hence there is no distinction in that regard. The mind-element, depending solely on the heart-base, performs the function of receiving immediately after the five sense-consciousnesses, operating at all five doors with respect to the five present objects (forms, etc.). The mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy, depending solely on the heart-base, arises as a resultant performing the function of investigating immediately after the resultant mind-element with respect to five present objects that are very desirable; and, following the impulsions, it performs the function of registration with respect to the six strong sense-sphere objects (which may be past, etc.), at all six doors. Thus, its door, object, function, and location are not fixed, hence it differs from the others in that regard. However, its basis remains fixed there, so there is no distinction in that respect. The same applies when it is accompanied by equanimity. Moreover, this consciousness, even when freed from doors, arises in the fortunate realms at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born blind, deaf, or insane, etc. It takes as its object one of the six kinds of sense-sphere objects (which may be past, etc.), such as kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign, presented by the force of kamma immediately after the death-consciousness of the previous life. From that moment onward, it performs the function of life-continuum throughout life and, at the end, the function of death. It also performs the functions of investigating and registering in the manner described. Thus it arises as a resultant in these five functional occasions. This is the distinction; the rest is the same.

Ettha ca vadhabandhādivasappavatte aniṭṭhārammaṇe khantipaṭisaṅkhānādivasena kusaluppattito tannibbattānaṃ paṭisandhiādiviññāṇānaṃ kammanimittañce ārammaṇaṃ hoti, aniṭṭheneva tena bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ iṭṭhavisaye uppannānaṃ kusalavipākānaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇesu anuppattito kammagatinimittameva tesaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti viññāyati. Vicāretvā yathā avirodho hoti, tathā gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ iṭṭhavisaye uppannakusalato nibbattānampi paṭisandhiādiviññāṇānaṃ kammanimittārammaṇatāya [V 0.0048] avirodho ñātabbo. Atītādibhedato pana aṭṭhannampi paccekamanantaratā heṭṭhā vuttanayena gahetabbā.

Here, when an unpleasant object arises in connection with execution, imprisonment, and so forth, due to the arising of wholesome states such as patience and reflection, if the kamma-sign becomes the object of the rebirth-linking consciousness and other resultant consciousnesses produced by that kamma, it must be an unpleasant object. Thus, it is understood that for wholesome resultants, since they do not arise in relation to unpleasant objects, their object can only be kamma or the destiny-sign. One should investigate this so that there is no contradiction. In this way, it should be understood that for rebirth-linking consciousness and other resultant consciousnesses produced by wholesome kamma that arose in relation to a desirable object, there is no contradiction in their taking a kamma-sign as object. Furthermore, for each of the eight consciousnesses, their relation to objects classified as past, etc., should be understood according to the method stated previously.

Ahetukakusalavipākā niṭṭhitā.

The unrooted wholesome resultants are concluded.

Sahetukakusalavipākavaṇṇanā

The Description of Rooted Wholesome Resultants

Alobhādivipākahetusampayuttā pana sahetukā, te sampayogato kāmāvacarakusalā viya aṭṭhavidhā. Somanassañāṇādisampayogo panettha āgamanādito veditabbo. Tihetukaṃ hi kāmāvacarakusalaṃ tihetukadvihetukapaṭisandhiyo datvā pavatte chasu dvāresu soḷasa vipākāni deti, duhetukaṃ pana kusalaṃ duhetukāhetukapaṭisandhiyo datvā pavatte chasu dvāresu tihetukarahitāni [M 0.0064] dvādasa vipākāni deti. Asaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikabhāvo panettha paccayavisesatopi hoti. Balavapaccayenāpi hi uppannaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ hoti, dubbalenāpi itaraṃ. Keci pana asaṅkhārikena sasaṅkhāravipākānaṃ, sasaṅkhārikena ca asaṅkhārikānaṃ uppattiṃ na icchanti. Yasmā panetāni paṭisandhidāyakato aññenāpi kammena pavatte akusalavipākāni pavattanti, paṭṭhāne ca “sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.1.102) vuttaṃ, tasmā ahetukapaṭisandhikassa puggalassa sugatiyaṃ pavatte sahetukānipi vipākāni pavattanti. Duggatiyaṃ, pana rūpāvacarabhūmiyañca ahetukāneva pavattanti. Tesupi atiiṭṭhe ārammaṇe somanassasahagatāni, iṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāsahagatānīti evaṃ āgamanādito sampayogabhedo veditabbo.

However, those associated with resultant roots such as non-greed are rooted; in terms of their association, they are eightfold, like the sense-sphere wholesome states. Here, their association with joy, knowledge, and so forth should be understood from the exposition. For a triple-rooted sense-sphere wholesome kamma, having given rise to triple-rooted and double-rooted rebirth-linking, produces sixteen resultants at the six doors during the course of existence. A double-rooted wholesome kamma, however, having given rise to double-rooted and rootless rebirth-linking, produces twelve resultants at the six doors during the course of existence, excluding the triple-rooted ones. Here, the distinction between uninstigated and instigated also arises from the difference in conditions. For what arises due to a strong condition is uninstigated, while the other arises due to a weak condition. Some, however, do not accept the arising of instigated resultants from uninstigated kamma, or uninstigated resultants from instigated kamma. But since these resultants also arise in the course of existence through kamma other than that which gives rebirth-linking, and since in the Paṭṭhāna it is said, “A rooted life-continuum is a condition for a rootless life-continuum by way of proximity condition” (Paṭṭhāna 3.1.102), therefore, for a person with rootless rebirth-linking, rooted resultants also arise in the course of existence in a happy destiny. In an unhappy destiny, however, and in the form-sphere plane, only rootless resultants arise. Even among these, when the object is extremely desirable, they are accompanied by joy; when it is moderately desirable, they are accompanied by equanimity. Thus, the distinctions of association should be understood from the exposition.

Dhammuddesādito pana yāva suññatavārapariyosānā kāmāvacarakusalasadisova sabbo vinicchayo, kevalañcettha yevāpanakesu karuṇāmuditā na santi sattārammaṇattā. Ekantaparittārammaṇā hi kāmāvacaravipākā. Viratiyopettha lokiyesu ekantakusalasabhāvattā na santi. “Pañcasikkhāpadā kusalā evā”ti (vibha. 715 ādayo) hi vuttaṃ. Phassādayo cettha [V 0.0049] vipākattā ādāse mukhanimittaṃ viya nirussāhasantā, kusalā pana mukhaṃ viya saussāhā. Saṅgahavāre ca pañcaṅgiko maggo hoti, ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

However, from the enumeration of states up to the conclusion of the section on emptiness, all the analysis is similar to that for sense-sphere wholesome states. The only difference here is that among the indefinite mental factors, compassion and appreciative joy are absent because they have beings as their object. For sense-sphere resultants have exclusively sense-sphere objects. The abstinences, too, are not found here among mundane states, because they are exclusively of a wholesome nature. For it is said, “The five training rules are wholesome only…” (Vibhaṅga 715 ff.). Here, contact and the other mental factors, being resultants, are without initiative, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, whereas the wholesome states are with initiative, like the face itself. And in the section on inclusion, the path has five factors—this is the distinction. The rest is just the same.

Visayādippabhedato pana yvāyaṃ kusalesu kammadvārapuññakiriyādhipatīhi bhedo vutto, so idha natthi aviññattijanakato, avipākadhammato, tathā appavattito ca. Hīnattikabhedo pana atthi hīnamajjhimappaṇītānaṃ kusalānaṃ vipākattā[M 0.0065], tathā dvārārammaṇādibhedo. Ete hi hadayavatthuṃ nissāya dvāravinimuttā hutvā devamanussesu dvihetukatihetukānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccāni, chadvāre chasu ārammaṇesu tadārammaṇakiccañca sādhayamānā evaṃ catūsu ṭhānesu vipaccanti. Evametesaṃ dvārārammaṇakiccaṭṭhānāni anibaddhāni, tato tehi bhedo hoti. Vatthu pana tattheva nibaddhaṃ, tato na bhedo. Atītādibhedato panetthāpi anantatā vuttanayā evāti.

However, regarding the distinctions by way of object and so forth, the division mentioned in the case of wholesome states by kamma-doors, meritorious deeds, and dominances is not present here. This is because resultants do not generate intimation, are not result-producing phenomena, and likewise do not initiate action. But the threefold distinction of inferior, middling, and superior does exist, due to their being the resultants of inferior, middling, and superior wholesome kamma, as do distinctions based on doors, objects, and so forth. For these resultants, relying on the heart-base and being independent of the doors, perform the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death for devas and humans with two or three roots, in the manner previously explained; and they accomplish the function of registration at the six doors with the six kinds of objects. Thus, they mature on four occasions. In this way, their doors, objects, functions, and occasions are not fixed, hence there is a division based on them. But the physical base is fixed in that respect, so there is no division based on it. As for the distinctions based on past and so forth, here too their endlessness is in accordance with the method previously explained.

Kāmāvacarasahetukakusalavipākā niṭṭhitā.

The Rooted Wholesome Resultants of the Sense-Sphere are concluded.

Rūpāvacaravipākavaṇṇanā

The Description of Form-Sphere Resultants

Rūpāvacaravipākāpi sampayogabhedato attano kusalā viya pañcavidhā honti. Sabbo cettha vinicchayabhedo kusale vuttanayo eva. Vipākabhāvato panettha yathā hatthiādīnaṃ chāyā taṃsadisā, evaṃ kusalāgamanato ca jhānaṅgādisampayuttadhammasamāyogo, paṭipadādibhedo ca hoti. Apicettha tividhāya paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyā paṭhamajjhānavipākā, tathā dutiyajjhānabhūmiyā dutiyajjhānavipākā tatiyajjhānavipākā ca, tatiyajjhānabhūmiyā catutthajjhānavipākā, vehapphalapañcasuddhāvāsavasena chabbidhāya catutthajjhānabhūmiyā pañcamajjhānavipākā ca vuttanayena paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccāni sādhayamānā hadayavatthuṃ nissāya dvāravinimuttāva kammanimittasaṅkhātapaññattārammaṇā hutvā vipaccantīti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

The form-sphere resultants, too, are fivefold due to differences in association, like their corresponding wholesome states. Here, all distinctions in analysis follow the method explained for the wholesome states. However, due to their resultant nature, just as the shadow of an elephant and so forth resembles its source, so too the combination of factors like jhāna constituents and associated states, and the distinctions based on the path and so forth, arise in accordance with the wholesome kamma that produced them. Moreover, here, in the three planes of the first jhāna, the first jhāna resultants arise; similarly, in the plane of the second jhāna, the second jhāna resultants and the third jhāna resultants arise; in the plane of the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna resultants arise; and in the sixfold fourth jhāna plane—namely, the Vehapphala and the five Pure Abodes—the fifth jhāna resultants arise. Performing the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, they depend on the heart-base, are independent of the doors, and take as their object the concept known as the kamma-sign. They mature accordingly—this is the distinction; the rest is just the same.

Rūpāvacaravipākā niṭṭhitā.

The Form-Sphere Resultants are concluded.

Arūpāvacaravipākavaṇṇanā

Description of Immaterial-Sphere Resultant States

Evaṃ [V 0.0050] arūpāvacaravipākāpi ārammaṇabhedato attano kusalā viya catubbidhā honti. Vinicchayo ca sabbo kusale [M 0.0066] vuttanayova. Kusalato cettha viseso rūpāvacaravipāke vuttanayena veditabbo.
