Kevalaṃ panettha kammanimittabhūtapaññattārammaṇo ākāsānañcāyatanavipāko paṭhamāruppabhūmiyaṃ, tathā mahaggatārammaṇo viññāṇañcāyatanavipāko dutiyāruppabhūmiyaṃ, kammanimittabhūtapaññattārammaṇo ākiñcaññāyatanavipāko tatiyāruppabhūkhiyaṃ, mahaggatārammaṇo nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavipāko catutthāruppabhūmiyañca avatthukā vuttanayena paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccāni sādhayamānāva pavattantīti ayameva viseso.

Similarly, the immaterial-sphere resultant states, too, are fourfold according to the difference in their objects, just like their corresponding wholesome states. The analysis here is entirely the same as explained for the wholesome states. The difference here, in relation to the wholesome, is to be understood in the manner described for the form-sphere resultant states. Merely, here, the resultant consciousness of the sphere of infinite space, which has as its object a concept that is a kamma-sign, arises in the first immaterial plane; likewise, the resultant consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness, which has a sublime object, arises in the second immaterial plane; the resultant consciousness of the sphere of nothingness, which has as its object a concept that is a kamma-sign, arises in the third immaterial plane; and the resultant consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which has a sublime object, arises in the fourth immaterial plane. These, being without a physical basis, function in the manner described, accomplishing the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death—this is the only difference.

Arūpāvacaravipākā niṭṭhitā.

The Immaterial-Sphere Resultant States are concluded.

Lokuttaravipākavaṇṇanā

Description of Supramundane Resultant States

Tathā lokuttaravipākāpi attano kusalā viya taṃtaṃmaggaphalattā catubbidhā, jhānaṅgayogabhedato paccekaṃ pañca pañca katvā vīsatividhāva honti. Vinicchayo cettha kusale vuttanayova. Kevalaṃ saṅgahavāre sotāpattimaggaphalaṃ sakadāgāmimaggaphalaṃ anāgāmimaggaphalanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ aññindriyaṃ, arahattaphalassa ca aññātāvindriyaṃ paññindriyaṭṭhāne gahetvā aṭṭhindriyatā, bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgādibodhipakkhiyadhammā, paṭipadādibhedo ca maggāgamanavaseneva hotīti veditabbo. Adhipatibhedopettha labbhati. Lokuttarakusalā hi attano phalānaṃ anantaruppattito, javanavuttito ca adhipatiṃ vidhātuṃ sakkonti, lokiyā pana viparītato na sakkonti. Tenāhu porāṇā “vipāke adhipatī natthi ṭhapetvā lokuttara”nti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 505). Vimokkhabhedato panete maggāgamanato tividhā honti suññataanimittaappaṇihitavimokkhavasena. Maggā hi vipassanāgamanato “suññato appaṇihito”ti dve nāmāni labhitvā saguṇārammaṇato pariyāyena [M 0.0067] animittātipi vuccanti, tasmā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano attano anantaraphalānaṃ nippariyāyato tīṇipi nāmāni denti. Aparabhāge pana phalasamāpattibhūtānaṃ na denti. Tattha vipassanāgamanatova magge vuttanayena [V 0.0051] duvidho nāmalābho veditabbo. Te ca na maggā viya ekacittakkhaṇikā, maggavīthiyaṃ pana dvattikkhattuṃ, phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ sakalampi divasaṃ appanājavanavaseneva nirantaraṃ mahaggatajavanāni viya pavattantīti ayaṃ viseso.

So too, the supramundane resultant states, like their wholesome counterparts, are fourfold by being the fruits of their respective paths, and when divided according to the jhāna factors, they become twentyfold, each being fivefold. The analysis here is the same as stated for the wholesome states. Only in the section on grouping, the faculty of knowing the unknown (aññindriya) is taken for the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning, while the faculty of the one who knows (aññātāvindriya) is taken for the fruit of arahantship, thereby counting as eight faculties in place of the faculty of wisdom. The enlightenment factors, path factors, and other qualities conducive to enlightenment, as well as the divisions by way of practice, should be understood to occur only by way of the path's arising. Here, the distinction of predominance is also found. For the supramundane wholesome states, being the immediate condition for their resultant fruits and functioning as impulsion, can establish predominance. But mundane states, being the opposite, cannot. Therefore, the ancients said: 'There is no predominance in resultants, except for the supramundane' (Dhs.A. 505). Furthermore, these are threefold by way of the approach to liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and desirelessness. For the paths, being approached through insight, obtain two names—'emptiness' and 'desirelessness'—and are conventionally called 'signless' because their objects are endowed with qualities. Thus, while standing in their own approachable state, they directly give all three names to their immediately following fruits. But in later stages, they do not give these names to the fruits that constitute the attainment of fruition. Here, the twofold acquisition of names should be understood in the manner stated for the path, which is solely from the approach through insight. And these (fruits), unlike the paths, are not of a single mind-moment's duration; in the path process, they occur two or three times, and in the fruition attainment process, they continue uninterrupted throughout the entire day by way of absorption-impulsion, like the sublime impulsion states. This is the distinction.

Lokuttaravipākā niṭṭhitā.

Supramundane Resultant States Concluded.

Akusalavipākā pana kāmāvacarāva, lobhādisampayuttahetu abhāvato ahetukā eva ca honti. Te sampayogato upekkhāsahagataṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tathā sotaghānajivhāviññāṇāni, tathā dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, upekkhāsahagatā manodhātu, tathā manoviññāṇadhātūti sattavidhā. Vinicchayo panesa sabbattha tādisāhetukakusalavipākesu vuttanayo eva. Kevalaṃ panāniṭṭhārammaṇatā, kāyaviññāṇassa dukkhasahagatatā, upekkhāsahagatamanoviññāṇadhātuyā uddhaccavajjitākusalapaccayā catūsu apāyesu paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutikiccāni, sugatiyañca santīraṇatadārammaṇakiccāni ca sādhanavasena pavatti ca viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

The unwholesome resultant states, however, are solely of the sense-sphere. Since they lack roots associated with greed and so forth, they are rootless. These are sevenfold by association: eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity; similarly ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness accompanied by pain; the mind-element accompanied by equanimity; and the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity. The analysis here follows the same method as stated for the corresponding rootless wholesome resultant states. Only the following are distinctions: the object being undesirable; body-consciousness being accompanied by pain; for the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is conditioned by unwholesome states other than restlessness, there are the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in the four woeful planes, and in happy destinies the functions of investigating and registering, as well as its occurrence by way of accomplishing these functions. The rest is the same.

Akusalavipākā niṭṭhitā.

Unwholesome Resultant States Concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca vipākābyākatā.

The Resultant-Indeterminate States are Concluded.

Ahetukakiriyāvaṇṇanā

Description of Rootless Functional States

Kiriyābyākatā pana kāmarūpārūpāvacaravasena tividhā. Tattha kāmāvacarakiriyā ahetukā sahetukāti duvidhā. Tattha sahajātahetuvirahitā ahetukā. Tā [M 0.0068] sampayogādito tividhā upekkhāsahagatā manodhātu, somanassasahagatā manoviññāṇadhātu, tathā upekkhāsahagatāti. Kiriyāti karaṇamattaṃ, kiccamattanti attho. Sabbesuyeva hi kiriyacittesu yaṃ āvajjanakiccadvayaṃ, taṃ ajavanavuttito moghapupphaṃ viya. Yaṃ javanavuttikaṃ, taṃ nirānusayasantānappavattito chinnamūlarukkhapupphaṃ viya aphalaṃ hoti. Taṃtaṃāvajjanajavanakiccasādhanavasena pavattattā pana kiccamattataṃ upādāya “kiriyā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha manodhātuyā vipākamanodhātuyaṃ vuttanayena [V 0.0052] sabbo vinicchayo veditabbo. Kevalaṃ pana pañcadvāre iṭṭhesu vā aniṭṭhesu vā pañcārammaṇesu pañcapasāde ghaṭṭitesu uppannabhavaṅgupacchedānantaraṃ tameva pañcārammaṇamārabbha hadayavatthuṃ nissāyevāvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pañcasupi dvāresu pavattatīti ayaṃ viseso.

The functional indeterminate states, however, are threefold according to the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere. Among these, the sense-sphere functional states are twofold: rootless and with roots. Here, those devoid of co-existent roots are rootless. These are threefold by association: the mind-element accompanied by equanimity, the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy, and similarly one accompanied by equanimity. 'Functional' means mere activity, mere function. For in all functional consciousnesses, the two functions of adverting are like barren flowers because they are not of the nature of impulsion. What is of the nature of impulsion is fruitless, like flowers on a tree with severed roots, due to its occurring in a continuity free from latent tendencies. But because they occur performing their respective functions of adverting and impulsion, they are called 'functional' in the sense of mere function. Here, the entire analysis of the mind-element should be understood in the same way as stated for the resultant mind-element. Only this distinction applies: in the five sense-doors, when desirable or undesirable fivefold objects strike the five sense faculties, after the life-continuum is interrupted, then, relying solely on the heart-base and taking that same fivefold object as its object, it performs the adverting function in all five doors.

Manoviññāṇadhātudvayampi yathākkamaṃ kusalavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayasadisaṃ, vīriyaṃ panettha adhikaṃ, vīriyūpatthambhova samādhi balavā hoti. Tato evettha saṅgahavāre vīriyasamādhimanosomanassajīvitindriyānaṃ pañcannaṃ vasena indriyasaṅgaho hoti, idhāpi balasaṅgaho nattheva. Yaṃ panettha padabhājanīye samādhivīriyānaṃ niddese “samādhibalaṃ vīriyabala”nti (dha. sa. 570-572) balavevacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ itarāhetukacittasampayuttehi imesaṃ balavataratādassanatthaṃ pariyāyato vuttaṃ. Tato eva hi saṅgahavāre “dve balāni hontī”ti na vuttaṃ, tasmā ahetukesu nippariyāyato balaṃ natthi evāti gahetabbaṃ.

The two mind-consciousness elements, in their order, are similar to the two rootless wholesome resultant mind-consciousness elements. However, effort is an additional factor here; concentration, being supported by effort, is strong. Therefore, in the section on grouping, the grouping of faculties occurs by way of five: effort, concentration, mind, joy, and vitality. Here too, the grouping of powers is not present. Moreover, in the analysis of terms, in the exposition of concentration and effort, the expressions 'power of concentration' and 'power of effort' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 570-572) are stated as synonyms for power by way of implication, to show their greater strength compared to factors associated with other rootless consciousnesses. Precisely for that reason, in the section on grouping, it is not stated 'there are two powers.' Therefore, it should be understood that in rootless states, there is certainly no power in the direct sense.

Visayādippabhedato panettha somanassasahagatā tāva hadayavatthuññeva nissāya pañcadvāre voṭṭhabbanakiccāya ca, manodvāre anuḷāresu chasu kāmāvacarārammaṇesu āvajjanakiccāya [M 0.0069] ca manoviññāṇadhātuyā anantaraṃ javanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā khīṇāsavānaññeva hasitaṃ uppādentī pavattati. Hasitaṃ hi somanassasahagatakāmāvacareheva javanehi, tesu asekhānaṃ pañcahi kiriyājavanehi, sekhānaṃ pana kusalehi ceva diṭṭhivippayuttalobhamūlehi cāti chahi, puthujjanānaṃ diṭṭhisampayuttehi cāti aṭṭhahīti terasahi cittehi uppajjati. Upekkhāsahagatā pana pañcadvāre hadayavatthuññeva nissāya santīraṇakiccāya vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuyā anantaraṃ voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ, manodvāre sabbesu chasupi ārammaṇesu savatthukā, avatthukā vā bhavaṅgacalanānantaraṃ āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pavattati. Ayaṃ hi tīsu bhavesu kassaci sacittakapuggalassa na kismiñci visaye na uppajjati, sabbaññutaññāṇasadisaṃ mahāgamanaṃ nāmetaṃ cittanti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ tādisameva.

Regarding the classification by objects and so on, first, the joy-accompanied consciousness, relying only on the heart-base, arises accomplishing the function of impulsion and producing laughter only for Arahants. For laughter arises from the joy-accompanied impulsion consciousnesses of the sense-sphere; it arises from thirteen types of consciousness: for non-trainees, from five functional impulsions; for trainees, from six (wholesome and greed-rooted states dissociated from wrong view); and for ordinary worldlings, from eight (the previous six plus two greed-rooted states associated with wrong view). The equanimity-accompanied consciousness, however, relying only on the heart-base, performs the function of determining at the five doors, immediately after the resultant mind-consciousness-element that performs the function of investigating. At the mind door, it performs the function of adverting toward all six objects, whether with a basis or without, immediately after the life-continuum vibrates. Indeed, for any individual possessing consciousness in the three planes, there is no object whatsoever in which this consciousness does not arise; this consciousness is called 'the great going,' similar to the knowledge of omniscience. This is the distinction; the rest is the same.

Ahetukakiriyā niṭṭhitā.

Rootless Functional States Concluded.

Sahetukakāmāvacarakiriyāvaṇṇanā

Description of Root-Accompanied Sense-Sphere Functional Consciousness

Alobhādikiriyāhetusampayuttā [V 0.0053] pana sahetukā, te sampayogato kusalā viya aṭṭhavidhā. Sabbopettha vinicchayo kusalesu vuttanayo eva. Kevalaṃ panettha viratiyo na santi, kusalā ca sekhaputhujjanānaṃ vuttanayena chasu dvāresu vatthuṃ nissāya vā anissāya vā javanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pavattanti, ime pana asekhānanti ayaṃ viseso. Kāmāvacarakiriyā.

Those associated with functional roots such as non-greed are with roots, and by way of association, they are eightfold, like the wholesome. Here, the entire analysis is just as the method stated for the wholesome. However, in this case, the abstinences are not present. And the wholesome states of trainees and ordinary people, by the method stated, arise in the six doors, relying on a basis or not relying on a basis, performing the function of impulsion. But these functional consciousnesses belong to the non-trainees—this is the distinction. Sense-sphere functional consciousness.

Rūpāvacarakiriyāvaṇṇanā

Description of Form-Sphere Functional Consciousness

Rūpāvacarakiriyā ca kusalā viya pañcavidhā. Vinicchayo ca tattha vuttanayo eva. Kevalaṃ hi kusalā sekhaputhujjanānaṃ paññattārammaṇā[M 0.0070], abhiññāvasena pavattaṃ pañcamajjhānaṃ sabbārammaṇañca hutvā manodvāre hadayavatthuññeva nissāya javanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā pavattanti, ime pana asekhānanti ayameva viseso. Rūpāvacarakiriyā.

Form-sphere functional consciousness is also fivefold, like the wholesome. And the analysis there is just as stated. However, the wholesome states of trainees and ordinary people have a concept as their object, and the fifth jhāna, occurring by way of direct knowledge and having all objects, performs the function of impulsion by relying solely on the heart-base at the mind-door. But these functional consciousnesses belong to the non-trainees—this alone is the distinction. Form-sphere functional consciousness.

Arūpāvacarakiriyāvaṇṇanā

The Description of Immaterial-Sphere Functional Consciousness

Arūpāvacarakiriyā ca kusalā viya catubbidhā. Vinicchayo ca tattha vuttanayo eva. Kevalaṃ hi kusalā sekhaputhujjanānaṃ savatthukā, avatthukā vā heṭṭhā vuttanayena yathāyogaṃ paññattimahaggatārammaṇā manodvāre javanakiccaṃ sāyemānā pavattanti, ime pana asekhānanti ayaṃ viseso. Arūpāvacarakiriyā.

Immaterial-sphere functional consciousness is also fourfold, like the wholesome. And the analysis there is just as stated. However, the wholesome states of trainees and ordinary people are with a basis or without a basis, as appropriate, by the method stated below, having conceptual or sublime objects, performing the function of impulsion at the mind-door. But these functional consciousnesses belong to the non-trainees—this is the distinction. Immaterial-sphere functional consciousness.

Kiriyābyākatā niṭṭhitā.

Functional Indeterminate States Concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Miscellaneous Discussion

Ettha [V 0.0054] ṭhatvā sabbe cittacetasikadhamme jātisaṅgahādito samodhānetvā pakiṇṇakakathā vattabbā. Yathāvuttāni hi cittāni kusalāni ekavīsati, akusalāni dvādasa, vipākāni chattiṃsa, kiriyāni vīsati cāti sabbānipi ekūnanavutividhāni, lokuttarānaṃ jhānaṅgayogabhedato cattālīsavidhattā ekavīsasataṃ vā honti. Tesu kāmāvacarāni catupaññāsa, rūpāvacarāni pannarasa, arūpāvacarāni dvādasa, lokuttarāni aṭṭha, cattālīsaṃ vā. Kāmāvacaresu ca kusalāni aṭṭha, vipākāni tevīsati, kiriyāni ekādasa, ahetukāni aṭṭhārasa. Sesāni pana catubhūmakānipi sahetukāni. Tesu ca jātito cittagaṇanā pubbe vuttāva[M 0.0071]. Cetasikā pana saddhā sati hirīottappaṃ alobho adoso kāyapassaddhādayo dvādasa, tatramajjhattatā amoho appamaññādvayaṃ, viratittayañca moho ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ uddhaccañca lobho diṭṭhi doso vicikicchā ca māno issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccaṃ thinaṃ middhañca phasso vedanā saññā cetanā ekaggatā jīvitindriyañca manasikāro ca vitakko vicāro pīti vīriyaṃ chando adhimokkho cāti dvepaññāsa honti.

Here, having established all consciousnesses and mental factors, the miscellaneous discussion should be presented by grouping them according to their class of origin and so forth. As previously stated, the wholesome consciousnesses are twenty-one, the unwholesome twelve, the resultant thirty-six, and the functional twenty—thus all together eighty-nine types. Or, when the supramundane are counted as forty by way of the combination of jhāna factors, they become one hundred and twenty-one. Among these, the sense-sphere consciousnesses are fifty-four, the form-sphere fifteen, the immaterial-sphere twelve, and the supramundane eight, or forty. In the sense-sphere, the wholesome are eight, the resultant twenty-three, the functional eleven, and the rootless eighteen. The remaining states, even those of the four planes, are with roots. Among them, the counting of consciousnesses by class of origin has been stated before. As for the mental factors, there are fifty-two: faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, the twelve beginning with tranquility of the mental body, equanimity, non-delusion, the two illimitables, and the three abstinences; delusion, shamelessness, recklessness, restlessness, greed, wrong view, hatred, doubt, conceit, envy, miserliness, worry, sloth, torpor; contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life faculty, attention, initial application, sustained application, joy, energy, desire, and determination.

Tattha tatramajjhattatā, appamaññādvayaṃ, mānādīni cha, manasikāro chando adhimokkho cāti dvādasa dhammā yathāṭhāne yevāpanakā eva, viratittayaṃ, uddhaccañca katthaci yevāpanakā. Tesu ca tatramajjhattatā manasikāro chando adhimokkho uddhaccaṃ viratiyoti ime ṭhapetvā sesā aṭṭha yathāṭhāne aniyatā eva, viratiyo pana katthaci aniyatā, ime pana ekādasa ṭhapetvā sesā ekacattālīsa dhammā niyatā eva. Tattha saddhādayo pañcavīsati dhammā kusalābyākatāyeva, mohādayo cuddasa akusalā eva, phassādayo terasa kusalākusalābyākatā tijātikā. Ekantato hi kusalā vā abyākatā vā dhammā natthi, kusalacittasampayuttasamaye pana kusalā, abyākatacittasampayuttasamaye abyākatā ca honti. Mohādayo pana sarūpeneva akusalā, itare ca taṃsampayogena sabbepi cete atthanā sampayuttacittabhedena bhedavantova hontīti veditabbā.

Here, equanimity, the two illimitables, the six beginning with conceit, attention, desire, and determination—these twelve states are invariably applicable in their respective places. The three abstinences and restlessness are applicable only in certain places. And among these, excluding equanimity, attention, desire, determination, restlessness, and the abstinences, the remaining eight are variable in their respective places. However, the abstinences are variable only in some places. Excluding these eleven, the remaining forty-one states are invariably fixed. Here, the twenty-five states beginning with faith are exclusively wholesome or indeterminate. The fourteen beginning with delusion are exclusively unwholesome. The thirteen beginning with contact are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. For among these, there are no states that are exclusively wholesome or exclusively indeterminate; however, when associated with a wholesome consciousness, they are wholesome, and when associated with an indeterminate consciousness, they are indeterminate. But the states beginning with delusion are, by their very nature, unwholesome. And all the others, through association with those, become different according to the difference in the consciousness with which they are associated. Thus it should be understood.

Tesu hi saddhādayo ekūnavīsati sabbesu kusalesu ceva sahetukābyākatesu cāti ekūnasaṭṭhicittesu uppajjanti, tato paccekaṃ ekūnasaṭṭhippabhedā ca honti. Evamaññepi ñātabbā[V 0.0055]. Amoho tesu ñāṇavippayuttāni dvādasa [M 0.0072] ṭhapetvā sesesu, appamaññā pana kāmāvacaresu sahetukakiriyakusalesu ceva pañcamajjhānavajjitarūpāvacaresu cāti aṭṭhavīsaticittesu, viratiyo pana kāmāvacarakusalesu, lokuttaresu cāti soḷasasu. Evamete pañcavīsati dhammā kusalābyākatesu uppajjanato kusalābyākatā nāma jātā. Akusalesu pana mohādayo cattāro dvādasasupi akusalacittesu uppajjanti, lobho aṭṭhasu lobhamūlesu, diṭṭhi tattha diṭṭhisampayuttesu, māno diṭṭhivippayuttesu, doso issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccaṃ paṭighasampayuttesu, thinamiddhaṃ pañcasu sasaṅkhārikesu, vicikicchā vicikicchāsampayutte evāti. Evamete cuddasapi sayaṃ akusalattā, akusalesveva uppajjanato ca akusalā nāma.

Indeed, among these, the nineteen mental factors beginning with faith arise in fifty-nine types of consciousness—namely, in all wholesome states and rooted indeterminate states—and thus each becomes of fifty-nine kinds. The rest should be understood in the same way. Non-delusion is present in the remaining states, except in the twelve types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge. The illimitables, however, arise in twenty-eight types of consciousness—namely, in rooted wholesome and functional states in the sense sphere, and in those of the form sphere except for the fifth jhāna. The abstinences arise in sixteen types of consciousness—namely, in wholesome states in the sense sphere and in supramundane states. Thus, these twenty-five mental factors, because they arise in wholesome and indeterminate states, are called 'wholesome and indeterminate.' In unwholesome states, delusion and the other three arise in all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. Greed arises in the eight types of greed-rooted consciousness; wrong view in those associated with wrong view; conceit in those dissociated from wrong view; hatred, envy, miserliness, and worry in those associated with aversion; sloth and torpor in the five prompted types; and doubt in the type associated with doubt. Thus, these fourteen mental factors are unwholesome by nature, and because they arise exclusively in unwholesome states, they are called 'unwholesome.'

Itaresu ca phassādayo satta dhammā sabbacittesu, na hi taṃ cittamatthi, yaṃ imesu ekenāpi vinā uppajjati. Sabbatthakā hi ete. Vitakkādayo pana yathāyogikā. Tesu hi vitakko tāva dvipañcaviññāṇavajjitakāmāvacaresu ceva ekādasasu paṭhamajjhānikarūpāvacaralokuttaresu cāti pañcapaññāsacittesu uppajjati. Vicāro pana tesu ceva tathā dutiyajjhānikacittesu cāti chasaṭṭhicittesu. Pīti catutthajjhānikavajjitasomanassasahagatesu. Vīriyaṃ dvipañcaviññāṇamanodhātusantīraṇattikavajjitesu. Chando ahetukamomūhavajjitesu. Adhimokkho dvipañcaviññāṇavicikicchāyuttavajjitesu. Evamete terasa kusalākusalābyākatesu uppajjanato tijātikā nāma jātā. Sampayuttacittabhedena cesaṃ paccekaṃ gaṇanābhedopi veditabbo. Yathā hi cittaṃ salakkhaṇato ekavidhampi sampayogāvatthādibhedeneva bhinnaṃ, tathā cetasikāpi paccekanti ñātabbā, visesaṃ pana nesaṃ vakkhāma.

Among the others, the seven mental factors beginning with contact are present in all consciousnesses, for there is no consciousness that arises without at least one of these. They are indeed universals. But the factors beginning with initial application are present according to their suitability. Among these, initial application arises in fifty-five types of consciousness: namely, in the sense-sphere consciousnesses (excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness) and in the eleven types of first-jhāna consciousness pertaining to the form-sphere and the supramundane. Sustained application arises in sixty-six types of consciousness: in those same fifty-five, as well as in the eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses. Joy arises in the consciousnesses accompanied by pleasant feeling, excluding those of the fourth jhāna. Energy arises in all consciousnesses except the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the mind-element, and the three types of investigating consciousness. Desire arises in all consciousnesses except the rootless and the delusion-rooted. Determination arises in all consciousnesses except the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and that associated with doubt. Thus, these thirteen factors are called 'of triple origin' because they arise in wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousnesses. Moreover, their individual enumeration should be understood according to the classification of associated consciousnesses. Just as consciousness, though one in its essential characteristic, is divided by differences in association, basis, and so on, so too should the mental factors be understood individually. However, we will explain their distinctions further.

Vatthusaṅgahe [M 0.0073] pana nesaṃ cittesu tāva kāmāvacaravipākamanodhātuhasitāni, dosasampayuttapaṭigharūpāvacarapaṭhamamaggāni cāti tecattālīsa cittāni heṭṭhā vuttanayena yathāsakaṃ vatthūni nissāyeva uppajjanti, arūpāvacaravipākāni pana anissāyeva, sesāni dvecattālīsa nissāyapi, āruppesupi uppajjanato anissāyapi. Arūpīnaṃ hi chapi vatthūni na santi, rūpīnaṃ pana ghānādīni tīṇi, sabbattha ca taṃtaṃvatthurahitānaṃ sabbattha niyataviññāṇānipi, asaññīnaṃ pana sabbānipi vatthuviññāṇāni na santi. Tesaṃ hi jīvitanavakameva rūpaṃ paṭisandhi, pavattiyaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ, maraṇakāle cuti ca hutvā pavattati. Yathā cettha cittānaṃ, evaṃ taṃsampayuttacetasikānampi vatthuto saṅgahabhedo veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tesu hi doso issā [V 0.0056] macchariyaṃ kukkuccañca hadayavatthuṃ nissāya kāmaloke eva uppajjati. Karuṇāmuditā pana rūpalokepi, na arūpe. Tattha hi rūpāvacarapubbabhāgānipi na uppajjanti, sesā pana sabbe nissāyapi anissāyapi tīsupi bhavesu uppajjanti. Tattha hi phassādayo satta chapi vatthūni, itare pana hadayamevāti, sesaṃ cittasamaṃ.

In the classification of bases, among these consciousnesses, first the sense-sphere resultant mind-element, the smiling consciousness, the consciousnesses associated with aversion, and the form-sphere first path consciousnesses—these forty-three consciousnesses arise dependent on their respective bases as previously stated. The immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses, however, arise independently. The remaining forty-two arise either dependently or independently, as they also arise in the immaterial-sphere. For immaterial beings, the six bases do not exist, while for form-beings, the three bases beginning with the nose are absent. And in all cases, for those lacking their respective bases, the corresponding consciousnesses also invariably do not arise. For the non-percipient beings, all consciousnesses related to bases are absent. For them, only the life-nonad of matter functions as rebirth-linking, as life-continuum during existence, and as decease at the time of death. Just as with the consciousnesses, so too should the classification of their associated mental factors be understood in terms of their bases. Here, however, there is a distinction: among them, hatred, envy, miserliness, and worry arise dependent on the heart-base only in the sense-sphere. Compassion and appreciative joy, however, arise in the form-sphere as well, but not in the immaterial-sphere. There, even the preparatory form-sphere consciousnesses do not arise. The rest arise in all three realms, either dependently or independently. Among them, the seven mental factors beginning with contact depend on all six bases, while the others depend solely on the heart-base. The rest is the same as with consciousness.

Kiccadvārasaṅgahe pana nesaṃ cittaṃ yathā ca cuddasahi kiccehi chadvārikadvāravinimuttabhāvena, evaṃ pavattikkamo veditabbo. Yadā hi kusalākusalabalena tīsu bhūmīsu sattā nibbattanti, tadā tesaṃ maraṇakāle yebhuyyena channaṃ dvārānamaññatarasmiṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ kammakammanimittagatinimittānamaññataraṃ gahetvā upekkhāsahagatavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayañceva aṭṭha mahāvipākāni, nava rūpārūpavipākāni ceti ekūnavīsati cittāni heṭṭhā vuttanayena yathāsakabhūmīsu paṭisandhi hutvā uppajjanti, tāneva bhavaṅgacutivasena dvāravinimuttāni nāma honti. Maraṇakāle hi [M 0.0074] sattānaṃ asaññisattavirahitānaṃ bhavantare paṭisandhijanakaṃ atītaṃ kammaṃ vā taṃkammakaraṇakāle visayopakaraṇādibhūtaṃ rūpādichabbidhampi atītādibhedaṃ kālavinimuttañca kammanimittaṃ vā upapajjamānabhavānurūpaṃ kapparukkhamātukucchinirayaggijālādigatinimittaṃ vā kammabalena yathārahaṃ channaṃ dvārānamaññatarasmiṃ sāyanhe pabbatacchāyā pathaviyaṃ viya cittasantāne allīyamānaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ upaṭṭhite ca tasmiṃ ārammaṇe kammabalena nirantaraṃ pavattamānacittasantānassa āyukkhayakammakkhayaubhayakkhayaupacchedakakammānamaññatarena paccāsannamaraṇassa tassa tassa vīthicittabhavaṅgānantaraṃ cuticittaṃ hoti, tadanantaraṃ kammakammanimittādīsu yathāgahitaṃ ārabbha yathārahaṃ tīsu bhavesu yaṃ kiñci paṭisandhicittaṃ bhavantare paṭhamacittaṃ hutvā uppajjati.

In the compendium of functions and doors, the process of occurrence of these consciousnesses should be understood according to the fourteen functions, and as occurring through the six doors or as being free from the doors. For when beings are born in the three realms through the force of wholesome or unwholesome kamma, at the time of their decease, an object—either kamma, a kamma-sign, or a destination-sign—usually presents itself at one of the six doors. Grasping one of these, the nineteen types of consciousness—namely, the two equanimity-accompanied resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements, the eight great resultants, and the nine form and formless resultants—arise as rebirth-linking in their respective realms, as previously explained. These same consciousnesses, when functioning as life-continuum and decease, are called 'door-freed.' At the time of decease, for beings other than the non-percipient, the past kamma that produces rebirth-linking in the next existence, or the sign of that kamma—which may be one of the six types of objects (such as form), classified as past, etc., and also timeless—or the sign of the destination, appropriate to the arising existence—such as a wish-fulfilling tree, a mother’s womb, or the flames of hell—appears at one of the six doors by the power of kamma, adhering to the stream of consciousness like the shadow of a mountain on the earth in the evening. When such an object has appeared, for one nearing decease due to the exhaustion of life-span, the exhaustion of kamma, the exhaustion of both, or an obstructive kamma, the decease-consciousness arises immediately after a cognitive process or the life-continuum. Following that, taking as its object what was grasped—whether kamma, kamma-sign, or destination-sign—a certain rebirth-linking consciousness arises as the first consciousness in the new existence, in one of the three realms as is appropriate.

Tattha ca duhetukāhetukacutiyānantaraṃ dasa kāmāvacarapaṭisandhiyova honti, na itarā, kāmāvacaratihetukāya cutiyā sabbāpi honti, rūpāvacarāya pana cutiyāpi ahetukapaṭisandhirahitā, arūpāvacarāya cutiyā heṭṭhimavajjitāruppapaṭisandhiyo ceva kāmāvacaratihetukapaṭisandhiyo ca, asaññīnaṃ pana rūpacutito bhavantare gahitapubbaṃ kammādimevārabbha ahetukarahitā kāmāvacarapaṭisandhiyova honti, na itarā. Puthujjanānaṃ, pana sotāpannasakadāgāmīnañca cutiyā suddhāvāsesu paṭisandhi na hoti, sekhānaṃ dvihetukāhetukāsaññipaṭisandhiyo, asekhānaṃ pana sabbāpi paṭisandhiyo na honti. Te hi cutito [V 0.0057] nirupadhisesanibbānena anupādāparinibbānappattā nāma honti. Evaṃ gahitapaṭisandhinirodhato paraṃ tadeva cittaṃ tasmiññevārammaṇe bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā cutipariyosānaṃ asati vīthicittuppāde supinampi adisvā niddokkamanakālādīsu [M 0.0075] aparimāṇasaṅkhampi nadīsotaṃ viya nirantaraṃ pavattati. Evaṃ ekūnavīsativiññāṇānaṃ paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattikkamo veditabbo.

Here, immediately after a two-rooted or rootless decease, there are only ten types of sense-sphere rebirth-linking, not others. After a three-rooted sense-sphere decease, all types are possible. After a form-sphere decease, however, rootless rebirth-linking is excluded. After a formless-sphere decease, rebirth-linking occurs only in the formless realms other than the lowest, and in the three-rooted sense-sphere. For the non-percipient beings, after decease in the form realm, in a future existence, only sense-sphere rebirth-linking excluding rootless occurs, based on previously performed kamma, not others. For ordinary persons, stream-enterers, and once-returners, rebirth-linking does not occur in the Pure Abodes. For trainees, two-rooted, rootless, and non-percipient rebirth-linkings are not possible. For non-trainees, however, no rebirth-linking occurs at all. They, upon decease, are said to attain the final Nibbāna without fuel for clinging, through the Nibbāna-element without residue. After the cessation of the rebirth-linking thus taken up, that same consciousness, becoming the life-continuum on that very object, continues up until the moment of decease. Without the arising of a cognitive process, even dreams are not seen. During times like entering deep sleep, it flows endlessly like a river, without interruption. Thus, the process of the nineteen kinds of consciousness should be understood in terms of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and decease.

Evaṃ pana vattamāne bhavaṅgasantāne yadā indriyaparipākamāgamma sabhāgapaccayantarasahitaṃ atimahantaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhudvāre ghaṭṭeti, tadā ghaṭṭanānubhāvena dvikkhattuṃ tattha bhavaṅgacalanaṃ hoti, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ vocchinditvā tasmiṃ rūpārammaṇe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tathā tadanantaraṃ cakkhuviññāṇadvaye yathārahamekaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tadanantaraṃ vipākamanodhātudvayā aññataraṃ sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ, tadanantaraṃ vipākamanoviññāṇadhātuttayā aññataraṃ santīraṇakiccaṃ, tadanantaraṃ upekkhāsahagatakiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ, tadanantaraṃ ekūnatiṃsakāmāvacarajavanesu yaṃ kiñci yathārahaṃ sattakkhattuṃ, chakkhattuṃ, maraṇakālādīsu pañcakkhattumeva vā javanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ, tadanantaraṃ ekādasasu tadārammaṇakiccesu mahāvipākasantīraṇesu yathārahamekaṃ sakiṃ, dvikkhattuṃ vā tadārammaṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgasantati eva pavattati. Evaṃ cakkhudvāre sattakiccāni chacattālīsa cittāni sambhavanti.

While the stream of the life-continuum is thus proceeding, when, upon the maturation of the faculties, a very distinct visible object, accompanied by a homogeneous proximate condition, impinges on the eye-door, then, due to the impact of impingement, the life-continuum vibrates twice. Immediately afterward, the life-continuum is interrupted, and the functional mind-element arises, performing the function of adverting to that visible object, and then ceases. Following that, one of the two eye-consciousnesses arises, performing the function of seeing, as is appropriate. Next, one of the two resultant mind-elements arises, performing the function of receiving. After that, one of the three resultant mind-consciousness-elements arises, performing the function of investigating. Then, the functional rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity arises, performing the function of determining. Following that, any one of the twenty-nine sense-sphere impulsion-consciousnesses arises, performing the function of impulsion seven times, six times, or—at the time of decease, etc.—only five times, as appropriate. Afterward, one of the eleven consciousnesses that perform the function of registering (the great resultants and investigating resultants) arises, performing its function once or twice, as is appropriate, and then ceases. Following that, the stream of the life-continuum resumes. Thus, in the eye-door, seven functions and forty-six types of consciousness can occur.

Yadā pana vuttanayena saddārammaṇādīni sotadvārādīsu ghaṭṭenti, tadāpi cakkhudvāre viya paccekañca chacattālīseva bhavanti. Kevalaṃ hettha āvajjanānantaraṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṭṭhāne sotaviññāṇādidvayāni yathākkamaṃ savanādikiccāni sādhayamānāni uppajjantīti. Evaṃ pañcadvāre atimahante pañcārammaṇe catupaññāsa kāmāvacaracittāneva sambhavanti. Keci panettha “sasaṅkhārikajavanāni pañcadvāre na uppajjanti pubbappayogāsambhavā, manodvāreyevetāni uppajjantī”ti vadanti.

When sounds and other objects impinge on the ear-door and so on in the manner described, then, just as with the eye-door, there are also forty-six types of consciousness for each door. Only here, after adverting, the two types of ear-consciousness and so on arise in place of eye-consciousness, performing their respective functions of hearing and so on in due order. Thus, in the five sense-doors, when the five sense-objects are very distinct, only fifty-four types of sense-sphere consciousness can arise. Some, however, say that prompted impulsion-consciousnesses do not arise in the five sense-doors due to the absence of prior application, and that they arise only in the mind-door.

Mahante [M 0.0076] pana tadārammaṇavajjitāni. Visayassa javanasamakālameva atītattā javanāvasāne bhavaṅgaṃ hoti. Paritte pana javanampi natthi. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ hettha javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā dvattikkhattuṃ pavattitvā nirujjhati, tato paraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ pana vāro “diṭṭhaṃ viya me[V 0.0058], sutaṃ viya me”tiādikathanakāle labbhati. Atiparitte pana voṭṭhabbanappādā asaṇṭhahanato bhavaṅgacalanamattameva, na āvajjanādīni. Āvajjanena hi bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite voṭṭhabbanaṃ appatvā antarā cakkhuviññāṇānantaraṃ cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otarissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, nāpi appavattamāne visaye pañcadvārikavīthicittāni pavattantīti. Ayaṃ pañcadvāre visayappavattibhedena cittappavattiniyamo.

But when the objects are great, the processes are devoid of registering consciousness. Since the object has passed by the time of impulsion, at the end of impulsion, the life-continuum occurs. But when the objects are faint, there is no impulsion. Here, determining takes the place of impulsion, occurring two or three times and then ceasing, after which the life-continuum occurs. This case is obtained at the time of making statements such as, “It is as if I saw, it is as if I heard.” But when the objects are very faint, due to the non-establishment of the arising of determining, there is merely a movement of the life-continuum; there is no adverting, etc. For when the life-continuum has been turned towards an object by adverting, it is not possible that the mind, without reaching determining, would descend into the life-continuum in the interval after eye-consciousness; nor do the five-door cognitive processes arise when the object is not occurring. This is the rule governing the arising of consciousness at the five sense-doors, according to the difference in the occurrence of objects.

Manodvāre pana chasu ārammaṇesu āpāthagatesu vuttanayena bhavaṅgacalanamanodvārāvajjanānantaraṃ kusalākusalaphalanāvajjanakiriyacittesu pañcapaññāsajavanakiccesu yaṃ kiñci kāmāvacarārammaṇamārabbha pavattati, tato pabhuti kāmāvacarārammaṇe tadārammaṇaṃ hoti. Appanājavane ayaṃ pavattikkamo – samathavipassanākammaṭṭhānikānaṃ hi yathāsakavisaye uppāditapubbabhāgabhāvanānaṃ “idāni appanā uppajjissatī”ti bhavaṅgacalanāvajjanāvasāne ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacarajavanesu aññatarasmiṃ yathārahaṃ parikammopacārānulomagotrabhunāmena catukkhattuṃ, tikkhattumeva vā uppajjitvā niruddhe catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā mahaggatajavanesu yaṃ kiñci paṭhamakappanābhiññābhūtaṃ ekavārameva, jhānasamāpattibhūtaṃ anantavārampi javati. Lokuttarajavanesu pana kusalāni ekasantāne ekavārameva javanti, tadanantaraṃ yathāsakaṃ phalacittañca dvattivāraṃ, phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ phalameva anantavārampi javati, nirodhasamāpattiyaṃ pana anupubbanirodhavasena [M 0.0077] paṭhamajjhānato yāvākiñcaññāyatanā yathākkamaṃ āvajjanaparikammādivaseneva samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhitassa gotrabhuto anantaraṃ catutthāruppajavane dvikkhattuṃ javitvā niruddhe yathāparicchinnakālañca cittaṃ na uppajjati, vuṭṭhānakāle ca āvajjanaparikammacittaniyāmena anāgāmiphalaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ vā yathārahamekavārameva uppajjati. Tattha ca kusalagotrabhuto anantaraṃ kusalañceva ādito phalattayañca appeti, kiriyāgotrabhuto kiriyaṃ, arahattaphalañca. Tatthāpi somanassasahagatato somanassasahagatameva, upekkhāsahagatato ca upekkhāsahagatameva appeti. Asekhānameva cettha arahattaphalakiriyājavanāni, yathāsakaṃ sekhānameva sesalokuttarāni, sekhaputhujjanānameva kusalākusalāni, tihetukānameva appanā honti, ayaṃ javananiyamo.

At the mind-door, however, when the six objects have come into range, in the manner stated, after the vibrating of the life-continuum and the mind-door adverting, whatever wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousness arises among the fifty-five types of impulsion, taking a sense-sphere object, from then on, with a sense-sphere object, registering consciousness occurs. The sequence of occurrence in absorption impulsion is as follows: For those who have undertaken serenity and insight meditation subjects, having previously cultivated the preliminary portion in their respective spheres, thinking, “Now absorption will arise,” after the vibrating of the life-continuum and adverting, in one of the knowledge-accompanied sense-sphere impulsions, according to suitability, four times—or only three times—named preparation, access, adaptation, and change-of-lineage, and after it has ceased, as the fourth or fifth moment, whatever first absorption or a supernormal knowledge-consciousness arises among the sublime impulsions, occurs once. That which is a jhāna attainment occurs an infinite number of times. In the supramundane impulsions, the wholesome ones occur once in a single continuity. Immediately after that, the respective fruition consciousness occurs two or three times. In the fruition attainment process, only the fruition occurs an infinite number of times. In the attainment of cessation, however, by successive cessation from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, for one who has emerged after entering in order, in the manner of adverting, preparation, etc., immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness, after the impulsion of the fourth immaterial sphere has arisen and ceased twice, consciousness does not arise for a period that has been defined. At the time of emerging, in accordance with the rule for adverting and preparation consciousness, the non-returner fruition or arahant fruition arises once according to suitability. And there, after a wholesome change-of-lineage, one attains the wholesome path and the first three fruitions; after a functional change-of-lineage, one attains the functional path and the Arahant fruition. There too, from a state accompanied by joy, one attains only that which is accompanied by joy; and from a state accompanied by equanimity, one attains only that which is accompanied by equanimity. Herein, the Arahantship fruition and functional impulsions are only for the non-trainees. The remaining supramundane ones are only for the trainees, each according to their level. The wholesome and unwholesome are for trainees and ordinary people. Absorptions are only for those with three roots. This is the rule of impulsion.

Appanājavanato paraṃ pana tadārammaṇaṃ natthi. Javanārammaṇesu hi kāmāvacarabhūtesveva kāmāvacarapaṭisandhikānameva atimahante, vibhūte ca visaye tadārammaṇamuppajjati. Atiiṭṭhe panārammaṇe [V 0.0059] santīraṇakiriyājavanatadārammaṇāni somanassasahagatāni, iṭṭhamajjhatte, aniṭṭhe ca upekkhāsahagatāni honti. Yadā pana domanassānantaraṃ somanassassa paṭṭhāne paṭikkhittattā somanassapaṭisandhikassa atiiṭṭhādīsu paṭighe javite tadārammaṇabhavaṅgāni na uppajjanti, tadā aññaṃ paricitapubbaṃ parittārammaṇamārabbha anāvajjanampi nirodhato vuṭṭhahantassa sāmaññaphalaṃ viya antarā upekkhāsahagatasantīraṇaṃ uppajjati, tamanantaritvā bhavaṅgaṃ hotīti ayaṃ tadārammaṇaniyamo.

After absorption impulsion, however, there is no registering consciousness. For registering consciousness arises only when the objects of impulsion are sense-sphere objects, and only for those whose rebirth-linking is in the sense-sphere, when the object is extremely great and clear. When the object is extremely desirable, the investigating, functional impulsion, and registering consciousnesses are accompanied by joy. With a moderately desirable or neutral object, and with an undesirable object, they are accompanied by equanimity. However, when, for one with a joyful rebirth-linking consciousness, repugnance has impelled regarding extremely desirable objects, etc., then because the basis for joy is rejected immediately after displeasure, registering consciousness and life-continuum do not arise. At that time, taking another previously familiar, limited object, an equanimous investigating consciousness arises in between, even without adverting—just as the fruition of recluseship arises for one emerging from cessation. Immediately following that, the life-continuum occurs. This is the rule regarding registering consciousness.

Evaṃ pana bhavaṅgānantaraṃ chadvāre āvajjanādīni vīthicittāni. Iti yāvatāyukaṃ imināva kamena cittaniyāmato viññāṇāni pavattanti. Vīthicittānantaraṃ, pana bhavaṅgānantaraṃ vā sabbapacchimaṃ [M 0.0078] taṃ ekūnavīsatividhaṃ bhavaṅgameva tasmiññevārammaṇe cutikiccañca sādhayamānaṃ pavattati, tasmiṃ niruddhe satto cuto nāma hoti. Tatopi cutito puna paṭisandhibhavaṅgavīthicutiyoti evaṃ punappunaṃ cittasantānaṃ yantayuttagoṇo viya bhavādīsu yāvānupādāya āsavehi na vimuccati, tāvāvicchinnaṃ pavattati eva. Evaṃ pavattamāne ca cittasantāne “tvaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ nāma hoti, tvaṃ tadanantaraṃ āvajjanaṃ…pe… tvaṃ tadanantaraṃ tadārammaṇaṃ nāma hoti, tvaṃ pana bhavaṅga”ntiādinā niyāmako kattā nāma natthi, cittaniyāmenevetaṃ pavattati.

Thus, after the life-continuum, process-consciousnesses, beginning with adverting, arise at the six doors. Thus, for as long as life lasts, consciousnesses occur in this very sequence, according to the order of consciousness. After process-consciousness, or after the life-continuum, that very last life-continuum, which is of nineteen types, occurs, performing the function of death on that very same object. When it ceases, the being is said to have died. From that death, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, process-consciousness, and death arise again and again. Just as an ox yoked to a machine, so too does the stream of consciousness flow on unbrokenly through the rounds of existence, etc., for as long as one is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. And while this stream of consciousness is thus occurring, there is no agent, no one who regulates, saying, “You are called life-continuum, you are the adverting that follows it… you are the registering that follows, and you are again the life-continuum.” Rather, it proceeds simply by the order of consciousness.

Pañcavidho hi niyāmo – bījaniyāmo utuniyāmo kammaniyāmo dhammaniyāmo cittaniyāmoti, tattha aṅkurapaṇṇadaṇḍapupphaphalādikkamena tesaṃ tesaṃ bījānaṃ aññoññavisadisarukkhatiṇagacchalatādisantāne attanā sadisaphaladānaṃ bījaniyāmo nāma. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye tesaṃ tesaṃ rukkhānaṃ ekappahārena pupphaphalapallavānaṃ gahaṇaṃ utuniyāmo nāma. Tassa tassa vā kusalākusalakammassa taṃtaṃsadisāsadisarūpārūpavipākadānaṃ, kammasarikkhakavipākadānañca kammaniyāmo nāma. Bodhisattānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇe, mātukucchito abhinikkhamane, abhisambodhidhammacakkappavattanādīsu ca dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni dhammaniyāmo nāma. Yathāvuttena bhavaṅgāvajjanādikiccakkameneva cittappavatti cittaniyāmo nāma. Iminā pana cittaniyāmena yathākkamaṃ kiccavantesu cetesu cittesu dvipañcaviññāṇamanodhātujavanāni yathāsambhavaṃ ekakiccaṭṭhānāni, sesāni pana dviticatupañcakiccaṭṭhānāni, tāni ca pubbe vuttāni, suviññeyyāni ca. Evaṃ ekadvārikādīni ca. Yathā ca cittānaṃ, evaṃ taṃsampayuttacetasikānampi [V 0.0060] kiccadvāravasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – kiccato hi sabbatthakā tāva satta cittaṃ viya cuddasa kiccāni karonti. Vitakkavicārādhimokkhā [M 0.0079] pana tayo dassanādipañcakiccāni vajjetvā nava, vīriyaṃ tato sampaṭicchanasantīraṇāni vajjetvā satta, pīti voṭṭhabbanāvajjanānipi vajjetvā santīraṇena saddhiṃ cha, viratiappamaññāvajjitā pana vīsati kusalābyākatā ceva chando ca santīraṇampi vajjetvā pañca, tato appamaññā tadārammaṇampi vajjetvā cattāri, viratiyo pana kusalā javanakiccameva karonti. Dvārato ca viratiyo manodvārikā eva, tathā karuṇāmuditā, dvāravinimuttā ca pana honti. Manodvāre eva hi duccaritaviramaṇaṃ sattapaññattiggahaṇañca hoti. Akusalā pana chadvārikā, tatthāpi mānaissāmacchariyakukkuccāni manodvārikānevāti keci. Avasesā chadvārikā ceva dvāravinimuttā ca. Sesaṃ cittasadisameva. Ārammaṇasaṅgaho pana nesaṃ parittārammaṇattike āvi bhavissatīti. Ayaṃ pakiṇṇakakathā.

There are five kinds of order—seed order, season order, kamma order, dhamma order, and mind order. Among these, the seed order is so called because it gives results similar to itself through the succession of sprouts, leaves, stems, flowers, fruits, etc., of various seeds, each producing trees, grass, shrubs, and creepers distinct from one another in their lineage. The season order is so called because it causes the simultaneous production of flowers, fruits, and shoots in those trees at certain times. The kamma order is so called because it gives results similar or dissimilar, in form or formless, to wholesome or unwholesome kamma, and because it produces results corresponding to kamma. The dhamma order is so called because of the appearance of the thirty-two portents at the rebirth-linking of Bodhisattas, their emergence from the mother’s womb, their supreme enlightenment, the turning of the Dhamma Wheel, and so forth. The mind order is so called because it is the occurrence of consciousness according to the sequence of functions such as life-continuum, adverting, etc., as previously described. By this mind order, among these consciousnesses performing their functions in sequence, the twofold five sense-consciousnesses, the mind-element, and the impulsions, as is possible, have a single function; the others have two, three, four, or five functions, as previously stated and as can be easily understood. Thus also for those with a single door, etc. Just as with consciousness, so too the associated mental factors should be classified according to their functions and doors. Here, however, is the distinction: in terms of function, the seven universals perform fourteen functions, just as consciousness does. But initial application, sustained application, and decision perform nine functions, excluding the five functions of seeing, etc. Energy performs seven functions, excluding from that receiving and investigating. Joy performs six functions, which include investigating but exclude determining and adverting. The twenty beautiful and indeterminate mental factors (excluding the abstinences and illimitables) and zeal, also excluding investigating, perform five functions. From that, the illimitables, also excluding registration, perform four functions. The abstinences, however, perform only the function of wholesome impulsion. In terms of doors, the abstinences are only mind-door factors, and so are compassion and appreciative joy, which are also door-free. For restraint from misconduct and the grasping of the concept of a being occur only in the mind-door. Unwholesome mental factors operate through the six doors, though some say that conceit, envy, miserliness, and worry occur only in the mind-door. The rest operate through the six doors and are also free from doors. The remainder is similar to consciousness. Their classification by object will become clear in the triad of limited objects. This is the miscellaneous discourse.

Cittuppādakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the arising of consciousness is completed.

Abyākatapadaṃ pana neva tāva niṭṭhitaṃ. Abyākatesu hi vipākābyākataṃ, kiriyābyākatañca vibhattaṃ, rūpābyākataṃ, pana nibbānābyākatañca avasiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha rūpābyākataṃ tāva bhūmito kāmāvacarameva, na bhinnaṃ, tathā sampayogatopi asambhavo eva. Sārammaṇadhammānameva, hi aññamaññasampayogo, na itaresanti. Dhammuddesato panetaṃ aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ – pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātu cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo rūpaṃ saddo gandho raso itthindriyaṃ purisindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ hadayavatthu kāyaviññatti vacīviññatti ākāso rūpassa lahutā mudutā kammaññatā rūpassa upacayo santati jaratā aniccatā kabaḷīkāro āhāroti. Padabhājanīye panettha kiñcāpi hadayavatthu na āgataṃ, upari pana paṭṭhānapāḷiyaṃ [M 0.0080] “yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca vattantī”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.8) sarūpeneva āgamissatīti taṃ idha gahitaṃ. Keci pana middharūpaṃ balarūpaṃ sambhavarūpaṃ jātirūpaṃ rogarūpanti imānipi pañca gahetvā “tettiṃsa rūpāni hontī”ti vadanti, te tesaṃ abhāvaṃ, antogadhabhāvañca vatvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Imesu hi middhaṃ rūpameva na hoti arūpadhammattā nīvaraṇānaṃ. Middheneva hi pacalāyikākārena rūpappavatti hoti, balarūpaṃ pana vāyodhātuyā antogadhaṃ taṃsabhāvattā, sambhavarūpaṃ āpodhātuyā, jātirūpaṃ [V 0.0061] upacayasantatīsu, rogarūpañca jaratāaniccatāsu pavisati sappaccayasamuṭṭhitarūpavikārabhedesu rogabyapadesatoti sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aṭṭhavīsatividhameva hoti. Ayaṃ dhammuddesato vinicchayo.

However, the indeterminate category is not yet fully concluded. Among the indeterminate, the resultant-indeterminate and the functional-indeterminate have been distinguished, but the material-indeterminate and the Nibbāna-indeterminate remain. First, the material-indeterminate is confined to the sense-sphere plane and is not further divided; similarly, association is impossible. For only phenomena with objects can associate with each other, not the others. In terms of the exposition of phenomena, it is of twenty-eight kinds, namely: the earth element, water element, fire element, air element, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odour, taste, femininity faculty, masculinity faculty, life faculty, heart-base, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, space, lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, growth of matter, continuity of matter, decay of matter, impermanence of matter, and physical nutriment. In the section on analysis of terms (Padabhājanīya), although the heart-base is not mentioned, it will be explicitly included later in the Paṭṭhāna text: "The material form on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element depend," etc. Therefore, it is included here. Some, however, taking these five—sloth-matter, strength-matter, origin-matter, birth-matter, and disease-matter—say, "There are thirty-three material phenomena." They should be refuted by stating their non-existence and their inclusion within other categories. For sloth is not a material phenomenon, being a non-material phenomenon among the hindrances. Sloth merely causes the occurrence of material form in a drowsy manner. Strength-matter is included within the air element due to its nature. Origin-matter is included within the water element. Birth-matter falls under growth and continuity. And disease-matter is classified under decay and impermanence, as 'disease' is a term for disturbances in conditionally arisen material phenomena. Thus, all material phenomena are only of twenty-eight kinds. This is the analysis in terms of the exposition of phenomena.

Lakkhaṇādito panettha kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu, patiṭṭhānarasā, sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātu, brūhanarasā, saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānā. Uṇhattalakkhaṇā tejodhātu, paripācanarasā, maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇā vāyodhātu, samudīraṇarasā, abhinīhārapaccupaṭṭhānā. Catassopi cetā sesabhūtattayapadaṭṭhānā. Rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā cakkhu, rūpesu āviñchanarasaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ pana yadetaṃ akkhikūpake patiṭṭhitaṃ nahārusuttakena matthaluṅgena ābaddhamaṃsayuttaṃ, yattha setampi atthi kaṇhampi lohitampi cattāripi mahābhūtāni, yañca semhussadattā setaṃ, pittussadattā kaṇhaṃ, ruhirussadattā lohitakaṃ, pathavussadattā patthiṇṇaṃ hoti, āpussadattā paggharati, tejussadattā [M 0.0081] paridayhati, vāyussadattā paribbhamati, yañca loke nīlapakhumasamākiṇṇaṃ kaṇhasukkamaṇḍalavicittaṃ nīluppaladalasannibhaṃ dīghaṃ puthulaṃ cakkhūti vuccati, tassa sasambhāracakkhuno setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe abhimukhe ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidese sattasu picupaṭalesu āsittatelaṃ picupaṭalāni viya satta akkhipaṭalāni byāpetvā dhāraṇanahāpanamaṇḍanabījanakiccāhi catūhi dhātīhi khattiyakumāro viya sandhāraṇābandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi catūhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ vaṇṇagandharasādīhi parivutaṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ pamāṇato ūkāsiramattaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā –

Here, in terms of characteristics and so forth: The earth element is characterized by hardness, its function is to provide a foundation, and its manifestation is receiving. The water element is characterized by flowing, its function is to promote growth, and its manifestation is cohesion. The fire element is characterized by heat, its function is maturing, and its manifestation is providing softness. The air element is characterized by distending, its function is impelling, and its manifestation is carrying forth. These four, moreover, have the remaining three elements as their proximate cause. The eye is characterized by sensitive material form capable of being impinged upon by visible objects, or it is characterized by sensitive material form arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to see. Its function is to grasp visible objects, its manifestation is serving as the basis for eye-consciousness, and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see. Moreover, this eye, which is established in the eye socket, bound by sinews to the brain, and composed of flesh—where white, black, red, and the four great elements exist; where the white part is due to an excess of phlegm, the black part due to an excess of bile, the red part due to an excess of blood, and the firmness due to the earth element; where it flows due to the water element, burns due to the fire element, and moves due to the air element—and which in the world is called the eye, being long and broad, surrounded by dark eyelashes, varied with black and white circles, resembling a blue lotus petal—this eye, surrounded by the white circle, with the black circle in the middle, stands facing outward in the place where the bodily formation arises. Just as oil spreads through seven layers of cotton, so too does it pervade the seven membranes of the eye. And just as a royal prince is sustained by four nurses performing the duties of holding, washing, adorning, and fanning, so too is the eye, aided by the four elements performing the duties of supporting, binding, maturing, and impelling, maintained by life, accompanied by color, scent, and taste, supported by climate, consciousness, and food. Measuring the size of a louse’s head, it stands accomplishing its appropriate role as the basis and door for eye-consciousness and so forth. This was also stated by the General of the Dhamma:

“Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpāni manupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumaṃ etaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpama”nti.

“By means of which sensitive eye-faculty, one perceives forms; this is limited and subtle, like a louse's head.”

Saddābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā sotaṃ, saddesu āviñchanarasaṃ, sotaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ[V 0.0062]. Idaṃ pana sasambhārasotabilassa anto tanutambalomācite aṅgulivedhakasaṇṭhāne padese vuttappakārāhi dhātuādīhi katūpakārānupālanaparivāropatthambhaṃ sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

The ear is characterized by sensitive material form capable of being impinged upon by sounds, or it is characterized by sensitive material form arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to hear. Its function is to grasp sounds, its manifestation is serving as the basis for ear-consciousness, and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to hear. This, however, within the ear-cavity with its constituents, in a place shaped like a finger-ring, covered with fine, copper-colored hairs, stands accomplishing its appropriate role as the basis and door for ear-consciousness and so forth, supported by the retinue of maintaining and helpful factors, such as the elements and others described in the aforesaid manner.

Gandhābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ, ghāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā ghānaṃ, gandhesu āviñchanarasaṃ, ghānaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ghāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0082]. Idañca sasambhāraghānabilassa anto ajapadasaṇṭhāne padese vuttappakāropakārānupālanaparivāropatthambhaṃ ghānaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

The nose is characterized by sensitive material form capable of being impinged upon by odours, or it is characterized by sensitive material form arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to smell. Its function is to grasp odours, its manifestation is serving as the basis for olfactory consciousness, and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to smell. This, moreover, within the nose-cavity with its constituents, in a place shaped like a goat's hoof, stands accomplishing its appropriate role as the basis and door for olfactory consciousness and so forth, supported by the retinue of maintaining and helpful factors of the kind described.

Rasābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā vā jivhā, rasesu āviñchanarasā, jivhāviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānā. Esā ca sasambhārajivhāmajjhassa upari uppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padese vuttappakāropakārānupālanaparivāropatthambhā jivhāviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānā tiṭṭhati.

The tongue is characterized by sensitive material form capable of being impinged upon by tastes, or it is characterized by sensitive material form arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to taste. Its function is to grasp tastes, its manifestation is serving as the basis for tongue-consciousness, and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to taste. This, moreover, above the middle of the tongue with its constituents, in a place resembling the tip of a lotus petal, stands accomplishing its appropriate role as the basis and door for tongue-consciousness and so forth, supported by the retinue of maintaining and helpful factors of the kind described.

Phoṭṭhabbābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo, phusitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo vā kāyo, phoṭṭhabbesu āviñchanaraso, kāyaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, phusitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhāno. Ayaṃ pana imasmiṃ kāye yāvatā upādinnā pathavīāpokoṭṭhāsā honti, tattha sabbattha kappāsapaṭale sneho viya anugato vuttappakāropakārānupālanaparivāropatthambho kāyaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamāno tiṭṭhati. Keci (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 600) pana “tejādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo cakkhu, vivaravāyuāpapathaviadhikānaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyā”ti vadanti. Apare (dha. sa. a. 600) “tejosabhāvaṃ cakkhu, ākāsapathaviāpavāyusabhāvā sotaghānajivhākāyā”ti vadanti. “Tejādisahakārittā, tejādiguṇarūpādivisayattā cā”ti kāraṇañca yathākkamaṃ vadanti. Te ca vattabbā – ko panevamāha “sahakārisabhāveheva indriyehi bhavitabba”nti, “rūpādayo vā tejādīnaṃ [M 0.0083] guṇā”ti. Avinibbhogesu hi bhūtesu “ayaṃ imassa guṇo, ayaṃ imassa guṇo”ti na labbhā vattunti. Athāpi vadeyyuṃ “tejādiadhikesu sambhāresu rūpādīnaṃ adhikabhāvadassanato [V 0.0063] icchitabbametaṃ ‘rūpādayo tejādīnaṃ guṇā’”ti, te vattabbā iccheyyāma, yadi āpādhikassa āsavassa gandhato pathaviadhike kappāse gandho adhikataro siyā, tejādhikassa ca uṇhodakassa vaṇṇatopi sītūdakassa vaṇṇo parihāyetha. Yasmā panetaṃ ubhayampi natthi, tasmā pahāyetha tametesaṃ nissayabhūtānaṃ visesakappanaṃ. Yathā avisesepi ekakalāpe bhūtānaṃ rūparasādayo aññamaññaṃ visadisā honti, evaṃ cakkhupasādādayopīti gahetabbametaṃ. Kiṃ panesaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ natthīti? No natthi. Kiṃ pana tanti? Kammameva nesaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ janakataṇhājanitānaṃ bhūtānaṃ visesato. Bhūtavisese hi sati pasādova nuppajjati. Samānānaṃ hi bhūtānaṃ pasādo, na visamānānanti porāṇā. Evaṃ kammavisesato visesavantesu cetesu cakkhusotāni asampattavisayaggāhakāni attano nissayaṃ anallīnanissayeva visaye viññāṇahetuttā. Ghānajivhākāyā pana sampattavisayaggāhakā nissayavasena ceva sayañca attano nissayaṃ allīne eva visaye viññāṇahetuttā.

The body is characterized by sensitive material form capable of being impinged upon by tangibles, or by sensitive material form arisen from kamma rooted in the desire to touch. Its function is to grasp tangibles, its manifestation is serving as the basis for body-consciousness, and its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch. Furthermore, this, in this body, wherever there are appropriated portions of the earth and water elements, stands pervading everywhere like oil in a cotton cloth, supported by the retinue of maintaining and helpful factors of the kind described, accomplishing its appropriate role as the basis and door for body-consciousness and so forth. Some (Dhs. A. 600) say: “The sensitive element of the elements predominated by fire is the eye; those predominated by space, wind, water, and earth are the ear, nose, tongue, and body.” Others (Dhs. A. 600) say: “The eye is of the nature of fire; the ear, nose, tongue, and body are of the nature of space, earth, water, and wind.” They also state the reason respectively: “Because of their cooperation with fire and other elements, and because visible forms and other objects are qualities of fire and the rest.” But they should be told: “Who says that the faculties must necessarily be of the nature of their cooperating elements? Or who says that visible forms and the rest are qualities of fire and the like?” For among inseparable elements, it is impossible to say, “This is the quality of this, and that is the quality of that.” Even if they were to argue, “Since visible forms and the like appear more prominently in materials predominated by fire and the rest, it should be accepted that visible forms and the like are qualities of fire and the rest,” they should be told: “We would accept this if the smell of an earth-predominated substance like cotton were greater than that of a water-predominated liquor, and if the color of cold water were to be less than the color of hot water, which is predominated by fire.” But since neither is the case, this assumption of a distinction among these supporting elements should be abandoned. Just as, even in a single undifferentiated group of elements, visible form, taste, and so on are dissimilar from one another, so too should eye-sensitivity and the rest be understood. Is there then no cause for their distinction? No, there is not none. What, then, is it? Kamma alone is their unique cause, due to the distinction of the elements produced by generative craving. For when there is an imbalance of the elements, sensitivity does not arise. The ancients say: “Sensitivity arises from balanced elements, not from imbalanced ones.” Thus, due to the distinction in kamma, among these distinct faculties, the eye and ear apprehend objects without contact, because they are a cause for consciousness regarding an object that is not clinging to their physical base. The nose, tongue, and body, however, apprehend objects by contact, because they are a cause for consciousness regarding an object that is clinging to their physical base, both by way of the base and by themselves.

Keci pana “cakkhusotānipi sampattavisayaggāhakāneva, dūre ṭhitesupi candarūpādīsu sīghayāyinayanaraṃsisaññogena, saddānañca paramparāyāgantvā sotabile ghaṭṭanena viññāṇuppattito. Teneva hi kuṭṭādiantaritesu, vicchiddapabbataleṇādigatesu ca rūpasaddesu viññāṇaṃ na [M 0.0084] uppajjatī”ti vadanti. Tesampi hi cakkhuno dūrāsannesu candarukkhādīsu anupalakkhitakālabhedena raṃsisamāyojanasāmatthiyaṃ, saddānampi dūrāsannānaṃ aviditatābhedaṃ āgantvā sotabilaghaṭṭanasāmatthiyaṃ viññāṇuppattihetubhūtaṃ upagantabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ tattheva ṭhitānaññeva viññāṇuppādanasāmatthiyopagamanaṃ. Kuṭṭaleṇādiantaritānañca rūpasaddānaṃ sahakāripaccayavirahato anāpāthagamanaṃ. Itarathā tesampi tādisesu indriyasaññogaṃ na dhāvitabbaṃ. Gamananivāraṇampi uppattinivāraṇameva, tatheva sahakāripaccayavirahato yādiseva tesaṃ indriyasaññogo hoti, tādise viññāṇuppatti hotīti gahetabbaṃ.

Some, however, argue that “the eye and ear also apprehend their objects only by contact, through the arising of consciousness via the connection of swiftly moving eye-rays even with distant objects like the moon, and via sounds arriving in succession and striking the ear-cavity. For this reason, consciousness does not arise with regard to forms and sounds that are obstructed by walls, or are within gapped mountains, caves, and so on.” For them too, it must be acknowledged that the eye’s ability to connect with rays from distant or near objects like the moon or trees, without perceptible temporal separation, and the ability of sounds from distant or near sources to arrive without a known difference and strike the ear-cavity, serve as the causes for the arising of consciousness. Beyond that, one must accept the ability of objects to produce consciousness while remaining just where they are. As for forms and sounds obstructed by walls, caves, and so on, their failure to come into range is due to the absence of cooperating conditions. Otherwise, for them too, in such cases, a connection with the sense faculty should not be denied. The prevention of the object's arrival is simply the prevention of the consciousness's arising. Just so, due to the absence of cooperating conditions, it should be understood that consciousness arises in accordance with the kind of connection that occurs with the sense faculty.

Cakkhu tāva dūre ṭhitānaṃ candādīnampi gahaṇato asampattaggāhakaṃ hotu, sotaṃ pana dūre rukkhaṃ chindantānaṃ, vatthaṃ dhovantānañca dūratova paññāyamānakāyavikārādinā saddhiṃ saddaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthatāya kathaṃ saṇikaṃ vavatthāpayamānaṃ taṃ asampattaggāhakaṃ hotīti? Tatthāpi ca kuṭhārivatthādīnaṃ paṭhamanipātasaddānaṃ mandatāya yathā hatthachijjamānasākhāpalāsacalanādisamuṭṭhitamandasaddānaṃ paramparāyāgamanaṃ natthi, tathā anāpāthagamanampi, pacchā pana ghaṭṭanānighaṃsassa balavatāya [V 0.0064] uppannamahāsaddānaṃ āgamanaṃ viya tattheva ṭhitānaññeva āpāthagamanaṃ hoti, itarathā dūrāsannādivavatthānāni na siyuṃ gandhādīnaṃ viya, tasmā asampattagocarānevetāni, ghānādīni ca sampattagocarānīti veditabbāni.

Let the eye, indeed, be a non-contact faculty, as it grasps objects like the moon even from a distance. But how can the ear be a non-contact faculty, when, in the case of those chopping a tree or washing clothes far away, it determines things slowly and is unable to grasp the sound simultaneously with the bodily movements discernible from afar? There, too, due to the faintness of the initial sounds from the striking of the axe, cloth, and so on, they do not come into range, just as there is no successive arrival of faint sounds arising from things like the movement of branches and leaves being broken by hand. But later, the loud sounds arising from the force of striking or rubbing reach the range of hearing as if they originate right there. Otherwise, distinctions like ‘far’ and ‘near’ would not obtain, as they do for smells and the like. Therefore, these (eye and ear) should be understood as having non-contact objects, while the nose and others have contact objects.

Ahisuṃsumārapakkhikukkurasiṅgālasadisāni cetāni. Yathā hi ahi nāma bahisittasammaṭṭhaṭṭhāne nābhiramati, taṃ vihāya tiṇapaṇṇagahanavammikādivisamajjhāsayova hoti, evaṃ [M 0.0085] cakkhupi sammaṭṭhabhittiādiṃ vihāya itthipurisapupphalatācittādivisamajjhāsayaṃ hoti. Yathā ca suṃsumāropi bahi caraṇaṃ vihāya udake bilajjhāsayo hoti, evaṃ sotampi vātapānacchiddādibilajjhāsayaṃ hoti. Yathā hi gijjhādipakkhīpi bhūmirukkhādiṃ vihāya ākāse pakkhandanajjhāsayo hoti, evaṃ ghānampi uddhaggaṃ hutvā gandhapavesakavātākaḍḍhanatthaṃ ākāsajjhāsayaṃ hoti. Yathā kukkuro bahigāmacāraṃ vihāya āmisagavesī gāmajjhāsayo mahānasādininnacitto hoti, evaṃ jivhāpi āpajjhāsayā hoti. Yathā ca siṅgālo bahisusānacāraṃ vihāya maṃsagavesī susānajjhāsayo hoti, evaṃ kāyopi anupādinnaṃ sukhasamphassasayanādiṃ labhitvāpi upādinnajjhāsayo hoti. Aññaṃ hi upādinnakaṃ alabhamānā sattā attano jaṇṇukāni urantaraṃ pavesetvā hatthatale sīsaṃ katvāpi nipajjanti. Ālokavivaravāyujalapathavipaccayāni cetāni viññāṇuppādakāni. Evametesaṃ pañcannaṃ pasādānaṃ lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadesanissayagocarajjhāsayappaccayabhedena vavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

These are like snakes, crocodiles, birds of prey, dogs, and jackals. For just as a snake does not delight in a place that is sprinkled and well-swept, but leaving it, is disposed to the unevenness of thickets of grass and leaves, anthills, and the like, so too the eye, leaving well-swept walls and the like, is disposed to the unevenness of forms such as women, men, flowers, and paintings. And just as a crocodile, leaving its roaming on land, has its lair in the water, so too the ear is disposed to holes such as window-apertures. For just as vultures and other birds of prey, leaving the ground and trees, are disposed to soaring into the sky, so too the nose, being upturned, is disposed to the sky for the purpose of drawing in the wind that brings scents. Just as a dog, leaving its roaming outside the village and seeking meat, is disposed to the village, with its mind inclined towards the kitchen and the like, so too the tongue is disposed to the water element. And just as a jackal, leaving its roaming outside the charnel ground and seeking flesh, is disposed to the charnel ground, so too the body, even having obtained an unclaimed pleasant touch, such as a bed, is still disposed to what is clung to. For beings, unable to find anything else that is clung to, lie down even by drawing their knees into their chest and placing their head on their palms. Light, aperture, air, water, and the earth element are the respective conditions for the arising of consciousness. Thus, the establishment of these five sensitivities is to be understood through the distinctions of their characteristic, function, manifestation, location, support, object, disposition, and condition.

Cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvarasaṃ, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, catumahābhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ, yathā cetassa, evaṃ sabbesampi upādārūpānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ, visesaṃ pana vakkhāma. Tayidaṃ rūpaṃ nīlapītalohitodātakāḷamañjiṭṭhasāmachāyātapaālokandhakārādivasena anekavidhaṃ. Keci pana “andhakāro nāma ālokābhāvamatto eva, tato eva tattha gatarūpāni na dissantī”ti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Yathā hi nīlameghamaṇiādīnaṃ chāyā ālokavisadisā vaṇṇāyatanabhūtā hoti, evaṃ bhitticchadanabhūmipabbatādicchāyā ca ghanībhūtā ghaṭarūpādicchādanato ālokavisadiso andhakāroti [M 0.0086] daṭṭhabbo, sotapaṭihananalakkhaṇo saddo, sotaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. So gītabherisaddādivasena anekavidho. Ghānapaṭihananalakkhaṇo gandho, ghānaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. So mūlagandhasāragandhādivasena anekavidho[V 0.0065]. Jivhāpaṭihananalakkhaṇo raso, jivhāviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. So mūlarasatacarasādīnaṃ vasena anekavidho.

Visible form has the characteristic of impinging on the eye. Its function is to be the objective field of eye-consciousness. It is manifested as its object-field. Its proximate cause is the four great elements. Just as for this, so too should the proximate cause of all derived material forms be understood; however, we will explain the specifics. This visible form is of many kinds—such as blue, yellow, red, white, black, crimson, dark brown, shadow, sunshine, light, and darkness. Some say, “Darkness is merely the absence of light, and for that reason forms that have gone there are not seen.” This is not correct. For just as the shadow of blue clouds, gems, and the like, being distinct from light, constitutes the color-base, so too the darkness from the shadow of walls, roofs, the ground, mountains, and the like—being solidified and obscuring forms such as pots—should be seen as distinct from light. Sound has the characteristic of impinging on the ear. Its function is to be the objective field of ear-consciousness. It is manifested as its object-field. It is of many kinds—such as the sounds of songs and drums. Smell has the characteristic of impinging on the nose. Its function is to be the objective field of nose-consciousness. It is manifested as its object-field. It is of many kinds—such as root scents, heartwood scents, and so on. Taste has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue. Its function is to be the objective field of tongue-consciousness. It is manifested as its object-field. It is of many kinds—such as root tastes, bark tastes, and so on.

Itthibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ itthindriyaṃ, itthīti pakāsanarasaṃ, itthiliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Purisabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ purisindriyaṃ, purisoti pakāsanarasaṃ, purisaliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Ubhinnampesaṃ itthipurisaliṅgādīnaṃ kāraṇabhāvo na sarasato atthi kenaci paccayena nesaṃ paccayabhāvassa paṭṭhāne anāgatattā, attano pana janakapaccayabhūtaāgamanatova. Itthipurisānaṃ paṭiniyataliṅganimittakuttākappabhāvānuguṇarūpānampi niyamena uppajjanato, liṅganimittādivohārānañca tappadhānato paccayabhāvo, indriyabhāvo ca pariyāyato vutto. Teneva hi itthiubhatobyañjanakassa purisindriyābhāvepi purisaliṅganimittādibyañjanaṃ, purisaubhatobyañjanakassa itthindriyābhāvepi itthiliṅganimittādibyañjanañca purimakammato eva uppajjati. Yadi hi nesaṃ taṃtaṃindriyeneva paṭiniyatabyañjanāni uppajjeyyuṃ, dutiyabyañjanassa abhāvo āpajjati. Na hi tesaṃ bhāvadvayaṃ atthi. Yadi siyā, sabbadāpi byañjanadvayassa bhāvappasaṅgo siyā. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa hi itthindriyameva vijjati, na itaraṃ. Tassa pana yadā itthiyaṃ rāgacittaṃ uppajjati, tadā purisabyañjanaṃ pātubhavati, itthibyañjanaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti. Tathā itarassa itaraṃ. Yasmā panesaṃ ekameva indriyaṃ niyataṃ[M 0.0087], tasmā itthiubhatobyañjanako sayampi gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parampi gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako paraṃ gaṇhāpeti, sayaṃ pana na gaṇhāti. Yathā tesaṃ ubhatobyañjanakānaṃ kammasahāyaṃ rāgacittameva byañjanakāraṇaṃ, na bhāvo, evaṃ pakatitthipurisānampi bhāvadvayajanakakammādipaccayo eva taṃtaṃliṅganimittādikāraṇanti gahetabbaṃ.
