Ubhayampi cetaṃ paṭhamakappikānaṃ pavatte samuṭṭhāti, tato aparabhāge paṭisandhiyameva, sabbesaṃ pana pavatte eva parivattati. Imesu ca purisaliṅgaṃ uttamaṃ, itthiliṅgaṃ hīnaṃ, tasmā purisaliṅgaṃ balavaakusalena antaradhāyati, itthiliṅgaṃ dubbalakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Itthiliṅgaṃ pana antaradhāyantaṃ dubbalākusalena antaradhāyati, itaraṃ balavakusalena patiṭṭhāti. Evaṃ ubhayampi sugatiyaṃ akusaleneva antaradhāyati, kusaleneva patiṭṭhāti. Kāyappasādo viya ca sakalasarīrabyāpakameva, na ca kāyappasādādīnaṃ ṭhitokāse tiṭṭhati.

The female faculty has the characteristic of being the female state; its function is to reveal 'this is a woman'; its manifestation is its being the cause of female marks, signs, behaviors, and appearances. The male faculty has the characteristic of being the male state; its function is to reveal 'this is a man'; its manifestation is its being the cause of male marks, signs, behaviors, and appearances. For both of these, the state of being the cause of female and male marks, etc., does not exist by their own essence, nor is there any condition that establishes their causal relationship beforehand, but only from the arrival of their own generative conditions. Since the forms appropriate to the fixed marks, signs, behaviors, and appearances of women and men arise invariably, and since the marks, signs, etc., are primarily dependent on them, their causal nature and their nature as faculties are stated indirectly. Thus, even in the absence of the male faculty in a hermaphrodite woman, male marks, signs, etc., appear only due to prior kamma. Similarly, in the absence of the female faculty in a hermaphrodite man, female marks, signs, etc., appear only due to prior kamma. If their respective fixed manifestations were to arise solely from their respective faculties, the absence of the second manifestation would ensue. For they do not possess a dual state. If they did, there would always be the consequence of the existence of dual manifestations. In a hermaphrodite woman, only the female faculty exists, not the other. But when a lustful thought arises in her, the male manifestation becomes evident, and the female manifestation becomes concealed. The same applies to the other. Since only one faculty is fixed in them, a hermaphrodite woman can both conceive and cause conception, while a hermaphrodite man can cause conception but cannot conceive himself. Just as for these hermaphrodites, lustful thoughts, aided by kamma, are the cause of their manifestations, not the faculty itself, so too for normal men and women, kamma and other conditions that produce the two faculties are to be understood as the cause of their respective marks, signs, etc. Both of these arise in the course of existence for beings of the first eon, but in later times, they arise only at rebirth-linking. However, for all beings, they change during existence. Among these, the male mark is superior, and the female mark is inferior. Therefore, the male mark disappears due to strong unwholesome kamma, while the female mark is established due to weak wholesome kamma. When the female mark disappears, it disappears due to weak unwholesome kamma, while the other is established due to strong wholesome kamma. Thus, in a happy destination, both disappear due to unwholesome kamma and are established due to wholesome kamma. And like body-sensitivity, it pervades the entire body, but it does not remain in the place where body-sensitivity, etc., are located.

Yadi evaṃ na sabbattha kāyabhāvindriyānīti? Nevaṃ paramatthato sabbattha, vinibbhujitvā panesaṃ [V 0.0066] okāsabhedaṃ paññāpetuṃ na sakkā rūparasādīnaṃ viya. Na hi paramatthato rūpe raso atthi. Yadi siyā, rūpaggahaṇeneva gahaṇaṃ gaccheyya. Evaṃ kāyabhāvindriyāni paramatthato na sabbattha, na ca sabbattha natthi vivecetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya heṭṭhā vuttalakkhaṇādivavatthānatopi cesaṃ asammissatā desato na vivekābhāvepi. Na kevalañca imāneva, sabbānipi rūpāni asammissāneva honti. Yathā hi pañcavaṇṇena kappāsena vaṭṭiṃ katvā dīpe jalite kiñcāpi jālā ekābaddhā viya honti, tassa tassa pana aṃsuno pāṭiyekkaṃ jālā aññamaññaṃ asammissāva. Evaṃ kāyabhāvindriyādīni ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samosaṭānipi bhinnaṭṭhānesu heṭṭhupariyādivasena natthi, tānipi asammissāneva honti.

If it is so, are the body faculty and the sex faculties not present everywhere? It is not so. In the ultimate sense, they are everywhere, but it is impossible to define their distinct locations by separating them, just as with form, taste, and so on. For in the ultimate sense, there is no taste in form. If there were, it would be grasped simply by grasping the form itself. Thus, in the ultimate sense, the body faculty and the sex faculties are not everywhere, nor are they not everywhere, due to the inability to distinguish them. And also because of their unmixed nature, as established from the analysis of their characteristics stated above, even when there is no distinction in terms of location. Not only these, but all material phenomena are unmixed. For just as when a wick is made from five-colored cotton and a lamp is lit, although the flames appear to be a single mass, the individual flame from each thread remains unmixed with the others. Similarly, although the body faculty, the sex faculties, and others are assembled in one place and do not exist in separate locations, such as above and below, they too remain entirely unmixed.

Sahajarūpānaṃ [M 0.0088] anupālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaṃyeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbadhammapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Atthikkhaṇe eva cetaṃ sahajarūpāni anupāleti udakaṃ viya uppalādīni, na bhaṅgakkhaṇe sayaṃ bhijjamānattā, yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannepi ca dhamme pāleti dhātī viya kumāraṃ, sayaṃpavattitadhammasambandheneva ca pavattati niyāmako viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent material phenomena. Its function is to make them continue. Its manifestation is the establishing of those same phenomena. Its proximate cause is the material phenomena to be sustained. At the moment of existence, it maintains the co-nascent material phenomena, like water sustaining lotuses and so on—not at the moment of dissolution, since it is itself dissolving. It also protects the phenomena produced by their respective conditions, like a nurse protecting a child. And it continues solely in connection with the phenomena that arise together with it, like a regulator. This should be understood.

Manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayalakkhaṇaṃ hadayavatthu, tāsaññeva dhātūnaṃ dhāraṇarasaṃ, ubbahanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ pana hadayavatthu yadetaṃ antosarīre dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ majjhe bāhirapattāni apanetvā adhomukhaṭṭhapitarattapadumamakulasaṇṭhānaṃ bahi maṭṭhaṃ, anto kosātakīphalassa abbhantarasadisaṃ, paññavantānaṃ thokaṃ vikasitaṃ, mandapaññānaṃ makuḷitaṃ, hadayamaṃsayamakaṃ parikkhipitvā vakkayakanakilomakapihakādayo tiṭṭhanti. Tassa sasambhārahadayamaṃsassa anto punnāgaṭṭhipatiṭṭhānamatte āvāṭake saṇṭhitaṃ addhapasatamattalohitaṃ saṇṭhāti. Tañca rāgacaritassa rattaṃ, dosacaritassa kāḷakaṃ, mohacaritassa maṃsadhovanaudakasadisaṃ, vitakkacaritassa kulatthayūsavaṇṇaṃ, saddhācaritassa kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ, buddhicaritassa acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ paṇḍaraṃ parisuddhaṃ niddhotajātimaṇi viya jutimantaṃ hoti, byāpetvā sandhāraṇādikiccehi bhūtehi katūpakāraṃ āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ vaṇṇādiparivutaṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnañceva taṃsampayuttānañca vatthubhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

The heart-base has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element. Its function is to sustain those same elements, and its manifestation is the upholding of them. This heart-base is located inside the body, between the two breasts. It has the shape of a red lotus bud placed facing downwards, with its outer petals as if removed. Externally, it is smooth, while internally, it resembles the inside of a luffa gourd. For the wise, it is slightly open, but for those of weak wisdom, it is closed. Surrounding the heart-flesh stand the kidneys, liver, lungs, spleen, and other organs. Within that heart-flesh with its constituents, in a cavity the size of a punnāga seed's base, there is about half a pasata measure of blood. For one of lustful temperament, this blood is red; for one of hateful temperament, dark; for one of deluded temperament, like water used to wash meat; for one of speculative temperament, the color of horse-gram soup; for one of faithful temperament, like the karnikara flower; for one of intellectual temperament, it is clear, bright, unstained, white, pure, and radiant like a polished Jati gem. Assisted by the elements through their functions of supporting and so on, maintained by life, surrounded by color and other qualities, upheld by temperature, mind, and nutriment, it stands, establishing the state of being the base for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and their associated states.

Abhikkamādippavattakacittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātuyā sahajarūpakāyasanthambhanasandhāraṇacalanassa paccayākāravikāralakkhaṇā kāyaviññatti, adhippāyappakāsanarasā, kāyavipphandanahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā[V 0.0067], cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātupadaṭṭhānā. Vacībhedappavattakacittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātuyā upādinnaghaṭṭanassa [M 0.0089] paccayākāravikāralakkhaṇā vacīviññatti, adhippāyappakāsanarasā, vacīghosassa hetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātupadaṭṭhānā. Ubhopetā kāyavipphandanavacīghosehi sayaṃ viññeyyattā, adhippāyaviññāpanato ca “kāyavacīviññattiyo”ti vuccanti. Cakkhusotapathasmiṃ hi ṭhatvā kenaci hatthavikārasīsukkhipanādikāyavikāre, sadde vā kate tathāpavattarūpasaddāyatanāni cakkhusotaviññeyyāni, na tāni viññattiyo, cittasamuṭṭhitakalāpagatāya pana vāyodhātuyā sahajātarūpakāyasandhāraṇacalanādīnaṃ paccayabhūto vikāro kāyaviññatti, tathā cittasamuṭṭhitapathavīdhātuyā upādinnaghaṭṭanassa paccayabhūto ākāravikāro vacīviññatti. Na ca tā cakkhusotaviññeyyā, tā pana manodvārikajavanehi tālapaṇṇādisaññāya udapānādīni viya yathāgahitakāyavikāravacīghosānusārena tiracchānānampi viññeyyā, tadanusāreneva “idañcidañca esa kāreti, vadati cā”ti adhippāyo ca viññeyyo hoti, tasmā sayaṃ viññeyyato, adhippāyaviññāpanato ca “viññattiyo”ti vuccanti.

Bodily intimation has the characteristic of a specific alteration which is the condition for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body, this alteration being caused by the wind element that arises from a mind initiating stepping forward and so on. Its function is to reveal intention. Its manifestation is its being the cause of bodily agitation. Its proximate cause is the wind element arisen from the mind. Verbal intimation has the characteristic of a specific alteration which is the condition for the striking of appropriated matter, this alteration being caused by the earth element that arises from a mind initiating the breaking forth of speech. Its function is to reveal intention. Its manifestation is its being the cause of vocal sound. Its proximate cause is the earth element arisen from the mind. Both of these are called "bodily and verbal intimations" because they are themselves knowable through bodily movement and vocal sound, and because they communicate intention. For when one is within range of the eye or ear, any bodily alteration such as hand gestures or head movements, or any sound made—these material forms and sound-objects are cognizable by the eye and ear, but they are not intimations. However, the alteration that is the condition for the supporting, moving, etc., of the co-nascent material body, and which is due to the wind element that has arisen from the mind and is present in material groups, is bodily intimation. Similarly, the alteration in mode that is the condition for the striking of appropriated matter, and which is due to the earth element that has arisen from the mind, is verbal intimation. These two are not cognizable by the eye or ear. Rather, they are cognizable through mind-door impulsion processes—just as one infers a well from a sign such as a palm leaf—and are knowable even by animals in accordance with the bodily alteration or vocal sound they have grasped. In accordance with that, the intention is also understood, as: "This person is doing such and such, and saying such and such." Therefore, because they are themselves knowable and because they communicate intention, they are called "intimations."

Tattha ca manodvārikajavanavīthiyaṃ sattasu kāmāvacarajavanesu kāyaviññattijanakesu purimehi chahi javanehi samuṭṭhitavāyodhātuyo upatthambhanasandhāraṇakiccameva kātuṃ sakkonti, abhikkamādiṃ pana nipphādetuṃ na sakkonti. Sattamajavanasamuṭṭhitā pana heṭṭhā chahi javanehi samuṭṭhitavāyodhātuyopatthambhaṃ labhitvā sattahi yugehi ākaḍḍhitabbabhāraṃ sakaṭaṃ sattamayugayuttagoṇo viya itarachayugayuttagoṇopatthambhaṃ labhitvā rūpakāyassa abhikkamapaṭikkamādiṃ kāretuṃ sakkoti, evaṃ vacīviññattijanakepi sattamajavanehi samuṭṭhitāya pathavīdhātuyāpi upādinnaghaṭṭanassa [M 0.0090] paccayabhāvo veditabbo. Idha pana purimajavanasamuṭṭhitāya upatthambhakattaṃ, sattamajavanasamuṭṭhitāya calanapaccayattañca natthi tesaṃ vāyodhātukiccattā, purimasahagatā pana pacchimā pathavīdhātu upādinnaghaṭṭanasamatthā hoti, sesaṃ tādisameva. Cittasamuṭṭhitakāye pana vāyodhātuyā calante tadupatthambhitatesamuṭṭhānikānampi calanato sakalakāyassa abhikkamādayo honti udake gacchante tattha patitatiṇapaṇṇāni viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In a mind-door cognitive process, among the seven sense-sphere impulsion moments that generate bodily intimation, the wind elements arisen from the first six impulsion moments can only perform the function of supporting and maintaining; they are incapable of producing movement such as stepping forward. However, the wind element arisen from the seventh impulsion moment, having gained the support of the wind elements arisen from the previous six impulsion moments, is able to cause the material body to step forward, step backward, and so forth—just as an ox yoked to the seventh yoke, having gained the support of the other six yoked oxen, can pull a cart that has to be pulled by seven yokes. Similarly, in the case of generating verbal intimation, the earth element arisen from the seventh impulsion moment should be understood as the condition for the striking of appropriated matter. Here, however, the earth element arisen from the earlier impulsion moments does not have the function of supporting, nor does the earth element arisen from the seventh impulsion moment have the function of being a condition for movement, because those are functions of the wind element. But the later earth element, accompanied by the earlier ones, is capable of striking the appropriated matter. The rest is similar. When the wind element produced by the mind moves in the mind-produced body, the entire body moves forward and so on, because the other co-arisen phenomena supported by it also move; just as when water flows, the grass and leaves that have fallen into it also move. This should be understood.

Rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇā ākāsadhātu, rūpapariyantappakāsanarasā, rūpamariyādapaccupaṭṭhānā, asamphuṭṭhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, chiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhānā, yāya paricchinnesu rūpesu “idamito uddhaṃ, adho, tiriya”nti ca hoti.

The space element has the characteristic of delimiting material form. Its function is to make manifest the boundaries of material form. Its manifestation is the limitation of material form, or the state of being untouched, or the state of being hollow and having openings. Its proximate cause is delimited material form. It is that by which, in delimited material forms, there arises the notion: 'this is above, this is below, this is across.'

Adandhatālakkhaṇā [V 0.0068] rūpassalahutā, rūpānaṃ garubhāvavinodanarasā, lahuparivattitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Athaddhatālakkhaṇā rūpassamudutā, rūpānaṃ thaddhabhāvavinodanarasā, sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, mudurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā rūpassakammaññatā, akammaññatāvinodanarasā, adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammaññatārūpapadaṭṭhānā. Etā pana tissopi aññamaññaṃ na vijahanti, garuthaddhaakammaññarūpapaṭipakkhabhāvena ca samuṭṭhitānaṃ utucittāhārajānaṃ lahumudukammaññabhūtānaṃ rūpānaṃ vikāratāya ca pariyāyato garuthaddhākammaññabhāvavinodanakiccā vuttā, na pana sabhāvato sayaṃ avijjamānattā.

The lightness of material form has the characteristic of unsluggishness. Its function is to eliminate the heaviness of material forms. Its manifestation is quick changeability. Its proximate cause is light material form. The softness of material form has the characteristic of non-rigidity. Its function is to eliminate the rigidity of material forms. Its manifestation is non-resistance to all activities. Its proximate cause is soft material form. The workability of material form has the characteristic of fitness for bodily activities. Its function is to eliminate unworkability. Its manifestation is an absence of debility. Its proximate cause is workable material form. These three, however, do not forsake one another. And because they are the opposite of heavy, rigid, and unworkable material forms, and because they are transformations of light, soft, and workable material forms arisen from temperature, mind, and nutriment, they are described figuratively as having the function of eliminating heaviness, rigidity, and unworkability—but not in the sense that these negative qualities exist in their own right, for they are themselves non-existent.

Ācayalakkhaṇo rūpassaupacayo, pubbantato rūpānaṃ ummujjāpanaraso, niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno, paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno. Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpassasantati, anuppabandhanarasā, anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā, anuppabandhakarūpapadaṭṭhānā[M 0.0091]. Ubhayampetaṃ jātirūpassevādhivacanaṃ. Sampiṇḍitānaṃ hi catusamuṭṭhānikarūpānaṃ paṭhamuppatti upacayo nāma, uparūparuppatti santati nāma. Teneva tāsaṃ padabhājanīye “yo rūpassa upacayo, sā rūpassa santatī”ti (dha. sa. 642) vuttaṃ, ākāranānattato pana visuṃ uddiṭṭhā.

The accumulation of form has the characteristic of growth. Its function is the emergence of forms from the past. Its manifestation is presentation as leading forward, or presentation as fullness. Its proximate cause is accumulated form. The continuity of form has the characteristic of unbroken flow. Its function is uninterrupted connection. Its manifestation is non-severance. Its proximate cause is continuously connecting form. Both of these are simply designations for the arising of form. For the initial arising of the fourfold-originated forms that have coalesced is called accumulation, while their subsequent arising is called continuity. Thus, in the analysis of terms, it is said: 'Whatever is the accumulation of form, that is the continuity of form' (Dhs. 642). However, due to the diversity of aspects, they are separately distinguished.

Rūpaparipākalakkhaṇā rūpassajaratā, upanayanarasā, sabhāvānapagamepi navabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā vīhipurāṇabhāvo viya, paripaccamānarūpapadaṭṭhānā. Khaṇe khaṇe bhijjamānāpi cesā upādinnesu khaṇḍadantādito, anupādinnesu rukkhalatādīsu vaṇṇavikārādito ca antarantarā ca suviññeyyavikārattā “pākaṭajarā, savīcijarā”ti ca vuccati, maṇikanakacandasūriyādīsu duviññeyyattā, nirantarattā ca “apākaṭajarā, avīcijarā”ti vuccati. Īdisesu hi kappavināsādikāle vikārato jarā paññāyeyya. Sabbadāpi pana apaññāyamānavikārattā arūpadhammesu jarā paṭicchannajarā nāma. Na ca tattha vaṇṇavikārādayo jarā tesaṃ cakkhuviññeyyato. Na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā, manoviññeyyā pana hoti. Yathā oghena paribhinnabhūmiādidassanena adiṭṭhopi ogho suviññeyyo hoti, evaṃ vikāradassanena jarāti gahetabbaṃ.

The aging of form has the characteristic of the maturing of form. Its function is leading to decay. Its manifestation is the absence of newness, even though its nature does not depart, like the state of old rice. Its proximate cause is maturing form. Though it breaks down moment by moment, in clung-to things like broken teeth, and in unclung-to things like trees and vines through discoloration, etc., because its changes are easily noticeable intermittently, it is called 'evident aging' or 'aging with intervals.' In things like gems, gold, the moon, and the sun, because the changes are hard to perceive and continuous, it is called 'non-evident aging' or 'aging without intervals.' In such cases, aging becomes apparent only at times of destruction, like at the end of an eon, through its transformation. But because its changes are imperceptible at all times in immaterial phenomena, aging there is called 'concealed aging.' Moreover, discoloration and so forth, which are cognizable by the eye, do not exist there. For aging is not cognizable by the eye, but is cognizable by the mind. Just as a flood, though unseen, can be easily inferred by observing the devastated land, so too aging should be understood by observing its effects.

Paribhedalakkhaṇā rūpassaaniccatā, saṃsīdanarasā, khayavayapaccupaṭṭhānā, paribhijjamānarūpapadaṭṭhānā. Na kevalañcetāni upacayādicatūhi gahitāni jātijarāmaraṇāni rūpadhammānameva[V 0.0069], arūpadhammānampi hontiyeva. Etāni ca imesaṃ sattānaṃ araññappavesakapaviṭṭhaparipātakapatitaghātakacorehi yathākkamaṃ sadisānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

The impermanence of form has the characteristic of destruction. Its function is disintegration. Its manifestation is decay and dissolution. Its proximate cause is destructible form. Not only are these four—beginning with accumulation—taken as birth, aging, and death for material phenomena, but they also apply to immaterial phenomena as well. And these should be regarded as similar, respectively, to one who leads into the forest, one who fells another who has entered, a killer of the fallen, and a thief.

Ojālakkhaṇo [M 0.0092] kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpāharaṇaraso, upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhāno, kabaḷaṃ katvā āharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhāno. Ayaṃ lakkhaṇādito vinicchayo.

Edible food has the characteristic of nutritive essence. Its function is the nourishing of form. Its manifestation is sustaining. Its proximate cause is the object to be eaten after making a mouthful. This is the analysis from the characteristics onwards.

Saṅgahato pana sabbampetaṃ rūpaṃ khandhato ekavidhaṃ rūpakkhandhova hoti, tathā ahetukaṃ sappaccayaṃ saṅkhataṃ lokiyaṃ sāsavaṃ saññojanīyaṃ oghanīyaṃ yoganīyaṃ nīvaraṇīyaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ saṃkilesikaṃ anārammaṇaṃ appahātabbantiādinā ca ekavidhaṃ, taṃ puna bhūtopādāyavasena duvidhaṃ, tathā nipphannānipphannādivasena ca. Tattha pathavīādīni cattāri mahābhūtāni bhūtarūpaṃ nāma, sesaṃ upādārūpaṃ nāma. Pathavīādayo sattarasa, kabaḷīkāro āhāro ceti aṭṭhārasavidhampi paramatthato vijjamānattā nipphannarūpaṃ nāma, itaraṃ anipphannarūpaṃ nāma. Cakkhādayo pañca pasādā, bhāvadvayaṃ, jīvitindriyanti aṭṭhavidhampi indriyarūpaṃ nāma, itaraṃ anindriyaṃ. Tāni indriyāni ceva hadayañcāti navavidhampi upādinnaṃ, itaraṃ anupādinnaṃ, pañca pasādā, cattāro rūpasaddagandharasā, āpodhātuvivajjitabhūtattayañcāti dvādasavidhampi oḷārikarūpaṃ, santikerūpaṃ, sappaṭigharūpañca, sesaṃ sukhumarūpaṃ, dūrerūpaṃ, appaṭigharūpañca. Pasādā, hadayañca vatthurūpaṃ, itaraṃ avatthurūpaṃ. Pasādā, viññattidvayañca dvārarūpaṃ, itaraṃ advāraṃ. Pasādā ajjhattikarūpaṃ, gocaraggāhikarūpañca, itaraṃ bāhiraṃ, agocaraggāhikarūpañca. Cattāri bhūtarūpāni, rūpagandharasaojā cāti idaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ avinibbhogarūpaṃ nāma, itaraṃ vinibbhogarūpaṃ.

Regarding its inclusion, all this form is, as an aggregate, of a single kind, being simply the aggregate of form. Likewise, it is of a single kind as being rootless, conditioned, compounded, mundane, with taints, subject to fetters, subject to floods, subject to yokes, subject to hindrances, clung to, defiled, without an object, not to be abandoned, and so forth. It is again twofold by way of primary and derived form, and likewise by way of produced and unproduced, and so forth. Herein, the four great elements—earth, etc.—are called primary form; the rest is called derived form. The seventeen kinds of form beginning with earth, and edible food, making eighteen kinds, are called produced form because they ultimately exist. The rest is called unproduced form. The five sense faculties—eye, etc.—the two sexes, and the life faculty, making eight kinds, are called faculty form; the rest is non-faculty form. Those faculties and the heart-base, making nine kinds, are called clung-to form; the rest is non-clung-to form. The five sense faculties, the four—visible form, sound, odor, and taste—and the three great elements excluding the water element, making twelve kinds, are called gross form, proximate form, and resistant form. The rest is subtle form, distant form, and non-resistant form. The sense faculties and the heart-base are called basis form; the rest is non-basis form. The sense faculties and the two kinds of intimation are called door form; the rest is non-door form. The sense faculties are internal form and object-apprehending form; the rest is external form and non-object-apprehending form. The four primary elements, visible form, odor, taste, and nutritive essence—this pure octad—is called inseparable form; the rest is separable form.

Cakkhu nacakkhūti evamādivasena ca duvidhaṃ hoti. Puna taṃ sanidassanattikavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ, sesamoḷārikarūpaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ, sabbampi sukhumarūpaṃ anidassanaappaṭighaṃ. Tathā kammajādittikavasena. Tattha navavidhaṃ upādinnarūpaṃ, suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, ākāso ca kammajaṃ nāma, viññattidvayaṃ, lahutādittayañca saddo [M 0.0093] ca akammajaṃ nāma, upacayādicatubbidhaṃ lakkhaṇarūpaṃ ajaṃ nāma. Suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, ākāso, viññattidvayaṃ, lahutādittayaṃ, saddo ca cittajaṃ nāma, tadavasesaṃ lakkhaṇarūpavirahitaṃ acittajaṃ nāma, lakkhaṇarūpaṃ ajaṃ nāma. Suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, ākāso, lahutādittayañca āhārajaṃ nāma, sesaṃ lakkhaṇavajjitaṃ [V 0.0070] anāhārajaṃ nāma, lakkhaṇaṃ ajaṃ nāma. Suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, ākāso, lahutādittayaṃ, saddo ca utujaṃ nāma, sesaṃ lakkhaṇavirahitaṃ anutujaṃ nāma, lakkhaṇaṃ ajaṃ nāma. Lakkhaṇāni hi jāyamānajīyamānaparibhijjamānadhammānaṃ sabhāvatāya kutoci jātivohāraṃ na labhanti bhesampi jātiādippasaṅgato. Na hi “jāti jāyati, jarā jīrati, maraṇaṃ mīyatī”ti voharituṃ yuttaṃ anavaṭṭhānato. Tadavasesānaṃ pana ākāsaviññattādianipphannānaṃ yadipi paramatthato avijjamānatāya na kutoci uppatti atthi, tathāpi tathā tathā pavattarūpaṃ upādāya nesaṃ vijjamānavohārasseva hetusamuppannavohārassāpi virodhābhāvato sahetukatā vuttā. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “rūpāyatanaṃ…pe… rūpassa upacayo rūpassa santati kabaḷīkāro āhāro. Ime dhammā cittasamuṭṭhānā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1202) jātiyāpi kutoci jātattaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ rūpajanakapaccayānaṃ kiccānubhāvalakkhaṇe diṭṭhattā rūpuppattikkhaṇe vijjamānataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, jarāmaraṇānaṃ pana rūpuppattikkhaṇe abhāvato na vuttaṃ. “Jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppanna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) idaṃ pana jarāmaraṇasīsena tathāpavattaviññāṇanāmarūpādīnameva gahitattā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ajjhattikaṃ, taṃ upādā, yaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ bāhiraṃ, taṃ atthi upādā, atthi no upādāti evamādinā nayenāpi tividhaṃ hoti.

It is also twofold by way of 'eye' and 'not-eye,' and so forth. Again, it is threefold according to the triad of the visible. Herein, the visible form base is visible and resistant, the remaining gross form is invisible and resistant, and all subtle form is invisible and non-resistant. Similarly, it is threefold according to the triad of kamma-originated, etc. Herein, the ninefold clung-to form, the pure octad, and space are called kamma-originated. The two kinds of intimation, the triad of lightness, etc., and sound are called non-kamma-originated. The fourfold characteristic form is called unoriginated. The pure octad, space, the two kinds of intimation, the triad of lightness, etc., and sound are called mind-originated. The remainder, excluding characteristic form, is called non-mind-originated. Characteristic form is called unoriginated. The pure octad, space, and the triad of lightness, etc., are called food-originated. The rest, excluding characteristics, is called non-food-originated. Characteristics are called unoriginated. The pure octad, space, the triad of lightness, etc., and sound are called temperature-originated. The rest, excluding characteristics, is called non-temperature-originated. Characteristics are called unoriginated. For characteristics, being the nature of phenomena that arise, age, and perish, do not receive the designation of being born from any cause, because this would imply that they too have birth, etc. For it is not proper to say, 'birth is born, aging ages, death dies,' as this leads to an infinite regress. However, regarding the remainder—space, intimation, etc., which are unproduced—though they do not exist ultimately and have no arising from anywhere, yet because their designation as existing and as causally produced is not contradicted, on account of their dependence on form that occurs in various ways, their causal conditionality is stated. But in the Pāḷi, where it is said, 'the visible form base... the accumulation of form, the continuity of form, edible food. These phenomena are mind-originated,' etc. (Dhs. 1202), even birth is spoken of as having some origin. This is said with reference to its presence at the moment of form's arising, as seen in the function and efficacy of form-producing conditions. Aging and death, however, are not mentioned because they are absent at the moment of form's arising. The statement, 'Aging and death, bhikkhus, are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen' (SN 12.20), should be understood as referring to consciousness, name-and-form, etc., which are included under the heading of aging and death. That form which is internal is clung-to; that form which is external is sometimes clung-to, sometimes not clung-to. In this way, it is also threefold.

Puna [M 0.0094] taṃ sabbaṃ diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nāma, saddo sutaṃ nāma, gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāni patvāva gahetabbato mutaṃ nāma, sesaṃ manasā viññātabbato viññātaṃ nāma. Tathā rūparūpacatukkādivasena catubbidhaṃ, tattha aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ nipphannaṃ rūparūpaṃ nāma, ākāso paricchedarūpaṃ nāma, viññattidvayaṃ, lahutādittayañca vikārarūpaṃ nāma, upacayādicatubbidhaṃ lakkhaṇarūpaṃ nāma. Tathā hadayavatthu vatthu, na dvāraṃ nāma, viññattidvayaṃ dvāraṃ, na vatthu nāma, cakkhādayo pañca pasādā vatthu ceva dvārañca nāma, sesaṃ neva vatthu na dvāraṃ nāmāti evamādinā nayena catubbidhaṃ.

Furthermore, all this is fourfold by way of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Herein, the visible-form base is called 'the seen'; sound is called 'the heard'; odor, taste, and tangible objects are called 'the sensed' because they are to be apprehended only upon contact; and the rest is called 'the cognized' because it is to be cognized by the mind. Likewise, it is fourfold by way of the fourfold division of form, etc. Herein, the eighteen kinds of produced form are called 'form-as-form'; space is called 'delimiting form'; the two intimations and the triad of lightness, etc., are called 'alteration form'; the fourfold [group] beginning with arising is called 'characteristic form'. Similarly, the heart-base is called a basis, not a door; the two intimations are called a door, not a basis; the five sense faculties beginning with the eye are called both basis and door; the rest is called neither basis nor door. By this and similar methods, it is fourfold.

Taṃ puna ekajādivasena pañcavidhaṃ. Navavidhaṃ hi upādinnarūpaṃ kammeneva, viññattidvayañca citteneva uppajjanato ekajaṃ nāma, saddo utucittehi uppajjanato dvijaṃ nāma, lahutādittayaṃ utucittāhārehi uppajjanato tijaṃ nāma, suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, ākāso ca catūhipi uppajjanato catujjaṃ nāma, lakkhaṇāni ajaṃ nāma. Evamādinā pañcavidhaṃ hoti.

That, again, is fivefold by way of being originated from a single source, etc. For the ninefold appropriated matter is produced by kamma alone, and the two intimations are produced by consciousness alone—thus they are called 'singly-originated'. Sound is produced by temperature and consciousness—thus it is called 'doubly-originated'. The triad of lightness, etc., is produced by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—thus it is called 'triply-originated'. The pure octad and space are produced by all four [sources]—thus they are called 'quadruply-originated'. The characteristics are called 'unoriginated'. By this and similar methods, it is fivefold.

Taṃ puna cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanaindriyaviññeyyavasena chabbidhaṃ. Sattaviññāṇadhātuviññeyyavasena [V 0.0071] sattavidhaṃ. Tadeva manoviññāṇadhātuviññeyyaṃ bhūtopādāyavasena dvidhā katvā aṭṭhavidhaṃ hoti. Tattha hi āpodhātu manoviññāṇeneva viññeyyaṃ bhūtarūpaṃ nāma, itaraṃ pasādasahitasukhumarūpaṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyopādāyarūpaṃ nāma. Tadeva puna manoviññāṇaviññeyyopādāyarūpaṃ indriyānindriyavasena dvidhā katvā navavidhaṃ hoti. Taṃ puna pasādavisayaāpodhātubhāvahadayajīvitaparicchedavikāralakkhaṇaāhāravasena dasavidhaṃ hoti.

Again, it is sixfold by way of being cognizable by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties. It is sevenfold by way of being cognizable by the seven consciousness elements. That same [matter] cognizable by the mind-consciousness element, when divided in two by way of primary and derived matter, becomes eightfold. Herein, the water element, cognizable only by mind-consciousness, is called primary matter; the remaining subtle matter together with the sense faculties is called derived matter cognizable by mind-consciousness. That same derived matter cognizable by mind-consciousness, when divided in two by way of faculty and non-faculty, becomes ninefold. Again, it becomes tenfold by way of the sense faculties, objects, the water element, gender, the heart-base, the life faculty, delimitation, alteration, characteristics, and nutriment.

Tadeva puna cakkhāyatanaṃ sotāyatanaṃ ghānāyatanaṃ jivhāyatanaṃ kāyāyatanaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ saddāyatanaṃ gandhāyatanaṃ [M 0.0095] rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ dhammāyatananti evaṃ āyatanato ekādasavidhaṃ hoti, tathā dhātuvasena. Tattha āpodhātuvivajjitabhūtattayaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbadhātu “kāyaviññeyyaṃ, kāyaviññāṇaviññeyya”nti ca vuccati, sukhumarūpaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ dhammadhātūti, tadeva pasādasahitaṃ “manoviññeyyaṃ, manoviññāṇaviññeyya”nti ca vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Again, by way of sense bases, it is elevenfold: the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, form-base, sound-base, odor-base, taste-base, tangible-base, and mind-object-base. It is likewise by way of the elements. Herein, the triad of primary elements, excluding the water element, constitutes the tangible-base and the tangible-element, and is also called 'cognizable by the body' and 'cognizable by body-consciousness'. Subtle matter is the mind-object-base and the mind-object-element; this same [subtle matter], together with the sense faculties, is also called 'cognizable by the mind' and 'cognizable by mind-consciousness'. The remainder is easily understood.

Kasmā panettha āpodhātuvivajjitānaññeva bhūtānaṃ phoṭṭhabbatā vuttā, nanu āpodhātupi sītavasena phusitvā veditabbāti? Na sītassāpi tejodhātuttā. Uṇhameva hi sītanti byapadissati. Kaṭhinākaṭhinataṃ upādāya rukkhādiviraḷacchāyā viya, taṃ vā upādāya sandacchāyādi, aññathā kassetaṃ sītattaṃ sabhāvaṃ siyā. “Āpodhātuyā” iti ce. Yadi evaṃ uṇhodakādīsu āpattaṃ na siyā āpotejānañca sahapavattānaṃ viruddhalakkhaṇattā, na ca sā tejosannidhāne sītattaṃ vihāya tiṭṭhati. Na hi sabhāvā kenaci sahabhāvena taṃsabhāvaṃ jahanti abhāvāpattito, nāpissā sītabhāvaṃ muñcitvā aparasabhāvo atthi, yena sahabhāvo yujjeyya. Yadi siyā “āpo sītatta”nti, bhāvadvayaṃ siyā aññoññavilakkhaṇasabhāvattā bhāvassa, athāpi na sītattaṃ, āpodhātuyā sarūpaṃ sītaguṇo, so ca uṇhasannidhāne vigacchati, guṇīrūpameva tiṭṭhatīti ce? Tadā tahiṃ sayaṃ aphoṭṭhabbāva āpodhātu, na niyataphassavatīti ca siyā, yo ca sītaphasso guṇoti suvutto, so amhehi tejodhātuvisesoti.

Why is tangibility stated here only for the other primary elements, excluding the water element? Is it not that the water element, too, is to be known by contact through coldness? No, because coldness itself is of the fire element. For it is heat itself that is designated as 'cold'. Otherwise, of what would this 'coldness' be the intrinsic nature? If it is said, 'Of the water element,' then in the case of hot water and so on, this would not apply, because the water and fire elements, co-existing, have mutually opposed characteristics. Nor does it (the water element) remain in the presence of the fire element while abandoning its cold nature. For intrinsic natures do not abandon their own nature through any association, as this would lead to their non-existence. Nor, having relinquished its cold nature, does it possess another intrinsic nature with which association would be fitting. If one were to say, 'Water is coldness,' there would be two states, as the intrinsic nature of one is different from the other. Or if it is said: 'Coldness is not the intrinsic form of the water element, but a quality of it, and this quality disappears in the presence of heat, while the substance itself remains'? In that case, the water element there would itself be intangible and would not invariably possess contact. And that cold contact, which is well-described as a quality, is, for us, a specific kind of fire element.

Ayameva visesoti ce, nanu sītattaṃ, uṇhattañca aññoññaviruddhaṃ, kathaṃ tejodhātuyā sabhāvaṃ siyāti? Nāyaṃ doso ekakalāpe tesaṃ sambhavābhāvato, bhinnakalāpesu [M 0.0096] pana pavattiyaṃ ālokandhakāranīlapītādīnaṃ vaṇṇāyatanatā viya tejodhātuttaṃ na virujjhatīti. Yadi āpodhātuyā na sītattaṃ sarūpaṃ, kiṃ panassā sarūpanti? Dravatā. Yadi evaṃ dravatāpi phusitvā [V 0.0072] ñātabbato phoṭṭhabbaṃ siyāti? Na sītādiṃ phusitvā manasāva vaṇṇaṃ disvā ñātabbato. Andhakāre sayantā hi atisītalatāya pattādiṃ phusitvā “udakaṃ etthā”ti āsaṅkitā honti, udakaṃ vā phusitvā sappādisaññino, tasmā aphoṭṭhabbameva āpodhātu, itarabhūtattayameva phoṭṭhabbanti gahetabbaṃ.

If it is said that this is the distinction, then are not coldness and heat mutually opposed? How could they both be the intrinsic nature of the fire element? This is not a fault, because of their non-existence together in a single material group (kalāpa). But when they occur in different material groups, their being the fire element is not contradicted, just as light and darkness, blue and yellow, etc., are [all] the visible-form base. If coldness is not the intrinsic nature of the water element, then what is its intrinsic nature? Fluidity. If so, since fluidity too is known by touching, should it not be tangible? No, because it is to be known by the mind alone after seeing its color, not by touching it as one does coldness, etc. For those lying in darkness, on touching something very cold like a bowl, become suspicious that 'there is water here'; or on touching water, they perceive it as a snake, etc. Therefore, it should be understood that the water element is indeed intangible; only the other three primary elements are tangible.

Kiṃ panetaṃ bhūtattayaṃ ekato ārammaṇaṃ katvā kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjituṃ sakkoti, na sakkotīti? Na sakkoti. Kasmā? Ābhujitavasena vā ussadavasena vā tesu ekamevārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjanato. Ābhujitavasena hi odanathāliyaṃ sitthaṃ gahetvā thaddhamudubhāvaṃ vīmaṃsantassa, uṇhodakabhājane vā hatthaṃ otāretvā uṇhabhāvaṃ vīmaṃsantassa, uṇhasamaye vā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā vātena sarīraṃ paharāpentassa ca tattha tattha kiñcāpi itaraṃ bhūtattayampi atthi, yathābhujitaṃ pana taṃtaṃpathavītejovāyodhātumeva yathākkamaṃ ārabbha kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Evaṃ ābhujitavasena ārammaṇaṃ karoti nāma. Ussadavasena pana bhuñjanasamaye sakkharaṃ ḍaṃsantassa, magge vā aggiṃ akkamantassa, balavavātena vā kaṇṇasakkhaliyampi paharantassa ca tattha tattha kiñcāpi itarabhūtattayampi atthi, yathāussadaṃ pana taṃtaṃpathavītejovāyodhātumevārabbha yathākkamaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Aggimhi vā nimuggasakalasarīrassa yadipi ekappahārena agginā kāyo ghaṭṭīyati, yasmiṃ yasmiṃ pana ṭhāne kāyappasādo ussanno hoti, yattha yattha vā pana visayaghaṭṭanānighaṃso balavā hoti, tattha tattheva paṭhamaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ [M 0.0097] uppajjati, pacchā itaraṭṭhānesu. Khaṇaparittatāya pana sahasā parivattitvā uppajjanavasena ekappahārena sakalasarīraṃ ḍayhamānaṃ viya khāyati. Na hi ekasmiṃ khaṇe bahūni viññāṇāni uppajjanti, byāpetvā vā ekaṃ. Ekekasmiṃ pana avinibbhoge kāyadasake ekameva kāyaviññāṇaṃ ussadavasena uppajjati, evaṃ itaravatthūsupi viññāṇānaṃ avinibbhoge padese ekekānameva uppatti veditabbā. Evaṃ ussadavasena ārammaṇaṃ karoti nāma.

But can these three elements together be the object on which body-consciousness arises, or can they not? They cannot. Why? Because it arises by taking only one element as object, either by way of attending to it or by way of its predominance. For instance, when someone takes a grain of rice from a pot and examines its firmness or softness by way of attending to it, or dips a hand into a vessel of hot water and examines its heat, or opens a window during hot weather and lets the wind strike the body—although the other two tangible elements are present in each case, body-consciousness arises by taking as its object that very earth, fire, or wind element respectively, according to what is attended to. This is called taking an object by way of attending to it. Similarly, when someone bites on a piece of gravel while eating, or steps on fire while walking on the road, or is struck forcefully by wind even on the earlobe—although the other two tangible elements are present in each case, body-consciousness arises by taking as its object that very earth, fire, or wind element respectively, according to its predominance. Even if the entire body is immersed in fire, and the body is contacted by the fire with a single impact, body-consciousness first arises in those places where the body-sensitivity is predominant, or where the friction of contact with the object is strong, and only afterwards in other places. However, due to the extreme brevity of a moment, by way of arising and revolving swiftly, it appears as if the entire body is burning simultaneously. For many consciousnesses do not arise in a single moment, nor does one pervade the whole. Rather, in each inseparable body-decad, only one body-consciousness arises by way of predominance. Similarly, in other bases too, the arising of single consciousnesses one by one should be understood to occur in an inseparable region. This is called taking an object by way of predominance.

Kena pana cittassa ārammaṇasaṅkanti hotīti? Ajjhāsayato, visayādhimattato vā. Nānāṭhānesu hi cittapaṭimādīni passitukāmassa paṭhamaṃ ekaṭṭhāne disvā tato itaraṭṭhānesu ca rūpāni passituṃ sarasenāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. Evaṃ ajjhāsayato saṅkanti hoti. Rūpārammaṇaṃ pana mahantampi passantassa sabbatūriyanigghose uṭṭhite taṃ vā suṇantassa manuññāmanuññe adhimattagandharasaphoṭṭhabbe [V 0.0073] indriyesu ghaṭṭite itaritare cittaṃ saṅkamati, evaṃ visayādhimattato saṅkanti hotīti ayamettha saṅgahato vinicchayo. Suññato, pana atītādivasena paccekaṃ anantappabhedato ca vinicchayo cittavibhattiyaṃ vuttanayānusārena yathānurūpaṃ veditabbo.

And how does the mind's transition to an object occur? Due to inclination or due to the intensity of the object. For one who wishes to see images, etc., in various places, after first seeing them in one place, a spontaneous adverting arises to see forms in other places as well—thus, transition occurs due to inclination. Moreover, when one is seeing even a large visual object, or when the sound of all musical instruments arises and one hears it, or when extremely pleasant or unpleasant smells, tastes, or tangibles strike the senses, the mind transitions from one to another—thus, transition occurs due to the intensity of the object. This is the determination here in summary. But the determination from the aspect of voidness, by way of past, etc., and from the aspect of infinite individual distinctions, should be understood as appropriate, following the method explained in the Analysis of Consciousness.

Samuṭṭhānato, panettha bhavayonīsu pavattikkamato ca pakiṇṇakakathā veditabbā – catusamuṭṭhānikāni hi rūpāni uppajjamānāni dvīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu dasakādikalāpavaseneva paṭisandhippavattīsu yathāsambhavaṃ samuppajjanti. Tattha kammajesu tāva vīsatiyā kāmāvacarakusalākusalehi kāmalokeyeva saṃsedajānaṃ, opapātikānañca cha vatthūni, bhāvadvaye aññataraṃ, jīvitañcāti aṭṭha rūpāni yathāsambhavaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya pātubhavanti. Tāni ca suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, jīvitañca jīvitanavakaṃ, tadeva navakaṃ cakkhunā saha [M 0.0098] cakkhudasakaṃ, sotena sotadasakaṃ, ghānena ghānadasakaṃ, jivhāya jivhādasakaṃ, kāyena kāyadasakaṃ, hadayavatthunā vatthudasakaṃ, bhāvaññatarena bhāvadasakañcāti nava kalāpā hutvā uppajjanti. Napuṃsakānaṃ panettha bhāvadasakaṃ natthi, tathā jaccandhādīnaṃ cakkhusotaghānadasakāni. Evaṃ aṇḍajajalābujānampi, tesaṃ pana paṭisandhicittena saha kāyavatthubhāvadasakāneva uppajjanti, tato pavattikāle jīvitanavakacakkhudasakādīni yathānurūpaṃ uppajjanti. Rūpabhave pana ghānadasakādittayaṃ, bhāvadasakadvayaṃ, udaragginavakañca natthi, sesāni pañcahi rūpāvacarakusalakammehi paṭisandhito pabhuti uppajjanti. Aññaññīnaṃ pana pañcamajjhānakusalena jīvitanavakameva. Evaṃ kāmarūpāvacarakammasamuṭṭhitā nava rūpakalāpā dvīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu yathāsambhavaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāva cuticittoparisattarasamacittassa ṭhiti, tāva cittassa uppādaṭhitibhaṅgasaṅkhātesu tīsu khaṇesu nirantaraṃ ajjhattasantāne eva uppajjanti, tato pabhuti anuppajjitvā cuticittena saha nirujjhanti.

Regarding its origin, the miscellaneous discussion should be understood here from the aspect of the process of occurrence in the realms of existence and modes of birth. For the material phenomena that arise, being of four origins, appear in the two realms of existence and four modes of birth, by way of kalāpas such as decads, as appropriate, at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Here, first, among those originating from kamma, the twenty sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome kammas produce, in the sense-sphere world, for moisture-born and spontaneous beings, six bases, one of the two sex-materialities, and the life faculty—these eight material phenomena appear appropriately from rebirth-linking onwards. These form the pure octad, and with the life faculty, the life-nonad. The same nonad, when combined with the eye, becomes the eye-decad; with the ear, the ear-decad; with the nose, the nose-decad; with the tongue, the tongue-decad; with the body, the body-decad; with the heart-base, the base-decad; and with one of the sex-materialities, the sex-decad—thus nine kalāpas arise. For neuter beings, however, the sex-decad does not exist here; similarly, for those born blind, etc., the eye-decad, ear-decad, and nose-decad are absent. The same applies to egg-born and womb-born beings; for them, however, only the body-decad, base-decad, and sex-decad arise together with their rebirth-linking consciousness. Then, during the course of existence, the life-nonad, eye-decad, and so on, arise as appropriate. In the fine-material realm, however, the triad beginning with the nose-decad, the two sex-decads, and the digestive fire nonad do not exist. The remaining arise from rebirth-linking onwards, produced by the five types of fine-material wholesome kamma. For non-percipient beings, only the life-nonad arises, produced by the fifth-jhāna wholesome kamma. Thus, the nine material kalāpas originating from kamma in the sense-sphere and fine-material realms arise continuously in the internal continuum, in the two realms of existence and four modes of birth, as appropriate, from rebirth-linking onwards, in the three moments of consciousness called arising, persistence, and dissolution, until the persistence of the seventeenth consciousness-moment before the death-consciousness. From then on they do not arise, but cease together with the death-consciousness.

Cittajāni pana pañcavokārabhave dvipañcaviññāṇaāruppavipākavajjitapañcasattaticittehi attano attano uppattikkhaṇe eva samuṭṭhāpitāni paṭhamabhavaṅgamupādāya cuticittapariyosānaṃ ajjhattasantāne eva suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, tadeva kāyaviññattiyā saha kāyaviññattinavakaṃ, vacīviññattisaddehi vacīviññattidasakaṃ, lahutādittayena lahutādekādasakaṃ, kāyaviññattilahutādīhi dvādasakaṃ, vacīviññattisaddalahutādīhi terasakañcāti cha kalāpā hutvā yathāyogaṃ pavattanti. Rūpajanakacittesu cettha somanassasahagatakāmāvacarajavanāni iriyāpathaviññattihasanasahitaṃ [V 0.0074] sabbaṃ cittajarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, sesakāmāvacarajavanābhiññāvoṭṭhabbanāni hasanavajjaṃ, appanājavanāni ca iriyāpathādivirahitameva, yathāpavattaṃ pana iriyāpathaṃ [M 0.0099] avinassamānaṃ upatthambhenti. Sesāni pana rūpāvacaravipākamanodhātutadārammaṇāni ekūnavīsati tampi na karonti, suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, saddanavakaṃ, lahutādekādasakaṃ, saddalahutādidvādasakañcāti cattāro kalāpe uppādenti, tatthāpi sabbesampi paṭisandhicittāni, arahantānaṃ cuticittāni, arūpabhavūpapannāni ca na kiñci rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, āruppavipākadvipañcaviññāṇāni sabbathā na uppādentīti.

Moreover, in the five-constituent existence, the mind-born phenomena, being originated by the seventy-five types of consciousness—excluding the ten sense-consciousnesses and the immaterial resultant consciousnesses—arise at their own moment of arising in the internal continuum, from the first life-continuum up to the death-consciousness. They proceed as appropriate, forming six kalāpas: the pure octad; the same with bodily intimation, forming the bodily intimation nonad; with vocal intimation and sound, forming the vocal intimation decad; with the triad of lightness, etc., forming the lightness-elevenfold; with bodily intimation and lightness, etc., forming the twelvefold; and with vocal intimation, sound, and lightness, etc., forming the thirteenfold. Among the consciousnesses that generate materiality here, the joy-accompanied sense-sphere javanas produce all mind-born materiality, including postures, intimations, and laughter. The remaining sense-sphere javanas, the higher knowledges, and the determining consciousness produce all except laughter. The absorption javanas are devoid of postures, etc., but they sustain the existing postures so they do not perish. The remaining nineteen—namely the fine-material resultants, the mind-element, and the registering consciousnesses—do not do even that; they produce four kalāpas: the pure octad, the sound nonad, the lightness-elevenfold, and the sound-lightness-etc. twelvefold. Among these, the rebirth-linking consciousnesses of all beings, the death-consciousnesses of Arahants, and those who have arisen in the immaterial existence do not produce any materiality. The immaterial resultant consciousnesses and the ten sense-consciousnesses do not produce any at all.

Āhārajāni pana kāmabhave eva ajjhohaṭāhāre ṭhitena ṭhitippattena ojāsaṅkhātena āhārena samuṭṭhitāni ajjhattasantāne eva suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, lahutādekādasakañcāti dve kalāpā hutvā yāvatāyukaṃ pavattanti, na rūpabhūmiyaṃ. Utujāni ajjhattikabāhirena tejodhātusaṅkhātena ṭhitippattena utunā ajjhattasantāne samuṭṭhitāni suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, saddanavakaṃ, lahutādekādasakaṃ, saddalahutādekādasakaṃ, saddalahutādidvādasakañcāti cattāro kalāpā hutvā yāvatāyukaṃ, bahiddhā pana pathavīpabbatadevabrahmavimānādīsu suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, samuddaghosādisaddanavakañcāti dve kalāpāva hutvā pavattanti. Ākāsalakkhaṇāni cettha sabbakalāpesu vijjamānānipi kalāpasaṅgahe vohārābhāvā na gaṇīyanti. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe cettha utucittāhārajāni na honti, na sabbatthāpi uppattikkhaṇe jarāmaraṇānīti evaṃ catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassa bhavayonīsu, paṭisandhippavattīsu ca pavattikkamo veditabbo.

Food-born material phenomena, however, arise only in the sense-sphere realm, originated by the nutriment, called nutritive essence, which has reached the stage of persistence, present in the ingested food. These arise internally in the continuity of being as the pure octad and the lightness-elevenfold, forming two kalāpas that persist for the duration of life; but not in the fine-material realm. Season-born material phenomena arise internally in the continuity of being by the temperature, called the heat element, which has reached the stage of persistence, whether internal or external. These arise as the pure octad, the sound nonad, the lightness-elevenfold, and the sound-lightness-etc. twelvefold, forming four kalāpas that persist for the duration of life. Externally, however, in the earth, mountains, divine and Brahmā abodes, etc., they arise as just the pure octad and the sound nonad, like the sound of the ocean, forming only two kalāpas that persist. Here, the characteristics of space, although present in all kalāpas, are not counted in the kalāpa enumeration due to the absence of conventional usage. At the moment of rebirth-linking, however, season-born, mind-born, and food-born material phenomena do not arise; nor, in any case, do decay and death arise at the very moment of origination. Thus, the process of occurrence for material phenomena originating from four causes should be understood in the various realms of existence, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of life.

Apica dvācattālīsāya koṭṭhāsānaṃ vasenāpi cettha tassa ajjhattaṃ, mahābhūtādivasena bahiddhā ca pavatti evaṃ veditabbā – ajjhattikā hi kesā lomā…pe… karīsaṃ matthaluṅganti ime vīsati pathavādhikakoṭṭhāsā, pittaṃ…pe… muttanti ime dvādasa āpādhikakoṭṭhāsā, yena ca santappati, yena [M 0.0100] ca jīrati, yena ca pariḍayhati, yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammāpariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti ime cattāro tejādhikakoṭṭhāsā, uddhaṃgamo adhogamo kucchisayo koṭṭhāsayo aṅgamaṅgānusārī assāsapassāso cāti ime cha vāyuadhikakoṭṭhāsāti dvecattālīsa koṭṭhāsā honti. Tesu udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pubbo muttanti ime cattāro koṭṭhāsā utujā. Evametesu ekekaṃ utujaṭṭhakameva hoti, sedo assu kheḷo siṅghāṇikāti ime cattāro utucittajā, tesu ekekasmiṃ dve dve aṭṭhakā honti. Asitādiparipācako [V 0.0075] tejo kammajova, tattha jīvitanavakameva. Assāsapassāso pana cittajova, tattha cittajasaddanavakameva. Ime dasa koṭṭhāse ṭhapetvā sesā dvattiṃsa catujā.

Moreover, regarding these forty-two parts, their occurrence internally and externally should be understood as follows: internally, hair of the head, body hair… and so on… feces, and brain—these twenty are parts predominated by the earth element; bile… and so on… urine—these twelve are parts predominated by the water element; that which warms, that which causes aging, that which consumes with fever, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested—these four are parts predominated by the fire element; upward-going winds, downward-going winds, winds in the stomach, winds in the intestines, winds coursing through the limbs, and inhalation and exhalation—these six are parts predominated by the air element. Thus, there are forty-two parts. Among these, the stomach contents, feces, pus, and urine—these four parts are temperature-originated. Thus, in each of these, there is only a temperature-originated octad. Sweat, tears, saliva, and nasal mucus—these four are temperature-and-mind-originated; in each of these, there are two octads. The fire that digests what is eaten, etc., is solely kamma-originated; therein, there is only the vitality nonad. Inhalation and exhalation, however, are solely mind-originated; therein, there is only a mind-originated sound-nonad. Excluding these ten parts, the remaining thirty-two are originated from all four causes.

Tattha aṭṭhasu tejovāyokoṭṭhāsesu ekekasmiṃ jīvitanavakañceva tīṇi ca utucittāhārajaṭṭhakāni honti, vāyokoṭṭhāsesu cettha utucittajasaddanavakampi hoti, sesesu catuvīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu kesalomanakhadantānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbattha dve kāyabhāvadasakāni, tīṇi ca aṭṭhakāni, maṃsamuttesu pana kesādīsu utujaṭṭhakameva hoti. Tāni ca yathāvuttadasakanavakaṭṭhakāni sakalasarīrabyāpīsu tacamaṃsaruhirādīsu, abyāpīsu ca kesādīsu koṭṭhāsesu avinibbhoge ekasmiṃ aṇupadese hontīti paccekaṃ anantāparimāṇā, anantadhātupaccayattā tesaṃ sarīrasmiṃ hi paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇāni anantāni cattāri mahābhūtāni ceva saupādārūpāni ca aññoññapaccayabhūtāni ajjhattaṃ dvācattālīsakoṭṭhāsasarīrārohapariṇāhasaṇṭhānādinā, bahiddhā ca pathavīpabbatādinā ca ākārena yathāpaccayaṃ samuppannāni. Māyākārādayo viya na bālajanappabodhakāni honti.

Here, among the eight components of fire and air, in each, there is one vitality nonad and three octads born of temperature, mind, and nutriment. In the air components, there is also a temperature-and-mind-originated sound-nonad. In the remaining twenty-four components—excluding the places devoid of flesh, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—everywhere there are the two decads of body-faculty and sex-faculty, and three octads. But in those devoid of flesh, such as hair, etc., there is only a temperature-originated octad. These, along with the aforementioned decads, nonads, and octads, pervade the entire body—both in the skin, flesh, blood, etc., that spread throughout, and in the components like hair, etc., that do not spread. Though indivisible in a single minute particle, they are individually infinite and immeasurable, due to the infinite conditions of elements. For in the body, the four great elements and derived matter, crushed into the finest particles, are infinite, being mutually conditioned, arising according to conditions, both internally as the forty-two components of the body’s height, girth, and shape, and externally as earth and mountains. Like a magician's creations, they are not for the understanding of the foolish.

Pathavīdhātu [M 0.0101] cettha sukhumasañcuṇṇā rajabhūtā eva āpodhātuyā saṅgahitā, tejodhātuyā anupālitā, vāyodhātuyā vitthambhitā, vaṇṇādīhi parivāritā na vikiriyamānā ajjhattaṃ itthipurisamigapakkhidevabrahmādisarīrabhāvaṃ, bahiddhā ca pathavīpabbatarukkhadevabrahmalokacandasūriyanakkhattamaṇikanakādibhāvañca upagacchati, yūsagatā bandhanabhūtā panettha āpodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā. Avasesānupālanavitthambhanaparipācanaparivāritā na paggharati, apaggharamānā pīṇitabhāvaṃ dasseti, usumattagatā tejodhātu sesadhātupatiṭṭhānasaṅgahavitthambhanaparivāritā imaṃ kāyaṃ paripāceti, vaṇṇasampattiñcassa apūtibhāvañca sādheti, vāyodhātu vitthambhanasamudīraṇasabhāvā sesadhātupatiṭṭhānasaṅgahānupālanaparivāritā vitthambheti cāleti, sarīravimānādīnaṃ gamanādipadavītiharaṇādīnaṃ ṭhitiñca sampādeti. Catassopi cetā sambhūya pathavīadhikatāya kesādibhāvaṃ, pathavīpabbatādibhāvañca, āpādhikatāya pittādibhāvaṃ, samuddajalādibhāvañca, vāyuadhikatāya uddhaṅgamavātādibhāvaṃ, pathavīsandhārakavātādibhāvañca, tejādhikatāya paripācakaggiādibhāvaṃ, narakaggiādibhāvañca sādhenti, yāsaṃ pakopena rogajarāmaraṇañceva kappavināsādayo ca honti. Evametāsaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇānaṃ dhātūnaṃ sañcayattā paccekaṃ [V 0.0076] anantāparimāṇā kalāpā eva ajjhattikakoṭṭhāsā honti, tathā bāhirāni rūpāni. Tāni ca tena tena paccayena tathātathākārena samuditāva uppajjanti ceva uppajjissanti ca.

The earth element here, finely pulverized, indeed becoming dust, is held together by the water element, maintained by the fire element, supported by the air element, and surrounded by color and other qualities. Without scattering, it internally takes on the form of bodies such as male and female, animals, birds, deities, and Brahmās, and externally the form of earth, mountains, trees, the realms of gods and Brahmās, the moon, the sun, stars, jewels, gold, and so forth. The water element here, being fluid and binding, is established on the earth element. Maintained, supported, ripened, and surrounded by the remaining elements, it does not flow away. Not flowing away, it shows a state of plumpness. The fire element, having the nature of heat, supported, held together, and sustained by the remaining elements, and surrounded by them, ripens this body. It achieves beauty of complexion and prevents its putrefaction. The air element, having the nature of supporting and impelling, supported, held together, maintained, and surrounded by the remaining elements, supports and moves. It accomplishes the stability of bodies, celestial mansions, and the like, and their movements such as walking and other postures. These four elements, combined together, through the predominance of the earth element, produce hair and the like, as well as earth, mountains and the like; through the predominance of the water element, bile and the like, as well as ocean water and the like; through the predominance of the air element, upward-moving winds and the like, as well as winds that support the earth; through the predominance of the fire element, digestive fire and the like, as well as the fires of hell. When these are disturbed, diseases, aging, and death occur, and even the destruction of the eon. Thus, due to the accumulation of these finely divided elements, countless immeasurable individual kalāpas exist as internal parts, and likewise external forms. These, assembled in such and such a way by such and such conditions, arise and will continue to arise.

Yadi paṭhamaṃ dhātuyo aṇurūpena ṭhatvā pacchā saṃyujjanti, tathā ṭhāne viniyogābhāvato aparenāpi pariyāyena cettha kammajaṃ kammapaccayaṃ kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārajaṃ [M 0.0102] āhārapaccayaṃ āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, utujaṃ utupaccayaṃ utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittajaṃ cittapaccayaṃ cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānanti evaṃ samuṭṭhānabhedo veditabbo. Tattha upādinnarūpaṃ kammajaṃ nāma, maṃsamuttakesalomadantasiṅghāṇikādi kammapaccayaṃ nāma, sampattikaramahāmeghapathavīpabbatādi, cakkaratanadevavimānādi ca kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Āhārato samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ āhārajaṃ nāma, kabaḷīkāro āhāro āhārajassa janako hutvā kammajassa anupālako hotīti tadanupālitaṃ kammajarūpaṃ āhārapaccayaṃ nāma, visabhāgāhāraṃ sevitvā ātape gacchantassa kāḷakuṭṭhādīni uppajjanti, idaṃ āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Kammajaututo samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakaṃ utujaṃ nāma, tasmiṃ utu aññaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, idaṃ utupaccayaṃ nāma, tasmimpi utu aññaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, idaṃ utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Evaṃ upādinnake tisso eva santatiyo ghaṭṭetuṃ sakkonti, anupādinnake pana valāhako utujaṃ nāma, vuṭṭhidhārā utupaccayaṃ nāma, deve pana vuṭṭhe pathavī gandhaṃ muñcati, bījāni viruhantīti evaṃ yaṃ anantaṃ santativasena pavattaṃ, etaṃ utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Cittato samuṭṭhitaṃ suddhaṭṭhakādi cittajaṃ nāma, cittena pacchājātapaccayabhāvena upatthambhito kāyo cittapaccayaṃ nāma, abhiññācittena bahiddhā samuṭṭhāpitahatthiassādikaṃ cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Pakiṇṇakakathā.

If the elements first stand in the form of atoms and later combine, then due to the absence of application in that case, here too, in another way, the following distinctions of origination should be understood: kamma-originated, kamma-conditioned, kamma-conditioned-temperature-originated; nutriment-originated, nutriment-conditioned, nutriment-conditioned-temperature-originated; temperature-originated, temperature-conditioned, temperature-conditioned-temperature-originated; mind-originated, mind-conditioned, mind-conditioned-temperature-originated. Therein, appropriated matter is called kamma-originated. Things devoid of flesh, such as hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, and nasal mucus, are called kamma-conditioned. Great clouds, the great earth, mountains, and divine mansions like the Wheel-Treasure, etc., which bring about prosperity, are called kamma-conditioned-temperature-originated. A pure octad arisen from nutriment is called nutriment-originated. Edible food, being the producer of nutriment-originated matter, becomes the sustainer of kamma-originated matter; thus, kamma-originated matter sustained by it is called nutriment-conditioned. When one consumes incompatible food and goes out in the sun, black leprosy and so on arise—this is called nutriment-conditioned-temperature-originated. A pure octad arisen from kamma-born temperature is called temperature-originated. In that, temperature produces another octad—this is called temperature-conditioned. In that, too, temperature produces another octad—this is called temperature-conditioned-temperature-originated. Thus, in appropriated matter, only these three continuities can be generated. In unappropriated matter, however, a cloud is called temperature-originated. A rain shower is called temperature-conditioned. When it has rained, the earth releases fragrance, and seeds sprout—thus, whatever occurs endlessly through a continuous series is called temperature-conditioned-temperature-originated. A pure octad and so on, arisen from the mind, is called mind-originated. The body, supported by the mind by way of the postnascence condition, is called mind-conditioned. Elephants, horses, and so on, produced externally by a mind of supernormal power, are called mind-conditioned-temperature-originated. Miscellaneous discussion.

Rūpābyākataṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The indeterminate which is form is concluded.

Nibbānābyākatavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Indeterminate Nibbāna

Nibbānābyākataṃ pana bhūmito lokuttarameva, dhammatopi ca ekameva, bhedo natthi, lakkhaṇādito pana santilakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0103] nibbānaṃ, nivattilakkhaṇaṃ, asaṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ vā, accutirasaṃ[V 0.0077], animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, asaṅkhatatāya panassa kārakahetuvirahato padaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, pāpakahetuvasena panetaṃ “dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā”tiādivacanato (vibha. 206) “ariyamaggapadaṭṭhāna”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṅgahato pana bhedābhāvā khandhesu saṅgahaṃ na gacchati, āyatanādīsu dhammāyatanadhammadhātūsu saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Suññato pana attasuññaṃ, salakkhaṇadhāraṇato anattakaṃ dhammamattaṃ, asaṅkhatatāya vā accantattā ca aniccatāsuññaṃ, dukkhatāsuññaṃ, rāgādisuññaṃ, nimittasuññanti pavattaṃ suññanti gahetabbaṃ.

The Indeterminate Nibbāna, however, from the standpoint of plane, is simply supramundane. And also by way of nature, it is just one; there is no division. From the perspective of characteristics, Nibbāna has the characteristic of peace, the characteristic of cessation, or the characteristic of being unconditioned. Its essence is immutability, and its manifestation is signless. Due to its unconditioned nature, it has no proximate cause, as it is devoid of a productive cause. However, by way of the cause for its attainment, it is proper to say that it has the Noble Path as its proximate cause, as stated in phrases like 'the path leading to the cessation of suffering' (Vibhaṅga 206). In terms of inclusion, since Nibbāna has no divisions, it is not included among the aggregates. It is, however, included among the sense-spheres and elements, specifically in the mental-object sense-sphere and the mental-object element. From the perspective of emptiness, Nibbāna is empty of self. By maintaining its own characteristic, it is merely a phenomenon that is without self. Due to its unconditioned nature and its being ultimate, it should be understood that it is empty of impermanence, empty of suffering, empty of defilements like greed, and empty of signs, and that it is empty of what is conditioned.

Bhedato pana santilakkhaṇādisabhāvato ekavidhampi kāraṇapariyāyato saupādisesanibbānadhātu, anupādisesanibbānadhātu ceti duvidhaṃ hoti. Sarasavasena pana parikappitākārabhedato suññataṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitanti tividhaṃ hoti. Saṅkhatadhammabhedamupādāya paṭikkhipitabbākārato na cittaṃ, na cetasikaṃ, na rūpaṃ, na atītaṃ, na anāgataṃ, na paccuppannaṃ, na maggo, na phalantiādinā anantappakāraṃ hoti.

Regarding divisions, however, from the intrinsic nature of having the characteristic of peace and so on, it is onefold. From the perspective of causal condition, it is twofold: the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. By way of its own essence, based on imagined aspects, it is threefold: void, signless, and desireless. Taking the classification of conditioned phenomena and the way of rejecting things as a basis, it is of infinite kinds, as in 'not mind, not mental factors, not matter, not past, not future, not present, not the path, not the fruit,' and so on.

Nibbānābyākataṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Indeterminate Nibbāna is completed.

Evaṃ imasmiṃ kusalattike avutto sabhāvadhammo nāma natthi. Asabhāvadhammesu panettha kiñcāpi rūpadhammānaṃ paricchedākāsalakkhaṇāni eva vuttāni, kasiṇādipaṭibhāganimittāni pana kasiṇugghāṭimākāso, viññāṇābhāvo, nirodhasamāpatti, tisso nāmapuggalaupādāpaññattiyo, arūpadhammānaṃ aniccatādilakkhaṇādayo ca na vuttā, tathāpi tesampi sabhāvadhammabyatirekābhāvato gahaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā ayaṃ tiko nippadesattikoti veditabbo[M 0.0104]. Yathā cettha, evaṃ ito paresupi tikadukesu paññattiggahaṇābhāvepi niravasesaparamatthaggahaṇeneva nippadesatā, vipariyāyato sappadesatā ca veditabbā. Yattha pana sammutiggahaṇaṃ atthi, tattha vakkhāma.

Thus, in this wholesome triad, there is no intrinsic phenomenon that is not stated. However, among non-intrinsic phenomena here, although only the characteristics of delimitation and space for material phenomena are stated, the counterpart signs of kasiṇas and so on, kasiṇa-removal space, the absence of consciousness, the attainment of cessation, the three designations—name, person, and concept—and the characteristics such as impermanence for immaterial phenomena are not mentioned. Yet, because even these are not separate from intrinsic phenomena, they are included. Therefore, this triad should be understood as an exhaustive triad. Just as here, so too in the triads and dyads that follow, even when conventional designations are not included, the inclusion of all ultimate realities without omission makes them exhaustive; the opposite, partiality, should be understood. But where conventional designations are included, we will explain.

Rūpanibbānakaṇḍo niṭṭhito.

The Section on Form and Nibbāna is completed.

Iti mohavicchedaniyā

Thus in the Mohavicchedanī,

Abhidhammamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanāya

in the Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix,

Kusalattikasaṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Wholesome Triad is completed.

Vedanāttikādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Feeling Triad and so on

Idāni [V 0.0078] kusalattikānantaraṃ vedanāttikādīnaṃ atthavaṇṇanā anuppattā, yasmā pana yvāyaṃ kusalattikassa –

Now, following the wholesome triad, the explanation of the meaning of the feeling triad and so on is due. But since this wholesome triad—

“Atthato bhūmibhedā ca, paccekaṃ sampayogato;

Uddesato ca dhammānaṃ, lakkhaṇādivibhāgato”ti. –

'By meaning, by division of planes, individually, by way of association; and by way of the designation of phenomena, and by way of the division of characteristics and so on.'

Ādinā mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā “kusalā tāva dhammā bhūmito catubbidhā honti kāmāvacarā…pe… lokuttarā”tievamādinā vinicchayanayo vutto, so eva sesattikadukānampi yathāyogaṃ hoti. Yathā hi ettha, evaṃ “sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā tāva dhammā bhūmito tividhā honti kāmāvacarā rūpāvacarā lokuttarā”tiādinā anukkamena sabbattikadukānampi paṇḍitehi sakkā vinicchayanayaṃ sallakkhetuṃ, tasmā taṃ vitthāranayaṃ vajjetvā nikkhepakaṇḍe, atthuddhārakaṇḍe ca vuttānusārato nātisaṅkhepavitthāranayena vedanāttikādīnaṃ tikadukānaṃ –

Having laid out the matrix with these terms, the method of analysis is explained, beginning with 'First, wholesome phenomena, by plane, are fourfold: sense-sphere… and supramundane,' and so on. This same method applies to the remaining triads and dyads as appropriate. Just as here, in the same way, with phrases like 'First, phenomena associated with pleasant feeling, by plane, are threefold: sense-sphere, form-sphere, and supramundane,' and so on, the wise can discern the method of analysis for all triads and dyads in sequence. Therefore, avoiding that method of elaboration, in accordance with what was stated in the sections on the matrix and the extraction of meaning, the treatment of triads and dyads such as the feeling triad and so on should be neither excessively brief nor excessively lengthy—

Padatthā taṃsarūpā ca, navattabbavibhāgato;

Vinicchayo vijānīyo, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ.

By word-meaning and by their intrinsic nature, and by way of the division of what should not be stated, the analysis should be understood in each case as appropriate.

Tattha [M 0.0105] vedanāttike padatthato tāva “sukhāya vedanāyā”tiādīsu sukha-saddo sukhavedanāsukhamūlasukhārammaṇasukhahetusukhapaccayaṭṭhānaabyābajjhanibbānādīsu dissati. Ayaṃ hi “sukhassa ca pahānā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.232; dha. sa. 165; vibha. 594) sukhavedanāya dissati. “Sukho buddhānamuppādo”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 194) sukhamūle. “Yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60) sukhārammaṇe. “Sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ puññānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.62; itivu. 22) sukhahetumhi. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ, yāva sukhā saggā (ma. ni. 3.255). Na te sukhaṃ pajānanti, ye na passanti nandana”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.11) ādīsu sukhapaccayaṭṭhāne. “Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā [V 0.0079] ete dhammā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.82) abyābajjhe. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 203-204; ma. ni. 215, 217) nibbāne. Idha panāyaṃ sukhavedanāyameva daṭṭhabbo.

Here, in the triad of feelings, firstly, regarding the meaning of the word: in phrases such as 'with pleasant feeling,' the word 'sukha' is seen in pleasant feeling, pleasant root, pleasant object, pleasant cause, a basis that is a condition for pleasure, non-affliction, Nibbāna, and so on. For instance, in passages such as 'and from the abandoning of pleasure,' it is seen as pleasant feeling. In 'The arising of Buddhas is pleasant,' it is seen as a pleasant root. In 'Because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, follows after pleasure, is inclined to pleasure,' it is seen as a pleasant object. In 'This, monks, is a designation for "pleasant," that is, meritorious deeds,' it is seen as a pleasant cause. In 'Monks, it is not easy to express in words how pleasant the heavens are,' and 'They do not know pleasure, those who do not see Nandana,' it is seen as a basis that is a condition for pleasure. In 'These are states of dwelling in ease in this very life,' it is seen as non-affliction. In 'Nibbāna is the supreme bliss,' it is seen as Nibbāna. Here, however, it should be understood as referring solely to pleasant feeling.

Vedanā-saddo “viditā vedanā uppajjantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.208) vedayitasmiṃ yeva vattati. Dukkha-saddo dukkhavedanādukkhavatthudukkhārammaṇadukkhapaccayadukkhapaccayaṭṭhānādīsu dissati. Ayaṃ hi “dukkhassa ca pahānā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.232; dha. sa. 165; vibha. 594) dukkhavedanāyaṃ dissati. “Jātipi dukkhā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.387; vibha. 190) dukkhavatthusmiṃ. “Yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhānupatitaṃ dukkhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60) dukkhārammaṇe. “Dukkho pāpassa uccayo”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 117) dukkhapaccaye. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ, yāva dukkhā nirayā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.250) dukkhapaccayaṭṭhāne. Idha panāyaṃ dukkhavedanāyameva daṭṭhabbo.

The term 'vedanā' in contexts such as 'with feeling arising, it is known' refers specifically to what is felt. The term 'dukkha' is seen in various contexts: painful feeling, basis of suffering, object of suffering, cause of suffering, a basis that is a condition for suffering, and so on. Here, in phrases like 'the abandoning of suffering,' it is seen as painful feeling. In phrases like 'birth is suffering,' it is seen as the basis of suffering. In phrases like 'because, Mahāli, form is suffering, bound to suffering, inclined to suffering,' it is seen as the object of suffering. In phrases like 'the accumulation of evil is suffering,' it is seen as the cause of suffering. In phrases like 'Monks, it is not easy to express in words how painful the hells are,' it is seen as a basis that is a condition for suffering. Here, however, it should be understood specifically as painful feeling.

Vacanattho [M 0.0106] panettha – sukhayati sattaṃ, suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhā, kāyikacetasikānaṃ sukhasomanassānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dukkhayatīti dukkhā, kāyikacetasikānaṃ dukkhadomanassānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na dukkhā na sukhāti adukkhamasukhā, upekkhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Evaṃ tīhi padehi pañcavidhāpi vedanā gahitā. Sabbāpi ārammaṇarasaṃ vediyanti anubhavantīti vedanā. Yo panāyaṃ tīsupi padesu sampayutta-saddo, tassattho – samaṃ pakārehi yuttāti sampayuttā, katarehi pakārehīti? “Atthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sahagatā sahajātā saṃsaṭṭhā ekuppādā ekanirodhā ekavatthukā ekārammaṇā”ti (kathā. 473) evaṃ vuttehi imehi ekuppādatādīhi catūhi pakārehi. Ukkaṭṭhaniddeso cesa. Āruppe hi vināpi ekavatthukabhāvaṃ sampayogo labbhatīti. Sesaṃ vuttatthameva. Ayaṃ tāvettha padatthato vinicchayo.

Here, the meaning of the word is as follows. It gladdens beings (sukhayati), or it thoroughly consumes (suṭṭhu khādati) and destroys (khanati) bodily and mental afflictions; thus it is 'sukha' (pleasant). This is a designation for bodily and mental pleasure and joy. It causes suffering (dukkhayati); thus it is 'dukkha' (painful). This is a designation for bodily and mental pain and sorrow. It is neither painful nor pleasant (na dukkhā na sukhā); thus it is 'adukkhamasukhā' (neither-painful-nor-pleasant). This is a designation for equanimity. The letter 'ma' serves as a euphonic consonant. Thus, with these three terms, all five kinds of feeling are included. All feelings are so called because they feel (vediyanti), that is, they experience (anubhavanti) the taste of their objects. Moreover, the term 'sampayutta' (associated) in all three phrases means 'connected in the same way' (samaṃ pakārehi yutta). In what ways? By these four ways, namely, having a single arising and so on, as stated: 'There are certain phenomena that are accompanied, co-arisen, conjoined, having a single arising, a single ceasing, a single basis, and a single object.' This is the superior explanation, for in the formless realms, association is possible even without having a single basis. The rest is as previously explained. This, then, is the analysis of the meaning of the terms here.

Taṃsarūpāti tassa padatthassa sarūpamattadassanato. Tattha sukhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, somanassasahagatāni aṭṭhārasa kāmāvacaracittāni, paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānikāni catucattālīsa rūpāvacaralokuttaracittāni cāti tesaṭṭhi cittāni sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā nāma[V 0.0080]. Tathā dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, dve domanassasahagatāni cāti tīṇi cittāni dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā nāma. Sesāni upekkhāsahagatāni pañcapaññāsa cittāni adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā nāma. Yathā ca cittānaṃ sukhādisampayogo, evaṃ taṃcittasampayuttānaṃ cetasikānampi. Na kevalañca ettheva, ito paresupi tikadukesu cittavaseneva taṃsampayuttacetasikānampi saṅgaho veditabbo[M 0.0107]. Yattha pana viseso hoti, tattha vakkhāma. Idha pana cetasikesu sappītikāni vedanāvajjitāni cha cetasikāni eva pañcahipi vedanāhi sampayuttāni, itarāni pana kāyikasukhadukkhavajjitāhi tīheva. Tesu ca pītivajjitā pañca yathāyogikā ceva moho ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ uddhaccaṃ thinaṃ middhañcāti ime ekādasa yathāyogaṃ tīhipi. Tatthāpi vitakkavicārā mahaggatalokuttarabhūtāya sukhāya eva, pīti pana sabbattha sukhāya eva, dosaissāmaccherakukkuccāni dukkhāya eva, vicikicchā upekkhāya eva, sesāni aṭṭhavīsatisomanassupekkhāhi eva vedanāhi sampayuttāni, tatthāpi karuṇāmuditā mahaggatabhūtāya sukhāya evāti ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ cittasampayogasadisaṃ. Ayaṃ sarūpato vinicchayo.

The analysis of the essential nature (taṃsarūpa) is the showing of the mere nature of the meaning of that term. Herein, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure; the eighteen sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by joy; and the forty-four fine-material-sphere and supramundane consciousnesses of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas—these sixty-three consciousnesses are said to be associated with pleasant feeling.
