Similarly, body-consciousness accompanied by pain and the two consciousnesses accompanied by grief—these three consciousnesses are said to be associated with painful feeling. The remaining fifty-five consciousnesses, being accompanied by equanimity, are said to be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Just as the association of consciousnesses with pleasure and so forth is thus, so too is the association of the mental factors connected with those consciousnesses. And not only here, but in the subsequent triads and dyads as well, the inclusion of the associated mental factors should be understood according to the consciousness. Where there is a distinction, we will explain it. Here, among the mental factors, the six mental factors that are accompanied by joy and exclude feeling are associated with all five feelings. The others, however, are associated with only three feelings, excluding bodily pleasure and pain. Among these, the five (particulars) excluding joy, as appropriate, and delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, restlessness, sloth, and torpor—these eleven are associated with the three feelings, as appropriate. Among these, initial application and sustained application, when they have become exalted and supramundane, are associated only with pleasant feeling. Joy, however, is everywhere associated only with pleasant feeling. Aversion, envy, stinginess, and remorse are associated only with painful feeling. Doubt is associated only with equanimous feeling. The remaining twenty-eight are associated only with joyful and equanimous feelings. Among these, compassion and appreciative joy, when they have become exalted, are associated only with pleasant feeling. This is the distinction. The rest is similar to the association with consciousness. This is the analysis by essential nature.

Navattabbavibhāgatoti imasmiṃ tike sabbā vedanā sabbaṃ rūpaṃ nibbānaṃ sammutiyoti ime dhammā “sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā”ti vā “dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā”ti vā “adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā”ti vā na vattabbā. Na hi vedanā vedanāya sampayuttā hoti rūpādayo vā, tasmā ime imasmiṃ tike na labbhanti. Ayañca sappadesattiko hoti. Yathā cettha, evaṃ ito paresupi tikadukesu navattabbayojanā. Yaṃ yasmiñca na vuttaṃ atthi, tassa sappadesatā veditabbā. Ito paraṃ pana yattha asaṅgahitā dhammā honti, tattha tesaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetvā “ime navattabbā”ti ettakameva vakkhāma, tenassa sappadesatāpi ñātabbā. Yattha pana asaṅgahitā natthi, taṃ nippadesanti vakkhāma. Tena tattha navattabbābhāvopi viññātabbo. Sabbattha pana mātikaṃ anuddharitvāva padatthaṃ, taṃsarūpavibhāgañca vakkhāma. Ayaṃ navattabbavibhāgato vinicchayo.

From the division of what is not to be stated (navattabbavibhāgato): in this triad, all feeling, all form, Nibbāna, and concepts—these phenomena—cannot be said to be ‘associated with pleasant feeling,’ or ‘associated with painful feeling,’ or ‘associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’ For a feeling is not associated with another feeling, nor are form and the like; therefore these are not found in this triad. And this is a partial triad (sappadesattika). As it is here, so too in the subsequent triads and dyads is the application of what cannot be stated. Wherever something is not stated, its partial nature (sappadesatā) should be understood. From here onward, wherever there are unincluded phenomena, we will indicate their classification and state just this: ‘These are not to be stated.’ By this, its partial nature will also be known. Wherever, however, there are no unincluded phenomena, we will declare it as ‘exhaustive’ (nippadesa). By this, the absence of what cannot be stated should also be understood. In all cases, however, we will explain the meaning of the terms and the analysis of their essential nature, without first quoting the matrix. This is the analysis by the division of what is not to be stated.

Vedanāttikaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Triad on Feeling is concluded.

Vipākattike [M 0.0108] aññamaññavisiṭṭhānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ pākāti vipākā, vipakkabhāvamāpannānaṃ arūpadhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Kiñcāpi arūpadhammā viya rūpadhammāpi kammasamuṭṭhānā [V 0.0081] atthi, anārammaṇattā pana te kammasarikkhakā na hontīti sārammaṇā arūpadhammāva kammasarikkhattā vipākāti vuttā bījasarikkhakaṃ phalaṃ viya. Yathā hi sālibījato nikkhantasīsameva sāliphalanti vuccati, na aṅkurādīni, tāni pana “sālijātāni, sālinibbattāni cā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ kammasadisā arūpadhammāva “vipākā”ti vuccanti, rūpadhammā pana kammajā “upādinnā”ti vuccanti. Vipākadhammadhammāti vipākasabhāvā dhammā. Yathā hi jātijarāsabhāvā sattā “jātidhammā jarādhammā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ vipākajanakaṭṭhena vipākasabhāvā vipākapakatikā dhammāti attho. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayasabhāvapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ, ayaṃ padattho.

In the Triad of Results, the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions, being distinct from each other, are called ‘results’ (vipākā); this is a designation for immaterial phenomena that have attained the state of being results. Although material phenomena, like immaterial phenomena, may arise from kamma, they are not similar to kamma because they lack an object. Therefore, only immaterial phenomena with an object are called ‘results,’ being similar to kamma, just like a fruit resembling its seed. Just as only the head of grain emerging from a rice seed is called ‘rice fruit,’ but not the sprouts and the like—those are called ‘born of rice’ and ‘produced from rice’—so too, only immaterial phenomena similar to kamma are called ‘results,’ while material phenomena produced by kamma are called ‘grasped’ (upādinnā). ‘Phenomena that are result-producing phenomena’ (vipākadhammadhammā) means phenomena whose nature is to produce a result. Just as beings whose nature is birth and aging are called ‘subject to birth’ and ‘subject to aging,’ so too, the meaning is phenomena whose nature and character it is to generate a result. The third term is stated by way of rejecting both natures. This is the meaning of the terms.

Tattha catūsu bhūmīsu chattiṃsa vipākacittāni vipākā nāma, tathā ekavīsati kusalāni, dvādasa akusalāni cāti tettiṃsa vipākadhammadhammā nāma, tīsu bhūmīsu vīsati kiriyacittāni, sabbañca rūpaṃ, nibbānañcāti ime nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā nāma. Cetasikesu pana cuddasa akusalā vipākadhammadhammā eva, viratiyo siyā vipākā, siyā vipākadhammadhammā, tadavasesā pana siyā vipākā, siyā vipākadhammadhammā, siyā nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammāti cittaṃ viya tividhā hontīti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ cittasamaṃ, idañca nippadesattikanti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, in the four planes, thirty-six resultant consciousnesses are called results. Likewise, twenty-one wholesome and twelve unwholesome states—these thirty-three are called result-producing phenomena. In the three planes, twenty functional consciousnesses, all material form, and Nibbāna—these are called neither-results-nor-result-producing-phenomena. Among the mental factors, however, the fourteen unwholesome ones are solely result-producing phenomena. The Abstinences may be results or result-producing phenomena. The remaining factors may be results, result-producing phenomena, or neither-results-nor-result-producing-phenomena—like consciousness, they are threefold. This is the distinction. The rest is similar to consciousness, and this should be understood as a triad without remainder.

Vipākattikaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Triad of Results is concluded.

Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena taṇhādiṭṭhīhi upetena kammunā ādinnā phalabhāvena gahitāti upādinnā, ārammaṇabhāvaṃ upagantvā upādānasambandhena upādānānaṃ hitāti upādāniyā, upādānassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Upādinnā ca [M 0.0109] te upādāniyā cāti upādinnupādāniyā, sāsavakammanibbattānaṃ rūpārūpadhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iminā nayena sesapadadvayepi paṭisedhasahito attho veditabbo.

Because they are taken up by kamma accompanied by craving and wrong view, by making them an object, and grasped as a result, they are called ‘grasped’ (upādinnā). Because they become an object and are connected through clinging, they are beneficial to the clingings, thus they are called ‘to be clung to’ (upādāniyā); this is a designation for those things that serve as the object-condition for clinging. They are both grasped and to be clung to, thus they are called ‘grasped and to be clung to’ (upādinnupādāniyā); this is a designation for material and immaterial phenomena produced by kamma with taints. In this way, the meaning of the remaining two terms should also be understood along with their negations.

Tattha dvattiṃsa lokiyavipākacittāni, nava kammajakalāpā ca upādinnupādāniyā nāma. Avasesalokiyacittāni ceva akammajarūpakalāpā ca anupādinnupādāniyā nāma. Lokuttaracittanibbānāni anupādinnaanupādāniyā nāma. Kiñcāpi khīṇāsavānaṃ upādānakkhandhā [V 0.0082] “amhākaṃ mātulatthero”tiādinā vadantānaṃ paresaṃ upādānassa ārammaṇapaccayā honti, maggaphalanibbānāni pana divasaṃ santattaayoguḷo viya makkhikāhi tejussadattā upādānehi anupādinnāneva. Asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikesupi eseva nayo. Cetasikesu pana kusalā anupādinnupādāniyā eva, karuṇāmuditā siyā upādinnupādāniyā, siyā anupādinnupādāniyā viratiyo pana siyā anupādinnupādāniyā, siyā anupādinnaanupādāniyā, sesā cittaṃ viya tividhā honti, idañca nippadesattikanti veditabbaṃ. Upādinnupādāniyattikaṃ.

Therein, the thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses and the nine kamma-produced material groups are called ‘grasped and to be clung to.’ The remaining mundane consciousnesses and the non-kamma-produced material groups are called ‘not grasped but to be clung to.’ The supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna are called ‘not grasped and not to be clung to.’ Although the aggregates subject to clinging of those whose taints are destroyed become objects of clinging for others when they say things like, ‘This is our maternal uncle, the elder,’ the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, like a red-hot iron ball during the day untouched by flies due to its fiery heat, remain ungrasped by the clingings. The same principle applies to the undefiled and non-defiling states. Among the mental factors, the wholesome ones are only ‘not grasped but to be clung to.’ Compassion and appreciative joy may be either ‘grasped and to be clung to’ or ‘not grasped but to be clung to.’ The abstinences may be either ‘not grasped but to be clung to’ or ‘not grasped and not to be clung to.’ The rest are threefold like consciousness; and this should be understood as a triad without remainder. The Triad of Grasped and To Be Clung To.

Saṃkilesetīti saṃkileso, vibādhati upatāpetīti attho. Saṃkilesena sampayuttā saṃkiliṭṭhā, saṃkilesasahagatāti attho. Attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanena saṃkilesaṃ arahanti, saṃkilese vā niyuttā tassa ārammaṇabhāvaṃ anatikkamanatoti saṃkilesikā, saṃkilesassa ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saṃkiliṭṭhā ca te saṃkilesikā cāti saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā. Sesapadadvayaṃ purimattike vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

It defiles, thus it is a defilement (saṃkilesa); the meaning is that it oppresses and torments. Those associated with defilement are defiled (saṃkiliṭṭha), meaning they are accompanied by defilement. Because they occur by making themselves an object, they are liable to defilement, or being engaged in defilement, they do not transcend being its object—thus they are defiling (saṃkilesikā). This is a designation for those things that are the object-condition for defilement. Being both defiled and defiling, they are called ‘defiled and defiling’ (saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā). The remaining two terms should be understood in the same way as explained in the preceding triad.

Tattha dvādasa akusalacittuppādā saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā nāma. Sesalokiyacittāni ceva sabbaṃ rūpañca [M 0.0110] asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā nāma. Lokuttaracittāni, nibbānañca asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikā nāma. Cetasikesu pana akusalā saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikāva, karuṇāmuditā asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikāva, sesakusalābyākatā siyā saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā, siyā asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikā, siyā asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikāti tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Saṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikattikaṃ.

Here, the twelve arisings of unwholesome consciousness are called ‘defiled and defiling.’ The remaining mundane consciousnesses and all material form are called ‘undefiled but defiling.’ The supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna are called ‘undefiled and undefiling.’ Among mental factors, the unwholesome ones are solely ‘defiled and defiling,’ while compassion and appreciative joy are solely ‘undefiled and undefiling.’ The remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors may be either ‘defiled and defiling,’ or ‘undefiled but defiling,’ or ‘undefiled and undefiling’—thus, they are threefold. This is a triad without remainder. The Triad of Defiled and Defiling.

Sampayogavasena vattamānena saha vitakkena savitakkā, tathā saha vicārena savicārā, savitakkā ca te savicārā cāti savitakkasavicārā. Ubhayarahitā avitakkaavicārā. Vitakkavicāresu vicārova mattā pamāṇametesanti vicāramattā, vicārato uttariṃ vitakkena saddhiṃ sampayogaṃ na gacchantīti attho. Avitakkā ca te vicāramattā cāti avitakkavicāramattā.

Those occurring in association with initial application are ‘with initial application’ (savitakkā); and similarly, those occurring with sustained application are ‘with sustained application’ (savicārā). Those that are both with initial application and with sustained application are ‘with initial application and sustained application’ (savitakkasavicārā). Those devoid of both are ‘without initial application and without sustained application’ (avitakka-avicārā). Among initial application and sustained application, sustained application alone is their measure or limit—thus they are ‘with sustained application only’ (vicāramattā), meaning they are not associated with initial application in addition to sustained application. Those that are without initial application and with sustained application only are ‘without initial application, with sustained application only’ (avitakkavicāramattā).

Tattha dvipañcaviññāṇavajjitakāmāvacaracittāni ceva ekādasa mahaggatalokuttarapaṭhamajjhānikacittāni [V 0.0083] ca taṃsampayuttesu vitakkavicāre ṭhapetvā sesā ca savitakkasavicārā nāma. Tesu vitakko ekādasa dutiyajjhānikamahaggatalokuttarāni ca taṃsampayuttesu vicāraṃ ṭhapetvā sesā ca avitakkavicāramattā nāma. Dutiyajjhānikesu vicāro, sesā pañcacattālīsa mahaggatalokuttaracittāni, dvipañcaviññāṇāni, taṃsampayuttā ca sabbañca rūpaṃ, nibbānañca avitakkaavicārā nāma. Apica kusalacetasikā savitakkasavicārāva, vitakko avitakkavicāramattova, vicāro pana dutiyajjhānikesu siyā avitakkaavicāro, savitakkacittesu siyā na vattabbo, avasesā pana sabbe cetasikā dhammā tidhāpi honti. Imasmiṃ pana tike vitakkasahajāto vicārova na vattabbo. Vitakkattikaṃ.

Here, the sense-sphere consciousnesses, excluding the ten sense-consciousnesses, the eleven sublime and supramundane first-jhāna consciousnesses, and the remaining mental factors associated with them (excluding initial and sustained application themselves), are called 'with initial application and sustained application.' Among these, initial application itself, the eleven sublime and supramundane second-jhāna consciousnesses, and the remaining mental factors associated with them (excluding sustained application itself), are called 'without initial application, with sustained application only.' Sustained application in the second-jhāna consciousnesses, the remaining forty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses, the ten sense-consciousnesses and their associated mental factors, all material form, and Nibbāna are called 'without initial application and without sustained application.' Furthermore, wholesome mental factors are solely 'with initial application and sustained application.' Initial application itself is solely 'without initial application, with sustained application only.' Sustained application, however, in the second jhānas may be 'without initial application and without sustained application,' and in consciousnesses with initial application it should not be classified. The remaining mental factors, however, are all threefold. In this triad, however, sustained application co-arisen with initial application should not be classified. The Triad of Initial Application.

Pītiyā [M 0.0111] saha ekuppādādibhāvaṃ gatāti pītisahagatā, pītisampayuttāti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Upekkhāti cettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā. Sā hi sukhadukkhākārappavattiṃ upekkhati majjhattākārasaṇṭhitattā tenākārena pavattatīti upekkhā. Iti vedanāttikato padadvayameva gahetvā nippītikasukhassa sappītikasukhato visesadassanavasena ayaṃ tiko vutto.

Having attained the state of co-arising, etc., with joy, it is 'accompanied by joy' (pītisahagatā); that is, it is associated with joy. The same principle applies to the other two terms as well. Here, by 'equanimity' (upekkhā) is meant the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant. For it overlooks the activity characterized by pleasure and pain, because it is established in a neutral state; it proceeds in that manner, therefore it is equanimity. Thus, taking only two terms from the Triad of Feelings, this triad is stated to show the distinction between happiness without joy and happiness with joy.

Tattha pīti pañcavidhā khuddikā khaṇikā okkantikā ubbegā pharaṇāti. Tattha khuddikā pīti sarīre lomahaṃsanamattameva kātuṃ sakkoti. Khaṇikā pīti khaṇe khaṇe vijjuppādasadisā hoti. Okkantikā pīti samuddatīraṃ vīci viya kāyaṃ okkamitvā okkamitvā bhijjati. Ubbegā pīti balavatī hoti kāyaṃ uddhaggaṃ katvā ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇappattā. Pharaṇāya pītiyā pana uppannāya sakalasarīraṃ dhamitvā pūritavatthi viya, mahatā udakoghena pakkhandapabbatakucchi viya ca anuparipphuṭaṃ hoti. Tattha pharaṇā rūpāvacaralokuttarāva, sesā kāmāvacarāva.

Herein, joy (pīti) is fivefold: minor joy (khuddikā), momentary joy (khaṇikā), showering joy (okkantikā), transporting joy (ubbegā), and pervasive joy (pharaṇā). Among these, minor joy is only able to cause the hairs on the body to stand on end. Momentary joy is like flashes of lightning from moment to moment. Showering joy breaks upon the body again and again, like waves upon the seashore. Transporting joy is powerful, making the body rise up, reaching the point of being able to leap into the air. When pervasive joy has arisen, the entire body is completely suffused, like an inflated bladder or like a mountain cavern inundated by a great flood of water. Among these, pervasive joy belongs only to the form sphere and the supramundane, while the rest belong only to the sense sphere.

Sukhaṃ pana kāyikaṃ, cetasikañceti duvidhaṃ hoti. Satipi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge iṭṭhārammaṇapaṭilābhatuṭṭhi pīti, paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ sukhaṃ. Yattha pīti, tattha sukhaṃ. Yattha sukhaṃ, tattha na niyamato pīti. Saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā pīti, vedanākkhandhasaṅgahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Kantārakhinnassa vanantodakadassanasavanesu viya pīti, vanacchāyāpavesanaudakaparibhogesu viya sukhaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye pākaṭabhāvato cetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Happiness (sukha), however, is twofold: bodily and mental. And although in some instances they are not dissociated, joy is the delight in obtaining a desirable object, while happiness is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been obtained. Where there is joy, there is happiness. Where there is happiness, there is not necessarily joy. Joy is included in the aggregate of formations; happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling. Joy is like when one exhausted in a wilderness sees and hears of water at the edge of a forest; happiness is like entering the forest shade and partaking of the water. And it should be understood that this is said on account of their distinct manifestation at each particular time.

Tattha [V 0.0084] sukhasahagatā, upekkhāsahagatā ca vedanāttike vuttāva, sukhasahagataṃ pana kāyaviññāṇaṃ, mahaggatalokuttaracatutthajjhānikacitte ca vajjetvā sesā pītisahagatā nāma, tattha pīti na pītisahagatā, sukhasahagatāva hoti[M 0.0112], sukhaṃ pana pītisahagataṃ nāma siyā na pītisukhasahagatā. Imasmiṃ tike dve domanassasahagatacittuppādā, dukkhasahagataṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ, rūpaṃ, nibbānañca navattabbā. Cetasikesu pana pīti sukhasahagatāva, vicikicchā upekkhāsahagatāva, lobhadiṭṭhimānā, pañcavīsati kusalābyākatā ca tidhāpi honti, cetasikasukhaṃ siyā pītisahagataṃ, paṭhamadutiyatatiyajjhānikesu catutthajjhānikesu siyā navattabbaṃ, kāyikaṃ pana sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ sabbā ca upekkhā doso issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccañca navattabbāva, sesā sattarasa dhammā siyā tidhāpi honti navattabbāpi. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pītittikaṃ.

Herein, those accompanied by pleasure and accompanied by equanimity have already been stated in the Triad of Feeling. However, excluding body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure and the sublime and supramundane consciousnesses of the fourth jhāna, the rest are called 'accompanied by joy.' Therein, joy is not 'accompanied by joy'; it is only 'accompanied by pleasure.' Pleasure, however, may be called 'accompanied by joy,' but not 'accompanied by joy-and-pleasure.' In this triad, the two consciousness-arisings accompanied by displeasure, body-consciousness accompanied by pain, form, and Nibbāna are 'not to be stated.' Among the mental factors, joy is only 'accompanied by pleasure'; doubt is only 'accompanied by equanimity'; greed, wrong view, and conceit, along with twenty-five wholesome and indeterminate states, can be of three kinds. Mental pleasure may be 'accompanied by joy' in the first, second, and third jhānas; in the fourth jhānas, it may be 'not to be stated.' Bodily pleasure, pain, displeasure, all equanimity, hatred, envy, stinginess, and worry are only 'not to be stated.' The remaining seventeen dhammas may be of three kinds or may be 'not to be stated.' The rest is easily understood. The Triad of Joy.

Dassanenāti sotāpattimaggena. So hi paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti vutto. Gotrabhu pana kiñcāpi paṭhamataraṃ passati, yathā pana rañño santikaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena āgato puriso dūratova rathikāya carantaṃ hatthikkhandhagataṃ rājānaṃ disvāpi “diṭṭho te rājā”ti puṭṭho disvāpi kātabbakiccassa akatattā “na passāmī”ti vadati, evameva nibbānaṃ disvā kattabbassa kilesappahānassa abhāvā “dassana”nti na vuccati. Taṃ hi ñāṇaṃ maggassa āvajjanaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Bhāvanāyāti sesamaggattayena. Sesamaggattayaṃ hi paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhasmiṃyeva dhamme bhāvanāvasena uppajjati, adiṭṭhapubbaṃ kañci na passati, tasmā “bhāvanā”ti vuccati. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ.

'By seeing' means by the path of stream-entry. For it is called 'seeing' because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna. However, although the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) consciousness sees it even earlier, it is like a man who has come to the king on some business: even though from afar he sees the king mounted on an elephant proceeding along the road, when asked, 'Have you seen the king?' he replies, 'I have not seen him,' because the task to be done has not been accomplished. Even so, although it sees Nibbāna, because the task to be done—the abandonment of defilements—has not been accomplished, it is not called 'seeing.' For that knowledge stands in the position of adverting to the path. 'By development' means by the remaining three paths. For the remaining three paths arise by way of development with regard to the very same Dhamma already seen by the first path; they do not see anything not previously seen, therefore this is called 'development.' The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

Tattha cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādā, vicikicchāsahagato cāti pañca dassanena pahātabbāva, uddhaccasahagato bhāvanāya eva pahātabbo, avasesā cha akusalacittuppādā apāyahetubhāvena pavattito, appavattito ca siyā dassanenapahātabbā, siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbā, akusalavajjitā [M 0.0113] pana sabbe cittuppādā, rūpaṃ, nibbānañca nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbā. Cetasikesu pana diṭṭhi vicikicchā issā macchariyaṃ kukkuccaṃ dassanenapahātabbāva, sesā akusalā siyā dassanenapahātabbā, siyā bhāvanāyapahātabbāti tijātikā terasavidhā honti, vuttāvasesā nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbāva. Yaṃ pana “sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena satta bhave [V 0.0085] ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāre ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, etthete nirujjhantī”tiādinā (cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 6) nayena kusalābyākatānampi pahānaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ tesaṃ maggānaṃ abhāvitattā ye uppajjeyyuṃ, te upanissayapaccayānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahīnattā pahīnāti imaṃ pariyāyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Dassanenapahātabbattikaṃ.

Herein, the four consciousness-arisings associated with wrong view and the one accompanied by doubt—these five are to be abandoned only by seeing. The one accompanied by restlessness is to be abandoned only by development. The remaining six unwholesome consciousness-arisings may be abandoned either by seeing or by development. However, all consciousness-arisings apart from the unwholesome, as well as form and Nibbāna, are to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development. Among the mental factors, wrong view, doubt, envy, stinginess, and worry are to be abandoned only by seeing. The remaining unwholesome factors may be abandoned either by seeing or by development; thus they are of three kinds and are thirteen-fold. The aforementioned remaining factors are to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development. Furthermore, that the abandonment of wholesome and indeterminate states is also permitted is stated with reference to the method in the passage beginning: 'Through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, with the cessation of formative consciousness, having established seven existences, whatever name-and-form might arise in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, these cease here' (Cūḷaniddesa 6). This is said with reference to the following perspective: whatever states would arise because those higher paths have not been developed, they are considered abandoned because the defilements that are their support condition have been abandoned. And this is a triad without remainder. The Triad of What is to be Abandoned by Seeing.

Dassanena pahātabbo hetu etesanti dassanenapahātabbahetukā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Tatiyapade pana nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbo hetu etesanti evamatthaṃ aggahetvā nevadassanenanabhāvanāya pahātabbo hetu etesaṃ atthīti evamattho gahetabbo. Itarathā hi ahetukānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ bhaveyya. Hetu eva hi tesaṃ natthi, yo dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbo siyā. Sahetukesupi hetuvajjānaṃ pahānaṃ āpajjati, na hetūnaṃ. Hetuyeva hi etesaṃ nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabboti vutto, na te dhammā. Ubhayampi cetaṃ anadhippetaṃ, tasmā vuttanayena attho gahetabbo. Ito paraṃ sabbo vinicchayo anantarattikasadisova. Kevalaṃ cetasikesu vicikicchuddhaccasampayutto moho dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbahetukesu na pavisati sahajātassa aññassa hetuno abhāvā, nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbahetukesu [M 0.0114] pana pavisati. Lobhadosamūlacittesu pana hetūsu moho lobhena ceva dosena ca sahetuko, lobhadosā ca mohenevāti ime pahātabbahetukapade paviṭṭhāti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Dassanenapahātabbahetukattikaṃ.

They are 'with a root to be abandoned by seeing' because they have a root that is to be abandoned by seeing. The same method applies to the second term. In the third term, however, the meaning should not be taken as 'they have a root that is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' but rather the meaning should be taken thus: 'their root is not one to be abandoned by seeing or by development.' Otherwise, the rootless states would not be included, for they have no root at all that could be abandoned by seeing or by development. And even in the case of states with roots, this would imply the abandonment of what is other than the roots, not the roots themselves. For it is their root that is said to be 'one to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development,' not the states themselves. Both of these interpretations are unintended; therefore, the meaning should be taken in the way that was stated. From this point on, the entire analysis is similar to the immediately preceding triad. The only distinction is that, among the mental factors, the delusion associated with doubt and restlessness is not included among those 'with a root to be abandoned by seeing or by development,' because it has no other co-arisen root; however, it is included among those 'with a root not to be abandoned by seeing or by development.' But in consciousnesses rooted in greed and hatred, delusion has greed and hatred as its co-arisen roots, and greed and hatred have delusion as their co-arisen root; thus these are included in the term 'with a root to be abandoned.' This is the specific difference; the rest is the same. The Triad of States with a Root to be Abandoned by Seeing.

Kammakilesehi ācīyatīti ācayo, paṭisandhicutigatipavattisaṅkhātānaṃ upādinnakkhandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā nipphādanabhāvena taṃ ācayaṃ gacchanti, yassa vā pavattanti, taṃ puggalaṃ yathāvuttameva ācayaṃ gamentīti ācayagāmino. Tato eva ācayasaṅkhātā cayā apetattā nibbānaṃ apetaṃ cayāti apacayo, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanato apacayaṃ gacchantīti apacayagāmino. Apica pākāraṃ iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī viya pavattaṃ ācinantā gacchantīti ācayagāmino. Teneva vaḍḍhakinā citaṃ citaṃ viddhaṃsayamāno puriso viya tadeva pavattaṃ apacinantā gacchantīti apacayagāmino. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ.

It is called 'accumulation' (ācaya) because it is accumulated by kamma and defilements. This is a designation for the appropriated aggregates, described as rebirth-linking, decease, destination, and the ongoing process of existence. Because they are the cause and bring it about, they lead to that accumulation; or, they lead the person for whom they occur to that accumulation as stated before—thus, they are 'leading to accumulation' (ācayagāmino). Because Nibbāna is devoid of that which is called the heap (caya) or accumulation (ācaya), it is 'devoid of the heap' (apacaya). Because they proceed with that as their object, they are 'leading to non-accumulation' (apacayagāmino). Furthermore, just as a bricklayer proceeds building up a wall, so they proceed accumulating the ongoing process of existence—thus, they are 'leading to accumulation'. Just as a man, dismantling what was built by that very bricklayer, proceeds dismantling that same ongoing process of existence—thus, they are 'leading to non-accumulation'. The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

Tattha lokiyakusalākusalāni ācayagāmino nāma, cattāri maggāni apacayagāmino nāma[V 0.0086], sabbāni vipākaphalakiriyāni, rūpaṃ, nibbānañca nevaācayagāmino na apacayagāmino nāma. Cetasikesu pana akusalā ācayagāmino eva, karuṇā muditā siyā ācayagāmino, siyā nevācayagāmino na apacayagāmino nāma, sesā tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Ācayagāmittikaṃ.

Herein, worldly wholesome and unwholesome states are called 'leading to accumulation'. The four paths are called 'leading to non-accumulation'. All resultant, fruit, and functional states, as well as form and Nibbāna, are called 'neither leading to accumulation nor leading to non-accumulation'. Among the mental factors, unwholesome states are solely 'leading to accumulation'. Compassion and sympathetic joy may be 'leading to accumulation', or they may be 'neither leading to accumulation nor leading to non-accumulation'. The rest can be of all three kinds. And this is an exhaustive triad. The Triad of Leading to Accumulation.

Tīsu sikkhāsu jātā, sattannaṃ vā sekhānaṃ etetipi sekhā, apariyositasikkhattā sayameva sikkhantītipi sekhā. Upari sikkhitabbābhāvato na sekhāti asekhā, vuddhippattā vā sekhātipi asekhā. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ.

They are 'trainees' (sekhā) because they are engaged in the three trainings, or because they are among the seven kinds of trainees. They are also 'trainees' because they are still training themselves, their training being uncompleted. They are 'non-trainees' (asekhā) because there is nothing further for them to train in; or, they are 'non-trainees' because they have attained the culmination of training. The third term is stated by way of rejecting both.

Tattha [M 0.0115] cattāri lokuttarakusalāni, heṭṭhimāni ca tīṇi sāmaññaphalānīti satta sekhā nāma, arahattaphalaṃ asekhā nāma, lokiyacittāni, rūpaṃ, nibbānañca nevasekhā nāsekhā nāma. Cetasikesu pana akusalā ca appamaññā ca nevasekhā nāsekhā eva, sesā tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Sekhattikaṃ.

Herein, the four supramundane wholesome states and the three lower fruits of recluseship—these seven are called 'trainees'. The fruit of arahantship is called 'non-trainee'. Mundane consciousnesses, form, and Nibbāna are called 'neither trainee nor non-trainee'. Among the mental factors, the unwholesome ones and the immeasurables are solely 'neither trainee nor non-trainee'; the rest can be of all three kinds. And this is an exhaustive triad. The Triad of Trainees.

Samantato khaṇḍitattā appamattakaṃ parittanti vuccati “parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍa”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.96) ādīsu viya. Kāmāvacaradhammā hi appānubhāvatāya parittā viyāti parittā. Kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya, mahantavipulaphalatāya, dīghasantānatāya ca mahantabhāvaṃ gatā, mahantehi vā uḷāracchandavīriyacittapaññehi gatā paṭipannātipi mahaggatā. Pamāṇakarā dhammā rāgādayo pamāṇaṃ nāma, ārammaṇato vā sampayogato vā natthi etesaṃ pamāṇaṃ, pamāṇassa ca paṭipakkhāti appamāṇā.

Because it is limited in every respect, a small amount is called 'limited' (paritta), as in such phrases as 'a small lump of cow dung' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.96). Indeed, sense-sphere phenomena are 'limited' because they are of lesser power. Those states that have 'gone to greatness' (mahaggata)—either because they are capable of suppressing the defilements, because they bear great and abundant fruit, or because they extend over a long continuum—are called 'developed'. Or, because they are attained or entered upon by means of lofty aspiration, energy, consciousness, and wisdom, they are also called 'developed'. The phenomena that create limitation, such as lust and so on, are called 'measure' (pamāṇa). Because there is no measure for them, either in terms of object or in terms of association, and because they are the opposite of measure, they are 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa).

Tattha catupaññāsa kāmāvacaracittāni, rūpañca parittā nāma, sattavīsati rūpārūpāvacaracittāni mahaggatā nāma, lokuttaracittāni, nibbānañca appamāṇā nāma. Cetasikesu pana akusalā parittā eva, appamaññā parittamahaggatā eva, viratiyo parittaappamāṇā eva, sesā tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Parittattikaṃ.

Herein, the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses and form are called 'limited'. The twenty-seven fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousnesses are called 'developed'. The supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna are called 'immeasurable'. Among the mental factors, the unwholesome ones are solely 'limited'; the immeasurables are 'limited' and 'developed'; the abstinences are 'limited' and 'immeasurable'; while the rest can be of all three kinds. And this is an exhaustive triad. The Triad of the Limited.

Parittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etesanti parittārammaṇā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Sayaṃ parittā vā hontu mahaggatā vā, parittādidhamme ārabbha pavattā tadārammaṇāti vuccanti.

They are 'with a limited object' (parittārammaṇā) because they have a limited object. The same principle applies to the remaining two terms. Whether they themselves are limited or developed, when they arise in relation to limited and other such phenomena, they are said to be 'with that as their object'.

Tattha [V 0.0087] tevīsati kāmāvacaravipākā, kiriyāmanodhātuahetukajavanañca parittārammaṇāva, viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusalavipākakiriyāni mahaggatārammaṇāva, aṭṭha lokuttaracittāni appamāṇārammaṇāva, akusalacittāni [M 0.0116] ca aṭṭha ñāṇavippayuttajavanāni ca siyā parittārammaṇā, siyā mahaggatārammaṇā, siyā navattabbārammaṇatāya na vattabbā, na kadāci appamāṇārammaṇā, aṭṭha ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacarajavanāni, abhiññā, manodvārāvajjanañcāti ekādasa tidhāpi honti navattabbāpi. Tesu ca kusalāni pañca arahattamaggaphalavajjitasabbārammaṇāni. Tatthāpi taṃtaṃsekhānameva yathāsakaṃ maggaphalāni ārammaṇāni honti, kiriyāni cha sabbathāpi sabbārammaṇāni, abhiññāvajjitarūpāvacarāni ceva cha ākāsānañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatanacittāni ca niyamena paññattārammaṇatāya, rūpanibbānānañca anārammaṇatāya sabbathā navattabbāti. Cetasikesu pana akusalā akusalacittasadisāva, viratiyo siyā parittārammaṇā, siyā appamāṇārammaṇā, karuṇāmuditā navattabbāva, sesā tidhāpi honti siyā navattabbāti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Parittārammaṇattikaṃ.

Herein, the twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, the functional mind-element, and the rootless impulsion are solely 'with a limited object'. The wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception are solely 'with a developed object'. The eight supramundane consciousnesses are solely 'with an immeasurable object'. The unwholesome consciousnesses and the eight javanas dissociated from knowledge may be 'with a limited object' or 'with a developed object', or, because their object is ineffable, they are indeterminate; they are never 'with an immeasurable object'. The eleven—the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge, the two supernormal knowledge consciousnesses, and mind-door adverting—can be of all three kinds, and also indeterminate. Among these, the five wholesome ones take all objects except the path and fruit of Arahantship. Even then, for the respective trainees, their own respective paths and fruits become objects. The six functional ones can, in all ways, take all objects. The fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, excluding the supernormal knowledges, and the six consciousnesses of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of nothingness, because their object is by rule a concept and because they do not take form or Nibbāna as an object, are in all cases indeterminate. Among the mental factors, the unwholesome ones are like the unwholesome consciousnesses. The abstinences may be 'with a limited object' or 'with an immeasurable object'. Compassion and sympathetic joy are solely indeterminate. The rest can be of all three kinds or indeterminate. The remainder is easily understood. The Triad of Having a Limited Object.

Hīnāti lāmakā, akusalā dhammā. Hīnapaṇītānaṃ majjhe bhavāti majjhimā, avasesā tebhūmakā rūpārūpadhammāva. Uttamaṭṭhena, atappakaṭṭhena ca paṇītā, lokuttaracittanibbānāni. Cetasikesu pana akusalā hīnāva, karuṇāmuditā majjhimāva, sesakusalābyākatā majjhimapaṇītāva, sesā tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Hīnattikaṃ.

'Inferior' (hīna) means base; these are the unwholesome states. 'Middling' (majjhima) means existing between the inferior and the excellent; these are the remaining phenomena of the three planes. 'Excellent' (paṇīta) means supreme and incomparably excellent; these are the supramundane consciousnesses and Nibbāna. Among the mental factors, the unwholesome are solely 'inferior'. Compassion and sympathetic joy are solely 'middling'. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate states are either 'middling' or 'excellent'. The rest can be of all three kinds. And this is an exhaustive triad. The remainder is easily understood. The Triad of the Inferior.

“Hitasukhāvahā me bhavissantī”ti evaṃ āsīsitāpi tathā abhāvato, asubhādīsuyeva subhantiādiviparītappavattito ca micchā sabhāvāti micchattā, vipākadāne sati khandhabhedānantarameva vipākadānato niyatā, micchattā ca te niyatā cāti micchattaniyatā. Vuttaviparītena atthena sammā sabhāvāti sammattā, sammattā ca te niyatā cāti sammattaniyatā. Ubhayathāpi na niyatāti aniyatā.

Although one wishes, 'May they bring me benefit and happiness,' they are of a wrong nature (micchā sabhāva) because they are not so, and also because they proceed in a distorted way, such as regarding the foul as beautiful; thus they are 'wrongness' (micchatta). Because they give their result immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates, they are 'fixed' (niyata). Since they are both wrongness and fixed, they are 'fixed in wrongness' (micchattaniyata). In the opposite sense to what has been said, they are of a right nature (sammā sabhāva), thus they are 'rightness' (sammatta). Since they are both rightness and fixed, they are 'fixed in rightness' (sammattaniyata). Because they are not fixed in either way, they are 'unfixed' (aniyata).

Ānantarikabhāvena [M 0.0117] pavattiyaṃ siyā micchattaniyatā, aññathā pavattiyaṃ siyā aniyatā. Ahetukaakiriyanatthikadiṭṭhīsu hi aññatarā diṭṭhi yassa niyatā, taṃ buddhasatampi vibodhetuṃ [V 0.0088] na sakkoti. Yena ca anantare eva attabhāve phaladānato ānantarikesu mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakasaṅghabhedakalohituppādakasaṅkhātesu pañcasu kammesu ekampi kammaṃ paṭighacittena kataṃ hoti, so sineruppamāṇepi suvaṇṇathūpe katvā sakalacakkavāḷaṃ pūretvā nisinnasambuddhappamukhaṃ saṅghaṃ yāvajīvaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahitvāpi tena kusalena ānantarikassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhituṃ na sakkoti, ānantarikena pana adhikena ānantarikaṃ paṭibāhati, tasmā niyatamicchādiṭṭhi ānantarikā ca maggaphalānaṃ, mahaggatānañca paṭibāhakatāya anantarameva niraye vipākadānato micchattaniyatā ca jātā, cattāro pana maggā sammattaniyatā nāma, sesacittarūpanibbānāni aniyatā nāma. Cetasikesu pana moho ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ uddhaccaṃ lobho diṭṭhi doso thinaṃ middhanti ime nava siyā micchattaniyatā, siyā aniyatā, sesaakusalā, karuṇā, muditā ca aniyatā eva, sesakusalābyākatā siyā sammattaniyatā, siyā aniyatā, tijātikā pana tidhāpi honti, idañca nippadesattikanti. Micchattattikaṃ.

If it occurs as an immediate consequence, it may be 'wrongly determined'; otherwise, if it occurs otherwise, it may be 'undetermined'. Among the views of no cause, no action, and no consequence, whichever view is determined for someone, even a hundred Buddhas cannot awaken them. And for one who, in the very next life, gives the result due to immediately effective kamma—among the five deeds known as killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an arahant, causing schism in the Sangha, and shedding a Buddha's blood—if even one such deed is done with a hateful mind, then even if they were to build a golden stupa the size of Mount Sineru, fill the entire world-system with it, and serve the Sangha headed by the fully enlightened Buddha for life with the four requisites, they still could not ward off the result of that immediately effective kamma. However, a greater immediately effective kamma can ward off a lesser one. Therefore, wrongly determined wrong view and the immediately effective kammas are called 'wrongly determined' because they obstruct the path, fruits, and sublime states, and because they yield their result immediately in hell. The four paths, however, are called 'rightly determined'. The remaining consciousnesses, form, and Nibbāna are called 'undetermined'. Among mental factors, delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, restlessness, greed, wrong view, hatred, sloth, and torpor—these nine may be 'wrongly determined' or may be 'undetermined'. The remaining unwholesome states, compassion, and sympathetic joy are solely 'undetermined'. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate states may be 'rightly determined' or may be 'undetermined'. Those belonging to the three natures, however, are also of three kinds. And this is the exhaustive triad. The Triad of Wrongly Determined States.

Nibbānaṃ maggati, kilese vā mārento gacchatīti maggo, ariyamaggo, so ārammaṇametesanti maggārammaṇā. Lokiyo aṭṭhaṅgikopi maggo paccayaṭṭhena etesaṃ hetūti maggahetukā, maggasampayuttā dhammā. Magge vā hetūti maggahetū, alobhādayo. Te etesaṃ hetūti maggahetukā. Sammādiṭṭhi sayaṃ maggo ceva hetu ca, iti maggabhūto hetu etesanti maggahetukā, lokuttarāva[M 0.0118]. Abhibhavitvā pavattanaṭṭhena maggo adhipati ārammaṇabhūto, sahajāto vā etesanti maggādhipatino, tadubhayaṃ.

One seeks Nibbāna by the path; or the path is that which goes destroying the defilements—the Noble Path. The path is their object, thus, 'having the path as object'. The mundane eightfold path, in the sense of being a condition, is a cause for these, thus, 'having the path as cause', or, states concomitant with the path. Or, the causes in the path are path-causes—non-greed and so on. These are their causes, thus, 'having the path as cause'. Right view is itself both path and cause; thus, for these, the cause is the path itself, thus, 'having the path as cause'—solely the supramundane. The path, by overcoming and occurring, is the dominant condition, being either the object or co-arisen, thus, 'having the path as dominance'—both (object and co-arisen).

Tattha rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānakusalakiriyā ca abhiññābhūtā, manodvārāvajjanañca siyā maggārammaṇā, siyā navattabbā, ariyānaṃ hi cetopariyaanāgataṃsañāṇāni paresaññeva maggacittassa jānanakāle maggārammaṇāni, pubbenivāsañāṇamanodvārāvajjanāni pana attano, paresañcāpi tadaññārammaṇakāle pana navattabbāni, cetopariyañāṇassa pana niyamena paracittavisayattā tena attanā adhigatamaggaṃ ariyā ālambituṃ na sakkonti, anāgataṃsañāṇena pana attano anāgate uppajjanakassa uparimaggassa avisayattā na sakkonti. Ariyā hi yathāsakaṃ, heṭṭhimañca maggaphalaṃ jānituṃ sakkonti, na uparimaṃ. Tāni pana abhiññājavanāni maggena asahajātattā na maggahetukāni. Maggaṃ garuṃkatvā appavattanato [V 0.0089] na maggādhipatīni. Na hi tāni kiñci ārammaṇaṃ adhipatiṃ karonti, antamaso lokuttaramapi. Kasmā? Attano mahaggatatāya rājānaṃ disvā tassa mātāpitaro viya, manodvārāvajjanaṃ pana attano ahetukatāya rājānaṃ disvā khujjaceṭakādayo viya. Cattāri maggaṭṭhacittāni sabbadā maggahetukā eva, tāneva ca vīmaṃsāvīriyānaṃ adhipatibhāvena pavattiyaṃ siyā maggādhipatino, itaresaṃ chandacittānaṃ adhipatibhāvena pavattiyaṃ siyā navattabbā, aṭṭha ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacarajavanāni siyā maggārammaṇā, siyā maggādhipatino, siyā navattabbā. Tāni hi attanā, parehi ca paṭividdhamaggapaccavekkhaṇakāle maggārammaṇā, attano maggaṃ garuṃkatvā paccavekkhaṇakāle maggādhipatino ca tathāappavattiyaṃ navattabbā ca honti. Ariyā hi paresaṃ maggaphalāni paccavekkhantā [M 0.0119] garuṃ karontāpi attano maggaphalāni viya garuṃ na karonti, api sammāsambuddhānaṃ. Tesu sotāpanno sotāpannānameva maggaphalāni jānituṃ sakkoti, nāññesaṃ, sakadāgāmī pana sakadāgāmīnampi, na anāgāmiarahantānaṃ, anāgāmī pana anāgāmīnampi, na arahantānaṃ, arahā pana sabbesampi maggaphalāni jānāti, sobhanalokiyacittarūpanibbānāni navattabbāneva. Cetasikesu pana viratiyo lokuttarakusale maggasadisāva, aññattha navattabbā, karuṇā, muditā, akusalā ca navattabbā, sesā tidhāpi honti navattabbā ca. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti. Maggārammaṇattikaṃ.

Here, the wholesome and functional consciousness of the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, which have become direct knowledges, and mind-door adverting may have the path as their object, or they may be indeterminate. For noble ones, the knowledge of others' minds and future knowledge have the path as their object only when knowing the path-consciousness of others. The knowledge of past lives and mind-door adverting, however, regarding one's own and also others', are indeterminate when the object is other than the path. The knowledge of others' minds, being necessarily concerned with others' minds, cannot take the path attained by oneself as an object. The future knowledge cannot take the higher path to be attained in one's own future as its object, as it is beyond its scope. Noble ones can know their own respective lower paths and fruits but not the higher ones. Those direct-knowledge javanas are not caused by the path because they do not arise together with it. They do not have the path as their dominant condition because they do not arise emphasizing the path. Indeed, they do not take any object as dominant, not even the supramundane. Why? Due to their exalted nature, like the parents seeing a king. The mind-door adverting, however, being rootless, is like a hunchbacked servant seeing a king. The four path-moment consciousnesses are always path-causal. And when they arise with investigation and energy as dominant, they may be path-dominant. When they arise with desire and consciousness as dominant, they may be indeterminate. The eight knowledge-associated sense-sphere javanas may have the path as their object, may have the path as their dominant condition, or may be indeterminate. When reviewing the path realized by oneself or others, they have the path as their object. When reviewing while emphasizing one's own path, they have the path as their dominant condition. Otherwise, when not arising in such a way, they are indeterminate. Noble ones, even when reviewing others' paths and fruits with respect, do not esteem them as they do their own—not even those of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. A stream-enterer can know only the paths and fruits of stream-enterers, not those of others. A once-returner can know those of once-returners but not non-returners or arahants. A non-returner can know those of non-returners but not arahants. An arahant can know all paths and fruits. The beautiful mundane consciousnesses, form, and Nibbāna are always indeterminate. Among mental factors, the abstinences in the supramundane wholesome are like the path; elsewhere, they are indeterminate. Compassion, appreciative joy, and the unwholesome are indeterminate. The rest are of three kinds, and indeterminate as well. The rest is easily understood. The Triad of Having the Path as Object.

Uppannāti ettha vattamānabhūtāpagataokāsakatabhūmiladdhavasena uppannā anekappabhedā honti. Tattha sabbampi uppādajarābhaṅgasamaṅgīsaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhataṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma, ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhaṃ anubhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ kusalākusalañca uppādādittayaṃ anuppatvā niruddhaṃ bhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ, sesasaṅkhatañca bhūtāpagatuppannaṃ nāma, “yānissa tāni pubbekatāni kammānī”ti evamādinā nayena vuttaṃ kammaṃ atītampi samānaṃ aññaṃ vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitattā, tathākatokāsañca vipākaṃ anuppannampi ekaṃsena uppajjanakato okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma, tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamūhataṃ akusalaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma. Ettha ca vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā bhūmi nāma, tesu khandhesu uppattārahakilesajātā bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma, tehi kilesehi sā bhūmi laddhā hotīti evametesu uppannesu idha vattamānuppannā adhippetā.

Here, 'arisen' refers to the diverse kinds of arising in terms of present-arisen, past-gone, opportunity-created-arisen, and realm-obtained-arisen. Therein, all conditioned phenomena accompanied by arising, decay, and dissolution are called 'presently arisen'; what has ceased after experiencing the flavor of its object is the state known as 'experienced and past'; wholesome and unwholesome kamma that has ceased after undergoing the triad of arising, etc., is called 'past-gone'; and the remaining conditioned phenomena are called 'past-arisen.' As stated in the phrase, 'Whatever deeds were previously performed,' even past kamma, though it is past, by obstructing another result, stands having made an opportunity for its own result. And a result for which an opportunity has been so made, though not yet arisen, is called 'opportunity-created-arisen' because it is certain to arise. In those various realms, unabandoned unwholesome states are called 'realm-obtained-arisen.' Here, the five aggregates of the three realms, which are the object of insight, are called 'realm.' The defilements capable of arising in those aggregates are called 'realm-obtained.' Because that realm is obtained by those defilements, it is said they are 'realm-obtained.' Among these various kinds of 'arisen,' 'presently arisen' is what is intended here.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – pubbantato uppādato paṭṭhāya yāva bhaṅgā pannā gatā pavattāti uppannā, paccuppannāti [V 0.0090] attho[M 0.0120]. Na uppannāti anuppannā. Pariniṭṭhitakāraṇekadesattā avassaṃ uppajjissantīti uppādino, ubhayenāpi anāgatāva dassitā. Ayaṃ hi tiko dvinnaṃ addhānaṃ vasena pūretvā dassito. Laddhokāsassa hi kammassa vipāko uppādī nāma. Yadi pana āyūhitakusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ sabbaṃ vipākaṃ dadeyya, assa okāso na bhaveyya. Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti dhuvavipākaṃ, addhuvavipākañca. Tattha pañcānantarikaaṭṭhasamāpatticatutthamaggādi dhuvavipākaṃ nāma. Taṃ pana kammaṃ khaṇappattampi atthi appattampi. Tattha khaṇappattaṃ uppannaṃ nāma, appattaṃ anuppannaṃ nāma. Tassa duvidhassa ca vipāko duvidho hoti khaṇappatto ca appatto ca. Tattha khaṇappatto uppanno nāma, appatto cittānantare vā uppajjatu, kappasatasahassātikkame vā dhuvapaccayaṭṭhena uppādī nāma hoti. Metteyyassa bodhisattassa maggo anuppanno nāma hoti, phalaṃ uppādī nāma. Tattha catūsu bhūmīsu vipāko, kammajarūpañca vattamānuppannā nāma, uppajjanārahā uppādino nāma, na pana vattabbā “anuppannā”ti. Kusalākusalakiriyā, kammajarūpañca siyā uppannā, siyā anuppannā, na pana vattabbā “uppādino”ti. Cetasikesu pana akusalā akusalacittasadisāva, sesā duvidhāpi honti, atītā, panettha nibbānañca navattabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti. Uppannattikaṃ.

Herein, this is the meaning of the words: 'Arisen' (uppannā) means 'present' (paccuppannā), referring to that which has come to be, proceeded, and occurred from the prior end, from its arising up to its dissolution. That which has not arisen is 'unarisen' (anuppannā). Because a portion of its cause is complete, it will certainly arise; this is 'about to arise' (uppādino). By both of these, the future is indicated. This triad is shown as being fulfilled by means of two time periods. For a kamma that has obtained its opportunity, its result is called 'about to arise.' If all accumulated wholesome and unwholesome kamma were to yield their results, there would be no opportunity. But this kamma is of two kinds: that with fixed results (dhuvavipāka) and that with unfixed results (addhuvavipāka). Among them, the five heinous crimes, the eight attainments, the fourth path, and so on are called 'fixed results.' Such kamma may either have reached its moment or not. Among them, that which has reached its moment is called 'arisen,' while that which has not is called 'unarisen.' The result of these two kinds is also twofold: that which has reached its moment and that which has not. Among them, that which has reached its moment is called 'arisen,' while that which has not—whether it arises in the next mind-moment or after the passing of a hundred thousand aeons—is called 'about to arise' because its condition is fixed. The path of the Bodhisatta Metteyya is called 'unarisen,' but its fruit is called 'about to arise.' In the four planes of existence, resultant consciousness and kamma-born materiality are called 'presently arisen.' That which is fit to arise is called 'about to arise,' but it should not be called 'unarisen.' Wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousness, and kamma-born materiality, may be either 'arisen' or 'unarisen,' but they should not be called 'about to arise.' Among mental factors, the unwholesome ones are similar to unwholesome consciousness. The rest may be of both kinds. Past states and Nibbāna are here indeterminate. The rest is easily understood. The Triad of the Arisen.

Attano sabhāvaṃ, uppādādikkhaṇaṃ vā patvā taṃ atikkamitvā itā gatā pattāti atītā. Tadubhayampi na āgatāti anāgatā. Taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca uppannāti paccuppannā, sabbe saṅkhatā nāmarūpadhammā. Na saṅkhatadhammesu tekālikabhāvaṃ appatto nāma atthi, sabbepi te tidhā honti. Nibbānaṃ panettha navattabbanti. Atītattikaṃ.

Having attained its own nature or the moment of arising and so forth, and having passed beyond it, it has departed, gone, and arrived—thus, it is 'past' (atītā). As both of these have not yet come—thus, they are 'future' (anāgatā). Having arisen in dependence on this or that cause—thus, it is 'present' (paccuppannā), which refers to all conditioned phenomena, that is, name-and-form. There is no conditioned phenomenon that has not attained the state of belonging to the three time periods; all of them are threefold. Herein, Nibbāna is indeterminate. The Triad of the Past.

Atītaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etesanti atītārammaṇā. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

They have a past object, thus they are 'of past object.' The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

Tattha [M 0.0121] kusalavipākakiriyāvasena chabbidhāni viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanāni heṭṭhā atītasamāpattiṃ ārabbha pavattito atītārammaṇāni, dvipañcaviññāṇamanodhātuyo paccuppannārammaṇāva, sesā ekādasa kāmāvacaravipākā, ahetukahasanacittañca tidhāpi honti, sesakāmāvacarakiriyakusalākusalā ca abhiññābhūtarūpāvacaracatutthajjhānakusalakiriyā ca tidhāpi honti navattabbā ca. Tesu kāmāvacarānaṃ atītādīsu chasu ārammaṇesu pavattivibhāgo heṭṭhā vuttova. Navattabbatā pana tesu ñāṇavippayuttajavanakusalānaṃ [V 0.0091] paññattārammaṇavaseneva, na nibbānārammaṇavasena, tesupi tihetukajavanāvajjanānaṃ maggaphalarūpārūpajjhānānaṃ, purecārikabhāvenāpi nibbānacatukkajjhānavisayānañca paccavekkhaṇabhāvenāpi navattabbatā veditabbā, abhiññānaṃ pana iddhividhañāṇassa tāva kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmetvā kāyasannissitaṃ katvā dissamānena kāyena gacchantassa atītaṃ pādakajjhānacittaṃ ārabbha pavattanato atītārammaṇaṃ, “anāgatesu rūpāni evaṃ hontū”ti adhiṭṭhahantassa anāgatārammaṇaṃ, kāyaṃ pana cittasannissitaṃ katvā adissamānena kāyena gamanakāle, ajjhattaṃ kumāravaṇṇādīnaṃ, bahiddhāpāsādakūṭāgārādīnañca paccuppannānaṃ nimmānakāle ca paccuppannārammaṇañca tāva hotīti evaṃ iddhividhassa chabbidhampi ajjhattikaṃ, bāhirañca tekālikaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the six types of consciousness—wholesome, resultant, and functional—of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, when arising by taking a past attainment as their object, have past objects. The two sets of five sense-consciousnesses and the mind-element have only present objects. The remaining eleven sense-sphere resultant states and the rootless smile-producing consciousness can be threefold. The remaining sense-sphere functional, wholesome, and unwholesome states, as well as the wholesome and functional consciousness of the fourth form-sphere jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges, can also be threefold and are also indeterminate. Among them, the analysis of the occurrence of the sense-sphere states in the six objects—past and so on—has been stated below. The indeterminacy, however, for the wholesome javanas dissociated from knowledge, is only by way of a concept-object, not by way of Nibbāna as object. Even for these, the indeterminacy of the three-rooted javanas and adverting, of the path, fruition, and form and formless jhānas, should be understood both by way of being precursors to the four jhānas that have Nibbāna as their object, and by way of reviewing them. As for the direct knowledges, in the case of the power of magical manifestation: when one transforms the mind by means of the body, makes it dependent on the body, and travels with a visible body, it has a past object because it arises taking a past basis-jhāna consciousness as its object. For one who resolves, 'May forms in the future be thus,' it has a future object. But when one makes the body dependent on the mind and travels with an invisible body, or at the time of creating present phenomena—such as the appearance of a youth internally, or palaces and mansions externally—it has a present object. Thus, it should be understood that the power of magical manifestation has a sixfold internal and external object pertaining to the three time periods.

Dibbasotassa kucchigataṃ ajjhattikaṃ, bāhirañca paccuppannaṃ saddāyatanamevārammaṇaṃ. Cetopariyañāṇassa atīte sattadivasabbhantare, anāgate sattadivasabbhantare ca paresaññeva cittaṃ atītañca anāgatañcārammaṇaṃ hoti. Sattadivasātikkame panetaṃ paracittaṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti. Atītaṃsaanāgataṃsañāṇānaṃ [M 0.0122] hi esa visayo, na etassa. Paccuppannacittajānanakāle panassa paccuppannamārammaṇaṃ hoti.

The divine ear has as its object only the present sound-base, internal and external, that has come within its range. For the knowledge of others' minds, the object is the past and future mind of others within seven days in the past and within seven days in the future. Beyond seven days, it is not able to know another's mind. For this is the domain of the knowledges concerning a portion of the past and a portion of the future, not of this knowledge. But at the time of knowing a present mind, its object is the present.

Paccuppannañca nāmetaṃ tividhaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ addhāpaccuppannañcāti. Tattha uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgappattaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ nāma. Santatipaccuppannaṃ pana duvidhaṃ rūpārūpavasena. Tattha ātapaṭṭhānā āgantvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhassa yāva andhakārabhāvo na vigacchati, antogabbhe vā vasitvā divā ātapaṭṭhānaṃ olokentassa yāva akkhīnaṃ phandanabhāvo na vūpasammati, ayaṃ rūpasantati nāma. Dve tayo javanavārā arūpasantati nāma, tadubhayaṃ santatipaccuppannanti veditabbaṃ. Ekabhavaparicchinnaṃ addhāpaccuppannaṃ nāma. Imasmiṃ pana cetopariyañāṇavisaye katipayajavanavārā addhāpaccuppannaṃ nāma. Tattha khaṇapaccuppannaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ na hoti āvajjanena saddhiṃ nirujjhanato. Na hi āvajjanajavanānaṃ ettha bhinnārammaṇatā yuttā. Rūpasantatipaccuppannaṃ pana katipayajavanavāraparicchinnaṃ addhāpaccuppannaṃ assa ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Iddhimā hi parassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo āvajjeti, taṃ āvajjitakkhaṇe paccuppannacittamārammaṇaṃ katvā teneva saha nirujjhati. Tato tadeva niruddhaṃ cittamālambitvā cattāri, pañca vā javanāni uppajjanti, tesaṃ pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ, sesāni kāmāvacarajavanāni[V 0.0092]. Tesañca ekārammaṇattepi iddhicittameva parassa cittaṃ jānāti, na itarāni. Yathā cakkhudvāravīthiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇameva rūpaṃ passati, na itarāni, tesu ca āvajjanameva nippariyāyato paccuppannārammaṇaṃ, itarāni pana addhāsantativasena pariyāyatoti gahetabbaṃ, evametassa atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ cittamevārammaṇaṃ hoti, tañca kho parasseva, na attano.

This 'present' is threefold: the momentary present, the continuity present, and the duration present. Herein, that which has reached arising, presence, and dissolution is called the momentary present. The continuity present is twofold, by way of form and formless. Herein, for one who, having come from a sunny place, has entered a dark chamber, as long as the impression of darkness does not disappear; or for one dwelling inside a chamber and looking out at a sunny place during the day, as long as the flickering of the eyes does not cease—this is called form-continuity. Two or three javana-processes are called formless continuity. Both should be understood as the continuity present. That which is limited to a single existence is called the duration present. In this domain of the knowledge of others' minds, however, a few javana-processes are called the duration present. Herein, the momentary-present mind is not an object for the knowledge of others' minds because it ceases together with the adverting consciousness. For it is not fitting here that the adverting and the javanas have different objects. However, the continuity-present of form, limited by a few javana-processes, which constitutes the duration-present, becomes its object. For one with psychic power, wishing to know another’s mind, adverts. At the moment of adverting, having taken the present mind as object, the adverting consciousness ceases together with it. Then, taking that very ceased mind as object, four or five javanas arise. The last of these is the psychic-power mind, while the rest are sense-sphere javanas. And though they have a single object, only the psychic-power mind knows the other’s mind, not the others. Just as in the eye-door cognitive process, only eye-consciousness sees the form, not the other consciousnesses. And among them, only adverting has the present as its object directly, while the others should be understood to have it indirectly by way of duration and continuity. Thus, for this knowledge, the past, future, and present mind is its object—and that, indeed, only of another, not of oneself.

Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ pana nāmagottakasiṇapaññattādianussaraṇe, nibbānānussaraṇe ca navattabbārammaṇaṃ, saṅkhatadhammānussaraṇe [M 0.0123] atītārammaṇameva. Tassa hi atītesu sāsavānāsavesu, ajjhattikabāhiresu ca dhammesu anārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi, buddhānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasamagatikaṃ hoti. Yathākammūpagañāṇassa ajjhattikaṃ, bāhirañca atītaṃ kusalākusalacetanāmattameva. “Cetopariyañāṇassa cittamevārammaṇaṃ hoti, na taṃsampayuttadhammā”ti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, paṭṭhāne pana “kusalā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammūpagañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.404) vuttattā cetopariyañāṇayathākammūpagañāṇānaṃ cittasampayuttāpi cetanāsampayuttāpi cattāro khandhā ārammaṇaṃ honti evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The knowledge of past lives, however, has an inexpressible object when recollecting names, clans, kasiṇa concepts, and so on, and when recollecting Nibbāna; in the recollection of conditioned phenomena, it has only a past object. For this knowledge, there is no phenomenon whatsoever—whether past, with or without taints, internal or external—that is not an object; it is on a par with the omniscient knowledge of the Buddhas. The knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma takes only past wholesome and unwholesome volition as its object, whether internal or external. The commentaries state, 'The knowledge of others' minds has only consciousness as its object, not the associated mental factors.' However, in the Paṭṭhāna, it is said: 'The wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object-condition for the knowledge of psychic powers, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future.' Therefore, it should be understood that for the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of the faring of beings according to their kamma, the four aggregates—those associated with consciousness and those associated with volition—do indeed serve as objects.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇassa pana ajjhattikaṃ, bāhirañca paccuppannaṃ vaṇṇāyatanamevārammaṇaṃ. Anāgataṃsañāṇassa chabbidhampi anāgatameva ajjhattañca bāhirañcārammaṇaṃ, idampi pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ viya anāgate sabbaññutaññāṇasadisanti. Evaṃ abhiññānaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannesu, navattabbesu ca ajjhattikabāhiresu chasu ārammaṇesu yathāyogaṃ pavatti veditabbā. Sesāni pannarasa rūpāvacaracittāni, ākāsānañcāyatanaākiñcaññāyatanakusalavipākakiriyāni, aṭṭha lokuttaracittāni, rūpanibbānāni ca navattabbāni. Cetasikesu pana appamaññā navattabbāva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Atītārammaṇattikaṃ.

The divine eye knowledge has only the present visible-form base as its object, both internal and external. For the knowledge of the future, all six kinds of future objects, both internal and external, are its objects. This knowledge, like the knowledge of past lives, is similar to the omniscient knowledge with regard to the future. Thus, the functioning of the higher knowledges should be understood as occurring in relation to the six objects—past, future, present, and inexpressible, both internal and external—as is appropriate. The remaining fifteen form-sphere consciousnesses; the wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness; the eight supramundane consciousnesses; and material form and Nibbāna are inexpressible. Among the mental factors, the immeasurables are indeed inexpressible. The rest is easily understood. The Triad of Past Objects.

“Evaṃ pavattamānā mayaṃ attāti gahaṇaṃ gamissāmā”ti iminā viya adhippāyena attānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā pavattāti ajjhattā. Ajjhatta-saddo panāyaṃ gocarajjhatte niyakajjhatte ajjhattajjhatte visayajjhatteti catūsu atthesu dissati. “Ajjhattarato [M 0.0124] samāhito”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 362) hi ayaṃ gocarajjhatte dissati. “Ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu [V 0.0093] (dī. ni. 2.373) niyakajjhatte. “Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanānī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.304) ajjhattajjhatte. “Ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.187) visayajjhatte, issariyaṭṭhāneti attho. Phalasamāpatti hi buddhānaṃ issariyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Idha panāyaṃ niyakajjhatte vattati, tasmā attano santāne pavattā pāṭipuggalikā rūpārūpadhammā idha ajjhattāti veditabbā. Tato bahibhūtā indriyabaddhā vā anindriyabaddhā vā rūpārūpapaññattiyo bahiddhā nāma, tatiyapadaṃ tadubhayavasena vuttaṃ.

It is called 'internal' (ajjhattā) because it proceeds by making the self its basis, as if with the intention, 'Thus occurring, we will grasp it as self.' The word 'ajjhatta' (internal) is found in four senses: internal as to sphere (gocarajjhatta), internal as to one's own (niyakajjhatta), intrinsically internal (ajjhattajjhatta), and internal as to domain (visayajjhatta). For instance, in 'delighting internally, composed' (Dhp. 362), it is found in the sense of internal as to sphere. In 'one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally' (DN 2.290), it is in the sense of internal as to one's own. In 'the six internal sense bases' (MN 3.239), it is in the sense of intrinsically internal. In 'having entered upon internal emptiness, one dwells' (MN 3.111), it is in the sense of internal as to domain, which means a state of mastery (issariyaṭṭhāna). For the fruition attainment of the Buddhas is called a state of mastery. Here, however, it is used in the sense of internal as to one's own. Therefore, the personal material and immaterial phenomena that occur in one's own continuity should be understood here as 'internal.' External to that, the material phenomena, immaterial phenomena, and concepts—whether bound to the sense faculties or not bound to the sense faculties—are called 'external.' The third term is stated with reference to both of these.

Tattha sabbāni cittacetasikāni indriyabaddharūpaṃ tidhā honti, anindriyabaddharūpaṃ, nibbānapaññattiyo ca bahiddhāva. Imasmiṃ hi tike kusalattike alabbhamānā paññattiyopi labbhanti ṭhapetvā ākiñcaññāyatanārammaṇaṃ, tadeva idha navattabbaṃ. Teneva hi bhagavatā anantarattike “kasiṇādipaññattārammaṇāni kāmarūpāvacarādicittāni bahiddhārammaṇāni, ākiñcaññāyatanañca navattabba”nti vuttaṃ, idañca nippadesattikaṃ. Ajjhattattikaṃ.

Therein, all consciousnesses, mental factors, and faculty-bound material form can be threefold. Non-faculty-bound material form, Nibbāna, and concepts are only external. In this triad, concepts not found in the wholesome triad are also included, with the exception of the object of the base of nothingness; that alone is inexpressible here. For this very reason, the Blessed One said in the immediately following triad, 'Consciousnesses of the sense sphere, form sphere, etc., that have kasiṇa concepts and so on as their object, have external objects, but the base of nothingness is inexpressible.' And this is an exhaustive triad. The Triad on the Internal.

Yathāvutte ajjhattādike ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattānaṃ vasena ayaṃ tiko vutto. Tattha chabbidhāni viññāṇañcāyatananevasaññānāsaññāyatanacittāni ajjhattārammaṇāneva, ākāsānañcāyatanattayaṃ, rūpāvacaralokuttaracittāni ca bahiddhārammaṇāneva, voṭṭhabbanavajjitā ahetukamahāvipākā tidhāpi honti, avasesā pana ākiñcaññāyatanavajjitāni āvajjanajavanāni, abhiññā ca siyā tidhāpi honti, ākiñcaññāyatanārammaṇassa āvajjanaparikammapaccavekkhaṇādibhāvappavattiyaṃ siyā navattabbāti. Tesaṃ [M 0.0125] ajjhattādiārammaṇatā anantarattike, heṭṭhā ca vuttanayānusārena ñātabbā, ākiñcaññāyatanattayaṃ, pana rūpanibbānāni ca navattabbāva. Cetasikesu pana appamaññāviratī bahiddhārammaṇāva, sesā tidhāpi honti navattabbā ca. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ajjhattārammaṇattikaṃ.

This triad is stated with reference to the occurrence of states that take the aforesaid internal, etc., as their object. Therein, the six kinds of sense consciousness, the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness, and the consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have only internal objects. The three consciousnesses of the base of infinite space, and the form-sphere and supramundane consciousnesses, have only external objects. The rootless and great resultant consciousnesses, excluding the determining consciousness, can be of three kinds. The remaining advertence and impulsion consciousnesses, excluding those related to the base of nothingness, and the higher knowledges can be of three kinds. When there is an occurrence of advertence, preparation, reviewing, etc., with the base of nothingness as object, it may be inexpressible. Their having internal, etc., objects should be understood according to the method stated in the immediately preceding triad and below. The three consciousnesses of the base of nothingness, as well as material form and Nibbāna, are indeed inexpressible. Among the mental factors, the immeasurables and the abstinences have only external objects; the rest can be of three kinds and also inexpressible. The rest is easily understood. The Triad on Internal Objects.

Daṭṭhabbabhāvasaṅkhātena saha nidassanenāti sanidassanā, paṭihananabhāvasaṅkhātena saha paṭighenāti sappaṭighā, sanidassanā ca te sappaṭighā cāti sanidassanasappaṭighā, rūpāyatanameva. Nīlādibhedamupādāya pana bahuvacananiddeso. Natthi etesaṃ daṭṭhabbabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ nidassananti anidassanā, anidassanā ca te vuttanayena sappaṭighā cāti anidassanasappaṭighā, [V 0.0094] sesāni oḷārikarūpāni. Tatiyapadaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena vuttaṃ, sukhumarūpacittacetasikanibbānāni anidassanaappaṭighā nāma, idañca nippadesattikanti veditabbaṃ. Sanidassanattikaṃ.

'With appearance' (sanidassanā) means with the appearance characterized as the state of being visible. 'With resistance' (sappaṭighā) means with the resistance characterized as the state of being struck. Those that are 'with appearance and with resistance' (sanidassanasappaṭighā) are the visible-form base alone. The plural designation is used on account of the distinctions of blue, etc. 'Without appearance' (anidassanā) means for which there is no appearance characterized as the state of being visible. Those that are 'without appearance and with resistance' (anidassanasappaṭighā), in the way stated, are the remaining gross material forms. The third term is stated by the negation of both: subtle material form, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna are called 'without appearance and without resistance.' This should be understood as an exhaustive triad. The Triad on the Visible.

Tikamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Triad Matrix is concluded.

Abhidhammadukamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Dual Matrix.

Dukamātikāya pana heṭṭhā anāgatapadatthavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma. Hetugocchake tāva hetū dhammāti ettha hetuhetu paccayahetu uttamahetu sādhāraṇahetūti catubbidhā hetū. Tattha alobhādayo cha dhammā hetuhetū nāma, upādārūpādīnaṃ mahābhūtādayo paccayahetū nāma, vipākuppattiyaṃ kusalākusalaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇañca uttamahetū nāma, saṅkhārādīnaṃ avijjādayo sādhāraṇahetū nāma. Idha pana hetuhetu adhippeto. Hetū dhammāti mūlaṭṭhena hetusaṅkhātā dhammā, “hetudhammā”tipi pāṭho, soyevattho. Na hetūti tesaññeva paṭikkhepavacanaṃ.

Now, in the Dual Matrix, we will hereafter explain only the meaning of the terms that have not yet been discussed. First, in the Cluster on Roots, regarding the phrase 'states that are roots,' there are four kinds of roots: root as root-cause (hetuhetu), root as condition (paccayahetu), root as supreme cause (uttamahetu), and root as general cause (sādhāraṇahetu). Among these, the six states beginning with non-greed are called 'root as root-cause.' The great elements and so on, for derived material form and so on, are called 'root as condition.' In the arising of a resultant, wholesome and unwholesome kamma, and desirable and undesirable objects, are called 'root as supreme cause.' For formations and so on, ignorance and so on are called 'root as general cause.' Here, however, 'root as root-cause' is intended. 'States that are roots' means states designated as roots in the sense of being an origin. The reading 'root-states' (hetudhammā) is also found, with the same meaning. 'States that are not roots' is the term negating those very states.

Tattha [M 0.0126] alobho adoso amohoti kusalābyākatā tayo, lobho doso mohoti akusalā tayo cāti ime cha dhammā hetū nāma. Ime ṭhapetvā avasesā cetasikā, sabbāni ca cittāni, rūpanibbānāni cāti ime dhammā na hetū nāma, idañca nippadesadukanti veditabbaṃ. Hetudukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Therein, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the three that are wholesome and indeterminate; greed, hatred, and delusion are the three that are unwholesome. These six states are called roots. Excluding these, the remaining mental factors, all consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna—these states are called 'not roots.' This should be understood as an exhaustive pair. The First Pair: on Roots.

Sampayogato pavattena saha hetunāti sahetukā. Tatheva pavatto natthi etesaṃ hetūti ahetukā.

'With roots' (sahetukā) means occurring together with a root by way of association. 'Rootless' (ahetukā) means states for which there is no root occurring in the same way.

Tattha ahetukacittavajjitāni ekasattati cittāni sahetukā nāma. Tesu dve mohamūlāni moheneva sahetukāni, aṭṭha lobhamūlāni lobhamohehi dvīhi, dve dosamūlāni dosamohehi, dvādasa ñāṇavippayuttakusalābyākatāni alobhādosehi, sesāni sattacattālīsa alobhādīhi tīhipi sahetukānīti, mohamūlesu pana moho, dvipañcaviññāṇaṃ, manodhātu, santīraṇattayaṃ, voṭṭhabbanaṃ, hasituppādakāni aṭṭhārasa cittāni, rūpanibbānāni cāti ime dhammā ahetukā nāma. Cetasikesu pana lobhadosā, vicikicchā ca moheneva sahetukā, diṭṭhimāno [V 0.0095] lobhamohehi dvīhi, issāmacchariyakukkuccāni dosamohehi, moho pana siyā lobhena, siyā dosenāti dvīhi sahetukopi mohamūlesu ahetukopi, thinamiddhāni siyā lobhamohehi, siyā dosamohehīti tīhipi sahetukāni, ahirikānottappauddhaccāni tathā ca kevalamohena ca, amoho pana alobhādoseheva dvīhi, alobho siyā adosāmohehi, siyā adosenāti [M 0.0127] dvīhi, adoso siyā alobhāmohehi, siyā alobhenāti dvīhi, sesā pana dvāvīsati kusalābyākatā siyā tīhi, siyā dvīhipi hetūhi sahetukā, chando pana yathāyogaṃ tīhi, pītidosavajjitehi pañcahi siyā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi, sesā ekādasa tijātikā chahi hetūhi sahetukāpi ahetukāpi, vedanā cettha domanassabhūtā dvihetukāva, somanassaupekkhā yathāyogaṃ dosavajjitehi pañcahi sahetukāpi ahetukāpi, sukhadukkhabhūtā ahetukāva, idañca nippadesadukanti. Dutiyaṃ.

Here, the seventy-one consciousnesses, excluding the rootless consciousnesses, are called 'with roots'. Among them, the two rooted in delusion are with delusion alone as their root; the eight rooted in greed are with greed and delusion as their two roots; the two rooted in hatred are with hatred and delusion as their two roots; the twelve wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge are with non-greed and non-hatred as their two roots; and the remaining forty-seven are with all three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—as their roots. However, delusion in the delusion-rooted consciousnesses; the two sets of fivefold sense consciousnesses; the mind element; the three investigating consciousnesses; the determining consciousness; and the smile-producing consciousness—these eighteen consciousnesses—along with material form and Nibbāna, are called 'rootless states'. Among the mental factors, greed, hatred, and doubt are with delusion alone as their root. Wrong view and conceit are with greed and delusion as their two roots. Envy, avarice, and worry are with hatred and delusion as their two roots. Delusion, however, may be with greed or with hatred, thus it is with two roots; but in the delusion-rooted consciousnesses, it is rootless. Sloth and torpor may be with greed and delusion or with hatred and delusion, thus they are with three roots.
