Shamelessness, recklessness, and restlessness are likewise associated with greed-and-delusion or hatred-and-delusion, and also with delusion alone. Non-delusion, however, is with non-greed and non-hatred as its two roots. Non-greed may be with non-hatred and non-delusion, or with non-hatred alone, thus it is with two roots. Non-hatred may be with non-greed and non-delusion, or with non-greed alone, thus it is with two roots. The remaining twenty-two wholesome and indeterminate mental factors may be with three roots or with two roots. Intention, depending on the case, may be with roots (with three roots) or rootless; likewise, joy, associated with the five roots excluding hatred, may be with roots or rootless. The remaining eleven mental factors of three origins may be with roots (with six roots) or rootless. Regarding feeling, that which is sorrow is always with two roots. Pleasant and neutral feelings, depending on the case and associated with the five roots excluding hatred, may be with roots or rootless. That which is happiness and suffering is always rootless. And this is the pair without residue. The second.

Ekuppādāditāya hetunā sampayuttāti hetusampayuttā. Hetunā vippayuttāti hetuvippayuttā. Ayaṃ hetusampayuttaduko anantare vuttasahetukadukena atthato ninnānākaraṇo. Sahetukaduko eva hi bhagavatā desanāvilāsena, tathā bujjhanakapuggalānaṃ vā ajjhāsayavasena hetusampayuttadukabhāvenāpi vutto. Evaṃ uparipi samānatthadukānaṃ vacane kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tatiyaṃ.

Because they are associated with a root by way of arising together and so forth, they are 'associated with roots'. Those dissociated from a root are 'dissociated from roots'. This pair, 'associated with roots,' is not different in meaning from the immediately preceding pair, 'with roots'. Indeed, the 'with roots' pair was taught by the Blessed One due to elegance in teaching, or according to the inclination of those who are to understand it, even as the 'associated with roots' pair. Similarly, the reason for stating other pairs with the same meaning should be understood in what follows. The third.

Catutthādayo pana yasmā paṭhamadukadutiyatatiyadukesu paṭhamapadena yojetvā dve dukā, paṭhamaduke ca pacchimapadaṃ dutiyadukena yojetvā ekaṃ dukanti tayo dukā desitā, tasmā tesaṃ padattho vuttanayova.

However, since the fourth and subsequent pairs are taught as three pairs—namely, two pairs formed by combining the first term of the first pair with the second and third pairs respectively, and one pair formed by combining the last term of the first pair with the second pair—therefore, the meaning of their terms is as previously stated.

Tattha ca yatheva “hetū ceva dhammā sahetukā ca, sahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū”ti ayaṃ duko sambhavati, tathā “hetū ceva dhammā ahetukā ca, ahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū”ti ayampi sambhavati. Iminā nayena hetusampayuttadukena yojanāyapi eko [M 0.0128] labbhati. Yathā ca “na hetū kho pana dhammā sahetukāpi, ahetukāpī”ti ayaṃ labbhati, tathā “hetū kho pana dhammā sahetukāpi, ahetukāpī”ti ayampi. Yathā cettha sahetukaduke dve dukā, evaṃ hetusampayuttadukepi “na hetū kho pana dhammā hetusampayuttāpi, hetuvippayuttāpī”ti ca “hetū kho pana dhammā hetusampayuttāpi, hetuvippayuttāpī”ti ca dve dukā labbhantīti aparepi pañca dukā hetugocchake yojetuṃ sakkā. Te pana bhagavatā vuttānusāreneva sakkā ñātunti chasu eva [V 0.0096] saṅgahitāti veditabbā. Tattha ye tāva ekasmiṃ citte dve tayo hetū ekato uppajjanti, te hetū ceva aññoññāpekkhāya sahetukā ca nāma. Sahetukacittesu pana hetuṃ ṭhapetvā sesā cittacetasikā dhammā sahetukā ceva na ca hetū nāma. Imasmiṃ duke sabbe ahetukadhammā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana hetuvajjitā akusalā ceva kusalābyākatā ca, chando ca sahetuko ceva na hetu eva, sesā tijātikā, tathā navattabbā ca, moho pana hetu ceva sahetuko ca navattabbo ca. Catutthaṃ.

Here, just as the pair 'states that are roots and states with roots; states with roots but not roots' arises, so too does the pair 'states that are roots and rootless states; rootless states but not roots' also arise. In this way, by combining with the 'associated with roots' pair, one more is obtained. Just as 'states that are not roots, however, may be with roots or rootless' is obtained, so too 'states that are roots, however, may be with roots or rootless' is also obtained. Just as here, in the case of the 'with roots' pair, two pairs arise, similarly, in the 'associated with roots' pair, two pairs are obtained: 'states that are not roots, however, may be associated with roots or dissociated from roots,' and 'states that are roots, however, may be associated with roots or dissociated from roots'. Thus, five more pairs can be included in the Root Cluster. However, these can be known only in accordance with what was stated by the Blessed One, so they should be understood as already encompassed by the six. Here, the two or three roots that arise together in a single consciousness are called both 'roots' and, in dependence on each other, 'with roots'. But in consciousnesses with roots, the remaining consciousness and mental factors, excluding the roots, are called 'with roots but not roots'. In this pair, all rootless states are not to be stated. But among mental factors, the unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate ones, excluding the roots, and also intention, are 'with roots but not a root'. The remaining mental factors of three origins are likewise not to be stated. Delusion, however, which is both a root and with roots, is also not to be stated. The fourth.

Anantaradukopi iminā dukena sabbathāpi sadisovāti. Pañcamaṃ.

The immediately following pair is in every way similar to this pair. The fifth.

Sahetukacittesu hetuvajjitā cittacetasikā dhammā nahetū sahetū nāma, ahetukacittarūpanibbānāni nahetū ahetukā nāma. Imasmiṃ pana duke cha hetū na vattabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

In consciousnesses with roots, the consciousness and mental factors devoid of roots are called 'not roots' and 'with roots'. Rootless consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are called 'not roots' and 'rootless'. However, in this pair, the six roots are not to be stated. The rest is easily understood. The sixth.

Hetugocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Root Cluster is completed.

Sattasu [M 0.0129] cūḷantaradukesu attano nipphādakena saha paccayenāti sappaccayā, cittacetasikarūpāni. Natthi etesaṃ uppāde vā ṭhitiyaṃ vā paccayo ahutvā bhavanassevābhāvāti appaccayā, nibbānameva. Desanāya panettha paramatāya sotapatitavasena bahuvacananiddeso kato. Evaṃ sanidassanādīsupi. Idañca ito parāni cha ca nippadesadukānīti veditabbāni. Tato parañca yattha “ime na vattabbā”ti na vakkhāma, taṃ nippadesanti gahetabbaṃ. Sappaccayadukaṃ.

In the seven minor intermediate pairs, 'with conditions' refers to consciousness, mental factors, and material form, because they are with their own producing conditions. 'Without conditions' refers to Nibbāna alone, for which there is no condition for its arising or persistence, because it does not come into being after not having been. Here, the plural designation is made for the sake of the ultimate teaching, by way of being heard. The same applies to 'with indication' and so forth. It should be understood that this and the six pairs following it are 'pairs without residue'. Furthermore, wherever we do not say, 'These are not to be stated,' that should be taken as 'without residue'. The With-Conditions Pair.

Paccayehi samāgantvā katāti saṅkhatā. Na saṅkhatāti asaṅkhatā. Idañca sabbathā sappaccayadukasadisameva. Sappaccayasaṅkhataubhayadukaṃ sabbathā sadisameva. Saṅkhatadukaṃ.

What is 'conditioned' is that which is made by the coming together of conditions. What is 'unconditioned' is that which is not conditioned. This pair is entirely similar to the 'with conditions' pair. Both the 'with conditions' pair and the 'conditioned' pair are entirely similar. The Conditioned Pair.

Rūpāyatanaṃ sanidassanaṃ nāma. Sesarūpacittacetasikanibbānāni anidassanā nāma. Sanidassanadukaṃ.

The visible-form base is called 'with indication'. The remaining material forms, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna are called 'without indication'. The With-Indication Pair.

Pasādavisayarūpāni [V 0.0097] dvādasa sappaṭighā nāma. Sesarūpacittacetasikanibbānāni appaṭighā nāma. Sappaṭighadukaṃ.

The twelve material forms—the sensitive material forms and the object material forms—are called 'with impact'. The remaining material forms, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna are called 'without impact'. The With-Impact Pair.

Avinibbhogavasena rūpaṃ etesaṃ atthīti rūpino, ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ vā rūpaṃ, taṃ etesaṃ atthīti rūpino, bhūtopādāyarūpameva. Na rūpino arūpino, cittacetasikanibbānāni. Rūpidukaṃ.

They are 'material' because they possess materiality which has the characteristic of being afflicted; or because they possess materiality in the sense of inseparability—this refers only to the primary and derived material forms. What is not material is 'immaterial'—consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna. The Material Pair.

Loko vuccati lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena vaṭṭaṃ, tasmiṃ pariyāpannabhāvena loke niyuttāti lokiyā, pañcupādānakkhandhā. Tato lokato tattha apariyāpannabhāvena uttiṇṇāti lokuttarā, ariyamaggaphalanibbānāni. Cetasikesu panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ asekhattike vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Lokiyadukaṃ.

The world (loka) is called 'the round' (vaṭṭa) in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating; what is 'mundane' means the five aggregates subject to clinging, because they are included in that world. What is 'supramundane' means the noble path, fruition, and Nibbāna, because they have transcended that world by not being included in it. Here, what should be stated regarding mental factors should be understood in the way stated in the 'non-trainee' triad. The Mundane Pair.

Kenaci [M 0.0130] viññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇādīsu kenaci ekena cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇādinā vā vijānitabbā. Kenaci na viññeyyāti teneva cakkhuviññāṇena vā sotaviññāṇādinā vā na kenaci vijānitabbāni. Evaṃ hi sati dvinnampi padānaṃ atthanānattato duko hoti. Padabhājanīyasmimpi “ye te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā, na te dhammā sotaviññeyyā”ti (dha. sa. 1101) ettakaṃ ekadukanti aggahetvā “ye te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā, na te dhammā sotaviññeyyā, ye vā pana te dhammā sotaviññeyyā, na te dhammā cakkhuviññeyyā”ti (dha. sa. 1101) ayameko dukoti veditabbo. Tassa pana rūpaṃ cakkhuviññeyyaṃ, saddo na cakkhuviññeyyoti ayamattho. Evaṃ sesesupi dukaparicchedo ñātabbo. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhunā vā cakkhuviññāṇena vā viññeyyaṃ nāma. Sesarūpārūpadhammā teneva cakkhunā vā cakkhuviññāṇena vā kenaci naviññeyyā. Evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyatabbiññāṇamūlikāsupi catūsu yojanāsu vibhāgo yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbo. Rūpādayo pana pañcavisayā manodhātuttayena kenaci viññeyyā. Sesarūpārūpadhammā teneva manodhātuttayena kenaci naviññeyyā. Kiñcāpi sāmaññato manoviññāṇena aviññeyyassa abhāvato pāḷiyaṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyavasena duko na vutto, tathāpi visesato vattabbova. Tathā hi chabbidhāpi kāmāvacaradhammā kāmāvacaravipākādinā manoviññāṇena kenaci viññeyyā, rūpārūpāvacaralokuttarapaññattiyo teneva kenaci naviññeyyā. Tathā kāmarūpārūpāvacarapaññattiyo akusalādinā [V 0.0098] kenaci viññeyyā, lokuttarā teneva kenaci naviññeyyā. Tathā nibbānaṃ lokuttarena kenaci viññeyyaṃ[M 0.0131], sesalokiyalokuttarā teneva kenaci naviññeyyāti iminā nayena rūpārūpāvacarādibhedena manoviññāṇena kenaci viññeyyāviññeyyadhammā yathāyogaṃ yojetabbā. Evaṃ sabbe dhammā kenaci viññeyyā, kenaci na viññeyyā nāma. Imasmiñca duke paññattiyopi labbhantīti veditabbāti. Kenaciviññeyyadukaṃ.

"Cognizable by some" means that they are to be cognized by any one among eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and so forth, such as by eye-consciousness or by ear-consciousness. "Not cognizable by some" means they are not to be cognized by that same eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness, and so forth. In this way, due to the difference in meaning between the two terms, the dyad arises. Even in the word-analysis, in the phrase, "Those phenomena that are cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear" (Dhs. 1101), instead of taking just this much as a single dyad, it should be understood as: "Those phenomena that are cognizable by the eye are not cognizable by the ear, and those phenomena that are cognizable by the ear are not cognizable by the eye" (Dhs. 1101). This is one dyad. Here, the meaning is that form is cognizable by the eye, but sound is not cognizable by the eye. The division of dyads should be understood in the same way for the remaining ones. In this context, the form-base is called cognizable by the eye or by eye-consciousness. The remaining material and immaterial phenomena are not cognizable by that same eye or eye-consciousness. Similarly, the distinction should be understood appropriately in the four applications rooted in ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. However, the five sense objects, such as form, are cognizable by any of the three mind-elements. The remaining material and immaterial phenomena are not cognizable by those same three mind-elements. Although, generally speaking, since there is nothing that is not cognizable by mind-consciousness, the dyad is not stated in the Pāli in terms of what is cognizable by mind-consciousness, nevertheless, it should be stated specifically. For example, all six kinds of sense-sphere phenomena are cognizable by some mind-consciousness, such as sense-sphere resultant consciousness, whereas form-sphere, formless-sphere, supramundane phenomena, and concepts are not cognizable by that same mind-consciousness. Similarly, phenomena of the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere, and concepts are cognizable by some, such as unwholesome consciousness, whereas supramundane phenomena are not cognizable by that same consciousness. Likewise, Nibbāna is cognizable by some supramundane consciousness, whereas the remaining mundane and supramundane phenomena are not cognizable by that same consciousness. In this way, phenomena cognizable and not cognizable by some mind-consciousness, according to their divisions such as form-sphere and formless-sphere, should be appropriately applied. Thus, all phenomena are called 'cognizable by some' and 'not cognizable by some'. And it should be understood that in this dyad, concepts are also included. The Dyad of 'Cognizable by Some'.

Cūḷantaradukā niṭṭhitā.

The Minor Intermediate Dyads are concluded.

Āsavagocchake āsamantato savantīti āsavā, cakkhutopi…pe… manatopi savanti, pavattantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammato yāvagotrabhuṃ, okāsato yāvabhavaggā savantīti vā āsavā, ete dhamme, etañca okāsaṃ antokaritvā pavattantīti attho. Antokaraṇattho hi ayaṃ ā-kāro. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādiāsavā viyātipi āsavā. Yadi ca cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena āsavā, ete eva bhavituṃ arahanti. Anādittā āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantītipi āsavā. Tato aññe no āsavā nāma.

In the Taint Cluster (Āsavagocchaka), they are called taints (āsavā) because they flow all around. They flow from the eye... and so forth... up to the mind; thus it is said that they occur. Or, they are taints because, from the standpoint of the Dhamma, they flow up to the gotrabhu (change of lineage) consciousness, and from the standpoint of location, they flow up to the highest existence, meaning they occur by encompassing these phenomena and this location. For this prefix 'ā-' indeed has the meaning of 'encompassing'. And they are also taints in the sense of being long-established, like the taints of liquor and so forth. And if they are taints in the sense of being long-established, then these alone are fit to be so. Or, they are taints because they cause the long, extensive suffering of saṃsāra to flow and seep forth from beginningless time. Other than these, there are no things called taints.

Tattha kāmāsavo bhavāsavo diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavoti ime cattāro āsavā nāma. Tattha aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittesu uppanno sabbopi lobho kāmāsavo nāma. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana “pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo kāmāsavo”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1102) ca, “diṭṭhisahajāto rāgo kāmāsavo na hoti, diṭṭhirāgo nāma hotī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1105) ca, “yo brahmānaṃ vimānakapparukkhābharaṇesu chandarāgo uppajjati, so kāmāsavo na hoti pañcakāmaguṇikassa rāgassa idheva pahīnattā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “kāmāsavo aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatesu [M 0.0132] cittuppādesu uppajjatī”ti (dha. sa. 1465) ca, “kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavo”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.3.1) ca vuttattā bhavāsavaṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso sabbopi lobho kāmāsavoti paññāyati diṭṭhisampayuttarāgassa, brahmānaṃ vatthābharaṇādīsu rāgassa ca bhavāsavattābhāvā. Diṭṭhivippayuttarāgo eva hi rūpārūpabhavapatthanāvasena pavattiyaṃ bhavāsavo hoti “rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ettha bhavarāgānusayo anusetī”tiādivacanato (yama. 2.anusayayamaka.2), na ca kāmāsavabhavāsavavinimutto lobho atthi. Yadi siyā, “lobho siyā āsavo, siyā no āsavo”ti pāḷiyaṃ vattabbo bhaveyya, “diṭṭhivippayuttalobhena sampayutto [V 0.0099] avijjāsavo siyā āsavasampayutto, siyā āsavavippayutto”ti ca vattabbo siyā. Padabhājanīye ca kāmāsavaniddese āgatassa “kāmesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. 1103) imassa padassa aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “pañcakāmaguṇesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. a. 1103) attho vutto, tassa pana padassa vatthukāmesu kilesakāmotipi atthayojanā sakkā kātuṃ tebhumakassa dhammassa vatthukāmattā, tattha sabbattha rāgassa ca kilesakāmattā. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā mahāniddese –

Here, the four taints are called the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. Among these, all greed that arises in the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed is called the taint of sensual desire. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, it is stated: "Lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is the taint of sensual desire" (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 1102), and "Lust arising together with wrong view is not the taint of sensual desire; it is called the lust of views" (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 1105), and also: "The desire that arises in Brahmās for their celestial mansions, wishing-trees, and ornaments is not the taint of sensual desire, because the lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure has already been abandoned here." In the Pāli, however, it is stated: "The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed" (Dhs. 1465), and "Dependent on the taint of sensual desire are the taint of views and the taint of ignorance" (Paṭṭhā. 3.3.1). Therefore, it is understood that all greed, except for the taint of existence, is the taint of sensual desire, since the lust associated with views and the lust for the garments and ornaments of Brahmās are not the taint of existence. For indeed, lust dissociated from views, when it occurs by way of longing for existence in the form or formless realms, becomes the taint of existence, as stated in passages like: "The latent tendency to craving for existence lies dormant in the form realm and the formless realm" (Yam. 2. Anusayayamaka.2). And there is no greed that is free from the taint of sensual desire or the taint of existence. If there were, the Pāli would have to state: "Greed might be a taint, it might not be a taint," and also: "The taint of ignorance associated with greed dissociated from views might be associated with taints, it might be dissociated from taints." In the word-analysis, in the explanation of the taint of sensual desire, the meaning of the phrase "desire for sensual pleasures" (Dhs. 1103) is given in the Aṭṭhasālinī as "desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (Dhs. A. 1103). However, that phrase can also be interpreted as referring to both objective sensual pleasures and defilement-sensual pleasures, since the Dhamma of the three realms is objective sensual pleasure, and the lust in all of them is defilement-sensual pleasure. This has been stated by the General of the Dhamma in the Mahāniddesa—

“Katame vatthukāmā? Manāpikā rūpā…pe… sabbepi kāmāvacarā dhammā, sabbepi rūpāvacarā dhammā, sabbepi arūpāvacarā dhammā…pe… ime vuccanti vatthukāmā.

"What are objective sensual pleasures? Pleasant forms... and so forth... all phenomena of the sense sphere, all phenomena of the form sphere, all phenomena of the formless sphere... and so forth... these are called objective sensual pleasures."

“Katame kilesakāmā? Chando kāmo rāgo kāmo…pe… yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo [M 0.0133] kāmanandī kāmataṇhā kāmasneho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ kāmogho kāmayogo kāmupādānaṃ kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ…pe… ime vuccanti kilesakāmā”ti (mahāni. 1).

"What are defilement-sensual pleasures? Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure... and so forth... whatever sensual desire for sensual pleasures, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual attachment, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, sensual obsession, the flood of sensual pleasure, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the clinging to sensual pleasure, the hindrance of sensual desire... and so forth... these are called defilement-sensual pleasures." (mahāni. 1).

Apicettha “kāmogho kāmayogo”tiādinā kilesakāmassa kāmoghādibhāvaṃ vadatā dhammasenāpatinā vatthukāmattavisayassa rāgassa āsavādibhāvo anuññāto, na pañcakaāmaguṇikasseva rāgassa. Na ca oghāsavesu koci viseso atthi. Aṭṭhasāliniyampi hi upādānagocchakassa padabhājanīye “kāmesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. 1220) imassa “vatthukāmesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. a. 1220) ayamevattho vutto. Tato aññesu hetuganthakilesagocchakesu lobhasseva anavasesapariyādānaṃ vuttaṃ, na itaragocchakesu. Tesu ca lobhassa pāḷianusārato olokiyamāne kilesakāmamattako. Anavasesalobhapariyādānaṃ paññāyati. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

Moreover, here, by stating the nature of defilement-sensual pleasure as the flood of sensual pleasure, the yoke of sensual pleasure, and so forth, the General of the Dhamma has approved the nature of taints, etc., for the lust that has objective sensual pleasure as its domain, not merely for the lust that has the five strands of sensual pleasure. And there is no distinction between floods and taints. Indeed, in the Aṭṭhasālinī too, in the word-analysis of the Upādāna Cluster, the meaning of "desire for sensual pleasures" (Dhs. 1220) is given as "desire for objective sensual pleasures" (Dhs. A. 1220). Furthermore, in other clusters such as the Root, Fetter, and Defilement clusters, the complete inclusion of greed alone is stated, not in other clusters. And when greed in those [other] clusters is examined according to the Pāli, it is evident that it is merely defilement-sensual pleasure. The complete inclusion of greed is evident. This should be understood after careful consideration.

Catūsu pana diṭṭhigatavippayuttacittesu uppanno rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgabhāvena, kāmajjhosānanikantibhāvena [V 0.0100] ca pavatto lobho bhavāsavo nāma. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana “sassatadiṭṭhisahajāto rāgo bhavāsavo”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1102) vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “bhavāsavo catūsu diṭṭhigatavippayuttalobhasahagatesū”ti (dha. sa. 1465) niyamitattā na sakkā gahetuṃ, adhippāyo pana gavesitabbo. Dvāsaṭṭhipabhedā sabbāpi diṭṭhi diṭṭhāsavo nāma. Aṭṭhavatthuko sabbopi moho avijjāsavo nāma. Tesu diṭṭhāsavo paṭhamena maggena pahīyati, kāmāsavo [M 0.0134] catūhipīti vattuṃ yuttaṃ, “tatiyenā”ti pana vuttaṃ. Bhavāsavo, avijjāsavo ca catutthena pahīyati. Imesañca kāmāsavabhavāsavānaṃ lobhasabhāvattā sabhāvato tayo dhammā vibhāgato cattāro āsavā nāma jātā. Ime ṭhapetvā sesā lokiyalokuttarā sabbe dhammā no āsavā nāma. Āsavadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

However, the greed that arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from views, occurring as desire and lust for the form and formless realms, and as attachment and delight, is called the taint of existence. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, it is stated: 'Lust associated with the eternalist view is the taint of existence' (Dhs. Aṭṭha. 1102). But in the Pāli text, since it is specified that 'the taint of existence is in the four [types of consciousness] accompanied by greed dissociated from views' (Dhs. 1465), this cannot be accepted. The intention, however, should be investigated. All sixty-two kinds of views are called the taint of views. All delusion concerning the eight objects is called the taint of ignorance. Among these, the taint of views is abandoned by the first path. The taint of sensual desire is abandoned by the third path, though it is proper to say by all four. The taint of existence and the taint of ignorance are abandoned by the fourth path. And since the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence are of the nature of greed, by their intrinsic nature there are three phenomena, which by division become the four taints. Apart from these, all remaining mundane and supramundane phenomena are not called taints. This is the first, the Dyad of Taints.

Attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattehi saha āsavehīti sāsavā, sabbe lokiyadhammā. Evaṃ pavattamānā natthi etesaṃ āsavāti anāsavā, nava lokuttaradhammāva. Cetasikā panettha lokiyaduke vuttasadisāva. Sāsavadukaṃ dutiyaṃ.

Tainted (sāsavā) means 'with taints'; these are all mundane phenomena, which proceed by taking the self as their object. Untainted (anāsavā) are those for which there are no taints when they occur; these are only the nine supramundane phenomena. The mental factors here are just as stated in the mundane dyad. This is the second, the Dyad of Tainted and Untainted.

Tatiyādīnaṃ catunnaṃ dukānaṃ padattho vuttanayova. Sesamettha hetugocchake vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – yathā tattha “na hetū kho pana dhammā sahetukāpi, ahetukāpī”ti ayaṃ osānaduko paṭhamaduke dutiyapadaṃ dutiyadukena yojetvā vutto, evamidha “no āsavā kho pana dhammā sāsavāpi, anāsavāpī”ti na vutto. Ayañca tattha tattha vuttanayena iha saṅgahitoti veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ saññojanagocchakādīsupi yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ.

The meaning of the terms of the four dyads beginning with the third is in the manner already stated. The remainder here should be understood according to the method explained in the Section on Roots. There is, however, this difference: just as there it was stated, 'But those phenomena that are not roots are either with roots or without roots'—this concluding dyad being formed by combining the second term of the first dyad with the second dyad—so here it is not stated, 'But those phenomena that are not taints are either tainted or untainted.' And this should be understood as being included here according to the method stated in various places. As it is here, so too should it be understood appropriately in the sections on fetters and so on.

Tattha dvādasa akusalacittuppādā āsavasampayuttā nāma. Dosamohamūlacittesu moho, kusalābyākatacittarūpanibbānāni ca āsavavippayuttā nāma. Cetasikesu pana mohaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā akusalā āsavasampayuttāva, moho pana tijātiko ca dvidhāpi hoti, sesā āsavavippayuttā evāti. Tatiyaṃ.

Here, the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness are called 'associated with taints.' Delusion in consciousness rooted in aversion and delusion, as well as wholesome and indeterminate states of consciousness, materiality, and Nibbāna, are called 'dissociated from taints.' Among mental factors, however, apart from delusion, the remaining unwholesome factors are associated with taints, while delusion, which is of three kinds, is also of both types. The rest are dissociated from taints. This is the third.

Cattāro [M 0.0135] āsavā āsavā ceva sāsavā ca nāma. Tadavasesā lokiyadhammā sāsavā ceva no ca āsavā nāma. Idha pana lokuttarā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana āsavāti vuttehi [V 0.0101] sesā akusalā, karuṇāmuditā ca sāsavā ceva no ca āsavā eva, sesā tathā ca na vattabbā ca. Catutthaṃ.

The four taints are called 'both taints and tainted.' The remaining mundane phenomena are called 'tainted, but not taints.' Here, however, the supramundane are not to be mentioned. Among mental factors, however, the remaining unwholesome factors apart from those designated as taints, as well as compassion and sympathetic joy, are 'tainted, but not taints'; the rest are otherwise and not to be spoken of in this way. This is the fourth.

Ye pana lobhamūlesu lobhamohā, lobhadiṭṭhimoho cāti dve tayo ekato katvā uppajjanti, te āsavā ceva āsavasampayuttā ca nāma. Dvādasa akusalacittāni ceva āsavavajjitā taṃsampayuttā ca āsavasampayuttā ceva no ca āsavā nāma. Idha pana āsavavippayuttā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana āsavavajjitā akusalā āsavasampayuttā ceva no ca āsavā eva, moho siyā āsavo ceva āsavasampayutto ca, siyā na vattabbo, tijātikā siyā āsavasampayuttā ceva no ca āsavā, siyā na vattabbā, kusalābyākatā na vattabbāva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pañcamaṃ.

Now, those taints that arise together in consciousness rooted in greed—either two, namely greed and delusion, or three, namely greed, wrong view, and delusion—are called 'both taints and associated with taints.' The twelve unwholesome states of consciousness, and the associated mental factors excluding the taints themselves, are called 'associated with taints but not taints.' Here, however, 'dissociated from taints' is not to be stated. Among mental factors, however, unwholesome factors excluding the taints are indeed 'associated with taints but not taints.' Delusion may be 'both a taint and associated with taints,' or it may not be stated. Factors belonging to the three categories may be 'associated with taints but not taints,' or they may not be stated. Wholesome and indeterminate factors are not to be stated at all. The rest is easily understood. This is the fifth.

Lokuttaravajjitā āsavavippayuttā sāsavā nāma. Lokuttarā āsavavippayuttā anāsavā nāma. Idha pana āsavasampayuttā na vattabbāva. Cetasikesu pana karuṇāmuditā āsavavippayuttā sāsavā eva, moho tathā ca na vattabbo ca, sesakusalābyākatā dvidhāpi honti, tijātikā dvidhāpi na vattabbāva, mohavajjitā pana akusalā na vattabbāva. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Phenomena dissociated from taints, excluding the supramundane, are called 'tainted.' Supramundane phenomena dissociated from taints are called 'untainted.' Here, however, those associated with taints are not to be mentioned at all. Among mental factors, however, compassion and sympathetic joy, being dissociated from taints, are indeed 'tainted.' Delusion is likewise and also not to be spoken of. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors are of both kinds. Factors belonging to the three categories are not to be spoken of as being of both kinds. And unwholesome factors, excluding delusion, are not to be spoken of at all. This is the sixth.

Āsavagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Taints is concluded.

Saṃyojanagocchake [M 0.0136] yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ puggalaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanā. Tato aññe no saṃyojanā.

In the Section on Fetters: because they fetter and bind in the cycle of existence the person in whom they are found, they are called 'fetters' (saṃyojanā). Others are not fetters.

Tattha kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ bhavarāgapaṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyaavijjāsaṃyojananti ime dasa dhammā saṃyojanā nāma. Tesu kāmabhavadiṭṭhiavijjāsaṃyojanāni āsavagocchake vuttanayāneva. “Anatthaṃ me acari, carati, carissati, piyassa me anatthaṃ acari, carati, carissati, appiyassa me atthaṃ acari, carati, carissatī”ti (dha. sa. 1066) evaṃ vuttehi navahi ākārehi sattesu, aṭṭhānakopavasena saṅkhāresu ca uppajjamāno sabbopi doso paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ nāma.

Here, the ten phenomena called fetters are: the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of craving for existence, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, envy, stinginess, and ignorance. Among these, the fetters of sensual desire, craving for existence, views, and ignorance are just as explained in the Section on Taints. All aversion that arises towards beings and, through groundless anger, towards formations, in the nine ways stated—'He has harmed me, is harming me, will harm me; he has harmed, is harming, will harm what is dear to me; he has benefited, is benefiting, will benefit what is not dear to me' (Dhs. 1066)—is called the fetter of aversion.

“Seyyohamasmi[V 0.0102], sadisohamasmi, hīnohamasmī”ti evaṃ tīhi ākārehi pavatto sabbo māno mānasaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Tattha seyyasseva sato puggalassa “seyyohamasmi, sadiso, hīno”ti ca tidhā māno uppajjati, tathā sadisahīnānampi. Tattha seyyassa seyyamānova yāthāvamāno. Tathā sadisassa sadisamāno, hīnassa hīnamāno ca. Tiṇṇampi itare dve dve mānā ayāthāvamānāti ñātabbā.

'I am better, I am equal, I am worse'—thus, all conceit that occurs in these three ways is called the fetter of conceit. Here, for a person who is in fact better, the conceit 'I am better,' 'I am equal,' or 'I am worse' arises in three ways. It is similar for one who is equal or worse. Here, for one who is better, the conceit 'I am better' is an accurate conceit. Likewise, for one who is equal, the conceit 'I am equal,' and for one who is worse, the conceit 'I am worse.' For all three, the other two conceits in each case should be understood as inaccurate conceits.

Satthudhammasaṅghasikkhāsu, pubbantāparantatadubhayapaṭiccasamuppannesu ca kaṅkhatāvasena pavattā sabbāpi vicikicchā vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma.

All doubt that occurs by way of uncertainty regarding the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the training, and regarding the past, the future, both the past and the future, and dependently arisen phenomena, is called the fetter of doubt.

Gosīlagovatādīhi suddhīti gahaṇākārappavattā diṭṭhi eva sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ nāma.

The view that occurs in the manner of grasping that 'purity comes through bovine practices, bovine vows, and so on' is itself the fetter of clinging to rites and rituals.

Tadavasesā diṭṭhi diṭṭhisaṃyojananti gahetabbaṃ.

The remaining views should be understood as the fetter of views.

Paralābhasakkāragarukāramānanavandanapūjanādīsu [M 0.0137] asahanākārena pavattā issā issāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Āvāsamacchariyaṃ kulalābhavaṇṇadhammamacchariyanti pañcavidhaṃ macchariyaṃ macchariyasaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Sakalārāmepi hi pariveṇovarakādīsu vā vasanto tattha aññassa vattasampannassa pesalassa bhikkhuno āgamanaṃ na icchati, āgatassāpi khippaṃ gamanaññeva icchati, idaṃ āvāsamacchariyaṃ nāma. Bhaṇḍanakārakādīnaṃ pana tattha vāsaṃ anicchato āvāsamacchariyaṃ nāma na hoti.

Envy that occurs in a manner of intolerance regarding others' gains, honor, respect, reverence, worship, and the like, is called the fetter of envy. The fivefold stinginess—stinginess regarding dwellings, families, gains, praise, and the Dhamma—is called the fetter of stinginess. For when one is dwelling in an entire monastery, or in a cell, a private room, and so on, one does not wish for the arrival there of another virtuous and amiable monk. And if one has arrived, one wishes only for their quick departure—this is called stinginess regarding dwellings. However, when one does not wish for quarrelsome persons and the like to reside there, it is not called stinginess regarding dwellings.

Attano pana upaṭṭhākakule vā ñātikule vā aññassa pesalassa upasaṅkamanaṃ anicchato kulamacchariyaṃ hoti, pāpapuggalassa anicchato pana na hoti. So hi tesaṃ pasādabhedāya paṭipajjatīti.

When one does not wish for another amiable person to approach one’s own supporter-family or family of relatives, this is stinginess regarding families. But when one does not wish for a wicked person to approach, it is not so, for such a person behaves in a way that would destroy their confidence.

Attanā labhanaṭṭhāne catupaccayaṃ labhante sīlavante disvā “mā labhantū”ti cintentassa lābhamacchariyaṃ hoti. Yo pana saddhādeyyaṃ vinipāteti, pūtibhāvampi gacchantaṃ aññassa na deti[V 0.0103], taṃ labhantaṃ disvā “sace imaṃ añño sīlavā labheyya, paribhogaṃ gaccheyyā”ti cintentassa macchariyaṃ nāma natthi.

When one sees virtuous ones receiving the four requisites in a place where one receives them oneself, and thinks, “May they not receive them,” this is stinginess regarding gains. However, for one who destroys what is given in faith, or does not give to another even what is decaying, but upon seeing someone else receive it thinks, “If another virtuous person were to receive this, it could be put to use,” this is not called stinginess.

Vaṇṇo nāma attanā sadiso sarīravaṇṇopi guṇavaṇṇopi. Tattha “rūpavā pāsādiko”ti parassa sarīravaṇṇaṃ, “sīlavā, dhutavā”tiādinā guṇavaṇṇañca attano vaṇṇabhaṇanaṭṭhāne vuccamānaṃ asahantassa duvidhaṃ vaṇṇamacchariyaṃ nāma hoti, apesalaṃ pana vipannaṃ pasaṃsitvā parisāsu upatthambhentaṃ disvā pāpagarahitāya asahantassa na hoti.

Praise (vaṇṇa) refers to both physical praise and the praise of virtues. Here, when one cannot bear another's physical praise—such as, 'He is handsome and pleasing'—or the praise of their virtues—such as, 'He is virtuous, an ascetic'—being spoken, this is called twofold stinginess regarding praise. However, when one sees a wicked and corrupt person being praised and supported in assemblies, and cannot bear it due to censure of evil, this is not stinginess.

Dhammoti pariyattiyeva, na paṭivedho ariyānaṃ tattha macchariyābhāvā. Pariyattiṃ pana guḷhaganthaṃ aññesaṃ akathetukāmassa dhammamacchariyaṃ nāma hoti, dhammānuggahena pana lolassa[M 0.0138], kālena samaṇo, kālena nigaṇṭhādi ca hutvā vicarantassa paveṇiāgataṃ tantiṃ “saṇhasukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ bhinditvā āluḷissati, amhākaṃ samayaṃ bhindissatī”ti ca na dentassa, puggalānuggahena vā pakatiyā saṭhassa māyāvino “saṇhasukhumadhammaṃ uggaṇhitvā aññaṃ byākaritvā nassissatī”ti na dentassa ca dhammamacchariyaṃ na hoti. Yathā ca bhikkhūnaṃ, evaṃ gahaṭṭhānampi pañcavidhaṃ macchariyaṃ yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Saṅkhepato pana gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ attasampattinigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ macchariyaṃ nāmāti gahetabbaṃ.

The Dhamma here refers only to the scriptures, not to realization, as the noble ones have no stinginess regarding that. One who is unwilling to explain the difficult passages of the scriptures to others has stinginess regarding the Dhamma. However, it is not stinginess for one who, being protective of the Dhamma, does not give the traditional teaching to a person who wanders about, at times being a recluse, at times a Jain, thinking, 'He will distort and confuse this subtle and profound teaching, and will disrupt our doctrine'; nor is it stinginess for one who, out of concern for the person, does not give it to someone who is by nature deceitful and fraudulent, thinking, 'Having learned this subtle and profound teaching, he will explain it otherwise and come to ruin.' Just as for monastics, so too for householders the five kinds of stinginess should be understood accordingly. In brief, for both householders and renunciants, stinginess is to be understood as having the characteristic of concealing one’s own attainments.

Imesu ca saṃyojanesu diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyāni sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti, paṭigho anāgāmimaggena, kāmarāgo catūhipīti vattabbaṃ, “tatiyenā”ti pana vuttaṃ. Mānabhavarāgaavijjā arahattamaggena. Tattha ca ayāthāvamāno paṭhamamaggena pahīyatīti daṭṭhabbo, imesaṃ kāmarāgabhavarāgānaṃ lobhasabhāvattā diṭṭhisīlabbataparāmāsānaṃ micchādiṭṭhisabhāvattā sabhāvato aṭṭheva dhammā dasa saṃyojanā nāma jātā. Ime dasa ṭhapetvā sesā lokiyalokuttaradhammā no saṃyojanā nāma. Sesaṃ āsavadukasadisaṃ. Saṃyojanadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Among these fetters, wrong view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. Aversion is abandoned by the path of non-returning, and sensual desire, it should be said, is abandoned by all four paths, though it has been stated 'by the third.' Conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance are abandoned by the path of arahantship. Here, it should be understood that unjustified conceit is abandoned by the first path. Because sensual desire and craving for existence have the nature of greed, and wrong view and clinging to rites and rituals have the nature of wrong view, by their nature eight phenomena become the ten fetters. Apart from these ten, the remaining worldly and supramundane phenomena are not called fetters. The rest is similar to the dyad of taints. The first dyad on fetters.

Ārammaṇabhāvaṃ upagantvā saṃyojanasaṃvaḍḍhanena saṃyojanānaṃ hitāti saṃyojaniyā, sāsavadhammā eva. Tathā nīvaraṇiyāti etthāpi. Na saṃyojaniyā asaṃyojaniyā, anāsavā. Sesaṃ sāsavadukasadisameva. Dutiyaṃ.

By becoming an object, they are conducive to the fetters by increasing them; thus they are called 'pertaining to fetters,' namely, the tainted phenomena. The same applies to 'pertaining to hindrances.' What does not pertain to fetters is 'not pertaining to fetters,' namely, the untainted. The rest is just like the dyad of the tainted. The second.

Tatiyādayopi [V 0.0104] āsavagocchake tatiyādisadisā eva, visesamattamevettha vakkhāma. Tattha hi dvādasākusalacittāni saṃyojanasampayuttā nāma, uddhaccasahagato moho, sesacittarūpanibbānāni saṃyojanavippayuttā nāma. Sesaṃ samameva. Tatiyaṃ.

The third and so forth are just like the third and so forth in the section on taints; we will mention here only the difference. Here, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are called 'associated with fetters,' as is the delusion accompanied by restlessness. The remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are called 'dissociated from fetters.' The rest is the same. Third.

Dasa [M 0.0139] saṃyojanāni saṃyojanā ceva saṃyojaniyā ca nāma. Tadavasesalokiyadhammā saṃyojaniyā ceva no ca saṃyojanā nāma. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Catutthaṃ.

The ten fetters are called both 'fetters' and 'pertaining to fetters.' The remaining worldly phenomena are called 'pertaining to fetters' but not 'fetters.' The rest is easily understood. Fourth.

Ye pana uddhaccavirahitesu ekādasasu akusalacittesu vicikicchāmohā dosamohā dosaissāmohā dosamacchariyamohā lobhamānamohā lobhadiṭṭhimohā cāti dve tayo ekato uppajjanti, te saṃyojanā ceva saṃyojanasampayuttā ca nāma. Dvādasākusalacittāni ceva saṃyojanavajjitataṃsampayuttā ca saṃyojanasampayuttā ceva no ca saṃyojanā nāma. Sesamidha anantaradukañca āsavagocchake pañcamachaṭṭhadukasadisameva. Kevalaṃ āsavapadaṭṭhāne saṃyojanapadameva viseso. Pañcamachaṭṭhadukāni.

Moreover, in the eleven unwholesome consciousnesses devoid of restlessness, the fetters of doubt-and-delusion, hatred-and-delusion, hatred-envy-and-delusion, hatred-stinginess-and-delusion, greed-conceit-and-delusion, and greed-wrong-view-and-delusion arise—two or three together. These are called both 'fetters' and 'associated with fetters.' The twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, and the mental factors associated with them other than the fetters themselves, are called 'associated with fetters' but not 'fetters.' The remainder here, and the immediately following dyad, are similar to the fifth and sixth dyads in the section on taints. The only difference is the term 'fetters' in place of the term 'taints.' The fifth and sixth dyads.

Saṃyojanagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on fetters is concluded.

Ganthagocchake yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena vaṭṭasmiṃ ganthenti ghaṭentīti ganthā. Tato aññe no ganthā.

In the section on bonds: because they bind and fasten a being in the cycle of existence by way of death and rebirth, they are called 'bonds.' Others are not bonds.

Tattha abhijjhākāyagantho, byāpādo, sīlabbataparāmāso, idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyaganthoti ime cattāro dhammā ganthā nāma. Tattha abhijjhā eva nāmakāyaṃ vuttanayena ganthetīti abhijjhākāyagantho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Sabbaññubhāsitampi paṭikkhipitvā “sassato loko, idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti iminā ākārena abhinivisanato sīlabbataparāmāsavirahitā sabbāpi diṭṭhi idaṃsaccābhiniveso nāma. Sesā vuttatthāva. Imesu ca pacchimā dve ganthā paṭhamena maggena pahīyanti, byāpādo tatiyena, abhijjhā catūhipi. Ime ca sabhāvato tayo dhammā cattāro [M 0.0140] ganthā nāma jātā. Ime pana ṭhapetvā sesā sabbe dhammā no ganthā nāma. Ganthadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Here, these four phenomena are called 'bonds': the bodily bond of covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and rituals, and dogmatic clinging to this as the truth. Among these, covetousness binds the mental and material body in the manner described—thus it is called 'the bodily bond of covetousness.' The same applies to the others. All views, excluding adherence to rites and rituals, that cling in this way—'The world is eternal, this alone is true, all else is false'—even rejecting the words of the Omniscient One, are called 'dogmatic clinging to this as the truth.' The rest are as previously explained. Among these, the last two bonds are abandoned by the first path; ill will by the third; and covetousness by all four paths. By their nature, these three phenomena become the four bonds. Setting these aside, all other phenomena are not called 'bonds.' The first dyad on bonds.

Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena [V 0.0105] ganthehi ganthitabbāti ganthaniyā. Na ganthaniyā aganthaniyā. Sesaṃ sāsavadukasadisameva. Dutiyaṃ.

Because they are to be bound by bonds by way of being objects or causes, they are called 'pertaining to bonds.' What does not pertain to bonds is 'not pertaining to bonds.' The rest is just like the dyad on taints. Second.

Mohamūlavajjitāni dasa akusalacittāni, diṭṭhivippayuttacittesu lobhaṃ, dosamūlesu ca dosaṃ ṭhapetvā taṃsampayuttā ca ganthasampayuttā nāma. Yathāvutto lobho, doso, mohamūlāni, kusalābyākatāni cittāni, rūpanibbānāni ca ganthavippayuttā nāma. Cetasikesu pana diṭṭhimānaissāmacchariyakukkuccathinamiddhāni ganthasampayuttā eva. Dosavicikicchā, kusalābyākatā ca ganthavippayuttā eva, sesā dvidhāpi honti. Tatiyaṃ.

The ten unwholesome consciousnesses devoid of a delusion-root, and their associated mental factors—excluding greed in the consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view, and hatred in the hatred-rooted consciousnesses—are called 'associated with bonds.' Greed and hatred as previously defined, the delusion-rooted consciousnesses, wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are called 'dissociated from bonds.' Among mental factors, wrong view, conceit, envy, stinginess, worry, sloth, and torpor are solely 'associated with bonds.' Hatred, doubt, and wholesome and indeterminate mental factors are solely 'dissociated from bonds'; the remaining are of both kinds. Third.

Cattāro ganthā ganthā ceva ganthaniyā ca nāma. Tadavasesā lokiyā ganthaniyā ceva no ca ganthā nāma. Tathā cetasikesu ganthavajjitā akusalā, appamaññā ca, sesā cetasikā pana tathā ca na vattabbā ca, idha pana lokuttarā na vattabbā. Catutthaṃ.

The four bonds are both 'bonds' and 'pertaining to bonds.' The remaining worldly phenomena are 'pertaining to bonds' but not 'bonds.' Thus, among mental factors, the unwholesome ones excluding the bonds, and the immeasurables, are 'pertaining to bonds but not bonds'; the remaining mental factors, however, can be both 'pertaining to bonds but not bonds' and 'not to be stated.' Here, however, the supramundane are 'not to be stated.' Fourth.

Diṭṭhi ganthāceva ganthasampayuttā ca nāma. Lobho tathā ca na vattabbo ca, ganthasampayuttesu ganthe ṭhapetvā sesā ganthasampayuttā ceva no ca ganthā nāma. Idha pana ganthavippayuttā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana mānaissāmacchariyakukkuccathinamiddhāni ganthasampayuttā ceva no ca ganthā eva, mohāhirikānottappauddhaccāni tijātikā ca siyā, tathā navattabbā ca, sesā na vattabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pañcamaṃ.

Wrong view is both 'a bond' and 'associated with bonds.' Greed can be both 'a bond and associated with bonds' and 'not to be stated.' Among things associated with bonds, the remainder, excluding the bonds themselves, are 'associated with bonds' but not 'bonds.' Here, however, things dissociated from bonds are 'not to be stated.' Among mental factors, conceit, envy, stinginess, worry, sloth, and torpor are only 'associated with bonds but not bonds.' Delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, and restlessness, being of three spheres, can be 'associated with bonds but not bonds' and can also be 'not to be stated.' The remaining are 'not to be stated.' The rest is easily understood. Fifth.

Lokuttaravajjitā ganthavippayuttā ganthaniyā nāma. Lokuttarā pana ganthavippayuttā aganthaniyā nāma. Idha pana ganthasampayuttā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana doso vicikicchā [M 0.0141] karuṇā muditā ganthavippayuttā ganthaniyā eva, mohāhirikānottappauddhaccalobhā tathā na vattabbā ca, sesā kusalābyākatā dvidhāpi honti, tijātikā pana dvidhāpi na vattabbā ca, sesā akusalāpi na vattabbā ca. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Excluding the supramundane, those dissociated from the bonds are called 'liable to be bound.' The supramundane, however, being dissociated from the bonds, are 'not liable to be bound.' Here, however, those associated with the bonds are not to be stated. Among the mental factors, hatred, doubt, compassion, and sympathetic joy are dissociated from the bonds and are only liable to be bound. Delusion, shamelessness, recklessness, restlessness, and greed are not to be stated as such. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate factors are of both kinds. But those of threefold origin are not to be stated as being of both kinds, and the remaining unwholesome factors are also not to be stated. Sixth.

Ganthagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on bonds is concluded.

Oghayogagocchakāni sabbathā āsavagocchakasadisāni. Padatthamattameva, hettha nāmamattañca viseso[V 0.0106]. Tattha yassa saṃvijjanti, taṃ vaṭṭasmiṃ ohananti osīdāpentīti oghā. Ārammaṇaṃ katvā atikkamanīyato oghehi atikkamitabbāti oghaniyā. Tathā yoganiyāti etthāpi. Vaṭṭasmiṃ yojentīti yogā. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

The sections on floods and yokes are in every way similar to the section on taints. The only difference here is in the meaning of the terms and the names themselves. Herein, because they plunge beings into the cycle of existence, causing them to sink, they are called 'floods.' Because they are to be overcome by the floods, they are called 'liable to floods.' It is similar also in the case of 'liable to yokes.' Because they yoke one to the cycle of existence, they are called 'yokes.' The rest is just the same.

Oghayogagocchakāni niṭṭhitāni.

The sections on floods and yokes are concluded.

Nīvaraṇagocchake cittaṃ nīvaranti pariyonandhantīti nīvaraṇā. Tattha kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇanti ime cha nīvaraṇā nāma. Tattha thinanti sappipiṇḍo viya avipphārikatāya cittassa ghanabhāvo, thaddhatāti attho. Medhatīti middhaṃ, akammaññabhāvo, pacalāyikabhāvakaroti attho. Idañca sekhaputhujjanānaṃ niddāya pubbabhāge, aparabhāge ca pacalāyanahetukaṃ uppajjati, na niddokkamanakāle. Khīṇāsavānampi hi karajakāyassa dubbalabhāvena asammissabhavaṅgasantativasena niddokkamanaṃ hoti, taṃ pana tesaṃ thinamiddhahetukaṃ na hoti, itaresameva hoti.

In the section on hindrances, because they hinder and envelop the mind, they are called 'hindrances' (nīvaraṇā). Herein, there are six hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt, and the hindrance of ignorance. Herein, 'sloth' (thina) is the denseness of the mind, its lack of diffusion, like a lump of ghee; the meaning is stiffness. 'Torpor' (middha) is derived from being inert; it is a state of unworkability, meaning that which causes drowsiness. This arises in trainees and ordinary people before and after sleep as a cause of drowsiness, but not at the time of emerging from sleep. Even for those whose taints are destroyed, emerging from sleep occurs due to the weakness of the body born of kamma and by way of the unmixed continuity of the life-continuum, but for them it is not caused by sloth and torpor; it is so only for others.

Keci [M 0.0142] pana rūpameva “middha”nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ, “thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇena nīvaraṇañceva nīvaraṇasampayuttañcā”ti arūpadhammehi sampayogavacanato arūpameva. Akusalañca “thinamiddhanīvaraṇassa pahīnattā”tiādipahānavacanato. Akusalā eva hi pahātabbā, tasmā āruppepi cetaṃ uppajjati. “Nīvaraṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca nīvaraṇo dhammo uppajjati na purejātapaccayā”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) etassa vibhaṅge “āruppe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhauddhaccaavijjānīvaraṇa”nti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. “Soppaṃ pacalāyikā”ti (dha. sa. 1163) padabhājanīye panassa phalūpacārena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Thinaṃ middhañcāti idaṃ dvayaṃ nīvaraṇaṭṭhāne ekanīvaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā uddhaccakukkuccañcāti idaṃ dvayaṃ. Tattha kukkuccanti “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ, kataṃ pāpa”ntiādinā uppajjamāno vippaṭisāro. Tenevassa padabhājanīye “cetaso vippaṭisāro manovilekho”ti ca vuttaṃ. “Akappiye kappiyasaññitā”tiādi pana kukkuccamūladassanatthaṃ. Evaṃsaññitāya hi kate vītikkame pacchā “duṭṭhu mayā kata”nti sudinnādīnaṃ viya vippaṭisāro uppajjati. Yaṃ pana vinaye “atha kho āyasmā sāriputto…pe… kukkuccāyanto na paṭiggahesī”ti (pāci. 204) kukkuccaṃ āgataṃ, taṃ nīvaraṇakukkuccaṃ[V 0.0107]. Na hi arahato nīvaraṇaṃ atthi, nīvaraṇavatirūpakaṃ pana “kappati, na kappatī”ti vīmaṃsanasaṅkhātaṃ vinayakukkuccaṃ nāmetanti veditabbaṃ. Sesanīvaraṇāni vuttatthāni eva. Imesu ca kukkuccavicikicchā paṭhamena maggena pahīyanti, byāpādo tatiyena, thinamiddhuddhaccāvijjā catutthena, kāmacchando catūhipīti vattabbaṃ, “tatiyenā”ti pana vuttaṃ. Ime ca sabhāvato aṭṭha dhammā cha nīvaraṇā nāma jātā, ime pana ṭhapetvā sesā no nīvaraṇā nāma. Nīvaraṇadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Some, however, say that 'torpor' (middha) is only material form, but this is not correct. Because of the statement of its association with immaterial phenomena—'The hindrance of sloth and torpor is both a hindrance and associated with the hindrance of ignorance'—it is itself immaterial. And it is unwholesome, because of statements about its abandonment, such as 'due to the abandoning of the hindrance of sloth and torpor.' For only unwholesome states are to be abandoned; thus, this also arises in the immaterial sphere. In the phrase, 'A hindering phenomenon arises in dependence on a hindering phenomenon, not through the pre-nascence condition' (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8), its analysis states, 'In the immaterial sphere, in dependence on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrances of sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance arise.' All this should be elaborated. In the word analysis of 'sleep and drowsiness' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1163), it should be understood that this is stated figuratively based on its result. 'Sloth and torpor'—these two are spoken of as a single hindrance in the context of hindrances. Similarly, 'restlessness and remorse'—these two are also a single hindrance. Herein, 'remorse' (kukkucca) refers to the regret that arises from thoughts like, 'Alas, I have not done what is good; I have done what is evil.' Therefore, in its word analysis, it is also said to be 'remorse of the mind, mental agitation.' Phrases like 'perceiving the unallowable as allowable' are given to show the root of remorse. For when a transgression is committed due to such a perception, regret arises afterward, thinking, 'I have acted wrongly,' as in the case of Sudinna and others. However, the remorse mentioned in the Vinaya, 'Then the Venerable Sāriputta... feeling remorseful, did not accept,' is not the hindrance of remorse. For an Arahant has no hindrances. Rather, it should be understood that what is called 'Vinaya remorse' is the scrutiny of 'Is this allowable or not allowable?', which only resembles a hindrance. The remaining hindrances are as previously explained. Among these, remorse and doubt are abandoned by the first path, ill will by the third, and sloth, torpor, restlessness, and ignorance by the fourth. Sensual desire should be said to be abandoned by the four paths, but it has been stated 'by the third.' By their nature, these eight phenomena become what are called the six hindrances. Apart from these, the remaining phenomena are not called hindrances. This is the first, the Hindrance Dyad.

Dutiyaṃ [M 0.0143] sāsavadukasadisameva. Dvādasa akusalacittāni nīvaraṇasampayuttā nāma. Sesacittarūpanibbānāni nīvaraṇavippayuttā nāma. Cetasikesu akusalā nīvaraṇasampayuttāva, kusalābyākatā nīvaraṇavippayuttāva, sesā dvidhāpi honti. Tatiyaṃ.

The second is just like the dyad on taints. The twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are called 'associated with the hindrances.' The remaining types of consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are called 'dissociated from the hindrances.' Among the mental factors, the unwholesome ones are only associated with hindrances, the wholesome and indeterminate ones are only dissociated from hindrances, and the remaining ones are of both kinds. The third.

Cha nīvaraṇā nīvaraṇā ceva nīvaraṇiyā ca nāma. Sesā lokiyā nīvaraṇiyā ceva no ca nīvaraṇā nāma. Lokuttarā na vattabbā. Sesaṃ āsavagocchake catutthasadisameva. Catutthaṃ.

The six hindrances are called both 'hindrances' and 'liable to hindrances.' The remaining worldly phenomena are called 'liable to hindrances' but not 'hindrances.' The supramundane are not to be stated. The rest is just like the fourth in the section on taints. The fourth.

Cha nīvaraṇā nīvaraṇā ceva nīvaraṇasampayuttā ca nāma. Tadaññe nīvaraṇasampayuttā pana nīvaraṇasampayuttā ceva no ca nīvaraṇā nāma. Tathā cetasikesu nīvaraṇavirahitā akusalā, tijātikā pana tathā ca na vattabbā ca, kusalābyākatā na vattabbāva. Idha pana nīvaraṇavippayuttā sabbe na vattabbā. Pañcamaṃ.

The six hindrances are called both 'hindrances' and 'associated with hindrances.' Others associated with hindrances, however, are called 'associated with hindrances' but not 'hindrances.' Similarly, among mental factors, the unwholesome factors that are not themselves hindrances, and those of the three origins, are both 'such' and 'not to be stated'; the wholesome and indeterminate are not to be stated at all. Here, however, all those dissociated from hindrances are not to be stated. The fifth.

Lokuttaravajjitā nīvaraṇavippayuttā nīvaraṇiyā nāma. Lokuttarā nīvaraṇavippayuttā anīvaraṇiyā nāma. Idha pana nīvaraṇasampayuttā na vattabbā. Cetasikesu pana karuṇāmuditā nīvaraṇavippayuttā nīvaraṇiyāva, kusalābyākatā dvidhāpi honti, tijātikā tathā ca na vattabbā ca, akusalā pana na vattabbāva. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Excluding the supramundane, those dissociated from the hindrances are called 'liable to hindrances.' The supramundane, being dissociated from hindrances, are called 'not liable to hindrances.' Here, however, those associated with hindrances are not to be stated. Among mental factors, compassion and sympathetic joy are dissociated from hindrances and are only liable to hindrances; the wholesome and indeterminate are of both kinds; those of the three origins are both 'such' and 'not to be stated'; but the unwholesome are not to be stated at all. The sixth.

Nīvaraṇagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the hindrances is concluded.

Parāmāsagocchake dhammānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ aniccādiākāraṃ atikkamitvā “nicca”ntiādivasena [V 0.0108] pavattamānā parato āmasantīti parāmāsā. Micchādiṭṭhi. Bahuvacananiddese kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Tadaññe sabbe dhammā no parāmāsā nāma. Parāmāsadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

In the section on graspings: Because they grasp wrongly, transgressing the true nature of phenomena as impermanent and so forth, and proceeding by way of 'permanent' and so on, they are called 'graspings' (parāmāsā). This is wrong view. The reason for the plural designation has already been stated. All other phenomena are not called 'graspings.' This is the first, the Grasping Dyad.

Parāmāsehi [M 0.0144] ārammaṇakaraṇavasena parāmaṭṭhattā parāmaṭṭhā. Sesaṃ āsavadukasadisameva. Dutiyaṃ.

Because they are grasped by the graspings by way of being made an object, they are called 'grasped.' The rest is just like the dyad on taints. The second.

Diṭṭhisampayuttacittesu diṭṭhivirahitā dhammā parāmāsasampayuttā nāma. Sesacittarūpanibbānāni parāmāsavippayuttā nāma. Idha pana diṭṭhi na vattabbā, sesacetasikesu pana mānadosaissāmacchariyakukkuccavicikicchā, kusalābyākatā ca parāmāsavippayuttā eva, sesā dvidhāpi honti. Tatiyaṃ.

In types of consciousness associated with wrong view, the phenomena devoid of wrong view are called 'associated with grasping.' The remaining types of consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are called 'dissociated from grasping.' Here, however, wrong view is not to be stated. Among the remaining mental factors, conceit, hatred, envy, avarice, remorse, and doubt, as well as the wholesome and indeterminate factors, are only dissociated from grasping. The rest are of both kinds. The third.

Diṭṭhi eva parāmāsā ceva parāmaṭṭhā ca nāma. Sesalokiyā parāmaṭṭhā ceva no ca parāmāsā nāma. Idha pana lokuttarā na vattabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Catutthaṃ.

Wrong view itself is called both 'grasping' and 'grasped.' The remaining worldly phenomena are called 'grasped' but not 'grasping.' Here, however, the supramundane are not to be stated. The rest is easily understood. The fourth.

Imasmiṃ pana gocchake “parāmāsā ceva dhammā parāmāsasampayuttā cā”ti ayaṃ duko na labbhati. Na hi diṭṭhi diṭṭhiyā sampayujjati. Pacchimaduke lokuttaravajjitā parāmāsavippayuttā parāmaṭṭhā nāma. Lokuttarā parāmāsavippayuttā aparāmaṭṭhā nāma. Idha pana parāmāso, taṃsampayuttā ca na vattabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

In this section, however, the pair 'graspings and phenomena associated with grasping' is not found. For wrong view is not associated with wrong view. In the last pair, those dissociated from grasping, excluding the supramundane, are called 'grasped'. The supramundane, dissociated from grasping, are called 'not grasped'. Here, however, grasping and what is associated with it are not to be stated. The rest is as stated before.

Parāmāsagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Grasping is concluded.

Mahantaradukesu ārammaṇaṃ aggahetvā appavattito saha ārammaṇenāti sārammaṇā, cittacetasikā. Natthi ārammaṇametesanti anārammaṇā, rūpanibbānāni. Sārammaṇadukaṃ.

In the great intermediate pairs, because they do not occur without taking an object, consciousness and mental factors are 'with an object' (sārammaṇā). Because there is no object for them, material phenomena and Nibbāna are 'objectless' (anārammaṇā). The Dyad on [Phenomena] with an Object.

Cintanaṭṭhena cittaṃ, cittatāya vā cittaṃ. Taṃ hi vatthudvārārammaṇakiccādibhedato, atītādibhedato ca attano vicittatāya cittanti vuccati cittakaraṇatāya vā. Lokasmiṃ hi cittakammato uttaritaraṃ cittaṃ nāma natthi, tasmimpi caraṇaṃ [M 0.0145] nāma cittaṃ aticittaṃ hoti. Yaṃ vā panaññampi loke sippajātaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ citteneva karīyati. Evaṃ tassa tassa cittassa nipphādakaṃ [V 0.0109] cittampi tatheva cittaṃ hoti. Yathā cintitassa vā anavasesassa anipphajjanato tatopi cittameva cittataraṃ, tathā yadetaṃ devamanussanirayatiracchānabhedāsu gatīsu kusalākusalakammanānattaṃ, tena tāsu gatīsu apadadvipadādiuccattanīcattādinānattaṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ attabhāve dīgharassathūlāthūlasuvaṇṇadubbaṇṇādilābhālābhādi cāti evamādi ajjhattaṃ cittaṃ, bahiddhā ca pathavīpabbatatiṇarukkhalatādidevabrahmavimānakapparukkhādibhūtaṃ kammapaccayaṃ cittaṃ, tampi citteneva kataṃ, tato cittameva cittataraṃ cintitaniyāmena sabbākārassa asambhavato. Evaṃ cintanaṭṭhena, cittavicittaṭṭhena, cittakaraṇaṭṭhena ca “citta”nti viññāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, tadeva viññāṇaṃ cittaṃ nāma. Cetasikarūpanibbānāni no cittā nāma. Cittadukaṃ.

Consciousness (citta) is so called by way of its characteristic of thinking (cintana) or by way of its variegated nature (cittatā). For it is called 'citta' by way of its own variegated nature due to distinctions of base, door, object, function, etc., and due to distinctions of past, etc., or by way of its act of making variegated. Indeed, in the world there is nothing more variegated than the work of consciousness; even in that, the activity called consciousness is exceedingly variegated. Whatever other skills exist in the world, all of them are accomplished by consciousness. Thus, the consciousness which produces each and every skill is also variegated in the same way. Just as not all that is thought comes to fruition, so too consciousness itself is more variegated than that. And as the diversity of wholesome and unwholesome kamma leads to various destinies among gods, humans, hell-beings, and animals—resulting in differences like footless, two-footed, high, low, etc., and within each existence, differences like long, short, coarse, fine, beautiful, ugly, gain, loss, etc.—so too internally, consciousness is variegated. Externally, the earth, mountains, grass, trees, creepers, divine mansions, Brahmā’s palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, etc., are all kamma-produced and variegated, and this too is done by consciousness. Thus, consciousness is even more variegated, since without the principle of thought, the existence of anything in any form is impossible. Therefore, consciousness (viññāṇa) should be understood as that which has the characteristic of thinking, as that which has the characteristic of being variegated, and as that which has the characteristic of making variegated. That very consciousness is called citta. Mental factors, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are not called citta. The Dyad on Consciousness.

Avippayogavasena cetasi niyuttā cetasikā, phassādayo dvipaññāsa dhammā. Cittarūpanibbānāni acetasikā nāma. Cetasikadukaṃ.

Mental factors (cetasikā) are the fifty-two mental states beginning with contact (phassa), which are yoked to consciousness by way of inseparability. Consciousness, material phenomena, and Nibbāna are called non-mental factors. The Dyad on Mental Factors.

Cetasikā eva cittasampayuttā nāma. Rūpanibbānāni cittavippayuttā nāma, idha pana cittaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Cittasampayuttadukaṃ.

Mental factors themselves are called 'associated with consciousness'. Material phenomena and Nibbāna are called 'dissociated from consciousness'; but here, consciousness is not to be stated. The Dyad on [Phenomena] Associated with Consciousness.

Nirantarabhāvūpagamanatāya uppādato yāva bhaṅgācittena saṃsaṭṭhāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhā. Ekato vattamānāpi nirantarabhāvaṃ anupagamanatāya cittena visaṃsaṭṭhāti cittavisaṃsaṭṭhā. Sesaṃ anantaradukasadisameva. Cittasaṃsaṭṭhadukaṃ.

By way of attaining an uninterrupted state, from arising until dissolution, they are blended with consciousness—thus, they are called 'blended with consciousness'. Though occurring together, by way of not attaining an uninterrupted state, they are unblended with consciousness—thus, they are called 'unblended with consciousness'. The rest is just like the preceding pair. The Dyad on [Phenomena] Blended with Consciousness.

Samuṭṭhahanti etenāti samuṭṭhānaṃ, cittaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ etesanti cittasamuṭṭhānā, cetasikāni ceva cittajarūpakalāpā ca[M 0.0146]. Cittaṃ, pana acittajarūpakalāpā, nibbānañca no cittasamuṭṭhānā nāma. Cittasamuṭṭhānadukaṃ.

That from which they arise is 'origination' (samuṭṭhāna). Those for which consciousness is the origination are 'consciousness-originated'—namely, mental factors and the material groups produced by consciousness. Consciousness itself, material groups not produced by consciousness, and Nibbāna are not called 'consciousness-originated'. The Dyad on [Phenomena] Originated by Consciousness.

Saha bhavantīti sahabhuno, cittena sahabhuno cittasahabhuno, cetasikāni ceva kāyavacīviññattiyo ca. Cittaṃ, pana viññattivajjitarūpanibbānāni ca no cittasahabhuno nāma. Cittasahabhudukaṃ.

Those that exist together are 'co-existent' (sahabhū). Those that are co-existent with consciousness are 'co-existent with consciousness'—namely, mental factors and bodily and verbal intimation. However, consciousness itself, as well as material phenomena excluding intimation, and Nibbāna, are not called 'co-existent with consciousness'. The Dyad on [Phenomena] Co-existent with Consciousness.

Anuparivattantīti [V 0.0110] anuparivattino, kiṃ anuparivattanti? Cittaṃ, cittassa anuparivattino cittānuparivattino. Sesaṃ anantaradukasadisameva. Cittānuparivattidukaṃ.

Those that revolve in accordance are 'revolving in accordance'. What do they revolve in accordance with? Consciousness. Those that revolve in accordance with consciousness are 'revolving in accordance with consciousness'. The rest is just like the preceding pair. The Dyad on [Phenomena] Revolving in Accordance with Consciousness.

Ito pare pana tayo dukā cetasikadukasadisāva, kevalaṃ padatthamattameva viseso. Tattha cittasaṃsaṭṭhā ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā eva cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānā. Cittasaṃsaṭṭhā ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā ca cittasahabhuno eva cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānasahabhuno, cittasaṃsaṭṭhā ca te cittasamuṭṭhānā ca cittānuparivattino eva cāti cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānānuparivattino. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Beyond these, the next three pairs are just like the Dyad on Mental Factors, differing only in the meaning of the terms. Here, those that are both blended with consciousness and originated by consciousness are 'blended and originated by consciousness'. Those that are blended with consciousness, originated by consciousness, and also co-existent with consciousness are 'blended, originated by consciousness, and co-existent with consciousness'. And those that are blended with consciousness, originated by consciousness, and also revolving in accordance with consciousness are 'blended, originated by consciousness, and revolving in accordance with consciousness'. The rest is easily understood.

Tadanantare pana ajjhattikaduke ajjhattajjhattaṃ ajjhattattike vuttavasena ajjhattāva ajjhattikā. Pasādarūpacittasaṅkhātāni cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Tato bahibhūtā bāhirā. Sesarūpacetasikanibbānapaññattisaṅkhātāni cha bāhirāyatanāni, idha pana paññattiyopi labbhanti. Ajjhattikadukaṃ.

Next, in the dyad on the internal, what is internal is 'internal' as explained in the internal triad. The six internal sense bases are designated as sensitive material phenomena and consciousness. What is external to those is 'external'. The six external sense bases are designated as the remaining material phenomena, mental factors, Nibbāna, and concepts; here, concepts are also obtained. The Dyad on the Internal.

Upādiyanteva bhūtāni, na bhūtā viya upādiyantīti upādā, catuvīsati upādārūpāni eva. Na upādiyantīti no upādā, catumahābhūtacittacetasikanibbānāni. Upādādukaṃ.

Because they are derived from the great elements, they are called 'derived' (upādā); these are only the twenty-four derived material phenomena. Because they are not derived, they are called 'not derived' (no upādā); these are the four great elements, consciousness, mental factors, and Nibbāna. The Dyad on the Derived.

Dvattiṃsa lokiyavipākacittāni, kammajarūpañca upādinnā nāma. Sesalokiyalokuttarāni, nibbānañca anupādinnā nāma[M 0.0147]. Sesaṃ upādinnupādāniyattike vuttānusārena ñātabbaṃ. Upādinnadukaṃ.

The thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses and kamma-produced material phenomena are called 'grasped' (upādinna). The remaining mundane and supramundane phenomena, and Nibbāna, are called 'not grasped' (anupādinna). The rest should be understood according to the explanation in the triad of the grasped and the graspable. The Dyad on the Grasped.

Mahantaradukā niṭṭhitā.

The Great Intermediate Dyads are concluded.

Upādānagocchakebhusaṃ ādiyantīti upādānā, daḷhaggāhaṃ gaṇhantīti attho. Daḷhattho hi ettha upa-saddo “upāyāso”tiādīsu viya. Tato aññe no upādānā. Tattha kāmupādānaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ attavādupādānanti ime upādānā nāma. Tattha vatthukāmesu uppanno kilesakāmova vuttanayena upādānanti kāmupādānaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tattha vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi attavādupādānaṃ nāma. Sesāni pubbe vuttāneva. Pacchimāni panettha tīṇi upādānāni tathāpavattadiṭṭhi eva. Tāni ca paṭhamena maggena pahīyanti, kāmupādānaṃ catūhipi[V 0.0111]. Ime ca sabhāvato dve dhammā vibhāgato caturupādānā nāma jātā. Ime pana ṭhapetvā sesā sabbe dhammā no upādānā nāma. Upādānadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

In the Section on Clinging, because they take up (ādiyanti) things intensely (bhusaṃ), they are 'clingings' (upādānā); the meaning is that they grasp firmly. Here, the prefix 'upa-' indeed has the sense of firmness, as in words such as 'upāyāso' (distress). Others are not clingings. Among these, the following are called clingings: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, and clinging to a doctrine of self. Herein, 'clinging to sensual pleasures' is the defilement of craving that arises regarding sense objects, which is a clinging in the manner stated. The same applies to the others. Among these, the twenty-based personality view is called 'clinging to a doctrine of self'. The rest have been previously explained. In this case, the latter three clingings are indeed views that have arisen in that way. These are abandoned by the first path, while clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned by all four paths. And these, which in essence are two phenomena, become the four clingings by way of classification. All other phenomena, apart from these, are called 'not-clinging'. The first is the Dyad on Clinging.

Upādāniyaduko saṃyojaniyadukasadisova. Dutiyaṃ.

The dyad on the clingable is similar to the dyad on the fetterable. The second.

Aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittāni, taṃsampayuttesu diṭṭhivippayuttalobhaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā ca upādānasampayuttā nāma. Diṭṭhivippayuttalobhadosamohamūlāni, kusalābyākatāni ca cittāni, rūpanibbānāni ca upādānavippayuttā nāma. Cetasikesu pana diṭṭhimānā upādānasampayuttāva, dosaissāmacchariyakukkuccavicikicchā, kusalābyākatā ca upādānavippayuttā eva. Sesā duvidhāpi honti. Tatiyaṃ.

The eight greed-accompanied consciousnesses, and their associated mental factors—except for greed in those consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view—are called 'associated with clinging'. The greed-rooted consciousnesses dissociated from wrong view, the hatred-rooted and delusion-rooted consciousnesses, as well as wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna, are called 'dissociated from clinging'. Among mental factors, however, wrong view and conceit are associated with clinging; hatred, envy, stinginess, worry, and doubt, as well as wholesome and indeterminate mental factors, are dissociated from clinging. The remaining mental factors can be of both kinds. The third.

Cattāri upādānāni upādānā ceva upādāniyā ca nāma. Tadavasesā lokiyā upādāniyā ceva no ca [M 0.0148] upādānā nāma. Idha pana lokuttarā na vattabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Catutthaṃ.

The four clingings are called both 'clingings' and 'clingable'. The remaining worldly states are called 'clingable' but not 'clingings'. Here, however, the supramundane states are not to be spoken of. The rest is as previously stated. The fourth.

Pañcamachaṭṭhadukā pāṭhato ganthagocchake pañcamachaṭṭhadukasadisāva, kevalaṃ pañcamaduke “cetasikesu māno upādānasampayutto ceva no ca upādāno eva, mohāhirikānottappauddhaccathinamiddhāni tijātikāni tathā ca na vattabbā cā”ti idañca, chaṭṭhaduke “cetasikesu dosaissāmacchariyakukkuccavicikicchā appamaññā upādānavippayuttā upādāniyā eva, mohāhirikānottappauddhaccalobhathinamiddhāni tathā ca na vattabbāni cā”ti ettakameva pāṭhato viseso, atthato pana nāmamattakova viseso. Seso suviññeyyova. Pañcamachaṭṭhāni.

The fifth and sixth dyads are similar in wording to the fifth and sixth dyads in the Section on Bonds, except that in the fifth dyad, it states: 'Among mental factors, conceit is associated with clinging but is not itself clinging. Delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, restlessness, sloth, and torpor are of three classes and are not to be spoken of in the same way.' And in the sixth dyad, it states: 'Among mental factors, hatred, envy, stinginess, worry, doubt, and the immeasurables are dissociated from clinging but are objects of clinging. Delusion, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, restlessness, greed, sloth, and torpor are likewise and are not to be spoken of in the same way.' This is the only difference in wording, but in meaning, the difference is merely a matter of name. The rest is easily understood. The fifth and sixth.

Upādānagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Clinging is concluded.

Kilesagocchake saṃkiliṭṭhattike vuttanayena padattho veditabbo. Lobho doso moho māno diṭṭhi vicikicchā thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime dasa dhammā kilesā nāma. Ime ca vuttatthā eva, idha pana lobho, hetuganthanīvaraṇaupādānagocchakesu lobho ca nippadesato catumaggavajjhopi ekeneva koṭṭhāsena ṭhito, sesagocchakesu so sabbopi lobho “kāmāsavo bhavāsavo”tiādinā [V 0.0112] dve dve koṭṭhāsā hutvā ṭhito, iminā pana aṭṭhakathāvacanenāpi bhavāsavādibyatiritto sabbo catumaggavajjhopi rāgo kāmāsavādīsu saṅgahito. Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ pana bhavarāgopi na pañcakāmaguṇikarāgamattovāti paññāyati, “āruppe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhanīvaraṇa”ntiādipāḷito (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) cetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassa rūpārūpabhūmīsu anuppajjanato. Imesu [M 0.0149] ca kilesesu diṭṭhivicikicchā paṭhamena maggena pahīyanti, doso tatiyena, lobhādayo catūhipi. Ime pana dasa dhamme ṭhapetvā sesā no kilesā nāma. Kilesadukaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

In the Section on Defilements, the meaning of the terms should be understood in the manner stated in the triplet of defiled states. Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread—these ten phenomena are called defilements. And these have been explained as above. Here, however, greed, in the sections on roots, bonds, hindrances, and clinging, stands as one category, even though it is to be abandoned by the four paths in its entirety. In the remaining sections, all that greed stands as two categories, such as 'the taint of sensuality and the taint of existence,' and so on. Moreover, according to this commentary passage, all craving, even that to be abandoned by the four paths, is included in the taint of sensuality, etc., apart from the taint of existence, etc. The hindrance of sensual desire, however, is understood to include even craving for existence, and is not merely craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure. This should be seen from the Pāli text, 'In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, there arises the hindrance of sloth and torpor,' etc. (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8), because craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure does not arise in the form and formless realms. Among these defilements, wrong view and doubt are abandoned by the first path, hatred by the third, and greed and the rest by all four paths. Apart from these ten phenomena, the rest are not called defilements. The first is the dyad of defilements.

Saṃkilesikaduko sāsavadukasadisova. Dutiyaṃ.

The dyad of corrupting factors is similar to the dyad of taints. The second.

Saṃkiliṭṭhaduko, kilesasampayuttaduko cāti dvepi samānatthāva. Te ca nīvaraṇagocchake tatiyadukasadisāva. Tatiyacatutthāni.

The dyad of defiled states and the dyad of states associated with defilements—these two indeed have the same meaning. And they are similar to the third dyad in the Section on Hindrances. The third and fourth.

Dasa kilesā kilesā ceva saṃkilesikā ca nāma. Sesā lokiyadhammā saṃkilesikā ceva no ca kilesā nāma. Idha pana lokuttarā na vattabbā. Sesaṃ nīvaraṇagocchake catutthadukasadisameva. Pañcamaṃ.

The ten defilements are called both defilements and corrupting factors. The remaining worldly phenomena are called corrupting factors but not defilements. Here, however, the supramundane states are not to be spoken of. The rest is similar to the fourth dyad in the Section on Hindrances. The fifth.

Chaṭṭhasattamadukānipi aññamaññaṃ samānatthāneva. Tāni chaṭṭhasattamāni nīvaraṇagocchake yathākkamaṃ pāṭhato pañcamachaṭṭhadukasadisāni, atthato pana nāmamattakova viseso. Seso suviññeyyo. Chaṭṭhasattamaaṭṭhamāni.

The sixth and seventh dyads are similar in meaning to each other. These sixth and seventh dyads, in the Section on Hindrances, are similar in wording to the fifth and sixth dyads respectively, but in meaning, the difference is merely a matter of name. The rest is easily understood. The sixth, seventh, and eighth.

Kilesagocchakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on Defilements is concluded.

Piṭṭhidukesu ādito cattāro dukā dassanenapahātabbattike, dassanenapahātabbahetuke ca vuttanayena veditabbā.
