Kevalaṃ pana tattha paṭhamattike vuttesu dassanenapahātabbe dhamme ṭhapetvā sesā idha paṭhamadukassa dutiyapade dassanenapahātabbesu pavisanti, bhāvanāyapahātabbe ṭhapetvā sesā idha dutiyaduke nabhāvanāyapahātabbesu pavisanti. Tattha ca dutiyattike vuttesu dassanenapahātabbahetuke ṭhapetvā [V 0.0113] sesā idha tatiyaduke nadassanenapahātabbahetuke, bhāvanāyapahātabbahetuke ca ṭhapetvā sesā idha catutthaduke nabhāvanāyapahātabbahetukesu pavisanti.

In the Posterior Dyads, the first four dyads are to be understood in the manner stated in the triplet of states to be abandoned by insight and the triplet of roots to be abandoned by insight. However, setting aside the phenomena to be abandoned by insight as mentioned in the first triplet, the remaining phenomena here enter into the states not to be abandoned by insight in the second term of the first dyad; and setting aside those to be abandoned by cultivation, the remaining phenomena here enter into the states not to be abandoned by cultivation in the second dyad. Furthermore, in the second triplet, setting aside the roots to be abandoned by insight as mentioned, the remaining phenomena here enter into the states not rooted in what is to be abandoned by insight in the third dyad; and setting aside the roots to be abandoned by cultivation, the remaining phenomena here enter into the states not rooted in what is to be abandoned by cultivation in the fourth dyad.

Padattho [M 0.0150] ca dassanena pahātabbo hetu etesaṃ atthīti dassanenapahātabbahetukā. Evaṃ bhāvanāyapahātabbahetukāti etthāpi attho veditabbo. Evaṃ hi sati ahetukānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ siyāti ettakameva viseso. Tikadvayameva hi bhagavā desanāvilāsena cattāro duke katvā desesi. Sesaṃ tādisameva. Cattāro dukā niṭṭhitā.

And the meaning of the term 'rooted in what is to be abandoned by insight' is that they have a root to be abandoned by insight. Similarly, the meaning of 'rooted in what is to be abandoned by cultivation' should be understood here too. This being so, the only difference is the non-inclusion of rootless states. Indeed, the Blessed One, with the elegance of his teaching, taught the two triplets by making them into four dyads. The rest is just the same. The four dyads are concluded.

Pañcapaññāsasavitakkacittesu vitakkavirahitā cittacetasikā dhammā savitakkā nāma. Vitakko, pana sesacittarūpanibbānāni ca avitakkā nāma. Pañcamaṃ.

In the fifty-five consciousnesses accompanied by applied thought, the phenomena of consciousness and mental factors, excluding applied thought itself, are called 'accompanied by applied thought.' Applied thought itself, however, along with the remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna, are called 'without applied thought.' The fifth.

Chasaṭṭhiyā savicāracittesu vicāravirahitā dhammā savicārā nāma. Vicāro, pana sesacittarūpanibbānāni ca avicārā nāma. Sesaṃ idha, anantare vuttaduke ca vitakkattike vuttānusārena ñātabbaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

In the sixty-six consciousnesses accompanied by sustained thought, the phenomena, excluding sustained thought itself, are called 'accompanied by sustained thought.' Sustained thought itself, however, along with the remaining consciousnesses, material phenomena, and Nibbāna, are called 'without sustained thought.' The rest here, and in the immediately preceding dyad, should be understood according to what has been stated in the triplet on applied thought. The sixth.

Ito paresu sappītikaduko, pītisahagataduko ca samānatthāva, te ca sukhasahagataupekkhāsahagatadukā cāti cattāropi dukā pītittike vuttanayāva. Kevalaṃ panetesaṃ dukānaṃ paṭhamaṃ padaṃ tattha pavisati, pītittike itarītarapadadvayasaṅgahitā, asaṅgahitā ca sabbe atthā heṭṭhā vuttanayenettha dukānaṃ dutiyapadesu atthato saṅgahitā, ime ca nippadesadukāti ayameva viseso. Sattamaaṭṭhamanavamadasamā.

Hereafter, the dyad of states accompanied by joy and the dyad of states associated with joy have the same meaning. These, along with the dyad of states accompanied by happiness and the dyad of states accompanied by equanimity—all four of these dyads are to be understood in the manner stated in the triplet on joy. However, only the first term of these dyads corresponds to a term there. All things that are included in the other two terms of the triplet on joy, and those that are not included at all, are here included in meaning in the second terms of these dyads, in the manner previously explained. This is the only difference, that these are exhaustive dyads. The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.

Tadanantaresu kāmāvacarāti ettha “heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito paranimmitavasavattī deve anto karitvā yaṃ tasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā”ti evaṃ (dha. sa. 1287) pāḷiyaṃ paricchinnānaṃ catunnaṃ apāyānaṃ, manussānaṃ, channaṃ devalokānañca vasena okāsato ekādasavidho kāmabhavo [M 0.0151] “kāmo”ti vuccati uttarapadalopena yathā “rūpūpapattiyā”tiādīsu rūpabhavo “rūpa”nti. Tasmiṃ kāme avacaranti pavattantīti kāmāvacarā. Yebhuyyato cetaṃ vuttaṃ rūpārūpesu cetesañca idha pavattito “thalacarā”tiādīsu viya. Kāmabhavasaṅkhāte vā kāme paṭisandhiṃ avacārentītipi kāmāvacarā, kusalākusalāni[V 0.0114]. Uddhaccasahagatacittaṃ pana abyākatacittasadisaṃ. Tadāyattatāya, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena vā kilesakāmo ettha avacaratītipi kāmāvacaraṃ. Kāmañcesa rūpārūpāvacaradhammesupi avacarati, ruḷhito pana “vadatīti vaccho”tiādīsu viya ime eva “kāmāvacarā”ti vuccanti. Apica kāmataṇhā rūpataṇhā arūpataṇhāti ettha vuttakāmataṇhāsaṅkhāto kāmo ettha avacaratītipi kāmāvacarā. Evaṃ brahmānaṃ vimānābharaṇādīsu chandarāgassāpi kāmataṇhābhāvo siddho, rūpataṇhāvisayānampi ca brahmānaṃ kammajarūpādīnaṃ kāmataṇhāyapi visayatāya kāmāvacaratā siddhā hoti. Na rūpārūpāvacarānaṃ tadabhāvato tadaññe na kāmāvacarā. Iminā nayena rūpāvacarādidukānampi padattho yathārahaṃ ñātabbo. Tattha catupaññāsa kāmāvacaracittāni, sabbañca rūpaṃ kāmāvacarā nāma. Sesacittanibbānāni na kāmāvacarā nāma. Cetasikesu vattabbaṃ pariyāpannaduke eva āvi bhavissati. Ekādasamaṃ.

Regarding 'of the sense sphere' (kāmāvacara) here: 'Having made Avīci hell the lower boundary and the Paranimmitavasavattī devas the upper limit—whatever is included within this interval is what moves within this sphere, is comprised within this sphere.' Thus, in the Pāli (Dhs. 1287), the elevenfold sense-sphere existence, defined by location as comprising the four lower realms, the human realm, and the six celestial realms, is called 'kāma' by elision of the latter part of the word, just as 'rūpa' is used for form existence in expressions like 'rebirth in the form realm' (rūpūpapatti). They move about (avacaranti) and occur (pavattanti) in that kāma, thus they are 'of the sense sphere' (kāmāvacara). This is said generally, since these also occur here in the form and formless spheres, similar to terms like 'land-dweller' (thalacara). Alternatively, wholesome and unwholesome states that cause rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the existence of the sense sphere (kāmabhava) are also 'of the sense sphere'. The consciousness accompanied by restlessness, however, is similar to an indeterminate consciousness. Or, because of its dependence on that (kāma), or because sensual desire (kilesakāma) moves about therein by way of being an object, it is 'of the sense sphere'. Although this sensual desire also moves about in form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena, by convention only these are called 'of the sense sphere', just as in expressions like 'it speaks (vadati), thus it is a calf (vaccha)'. Moreover, the kāma which is sensual craving, mentioned in 'sensual craving, form craving, formless craving,' moves about therein, thus these are 'of the sense sphere'. In this way, the nature of sensual craving is established even for the desire and longing (chandarāga) of Brahmās for celestial mansions, ornaments, and so forth. And since the kamma-born form, etc., of Brahmās, which are objects of form craving, are also objects of sensual craving, their nature as 'of the sense sphere' is established. Because form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena lack that (sensual craving), those other than these are not 'of the sense sphere'. By this method, the meaning of the terms in the dyads beginning with 'of the form sphere' should be understood as appropriate. Therein, the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses and all material form are called 'of the sense sphere'. The remaining consciousnesses and Nibbāna are not called 'of the sense sphere'. What is to be said regarding mental factors will become clear in the dyad of the included. The eleventh.

Pannarasa rūpāvacaracittāni rūpāvacarā nāma. Sesacittarūpanibbānāni na rūpāvacarā nāma. Dvādasamaṃ.

The fifteen form-sphere consciousnesses are called 'of the form sphere' (rūpāvacara). The remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are not called 'of the form sphere'. The twelfth.

Dvādasa arūpāvacaracittāni arūpāvacarā nāma. Sesacittarūpanibbānāni na arūpāvacarā nāma. Terasamaṃ.

The twelve formless-sphere consciousnesses are called 'of the formless sphere' (arūpāvacara). The remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna are not called 'of the formless sphere'. The thirteenth.

Tebhūmakavaṭṭe pariyāpannā antogadhāti pariyāpannā, lokiyadhammāva. Tattha na pariyāpannāti apariyāpannā, lokuttarā. Cetasikesu pana kāmāvacarādidukānaṃ catunnampi [M 0.0152] sādhāraṇo vinicchayo evaṃ veditabbo – akusalacetasikā kāmāvacarāva, appamaññā kāmarūpāvacarā, viratiyo pana kāmāvacarapariyāpannā, vitakkavicārapītiyo pana kāmarūpāvacarapariyāpannā, sesā catubhūmakāti. Cuddasamaṃ.

Those included in, contained within, the round of the three planes are 'included' (pariyāpanna); these are the worldly phenomena. Those not included therein are 'not included' (apariyāpanna); these are the supramundane phenomena. Regarding the mental factors, the common determination for all four dyads beginning with 'of the sense sphere' should be understood thus: unwholesome mental factors are only of the sense sphere; the immeasurables are of the sense and form spheres; the abstinences are included in the sense sphere; applied thought, sustained thought, and joy are included in the sense and form spheres; the rest are of the four planes. The fourteenth.

Vaṭṭamūlaṃ chindantā nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vaṭṭato nīyantīti niyyānikā, cattāri lokuttaramaggacittāni. Iminā lakkhaṇena na niyyantīti aniyyānikā, sesacittarūpanibbānāni. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pañcadasamaṃ.

Cutting off the root of the round of existence, having taken Nibbāna as their object, they lead out from the round, thus they are 'leading out' (niyyānika); these are the four supramundane path consciousnesses. Those that do not lead out by this characteristic are 'not leading out' (aniyyānika); these are the remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna. The rest is easily understood. The fifteenth.

Cutiyā [V 0.0115] vā attano vā pavattiyā anantaraṃ phaladāne niyatattā niyatā, micchattaniyatā, sammattaniyatā ca. Tathā aniyatattā aniyatā, sesadhammā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Soḷasamaṃ.

Because they are fixed on giving their fruit immediately after death or after their own occurrence, they are 'fixed' (niyata); these are those fixed in wrongness and those fixed in rightness. Similarly, because they are not fixed, they are 'unfixed' (aniyata); these are the remaining phenomena. The rest is as explained. The sixteenth.

Aññe dhamme uttaranti atikkamantīti uttarā, attānaṃ uttarituṃ samatthehi saha uttarehīti sauttarā, lokiyāva. Natthi etesaṃ uttarāti anuttarā, lokuttarā. Sattarasamaṃ.

They surpass, they overcome other phenomena, thus they are 'superior' (uttara). They are 'with a superior' (sauttara) because they are together with what is superior or with what is capable of surpassing them; these are the worldly phenomena. There is nothing superior to these, thus they are 'unsurpassed' (anuttara); these are the supramundane phenomena. The seventeenth.

Raṇanti kandanti etehīti raṇā, yehi abhibhūtā sattā nānappakārato paridevanti, tesaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tehi sampayogavasena, pahānekaṭṭhatāvasena ca saha raṇehīti saraṇā. Etenākārena natthi etesaṃ raṇāti araṇā.

Beings make noise (raṇanti), they cry out (kandanti) because of these, thus they are 'strife' (raṇa); this is a designation for the unwholesome roots, by which beings, when overcome, lament in various ways. They are 'with strife' (saraṇa) because they are together with strife by way of association and by way of sharing the single nature of being abandoned. By this reasoning, those for which there is no strife are 'without strife' (araṇa).

Tattha dvādasa akusalacittāni saraṇā nāma. Saraṇadhammesu cettha lobhadosamohā raṇā ceva saraṇā ca, tesu lobhadosā moheneva sampayogato saraṇā, tathā vicikicchuddhaccasahagatacittaṃ, taṃsampayuttā ca. Moho pana tesu sampayogato saraṇo, diṭṭhisampayuttarāgena, pana bhavarāgena ca raṇabhūtena pahānekaṭṭhatāvaseneva saraṇo[M 0.0153]. Lobhadosamohamūlasampayuttesu pana moho lobhena ceva dosena ca, sesā lobhamohena ceva dosamohena ca sampayogato saraṇāti veditabbā. Sabbāni kusalābyākatacittāni, rūpanibbānāni ca araṇā nāma. Cetasikesu pana akusalā saraṇāva, kusalābyākatā araṇāva, tijātikā pana dvidhāpi hontīti. Aṭṭhārasamaṃ.

Herein, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are called 'with strife' (saraṇa). Among these phenomena with strife, greed, hatred, and delusion are both 'strife' (raṇa) and 'with strife' (saraṇa). Among them, greed and hatred are 'with strife' through association with delusion; similarly, the consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness, and its associated states, are 'with strife'. Delusion, however, is 'with strife' through association with them. And in the case of greed associated with wrong view and greed for existence, which are 'strife', delusion is 'with strife' only by way of being of a single nature with their abandonment. In those states associated with the roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, it should be understood that delusion is 'with strife' through association with greed and with hatred, and the remaining factors are 'with strife' through association with greed-and-delusion and with hatred-and-delusion. All wholesome and indeterminate consciousnesses, as well as material form and Nibbāna, are called 'without strife' (araṇa). Among the mental factors, the unwholesome are only 'with strife'; the wholesome and indeterminate are only 'without strife'; while those of the three kinds can be both. The eighteenth.

Piṭṭhidukā niṭṭhitā.

The preceding dyads are concluded.

Abhidhammadukamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Dyad Matrix is concluded.

Suttantikadukamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Suttanta Dyad Matrix

Suttantikadukesu vedeti, vividhena vā ākārena jānātīti vijjā, vipassanāñāṇamanomayiddhichaabhiññāvasappavattā paññā, tasmiṃ vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vijjāsabhāve [V 0.0116] vattantīti vijjābhāgino. Tā eva vijjā, taṃ vā vijjaṃ sampayogavasena bhajantītipi vijjābhāgino, aṭṭhavidhavijjāsampayuttadhammā. Tāsu yā kāci ekā vijjā vijjā, sesā vijjābhāginoti evaṃ vijjāpi vijjāsampayuttadhammāpi vijjābhāginotveva veditabbā, idha pana vijjāsampayuttā dhammāva adhippetā. Na vijānātīti avijjā, catusaccacchādakavasena catubbidho moho, tasmiṃ avijjābhāge avijjākoṭṭhāse avijjāsabhāve vattantīti avijjābhāgino. Tā eva avijjā, taṃ vā avijjaṃ sampayogavasena bhajantītipi avijjābhāgino, avijjāsampayuttadhammā. Evaṃ avijjāpi avijjāsampayuttadhammāpi avijjābhāginotveva veditabbā, idha pana avijjāsampayuttadhammāva adhippetā.

In the Suttanta dyads: one knows (vedeti), or one knows in various ways (vividhena ākārena jānāti), thus it is 'knowledge' (vijjā). Wisdom (paññā) that proceeds by way of insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six higher knowledges is knowledge. Those that exist in that portion of knowledge, in that division of knowledge, in that nature of knowledge, are 'partaking of knowledge' (vijjābhāgino). Those very knowledges, or those that partake of that knowledge by way of association, are also 'partaking of knowledge'; these are the phenomena associated with the eight kinds of knowledge. Among these, any single knowledge is 'knowledge', while the rest are 'partaking of knowledge'. Thus, both knowledge itself and the phenomena associated with knowledge should be understood as 'partaking of knowledge'. Here, however, only the phenomena associated with knowledge are intended. One does not know (na vijānāti), thus it is 'ignorance' (avijjā); this is the fourfold delusion that obscures the four truths. Those that exist in that portion of ignorance, in that division of ignorance, in that nature of ignorance, are 'partaking of ignorance' (avijjābhāgino). That very ignorance, or those that partake of that ignorance by way of association, are also 'partaking of ignorance'; these are the phenomena associated with ignorance. Thus, both ignorance itself and the phenomena associated with ignorance should be understood as 'partaking of ignorance'. Here, however, only the phenomena associated with ignorance are intended.

Tattha arahattamaggacittaṃ, paññāvirahitataṃsampayuttā ca vijjābhāgino ca ñāṇasampayuttakāmāvacarajavanāni, ñāṇavirahitataṃsampayuttā [M 0.0154] ca vipassanābhāvena pavattiyaṃ vijjābhāgino, aññadā na vattabbā. Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānikajavanacittāni, paññāvirahitataṃsampayuttā ca manomayiddhibhāvena ca pañcābhiññābhāvena ca pavattiyaṃ vijjābhāgino, aññadā na vattabbā. Tattha dvādasākusalacittāni, avijjāvirahitataṃsampayuttā ca avijjābhāginova, idha pana avijjā, sesacittarūpanibbānāni ca na vattabbāva. Cetasikesu pana mohaappamaññā na vattabbāva, sesā kusalābyākatā siyā vijjābhāgino, siyā na vattabbā, tijātikā dvidhāpi na vattabbā ca. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Paṭhamaṃ.

Herein, the Arahantship path-consciousness and the factors associated with it apart from wisdom are 'partaking of knowledge'. And the knowledge-associated sense-sphere javanas and the factors associated with them apart from knowledge, when occurring as insight, are 'partaking of knowledge'; at other times, they are not to be so called. The fourth-jhāna form-sphere javana consciousnesses, and the factors associated with them apart from wisdom, when occurring as mind-made psychic power or as the five higher knowledges, are 'partaking of knowledge'; at other times, they are not to be so called. Here, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, and the factors associated with them apart from ignorance, are indeed 'partaking of ignorance'. But here, ignorance itself, along with the remaining consciousnesses, material form, and Nibbāna, are not to be so called. Among the mental factors, delusion and the immeasurables are not to be so called. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate mental factors may be 'partaking of knowledge', or may not be so called. And those of three kinds are not to be so called in either way. The rest is easily understood. The first.

Puna anajjhottharaṇavasena kilesandhakāraṃ viddhaṃsetuṃ asamatthatāya vijju upamā etesanti vijjūpamā, ādito tīsu maggesu ñāṇaṃva. Nissesaṃ viddhaṃsanasamatthatāya vajiraṃ upamā etesanti vajirūpamā, arahattamagge ñāṇaṃ. Yathā hi meghandhakāre maggapaṭipannassa paṭicchādanaandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā vijjuyā uppannakkhaṇe cātudisā maggā pākaṭā honti, vijjuyā niruddhāya puna andhakāro ottharitvā maggaṃ paṭicchādeti, evaṃ vipassanāyānikassa yathāsakaṃ saccacchādakakilesandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā tīsu maggesu yathākkamaṃ uppannesu cattāri saccāni pākaṭāni honti, tesu niruddhesu puna avasiṭṭhakilesandhakāro catusaccaṃ paṭicchādeti, tasmā tīsu maggesu paññā vijjūpamā vuttā. Yathā pana vajirassa abhejjo pāsāṇo nāma natthi, tañca nissesato vajiraṃ khepeti, vajirena ca gatamagge pāsāṇassa puna [V 0.0117] pākatikabhāvo natthi, evaṃ arahattamaggañāṇassa avajjhakileso nāma natthi, tañca nissesato arahattamaggañāṇaṃ khepeti, tena ca khepite kilese avasiṭṭhakilesābhāvato tassa puna paccudāvattanaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā [M 0.0155] catutthamagge paññā vajirūpamā vuttā. Paññā eva hettha siyā vijjūpamā, siyā na vattabbā ca hoti. Sesacetasikacittarūpanibbānāni pana sabbāni na vattabbāneva. Dutiyaṃ.

Again, because by way of not completely overwhelming they are unable to destroy the darkness of defilements, they have lightning as a simile, thus they are 'lightning-like'—this is the knowledge in the first three paths. Because they are able to destroy without remainder, they have a diamond as a simile, thus they are 'diamond-like'—this is the knowledge in the path of Arahantship. For just as, in the darkness of clouds, for one who has entered upon a path, when lightning arises and dispels the obscuring darkness, the paths in the four directions become manifest, but when the lightning has ceased, darkness again spreads and conceals the path; so too, for one practicing insight, when the darkness of defilements that conceals the respective truths is dispelled as the three paths arise in sequence, the four truths become manifest. But when those paths have ceased, the remaining darkness of defilements again conceals the four truths. Therefore, the wisdom in the three paths is said to be 'lightning-like.' And just as there is no rock that cannot be split by a diamond, and the diamond destroys it without remainder, and on the path traversed by the diamond the rock does not return to its natural state; so too, there is no defilement that cannot be destroyed by the knowledge of the Arahantship path, and that knowledge destroys it without remainder. And when the defilements have been destroyed by it, because of the absence of remaining defilements, there is no such thing as their returning again. Therefore, the wisdom in the fourth path is said to be 'diamond-like.' Here, wisdom itself may be 'lightning-like,' or it may not be so called. But all the other mental factors, consciousness, materiality, and Nibbāna cannot be described as such. Second.

Bālesu ṭhitattā, yattha ṭhitā tadupacārena bālā, bālakarattā vā bālā, dvādasākusalacittāni. Idha pana ahirikañca anottappañca bālā nāma. Paṇḍitesu ṭhitattā paṇḍitā, paṇḍitakarattā vā paṇḍitā, ekavīsati kusalacittāni. Idha pana hirī ca ottappañca paṇḍitā nāma. Sesacittarūpanibbānāni na vattabbāni. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Tatiyaṃ.

Because they are established in foolish things, or by extension from where they are established, they are 'fools'; or because they make one a fool, they are 'fools'—these are the twelve unwholesome states of consciousness. Here, however, shamelessness and lack of moral dread are called 'fools.' Because they are established in wise things, they are 'wise'; or because they make one wise, they are 'wise'—these are the twenty-one wholesome states of consciousness. Here, however, moral shame and moral dread are called 'the wise.' The remaining states of consciousness, materiality, and Nibbāna are not to be so called. The rest is easily understood. Third.

Kaṇhāti kāḷakā, cittassa apabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Sukkāti odātā, pabhassarabhāvakaraṇā. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ bāladukasadisameva. Catutthaṃ.

'Black' means dark, because it makes the mind non-radiant. 'White' means bright, because it makes the mind radiant. The rest is all just like the dyad of fools. Fourth.

Idha ceva samparāye ca tapentīti tapanīyā. Na tapanīyā atapanīyā. Sesaṃ bāladukasadisameva. Pañcamaṃ.

Because they torment both here and in the future life, they are 'tormenting' (tapanīyā). What is not tormenting is 'non-tormenting' (atapanīyā). The rest is similar to the dyad of fools. Fifth.

“Sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhako”tiādayo viya vacanamattameva adhikāraṃ katvā pavattā adhivacanā nāma. Nāmadheyyanti tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ nāmāni. Tāni catubbidhāni sāmaññanāmaṃ guṇanāmaṃ kittimanāmaṃ opapātikanāmanti. Tattha paṭhamakappikesu mahājanena sammannitvā ṭhapitattā “mahāsammato”ti rañño nāmanti evarūpaṃ sāmaññanāmaṃ nāma. “Dhammakathiko paṃsukūliko kāḷo rasso”ti evarūpaṃ guṇato āgataṃ, “bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādīnipi tathāgatassa anekāni nāmasatāni guṇanāmaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana jātassa kumārassa ñātakā kappetvā pakappetvā “ayaṃ asuko nāmā”ti nāmaṃ karonti, idaṃ kittimanāmaṃ [M 0.0156] nāma. Yā pana purimapaññatti aparapaññattiyaṃ nipatati, seyyathidaṃ – purimakappepi cando cando eva, etarahipi anāgatepi cando eva. Tathā “sūriyo samuddo pathavī rūpaṃ vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ nibbāna”ntievamādi opapātikanāmaṃ nāma. Tāni puna vijjamānapaññatti avijjamānapaññatti vijjamānenaavijjamānapaññatti avijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti [V 0.0118] vijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti avijjamānenaavijjamānapaññattīti evaṃ nāmapaññattivasena chabbidhāni honti.

Designations (adhivacanā) are those that arise by taking a mere word as their basis, like 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' (Increase of Fortune) and 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka' (Increase of Wealth). Names (nāmadheyyāni) are the names of various phenomena. They are of four kinds: common names (sāmaññanāma), names derived from qualities (guṇanāma), created names (kittimanāma), and spontaneously arisen names (opapātikanāma). Among these, a common name is one like 'Mahāsammato' (The Great Elect), the name of the king, which was established by the great populace in the first aeon. A name derived from qualities is one that comes from a quality, like 'Dhammakathika' (Preacher of Dhamma), 'Paṃsukūlika' (Rag-Robe Wearer), 'Kāḷa' (The Dark One), 'Rassa' (The Short One); and the many hundreds of names of the Tathāgata such as 'Bhagavā' (The Blessed One), 'Arahaṃ' (The Worthy One), 'Sammāsambuddho' (The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One) are also names derived from qualities. A created name is one that relatives conceive and fashion for a newborn child, declaring, 'This one shall be named so-and-so.' A spontaneously arisen name is one where an earlier designation persists in a later designation—for example, the moon was 'cando' in a past aeon, is 'cando' now, and will be 'cando' in the future. Similarly, 'sūriyo' (the sun), 'samuddo' (the ocean), 'pathavī' (the earth), 'rūpaṃ' (materiality), 'vedanā' (feeling), 'saññā' (perception), 'saṅkhārā' (formations), 'viññāṇaṃ' (consciousness), and 'nibbāna' (Nibbāna)—these are all spontaneously arisen names. Furthermore, by way of name-designation (nāmapaññatti), these are sixfold: designation of what exists (vijjamānapaññatti), designation of what does not exist (avijjamānapaññatti), designation of what does not exist by means of what exists (vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti), designation of what exists by means of what does not exist (avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti), designation of what exists by means of what exists (vijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti), and designation of what does not exist by means of what does not exist (avijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti).

Tattha paramatthato upalabbhamānā yathāvuttadvāsattatividhā nāmarūpadhammā vijjamānā nāma, tesaṃ pakārehi ñāpanato paññatti vijjamānapaññatti nāma, “cittaṃ phasso pathavī rūpaṃ nibbāna”ntiādayo paramatthavācakā saddā. Upādinnanāmarūpadhamme pana upādāya paññattā sattapuggalaitthipurisadevamanussatiracchānādibhedā, anupādinnarūpadhamme upādāya paññattā bhūmipabbatarukkhasakaṭacandasūriyanakkhattadisākālakasiṇādibhedā ca paramatthato anupalabbhamānā avijjamānā nāma, tesaṃ paññatti avijjamānapaññatti nāma. Tathā “attā bhūmī”tiādayo atthapaññattivācakā saddā ca cittasantativaṇṇupagantiādi vijjamānatthavācakā saddā vijjamānenaavijjamānapaññatti nāma. “Purisassa cittaṃ, meghavaṇṇo”tiādīsu avijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti nāma. “Cittalahutā pathavīgandho”tiādi vijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti nāma. “Manussasarīraṃ rukkhasākhā”tiādi avijjamānenaavijjamānapaññatti nāma. Evaṃ chabbidhāpi cetā adhippāyaṃ viññāpetukāmatācittasamuṭṭhāpitasaviññattisaddānusārena ñātasaṅketassa sotaviññāṇavīthianantaraṃ uppannehi manodvārikaviññāṇehi “imassedaṃ nāma”nti anekasaddesu ekattamāropetvā vavatthāpitā atthābhimukhaṃ namanato pakārehi atthassa ñāpanato “nāmapaññattī”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ [M 0.0157] adhivacanānaṃ pathā atthā adhivacanapathā, sammutiparamatthabhedā sabbe dhammā saddavacanīyasabhāvā. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Therein, the seventy-two kinds of name-and-form phenomena as described, being found in the ultimate sense, are called 'existing' (vijjamānā). The designation by which they are made known through their modes is called 'designation of what exists' (vijjamānapaññatti); for example, words denoting ultimate realities such as 'mind,' 'contact,' 'earth,' 'materiality,' and 'Nibbāna.' However, designations based on appropriated name-and-form phenomena—such as beings, persons, women, men, devas, humans, animals, and so forth—and designations based on unappropriated materiality phenomena—such as lands, mountains, trees, carts, the moon, the sun, stars, directions, time, and kasinas—are called 'non-existent' (avijjamānā) because they are not found in the ultimate sense; their designation is called 'designation of what does not exist' (avijjamānapaññatti). Similarly, words denoting meaning-designations (atthapaññattivācakā saddā) like 'self' and 'earth,' and words denoting existing meanings (vijjamānatthavācakā saddā) such as 'the continuity of mind' and 'the succession of color,' are called 'designation of what does not exist by means of what exists' (vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti). In expressions like 'a man’s mind' and 'the color of a cloud,' they are called 'designation of what exists by means of what does not exist' (avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti). In phrases like 'the lightness of mind' and 'the smell of earth,' they are called 'designation of what exists by means of what exists' (vijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti). In statements like 'a human body' and 'a tree branch,' they are called 'designation of what does not exist by means of what does not exist' (avijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti). Thus, all six of these types are established by the mind-door consciousnesses that arise immediately after the ear-consciousness process has apprehended a known convention. This occurs in accordance with the sounds of verbal intimation produced by the mind's intention to communicate meaning, by imposing unity upon multiple sounds and determining them as 'this is such-and-such a name.' Because they incline towards meaning and reveal meaning through various modes, they are called 'name-designations' (nāmapaññatti). The scope of these designations constitutes the 'paths of terms' (adhivacanapathā). All phenomena, whether distinguished as conventional or ultimate, are of a nature to be expressed by words. Sixth.

Ito paraṃ dve dukā adhivacanadukasadisāva, kevalaṃ padatthamattameva viseso. Tattha abhisaṅkharontīti saṅkhārāti evaṃ niddhāretvā sahetukaṃ katvā vuccamānā nirutti nāma, “takko vitakko saṅkappo”ti evaṃ tena tena pakārena ñāpanato paññatti nāma, yathāvuttanāmapaññattiyova. Na hi adhivacananiruttipaññattīsu atthato kocipi bhedo atthi, nibbattinimittabhedadassanatthaṃ pana nesaṃ vibhāgena padattho dassito. Imesu ca tīsu dukesu paññattisahitā sabbe dhammā labbhanti, anantare nāmarūpaduke paññattirahitāti ime cattāro dukā imesu suttantikadukesu nippadesā, sesā pana aṭṭhatiṃsāpi sappadesāti veditabbā. Sattamaṭṭhamāni.

The two dyads that follow are similar to the dyad of designation; the only difference is in the meaning of the terms. Here, an etymological explanation given with its cause, such as defining 'formations' (saṅkhārā) by 'they construct,' is called 'expression' (nirutti). Making something known in various ways, such as 'thinking, initial thought, intention,' is called 'concept' (paññatti), which is just like the name-concepts mentioned before. Indeed, there is no difference in meaning among designation, expression, and concept. However, the meaning of the terms is shown separately in order to illustrate the differences in their origin and characteristics. In these three dyads, all phenomena are included along with concepts, but in the immediately following name-and-form dyad, they are without concepts. These four dyads, among the Suttanta dyads, are exhaustive; but the remaining thirty-eight should be understood as non-exhaustive. Seventh and eighth.

Nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena, namanaṭṭhena, nāmanaṭṭhena ca nāmaṃ, arūpakkhandhanibbānāni. Tāni hi sabbadāpi [V 0.0119] vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ nibbānanti opapātikanāmavasena attano nāmaṃ karontāva pavattanti candasūriyādayo viya. Na hi tesaṃ sāmaññaguṇakittimavasena nāmakaraṇakiccaṃ atthīti. Evaṃ nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena nāmaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ pana namanaṭṭhena, aññamaññaṃ tattha nāmanaṭṭhena ca cattāro arūpakkhandhāva nāmaṃ. Nibbānaṃ pana ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatāya attani anavajjadhammānaṃ nāmanaṭṭheneva nāmaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ruppanaṭṭhena rūpaṃ, rūpakkhandho. Navamaṃ.

By the characteristic of naming, by the characteristic of inclining, and by the characteristic of designation, 'name' refers to the formless aggregates and Nibbāna. For these—feeling, perception, formations, consciousness, and Nibbāna—always proceed by assigning a name to themselves by way of spontaneously arising names, just like the sun and moon. Indeed, their function of naming does not exist by way of common qualities or convention. Thus, 'name' should be understood by the characteristic of naming. Moreover, by the characteristic of inclining towards an object, and by the characteristic of mutual designation therein, the four formless aggregates alone are 'name'. But Nibbāna, on account of being a dominant support condition for objects and by causing blameless phenomena to incline towards itself, should be understood as 'name' solely by the characteristic of designation. By the characteristic of being afflicted, 'form' refers to the aggregate of form. The ninth (dyad).

Avijjāti dukkhādipaṭicchādako sabbo moho. Bhavataṇhāti bhavapatthanāvasena pavatto lobho. Tathā appavatto panettha lobho, sesacetasikacittarūpanibbānāni ca na vattabbāni. Ito paraṃ pana evaṃ navattabbavibhāgaṃ adassetvā padatthasarūpamattameva dassayissāma, dassitāvasesā na vattabbāti gahetabbā. Dasamaṃ.

Ignorance (avijjā) is all delusion that conceals suffering and so forth. Craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is the greed that proceeds by way of longing for existence. Likewise, greed that does not proceed in that way here, along with the remaining mental factors, consciousness, form, and Nibbāna, are not to be mentioned. But hereafter, without showing such distinctions of what is not to be mentioned, we will show only the mere essential meaning of the terms, it being understood that what is left unshown is not to be mentioned. The tenth (dyad).

Bhavo [M 0.0158] vuccati sassataṃ. “Bhavissati attā ca loko cā”ti sassatavasena uppajjanakadiṭṭhi bhavadiṭṭhi nāma. Vibhavo vuccati ucchedo. “Na bhavissati attā ca loko cā”ti ucchedavasena uppajjanakadiṭṭhi vibhavadiṭṭhi nāma. Ubhayenāpi micchādiṭṭhi gahitā. Tathā anantaresupi tīsu dukesu. Ekādasamaṃ.

Existence (bhava) is called eternalism (sassata). 'The self and the world will exist'—this view arising by way of eternalism is called the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi). Non-existence (vibhava) is called annihilationism (uccheda). 'The self and the world will not exist'—this view arising by way of annihilationism is called the view of non-existence (vibhavadiṭṭhi). Both are taken as wrong view. Similarly, in the three immediately following dyads as well. The eleventh (dyad).

Khandhapañcakaṃ “attā ca loko cā”ti gahetvā “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti pavattā diṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhi nāma. Tathā “ucchijjissatī”ti pavattā diṭṭhi ucchedadiṭṭhi nāma. “Antavā”ti pavattā antavādiṭṭhi nāma. “Anantavā”ti pavattā anantavādiṭṭhi nāma. Pubbantaṃ anugatā brahmajāle vuttanayena atītakoṭṭhāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattā aṭṭhārasavidhā pubbantānudiṭṭhi nāma. Aparantaṃ anugatā tattheva āgatanayena anāgatakoṭṭhāsaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattā catucattālīsavidhā aparantānudiṭṭhi nāma. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana brahmajāle (dī. ni. 1.28), tadaṭṭhakathāya (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.28) ca veditabbo. Dvādasamaterasamacuddasamāni.

Taking the five aggregates as 'the self and the world,' the view that arises, 'the self and the world are eternal,' is called the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). Similarly, the view that arises, 'it will be destroyed,' is called the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The view that arises, 'it is finite,' is called the view of finiteness (antavādiṭṭhi). The view that arises, 'it is infinite,' is called the view of infiniteness (anantavādiṭṭhi). Views concerning the past (pubbantaṃ anugatā), which take the past portion as their object according to the method stated in the Brahmajāla, are the eighteen kinds of views regarding the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi). Views concerning the future (aparantaṃ anugatā), which take the future portion as their object according to the method stated therein, are the forty-four kinds of views regarding the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi). This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood from the Brahmajāla (Dī. Ni. 1.28) and its commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.28). The twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth (dyads).

Ahirikadukaṃ, hiridukañca suviññeyyameva. Pañcadasamasoḷasamāni.

The dyad of shamelessness (ahirikadukaṃ) and the dyad of moral shame (hiridukaṃ) are indeed easy to understand. The fifteenth and sixteenth (dyads).

Dukkhaṃ [V 0.0120] vaco etasmiṃ vippaṭikūlagāhimhi vipaccanīkasāte anādare puggaleti dubbaco, sahadhammikaṃ dassetvā ovadiyamāne anādarakārako puggalo, tassa kammaṃ dovacassaṃ, tassa bhāvo dovacassatā, anādaravasena pavattā dve paṭighacittā, taṃsampayuttā ca. Pāpā assaddhādayo puggalā etassa mittāti pāpamitto, tassa bhāvo pāpamittatā, pāpapuggalesu daḷhabhattivasena, kāyacittehi taṃsevanātanninnatāvasena ca pavattāni aṭṭha lobhacittāni. Sattarasamaṃ.

Speech is difficult for this person who is resistant, hostile, disagreeable, and disrespectful—thus, 'difficult to speak to' (dubbaca). When being admonished with a teaching in accordance with the Dhamma, such a person acts with disrespect. Their action is disobedience (dovacassaṃ); their state is disobedience (dovacassatā). Due to disrespect, two consciousnesses rooted in aversion arise, along with their associated mental factors. Evil persons, the faithless, and so forth, are their friends—thus, 'evil companion' (pāpamitto). Their state is having evil companions (pāpamittatā). Through strong devotion to wicked people and through bodily and mental inclination toward serving them, eight consciousnesses rooted in greed arise. The seventeenth (dyad).

Sovacassatā[M 0.0159], kalyāṇamittatā ca vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbā. Atthato pana tathāpavattāni sahetukakāmāvacarakusalakiriyacittāni. Aṭṭhārasamaṃ.

Tractability (sovacassatā) and good companionship (kalyāṇamittatā) should be understood as the opposites of what has been stated. In meaning, however, they are wholesome and functional sense-sphere consciousnesses with roots that arise accordingly. The eighteenth (dyad).

Pañcasu, sattasu vā āpattīsu kusalabhāvo āpattikusalatā, saha vatthunā tāsaṃ āpattīnaṃ āpajjanaparicchedajānanavasena pavattā kāmāvacarajavanapaññā. Āpattīhi vuṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā, vuṭṭhānavidhānena saddhiṃ āpattivuṭṭhānaparicchedajānanavasena pavattā yathāvuttacittasampayuttapaññāva. Ekūnavīsatimaṃ.

Skillfulness in the five or seven offenses is skill in offenses (āpattikusalatā), which is sense-sphere javana wisdom arising through the knowledge that discerns the occurrence and limitations of those offenses together with their basis. Skillfulness in emerging from offenses is skill in emerging from offenses (āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā), which is wisdom associated with the aforementioned consciousness, arising through the knowledge that discerns the limitations of emerging from offenses together with the method of emergence. The nineteenth (dyad).

Samāpajjitabbato samāpatti, tāsu lokiyalokuttarāsu savitakkasavicārādīsu samāpattīsu kusalatā samāpattikusalatā, saha parikammena appanāparicchedajānanavasena pavattā paññā. Samāpattīhi vuṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā, yathāparicchinnakāleyeva tāhi vuṭṭhānakapaññā kāmāvacarajavanapaññāva. Vīsatimaṃ.

From the fact that it should be attained, it is called 'attainment' (samāpatti). Skillfulness in those attainments—mundane and supramundane, with initial thought and sustained thought, and so forth—is called skill in attainments (samāpattikusalatā). It is wisdom that arises through knowing the limits of absorption together with preparatory work. Skillfulness in emerging from attainments is called skill in emerging from attainments (samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā). It is the wisdom of the sense-sphere javana that arises at the precisely determined moment of emerging from them. The twentieth (dyad).

Aṭṭhārasasu dhātūsu kusalabhāvo dhātukusalatā, savanadhāraṇapaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇapaññā. Tāsaññeva dhātūnaṃ manasikāre kusalabhāvo manasikārakusalatā, tāsaṃ sammasanapaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇapaññā. Esa nayo āyatanakusalatāyapi. Tattha hi savanadhāraṇapaccavekkhaṇā kāmāvacarāva, paṭivedho lokuttarova, sammasanaṃ kāmāvacaralokuttaraṃ. Aññamaññaṃ paṭicca sahitaṃ phalaṃ uppādetīti paṭiccasamuppādo, avijjādīhi niddiṭṭho paccayasamūho, tasmiṃ dvādasaṅge anulomapaṭiccasamuppāde kusalabhāvo paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā, “iminā paccayena idaṃ hotī”ti jānanavasena pavattā lokiyajavanapaññāva. Ekavīsatimadvāvīsatimāni.

Skillfulness in the eighteen elements is skill in elements (dhātukusalatā), which is the wisdom of hearing, retaining, penetrating, and reviewing. Skillfulness in attention to those same elements is skill in attention (manasikārakusalatā), which is the wisdom of contemplating, penetrating, and reviewing them. This method applies to skill in the sense bases (āyatanakusalatā) as well. Therein, hearing, retaining, and reviewing are only mundane, while penetration is only supramundane. Contemplation is both mundane and supramundane. Because, in dependence on one another, a combined result is produced, it is called 'dependent origination' (paṭiccasamuppādo); it is the collection of conditions indicated by ignorance and so forth. In that twelve-linked dependent origination in forward order, skillfulness is called skill in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā), which is the mundane javana wisdom that arises through knowing, 'With this as condition, this comes to be.' The twenty-first and twenty-second (dyads).

Tiṭṭhati [M 0.0160][V 0.0121] ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, kāraṇaṃ, tasmiṃ ṭhāne kusalatā ṭhānakusalatā. Na ṭhāne kusalatā aṭṭhānakusalatā. Tevīsatimaṃ.

A result stands therein, its occurrence being dependent on it—thus, 'basis' (ṭhāna), which is a cause. Skillfulness in that basis is skill in what is possible (ṭhānakusalatā). Skillfulness in what is not a basis is skill in what is impossible (aṭṭhānakusalatā). The twenty-third (dyad).

Ujubhāvo ajjavo. Mudubhāvo maddavo. Kāyacittujukatāmudukatādvayaṃ. Catuvīsatimaṃ.

Uprightness (ujubhāvo) is rectitude (ajjavo). Gentleness (mudubhāvo) is mildness (maddavo). This is the twofold quality of rectitude and mildness in body and mind. The twenty-fourth (dyad).

Adhivāsanasaṅkhātā khamanaṃ khanti, tathāpavattakāmāvacarajavanāni. Pāpato suṭṭhu orato viratoti sorato, tassa bhāvo soraccaṃ. Kāyavacīmanosaṃvarasīlasaṅkhātāni lokiyalokuttarajavanāni. Pañcavīsatimaṃ.

Endurance, known as forbearance, is patience (khanti), as are the sense-sphere javana moments that arise accordingly. One who is well-restrained, turned away, and abstaining from evil is 'well-restrained' (sorato); the state of that is 'tractability' (soraccaṃ). This is the mundane and supramundane javana moments known as the virtue of restraint of body, speech, and mind. The twenty-fifth (dyad).

Sammodakapiyavāditāsaṅkhāto sakhilabhāvo sākhalyaṃ, yathā parehi saddhiṃ attano chiddaṃ vivaraṃ na hoti, evaṃ dhammāmisehi paṭisantharaṇaṃ paṭicchādanaṃ paṭisanthāro. Āgantukassa hi paccuggamanapattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇaāsanadānabījanapādadhovanamakkhanādinā, pānīyena āpucchanena, kāle āgatassa yāguādīnaṃ, vikāle pānakādīnañca dānena, punadivase piṇḍāya caraṇaṭṭhānadassanapavesananikkhamanakālārocanādinā ca pabbajitā, gahaṭṭhānañca vinaye āgatanayena yathānurūpaṃ āmisapaṭisanthāro kātabbo. Āgantukaṃ pana upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe katarabhāṇakā”ti apucchitvā “ācariyupajjhāyā vo kataraṃ ganthaṃ vaḷañjentī”ti pucchitvā tassa visaye pañhapucchanena sace na sakkoti, sayaṃ kathetvā dānena, dhammakathanapañhavissajjanakammaṭṭhānakathanakukkuccadiṭṭhivinodanādinā, parivāsādivinayakammakaraṇena, pabbājanaupasampadādinā ca dhammapaṭisanthāro kātabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panāyaṃ saddhiṃ ānisaṃsadīpakavatthūhi aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1351) ñātabbo. Etasmiṃ duvidhe paṭisanthāre kusalabhāvo paṭisanthārakusalatā, tathāpavattakāmāvacarajavanāni eva. Chabbīsatimaṃ.

Amiability (sākhalyaṃ) is a friendly nature (sakhilabhāvo), reckoned as pleasant and amiable speech, whereby one's own faults and weaknesses are not revealed to others. Thus, hospitality (paṭisanthāro) is welcoming and concealing with the Dhamma and with material offerings. For a guest, material hospitality should be shown by going out to meet them, receiving their bowl and robe, offering a seat, giving water for washing feet and anointing them, providing drinking water, inquiring after them, giving gruel and so forth at the proper time, and drinks and so forth at the wrong time; on the next day, by showing them the place for the alms-round, and informing them of the times for entering and leaving. For both the ordained and for householders, material hospitality should be performed appropriately according to the method stated in the Vinaya. Furthermore, on approaching a guest, without asking, 'Of which recitation tradition are you?', one should ask, 'Which text do your teachers and preceptors practice?' By asking questions on that subject, if the guest is unable to answer, one should give by explaining it oneself. Hospitality through the Dhamma should be performed by giving teachings, answering questions, discussing meditation subjects, dispelling scruples and wrong views, performing Vinaya acts such as probation, and conducting the going forth and higher ordination. This is the summary here. For a detailed account, this should be understood along with the illustrative stories showing the benefits in the Aṭṭhasālinī (DhsA. 1351). Skill in these two kinds of hospitality is skill in hospitality (paṭisanthārakusalatā); it is just the sense-sphere javanas that have arisen in such a way. The twenty-sixth.

Indriyesu [M 0.0161] manacchaṭṭhesu āpāthagatarūpādīsu ārammaṇesu nimittagahaṇādinā indriyasaṃvarabhedasaṅkhāto aguttadvārabhāvo indriyesu aguttadvāratā. Paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena bhojane mattaṃ ajānanabhāvo bhojane amattaññutā, tathāpavattaakusalacittāni. Sattavīsatimaṃ.

Unguardedness in the sense faculties (indriyesu aguttadvāratā) is the state of having unguarded doors, reckoned as the breaking of sense-faculty restraint, which consists in grasping at signs and so on in objects, such as forms, that have come into the range of the six sense faculties with mind as the sixth. Immoderation in food (bhojane amattaññutā) is the state of not knowing the measure in food with regard to its acceptance and consumption. These are the unwholesome states of consciousness that have arisen in such a way. The twenty-seventh.

Anantaradukepi [V 0.0122] vuttapaṭipakkhavasena kāmāvacarasahetukakusalakiriyacittāni veditabbāni. Aṭṭhavīsatimaṃ.

In the immediately following pair also, sense-sphere wholesome and functional consciousnesses accompanied by roots should be understood by way of being the opposite of what has been stated. The twenty-eighth.

Sativippavāsasaṅkhāto muṭṭhasatibhāvo muṭṭhassaccaṃ, sabbe akusalā dhammā, asampajānanabhāvo asampajaññaṃ, moho. Ekūnatiṃsatimaṃ.

Lapsed mindfulness (muṭṭhassaccaṃ) is the state of lapsed mindfulness, reckoned as the absence of mindfulness; it comprises all unwholesome states. Lack of clear comprehension (asampajaññaṃ) is the state of not clearly comprehending; it is delusion. The twenty-ninth.

Anantaraduke catubhūmikā satipaññāva vuttā. Tiṃsatimaṃ.

In the immediately following pair, it is mindfulness and wisdom pertaining to the four planes that are stated. The thirtieth.

Appaṭisaṅkhāne appaṭivānasaṅkhāte akampiyaṭṭhena yonisodassanasaṅkhātaṃ paṭisaṅkhānameva balanti paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ, kāmāvacarapaññāva. Sattabojjhaṅgādibhāvanāvasena pavattā catubhūmakadhammā bhāvanābalaṃ. Ekatiṃsatimaṃ.

The power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ) is reflection itself as a power, reckoned as wise consideration, which is unshakable in nature and reckoned as not turning back in the face of non-reflection. It is just wisdom pertaining to the sense sphere. The power of development (bhāvanābalaṃ) consists of the phenomena of the four planes that proceed by way of the development of the seven factors of enlightenment and so on. The thirty-first.

Paccanīkadhamme sametīti samatho, so tividho cittasamatho adhikaraṇasamatho sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti. Tattha ca pubbabhāgāsu aṭṭhasamāpattīsu ekaggatā cittasamatho nāma, sammukhāvinayādi sattavidho adhikaraṇasamatho nāma, nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho nāma. Idha pana catubhūmako samādhi adhippeto. Aniccādivasena vividhenākārena passatīti vipassanā, lokiyalokuttarā vipassanāpaññāva. Bāttiṃsatimaṃ.

Because it calms opposing states, it is called tranquility (samatha). It is threefold: tranquility of mind (cittasamatha), settlement of disputes (adhikaraṇasamatha), and the calming of all formations (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha). Among these, one-pointedness in the eight preliminary attainments is called tranquility of mind; the sevenfold settlement of disputes, such as resolution in the presence, is called settlement of disputes; and Nibbāna is called the calming of all formations. Here, however, concentration pertaining to the four planes is intended. Because it sees in various ways by means of impermanence and so on, it is called insight (vipassanā). It is just mundane and supramundane insight-wisdom. The thirty-second.

Samathova taṃ ākāraṃ gahetvā puna pavattetabbassa samathassa nimittanti samathanimittaṃ. Paggāhanimittepi eseva nayo. Catubhūmakasamādhivīriyāni eva. Tettiṃsatimaṃ.

The sign of tranquility (samathanimittaṃ) is tranquility itself, which, having grasped that aspect, serves as a sign for the tranquility that is to be developed again. This same method applies to the sign of exertion. They are just concentration and energy pertaining to the four planes. The thirty-third.

Anantaradukepi [M 0.0162] vīriyasamādhī eva vuttā. Catuttiṃsatimaṃ.

In the immediately following pair also, it is energy and concentration that are stated. The thirty-fourth.

Sīlavināsikā asaṃvarasaṅkhātā sīlassa vipattīti sīlavipatti, tathāpavattā akusaladhammā. Sammādiṭṭhiyā vipatti diṭṭhivipatti, micchādiṭṭhi eva. Pañcatiṃsatimaṃ.

Failure in virtue (sīlavipatti) is the failure of virtue, reckoned as lack of restraint, which is destructive of virtue; it comprises the unwholesome states that have arisen in such a way. Failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti) is the failure of right view; it is just wrong view. The thirty-fifth.

Soraccameva sīlassa sampādanato sīlaparipūraṇato sīlassa sampadāti sīlasampadā. Diṭṭhipāripūribhūtaṃ [V 0.0123] ñāṇameva diṭṭhiyā sampadāti diṭṭhisampadā. Catubhūmakā sīlapaññāva. Tathā anantaradukepi. Chattiṃsatimaṃ.

Accomplishment in virtue (sīlasampadā) is gentleness itself, because it accomplishes virtue and fulfills virtue. Accomplishment in view (diṭṭhisampadā) is knowledge itself, which has become the fulfillment of view. These are just virtue and wisdom pertaining to the four planes. Likewise in the immediately following pair. The thirty-sixth.

Visuddhibhāvaṃ sampattā sīlasaṅkhātā sīlassa visuddhi sīlavisuddhi. Nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ visuddhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthā dassanasaṅkhātā diṭṭhiyā visuddhi diṭṭhivisuddhi. Sattattiṃsatimaṃ.

Purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is the purity of virtue, which is reckoned as virtue that has attained the state of purity. Purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) is the purity of view, which is reckoned as vision and is capable of leading to the purity called Nibbāna. The thirty-seventh.

Kammassakatāsaccānulomikamaggaphalasampayuttapaññā diṭṭhi visuddhi nāma. Yathādiṭṭhissa tadanurūpaṃ padhānaṃ yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhatiṃsatimaṃ.

Wisdom associated with the path and fruit, which is in conformity with the truth of ownership of kamma, is called purification of view. The striving of one who has seen, which is in accordance with that view, is called 'striving according to what is seen'. The thirty-eighth.

Saṃvegajanakāni jātijarābyādhimaraṇasaṅkhātāni kāraṇāni saṃvejanīyaṭṭhānāni nāma, tesu jātiādipaṭiccasamuppannabhayasaṅkhātaṃ saṃvijanaṃ saṃvego nāma, tathāpavattakusalādi eva. Evaṃ saṃvegajātassa yoniso upāyena padhānaṃ saṃviggassa yoniso padhānaṃ, lokiyalokuttaravīriyameva. Ekūnacattālīsatimaṃ.

The causes that generate a sense of urgency, reckoned as birth, aging, sickness, and death, are called grounds for urgency. In regard to these, the agitation, reckoned as the fear dependently arisen from birth and so on, is called urgency (saṃvega); it is just the wholesome states and so on that have arisen in such a way. Thus, the striving of one in whom urgency has arisen, by means of a wise method, is the wise striving of one who is urgent; it is just mundane and supramundane energy. The thirty-ninth.

Kusaladhammapūraṇe asantuṭṭhibhāvo asantuṭṭhitā. Yo pana dānaṃ datvā tato tena asantuṭṭho hutvā saraṇagamanaṃ ākaṅkhati, tato pañcasīlādiṃ, pabbajjaṃ, buddhavacanānaṃ uggaṇhanaṃ, samathavipassanaṃ, tato tenāpi asantuṭṭho anukkamena arahattaṃ gaṇhāti, ayaṃ asantuṭṭhitā kusalesu dhammesu. Adhikusaladhammānaṃ bhāvanāya ukkaṇṭhamāno padhānaṃ paṭivāpeti nivattāpetīti paṭivāni, na paṭivāni [M 0.0163] appaṭivāni, tassa bhavo appaṭivānitā. Arahattaṃ appatvā padhānasmiṃ anivattanatā anosakkanatā, tathāpavattalokiyalokuttarakusalā dhammā. Cattālīsatimaṃ.

Non-contentment (asantuṭṭhitā) is the state of being non-content in the fulfillment of wholesome qualities. One who, having given a gift, remains non-content with that and aspires to take refuge, then to observe the five precepts and so forth, to go forth into homelessness, to learn the Buddha's teachings, to practice serenity and insight, and still remains non-content with that, gradually attains arahantship—this is non-contentment in wholesome qualities. One who, being dissatisfied with the development of higher wholesome qualities, causes their striving to recede or turn back is called 'one who recedes' (paṭivāni). One who does not recede is 'non-receding' (appaṭivāni). The state of that is non-recedingness (appaṭivānitā). It is not turning back from striving, not drawing back, until arahantship is attained; it comprises the mundane and supramundane wholesome states that have arisen in such a way. The fortieth.

Vijānanato vijjā, pubbenivāsacutūpapātaāsavakkhayañāṇāni. Vimuccanato vimutti, aṭṭha samāpattiyo, nibbānañca. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo hi ārammaṇe adhimuccanato, sayaṃ vikkhambhitakilesehi vimuccanaṭṭhena ca vimuttīti vuttā, nibbānaṃ pana sabbakilesehi accantavimuccanaṭṭhena. Ekacattālīsatimaṃ.

Because of knowing, it is knowledge (vijjā): the knowledges of past lives, the passing away and rebirth of beings, and the destruction of the taints. Because of being liberated, it is liberation (vimutti): the eight attainments and Nibbāna. The eight attainments are called 'liberation' because of being resolved upon an object and because they are a liberation from the defilements suppressed by them. Nibbāna, however, is so called because it is the ultimate liberation from all defilements. The forty-first.

Kilesakkhayakaresu [V 0.0124] catūsu ariyamaggesu ñāṇaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ nāma. Paṭisandhivasena anuppādabhūte taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesānaṃ anuppādapariyosāne uppannaariyaphale ñāṇaṃ anuppāde ñāṇaṃ nāma. Sesaṃ sabbattha suviññeyyameva. Dvācattālīsatimaṃ.

Knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge in the four noble paths that cause the destruction of defilements. Knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge in the arisen noble fruit—which has become non-arising by way of rebirth-linking—at the conclusion of the non-arising of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path. The rest is easily understood everywhere. The forty-second.

Suttantikadukamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Suttantika Pairs Matrix is concluded.

Mohavicchedaniyā abhidhammamātikatthavaṇṇanāya

The Dispelling of Delusion: An Explanation of the Abhidhamma Matrix.

Dhammasaṅgaṇīmātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Mātikā is concluded.

2. Vibhaṅgamātikā

2. The Matrix of the Vibhaṅga

Idāni [M 0.0164][V 0.0125] dhammasaṅgaṇīmātikānantaraṃ vibhaṅgamātikāya atthavaṇṇanā anuppattā. Tassā pana –

Now, after the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Matrix, the explanation of the meaning of the Vibhaṅga Matrix is next in order. As for that –

Atthato dhammabhedena, vibhaṅganayadassanā;

Pāḷimuttanayā cāpi, hoti saṃvaṇṇanānayo.

The method of explanation proceeds: by way of meaning, by the division of phenomena, by showing the method of analysis, and also by methods independent of the Pāḷi text.

Sā panesā aṭṭhārasannaṃ vibhaṅgānaṃ ādimhi ṭhapitā aṭṭhārasavidhā hoti – khandhavibhaṅgamātikā-āyatana-dhātu-sacca-indriya-paccayākāra-satipaṭṭhāna-sammappadhāna-iddhipādabojjhaṅga-maggaṅgajhāna-appamaññā-sikkhāpada-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa-khuddakavatthu-dhammahadayavibhaṅgamāti

This, placed at the beginning of the eighteen Vibhaṅgas, is eighteenfold: the Matrix of the Analysis of Aggregates, of Sense Bases, of Elements, of Truths, of Faculties, of Dependent Origination, of Foundations of Mindfulness, of Right Exertions, of Bases of Power, of Factors of Enlightenment, of Path Factors, of Jhānas, of Illimitables, of Training Rules, of Analytical Knowledges, of Knowledges, of Minor Topics, and of the Heart of the Dhamma.

Khandhavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of Aggregates

Tattha ādibhūtāya khandhavibhaṅgamātikāya atthato tāva – pañcakkhandhāti ettha pañcāti gaṇanaparicchedo, tena na tato heṭṭhā, na uddhanti dasseti. Khandhāti paricchinnadhammanidassanaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ khandha-saddo sambahulesu ṭhānesu nipatati rāsimhi guṇe paṇṇattiyaṃ ruḷhiyanti. Tattha “mahāudakakkhandho”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.1037; a. ni. 4.51; 5.45; 6.37) hi rāsito khandho nāma. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.355) guṇato. “Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandha”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.241) paṇṇattito. “Viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 63) ekampi cittaṃ ruḷhito khandho nāma, svāyamidha rāsito adhippeto. Rāsaṭṭho hi khandha-saddo, koṭṭhāsaṭṭhotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Lokasmiṃ hi iṇaṃ gahetvā codiyamānā “dvīhi khandhehi dassāma[V 0.0126], tīhi khandhehi dassāmā”ti vadanti, tasmā khandhoti koṭṭhāsoti vuttaṃ [M 0.0165] hoti. Rūpakkhandhoti ettha ruppatīti rūpaṃ, sītuṇhādīhi pasiddhākārena ruppati ghaṭṭīyati, pīḷiyatīti attho. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here, first by way of meaning, in the primary Matrix of the Analysis of Aggregates—regarding “the five aggregates”: here, “five” is a numerical delimitation, thereby indicating neither below nor above that. “Aggregate” is a designation for delimited phenomena. Here, this word “khandha” occurs in many places in the sense of a heap, a quality, a designation, and common usage. For example: in phrases like “a great mass of water” (mahāudakakkhandho) and so on, it refers to mass. In phrases like “the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration” and so on, it refers to quality. In phrases like “the Blessed One saw a large log” and so on, it refers to designation. In phrases like “consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness” and so on, even a single mind-moment is, through common usage, called an aggregate. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of a heap. Indeed, the word “khandha” has the meaning of a heap, and it is also fitting to say it has the meaning of a portion. For in the world, when people take a loan and are pressed for repayment, they say, “We will pay in two portions, we will pay in three portions.” Therefore, “khandha” is said to mean “portion.” Regarding “form aggregate” (rūpakkhandho): here, “form” (rūpa) is so called because it is afflicted (ruppati). It is afflicted, struck, or oppressed by cold, heat, etc., in a well-known manner. For this has been said by the Blessed One –

“Ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccati. Kena ruppati? Sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jighacchāyapi ruppati, pipāsāyapi ruppatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.79).

“It is afflicted, monks, therefore it is called form. By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, it is afflicted by heat, it is afflicted by hunger, it is afflicted by thirst,” and so on. (SN 3.79)

Rūpañca taṃ khandho cāti rūpakkhandho, rūparāsi rūpakoṭṭhāsoti attho. Vedanākkhandhādīsupi eseva nayoti ayaṃ tāvettha atthato saṃvaṇṇanānayo.

That is form, and it is an aggregate; thus, “form aggregate” means a mass of form, a portion of form. The same method applies to the feeling aggregate and the others. This, then, is the method of explanation here by way of meaning.

Dhammabhedato panettha heṭṭhā kusalattike vibhattā atītādibhedabhinnā sabbe rūpadhammā rūpakkhandho nāma. Tathā catubhūmakā vedanāsaññāyo vedanākkhandho nāma, saññākkhandho nāma. Vedanāsaññā pana ṭhapetvā sesā phassādayo paññāsa cetasikā saṅkhārakkhandho nāma. Pañcasu khandhesu nibbānameva asaṅgahitaṃ, upādānakkhandhesu pana sabbe lokuttaradhammā. Ayameva hi khandhehi upādānakkhandhānaṃ viseso. Khandhā avisesato vuttā, upādānakkhandhā sāsavopādāniyabhāvena visesetvā. Idha pana avisesena vuttattā nibbānaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā sabbe dhammā saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti ayaṃ dhammabhedato saṃvaṇṇanānayo.

Here, by way of the division of phenomena, all material phenomena, differentiated by distinctions such as past, etc., as analyzed below in the section on the threefold wholesome, are called the aggregate of form. Similarly, feelings and perceptions pertaining to the four planes are called the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception, respectively. Excluding feeling and perception, the remaining fifty mental factors beginning with contact are called the aggregate of mental formations. Among the five aggregates, only Nibbāna is not included; however, among the aggregates of clinging, all supramundane phenomena are excluded. This is precisely the distinction between the aggregates and the aggregates of clinging: the aggregates are spoken of without distinction, whereas the aggregates of clinging are distinguished by their nature of being with taints and subject to clinging. Here, however, since they are spoken of without distinction, all phenomena except Nibbāna are included. This is the method of explanation by way of the division of phenomena.

Vibhaṅganayadassanāti vibhaṅgapāḷiyā āgataatthanayadassanato. Vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ hi suttantabhājanīyaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyaṃ pañhāpucchakanti tīhi nayehi khandhavibhaṅgo vibhatto. Tathā āyatanavibhaṅgādayo. Kevalaṃ hi indriyavibhaṅge, sikkhāpadavibhaṅge ca suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi. Paccayākāravibhaṅge pañhāpucchakaṃ natthi. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu pana tīsu tayopi nayā [M 0.0166] na santi. Tesu hi ñāṇavibhaṅgo ekavidhato paṭṭhāya yāva dasavidhā vibhatto, khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgo ekavidhato paṭṭhāya yāva dvāsaṭṭhipabhedā vibhatto, dhammahadayavibhaṅgo pana sabbasaṅgahādīhi dasahi vārehi vibhatto, tasmā tesaṃ tesaṃ nayānaṃ mukhamattadassanavasena tattha tattha saṃvaṇṇanā bhavissanti. Tatridaṃ khandhavibhaṅge tiṇṇaṃ nayānaṃ mukhamattadassanaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – suttantabhājanīye tāva rūpakkhandho –

“Showing the method of analysis” means showing the method of meaning that occurs in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi. For in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, the analysis of aggregates is divided by three methods: the Suttanta exposition, the Abhidhamma exposition, and the method of questioning. Likewise, the analyses of sense bases and so on. However, in the analysis of the faculties and the analysis of the training rules, there is no Suttanta exposition. In the analysis of dependent origination, there is no method of questioning. However, in the three analyses beginning with the analysis of knowledge, none of the three methods exist. For among these, the analysis of knowledge is divided from one kind up to ten kinds, the analysis of minor topics is divided from one kind up to sixty-two distinctions, and the analysis of the heart of the Dhamma is divided by ten turns beginning with the all-embracing summary. Therefore, in each of those cases, explanations will occur by way of showing merely the outline of those methods. Here, in the analysis of aggregates, is merely a showing of the outline of the three methods. Namely – first in the Suttanta exposition, the aggregate of form is –

“Tattha [V 0.0127] katamo rūpakkhandho? Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, tadekajjhaṃ abhisaññūhitvā abhisaṅkhipitvā ayaṃ vuccati rūpakkhandho”ti (vibha. 2) –

“And what, herein, is the aggregate of form? Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near; all gathered together and lumped together, this is called the aggregate of form.” (Vibh. 2)

Evaṃ uddisitvā vitthārato vibhatto, tathā vedanākkhandhādayopi. Tattha niyakajjhattaṃ nāma ajjhattarūpaṃ ajjhattaṃ nāma, tato aññaṃ parapuggalagataṃ, aviññāṇañca bahiddhā nāma, tathā vedanādayopi. Pasādavisayarūpaṃ pana oḷārikaṃ nāma, sesaṃ sukhumaṃ nāma. Aniṭṭharūpaṃ hīnaṃ nāma, iṭṭharūpaṃ paṇītaṃ nāma.

Having thus outlined it, it is analyzed in detail; the same applies to the aggregates of feeling and so on. Herein, “internal” (ajjhattaṃ) refers to one’s own internal form; that which belongs to another person, and that which is without consciousness, is called “external” (bahiddhā). The same applies to feeling and so on. Furthermore, sense-organ matter and sense-object matter are called “gross,” while the remainder is called “subtle.” Undesirable form is called “inferior,” while desirable form is called “superior.”

Nanu iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ nāma pāṭekkaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ nāma natthi, ekaṃ ekaccassa iṭṭhaṃ hoti manāpaṃ, tadeva aññassa ca aniṭṭhaṃ hoti. Vatthādīni hi sūkarādīnaṃ nappiyāni honti, na manussādīnaṃ, tesañca vatthābharaṇādīni piyāni, na sūkarādīnanti, tasmā rucivaseneva iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā gahetabbā? Na, iṭṭhāniṭṭhānaṃ pāṭekkaṃ vibhattattā. Kusalakammajaṃ hi kusalavipākavisayova iṭṭhaṃ nāma, akusalakammajaṃ akusalavipākavisayova aniṭṭhaṃ nāma, saññāvipallāsena pana koci [M 0.0167] iṭṭhameva buddharūpādiṃ javanakkhaṇe aniṭṭhato manasi karoti, aniṭṭhañca nirayaggisatthavisādiṃ iṭṭhato manasi karoti. Javanehi eva vipallāsabhāvo, na vipākehīti vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ niyataṃ veditabbaṃ.

Is it not that what is desirable and undesirable is not individually distinguished? What is desirable and pleasing to one person might be undesirable to another. For clothes and such are not dear to pigs and the like, but they are to humans and others; and clothes, ornaments, and such are dear to them, but not to pigs and the like. Therefore, should desirability and undesirability be determined solely by preference? No, because desirable and undesirable things are individually distinct. For what arises from wholesome kamma is called desirable, being the object of wholesome vipāka; what arises from unwholesome kamma is called undesirable, being the object of unwholesome vipāka. However, due to the distortion of perception, someone may, at the moment of the javana, regard what is actually desirable—such as the form of the Buddha—as undesirable, or regard what is actually undesirable—such as the fires of hell, a weapon, or poison—as desirable. The state of distortion exists only in the javana moments, not in the vipāka; thus, what is desirable and undesirable should be understood as fixed based on vipāka.

Sammohavinodaniyā pana vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya –

However, in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary on the Vibhaṅga –

“Sukhasamphassaṃ hi gūthakalalaṃ cakkhudvāraghānadvāresu aniṭṭhaṃ, kāyadvāre iṭṭhaṃ hoti. Cakkavattino maṇiratanena pothiyamānassa, suvaṇṇasūle uttāsiyamānassa ca maṇiratanasuvaṇṇasūlāni cakkhudvāre iṭṭhāni honti, kāyadvāre aniṭṭhānī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 6) –

“Indeed, feces and mire, which are pleasant to the touch, are undesirable at the eye-door and nose-door, but desirable at the body-door. For a wheel-turning monarch, when being beaten with a jewel treasure and being impaled with a golden needle, the jewel treasure and golden needle are desirable at the eye-door, but undesirable at the body-door.” (Vibh. aṭṭha. 6)

Evaṃ dvāravasena ekasseva vatthuno iṭṭhatā, aniṭṭhatā ca vuttā. Sā ca ekakkhaṇe na yuttā ekakalāpagatabhūtopādāyarūpānaṃ ekasāmaggiyamuppattito. Na hi bhūtesu akusalavasena aniṭṭhesu [V 0.0128] uppajjantesu tadupādāyarūpādikusalena iṭṭhāni uppajjanti, bhinnakkhaṇe pana iṭṭhāni maṇiratanādīni tehi pothiyamānassa akusalapaccayena utunā aniṭṭhāni vipariṇamanti, kusalapaccayena aniṭṭhāni gūthakalalādīni iṭṭhānīti, ayaṃ no attanomati. Evaṃ vibhattesu ca iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu taṃ taṃ rūpaṃ upādāyupādāya hīnaṃ, paṇītañca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sukhumaṃ pana rūpaṃ dūrerūpaṃ nāma, oḷārikaṃ santikerūpaṃ nāma. Taṃ taṃ vā pana rūpaṃ upādāyupādāya rūpaṃ dūre santike daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, by way of doors, the desirability and undesirability of a single object have been stated. However, this is not appropriate in a single moment, because the primary elements and derived material forms, which are contained in a single kalāpa, arise in a single aggregation. For when undesirable primary elements arise due to an unwholesome cause, desirable derived material forms and so on do not arise through a wholesome cause. But in separate moments, desirable things like gems and jewels, when struck by them, are transformed and become undesirable through temperature conditioned by an unwholesome cause; conversely, undesirable things like feces and mire become desirable through a wholesome cause. This is our own view. Thus, when desirable and undesirable things are distinguished, each form should be seen as inferior or superior in relation to that particular form. Subtle form is called ‘distant form,’ while coarse form is called ‘near form.’ Or, each form should be seen as distant or near in relation to that particular form. The rest is just as stated.

Vedanādīsu pana akusalā vedanā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Kusalākusalā oḷārikā, abyākatā sukhumā. Dukkhā vedanā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Sukhadukkhā vā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Asamāpannassa vā vedanā oḷārikā, samāpannassa sukhumā. Sāsavā oḷārikā[M 0.0168], anāsavā sukhumā. Taṃ taṃ vā pana vedanaṃ upādāyupādāya oḷārikasukhumatā daṭṭhabbā. Akusalā vedanā kusalābyākatāhi dūre, tā ca tāya dūreti evaṃ jātisabhāvapuggalabhūmibhedato vuttanayena dūrevedanā daṭṭhabbā, kusalā vedanā kusalāya santiketi evaṃ jātiādisāmaññato santikevedanā daṭṭhabbā. Taṃ taṃ vā pana vedanaṃ upādāyupādāya vedanā dūresantike daṭṭhabbā. Evaṃ saññākkhandhādīsupi yathānurūpaṃ oḷārikasukhumatādayo veditabbāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana vibhaṅgapāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu (vibha. 8 ādayo; vibha. aṭṭha. 8 ādayo) gahetabboti ayaṃ suttantabhājanīyanayo.

Now, among feelings and so on, unwholesome feelings are gross, while the others are subtle. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross, while indeterminate feelings are subtle. Painful feeling is gross, while the others are subtle. Or, pleasant and painful feelings are gross, while the other is subtle. Or, the feeling of one not in attainment is gross, while that of one in attainment is subtle. Feelings with taints are gross, while feelings without taints are subtle. Or, the grossness and subtlety should be seen in relation to each particular feeling. Unwholesome feelings are distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings, and those are distant from them. Thus, 'distant feeling' should be understood in the manner stated, in terms of difference in birth, nature, person, and plane. Wholesome feelings are near to wholesome feelings. Thus, 'near feeling' should be understood in terms of similarity in birth, etc. Or, feelings should be seen as distant or near in relation to each particular feeling. Similarly, in the case of the aggregate of perception and the others, grossness, subtlety, and so on should be understood as appropriate. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken from the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi and its commentaries (Vibhaṅga 8 ff.; Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 8 ff.). This is the Suttanta method of analysis.

Abhidhammabhājanīyanaye rūpakkhandhassa tāva ekavidhādito yāva ekādasavidhā rūpakaṇḍe vuttanayena veditabbā. Vedanākkhandho pana ekavidho phassasampayutto, duvidho sahetukadukavasena, tividho kusalattikavasena, catubbidho catubhūmakavasena, pañcavidho sabhāvabhedena, chabbidho chadvārikavasena, sattavidho sattaviññāṇasampayogavasena, aṭṭhavidho tesu kāyaviññāṇasampayuttaṃ sukhadukkhavasena dvidhā bhinditvā, navavidho tesu manoviññāṇasampayuttaṃ kusalattikavasena tidhā bhinditvā, dasavidho tesu kāyaviññāṇasampayuttaṃ duvidhā, manoviññāṇasampayuttañca tidhā bhinditvāti evaṃ sahetukadukamūlaṃ paṭhamavāraṃ vatvā puna kusalattikaṭṭhāne vedanāttikapītittikasanidassanattikavajjite sabbattike yojetvā yāva dasavidhā, aparepi aṭṭhārasa vārā vuttā. Yathā cettha sahetukadukamūlikā sabbattikayojanā, evaṃ hetusampayuttadukādīsu anurūpadukamūlikāpi saraṇadukapariyosānā paccekaṃ sabbattikayojanāpi veditabbāti [V 0.0129] ayaṃ dukamūlako yojanānayo. Yathā ca ekekadukena sabbattikayojanāvasena dukamūlako [M 0.0169] nayo vutto, evaṃ ekekattikena yathānurūpaṃ sabbadukayojanāvasena tikamūlako, tadubhayamissakavasena ubhatovaḍḍhanako ca nayo veditabbo. Yathā cettha vedanākkhandhe, evaṃ saññākkhandhādīsupi yathārahaṃ dukamūlakādinayā veditabbāti ayaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyanayo.

In the Abhidhamma method of analysis, the aggregate of form should first be understood in the manner stated in the section on form, from the singlefold division up to the elevenfold division. The aggregate of feeling, however, is singlefold as associated with contact, twofold according to the dyad of being with or without roots, threefold according to the triad of wholesome states, fourfold according to the four planes, fivefold according to distinctions of inherent nature, sixfold according to the six sense doors, sevenfold according to association with seven types of consciousness, eightfold by dividing feeling associated with body-consciousness into pleasure and pain, ninefold by dividing feeling associated with mind-consciousness into the triad of wholesome states, and tenfold by dividing feeling associated with body-consciousness into twofold and that associated with mind-consciousness into threefold. Thus, having first explained the dyad rooted in being with or without roots, it is then combined with all triads—except the triads of feeling, joy, and the visible—up to the tenfold division. Additionally, eighteen other rounds are mentioned. Just as here the combination with all triads is based on the dyad rooted in being with or without roots, so too in the case of dyads beginning with that of being associated with roots, the combination with all triads should be understood individually according to the appropriate dyadic root, up to the dyad ending with having refuge or not having refuge. This is the method of combination based on dyadic roots. And just as the method based on dyadic roots is explained by combining each dyad with all triads, so too the method based on triadic roots is understood by combining each triad with all dyads as appropriate, and the method of mutual augmentation by combining both. As in the case of the aggregate of feeling here, so too in the aggregates of perception and the rest, the methods based on dyadic roots and so on should be understood as appropriate. This is the Abhidhamma method of analysis.

Pañhāpucchakanaye pana pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ kati kusalā, kati akusalā, kati abyākatā, kati sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā…pe… kati saraṇā, kati araṇāti? Rūpakkhandho abyākato, cattāro khandhā siyā kusalā, siyā akusalā, siyā abyākatā, rūpaṃ, vedanā ca vedanāttike na vattabbā, sesā tidhāpi honti, rūpaṃ nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammaṃ, siyā upādinnupādāniyaṃ, siyā anupādinnupādāniyaṃ, asaṃkiliṭṭhasaṃkilesikaṃ, sesā cattāro khandhā tīhi tikehi tidhāpi honti. Rūpaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ, tayo khandhā tidhāpi honti, saṅkhārakkhandho tidhā ca na vattabbo ca. Rūpaṃ na vattabbaṃ, vedanā siyā pītisahagatā, na vattabbā, tayo tidhā ca na vattabbā ca. Rūpaṃ nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbaṃ, nadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbahetukaṃ, nevācayagāminaapacayagāmi, nevasekhaṃnāsekhaṃ, parittaṃ, sesā tidhāpi honti. Parittārammaṇattike rūpaṃ anārammaṇaṃ, sesā tidhā ca na vattabbā ca. Rūpaṃ majjhimaṃ, aniyataṃ, sesā tidhāpi. Maggārammaṇattike ca rūpaṃ anārammaṇaṃ, sesā tidhāpi vā na vattabbā. Uppannātītattikesu pañcapi tidhā honti. Atītārammaṇattike rūpaṃ anārammaṇaṃ, sesā tidhā ca na vattabbā ca. Ajjhattattike pañcapi tidhā honti. Ajjhattārammaṇattike rūpaṃ anārammaṇaṃ, sesā tidhāpi na vattabbā ca. Cattāro khandhā anidassanaappaṭighā, rūpakkhandho tidhāpi hoti.

In the method of questioning, how many of the five aggregates are wholesome, how many unwholesome, how many indeterminate, how many associated with pleasant feeling... and so on... how many are with refuge, how many are without refuge? The aggregate of form is indeterminate. The other four aggregates may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. In the feeling triad, form and feeling cannot be stated. The remaining aggregates are threefold. Form is neither a result nor productive of a result; it may be clung-to and a basis for clinging, or not clung-to but a basis for clinging; it is undefiled but a basis for defilement. The other four aggregates are threefold in these three triads. Form is without applied and sustained thought. Three aggregates are threefold, and the aggregate of formations is threefold and cannot be stated. In the joy triad, form cannot be stated. Feeling may be accompanied by joy or cannot be stated. Three aggregates are threefold and cannot be stated. Form is neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation, nor is it a root of what is to be abandoned by seeing or cultivation; it neither leads to accumulation nor to dispersion; it is neither of a trainee nor of one beyond training; it is limited. The remaining aggregates are threefold. In the triad of limited objects, form is objectless. The remaining aggregates are threefold or cannot be stated. Form is middling and unfixed. The remaining aggregates are threefold. In the triad of path-objects, form is objectless. The remaining aggregates are threefold or cannot be stated. In the triads of the arisen and the past, all five aggregates are threefold. In the triad of past objects, form is objectless. The remaining aggregates are threefold or cannot be stated. In the internal triad, all five aggregates are threefold. In the triad of internal objects, form is objectless. The remaining aggregates are threefold or cannot be stated. The four aggregates are invisible and non-resistant. The aggregate of form is threefold.

Cattāro [M 0.0170] khandhā nahetū, saṅkhārakkhandho siyā hetu, siyā na hetu. Rūpaṃ ahetukaṃ, hetuvippayuttaṃ, sesā dvidhāpi. Tayo khandhā siyā sahetukā ceva na ca hetū, siyā na vattabbā ca, saṅkhārakkhandho dvidhā ca na vattabbo ca, rūpaṃ na vattabbameva. Tathā anantaradukepi. Rūpaṃ nahetuahetukaṃ, tayo dvidhāpi, saṅkhārakkhandho dvidhā ca na vattabbo ca. Pañcapi sappaccayā, saṅkhatā, cattāro anidassanā, appaṭighā, rūpaṃ dvidhāpi. Rūpaṃ rūpī, sesā arūpino. Rūpaṃ lokiyaṃ, sesā dvidhāpi. Pañcapi kenaci viññeyyā, na ca kenaci viññeyyā ca. Cattāro no āsavā, saṅkhārā dvidhāpi, na vattabbā ca. Rūpaṃ sāsavo, āsavavippayutto[V 0.0130], sesā dvidhāpi. Rūpaṃ sāsavā ceva no ca āsavā, tayo tathā ca na vattabbā ca. Saṅkhāro dvidhā ca na vattabbo ca.
