Rūpaṃ na vattabbameva, tayo siyā āsavasampayuttā ceva no ca āsavā, siyā na vattabbā, saṅkhāro dvidhā ca na vattabbo ca. Rūpaṃ āsavavippayuttaṃ sāsavañca, sesā dvidhā ca na vattabbā ca. Iminā nayena saṃyojanagocchakādīsupi yojanā veditabbā. Kevalaṃ hi parāmāsasampayuttaduke rūpaṃ parāmāsavippayuttaṃ, tayo dvidhāpi, saṅkhāro dvidhāpi, diṭṭhivasena na vattabbo ca. Tatiye ettakameva viseso. Rūpaṃ anārammaṇaṃ, sesā sārammaṇā. Viññāṇaṃ cittaṃ, sesā no cittā. Tayo cetasikā, dve acetasikā. Tayo cittasampayuttā, rūpaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Tathā cittasaṃsaṭṭhadukepi. Tayo cittasamuṭṭhānā, viññāṇaṃ no cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Rūpaṃ dvidhāpi. Tathā anantaradukadvayepi. Tayo cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānā, dve no cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānā. Tathā anantaradukadvayepi. Viññāṇaṃ ajjhattikaṃ, tayo bāhirā, rūpaṃ dvidhāpi. Cattāro no upādā. Rūpaṃ dvidhāpi. Pañcapi siyā upādinnā, siyā anupādinnā, no upādānā.

The four aggregates are not roots; the formation aggregate may be a root or may not be a root. Form is rootless, dissociated from roots; the rest are twofold. Three aggregates may be with roots and also not with roots, or may be indeterminate; the formation aggregate is twofold and also indeterminate; form is solely indeterminate. Similarly in the immediately following dyad. Form is not a root and is rootless; the three are twofold; the formation aggregate is twofold and also indeterminate. All five are with conditions, are conditioned; four are invisible, non-resistant; form is twofold. Form is material; the rest are immaterial. Form is mundane; the rest are twofold. All five are knowable by some and also not knowable by some. Four are not taints; formations are twofold and also indeterminate. Form is with taints, dissociated from taints; the rest are twofold. Form is both with taints and not with taints; the three are likewise and also indeterminate; the formation aggregate is twofold and also indeterminate. Form is solely indeterminate; the three may be associated with taints and also not associated with taints, or may be indeterminate; the formation aggregate is twofold and also indeterminate. Form is dissociated from taints and with taints; the rest are twofold and also indeterminate. In this way, the application should be understood in the sections on fetters and so on. Only in the dyad of things associated with adherence is form dissociated from adherence; the three are twofold; the formation aggregate is twofold; and, in terms of view, it is indeterminate. In the third, this much is the only distinction. Form is without an object; the rest are with objects. Consciousness is mind; the rest are not mind. Three are mental factors; two are not mental factors. Three are associated with mind; form is dissociated from mind. Consciousness is indeterminate. Similarly in the dyad of mental conjunction. Three arise from mind; consciousness does not arise from mind. Form is twofold. Similarly in the two immediately following dyads. Three are conjoined with and arise from mind; two are not conjoined with and do not arise from mind. Similarly in the two immediately following dyads. Consciousness is internal; the three are external; form is twofold. Four are not objects of clinging; form is twofold. All five may be clung-to or may not be clung-to; they are not clinging.

Kilesagocchako [M 0.0171] vuttanayova. Rūpaṃ nevadassanenanabhāvanāya pahātabbaṃ, sesā dvidhāpi. Evaṃ yāvapītidukā yojanā veditabbā.

The section on defilements is as stated before. Form is to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by development, while the rest are twofold. Thus, the application should be understood up to the dyad of joy.

Rūpaṃ na vedanā, na sukhā, na sukhasahagatā, sesā dvidhāpi. Tathā anantaradukepi. Rūpaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, sesā dvidhāpi. Evaṃ yāva saraṇadukā yojanā veditabbā. Ayaṃ pañhāpucchakanayo.

Form is not feeling, not pleasant, not accompanied by pleasure; the remaining are twofold. Similarly, in the immediately following dyad. Form belongs to the sense-sphere; the remaining are twofold. Thus, up to the dyad of things with defilement, the application should be understood. This is the method of questioning.

Ime pana nayā vitthārato pāḷiaṭṭhakathāhi ñātabbā. Atthavinicchayo ca nesaṃ dhammasaṅgaṇīmātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanāya vuttānusārena ñātabbo. Ito paraṃ atirekaṃ avatvā apubbameva vaṇṇayissāmāti ayaṃ vibhaṅganayadassanato saṃvaṇṇanānayo.

Now, these methods should be understood in detail from the Pāli text and the commentaries. And the analysis of their meaning should be understood according to the manner stated in the commentary on the meaning of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī matrix. Beyond this, without saying anything further, we will explain what has not been explained before—this is the method of exposition showing the method of the Vibhaṅga.

Idāni panettha –

Now here:

Kamatonūnādhikato, daṭṭhabbasamabhedato;

Pāḷimuttanayo ñeyyo, khandhakosallamicchatā.

By sequence, by being neither deficient nor excessive, By the various ways of seeing and by similes; The method independent of the text should be known By one desiring skill in the aggregates.

Tattha [V 0.0131] kamatoti ettha uppattikkamo pahānakkamo paṭipattikkamo bhūmikkamo desanākkamoti bahuvidhesu kamesu khandhānaṃ desanākkamova yujjati, na itare, asambhavā. Abhedena hi pañcasu khandhesu attaggāhapatitaṃ veneyyajanaṃ samūhaghanavinibbhogadassanena attaggāhato mocetukāmo bhagavā hitakāmo tassa tassa janassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ cakkhuādīnaṃ visayabhūtaṃ oḷārikaṃ paṭhamaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ desesi, tato iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayasaṃvedakaṃ oḷārikaṃ vedanaṃ, yaṃ vedeti, taṃ sañjānātīti evaṃ vedanāvisayassa ākāraggāhikaṃ saññaṃ, saññāvasenābhisaṅkhārake saṅkhāre, tesaṃ vedanādīnaṃ nissayādhipatibhūtaṃ viññāṇanti ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Herein, regarding 'by sequence': Among the many kinds of sequences—such as the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, the order of stages, or the order of teaching—only the order of teaching the aggregates is appropriate here, not the others, as they are impossible. For the Blessed One, wishing for the welfare of beings to be trained who had fallen into grasping a self in the five aggregates taken as an undifferentiated whole, and desiring to free them from that self-grasping by showing them the analysis of the compact mass, first taught the gross material aggregate, which is the object of the eye and so forth, for the sake of its easy comprehension by each person. Then, he taught the gross feeling that experiences desirable and undesirable objects; then, with the words, 'What one feels, that one perceives,' he taught perception, which grasps the characteristics of the object of feeling; then, the formations, which fashion things by way of perception; and then consciousness, which is the support and dominant factor for those feelings and so on. This, then, is the sequence here.

Anūnādhikatoti [M 0.0172] kasmā pana bhagavatā pañceva khandhā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti? Sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgahato, attattaniyaggāhavatthussa etapparamato, aññesañca tadavarodhato. Anekappabhedesu hi saṅkhatadhammesu sabhāgavasena saṅgayhamānesu rūpaṃ rūpasabhāgekasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti, vedanā vedanāsabhāgekasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti. Esa nayo saññādīsupi, tasmā sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgahato pañceva vuttā. Etaparamañcetaṃ attattaniyaggāhavatthu, yadidaṃ rūpādayo pañca, tasmā attattaniyaggāhavatthussa etaparamatopi pañceva vuttā. Yepi caññe sīlādayo pañca dhammakkhandhā vuttā, tepi saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannattā ettheva avarodhaṃ gacchanti, tasmā aññesaṃ tadavarodhatopi pañceva vuttāti ayaṃ anūnādhikato.

Regarding 'neither deficient nor excessive': Why did the Blessed One teach only five aggregates, neither deficient nor excessive? Because of the inclusion of all conditioned things by way of their common nature, because they are the ultimate extent of the object of grasping as self and what belongs to self, and because of the inclusion of others within them. For among the many varieties of conditioned phenomena, when gathered together according to their common nature, form becomes one aggregate by way of including things sharing the nature of form; feeling becomes one aggregate by way of including things sharing the nature of feeling. This method applies to perception and the others as well. Therefore, because of the inclusion of all conditioned things by way of their common nature, only five are taught. Moreover, these five, namely, form and so on, are the ultimate extent of the object of grasping as self and what belongs to self; therefore, because they are the ultimate extent of the object of grasping as self and what belongs to self, only five are taught. And whatever other aggregates of qualities, such as the five aggregates of virtue, etc., are taught, those too, being included within the aggregate of formations, come to be included right here. Thus, because of the inclusion of others within them, only five are taught. This is the meaning of 'neither deficient nor excessive'.

Daṭṭhabbasamabhedatoti daṭṭhabbabhedato, upamābhedato ca. Tattha daṭṭhabbabhedato tāva pañcupādānakkhandhā sāmaññato ukkhittāsikapaccatthikato, bhārato, khādakato, aniccadukkhaanattasaṅkhātavadhakato ca daṭṭhabbā. Visesato pana pheṇapiṇḍaṃ viya rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, udakabubbuḷamarīcikakadalikkhandhamāyā viya yathākkamaṃ vedanādayo daṭṭhabbā. Yathā hi pheṇapiṇḍo vimaddāsaho, so ca pattathālakādiatthaṃ gahitopi tamatthaṃ na sādheti, bhijjati, evaṃ rūpampi vimaddāsahaṃ, tañca subhādivasena gahitampi na tathā tiṭṭhati, asubhādiyeva hoti.

Regarding 'By the various ways of seeing and by similes': this means by the various ways they are to be seen, and by the various similes. Herein, first, by the various ways they are to be seen: the five aggregates subject to clinging should be seen in general as an enemy with a raised sword, as a burden, as a devourer, and as executioners known as impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Specifically, however, form should be seen as like a lump of foam, while feeling and the rest should be seen in order like a water bubble, a mirage, a plantain trunk, and an illusion. For just as a lump of foam cannot withstand being crushed, and though taken for the purpose of a bowl or a dish, it does not serve that purpose but breaks apart, so too is form unable to withstand being crushed, and though grasped as beautiful and so on, it does not remain so but becomes foul and the like.

Yathā vā pheṇapiṇḍo anekasandhighaṭito bahunnaṃ udakasappādipāṇakānaṃ āvāso, ādito cesa badarapakkamatto hutvā anupubbavaḍḍhanako uṭṭhitamattopi cesa bhijjati, thokaṃ gantvāpi, samuddaṃ patvā pana avassameva bhijjati[M 0.0173], evaṃ rūpampi chiddāvachiddaṃ anekasandhighaṭitaṃ [V 0.0132] asītikimikulavokiṇṇaṃ, ādito cetaṃ kalalamattaṃ hutvā anupubbavaḍḍhanakaṃ, kalalamattepi cetaṃ bhijjati, abbudādibhāvepi āyukkhayaṃ patvā avassameva bhijjati. Evaṃ pheṇapiṇḍasadisaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Or, just as a lump of foam is joined together with many connections, a dwelling for many water creatures like snakes, and though it starts as the size of a ripe jujube fruit and grows gradually, it bursts as soon as it has arisen. Even if it travels a short distance, upon reaching the ocean, it inevitably bursts. Similarly, material form is also full of holes and fissures, joined together with many connections, and infested with eighty families of worms. Though it begins as a mere 'kalala', it grows gradually; yet it breaks apart even in the 'kalala' stage, and in the 'abbuda' stage and so on, having reached the exhaustion of the life-span, it inevitably breaks apart. Thus, it should be seen as similar to a lump of foam.

Yathā pana bubbuḷo muhuttaramaṇīyo agayhupago na ciraṭṭhitikova, evaṃ vedanāpi. Yathā ca bubbuḷo udakatalaṃ, udakabinduṃ, udakajallakaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā puṭaṃ katvā gahaṇavātañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca uppajjati, evaṃ vedanāpi vatthuṃ, ārammaṇaṃ, kilesajallaṃ, phassasaṅghaṭṭanañcāti cattāri kāraṇāni paṭicca uppajjatīti sā bubbuḷasadisā daṭṭhabbā.

Just as a bubble is momentarily delightful, ungraspable, and not long-lasting, so too is feeling. And just as a bubble arises dependent on four causes—the surface of the water, a drop of water, the film of water, and the wind that gathers it and forms it into a pocket—so too does feeling arise dependent on four causes: the physical basis, the object, the film of defilement, and the impact of contact. Thus, it should be seen as similar to a bubble.

Yathā pana marīcikā jalāsayādibhāvena vippalambhikā, evaṃ saññāpi niccādibhāvenāti marīcisadisā daṭṭhabbā. Yathā pana kadalikkhandho agayhupago bahuvaṭṭisamodhāno, evaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhopi agayhupagoniccādisāravirahito, phassādibahudhammasamodhāno ca hotīti so kadalikkhandhasadiso daṭṭhabbo. Yathā pana māyā asuvaṇṇarajatādirūpānipi tathā gāhāpetvā mahājanaṃ vañceti, evaṃ viññāṇampi aniccādirūpaṃ teneva cittena āgacchantaṃ viya niccādito ca gāhāpetvā vañcetīti taṃ māyāsadisaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuttañca –

Just as a mirage deceives by appearing as a body of water and the like, so too should perception be seen as similar to a mirage, for it deceives by appearing as permanent and so forth. Just as a banana trunk is without a core and composed of many sheaths, so too should the aggregate of formations be seen as being without a core, devoid of the essence of permanence and the like, and composed of many phenomena such as contact. Thus, it should be regarded as similar to a banana trunk. Just as a magic trick deceives a great crowd by making them grasp what are not forms of gold, silver, and the like as if they were, so too does consciousness, though itself impermanent, deceive by causing one to grasp it as permanent and so forth, as if it were arising with that very consciousness. Therefore, it should be seen as similar to a magic trick. And it is said—

“Pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ rūpaṃ, vedanā bubbuḷūpamā;

Marīcikūpamā saññā, saṅkhārā kadalūpamā;

Māyūpamañca viññāṇaṃ, desitādiccabandhunā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 3.95);

‘Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a water bubble; perception is like a mirage, formations like a plantain trunk; and consciousness is like an illusion—so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.’ (SN 22.95)

Ayamettha daṭṭhabbabhedo.

This is the distinction in what is to be seen here.

Upamābhedato ca pana gilānasālūpamo rūpupādānakkhandho, gelaññūpamo vedanupādānakkhandho, gelaññasamuṭṭhānūpamo saññupādānakkhandho, asappāyasevanūpamo saṅkhārupādānakkhandho[M 0.0174], gilānūpamo viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Apica cārakakāraṇaaparādhakāraṇakārakaaparādhikūpamā ete bhājanabhojanabyañjanaparivesakabhuñjakūpamā cāti ayamettha upamābhedo. Evaṃ pāḷimuttakavinicchayanayo ñeyyo.

Regarding the distinctions in similes: the form clinging-aggregate is like an infirmary, the feeling clinging-aggregate is like sickness, the perception clinging-aggregate is like the arising of sickness, the formations clinging-aggregate is like consuming what is unsuitable, and the consciousness clinging-aggregate is like a sick person. Furthermore, these are also like a prison, the cause of imprisonment, the offense, the perpetrator, and the offender; and like a vessel, food, seasoning, a server, and an eater. This is the distinction in similes here. Thus, the method of judgment independent of the Pāḷi should be understood.

Khandhavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the Analysis of the Aggregates is concluded.

Āyatanavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Sense Bases

Āyatanavibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0133] pana atthato tāva – dvādasāyatanānīti ettha āyatanato, āyānaṃ tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatanāni. Cakkhurūpādīsu hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇā cittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādinā kiccena āyatanti upaṭṭhahanti ghaṭenti vāyamanti, te ca pana āyabhūte dhamme etāni tanonti vitthārenti, idañca atīva āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ nayanteva, pavattayantīti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā “āyatanānī”ti vuccanti.

Now, as to the meaning in the matrix of the Analysis of the Sense Bases—first, regarding ‘the twelve sense bases.’ Here, they are called ‘sense bases’ (āyatanāni) because they are a place of resort (āyatana), because they stretch out (tanana) what arrives (āya), and because they lead on (nayana) what is long (āyata). For, with regard to the eye, forms, and so on, the mental phenomena of consciousness and its concomitants, which have their respective doors and objects, exert themselves (āyatanti)—that is, they are present, they strive, they endeavour—through their respective functions of experiencing and so on. And these bases stretch out (tanonti) and expand (vitthārenti) those phenomena that have become arrivals (āyabhūte). And they lead on (nayanteva)—that is, they cause to continue (pavattayanti)—this exceedingly long (āyataṃ) suffering of saṃsāra. Therefore, they are called ‘sense bases’.

Apica nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, ākaraṭṭhena, samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, sañjābhidesaṭṭhena, kāraṇaṭṭhena ca sāsane, loke ca “āyatana”nti vuccanti. Cakkhuādīsu hi te te cittacetasikā dhammā tadāyattavuttitāya nivasanti, tesu ca ākarabhūtesu ākiṇṇā vatthārammaṇavasena ca samosaranti, cakkhādayova nesaṃ sañjātideso, kāraṇañca, tasmā nivāsaṭṭhānādinā atthena cakkhādīni āyatanānīti veditabbāni.

Furthermore, in the Teaching and in the world, they are called 'āyatana' by way of the meanings of dwelling-place, mine, meeting-place, place of origination, and cause. For in the eye and so forth, those consciousnesses and mental factors dwell dependent on them; and in these, which are like mines, they are accumulated; and they converge by way of base and object. The eye and so forth are their place of origination and their cause. Therefore, the eye and so forth should be understood as āyatana by way of the meanings of dwelling-place and so forth.

Cakkhāyatanantiādīsu cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ assādeti, vibhāveti cāti attho. Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ. Vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ [M 0.0175] hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Sappatīti saddo, udāharīyatīti attho. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Gandhayatīti gandho, attano vatthuṃ sūcayatīti attho. Jīvitaṃ avhāyatīti jivhā. Rasanti taṃ sattāti raso, assādentīti attho. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti kāyo, uppattideso. Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Manatīti mano. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Cakkhu ca taṃ yathāvuttenatthena āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammā ca te āyatanañcāti dhammāyatananti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

In ‘eye base’ and so forth, ‘eye’ (cakkhu) is so called because it ‘sees’ (cakkhati); the meaning is that it enjoys (assādeti) and reveals (vibhāveti) form. ‘Form’ (rūpa) is so called because it ‘takes form’ (rūpayati); the meaning is that by undergoing alteration in appearance, it reveals a state that is pleasing to the heart. ‘Ear’ (sota) is so called because it ‘hears’ (suṇāti). ‘Sound’ (sadda) is so called because it ‘is sounded’ (sappati); the meaning is that it is uttered. ‘Nose’ (ghāna) is so called because it ‘smells’ (ghāyati). ‘Odor’ (gandha) is so called because it ‘gives off a scent’ (gandhayati); the meaning is that it indicates its own physical basis. ‘Tongue’ (jivhā) is so called because it ‘calls to’ (avhāyati) life (jīvitaṃ). ‘Taste’ (rasa) is so called because beings ‘savor’ (rasanti) it; the meaning is that they enjoy it. ‘Body’ (kāya) is so called because it is the ‘abode’ (āya) of contemptible (kucchita) and defiled (sāsava) things; it is their place of origin. ‘Tangible’ (phoṭṭhabba) is so called because it is ‘touched’ (phusīyati). ‘Mind’ (mano) is so called because it ‘thinks’ (manati). ‘Phenomena’ (dhammā) are so called because they ‘bear’ (dhārenti) their own characteristics. The eye, and that which is a base in the aforementioned sense, is the ‘eye base’… and those phenomena, and that which is a base, is the ‘phenomena base’—this, for now, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedato panettha sabbampi viññāṇaṃ manāyatanaṃ nāma. Cetasikasukhumarūpanibbānāni dhammāyatanaṃ nāma. Sesāni suviññeyyāni. Imesu ca āyatanesu atītādibhedabhinnā, kālavinimuttā ca lokiyalokuttarā sabbe nāmarūpadhammā, paññattiyo ca saṅgahitāti veditabbā. “Jāti dvīhi khandhehi ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā saṅgahitā”tiādivacanato (dhātu. 71) hi [V 0.0134] rūpārūpalakkhaṇānaṃ jātijarābhaṅgānaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhadhammāyatanadhammadhātūsu saṅgahitattā itarāsampi paññattīnaṃ yathārahaṃ tattha saṅgahitabhāvo veditabboti ayamettha dhammabhedo.

In terms of the classification of phenomena here, all consciousness is called the mind base (manāyatana). Mental factors, subtle materiality, and Nibbāna are called the phenomena base (dhammāyatana). The rest are easily understood. And in these bases, all mental and material phenomena—those divided into past and so forth, those free from time, whether mundane or supramundane—as well as concepts, should be understood as included. For, from the statement, ‘Birth is included in two aggregates, one base, and one element’ (Dhātukathā 71), it should be understood that because birth, aging, and disintegration—the characteristics of the material and immaterial—are included in the formations aggregate, the phenomena base, and the phenomena element, other concepts are also to be understood as included there as appropriate. This is the classification of phenomena here.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīye tāva “cakkhuṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā vipariṇāmadhammaṃ. Rūpā aniccā dukkhā anattā vipariṇāmadhammā…pe… dhammā aniccā dukkhā anattā vipariṇāmadhammā”ti (vibha. 154) evaṃ visayivisayāyatanavasena āyatanāni vuttānīti ayaṃ suttantabhājanīyanayo.

Here, in the Suttanta exposition, it is first stated: 'The eye is impermanent, suffering, not-self, subject to change. Forms are impermanent, suffering, not-self, subject to change… mental phenomena are impermanent, suffering, not-self, subject to change' (Vibhaṅga 154). Thus, the sense bases are stated by way of subject and object. This is the method of the Suttanta exposition.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana pasādavisayāyatanāni tāva “tattha katamaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ? Yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya [M 0.0176] pasādo”tiādinā (vibha. 156) rūpakaṇḍe (dha. sa. 597) vuttanayena vibhattāni. Manāyatanaṃ pana ekavidhato paṭṭhāya yāvadasavidhā vedanākkhandhe vuttanayena vibhattaṃ. Dhammāyatanaṃ pana “tattha katamaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ? Vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho, yañca rūpaṃ anidassanaappaṭighaṃ dhammāyatanapariyāpannaṃ asaṅkhatā ca dhātū”ti (vibha. 167) uddisitvā “tattha katamo vedanākkhandho”tiādinā (vibha. 167) vedanākkhandhādīsu vuttanayena vibhattaṃ. Sukhumarūpanibbānāni rūpakaṇḍe vuttanayānevāti ayaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyanayo.

In the Abhidhamma analysis, the sensitivity bases and object bases are first analyzed according to the method stated in the Rūpakaṇḍa (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 597), beginning: ‘Herein, what is the eye base? It is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements…’ (Vibhaṅga 156). The mind base, however, is analyzed starting from its single aspect up to its ten aspects, following the method explained in the section on the feeling aggregate. The phenomena base is defined as: ‘Herein, what is the phenomena base? It is the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and whatever form is invisible and non-resistant, included in the phenomena base, as well as the unconditioned element’ (Vibhaṅga 167), and then it is further analyzed in the sections on the feeling aggregate and so forth, beginning with ‘Herein, what is the feeling aggregate?’ Subtle form and Nibbāna are explained according to the method given in the Rūpakaṇḍa. This is the method of the Abhidhamma analysis.

Pañhāpucchakanayaṃ pana ito paraṃ vitthārato adassetvā tikadukānaṃ ādiantehi ceva visesatthadīpakehi ca tikadukehi yojetvā dassayissāma, sesehipi tikadukehi yojanānayo khandhe vuttanayena sakkā ñātunti. Kathaṃ dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇāti? Dasāyatanā abyākatā, dvāyatanā siyā kusalā, siyā akusalā, siyā abyākatā. Vedanāttike dasāyatanāni na vattabbāni, manāyatanaṃ tidhāpi, dhammāyatanaṃ tidhā na vattabbañca…pe… rūpāyatanaṃ sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ, navāyatanāni anidassanasappaṭighāni, manāyatanadhammāyatanāni anidassanaappaṭighāni, ekādasāyatanāni na hetū, dhammāyatanaṃ siyā hetu, siyā na hetu…pe… ekādasāyatanāni sappaccayāni, dhammāyatanaṃ siyā sappaccayaṃ, siyā appaccayaṃ…pe… dasāyatanāni rūpaṃ, manāyatanaṃ arūpaṃ, dhammāyatanaṃ dvidhāpi…pe… dasāyatanāni araṇāni, dvāyatanāni siyā saraṇāni, siyā araṇānīti ayaṃ pañhāpucchakanayo.

Now, we shall demonstrate the method of questioning, not in full detail, but by applying the first and last of the triads and dyads, as well as those that clarify special meanings. The method of applying the remaining triads and dyads can be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the aggregates. How many of the twelve sense bases are wholesome… how many are free from defilements? Ten sense bases are indeterminate. Two sense bases may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. In the triad of feeling, ten sense bases are not applicable. The mind base is threefold. The phenomena base is threefold and also not applicable… The form base is visible and resistant. Nine sense bases are invisible and resistant. The mind base and phenomena base are invisible and non-resistant. Eleven sense bases are not roots. The phenomena base may be a root or may not be a root… Eleven sense bases are conditioned. The phenomena base may be conditioned or may be unconditioned… Ten sense bases are form. The mind base is formless. The phenomena base is twofold… Ten sense bases are free from defilements. Two sense bases may be with defilements or may be free from defilements. This is the method of questioning.

Idāni [V 0.0135] pana –

Now, then—

Kamato tāvattato ca, tesaṃ daṭṭhabbabhedato;

Pāḷimuttanayenettha, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

By way of order, by way of extent, and by way of their discernible distinctions, the decision here should be understood by the method beyond the Pāḷi text.

Tattha [M 0.0177] kamatoti idhāpi desanākkamova yujjati. Ajjhattikesu hi āyatanesu sanidassanasappaṭighavisayattā cakkhāyatanaṃ pākaṭanti paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ, tato anidassanasappaṭighavisayāni sotāyatanādīni. Atha vā dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyahetubhāvato bahūpakārattā cakkhusotāyatanāni paṭhamaṃ desitāni, tato ghānāyatanādīni tīṇi, pañcannampi pana gocaravisayattā ante manāyatanaṃ, cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ gocarattā tesaṃ anantaraṃ rūpāyatanādīni. Apica viññāṇuppattikāraṇavavatthānatopi ayametesaṃ kamo veditabbo. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.421; saṃ. ni. 4.60, 113; mahāni. 107) ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Here, by 'order' is meant the order of teaching, and this is fitting here. Among the internal sense bases, the eye-base is taught first because it is evident, its object being visible and impinging. Then come the ear-base and others, whose objects are invisible but impinging. Alternatively, the eye and ear bases are taught first because they are the cause of unsurpassed seeing and unsurpassed hearing, and are therefore of great benefit. Next are the three beginning with the nose-base. Then, the mind-base is last, as it is the resort for the five. Because the form-base and so forth are the objects for the eye-base and others, they follow immediately after them. Moreover, this sequence should also be understood from the arrangement of the conditions for the arising of consciousness. For it was said: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises… dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises' (MN 3.421; SN 4.60, 113; Mahāni. 107). This, then, is the order here.

Tāvattatoti tāvabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – cakkhādayopi hi dhammā eva, evaṃ sati dhammāyatanamicceva avatvā kasmā dvādasāyatanāni vuttānīti ce? Chaviññāṇakāyuppattiyā dvārārammaṇavavatthānato ayametesaṃ bhedo hotīti dvādasa vuttāni. Cakkhuviññāṇavīthipariyāpannassa hi viññāṇakāyassa cakkhāyatanameva uppattidvāraṃ, rūpāyatanamevārammaṇaṃ. Tathā itarāni itaresaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa pana bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto manāyatanekadesova uppattidvāraṃ, asādhāraṇañca dhammāyatanaṃ ārammaṇanti. Iti channaṃ viññāṇakāyānaṃ uppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato dvādasa vuttānīti ayamettha tāvattatā.

‘Tāvattatā’ means ‘being just that much.’ This is what is said: The eye and so forth are indeed just phenomena. This being so, why are the twelve sense bases mentioned instead of simply stating ‘the phenomena-base’ (dhammāyatana)? This distinction among them is due to the arrangement of doors and objects for the arising of the six bodies of consciousness; therefore, twelve are spoken of. For the body of consciousness comprised in the eye-consciousness process, the eye-base itself is the door of arising, and the form-base itself is the object. Similarly for the others with their respective counterparts. For the sixth, however, a part of the mind-base known as the life-continuum mind is the door of arising, and the phenomena-base is the specific object. Thus, because the doors of arising and objects for the six bodies of consciousness are differentiated, they are spoken of as twelve. This here is the meaning of ‘tāvattatā’.

Daṭṭhabbabhedatoti ettha pana sabbāni cetāni āyatanāni anāgamanato, aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Na hi tāni pubbe udayā kutoci āgacchanti, napi uddhaṃ vayā kuhiñci gacchanti[M 0.0178], atha kho pubbe udayā appaṭiladdhasabhāvāni uddhaṃ vayā paribhinnasabhāvāni, pubbantāparantavemajjhe paccayāyattavuttitāya avasāni pavattanti, tasmā anāgamanato, aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Tathā nirīhato, abyāpārato ca. Na hi cakkhurūpādīnaṃ evaṃ hoti [V 0.0136] “aho vata amhākaṃ sāmaggiyaṃ viññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjeyyā”ti, na ca tāni viññāṇuppādanatthaṃ dvārabhāvena, vatthubhāvena, ārammaṇabhāvena vā byāpāramāpajjanti, atha kho dhammatāvesā yaṃ cakkhurūpādisāmaggiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīni sambhavanti, tasmā nirīhato, abyāpārato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Apica ajjhattikāni suñño gāmo viya daṭṭhabbāni dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitattā, bāhirāni gāmaghātakacorā viya. Tathā ajjhattikāni chapāṇakā viya daṭṭhabbāni, bāhirāni tesaṃ gocarā viyāti ayamettha daṭṭhabbabhedo. Evaṃ pāḷimuttanayenettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Here, as to the distinction in what is to be seen: all these sense bases should be seen as without coming and without going. For before their arising they do not come from anywhere, nor after their ceasing do they go anywhere. Rather, before their arising they are of a nature not yet obtained, and after their ceasing they are of a nature broken up; between the beginning and the end, they proceed powerlessly, dependent on conditions. Therefore, they should be seen as without coming and without going. Similarly, they should be seen as without striving and without activity. For it is not the case that the eye, forms, and so on, think: 'Oh, may consciousness arise from our combination!' Nor do they engage in activity as doors, bases, or objects for the arising of consciousness. Rather, it is simply due to the nature of things that eye-consciousness and so on arise when the eye, forms, and so on come together. Therefore, they should be seen as without striving and without activity. Furthermore, the internal sense bases should be seen as like an empty village—because they are devoid of the nature of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The external sense bases should be seen like village-destroying thieves. Likewise, the internal sense bases should be seen like six animals, and the external sense bases like their feeding grounds. This is the distinction in how they should be seen here. Thus, the analysis here should be understood according to the method beyond the Pāḷi.

Āyatanavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Sense Bases is concluded.

Dhātuvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Elements

Dhātuvibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – aṭṭhārasa dhātuyoti ettha vidahati, dhīyate, vidhānaṃ, vidhīyate etāya, ettha vā dhīyatīti dhātu. Lokiyā hi dhātuyo kāraṇabhāvena vavatthitā. Anekappakāraṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ vidahanti nipphādenti, sattehi ca dhīyante dhārīyanti, dukkhavidhānamattameva cetā, etāhi ca kāraṇabhūtāhi saṃsāradukkhaṃ sattehi anuvidhīyati, yathāvihitañca dukkhaṃ etāsveva dhīyati ṭhapīyatīti etehi atthehi yathāsambhavaṃ “dhātuyo”ti vuccanti.

Now, in the exposition of the meaning of the matrix of the Analysis of the Elements, first as to the meaning: in the phrase 'the eighteen elements,' they are called 'dhātu' because they establish (vidahati), are held (dhīyate), are an arrangement (vidhānaṃ), are that by which something is arranged (vidhīyate etāya), or that in which something is held (ettha vā dhīyati). For worldly elements are established as having the nature of a cause. They establish and produce the manifold suffering of the cycle of existence, and are held and borne by beings. These are merely an arrangement of suffering; and by these causal elements, the suffering of the cycle of existence is conformed to by beings; and the suffering thus arranged is held and placed in them. For these reasons, as is appropriate, they are called 'elements.'

Yathā [M 0.0179] vā sarīrasaṅkhātassa samudāyassa avayavabhūtesu rasasoṇitādīsu aññamaññaṃ visabhāgalakkhaṇaparicchinnesu dhātusamaññā, evametesupi pañcakkhandhasaṅkhātassa attabhāvassa cakkhādīsu dhātusamaññā veditabbā. Lokiyalokuttarasādhāraṇatthavasena pana attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo. Nijjīvamattānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttenatthena cakkhu ca taṃ dhātu cāti cakkhudhātu. Evaṃ sesesupīti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

Just as the designation 'element' is applied to the components of the aggregate called the body—such as bodily fluids, blood, and so on—which are mutually distinct and delimited by different characteristics, so too should the designation 'element' be understood in relation to the eye and so on, which are components of the individual existence called the five aggregates. Moreover, in a sense common to both the mundane and supramundane, they are called 'elements' because they bear their own intrinsic nature. This is a designation for what is merely non-sentient. Therefore, in the sense explained above, 'the eye and that element' is 'the eye-element.' Thus it is for the rest. This, then, is the meaning of the term here.

Dhammabhedato panettha āyatanesu vuttanayena veditabbo. Apica pañcadvārāvajjanasampaṭicchanadvayaviññāṇaṃ [V 0.0137] manodhātu nāma. Pañcaviññāṇamanodhātuvajjitaṃ pana sabbampi viññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu nāma. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Here, as to the classification of phenomena, it should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition on the sense bases. Furthermore, the five-door-adverting consciousness and the two receiving-consciousnesses are called the mind-element. However, all consciousness apart from the five sense-consciousnesses and the mind-element is called the mind-consciousness-element. The rest is easily understood.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīye tāva – “pathavīdhātu āpo tejo vāyo ākāsaviññāṇadhātū”ti cha dhātuyo uddisitvā ādito pañca ajjhattikabāhiravasena, pacchimā ca cha viññāṇavasena vibhattā, aparāpi “sukhadhātu dukkhasomanassadomanassupekkhāavijjādhātū”ti cha dhātuyo uddisitvā tathā tathā vibhattā, puna aparāpi “kāmadhātu byāpādavihiṃsānekkhammaabyāpādaavihiṃsādhātū”ti cha dhātuyo uddisitvā, evaṃ tīhi chakkehi paccekaṃ tebhūmakā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo sarūpato, lakkhaṇāhārato, nissayavisayapayogavinābhāvādito ca vuttāti veditabbāti ayaṃ suttantabhājanīyanayo.

Here, from the perspective of the analytical method, first in the Suttanta classification: having specified six elements—'earth-element, water-element, fire-element, air-element, space-element, and consciousness-element'—the first five are classified by way of internal and external, and the last is classified by way of the six consciousnesses. Having specified another six elements—'pleasure-element, pain-element, joy-element, displeasure-element, equanimity-element, and ignorance-element'—they are classified in various ways. And again, having specified another six elements—'sensual-desire-element, ill-will-element, harmfulness-element, renunciation-element, non-ill-will-element, and non-harmfulness-element'—thus, by means of these three sets of six, eighteen elements pertaining to the three realms are explained individually in terms of their nature, characteristics, nutriment, support, object, application, non-separation, and so on. This should be understood as the method of the Suttanta classification.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana sarūpeneva aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo uddisitvā pasādavisayadhātuyo āyatane vuttanayena vibhattā, satta viññāṇadhātuyo pana –

In the Abhidhamma classification, however, the eighteen elements are specified simply by their own nature. The sensitivity-elements and object-elements are classified in the way explained in the exposition on the sense bases. But the seven consciousness-elements are:

“Tattha katamā cakkhuviññāṇadhātu? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Ayaṃ vuccati cakkhuviññāṇadhātu…pe… kāyaviññāṇadhātu.

"Herein, what is the eye-consciousness-element? The consciousness that arises dependent on the eye and forms... (and so on) ...is the eye-consciousness-element. This is called the eye-consciousness-element... (and so on) ...up to the body-consciousness-element."

“Tattha [M 0.0180] katamā manodhātu? Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā…pe… kāyaviññāṇadhātuyā…pe… niruddhasamanantarā uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… sabbadhammesu vā pana paṭhamasamannāhāro uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… ayaṃ vuccati manodhātu.

"Herein, what is the mind-element? The consciousness that arises immediately after the cessation of the eye-consciousness-element... (and so on)... or of the body-consciousness-element... (and so on)... Or the consciousness that arises as the first adverting to all phenomena... (and so on)... this is called the mind-element."

“Tattha katamā dhammadhātu? Vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho, yañca rūpaṃ anidassanaṃ appaṭighaṃ dhammāyatanapariyāpannaṃ, asaṅkhatā ca dhātu…pe… ayaṃ vuccati dhammadhātu.

"Herein, what is the phenomena-element? The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, and that form which is invisible, non-impinging, and included in the phenomena-base, and the unconditioned element... (and so on) ...this is called the phenomena-element."

“Tattha katamā manoviññāṇadhātu…pe… manodhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarā [V 0.0138] uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… ayaṃ vuccati manoviññāṇadhātū”ti (vibha. 184) –

"Herein, what is the mind-consciousness-element? ... (and so on) ...the consciousness that arises immediately after the mind-element has arisen and ceased ... (and so on) ...the consciousness that arises dependent on the mind and phenomena ... (and so on) ...This is called the mind-consciousness-element." (Vibh. 184)

Evaṃ vibhattā. Tattha sabbadhammesu vā pana paṭhamasamannāhāroti ettha pañcaviññāṇavisayesu sabbadhammesūti evaṃ attho gahetabbo. Manodhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarāti ettha pana pi-kāro sampiṇḍanattho, tasmā manodhātuyāpi santīraṇavoṭṭhabbanādimanoviññāṇadhātuyāpīti evamattho gahetabbo. Manañca paṭiccātiādīsu manodvāre bhavaṅgamanañceva catubhūmakadhammārammaṇañca paṭicca sahāvajjanakajavanaṃ nibbattatīti attho. Ayaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyanayo.

Thus it is classified. Herein, in the phrase "or the first adverting to all phenomena," the meaning should be understood as "to all phenomena" referring to the objects of the five sense-consciousnesses. In the phrase "having arisen and ceased immediately after the mind-element," the particle "pi" serves the purpose of combination. Therefore, the meaning should be taken as "also in the mind-element, and also in the mind-consciousness element beginning with investigating and determining." In the phrases "dependent on the mind," etc., the meaning is that in the mind-door, dependent on both the life-continuum mind and the objective phenomena of the four planes, the impulsion consciousness arises together with the adverting consciousness. This is the method of classification according to the Abhidhamma.

Pañhāpucchakanaye pana aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇāti? Soḷasa dhātuyo abyākatā, dve dhātuyo tidhāpi honti…pe… dasa dhātuyo nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā, pañca dhātuyo vipākā, manodhātu siyā vipākā, siyā nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā, dve dhātuyo tidhāpi [M 0.0181] honti. Dasa dhātuyo upādinnupādāniyā, saddadhātuyo anupādinnupādāniyā, pañca dhātuyo siyā upādinnupādāniyā, siyā anupādinnupādāniyā, dve dhātuyo tidhāpi…pe… dasa dhātuyo siyā uppannā, siyā uppādino, saddadhātu siyā uppannā, siyā anuppannā, siyā na vattabbā uppādinoti, cha dhātuyo tidhāpi. Dhammadhātu tidhāva…pe… rūpadhātu sanidassanasappaṭighā, nava dhātuyo anidassanasappaṭighā, aṭṭha dhātuyo anidassanaappaṭighā. Sattarasa dhātuyo na hetū, dhammadhātu dvidhāva…pe… soḷasa dhātuyo araṇā, dve dhātuyo dvidhāpīti ayaṃ pañhāpucchakanayo.

Now, in the method of questioning: regarding the eighteen elements, how many are wholesome... (and so on) ...how many are free from defilements? Sixteen elements are indeterminate, two elements are threefold... (and so on) ...ten elements are neither result nor result-producing phenomena, five elements are results, the mind element may be a result or neither result nor result-producing phenomena, two elements are threefold. Ten elements are clung to and fuel for clinging, the sound element is not clung to but is fuel for clinging, five elements may be clung to and fuel for clinging or not clung to but fuel for clinging, two elements are threefold... (and so on) ...ten elements may be arisen or arising, the sound element may be arisen, may be unarisen, or cannot be said to be arising, six elements are threefold. The phenomena element is threefold... (and so on) ...the form element is visible and impinging, nine elements are invisible and impinging, eight elements are invisible and non-impinging. Seventeen elements are not roots, the phenomena element is twofold... (and so on) ...sixteen elements are free from defilements, two elements are twofold. This is the method of questioning.

Idāni panetāsaṃ –

Now, as for these—

Kamatāvattato daṭṭhabbā, paccayānaṃ vibhāgato;

Dhātūnamidha viññeyyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

They should be seen from their order and extent, and from the analysis of conditions; here, the analysis of the elements should be understood, according to the method beyond the Pāḷi text.

Tattha kamato tāva idhāpi desanākkamova yujjati. So ca panāyaṃ hetuphalānupubbavavatthānavasena [V 0.0139] vutto. Cakkhudhātu rūpadhātūti idaṃ hi dvayaṃ hetu, cakkhuviññāṇadhātūti idaṃ phalaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha. Ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Here, first, with regard to order, the order of teaching is appropriate here also. And this order is stated in terms of the sequential arrangement of cause and effect. For the eye-element and the form-element—these two are the cause; the eye-consciousness-element—this is the effect. The same applies everywhere. This, then, is the order here.

Tāvattato pana yā idha suttantabhājanīye tīhi chakkehi vuttā dhātuyo ceva, tesu tesu suttābhidhammapadesesu “ābhādhātu…pe… anekadhātunānādhātuloko”tiādinā āgatā cāti aññāpi bahudhātuyo dissanti, tāsampi vasena paricchedaṃ avatvā kasmā aṭṭhāraseva vuttāti? Tāsampi tadantogadhattā.

Now, as to the extent: although the elements mentioned here in the Suttanta classification by the three sets of six, as well as many other elements found in various Sutta and Abhidhamma passages—such as "the light element... (and so on) ...the world of diverse elements, the world of various elements"—are seen, why are only the eighteen mentioned without stating a classification of them as well? Because they are included within those.

Apica vijānanasabhāve viññāṇe jīvasaññīnaṃ tassā cakkhuviññāṇādibhedena anekataṃ, cakkhurūpādipaccayāyattavuttitāya aniccatañca pakāsetvā tasmiṃ dīgharattānusayitajīvasaññāsamūhananatthañca aṭṭhāraseva vuttā. Kiñca bhiyyo [M 0.0182] – veneyyajjhāsayavasena ca. Veneyyā hi arūpamūḷho rūpamūḷho ubhayamūḷhoti tividhā honti. Tesaṃ tiṇṇampi yathākkamaṃ nātisaṅkhepavitthārato arūpabhedavibhāvinī khandhadesanā, rūpabhedavibhāvinī āyatanadesanā, tadubhayabhedavibhāvinī dhātudesanā sappāyāti veneyyajjhāsayavasena aṭṭhāraseva vuttāti. Vuttañca –

Moreover, in consciousness, which is of the nature of cognizing, for those who perceive a living being, its multiplicity is shown by way of divisions such as eye-consciousness, and so forth, and its impermanence is revealed by its dependence on conditions such as the eye and form. And for the uprooting of the perception of a living being that has long been latent in it, only eighteen elements are stated. Furthermore, they are stated according to the inclinations of those to be trained. For those to be trained are of three kinds: those deluded by the formless, those deluded by form, and those deluded by both. For these three, respectively, the teaching of aggregates, neither too concise nor too extensive, is suitable for revealing the distinctions of the formless; the teaching of sense bases is suitable for revealing the distinctions of form; and the teaching of elements is suitable for revealing the distinctions of both. Thus, according to the inclinations of those to be trained, only eighteen elements are stated. And it is said:

“Saṅkhepavitthāranayena tathā tathā hi,

Dhammaṃ pakāsayati esa yathā yathāssa;

Saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena,

Veneyyasattahadayesu tamo payātī”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 183);

"For in this way or that, he explains the Dhamma, briefly or in detail, according to what is suitable; the darkness in the hearts of beings to be taught vanishes in an instant, struck by the Dhamma’s radiance." (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 183)

Ayamettha tāvattatā.

This here is the extent.

Daṭṭhabbato panetā sabbāpi saṅkhatā dhātuyo pubbantāparantavivittato, dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasuññato, paccayāyattavuttito ca daṭṭhabbā. Visesato panettha bheritalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu daṭṭhabbā, daṇḍo viya rūpadhātu, saddo viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā tissopi cetā yathākkamaṃ ādāsatalamukhamukhanimittāni viya. Tathā tilayantacakkatelāni viya, adharāraṇīuttarāraṇīaggī viya ca daṭṭhabbā. Esa nayo sotadhātuādīsupi. Manodhātu pana yathāsambhavato cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbā. Dhammadhātuyaṃ pana vedanā sallasūlamiva[V 0.0140], saññā rittamuṭṭhi viya, saṅkhārā visarukkhamiva, sukhumarūpaṃ khuracakkaṃ viya, asaṅkhatā dhātu khemantabhūmi viya ca daṭṭhabbā, manoviññāṇadhātu pana makkaṭo viya, assakhaḷuṅko viya, yatthakāmanipātito vehāsakkhittadaṇḍo viya, raṅganaṭo viya ca daṭṭhabbā. Ayamettha daṭṭhabbatā.

Moreover, all these conditioned elements should be seen as devoid of a beginning and an end, empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood, and as dependent on conditions for their occurrence. Specifically, here, the eye element should be seen like the surface of a drum, the form element like a drumstick, and the eye-consciousness element like sound. Similarly, those three should be seen in order like a mirror surface, a face, and its reflection. They should also be seen like the sesame seeds, the wheel of the oil press, and the oil; or like the lower fire-stick, the upper fire-stick, and the fire. This same method applies to the ear element and so on. The mind element, however, should be seen as preceding and following the eye-consciousness element and others, as appropriate, like a scout and a rear guard. In the case of the mental-object element, feeling should be seen like a dart or a spear, perception like an empty fist, formations like a poisonous tree, subtle materiality like a razor-wheel, and the unconditioned element like a safe land. The mind-consciousness element, however, should be seen like a monkey, like an unbroken colt, like a stick thrown into the air that falls wherever it may, and like an actor on a stage. This is how they should be seen here.

Paccayānaṃ [M 0.0183] vibhāgato panettha cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā cakkhu nissayapaccayo, rūpaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, kiriyāmanodhātu anantarapaccayo, tayo arūpino khandhā sahajātapaccayo. Evaṃ sotaviññāṇādīsupi. Manoviññāṇadhātuyā pana manodhātu anantarapaccayo, dhammadhātu ārammaṇapaccayo, sampayuttanissayasahajātādipaccayoti ayaṃ paccayavibhāgo. Evaṃ viññeyyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

Now, from the division of conditions, here for the eye-consciousness element, the eye is the dependence condition, visible form is the object condition, the functional mind-element is the contiguity condition, and the three immaterial aggregates are the co-arising condition. Similarly for ear-consciousness and the others. For the mind-consciousness element, however, the mind-element is the contiguity condition, the mental-object element is the object condition, and there are the associated, dependence, co-arising, and other conditions. This is the analysis of conditions. Thus should be understood the determination independent of the Pāḷi text.

Dhātuvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of Elements is complete.

Saccavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of Truths

Saccavibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – cattāri ariyasaccānīti etthāyaṃ sacca-saddo anekesu atthesu dissati. Seyyathidaṃ – “saccaṃ bhaṇe na kujjheyyā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 224) vācāsacce. “Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.433) viratisacce. “Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā, pavādiyāse kusalāvadānā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 891) diṭṭhisacce. “Ekaṃ hi saccaṃ, na dutiyamatthī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 890) paramatthasacce, nibbāne ceva magge ca. “Catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ kati kusalā”tiādīsu (vibha. 216) ariyasacce. Svāyamidhāpi ariyasacce vattati. Kenaṭṭhena saccāni? Tathaṭṭhena. Koyaṃ tathaṭṭho nāma? Yo paññācakkhunā upaparikkhamānānaṃ māyāva viparīto, marīcīva visaṃvādako, titthiyānaṃ atthā viya anupalabbhamānasabhāvo ca na hoti, atha kho bādhanappabhavasantiniyyānabhūtena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvena ariyañāṇassa gocaro hoti. Ayaṃ tathaṭṭho saccaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Vuttañca –

Now, in the matrix of the analysis of truths, as to their meaning first—the four noble truths—here, the term "truth" (sacca) is seen in various senses. For example: "Speak the truth, do not be angry" (Dhammapada 224)—this refers to verbal truth. "Those ascetics and brahmins who are established in truth" (Jātaka 2.21.433)—this refers to abstention as truth. "Why do those disputants, skilled in their own doctrines, proclaim various truths?" (Sutta Nipāta 891)—this refers to doctrinal truth. "Indeed, there is one truth, there is not a second" (Sutta Nipāta 890)—this refers to ultimate truth, in both Nibbāna and the path. "Of the four noble truths, how many are wholesome?" (Vibhaṅga 216)—this refers to the noble truth. Here too, it applies to the noble truth. In what sense are they truths? In the sense of actuality. What is this "actuality"? It is that which, when examined with the eye of wisdom, is not false like an illusion, not deceptive like a mirage, and does not have a non-existent nature like the tenets of other schools; but rather, by way of being affliction, origin, peace, and leading out, it is the domain of noble knowledge, in its genuine and undistorted nature. This actuality should be understood as the meaning of truth. And it is said:

“Iti [M 0.0184][V 0.0141] tacchāvipallāsabhūtabhāvaṃ catūsupi;

Dukkhādīsvavisesena, saccaṭṭhaṃ āhu paṇḍitā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 189; sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.14).

"Thus, in all four, regarding suffering and the rest without exception, the wise declare the meaning of truth as the state of being real, unperverted, and actual." (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 189; Sārattha. Ṭī. Mahāvagga 3.14)

Ariyāni ca tāni saccāni cāti ariyasaccāni. Ariyānīti uttamāni, avisaṃvādakānīti attho. Ariyehi buddhādīhi paṭivijjhitabbāni saccāni, ariyassa vā sammāsambuddhassa santakāni saccāni tena uppāditattā, pakāsitattā ca, ariyabhāvakarāni vā saccāni tesaṃ abhisambuddhattā ariyabhāvasiddhitoti ariyasaccāni. “Dukkhaṃ ariyasacca”ntiādīsu pana du-iti ayaṃ saddo kucchite dissati. Kucchitaṃ hi puttaṃ “duputto”ti vadanti. Khaṃ-saddo pana tucche. Tucchaṃ hi ākāsaṃ “kha”nti vuccati. Idañca paṭhamasaccaṃ kucchitaṃ anekopaddavādhiṭṭhānato, tucchaṃ bālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitato, tasmā kucchitattā, tucchattā ca “dukkha”nti vuccati. Saṃ-iti ca ayaṃ saddo “samāgamo, sameta”ntiādīsu saṃyogaṃ dīpeti. U-iti ayaṃ saddo “uppannaṃ udita”ntiādīsu uppattiṃ. Aya-saddo pana kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Idañca dutiyasaccaṃ avasesapaccayasamāyoge sati dukkhassuppattikāraṇanti “dukkhasamudayo”ti vuccati.

They are noble and they are truths, thus they are the noble truths. 'Noble' means supreme, that is, non-deceptive. They are truths to be penetrated by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas; or they are the truths belonging to the noble, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, because they were produced and proclaimed by him; or they are truths that make one noble, since the state of nobility is achieved by fully understanding them—thus they are called the noble truths. In the phrase 'the noble truth of suffering,' however, the syllable 'du' is seen in the sense of 'contemptible.' For a contemptible son is called a 'duputto.' The syllable 'kha,' however, signifies 'empty.' For empty space is called 'kha.' And this first truth is contemptible because it is the foundation of many dangers, and empty because it is devoid of the permanence, beauty, happiness, and self imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because it is contemptible and empty, it is called 'suffering.' The syllable 'saṃ' denotes connection, as in 'coming together' or 'assembled.' The syllable 'u' signifies arising, as in 'arisen' or 'appeared.' The syllable 'aya,' however, indicates cause. And this second truth is called 'the origin of suffering' because it is the cause for the arising of suffering when there is a conjunction of the remaining conditions.

Tatiyasaccaṃ pana yasmā ni-saddo abhāvaṃ, rodha-saddo cārakaṃ dīpeti, tasmā abhāvo ettha, etasmiṃ vā adhigate saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkhanirodhassa sabbagatisuññattā, tappaṭipakkhattā cāti “dukkhanirodha”nti vuccati, dukkhassa vā anuppādanirodhapaccayattā. Catutthaṃ pana yasmā etaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati, sattaṃ vā taṃ gamayati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhattā, paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā, tasmā “dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti vuccati.

Regarding the third truth, since the prefix 'ni-' denotes absence and the word 'rodha' denotes a prison, it is called 'cessation' (nirodha) because there is an absence of that prison. Or, it is so called because, when it is realized, it is empty of all destinations and is the opposite of that suffering designated as the prison of saṃsāra; or because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering. The fourth truth, however, is called 'the path leading to the cessation of suffering' because it leads to the cessation of suffering, or because it guides a being toward it by way of object, being oriented towards that, and because it is the path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering.

Apica [M 0.0185] dukkhādīnaṃ cattāro cattāro atthā vibhattā tathā avitathā anaññathā, ye dukkhādīni abhisamentehi abhisametabbā. Yathāha –

Furthermore, the four meanings of each of suffering and so forth are analyzed as true, not unreal, and not otherwise, which should be fully understood by those who fully comprehend suffering and the rest. As it is said:

“Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho, ime cattāro dukkhassa dukkhaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho nidānaṭṭho saṃyogaṭṭho palibodhaṭṭho [V 0.0142] …pe… nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho asaṅkhataṭṭho amataṭṭho…pe… maggassa niyyānaṭṭho hetvaṭṭho dassanaṭṭho ādhipateyyaṭṭho…pe… anaññathā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.8).

"For suffering, the meanings are oppression, being conditioned, burning, and alteration. These four are the meanings of suffering as suffering: they are true, not unreal, not otherwise. For the origin, the meanings are accumulation, source, connection, and obstruction... For cessation, the meanings are escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless... For the path, the meanings are leading out, cause, seeing, and dominance... not otherwise." (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.8)

Evaṃ vibhattānaṃ catunnaṃ catunnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena dukkhādīni veditabbāni. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

Thus, suffering and so forth are to be understood in terms of the four meanings for each, so analyzed. This, firstly, is the meaning of the words here.

Dhammabhedato pana taṇhāvajjitā sabbalokiyadhammā, saṃkilesikavajjitā vā dukkhasaccaṃ nāma, taṇhā pana sabbā akusalā vā lokiyakusalā vā dhammā samudayasaccaṃ nāma, nibbānaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ nāma, lokuttarakusalacittasampayuttāni aṭṭhamaggaṅgāni dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ nāma. Imehi pana maggaṅgehi sampayuttā cittacetasikā dhammā ceva sāmaññaphalāni cettha asaṅgahitānīti veditabbāni. Tāni hi “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato saṅkhāradukkhasaṅgahitānipi. Yāya pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena na honti, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti na vuccanti, tāni ṭhapetvā sabbe lokiyalokuttaradhammā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Ayaṃ dhammabhedo.

Regarding the division of phenomena, however, all worldly phenomena apart from craving, or apart from defiling states, are called the truth of suffering. Craving, however, and all unwholesome or worldly wholesome phenomena, are called the truth of the origin. Nibbāna is called the truth of cessation. The eight path factors associated with supramundane wholesome consciousness are called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. It should be understood that the consciousness and mental factors associated with these path factors, as well as the fruits of recluseship, are not included here. For although they are included in the suffering of formations according to the statement, 'Whatever is impermanent is suffering' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.15), they are not in reality that truth by the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, and thus they are not called 'the noble truth of suffering.' Setting those aside, it should be seen that all worldly and supramundane phenomena are included in the four truths. This is the division of phenomena.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīye dukkhasaccaṃ tāva –

Here, according to the method of the Vibhaṅga, in the Suttanta analysis, first is the truth of suffering:

“Tattha [M 0.0186] katamaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ? Jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho, piyehi vippayogo dukkho, yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkhaṃ, saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (vibha. 190) –

"Herein, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the pleasant is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering." (Vibh. 190)

Uddisitvā vibhattaṃ. Tattha dukkhaṃ tividhaṃ hoti dukkhadukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ saṅkhāradukkhanti. Tattha dukkhadukkhaṃ duvidhaṃ pariyāyadukkhaṃ nippariyāyadukkhanti. Tattha kāyikacetasikadukkhadomanassavedanā nippariyāyadukkhaṃ nāma, tadavasesā pana dukkhadukkhassa vatthubhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā pariyāyadukkhaṃ nāma. Sukhasomanassavedanā vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ nāma. Sabbe pana pañcupādānakkhandhā, sabbasaṅkhatā vā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ nāma. Imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dukkhānaṃ vasena yathāyogaṃ tīsu [V 0.0143] bhavesu jātiādīnaṃ dukkhadukkhatā veditabbā. Kāmabhavasmiṃ hi jāti tāva sayaṃ na dukkhā, apāyagatimanussagatiādīsu pana nirayaggisantāpādimūlakaṃ, gabbhokkantikādimūlakaṃ, jighacchāpipāsādimūlakañca dukkhaṃ tassa sabbassa kāyikacetasikadukkhassa vatthubhāvena pariyāyato dukkhanti. Tathā jarāmaraṇādayopi. Kevalaṃ jarā kāyadubbalatāmūlassa, puttadārādiparibhavamūlassa ca, maraṇaṃ pana māraṇantikavedanābhūtassa, nirayādigatinimittadassanamūlassa ca dukkhassa vatthubhāvato, sokādayo sokādimūlassa kāyikacetasikadukkhassa vatthubhāvattā ceva sayaṃ dukkhattā ca dukkhāti veditabbā. Vipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhatā cesaṃ pasiddhāyeva. Evaṃ kāmabhave jātiādīnaṃ tīhipi dukkhehi dukkhatā veditabbā. Rūpārūpabhavesu pana yasmā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā na santi, tasmā tattha jātiādīnaṃ [M 0.0187] vipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhavasena ca dukkhatā veditabbā, na dukkhadukkhavasenāti ayaṃ dukkhasacce nayo.

Having been stated, it is now analyzed. Herein, suffering is threefold: suffering as pain, suffering due to change, and suffering due to formations. Herein, suffering as pain is twofold: indirect suffering and direct suffering. Herein, bodily and mental painful feelings and displeasure are called direct suffering, while the remaining five aggregates subject to clinging, which serve as the basis for suffering as pain, are called indirect suffering. Pleasant and joyful feelings are called suffering due to change. All five aggregates subject to clinging, or all conditioned phenomena, are called suffering due to formations. By means of these three kinds of suffering, the nature of birth and so on as suffering as pain should be understood in the three planes of existence, as is appropriate. For in the plane of sensual desire, birth itself is not painful, but it is indirectly suffering because it serves as the basis for all bodily and mental pain rooted in such things as the torment of hell-fire, conception in the womb, and hunger and thirst. Similarly for aging, death, and the rest. Aging is suffering because it is the basis for pain rooted in bodily weakness and in humiliation by one's children and wife; death is suffering because it is the basis for the pain of dying and for that rooted in seeing signs of a future destination in hell or another such realm. Sorrow and the like are to be understood as suffering both because they are the basis for bodily and mental pain rooted in sorrow, and because they are suffering in themselves. Their nature as suffering due to change and suffering due to formations is well-established. Thus, in the plane of sensual desire, birth and so on should be understood as suffering in all three ways. However, in the planes of form and formlessness, because sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are absent, the suffering of birth and so on there should be understood only in terms of suffering due to change and suffering due to formations, not in terms of suffering as pain. This is the method regarding the truth of suffering.

Samudayasaccaṃ pana “kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā”ti (vibha. 203) tattakameva uddisitvā “sā kho panesā taṇhā kattha uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti (vibha. 203) pucchitvā channaṃ channaṃ indriyavisayaviññāṇaphassavedanāsaññācetanātaṇhāvitakkavicārānaṃ visayabhūtānaṃ vasena taṇhāya “etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti evaṃ uppattiṃ pakāsetvā vitthārato vibhattaṃ.

The truth of the origin, however, after being stated merely as “craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence” (Vibh. 203), is analyzed in detail. This is done by first asking, “But where does this craving arise when it arises?” (Vibh. 203), and then explaining its arising by showing that “it is here that this craving arises when it arises,” with respect to the sixfold groups of sense faculties, sense objects, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, intention, craving, thought, and examination, which are its objects.

Nirodhasaccaṃ pana “tassā eva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti (vibha. 204) vatvā puna “sā kho panesā taṇhā kattha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”ti (vibha. 204) pucchitvā samudayasacce vuttaindriyādīnaṃ vasena paṭilomato taṇhāya nirodhaṃ pakāsetvā vitthārato vibhattaṃ. Tattha asesavirāganirodhotiādīni padāni nibbānavevacanāni. Nibbānaṃ hi āgamma taṇhā asesā virajjati, nirujjhati, cajīyati, paṭinissajjīyati, muccati, na allīyati, tasmā “asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti vuccati. Ekameva hi nibbānaṃ, nāmāni panassa sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ nāmapaṭipakkhavasena anekāni honti.

The truth of cessation, however, is stated as, “The complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandonment, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment” (Vibh. 204). Then, having asked, “But where does this craving, when ceasing, cease?” (Vibh. 204), and having revealed the cessation of craving in reverse order by way of the faculties and so forth mentioned in the truth of origin, it is analyzed in detail. Here, the terms “complete fading away and cessation,” and so forth, are synonyms for Nibbāna. For it is in dependence on Nibbāna that craving completely fades away, ceases, is abandoned, is relinquished, is released, and does not cling; therefore, it is called “complete fading away and cessation, abandonment, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.” Indeed, Nibbāna is one, but its names are many, being the opposite of the names of all conditioned phenomena.

Nanu pāṭekkaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma natthi, kilesakkhayamattameva nibbānaṃ, teneva ca tāsu tāsu [V 0.0144] suttābhidhammadesanāsu “rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.314) vuttanti ce? Na, arahattanibbānānaṃ ekatāpajjanato. Arahattampi hi “yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo, idaṃ vuccati arahatta”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.314) rāgādīnaṃ parikkhayante uppannattā upacārena [M 0.0188] arahattaṃ rāgakkhayādibhāvena vuccati, tathā rāgādīnaṃ khayahetuttā nibbānampi rāgakkhayādibhāvena vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Itarathā nibbānassa bahuttaṃ āpajjati rāgādīnaṃ bahunnaṃ khayassāpi bahuttā. Sabbakilesānampi khayassa ekattena paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhiādīnaṃ khaye sabbakilesakkhayo āpajjati, oḷārikattañcassa siyā tiracchānānampi uppannarāgakkhayassa pākaṭattena nibbānappattito, gotrabhūkkhaṇepi ca rāgādikkhayo hoti gotrabhuno nibbānavisayattā, maggassa pana nibbānārammaṇatāappasaṅgo. Na hi attanā khepiyamānakilesakkhayamārabbha maggo uppajjati, abhāvo cassa āpajjati rāgādikkhayabhūtassa pana abhāvassa pakkhavasena tuccharūpattā, tassāpi bhāvattābhāvāva vivekalakkhaṇaṃ na siyā, saṅkhatatā cassa siyā. Na hi kadāci upalabbhamānaṃ asaṅkhataṃ bhavitumarahati sabbesampi ahetukattāpattito, saṅkhatattepi cassa na nibbānattaṃ uppattijarābhaṅgasamaṅgitāya dukkhattā, tathā ca abhāvassāpi abhāvo, anavaṭṭhānañca khīṇānampi rāgādīnaṃ puna uppajjanaṃ yesaṃ tesameva abhāvo abhāvassa vinaṭṭhattā.

Is it not the case that there is no such thing as a separate Nibbāna, and that Nibbāna is merely the destruction of defilements? For this reason, in various suttas and Abhidhamma teachings, it is said, “the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred,” and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 4.314). No, for that would entail the identity of arahantship and Nibbāna. For even arahantship is described as, “Friend, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this is called arahantship” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.314). Since arahantship arises with the complete destruction of lust and so on, it is figuratively called the destruction of lust and so on. Similarly, it should be understood that because it is the cause of the destruction of lust and so on, Nibbāna too is spoken of as the destruction of lust and so on. Otherwise, Nibbāna would become multiple, since the destruction of many defilements like lust would also be multiple. And if the destruction of all defilements were a single thing, then with the destruction of wrong view and so on by the first path, the destruction of all defilements would occur. This would be a gross conclusion, for even in animals the destruction of arisen lust is evident, which would entail the attainment of Nibbāna. And at the moment of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), the destruction of lust and so on occurs because change-of-lineage has Nibbāna as its object; but then it would follow that the path does not have Nibbāna as its object. For the path does not arise by taking as its object the destruction of defilements that it is itself destroying. And this [destruction] would be non-existent, for the non-existence that is the destruction of lust and so on is, by its nature as non-existence, void. And since that [non-existence] is also a state, it would not have the characteristic of seclusion, and it would be conditioned. For what is at some time perceived cannot be unconditioned, as this would entail that all things are uncaused. And even if it were conditioned, it would not be Nibbāna, because being endowed with arising, aging, and dissolution, it would be suffering. And thus there would be the non-existence of non-existence, and instability, and the re-arising of even the destroyed lust and so on, since the non-existence of those very things would be destroyed when that non-existence itself has perished.

Apica kāraṇantarena vā bhāve uppanne rāgādīnaṃ na kāci hāni hoti. Na hi aññassuppattiyaṃ aññaṃ vigacchati. Abhāvo bhāvassa virodhi, virodhisannidhāne ca itaraṃ vigacchatīti ce? Kimidaṃ vigamanaṃ nāma. Yadi tampi bhāvarūpaṃ, samānadosatā cassa siyā anavaṭṭhānañca, na ca atthasiddhi. Yadi tuccharūpaṃ, kiṃ paṭhamamevassa tuccharūpatāya upagatāya dūrampi gantvā upagantabbāti siddhā, rāgādikkhayabhūtassa nibbānassa tuccharūpatāya abhāvo, na ca abhāvo eva nibbānaṃ. Atītānāgatadosānamabhāve nibbānappattiyā abhāvato vattamānānañca [M 0.0189] abhāvo nāma. Abhāvo nāma na kilesavigamamatto, api tu anuppattibhāvena. Accantavigamo nibbānenāpi sampādīyatīti ce? Na, tassa kāraṇabhāvā. Vipassanā kāraṇamiti ce? Na, attādivikappajanakasaṅkhatadhammadassanena vinā anattādivikappabhūtāya vipassanāya anuppattito. Yadi hi uppajjeyya, tāya sabbepi sattā vimuttā eva siyuṃ, no ca kadāci na puccheyya viruddhadhammadassanābhāvā. Na hi dassanaṃ vinā vikappo sambhavati, na ca attāti vikappajanakarūpādidassanameva tabbiruddhavikappajanakaṃ [V 0.0145] hoti. Buddhānañca paramparopadesena rūpādīsu vipassanāvikappo uppajjatīti ce? Na, tesampi viruddhadassanābhāvena vipassanāvikappānuppattito. Na hi yādisāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā yādisaṃ kāriyaṃ uppajjati, tādisāya eva tabbiruddhaṃ uppajjati ahetukattappasaṅgato. Na ca viruddhadassanābhāvena ekassa vipassanāvikappajanakasāmatthiyābhāvato tādisānaṃ paramparāyapi tabbhāvo, tadupadeso ca sambhavati. Tilakkhaṇūpadesanānantarikatāya pana buddhānaṃ nibbānasacchikiriyā siddhi, tenevassa kilesānamaccantappahānassa, vipassanopadesasāmatthiyassa ca siddhīti nibbānameva tadubhayakāraṇaṃ, nāññanti gahetabbaṃ.

Moreover, if a state were to arise for another reason, there would be no decrease in lust and so on. For when one thing arises, another does not cease. If it is said, “Absence is the opposite of presence, and in the presence of the opposite, the other ceases,” then what is this cessation? If that too is a form of existence, it would share the same faults and lack stability, and the purpose would not be achieved. If it is of a void nature, why go to great lengths to attain it, when its void nature is present from the very beginning? It is established that the destruction of lust and so on is of a void nature, a non-existence; but non-existence itself is not Nibbāna. Since the attainment of Nibbāna does not occur through the mere non-existence of past and future defilements, it must be the non-existence of present ones that is meant. “Absence” does not merely mean the removal of defilements but also their non-arising. If it is said that complete cessation is accomplished by Nibbāna, [we say] no, because of its being the cause. If it is said, “Insight is the cause,” no, because without seeing conditioned phenomena that generate the conception of self and so on, insight, which is the conception of non-self and so on, does not arise. If it were to arise, all beings would be liberated by it, and they would never question, because there would be no seeing of contradictory phenomena. For without seeing, conceptions do not arise, and the seeing of form, etc., which generates the conception of self, is not what generates the opposing conception. If it is said, “For the Buddhas, the conception of insight arises in forms, etc., through successive instruction,” no, because even for them, without seeing contradictory phenomena, the conception of insight does not arise. For when a certain causal assemblage produces a certain effect, the opposite does not arise from that same assemblage, as that would entail causelessness. And because, due to the absence of seeing contradictory phenomena, a single person lacks the capacity to generate the conception of insight, such a state cannot arise even in a succession of such teachers, nor can their instruction be valid. However, the realization of Nibbāna by the Buddhas is accomplished immediately following the teaching on the three characteristics. By that means, the complete abandonment of defilements and the capacity for insight instruction are both achieved. Therefore, it should be understood that Nibbāna itself is the cause of both, and nothing else.

Kasmā pana nibbānadassanena rāgādīnaṃ accantappahānaṃ, tilakkhaṇañca hoti. Na hi aññassa dassanena itararāgappahānaṃ, tilakkhaṇañāṇañca yuttanti? Na, asaṅkhatadassanena saṅkhatassa vā dosassa vā pākaṭattā. Diṭṭhaaccantasukhānaṃ hi vaṭṭasukhe, tannissayārammaṇādīsu ca sukhābhimāno, vaṭṭābhirati ca pahīyati diṭṭhaparatīrassa nāvikassa nāvāyekadese sukhābhimānābhiratiyo viya. Apica saṅkhatadhammesu allinā rāgādayo asaṅkhatadhamme saṇṭhātuṃ na [M 0.0190] sakkonti aggikkhandhe viya makkhikā, thale viya ca jalacarā, nibbānadassanena pahīnadosassa cittassa yāthāvato tesu saṅkhatesu tilakkhaṇadassanaṃ sambhavati bhesajjālepena vihatakācatimirādidosassa cakkhuno ghaṭādirūpadassanaṃ viya, diṭṭhadosesu cassa saṅkhāresu na puna rāgādīnamuppatti ñātā sucibhāve viya vaccakūpeti veditabbaṃ.

Why then, through the vision of Nibbāna, is there complete abandonment of lust and so forth, and also the knowledge of the three characteristics? Is it not fitting that the abandonment of lust for other things and the knowledge of the three characteristics should occur through the vision of something else? No, because the vision of the unconditioned makes the conditioned and its defects manifest. For one who has seen ultimate bliss, the conceit of happiness in the round of existence, in its supports and objects, and delight in the round are abandoned—just as a sailor who has seen the far shore abandons the conceit of happiness and delight in a mere part of his boat. Moreover, lust and other defilements clinging to conditioned phenomena cannot remain in the unconditioned phenomenon—like flies on a mass of fire or aquatic creatures on dry land. For a mind that has abandoned defilements through the vision of Nibbāna, the true seeing of the three characteristics in those conditioned things becomes possible—just as an eye freed from the defects of cataracts, darkness, and so on by a medicinal ointment sees forms like pots and so forth. And it should be understood that for one who has seen the faults in conditioned formations, lust and so forth do not arise again—just as there is no delight in a cesspit that is known to be clean.

Kasmā pana kesañci sattānaṃ eva nibbānasacchikiriyāsambhavo, na sabbesanti? Anādibuddhaparamparopadesasāpekkhattā, tesañca upadesakānaṃ sabbattha sabbadā abhāvato, sotūnañca khaṇasampattiyā accantadullabhattā, cakkavāḷānañca anantattā, tasmā keci eva buddhuppādakāle tilakkhaṇopadesalābhena nibbānaṃ sacchikaronti, na sabbeti gahetabbaṃ.

Why then is the realization of Nibbāna possible for some beings, but not for all? Because it depends on instruction passed down through a beginningless lineage of Buddhas, and because those who give such instruction are not present everywhere at all times. Moreover, the attainment of the opportune moment for hearers is exceedingly rare, and the number of world-systems is infinite. Therefore, it should be understood that only some beings, obtaining the teaching of the three characteristics at the time of a Buddha's arising, realize Nibbāna—not all.

Kathaṃ panettha rāgādīnaṃ accantavigamo nibbānena sādhīyatīti? Na tāva so, atītānāgatānaṃ tesamidāni abhāvā, pubbe ca tassa vijjamānattā, vattamānānaṃ sarasanirodhato. Kathañcassa tuccharūpassa nibbānassa hetutte yathāvuttadosānamavasaroti ce? Na, tassa bhāvarūpattā. Pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyā hi nibbānamārabbha anusayājananabhāvena uppannamaggā eva [V 0.0146] kilesānamanuppādanirodho taduppattiyā āyatiṃ uppajjanārahānaṃ anuppattito aggisannidhāne aṅkurājanakabhāvena uppannasālikkhandhassa bījatābhāvarūpatā viya. Na hi abhāvo nāma koci paramatthato atthi, yo kāraṇena janīyati tabbiruddhakkhaṇuppādanabhāvovuppādanaṃ anekakkhaṇuppādanena khandhakārābhāvuppādanaṃ viya, tasmā kilesānaṃ anuppattinirodhasaṅkhātassa ariyamaggassa upanissayattā upanissayopacārena nibbānaṃ “asesavirāganirodho”tiādinā vuttaṃ. Sarūpeneva kasmā na vuttanti ce? Abhisukhumattā, anupaladdhapubbattā ca, sukhumatā cassa bhagavato [M 0.0191] appossukkatāvacanato, ariyena cakkhunā passitabbato ca veditabbā.

How then is the complete cessation of lust and so forth accomplished through Nibbāna here? Not so, because of the non-existence of past and future defilements now, and because they existed before, and because of the cessation of the present ones by their own nature. And how can there be no opportunity for the faults previously stated, if Nibbāna, which is of an insubstantial nature, were a cause? Not so, because it is of the nature of existence. For, with the preliminary practice directed towards Nibbāna, the arisen path, by its nature of not giving rise to latent tendencies, is itself the non-arising-cessation of defilements. By its arising, future defilements that could arise do not arise, just as the seed-nature is absent in a rice stalk that has arisen near a fire, due to the fire's sprout-preventing nature. Indeed, there is ultimately no such thing as non-existence that is produced by a cause; rather, it is the production of a state which is the arising of a moment opposed to it, like the production of the absence of the conditions for a pot. Therefore, Nibbāna is called 'the cessation without remainder' and so forth by way of figurative expression, because it is the decisive support for the Noble Path, which is designated as the cessation of the non-arising of defilements. Why then is it not described in terms of its own nature? Because of its extreme subtlety, because it has never been apprehended before, and because its subtlety is indicated by the Blessed One’s statement of disinclination, and because it is to be known only by the noble eye.

Ettha pana paravādī āha – “nattheva nibbānaṃ anupalabbhanīyato”ti. Na anupalabbhanīyaṃ tassa siddhattā. Upalabbhati hi taṃ tadanurūpapaṭipattiyā ariyehi. Apica nibbānaṃ natthīti na vattabbaṃ sabbasattānaṃ viruddhadhammānaṃ bhāvena apavaggābhāvappasaṅgato. Na ca taṃ yuttaṃ uṇhādipaṭipakkhassa sītādino viya bhavapaṭipakkhassa nibbānassapi avassaṃbhāvā. Vuttañca –

Here, however, another sectarian says, 'Nibbāna simply does not exist because it is unapprehendable.' It is not unapprehendable, for it is established. Indeed, the noble ones apprehend it through the appropriate practice. Moreover, one should not say that Nibbāna does not exist, because that would lead to the consequence of there being no release for all beings, given the existence of conflicting states. Nor is that reasonable, for just as cold must exist as the opposite of heat, so too Nibbāna must necessarily exist as the opposite of becoming. And it has been said:

“Yathāpi uṇhe vijjante, aparaṃ vijjati sītalaṃ;

Evaṃ tividhaggi vijjante, nibbānaṃ icchitabbaka”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.11) –

“Just as when heat exists, coolness is found, so too, when the threefold fire exists, Nibbāna is to be desired.”
