Ādi. Accantanirodhahetuno vipassanopadesassa dassanato ca attheva nibbānaṃ taṃ vinā tassāsambhavatoti vuttovāyamattho. Tadetaṃ purimāya koṭiyā abhāvato appabhavaṃ, tatova ajarāmaraṇaṃ, niccañca hotīti aṇuādīnampi niccabhāvapatti nibbānasseva niccattāti ce? Na, bhinnādhikaraṇattena hetulakkhaṇassānupapattito. Aṇuādīnampi asaṅkhatatā iti ce? Na, asaṅkhatatāsiddhito asaṅkhatānañcānekattānupapattito. Yadi hi asaṅkhataṃ nāma bhaveyya, ekeneva bhavitabbaṃ desakālasabhāvabhedassa kāraṇabhedakattā, bhinnasabhāvānampi ahetukatte atippasaṅgato.

And so forth. And because the instruction on insight, the cause of absolute cessation, is found, Nibbāna indeed exists; without it, that instruction would be impossible—this is the meaning conveyed. Since it has no prior limit, it is unoriginated; for that very reason, it is ageless and deathless, and it is permanent. If it is asked whether atoms and so forth also attain permanence, just as Nibbāna is permanent: No, because their basis is different, and because the characteristic of a cause is inapplicable. If it is asked whether atoms and so forth are also unconditioned: No, because their unconditioned nature is not established, and because a multiplicity of unconditioned things is untenable. For if there were such a thing as the unconditioned, it would have to be singular, since differences in location, time, and nature are due to a difference of cause; and if things of distinct natures were without cause, this would lead to an absurd consequence.

Saṅkhatehi sabhāvabhinnassa nibbānassa kathaṃ ahetukatāti ce? Asaṅkhatasabhāvena saṅkhatasabhāvehi bhinnassa kāraṇānapekkhattā. Asaṅkhatatte hi samāne bhavasabhāvabhedo [M 0.0192] kāraṇabhedaṃ sūcayati[V 0.0147], tasmā ekameva niccaṃ bhavitumarahati, tañca yathāvuttayuttito, sabbaññuvacanato ca paramatthato vijjamānaṃ nibbānameva. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ bhagavatā “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti (itivu. 43). Ayaṃ dukkhanirodhasacce nayo.

If it is asked how Nibbāna, being distinct in nature from conditioned things, can be without a cause: Because, being of an unconditioned nature and distinct from conditioned natures, it does not depend on causes. For, if things were the same in being unconditioned, a difference in their individual natures would indicate a difference in their causes. Therefore, only one thing can rightly be eternal, and that, according to the reasoning stated above and the words of the All-Knowing One, is Nibbāna itself, which exists in an ultimate sense. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned' (Itivuttaka 43). This is the method regarding the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

Itaraṃ pana “sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti uddisitvā vitthārato vibhattaṃ. Vinicchayo panettha maggaṅgavibhaṅge āvi bhavissatīti ayaṃ suttantabhājanīyanayo.

As for the other truth, it is indicated as 'right view... right concentration' and analyzed in detail. The detailed analysis here will become manifest in the Analysis of the Path Factors. This is the method of the Suttanta exposition.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana –

In the Abhidhamma exposition:

“Cattāri saccāni dukkhaṃ dukkhasamudayo dukkhanirodho dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Tattha taṇhā dukkhasamudayo. Avasesā sāsavadhammā…pe… dukkhaṃ. Taṇhāya pahānaṃ dukkhanirodho. Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti (vibha. 206) –

“The four truths are: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Here, craving is the origin of suffering. The remaining phenomena with taints... are suffering. The abandonment of craving is the cessation of suffering. The Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

Vatvā aṭṭha maggaṅgāni vitthārato niddisitvā “avasesā dhammā dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya sampayuttā”ti (vibha. 206 ādayo) evaṃ paṭhamavāre cattāri saccāni vibhattāni. Tāni puna aparehipi “taṇhā, avasesā ca kilesā samudayo, tathā taṇhā, avasesā ca kilesā, avasesā ca akusalā samudayo, tathā taṇhā, avasesā ca kilesā, avasesā ca akusalā, tīṇi ca kusalamūlāni, sāsavāni samudayo, tathā taṇhā, avasesā ca kilesā, avasesā ca akusalā, tīṇi ca kusalamūlāni, sāsavāni, avasesā ca sāsavakusaladhammā samudayo. Avasesā sāsavadhammā dukkhaṃ, tassa tassa samudayassa pahānaṃ nirodho, aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo paṭipadā”ti [M 0.0193] imehi vārehi vibhattāni. Tattha “ariyasaccānī”ti avatvā nippadesato paccayasaṅkhātaṃ samudayaṃ dassetuṃ “saccānī”ti vuttaṃ. Ariyasaccesu hi taṇhāva samudayo, na itare. Na ca kevalaṃ taṇhāva dukkhaṃ samudāneti, avasesā kusalākusalāpi paccayaṃ samudānentiyevāti tepi samudayato dassetuṃ “saccāni”tveva vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ yasmā aṭṭhaṅgiko maggova paṭipadāti. Sampayuttā pana phassādayo sabbepi dhammā paṭipadā eva, tasmā taṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ sabbasaṅgāhikavārepi sabbāni vibhattāni[V 0.0148]. Ettha hi ariyadhanāneva saṅgahitāni. Sesaṃ sadisamevāti ayaṃ abhidhammabhājanīyanayo.

Having pointed out the eight path factors in detail and having stated, 'The remaining phenomena are associated with the path leading to the cessation of suffering' (Vibh. 206 ff.), thus the four truths are analyzed in the first section. They are further analyzed in other sections as follows: 'Craving and the remaining defilements are the origin; likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, and the remaining unwholesome states are the origin; likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots that are with taints are the origin; likewise, craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots that are with taints, and the remaining wholesome phenomena that are with taints are the origin. The remaining phenomena with taints are suffering; the abandonment of each respective origin is cessation; the eightfold path is the path'—thus they are analyzed in these sections. Here, without saying 'Noble Truths,' the term 'truths' is used to show comprehensively the origin, which is designated as a condition. For in the Noble Truths, craving alone is the origin, not the other states. And not only does craving bring forth suffering—the remaining wholesome and unwholesome states also bring forth its condition—so to show them also as an origin, the term 'truths' is used. Furthermore, although only the eightfold path is the path, all associated phenomena such as contact, etc., are also the path. Therefore, to illustrate this principle, all are analyzed in the all-inclusive section. Here, only the noble states are included. The rest is similar. This is the method of the Abhidhamma exposition.

Pañhāpucchakanaye pana catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇā? Samudayasaccaṃ akusalaṃ, nirodhasaccaṃ abyākataṃ, dukkhasaccaṃ tidhāpi. Samudayo savitakkasavicāro, nirodho avitakkaavicāro, maggo tidhāpi, dukkhaṃ tidhāpi, na vattabbaṃ ca. Tīṇi saccāni anidassanaappaṭighāni, dukkhaṃ tidhāpi. Samudayo hetu, nirodho na hetu, sesā dvidhāpi. Dve saccāni lokiyāni, magganirodhā lokuttarā. Samudayasaccaṃ saraṇaṃ, dve saccāni araṇāni, dukkhaṃ duvidhāpi. Ayaṃ pañhāpucchakanayo. Idāni panettha –

In the method of questioning: Of the four noble truths, how many are wholesome... how many are taintless? The truth of origin is unwholesome, the truth of cessation is indeterminate, the truth of suffering is threefold. The origin is with applied and sustained thought; cessation is without applied and without sustained thought; the path is threefold; suffering is threefold and also not specifiable. Three truths are invisible and non-resistant; suffering is threefold. The origin is a cause; cessation is not a cause; the remaining two are twofold. Two truths are worldly; the path and cessation are supramundane. The truth of origin is with defilement; two truths are taintless; suffering is twofold. This is the method of questioning. Now here:

Kamatonūnādhikato, lakkhaṇādīhi suññato;

Ñāṇakiccopamā ñeyyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

The analysis freed from the Pāli text is to be known by way of sequence, deficiency, and excess; by voidness of characteristics and so forth; and by knowledge, function, and simile.

Tattha kamato tāva idhāpi desanākkamova yujjati. Ettha oḷārikattā, sabbasattasādhāraṇattā ca suviññeyyanti dukkhasaccaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ, tato tasseva hetudassanatthaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, tato “hetunirodhā bhavanirodho”ti ñāpanatthaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, tadadhigamupāyadassanatthaṃ ante maggasaccaṃ. Bhavasukhassādagadhitānaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ dukkhamāha, tato “bhavaṃ [M 0.0194] neva ahetukaṃ āgacchati, na issaranimmānādinā hoti, ito pana hotī”ti ñāpanatthaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, tato sahetukena dukkhena abhibhūtattā saṃviggamānasānaṃ tannissaraṇadassanena assāsajananatthaṃ nirodhaṃ, tato nirodhasampāpakaṃ magganti ayamettha kamo.

Here, first, the order of exposition is appropriate. Here, because it is gross, common to all beings, and thus easily understood, the truth of suffering is stated first; then, to show its cause, the truth of the origin; then, to make known that 'with the cessation of the cause there is the cessation of existence,' the truth of cessation; and at the end, to show the means of attaining that, the truth of the path. For those attached to the pleasure of existence, suffering is stated first to generate a sense of urgency; then, to make known that 'existence does not arise without a cause, nor does it arise from the creation of a supreme being, etc., but it arises from this,' the truth of origin; then, to give relief to those whose minds are agitated by being overwhelmed by suffering with a cause, by showing cessation as an escape from that; and finally, the path as the means to achieve cessation. This is the order here.

Anūnādhikato pana kasmā cattāri eva saccānīti ce? Tato aññassa asambhavato, aññatarassa ca anapaneyyato. Apica pavattimācikkhanto bhagavā sahetukaṃ ācikkhati, nivattiñca saupāyaṃ. Iti pavattinivattitadubhayahetūnaṃ etaparamato cattāri eva vuttānīti ayametthānūnādhikato.

Why, then, are there only four truths, neither more nor less? Because no other is possible, and none of these can be removed. Moreover, the Blessed One, in explaining occurrence, explains it with its cause, and cessation with its means. Thus, because these four are the ultimate in regard to occurrence, cessation, and their respective causes, only four are stated. This is why there are neither more nor less.

Lakkhaṇādīhi panettha lakkhaṇato bādhanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, santāpanarasaṃ, pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pabhavalakkhaṇaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, anupacchedakaraṇarasaṃ, palibodhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Santilakkhaṇaṃ [V 0.0149] nirodhasaccaṃ, accutirasaṃ, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ maggasaccaṃ, kilesapahānakaraṇarasaṃ, vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Apica pavattipavattakanivattinivattakalakkhaṇāni paṭipāṭiyā, tathā saṅkhatataṇhāasaṅkhatadassanalakkhaṇāni cāti imānettha lakkhaṇāni.

By way of characteristics, here the truth of suffering has the characteristic of affliction, its function is to scorch, and its manifestation is occurrence. The truth of origin has the characteristic of origination, its function is to not cut off, and its manifestation is impediment. The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace, its function is to not fall away, and its manifestation is signlessness. The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out, its function is to abandon defilements, and its manifestation is emergence. Furthermore, the characteristics of occurrence, causing occurrence, cessation, and causing cessation follow in sequence; and similarly, the characteristics of the conditioned, craving, the unconditioned, and seeing. These are the characteristics here.

Suññato panetāni yathākkamaṃ vedakakārakanibbutagamakābhāvato suññāni. Vuttañca –

By way of emptiness, these are empty in due order, being devoid of an experiencer, a doer, one who is extinguished, and one who goes. And it is said:

“Dukkhameva hi, na koci dukkhito,

Kārako na, kiriyāva vijjati;

Atthi nibbuti, na nibbuto pumā,

Maggamatthi, gamako na vijjatī”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 189);

“Suffering alone exists, but no sufferer is found; A doer is not, though action is found; Nibbāna exists, but no person who is extinguished; The path exists, but no traveler is found.”

Atha [M 0.0195] vā –

Or:

Dhuvasubhasukhattasuññaṃ,

Purimadvayamattasuññamamatapadaṃ;

Dhuvasubhasukhaattavirahito,

Maggo iti suññato tesu. (vibha. aṭṭha. 189);

“The first is empty of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self; the first two are empty of self, and the deathless state is empty of what pertains to self; the path is devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. Thus is the emptiness in them.”

Nirodhasuññāni vā tīṇi. Nirodho ca sesattayasuñño. Phalasuñño vā hettha hetu samudayamaggesu dukkhanirodhānaṃ abhāvā pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya. Hetusuññañca phalaṃ dukkhasamudayānaṃ, nirodhamaggānañca asamavāyā, na hetusamavetaṃ hetuphalaṃ. Hetuphalasamavāyavādīnaṃ dviaṇukādīni viyāti ayamettha suññatā.

Or, three truths are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the remaining three. Or, here, the cause is empty of the fruit, because suffering and cessation are absent in their causes, origin and path, just as for the proponents of primal nature, primal nature is empty of its manifestations. And the fruit is empty of the cause, because of the non-conjunction of suffering and origin with cessation and path, nor does the fruit of a cause inhere in the cause, unlike the dyads and so on of those who advocate for the conjunction of cause and fruit. This is the emptiness here.

Ñāṇakiccatoti ettha duvidhaṃ saccañāṇaṃ anubodhañāṇaṃ, paṭivedhañāṇañca. Tattha anubodhañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ, taṃ anussavādivasena nirodhe, magge ca pavattati. Paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, taṃ saccāvabodhapaṭipakkhakilese khepentaṃ nirodhamārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccato cattāripi saccāni paṭivijjhati. Yaṃ panetaṃ lokiyaṃ, tattha dukkhañāṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavanavasena pavattamānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ nivatteti, samudayañāṇaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ, nirodhañāṇaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiṃ, maggañāṇaṃ [V 0.0150] akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ. Dukkhañāṇaṃ vā tesu dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvarahitesu khandhesu dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasaññāsaṅkhātaṃ phale vippaṭipattiṃ, samudayañāṇaṃ “issarapadhānakālasabhāvādīhi loko pavattatī”ti akāraṇe kāraṇābhimānappavattaṃ hetumhi vippaṭipattiṃ, nirodhañāṇaṃ arūpalokādīsu apavaggaggāhabhūtaṃ nirodhe vippaṭipattiṃ, maggañāṇaṃ kāmasukhallikaattakilamathānuyogappabhede avisuddhimagge visuddhimaggaggāhavasena pavattaṃ upāye vippaṭipattiṃ nivatteti. Idamettha ñāṇakiccaṃ.

Regarding the function of knowledge, here there are two kinds of knowledge of the truths: knowledge of comprehension and knowledge of penetration. Among them, knowledge of comprehension is mundane; it occurs with regard to cessation and the path by way of tradition and so on. Knowledge of penetration is supramundane; dispelling the defilements that are contrary to the understanding of the truths, it takes cessation as its object and functionally penetrates all four truths. As for this mundane knowledge, knowledge of suffering, functioning by overcoming obsession, abandons the identity view; knowledge of origin abandons the annihilationist view; knowledge of cessation abandons the eternalist view; and knowledge of the path abandons the view of non-action. Or, knowledge of suffering abandons misapprehension regarding the fruit, which is the perception of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self in the aggregates that are devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. Knowledge of origin abandons misapprehension regarding the cause, which arises from the conceit of a cause in a non-cause, such as thinking 'the world proceeds from a supreme being, primal matter, time, intrinsic nature, etc.' Knowledge of cessation abandons misapprehension regarding cessation, which consists of grasping the formless realms and so on as liberation. Knowledge of the path abandons misapprehension regarding the means, which arises by grasping an impure path—divided into indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification—as the pure path. This is the function of knowledge here.

Upamāto [M 0.0196] panettha bhāro viya hi dukkhasaccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, bhārādānamiva samudayasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanamiva nirodhasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanupāyo viya maggasaccaṃ. Apica rogatannidānatadupasamabhesajjehi, orimatīramahoghapārimatīrataṃsampāpakopāyehi cāti evamādīhi yathākkamaṃ yojetvāpi etāni upamāto veditabbāni. Ayamettha upamā. Evaṃ ñeyyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

By way of simile, here the truth of suffering should be seen as a burden, the truth of origin as taking up the burden, the truth of cessation as laying down the burden, and the truth of the path as the means of laying down the burden. Furthermore, these should also be understood by applying in due order similes such as disease, its cause, its pacification, and the medicine; or this shore, the great flood, the far shore, and the means to reach it, and so on. This is the simile here. Thus, the analysis apart from the canonical text is to be understood.

Saccavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the matrix of the Analysis of the Truths is concluded.

Indriyavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of the Faculties

Indriyavibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – dvāvīsati indriyānīti ettha indriyaṭṭhasambhavato indriyāni. Ko panesa indriyaṭṭho nāmāti? Indaliṅgaṭṭho, indadesitaṭṭho, indadiṭṭhaṭṭho, indasiṭṭhaṭṭho, indajuṭṭhaṭṭho ca, so sabbopi idha yathāyogaṃ yujjati. Kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ indo nāma kammesu kassaci issariyābhāvato, tenevettha kammasañjanitāni tāva indriyāni attano janakakammaṃ ulliṅgenti, tena ca siṭṭhānīti indaliṅgaṭṭhena, indasiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Sammāsambuddho pana paramissariyabhāvato indo, tato sabbānipetāni indriyāni bhagavatā yathābhūtato pakāsitāni, abhisambuddhāni cāti indadesitaṭṭhena, indadiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Teneva bhagavatā kānici gocarāsevanāya, kānici bhāvanāsevanāya sevitānīti indajuṭṭhaṭṭhenapi indriyāni. Apica ādhipaccasaṅkhātena issariyaṭṭhenāpi etāni indriyāni.

In the matrix of the Analysis of the Faculties, first, as to the meaning of “twenty-two faculties”: they are called faculties because the meaning of 'indriya' is present. But what is this meaning of 'indriya'? It is the meaning of being indicated by an 'Inda,' declared by an 'Inda,' seen by an 'Inda,' fashioned by an 'Inda,' and frequented by an 'Inda'; all of these apply here as appropriate. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called 'Inda' because no one has lordship over kamma. Therefore, here, the faculties generated by kamma first indicate their originating kamma, and they are fashioned by it; thus they are 'indriyas' by the meaning of being indicated by an 'Inda' and fashioned by an 'Inda.' Moreover, the Perfectly Enlightened One is an 'Inda' due to his supreme lordship. Hence, all these faculties were declared by the Blessed One as they truly are and were fully comprehended by him; therefore, they are 'indriyas' by the meaning of being declared by an 'Inda' and seen by an 'Inda.' For that very reason, some faculties were frequented by the Blessed One by way of resorting to their domain, and some by way of resorting to development; thus, they are also 'indriyas' by the meaning of being frequented by an 'Inda.' Additionally, these are faculties by the meaning of sovereignty, in the sense of supremacy.

Cakkhundriyantiādīsu [V 0.0151] cakkhādīnaṃ padattho heṭṭhā pakāsito. Pacchimesu pana tīsu pubbabhāge anaññātaṃ amataṃ padaṃ, catusaccadhammaṃ vā jānissāmīti evaṃ paṭipannassa uppajjanato[M 0.0197], indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Ājānanato aññā eva indriyanti aññindriyaṃ. Aññātāvino catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitañāṇakiccassa khīṇāsavassa indriyanti aññātāvindriyaṃ. Tattha ca pasādindriyānantaraṃ cakkhuviññāṇādivīthicittappavattiyaṃ rūpādīnaṃ niyatabhāvassa, attano tikkhamandatānuvidhānassa ca āpādanato ādhipaccaṃ veditabbaṃ. Manindriyādīnaṃ pana attano attano vijānanādilakkhaṇe ādhipaccaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

In 'the eye faculty' and so on, the meaning of the terms 'eye' and so forth has been explained previously. In the last three, however, the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' arises in one who, in the preliminary stage, has undertaken to know the unknown, which is the deathless state or the Dhamma of the four truths; and because the meaning of 'indriya' is present, it is the 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty. Because of knowing, 'final knowledge' itself is the faculty; hence, it is the 'faculty of final knowledge.' For one who has known, an arahant whose task of knowledge in the four truths is completed and whose taints are destroyed, it is the 'faculty of one-who-has-known.' Therein, dominance should be understood with regard to the sense faculties, beginning with the eye, as the production of the fixed nature of their objects, such as form, and as conforming to their own sharpness or dullness in the cognitive process of eye-consciousness and so on, which occurs immediately after the sense faculty. For the mind faculty and others, however, dominance should be understood in their respective characteristics of cognizing and so forth. The rest is easily understood. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedato panettha jīvitindriyaṃ rūpārūpavasena dvidhā. Sukhindriyādīni pañca vedanābhāvato ekadhammo, tathā paññindriyādīni cattāri amohabhāvato. Sesāni pana indriyāni ekekadhammā evāti evaṃ paramatthato soḷasa dhammāva dvāvīsatindriyabhāvena desitāni. Sesāni panettha cetasikarūpanibbānāni asaṅgahitānīti ayaṃ dhammabhedo.

Regarding the division of phenomena here, the life faculty is twofold, by way of form and formless. The five faculties, beginning with the pleasure faculty, are a single phenomenon by virtue of being feeling. Similarly, the four faculties, beginning with the wisdom faculty, are a single phenomenon by virtue of being non-delusion. The remaining faculties, however, are each a single phenomenon. Thus, in ultimate reality, there are only sixteen phenomena, though they are taught as twenty-two faculties. The remaining phenomena here—mental factors, material phenomena, and Nibbāna—are not included. This is the division of phenomena.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīyaṃ nāma na gahitaṃ. Kasmā? Suttante imāya paṭipāṭiyā dvāvīsatiyā indriyānaṃ anāgatattā. Suttantasmiṃ hi katthaci dve indriyāni kathitāni, katthaci tīṇi, katthaci pañca, evaṃ pana nirantaraṃ dvāvīsati āgatāni nāma natthi. Abhidhammabhājanīyepi viseso natthi.

In the method of exposition, the Suttanta Exposition is not included here. Why? Because in the Suttanta, the twenty-two faculties do not appear in this sequence. In the Suttantas, sometimes two faculties are mentioned, sometimes three, sometimes five, but never continuously all twenty-two. There is also no distinction in the Abhidhamma Exposition.

Pañhāpucchakanaye pana dvāvīsatiyā indriyānaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇāti? Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ kusalaṃ, domanassindriyaṃ akusalaṃ, saddhāsatipaññāaññindriyāni cattāri kusalābyākatāni, manajīvitasomanassaupekkhāvīriyasamādhindriyāni cha tidhāpi, sesāni dasa abyākatāni. Cha indriyāni siyā sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, siyā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttāti, tīṇi tidhāpi, jīvitaṃ tidhā ca na vattabbañca, dvādasindriyāni na vattabbāni [M 0.0198] eva. Tīṇi vipākāni, dve vipākadhammadhammāni, rūpindriyāni satta nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammāni, aññindriyaṃ siyā vipākaṃ, siyā vipākadhammadhammaṃ, navindriyāni tidhāpi. Navindriyāni upādinnupādāniyāni, domanassindriyaṃ anupādinnupādāniyaṃ, tīṇi anupādinnaanupādāniyāni, nava tidhāpi. Domanassindriyaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ, upekkhindriyaṃ [V 0.0152] tathā ca avitakkaavicārañca, nava avitakkaavicārāni, ekādasa tidhāpi. Satta rūpindriyāni ceva sukhadukkhadomanassindriyāni cāti dasa parittāni, pacchimāni tīṇi appamāṇāni, sesāni nava tidhāva. Tattha ca somanassindriyaṃ rūpāvacaravaseneva mahaggataṃ, tadavasesāni arūpāvacaravasenāpīti veditabbaṃ. Pañcindriyāni anidassanasappaṭighāni, sattarasa anidassanaappaṭighāneva.

In the method of questioning, regarding the twenty-two faculties: how many are wholesome… how many are taintless? The 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' faculty is wholesome, the grief faculty is unwholesome, the faculties of faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and final knowledge are four that are wholesome or indeterminate, the faculties of mind, life, joy, equanimity, energy, and concentration are six that are threefold, and the remaining ten are indeterminate. Six faculties may be associated with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, three are threefold, the life faculty is threefold and also not to be stated, twelve faculties are not to be stated. Three are resultant, two are resultant-producing phenomena, the seven material faculties are neither resultant nor resultant-producing phenomena, the faculty of final knowledge may be resultant, or it may be a resultant-producing phenomenon, nine faculties are threefold. Nine faculties are clung to and clinging, the grief faculty is not clung to but clinging, three are neither clung to nor clinging, nine are threefold. The grief faculty is with applied and sustained thought, the equanimity faculty is likewise and also without applied and sustained thought, nine are without applied and sustained thought, eleven are threefold. The seven material faculties and the faculties of pleasure, pain, and grief—these ten are limited, the last three are immeasurable, the remaining nine are threefold. Among them, the joy faculty is sublime only in the form realm, the rest should be understood as sublime also in the formless realm. Five faculties are invisible and impingent, seventeen are invisible and non-impingent.

Paññindriyādīni cattāri hetū, sesā na hetū…pe… domanassindriyaṃ saraṇaṃ, manajīvitasomanassaupekkhāvīriyasamādhindriyāni dvidhāpi, sesāni pannarasa araṇānevāti ayaṃ pañhāpucchakanayo.

The wisdom faculty and the three others are roots, the rest are not roots... the grief faculty is tainted, the faculties of mind, life, joy, equanimity, energy, and concentration are in both ways, the remaining fifteen are taintless—this is the method of questioning.

Indriyesu panetesu, pāḷimuttavinicchayo;

Kamato dāni viññeyyo, tattha kosallamicchatā.

Now, regarding these faculties, the decision beyond the Pāḷi text; one should now understand them in sequence, desiring skill therein.

Kamatoti ayampi desanākkamova. Tattha ajjhattadhamme pariññāya ariyabhūmipaṭilābho hotīti attabhāvapariyāpannāni cakkhundriyādīni paṭhamaṃ desitāni. So manussattabhāvo yaṃ dhammaṃ upādāya “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā saṅkhaṃ gacchati, “ayaṃ so”ti nidassanatthaṃ tato itthindriyaṃ, purisindriyañca. So duvidhopi jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhavuttīti ñāpanatthaṃ tato jīvitindriyaṃ. Yāva tassa pavatti, tāva etesaṃ vedayitānaṃ anivatti. Yañca kiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ sukhaṃ dukkhanti ñāpanatthaṃ tato sukhindriyādīni. Tannirodhatthaṃ pana ete dhammā bhāvetabbāti paṭipattidassanatthaṃ tato saddhādīni. “Imāya paṭipattiyā esa dhammo paṭhamaṃ attani pātubhavatī”ti paṭipattiyā [M 0.0199] amoghabhāvadassanatthaṃ tato anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Tasseva phalattā, tato anantaraṃ bhāvetabbattā ca tato aññindriyaṃ. Ito paraṃ bhāvanāya imassa adhigamo, adhigate ca pana imasmiṃ natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti ñāpanatthaṃ ante paramassāsabhūtaṃ aññātāvindriyaṃ desitanti evaṃ kamato pāḷimuttavinicchayanayo viññeyyo.

This is also the sequence of exposition. Herein, the attainment of the noble stage comes about through the full understanding of internal phenomena; therefore, first, the faculties of the eye and so on, which pertain to one's own existence, are taught. That human existence, by virtue of which one is designated as 'woman' or 'man,' is indicated for the purpose of example by the feminine faculty and the masculine faculty. Since this twofold existence is bound up with the function of the life faculty, the life faculty is then taught to make this known. As long as its continuity lasts, so long do these feelings not cease. To make known that whatever is felt is all either pleasure or pain, the faculties of pleasure and so on are then taught. However, for their cessation, these phenomena must be developed; thus, to show the path of practice, the faculties of faith and so on are then taught. To show the unfailing nature of practice—'by this practice, this phenomenon first becomes manifest in oneself'—the faculty of 'I-shall-know-the-unknown' is then taught. Because the faculty of knowledge is the fruit of that and should be developed immediately after that, it is then taught. Beyond this, its attainment comes from development, and once this is attained, there is nothing further to be done; thus, the faculty of one-who-has-known, being the ultimate solace, is taught last. In this way, the method of determination beyond the Pāḷi text, in sequence, should be understood.

Indriyavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Exposition of the Faculties is concluded.

Paccayākāravibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of Dependent Arising

Paccayākāravibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0153] pana atthato tāva – avijjāpaccayātiādīsu avindiyaṃ kāyaduccaritādiṃ vindati paṭilabhati, vindiyaṃ vā kāyasucaritādiṃ na vindati, dhammānaṃ vā yathāsabhāvaṃ aviditaṃ karoti, antavirahite vā saṃsāre satte javāpeti, avijjamānesu vā javati, vijjamānesu vā na javatīti avijjā. Paṭicca phalameti etasmāti paccayo, dhammānaṃ uppattiyā, ṭhitiyā ca upakārako dhammo. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo, tasmā avijjāpaccayā. Saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti saṅkhārā.

Now, as to the meaning in the Matrix of the Analysis of the Mode of Conditions: in phrases such as 'conditioned by ignorance,' 'ignorance' means that one finds and obtains what should not be found, such as bodily misconduct, etc., or does not find what should be found, such as bodily good conduct, etc.; or it makes unknown the true nature of phenomena; or it propels beings in the endless cycle of existence; or it rushes towards what does not exist, or does not rush towards what exists. 'Condition' (paccayo) means that from which a result comes, a phenomenon that assists in the arising and persistence of phenomena. That ignorance is also a condition, thus 'ignorance-condition' (avijjāpaccayo); therefore, 'conditioned by ignorance' (avijjāpaccayā). 'They condition the conditioned'—thus, formations (saṅkhārā).

Ito paraṃ saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇantiādīsu vuttaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Avuttesu pana vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Namatīti nāmaṃ, ruppatīti rūpaṃ, nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpanti ekadesasarūpekasesanayena veditabbaṃ. Āye tanoti, āyatañca nayatīti āyatanaṃ, chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatananti ekasesanayena veditabbaṃ. Phusatīti phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Paritassatīti taṇhā. Upādiyatīti upādānaṃ. Bhavati, bhāvayati cāti bhavo. Jananaṃ jāti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā. Maranti etenāti [M 0.0200] maraṇaṃ. Socanaṃ soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhayati, uppādaṭṭhitivasena dvidhā khaṇatītipi dukkhaṃ. Dummanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso. Sambhavantīti nibbattanti. Na kevalañca sokādīheva, atha kho avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantītiādinā sabbapadehipi sambhavanti-saddassa yojanā kātabbā. Evaṃ hi paccayapaccayuppannavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

Henceforth, what is stated in 'conditioned by formations, consciousness,' etc., should be understood in the manner already explained. As for what is not stated, 'consciousness' (viññāṇaṃ) means 'that which cognizes.' 'Name' (nāmaṃ) means 'that which bends,' and 'material form' (rūpaṃ) means 'that which is afflicted.' 'Name and material form' (nāmarūpaṃ) should be understood by way of the figure of speech of retaining a single form from a part. 'Sense base' (āyatanaṃ) means 'that which extends' and 'that which leads to extension.' 'The sixth sense base' (chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ) and 'the six sense bases' (saḷāyatanaṃ) should be understood by way of the figure of speech of retaining a single form. 'Contact' (phasso) means 'that which contacts.' 'Feeling' (vedanā) means 'that which feels.' 'Craving' (taṇhā) means 'that which thirsts.' 'Clinging' (upādānaṃ) means 'that which clings.' 'Existence' (bhavo) means 'that which becomes' and 'that which causes to become.' 'Birth' (jāti) means 'generating.' 'Aging' (jarā) means 'decaying.' 'Death' (maraṇaṃ) means 'that by which one dies.' 'Sorrow' (soko) means 'sorrowing.' 'Lamentation' (paridevo) means 'lamenting.' 'Suffering' (dukkhaṃ) means 'that which afflicts,' and also 'that which excavates' in two ways: by way of arising and by way of persistence. 'Mental distress' (domanassaṃ) means 'the state of mental distress.' 'Anguish' (upāyāso) means 'intense anguish.' 'They originate' (sambhavanti) means 'they come into being.' And not only with sorrow and the like, but also with 'conditioned by ignorance, formations arise,' etc.—the word 'sambhavanti' should be applied to all terms. In this way, the analysis of conditions and their resultant phenomena is accomplished.

Evanti niddiṭṭhanayanidassanaṃ, tena avijjādīheva kāraṇehi, na issaranimmānādīhīti dasseti. Etassāti yathāvuttassa. Kevalassāti asammissassa, sakalassa vā, dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkhasamūhassa, na sattassa, na sukhasubhādīnaṃ. Samudayoti nibbatti, hotīti sambhavati. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

'Thus' (evaṃ) is a demonstration of the method as pointed out, thereby showing that it is caused by ignorance and so on, not by creation by a lord, etc. 'Of this' (etassa) refers to what has been stated. 'Of the whole' (kevalassa) means of the unmixed, or of the entire. 'Mass of suffering' (dukkhakkhandhassa) means a heap of suffering, not of a being, nor of pleasure, beauty, and so on. 'Origin' (samudayo) means arising; 'comes to be' (hoti) means comes into being. This, then, is the meaning of the words here.

Dhammabhedato panettha avijjāti suttantapariyāyena dukkhādīsu catūsu, abhidhammapariyāyena pubbantādīhi saddhiṃ aṭṭhasu vā ṭhānesu aññāṇaṃ. Saṅkhārā pana puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā tayo, kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārā tayo cāti chabbidhā. Tattha aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā, pañca rūpāvacarakusalacetanā [V 0.0154] ceti terasa cetanā puññābhisaṅkhāro nāma. Dvādasa akusalacetanā apuññābhisaṅkhāro nāma. Catasso arūpāvacarakusalacetanā āneñjābhisaṅkhāro nāma. Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ eva dvārato pavattidassanatthaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhārādittiko vutto.

As for the classification of phenomena here, 'ignorance' (avijjā) is non-knowledge in four instances, such as in suffering, according to the Suttanta method, or in eight instances, including the past, etc., according to the Abhidhamma method. Formations (saṅkhārā), however, are of six kinds: the three formations of merit, demerit, and imperturbability; and the three formations of body, speech, and mind. Among these, thirteen volitions—eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and five wholesome volitions of the form-sphere—are called the meritorious formation. Twelve unwholesome volitions are called the demeritorious formation. Four wholesome volitions of the formless-sphere are called the imperturbable formation. This triad of formations is stated to show the occurrence of these three formations through their respective doors.

Aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā ceva dvādasākusalacetanā ca kāyadvāre pavattiyaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīdvāre pavattiyaṃ vacīsaṅkhāro, etā ceva manodvāre pavattiyaṃ, manodvāre eva pavattanakā rūpārūpakusalacetanā ca cittasaṅkhāroti vuccanti. Abhiññācetanā, panettha uddhaccacetanā ca parato paṭisandhiviññāṇapaccayabhāve apanetabbāpi [M 0.0201] avijjāpaccayā sambhavato idha gahetabbāvāti ayaṃ tiko purimattikameva pavisatīti atthato lokiyakusalākusalacetanāva avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti veditabbaṃ. Idañca suttantabhājanīyanayena, abhidhammabhājanīyanayena pana lokiyalokuttare ekekacittakkhaṇe dvādasaṅgassa paṭiccasamuppādassa gahaṇato sabbāpi cetanā saṅkhārāti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ viññāṇanāmarūpādīsupi sabbacittasampayuttavasena ca dhammabhedo veditabbo. Suttantabhājanīyanayeneva pana dassayissāma.

The eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and the twelve unwholesome volitions, when occurring through the body door, are called bodily formations; when occurring through the speech door, they are called verbal formations; and these same, when occurring through the mind door, along with the wholesome volitions pertaining to form and formlessness that occur exclusively through the mind door, are called mental formations. Here, the volition of higher knowledge (abhiññācetanā) and the volition of restlessness (uddhaccacetanā), though they should be excluded later from being conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness, are to be included here because they arise conditioned by ignorance. Thus, this triad is included in the previous triad, and essentially, only mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions are to be understood as formations conditioned by ignorance. This is according to the Suttanta method. However, according to the Abhidhamma method, since the twelve links of dependent origination are included in each moment of consciousness, whether mundane or supramundane, all volitions are to be understood as formations. Similarly, the distinctions among consciousness, name-and-form, and the other factors are to be understood in terms of their association with all types of consciousness. Nevertheless, we will present this according to the Suttanta method.

Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇañca cakkhuviññāṇādichabbidhaṃ bāttiṃsalokiyavipākaviññāṇameva hoti, lokuttarāni pana vaṭṭakathāya na yujjantīti na gahitāni. Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ pana sabbalokiyaviññāṇasampayuttā tayo arūpino khandhā. Rūpaṃ sabbāni bhūtupādāyarūpāni. Saḷāyatanaṃ manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni. Phasso cakkhusamphassādiko chavipākaphasso, tathā vedanāpi. Taṇhā rūpataṇhādibhedato chabbidho lobho. Upādānaṃ kāmupādānādito catubbidhā lobhadiṭṭhiyova. Bhavo pana duvidho kammabhavo, upapattibhavoti. Tattha kammabhavo tebhūmakakusalākusalacetanā ca taṃsampayuttā abhijjhādayo ca. Upapattibhavo pana kammābhinibbattā pañcapi khandhā. So pabhedato kāmarūpārūpabhavā tayo, saññā asaññā nevasaññānāsaññā bhavā tayo, ekacatupañcavokārabhavā tayoti navavidho niddiṭṭho. Jātiādīni pubbe vuttāni. Tesu jātiggahaṇena viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanāva gahitā tadavinābhāvato. Tathā jarāmaraṇaggahaṇenāpi tesaññeva pākabhedattā. Sokādayo pana jarāmaraṇena dvādasamena aṅgena ekasaṅkhepaṃ katvā vuttā, na visuṃ aṅgabhāvena. Kimatthanti ce? Bhavacakkassa avicchedadassanatthaṃ. Sokādito [M 0.0202] hi avijjā siddhā hoti avijjāvippayogato[V 0.0155], avijjāsamuppattito ca. Jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa hi bālasseva te sambhavanti, tehi ca avijjāya siddhāya puna avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti evaṃ hetuphalaparamparāya bhavacakkaṃ avicchinnaṃ, anādikaṃ, apariyantaṃ, apariyosānañca hoti.

Conditioned by formations, consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) is indeed the sixfold mundane resultant consciousness, such as eye-consciousness, etc., totaling thirty-two types. Supramundane consciousness, however, is not included here, as it is not relevant to the discussion of the cycle of existence. Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpaṃ) refers to the three immaterial aggregates associated with all mundane consciousness, and material form (rūpaṃ) refers to all primary elements and derived material forms. The six sense bases (saḷāyatanaṃ) are the faculties with the mind as the sixth. Contact (phasso) is the sixfold resultant contact, such as eye-contact, etc.; similarly, feeling (vedanā) also. Craving (taṇhā) is sixfold greed, differentiated as craving for forms, etc. Clinging (upādānaṃ) is indeed fourfold greed and wrong view, such as sensual clinging, etc. Existence (bhavo), however, is twofold: kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Among these, kamma-existence consists of wholesome and unwholesome volitions pertaining to the three realms, along with associated mental factors like covetousness, etc. Rebirth-existence consists of the five aggregates produced by kamma. It is further classified into nine types: the three existences of the sensual, form, and formless realms; the three existences of percipient, non-percipient, and neither percipient nor non-percipient; and the three existences of one, four, or five aggregates. Birth and the others have been previously explained. Among these, by the inclusion of birth, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are implicitly included due to their inseparability. Similarly, by the inclusion of aging and death, the same are implied, as they are variations in the ripening of those same aggregates. Sorrow and the others, however, are stated by way of a single summary under the twelfth link, aging-and-death, and not as separate links. If it is asked 'For what purpose?', it is to demonstrate the unbroken continuity of the cycle of existence. For from sorrow and the like, ignorance is established, both by its absence when ignorance is abandoned and by its arising when ignorance is present. Indeed, for a fool struck by aging and death, these arise; and when ignorance is thereby established, the cycle continues: 'conditioned by ignorance, formations arise,' etc. Thus, the cycle of existence, by this succession of causes and effects, is unbroken, beginningless, endless, and without conclusion.

Yadi evaṃ, kasmā avijjā ādito vuttāti? Padhānadassanatthaṃ pana ādito vuttā. Tiṇṇaṃ hi vaṭṭānaṃ avijjā padhāno hetu tassā bhāve bhāvato, nirodhena ca nirujjhanato. Evaṃ avijjādīhi dvādasahi aṅgehi suttantabhājanīyanayena sabbe lokiyadhammāva paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena vuttāti veditabbā. Abhidhammapariyāyena pana lokuttarāpīti ayamettha dhammabhedo.

If so, why is ignorance mentioned first? It is mentioned first, however, for the purpose of showing its preeminence. For ignorance is the primary cause of the three rounds of existence—by its presence, they come into being, and by its cessation, they cease. Thus, it should be understood that all mundane phenomena are described in terms of conditionality and conditioned arising through these twelve factors beginning with ignorance, according to the method of the Suttanta exposition. However, according to the Abhidhamma method, even the supramundane is included—this is the distinction in the teaching here.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha pañhāpucchakanayo natthi, suttantabhājanīyanayāpi dhammabhede vuttanayeneva vitthārato vibhattāti veditabbo. Abhidhammabhājanīye pana –

In this method of analysis, there is no approach of asking questions. And it should be understood that the Suttanta exposition is also analyzed in detail in the same way as was stated in the classification of phenomena. But in the Abhidhamma exposition—

“Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmaṃ, nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ, chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jāti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

‘Conditioned by ignorance, formations arise; conditioned by formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name arises; conditioned by name, the sixth sense base arises; conditioned by the sixth sense base, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; conditioned by birth, aging and death arise. Thus arises this entire mass of suffering.’

“Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro…pe… viññāṇapaccayā nāmaṃ, nāmapaccayā phasso…pe… samudayo hoti.

‘Conditioned by ignorance, formations arise…conditioned by consciousness, name arises; conditioned by name, contact arises…thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.’

“Avijjāpaccayā…pe… viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ, chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso…pe… samudayo hoti.

‘Conditioned by ignorance…conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises; conditioned by name-and-form, the sixth sense base arises; conditioned by the sixth sense base, contact arises…thus arises this entire mass of suffering.’

“Avijjāpaccayā [M 0.0203] …pe… viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso…pe… samudayo hotī”ti (vibha. 243) –

‘Conditioned by ignorance…conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the sixth sense base, contact arises…thus arises this entire mass of suffering.’ (Vibh. 243)

Evaṃ paccayacatukkaṃ, puna “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro avijjāhetuko”tiādinā (vibha. 244) vuttanayeneva [V 0.0156] hetucatukkaṃ, puna “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro avijjāsampayutto”tiādinā (vibha. 245) sampayuttacatukkaṃ, puna “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro, saṅkhārapaccayāpi avijjā”tiādinā (vibha. 246) aññamaññapaccayacatukkanti evaṃ avijjāmūlakāni cattāri catukkāni vuttāni. Evaṃ “saṅkhārapaccayā avijjā”tiādinā saṅkhārādimūlakādiupādānamūlakapariyosānāni aṭṭhasu padesu cattāri cattāri catukkānīti bāttiṃsa catukkāni mātikaṃ katvā nikkhipitvā puna akusalakusalavipākakiriyacittesu lokiyalokuttaresu ekekasmiṃ citte yathānikkhittehi chattiṃsabāttiṃsamātikācatukkehi vitthārato yathānurūpaṃ paccayākāro vibhatto. Idañca yasmā na kevalaṃ ayaṃ paccayākāro nānācittesu eva hoti, ekacittepi hotiyeva. Nāpi vaṭṭacitte eva hoti, taṇhābhāvato vivaṭṭacittepi, tasmā taṃ nippadesato ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ paccayākāraṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva hettha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti avatvā “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”ti ekavacanena vuttaṃ ekacittakkhaṇe bahucetanābhāvā. Tattha yadetaṃ paṭhamacatukkaṃ, tattha paṭhamavāro nāmarūpaṭṭhāne nāmaṃ, saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne chaṭṭhāyatanañca gahetvā rūpārūpādisabbabhavasādhāraṇavasena, ekacittakkhaṇapariyāpannadhammaggahaṇavasena ca rūpaṃ chaḍḍetvā vutto rūpassa sabbabhavāsādhāraṇattā, bahucittakkhaṇikattā ca. Dutiyo nāmarūpaṭṭhāne nāmaṃ, “nāmapaccayā phasso”ti saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne phassameva [M 0.0204] gahetvā phassassa saḷāyatanaṃ vināpi paccayavisesasambhavadassanavasena ceva mahānidānasuttanayadassanavasena (dī. ni. 2.95 ādayo) ca vutto. Tatiyo saḷāyatanaṭṭhāne chaṭṭhāyatanameva gahetvā gabbhaseyyakānaṃ aparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ, rūpabhavikādīnañca vasena vutto. Catuttho “nāmapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti evaṃ itarāyatanehipi saḷāyatanassa visesato phassapaccayataṃva dassetvā opapātikānaṃ, paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ kāmabhavikānañca vasena vutto. Evaṃ dutiyacatukkādīsupi.

Thus, the fourfold condition; again, the fourfold cause, beginning with 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formation is with ignorance as cause,' etc., as stated in the Vibhaṅga (244); again, the fourfold association, beginning with 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formation is associated with ignorance,' etc., as stated in the Vibhaṅga (245); again, the fourfold mutual condition, beginning with 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formation; and with volitional formation as condition, ignorance,' etc., as stated in the Vibhaṅga (246). In this way, four sets of four, rooted in ignorance, are explained. Similarly, beginning with 'with volitional formation as condition, ignorance,' etc., up to clinging as the final root, four sets of four are explained in eight sections, making thirty-two sets of four. Having laid out this matrix, the mode of conditions is analyzed in detail according to the appropriate method, using the thirty-six and thirty-two fourfold sets of the matrix in each mundane and supramundane consciousness, whether unwholesome, wholesome, resultant, or functional. And this is because this mode of conditions is not only found in various types of consciousness but also in a single moment of consciousness. Nor is it limited to consciousness in the round of existence; due to the absence of craving, it is also found in consciousness that unrolls the round. Therefore, it is explained here to show completely the momentary mode of conditions in a single consciousness. For this reason, instead of saying 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' it is stated in the singular, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formation,' because in a single moment of consciousness, there is no multiplicity of volitions. Here, in the first set of four, the first instance refers to name at the stage of name-and-form, and the sixth sense base at the stage of the sixfold sense base, encompassing all realms, both material and immaterial, and so on, as common to all existence, and referring to phenomena included in a single moment of consciousness. Form is excluded because it is not common to all existences and lasts for many mind-moments. The second instance refers to name at the stage of name-and-form, and taking only contact, 'with name as condition, contact,' at the stage of the sixfold sense base, to show the possibility of a special conditionality of contact even without the six sense bases, following the method of the Great Discourse on Causation (Dīgha Nikāya 2.95, etc.). The third instance refers only to the sixth sense base at the stage of the sixfold sense base, explaining it in relation to beings in the womb with incomplete sense bases and for those in the realm of form and so on. The fourth instance states, 'with name as condition, the sixfold sense base; with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact,' thus showing the specific conditionality of contact through the six sense bases even with respect to other sense bases, explaining it in relation to spontaneously born beings, those with complete sense bases, and those in the sensual realm. Similarly for the second set of four and so on.

Sabbatthāpi cettha yasmā sokādayo sabbe ekacittakkhaṇe na sambhavanti, sabbasmiñca citte, bhave ca nappavattanti, tasmā na gahitā. Jātijarāmaraṇāni panettha arūpadhammānaṃ lakkhaṇamattāni, tāni ca acittakkhaṇamattānipi samānāni cittakkhaṇe antogadhattā pariyāyato paccayuppanne katvā aṅgaparipūraṇatthaṃ gahitāni. Bhavoti cettha upādānādipaccayavirahitā cattāro arūpino khandhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānanti ettha kāmupādānaṃ vajjetvā tīṇi upādānāni eva gahetabbāni[V 0.0157]. Dvinnampi ekalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekakkhaṇe asambhavā lobhamūlavirahitesu dosamohamūlesu ceva kusalābyākatesu ca cittesu vedanāpaccayā paṭighaṃ vicikicchā uddhaccanti evaṃ taṇhāṭhāne yathāyogaṃ paṭighādayo tayo. Tesu vicikicchāvajjitesu ceva diṭṭhivippayuttesu ca upādānaṭṭhāne adhimokkho gahito. Vicikicchāya pana saddhiṃ adhimokkhassāpi asambhavā vicikicchāpaccayā bhavoti ca gahito. Upādānaṭṭhāne ca adhimokkho ca gahito. Lokiyānañcettha kusalābyākatānaṃ upanissayavasena avijjāpaccayatā vuttā. Lokuttarānaṃ pana yasmā appahīnāvijjo avijjāya pahānatthaṃ, paṭippassambhanatthañca lokuttaraṃ [M 0.0205] bhāveti, tasmā samatikkamanavasena avijjāpaccayatā vuttā, na sahajātavasena. Teneva tesaṃ niddesavāresu “tattha katamā avijjā”ti avibhajitvā “tattha katamo avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”ti (vibha. 240) vibhattaṃ. Kiriyadhammānaṃ pana kenaci pariyāyena avijjāmūlakattaṃ natthīti “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”ntiādinā saṅkhāramūlakādiko nayo vutto, na avijjāmūlako. Apica lokiyakusalādīsu tesaṃ dhammānaṃ dukkhasaccapariyāpannattā “evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti (vibha. 225) evaṃ appanā katā, lokuttarakusalādīsu “evametesaṃ dhammāna”nti. Ayaṃ lokiyato lokuttarānaṃ desanāya visesoti ayaṃ abhidhammabhājanīye nayo.

In all cases here, because sorrow and the like do not all arise in a single mind-moment, nor do they occur in every consciousness or in every becoming, they are not included. Birth, aging, and death here are merely the characteristics of formless phenomena, and even though they are not just a single mind-moment, they are included by way of being encompassed within a mind-moment, having been treated figuratively as conditionally arisen for the purpose of completing the factors. Here, 'becoming' refers to the four formless aggregates devoid of conditions such as clinging. In 'craving as a condition for clinging,' here, excepting sensual clinging, the other three types of clinging should be taken. Due to the impossibility of two phenomena with the same characteristic arising in a single moment—in mind-states devoid of greed-roots, that is, in those rooted in hatred and delusion, and in wholesome and indeterminate states—feeling as a condition gives rise to aversion, doubt, and restlessness. Thus, in place of craving, aversion and the other two arise as appropriate. Among these, in those without doubt and dissociated from wrong view, determination is taken in the place of clinging. But since determination cannot arise together with doubt, 'becoming is conditioned by doubt' is also taken. And determination is taken in the place of clinging. For worldly wholesome and indeterminate states, their conditionality by ignorance is stated by way of decisive support. For supramundane states, however, because one whose ignorance is not yet abandoned cultivates the supramundane for the purpose of abandoning and calming ignorance, their conditionality by ignorance is stated by way of transcending, not by way of co-nascence. For this reason, in the sections of exposition, without analyzing 'what is ignorance here,' it is analyzed as 'what here is the volitional formation conditioned by ignorance?' (Vibh. 240). As for functional phenomena, since they are in no way rooted in ignorance, the method beginning with volitional formation as root is stated, in phrases like 'volitional formation as a condition for consciousness,' not the method with ignorance as root. Furthermore, because these phenomena in worldly wholesome and indeterminate states are included in the truth of suffering, the application is made as 'Thus arises this entire mass of suffering' (Vibha. 225). For supramundane wholesome states, it is 'Thus for these phenomena.' This is the distinction in the teaching between the worldly and the supramundane; this is the method in the Abhidhamma analysis.

Idāni paccayanayā, kārakādīhi suññato;

Mūladdhasandhisaṅkhepākāravaṭṭavibhāgato.

Now, from the way of conditions, from being empty of an agent and so on; from the root, the time-period, the connection, the summary, the mode, the round, and the division.

Vāraṇopamatopettha, gambhīranayabhedato;

Yathārahaṃ vijānīyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

Here, from the simile of the elephant and from the distinction of profound methods, the analysis beyond the Pāli text should be understood as is appropriate.

Tattha paccayanayo sāmaññato, visesato cāti duvidho hoti. Tattha tabbhāvabhāvimattatāpakāsako sāmaññato paccayanayo. Visesato pana paṭṭhāne āgatesu hetupaccayādicatuvīsatiyā paccayesu yathānurūpaṃ paccayavisesuppannamattatāpakāsako. Sā ca nesaṃ catuvīsatiyā paccayānaṃ vibhāgatā paṭṭhānamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanāya āvi bhavissati. Tattha sāmaññato saṅkhārādayo avijjādipaccayabhāve eva bhāvinoti veditabbā. Yassa hi catūsu saccesu, pubbantādīsu ca avijjā appahīnā hoti, so dukkhe tāva pubbantādīsu ca aññāṇena [V 0.0158] tīsu [M 0.0206] bhavesu jātijarārogamaraṇādianekādīnavavokiṇṇaṃ puññaphalasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhaṃ dukkhato ajānanto sukhasaññāya patthetvā tīhi dvārehi puññāneñjābhisaṅkhāre ārabhati. Samudaye aññāṇena dukkhahetubhūtesupi taṇhāparikkhāresu dukkhahetukaṃ āpāyikādidukkhaṃ, dukkhahetubhūtesu kāmūpasevanādīsu ca ādīnavaṃ apassanto sukhahetusaññāya ceva kilesābhibhūtatāya ca tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati. Nirodhe, pana magge ca aññāṇena anirodhabhūte gativisese nirodhasaññī, nirodhassa ca vā amaggabhūtesupi yaññāmaratapādīsupi nirodhamaggasaññī hutvā tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇena “ahetū appaccayā sattā uppajjanti, na honti paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā “attāva jānāti vā na jānāti vā, sova saṅkhāre saṅkharoti, sova paṭisandhiyaṃ uppajjati, tassa aṇuissarādayo kalalādibhāvena sarīraṃ saṇṭhāpentā indriyāni sampādenti, sova indriyasampanno phusati, vedayati, taṇhiyati, upādānādīni ca karotī”ti vā “sabbe sattā niyatisaṅgatibhavapariṇatā”ti vā vikappeti. So evaṃ avijjāya andhīkato –

Herein, the method of conditions is twofold: general and specific. The general method of conditions reveals merely that something comes to be when that is present. The specific method, however, reveals merely that something is produced by a specific condition, as is appropriate among the twenty-four conditions, beginning with the root condition, taught in the Paṭṭhāna. The detailed classification of these twenty-four conditions will become clear in the exposition of the meaning of the Paṭṭhāna matrix. Herein, it should be understood that formations and so on come to be only when conditioned by ignorance and so forth. For one whose ignorance regarding the four truths, the past end, and so on, has not been abandoned, does not know as suffering the suffering due to the alteration of formations—which is designated as the fruit of merit and is fraught with many dangers such as birth, aging, sickness, and death in the three realms. Instead, perceiving it as happiness, they aspire to it and engage in meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations through the three doors. Through ignorance of the origin, not seeing the suffering of the lower realms, which has suffering as its cause, in the accessories of craving, which are causes of suffering, nor the danger in indulging in sensual pleasures and so on, which are also causes of suffering, and perceiving these as sources of happiness while being overcome by defilements, they engage in all three kinds of formations. Through ignorance of cessation and the path, perceiving as cessation a particular state of existence that is not cessation, and perceiving as the path to cessation practices that are not the path, such as sacrifices and asceticism, they engage in all three kinds of formations. Through ignorance regarding phenomena arisen by specific conditionality and dependent origination, they misconceive: 'Beings arise without cause or condition; they do not exist after death,' or 'The self knows or does not know; it is the self that fabricates formations, it is the self that arises at rebirth-linking; for it, atoms, Isvara, and so on, establish the body in stages like the embryo and perfect the faculties; endowed with faculties, it is the self that makes contact, feels, craves, and performs clinging and so on,' or 'All beings are determined by fate, by association, or by transformation.' Thus blinded by ignorance—

“Yathāpi nāma jaccandho, naro apariṇāyako;

Ekadā yāti maggena, ummaggenāpi ekadā.

Just as a man born blind, without a guide, sometimes goes by the path, and sometimes by a false path.

“Saṃsāre saṃsaraṃ bālo, tathā apariṇāyako;

Karoti ekadā puññaṃ, apuññamapi ekadā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅgārapadaniddesa) –

“So too the fool wandering in saṃsāra, without a guide; sometimes he performs merit, and sometimes demerit.”

Vuttanayena tividhe saṅkhāre abhisaṅkharotīti. Kiṃ panettha ekāva avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, nanu ekasmā [M 0.0207] kāraṇā ekaṃva kāriyaṃ uppajjati, anekaṃ kāriyaṃ na uppajjati, anekasmā vā ekanti, anekasmā kāraṇā anekaṃ kāriyaṃ uppajjatīti? Saccaṃ, padhānattapākaṭattaasādhāraṇattadīpanatthaṃ panettha anekesu kāraṇesupi ekā avijjā eva paccayabhāvena niddiṭṭhā “phassapaccayā vedanā (udā. 3), semhasamuṭṭhānā ābādhā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 10.60; mahāni. 5; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128) viya. Avijjā hi padhāno hetu, saṅkhārānaṃ pākaṭo, asādhāraṇo ca taṇhādihetūnampi hetuttā, na vatthārammaṇādīni [V 0.0159] khīṇāsavassa tesaṃ sambhavepi saṅkhārānaṃ abhāvāti. Evaṃ tāvettha vaṭṭasaṅkhārānaṃ avijjāya eva bhāve bhāvo veditabbo. Tathā viññāṇassāpi upacitakammābhāve abhāvato, sabbattha sabbesañca sabbavipākaviññāṇuppattippasaṅgato ca saṅkhārānaṃ eva bhāve bhāvo veditabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ uparipi nāmarūpādīnaṃ viññāṇādibhāve bhāvo yathānurūpaṃ anubhavayuttīhi ñātabboti ayaṃ sāmaññato paccayanayo.

According to the stated method, one fabricates the threefold formations. But here, is ignorance alone the condition for formations? Is it not that from a single cause only a single effect arises, not multiple effects; or from multiple causes, a single effect; or from multiple causes, multiple effects? True, but here, even among multiple causes, ignorance alone is shown as the condition in order to emphasize its prominence, its manifest nature, and its uncommonness—just as in statements such as “feeling is conditioned by contact” and “illnesses arise from phlegm.” For ignorance is the primary cause, the most evident, and an uncommon cause of formations, being a cause even for craving and other causes; base, object, and so on are not such, for even when these exist for one whose taints are destroyed, formations do not arise. Thus, here it should be understood that the formations of the round of existence exist precisely because of the presence of ignorance. Similarly, since consciousness does not arise without accumulated kamma, and to avoid the consequence that all resultant consciousness would arise everywhere for everyone, it should be understood that consciousness exists precisely because of the presence of formations. Just as it is here, so too in what follows—the existence of name-and-form, etc., should be understood as dependent on consciousness, etc., in accordance with what is appropriate, by means of experience and reasoning. This is the general method of conditions.

Visesato pana avijjā puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ tāva ārammaṇapaccayena, upanissayapaccayena cāti dvidhā paccayo hoti. Sā hi avijjaṃ ārabbha sammasanādivasena uppattiyaṃ kāmāvacarānaṃ, abhiññācittena samohacittassa jānanakāle rūpāvacarānañca puññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ tāva ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo hoti, avijjāsamatikkamanatthāya pana avijjāsammūḷhatāya kāmarūpabhavasampattiyo patthetvāva kāmarūpāvacarapuññāni karontassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo hoti. Apuññābhisaṅkhārānaṃ panesā avijjaṃ ārabbha rāgādīnaṃ uppajjanakāle ārammaṇādipaccayena avijjāsammūḷhatāya pāṇātipātādīni karontassa nissayapaccayena, dutiyajavanādīnaṃ [M 0.0208] anantarūpanissayāsevananatthivigatapaccayehi yaṃ kiñci akusalaṃ karontassa hetusahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayehīti evaṃ anekadhā paccayo hoti, āneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ pana ekena upanissayapaccayeneva paccayo hoti.

Specifically, ignorance serves as a condition for meritorious formations in two ways: as an object condition and as a decisive support condition. For it acts as an object condition for meritorious formations of the sense-sphere when they arise by way of contemplation, etc., taking ignorance as their object; and for meritorious formations of the form-sphere when a mind of direct knowledge knows a mind associated with delusion. However, for one who, for the sake of overcoming ignorance, yet being deluded by ignorance, aspires to attainments in the sense-sphere and form-sphere and performs meritorious deeds of those spheres, it serves as a decisive support condition. As for demeritorious formations, it becomes a condition in various ways: as an object condition, etc., when lust and other defilements arise taking ignorance as their object; as a support condition for one who, being deluded by ignorance, kills living beings, etc.; for one performing any unwholesome act, it is a condition for the second impulsion onwards by way of immediately proximate, decisive support, repetition, absence, and non-disappearance conditions; and it is a condition by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. For imperturbable formations, however, it serves as a condition solely through the decisive support condition.

Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇapade pana tayopi saṅkhārā viññāṇassa yathārahaṃ tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhipavattīsu kammapaccayena ceva upanissayapaccayena cāti dvidhā paccayā honti. Abhidhammabhājanīyanayena sahajātassa viññāṇassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttakammatthiavigatādipaccayehi paccayā honti.

In the phrase 'consciousness is conditioned by formations,' all three kinds of formations serve as conditions for consciousness, as appropriate, in the three realms of existence, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of life, in two ways: as kamma condition and as decisive support condition. According to the Abhidhamma method of analysis, for co-nascent consciousness, they are conditions by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, kamma, presence, non-disappearance, and other conditions.

Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpapade pana viññāṇaṃ vipākabhūtaṃ, avipākabhūtañca nāmassa kevalassa vā rūpamissakassa vā paṭisandhipavattīsu sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttavipākaāhāraindriyaatthiavigatapaccayehi yathārahaṃ navadhā, aṭṭhadhā vā paccayo hoti. Paṭisandhiyaṃ vipākaviññāṇaṃ vatthurūpassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhāraindriyavippayuttaatthi avigatapaccayehi navadhā paccayo hoti. Ṭhapetvā pana vatthurūpaṃ sesarūpassa teheva aññamaññapaccayarahitehi aṭṭhahi paccayo hoti. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṃ pana ekavokārapañcavokārabhavesu [V 0.0160] kammajarūpassa suttantikapariyāyena upanissayavasena paccayo hoti. Pavattiyaṃ pana sabbampi viññāṇaṃ tassa tassa nāmarūpassa yathārahaṃ paccayo hoti. Tattha arūpabhave viññāṇaṃ nāmasseva, asaññibhave rūpasseva, pañcavokārabhave nāmarūpassa paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpanti nibbacanaṃ katanti.

In the phrase 'name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness,' consciousness, whether resultant or non-resultant, conditions name alone, or name together with form, at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, in nine ways or eight ways as appropriate, through the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, result, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. At rebirth-linking, resultant consciousness conditions the material-basis by way of nine conditions: co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. But, excluding the material-basis, it conditions the remaining material phenomena through eight conditions, with the condition of mutuality removed. Volitional consciousness, in one-constituent and five-constituent existences, conditions kamma-produced materiality by way of decisive support, according to the Suttanta method. In the course of existence, all consciousness appropriately conditions its corresponding name and form. Here, it should be understood that in the formless realm, consciousness conditions only name; in the non-percipient realm, only form; and in the five-constituent existence, both name and form. For this reason, the term is defined thus: 'Name, and form, and name-and-form are "name-and-form".'

Nāmarūpapaccayā [M 0.0209] saḷāyatanapade pana nāmaṃ vipākabhūtaṃ, avipākabhūtañca arūpabhave chaṭṭhāyatanassa avakaṃsato sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttavipākaatthiavigatavasena yathārahaṃ sattadhā paccayo hoti. Itaresaṃ panetaṃ pañcannaṃ cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ pañcavokārabhave paṭisandhiyaṃ catumahābhūtasahāyaṃ hutvā sahajātanissayavipākavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chadhā paccayo hoti. Kiñci panettha hetupaccayena, kiñci āhārapaccayena cāti tesaṃ vasena sabbavāresu ukkaṃsāvakaṃso veditabbo. Pavatte pana cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vipākamavipākampi nāmaṃ pacchājātavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena catudhā paccayo hotīti. Evaṃ tāva nāmameva saḷāyatanassa paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases,' name, being resultant and non-resultant, is a condition for the sixth sense base in the Formless Realm, by way of inclusion, in seven ways as appropriate: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, result, presence, and non-disappearance. For the other five—the eye-base and so on—in the five-constituent existence at rebirth, being associated with the four great elements, it is a condition in six ways: by way of co-nascence, support, result, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Herein, something is by way of root-condition, something by way of nutriment-condition; according to these, the prominence and inclusion in all cases should be understood. But in the course of existence, for the five—the eye and so on—name, both resultant and non-resultant, is a condition in four ways: by way of post-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should be understood that name alone is a condition for the six sense bases.

Rūpaṃ pana vatthubhūtaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chadhā paccayo hoti. Catumahābhūtarūpaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ, pavatte ca sahajātanissayaatthiavigatapaccayehi catudhā paccayo hoti. Rūpajīvitindriyaṃ pana indriyaatthiavigatavasena tividhā. Tathā āhāro āhāratthiavigatavasena. So ca āhārūpajīvīnaṃ pavatteyeva, no paṭisandhiyaṃ. Tāni pana pañca cakkhāyatanādīni pañcaviññāṇasaṅkhātassa chaṭṭhassa manāyatanassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chadhā paccayā honti pavatteyeva, no paṭisandhiyaṃ. Tathā pañcaviññāṇavirahitamanāyatanassa vatthurūpaṃ nissayapurejātavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena pañcadhā paccayo hotīti. Evaṃ rūpameva chaṭṭhāyatanassa, saḷāyatanassa ca paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ. Khandhattayavatthurūpasaṅkhātaṃ pana nāmarūpaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa paṭisandhiyaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttavippayuttavipākaatthiavigatādivasena yathārahaṃ paccayo hotīti. Evaṃ [M 0.0210] nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca yathārahaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanassa, saḷāyatanassa ca paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Material form, being the physical base, is a condition in six ways for the sixth sense base at rebirth: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. The four great elements are a condition for the five sense bases—the eye and so on—at rebirth and during the course of existence in four ways: by way of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance. The material life faculty, however, is a condition in three ways: by way of faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. Similarly, nutriment is a condition in three ways: by way of nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance. But this nutriment applies only during the course of existence, not at rebirth. Those five sense bases—the eye and so on—are conditions for the sixth mind-base, reckoned as the fivefold consciousness, in six ways during the course of existence only, not at rebirth: by way of support, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Likewise, the physical base is a condition for the mind-base when it is devoid of the fivefold consciousness in five ways: by way of support, pre-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should be understood that material form alone is a condition for the sixth sense base and for the six sense bases. But name-and-form, reckoned as the three mental aggregates and the physical base, is a condition for the sixth sense base at rebirth in various appropriate ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, dissociation, result, presence, non-disappearance, and so on. Thus, it should be understood that name, form, and name-and-form are conditions for the sixth sense base and for the six sense bases in their respective ways.

Saḷāyatanapaccayā phassapade pana chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ vipākaṃ, avipākañca sabbattha sampayuttaphassassa [V 0.0161] sahajātādivasena navadhā, aṭṭhadhā vā paccayo hoti. Cakkhāyatanādīni pañca yathākkamaṃ pavatte cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttaatthiavigatavasena chadhā, rūpāyatanādīni pañca tesaṃ ārammaṇapurejātaatthiavigatavasena tidhā. Manosamphassassa pana tāni, dhammārammaṇañca tathā ca ārammaṇādhipatimattena cāti bahudhā paccayā honti. Evaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca chabbidhassāpi phassassa paccayo hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'dependent on the six sense bases, contact arises,' the sixth sense base, being resultant and non-resultant, is a condition for its associated contact in all cases, in nine ways or eight ways, by way of co-nascence and so on. The five bases—the eye-base and so on—are conditions for the five kinds of contact—eye-contact and so on—in the course of existence, respectively, in six ways: by way of support, pre-nascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. The five sense objects—form-object and so on—are conditions for them in three ways: by way of object, pre-nascence, presence, and non-disappearance. For mind-contact, those sense objects and mental objects are conditions in many ways, including by way of object and predominance. Thus, it should be understood that the sixth sense base and the six sense bases are conditions for all six kinds of contact.

Phassapaccayā vedanāpade sabbopi phasso sahajātānaṃ vedanānaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayavipākaāhārasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena aṭṭhadhā, sattadhā vā paccayo hoti, asahajātānaṃ upanissayavasenevāti.

In the phrase 'dependent on contact, feeling arises,' all contact is a condition for co-nascent feelings in eight ways, or seven ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance. For non-co-nascent feelings, it is a condition only by way of decisive support.

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhāpade vipākavedanā anusayapatitāya taṇhāya upanissayavasena, sahajātādivasena ca paccayo hoti. Yasmā pana –

In the phrase 'dependent on feeling, craving arises,' resultant feeling is a condition for craving that is a latent tendency by way of decisive support, and by way of co-nascence and so on. For:

Dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayati, sukhī bhiyyopi icchati;

Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā;

Taṇhāya paccayā tasmā, honti tissopi vedanāti. (visuddhi. 2.644);

One who is suffering longs for happiness; one who is happy desires even more. Equanimity, being peaceful, is also spoken of as happiness. Therefore, all three feelings are conditions for craving. (Visuddhimagga 2.644)

Taṇhāpaccayā upādānapade taṇhā asahajātā catunnampi upādānānaṃ upanissayavasena ceva anantarādivasena ca, sahajātā pana kāmupādānavajjitānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ hetusahajāta aññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatavasena sattadhā paccayo hoti.

In the phrase 'dependent on craving, clinging arises,' craving, when non-co-nascent, is a condition for all four types of clinging by way of decisive support and by way of immediacy, and so on. Co-nascent craving, however, is a condition in seven ways for the three types of clinging other than clinging to sensual pleasures: by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

Upādānapaccayā [M 0.0211] bhavapade catubbidhampi upādānaṃ asahajātassa sabbakammabhavassa ceva upapattibhavassa ca upanissayavaseneva paccayo hoti, sahajātassa pana kammabhavassa hetusahajātādivasena paccayo hoti.

In the phrase 'dependent on clinging, becoming arises,' all four types of clinging are a condition for non-co-nascent becoming—both for all kamma-becoming and for rebirth-becoming—only by way of decisive support. For co-nascent kamma-becoming, however, they are a condition by way of root, co-nascence, and so on.

Bhavapaccayā [V 0.0162] jātipade bhavoti kammabhavova adhippeto, so ca jātiyā kammapaccayaupanissayapaccayavasena dvidhā paccayo hoti.

In the phrase 'dependent on becoming, birth arises,' 'becoming' is intended to mean only kamma-becoming. This is a condition for birth in two ways: by way of kamma condition and by way of decisive support condition.

Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇādipade jāti pana jarāmaraṇānaṃ, sokādīnañca tabbhāvabhāvībhāvamattato suttantikanayena upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo hotīti ayaṃ tāvettha paccayanayo.

In the phrase 'dependent on birth, aging, death, etc. arise,' birth is a condition for aging and death, and for sorrow and the rest, merely by the fact of their existence and coming into being. Thus, according to the Suttanta method, it is a condition that falls under the category of decisive support. This, then, is the method of conditions here.

Kārakādīhi suññato panete avijjādayo dvādasa dhammā yasmā evaṃ paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhā aññanirapekkhā hutvā avicchinnā anādikā pavattanti, tasmā tato aññena brahmādinā kārakena, pakatiaṇukālādihetunā vā kārakavedakarūpena paraparikappitena attanā vā rahitā. Na cete attā, na attani, na attavanto, suññā ete attena vā attaniyena vā dhuvabhāvena vā subhabhāvena vā sukhabhāvena vāti ayaṃ kārakādīhi suññatā.

Regarding emptiness of an agent and so on: because these twelve factors, ignorance and so on, proceed interconnected as conditions and conditioned phenomena, without reference to anything else, uninterrupted and without beginning, they are therefore devoid of any other agent such as Brahmā, or of any cause such as nature, atoms, or time, or of a self conceived by others in the form of an agent or experiencer. And these are not a self, not in a self, not possessed of a self. They are empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of beauty, or of happiness. This is emptiness of an agent and so on.

Mūladdhasandhisaṅkhepākāravaṭṭavibhāgatoti ettha mūlato tāva avijjā, taṇhā cāti dve dhammā mūlanti veditabbā. Addhato panettha avijjā, saṅkhārāti dve aṅgāni atīto addhā, viññāṇādīni bhavāvasānāni aṭṭha paccuppanno addhā, jāti ceva jarāmaraṇañcāti dve anāgato addhāti tayo addhā veditabbā. Sandhito pana saṅkhārānaṃ, paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhi, vedanāya ca taṇhāya ca antarā eko phalahetusandhi, bhavassa [M 0.0212] ca jātiyā ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhi cāti tayo sandhī veditabbā. Saṅkhepato pana sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitā cattāro saṅkhepā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – avijjāsaṅkhārā eko saṅkhepo, viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā dutiyo, taṇhupādānabhavā tatiyo, jātijarāmaraṇāni catutthoti evaṃ cattāro saṅkhepā veditabbā.

Regarding the division into roots, time periods, connections, summaries, modes, and rounds: First, as to the roots, it should be understood that two things are the roots: ignorance and craving. As to the time periods, it should be understood that there are three: ignorance and formations are two links belonging to the past period; the eight links from consciousness to becoming belong to the present period; birth and aging-and-death are two links belonging to the future period. As to the connections, it should be understood that there are three: one cause-to-result connection between formations and rebirth-linking consciousness; one result-to-cause connection between feeling and craving; and one cause-to-result connection between becoming and birth. As to the summaries, it should be understood that there are four, demarcated by the connections: ignorance and formations are the first summary; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the second; craving, clinging, and becoming are the third; birth and aging-and-death are the fourth.

Ākārato panettha –

As to the modes:

Atīte hetuyo pañca, idāni phalapañcakaṃ;

Idāni hetuyo pañca, āyatiṃ phalapañcakanti. –

Five causes in the past; a pentad of results in the present. Five causes in the present; a pentad of results in the future.

Evaṃ [V 0.0163] vīsati ākārā honti.

Thus, there are twenty aspects.

Ettha hi sarūpato vuttā avijjāsaṅkhārā, tesaṃ gahaṇena tadavinābhāvato gahitā taṇhupādānabhavāti ime pañca dhammā atīte hetuyo nāma, sarūpato vuttā viññāṇādayo pañca dhammā idāni phalapañcakaṃ nāma, sarūpato pana vuttā taṇhupādānabhavā, tesaṃ gahaṇena tadavinābhāvato gahitā avijjāsaṅkhārāti ime pañca idāni hetuyo nāma. Jātiādiapadesena vuttā viññāṇādayo pañca dhammā āyatiṃ phalapañcakaṃ nāmāti evaṃ vīsati ākārā veditabbā. Vaṭṭato panettha saṅkhārabhavā kammavaṭṭaṃ, avijjātaṇhupādānā kilesavaṭṭaṃ, sesāni vipākavaṭṭanti tīṇi vaṭṭāni honti. Yāva ca tesu kilesavaṭṭaṃ ariyamaggena na upacchijjati, tāva idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ anupacchinnaṃ pavattatīti ayamettha mūladdhasandhisaṅkhepākāravaṭṭavibhāgo.
