Here, ignorance and formations are stated in their own form; by grasping them, craving, clinging, and becoming are also taken, being inseparable from them—these five phenomena are called the past causes. Consciousness and the other four phenomena are stated in their own form—these five are now called the present results. Craving, clinging, and becoming, however, are stated in their own form; by grasping them, ignorance and formations are also taken, being inseparable from them—these five are now called the present causes. Consciousness and the other four phenomena, stated by way of designation as birth and so forth, are called the future results. Thus, these twenty aspects should be understood. From the standpoint of the round, formations and becoming here constitute the kamma round; ignorance, craving, and clinging constitute the defilement round; the remaining factors are the result round—thus, there are three rounds. And as long as the defilement round is not cut off by the Noble Path, this wheel of existence continues unbroken. This here is the analysis of the root, the time-periods, the connections, the summary, the modes, and the round.

Vāraṇopamatoti [M 0.0213] ettha vāraṇato tāva – “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti idamahetukavisamahetukadassananivāraṇaṃ, “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti ucchedaattasaṅkantidassananivāraṇaṃ, “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti attāti parikappitavatthubhedadassanato ghanasaññānivāraṇaṃ, “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādi attā passati…pe… vijānāti phusati, vedayati, taṇhiyati, upādiyati, bhavati, jāyati, jīyati, mīyatīti evamādidassananivāraṇanti idamettha micchādassananivāraṇaṃ.

Regarding prevention and simile: Here, first, regarding prevention—'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations' is the prevention of the view of causelessness or of disparate causes; 'With volitional formations as condition, consciousness' is the prevention of the view of annihilation or the transmigration of a self; 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form' is the prevention of the perception of compactness due to seeing the division of an entity conceived as a self; 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,' and so on—'a self sees... cognizes, contacts, feels, craves, clings, becomes, is born, ages, dies'—is the prevention of such views as these. This here is the prevention of wrong views.

Upamāto panettha andho viya avijjā, tassa upakkhalanaṃ viya saṅkhārā, patanaṃ viya viññāṇaṃ, tena gaṇḍapātubhāvo viya nāmarūpaṃ, tassa gaṇḍabhedapīḷakā viya saḷāyatanaṃ, tassa saṅghaṭṭanaṃ viya phasso, tajjanitadukkhaṃ viya vedanā, dukkhassa paṭikārābhilāso viya taṇhā, asappāyaggahaṇaṃ viya upādānaṃ, asappāyālepanaṃ viya bhavo, tena gaṇḍavikārapātubhāvo viya jāti, tabbikārabhedo viya jarāmaraṇaṃ. Yathāsabhāvadassananivāraṇādito vā ete avijjādayo akkhipaṭalādi upamāhipi veditabbāti ayamettha upamā.

As for the simile here: ignorance is like a blind man; his stumbling is like volitional formations; his falling is like consciousness; the appearance of a boil from that is like name-and-form; the bursting and sores of that boil are like the six sense bases; its contact is like contact; the pain produced by that is like feeling; the desire for a remedy for the pain is like craving; grasping unsuitable things is like clinging; smearing with unsuitable things is like becoming; the appearance of the boil’s degeneration from that is like birth; the breaking up of that degeneration is like aging-and-death. Alternatively, these, beginning with ignorance, should be understood by similes such as a cataract, etc., due to the prevention of seeing their true nature. This is the simile here.

Gambhīranayabhedatoti ettha gambhīrabhedo tāva imesaṃ avijjādīnaṃ paccekaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīratā veditabbā. Ime hi avijjādayo dhammā yenākārena yadavatthā ca saṅkhārādīnaṃ [V 0.0164] phalānaṃ paccayā honti, so nesaṃ paccayaṭṭho duravabodhato gambhīroti ayamettha dhammagambhīratā. Dhammoti hetu “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720) vacanato. Jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ phalānaṃ jātiādīhi paccayehi sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho duravabodhato gambhīroti ayaṃ atthagambhīratā. Atthoti phalaṃ “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ [M 0.0214] atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720) vacanato. Tesaṃ pana hetūnaṃ, phalānañca tena tenākārena aviparītato desanāpi sabbaññutaññāṇasseva gocarato gambhīrāti ayaṃ desanāgambhīratā. Yo panesaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ adassanāyūhanādisabhāvo, so mandapaññehi duppariyogāhattā gambhīroti ayaṃ paṭivedhagambhīratāti ayamettha gambhīrabhedo.

Regarding the distinction of depth and method: Here, first, the distinction of depth should be understood as the profundity of phenomenon, meaning, teaching, and penetration for each of these, beginning with ignorance. For these phenomena of ignorance, etc., are profound because the manner and the state in which they serve as conditions for the results of volitional formations, etc., is hard to comprehend—this is the profundity of the phenomenon here. 'Phenomenon' refers to cause, as it is said, 'Knowledge regarding the cause is analytical knowledge of the phenomenon' (Vibh. 720). The state of being produced and arisen for results like aging-and-death from conditions like birth is hard to comprehend—this is the profundity of meaning here. 'Meaning' refers to the result, as it is said, 'Knowledge regarding the cause and result is analytical knowledge of meaning' (Vibh. 720). Moreover, the teaching of these causes and results in their various aspects, without distortion, is profound because it is the domain of omniscient knowledge alone—this is the profundity of the teaching here. The inherent nature of these, beginning with ignorance and volitional formations, such as non-seeing, accumulating, etc., is profound because it is hard for those of weak wisdom to grasp—this is the profundity of penetration here. This is the distinction of depth here.

Nayabhedo panettha ekattanayo nānattanayo abyāpāranayo evaṃdhammatānayoti imesaṃ catunnaṃ atthanayānaṃ vasena veditabbo. Tattha hi “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti evaṃ bījassa aṅkurādibhāvena rukkhabhāvappatti viya santānānupacchedo ekattanayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto hetuphalasambandhena santānānupacchedāvabodhato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto hetuphalasambandhena pavattamānassa santānānupacchedassa ekattaggahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

Here, the distinction of method should be understood in terms of these four methods of interpretation: the method of unity, the method of diversity, the method of non-operation, and the method of suchness. Among these, the statement 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises,' illustrates the method of unity, called the unbroken continuity of the stream, like the attainment of the state of a tree by a seed through the stages of sprout and so forth. One who sees this rightly abandons the view of annihilation by understanding the unbroken continuity of the stream through the connection of cause and effect. However, one who sees wrongly clings to the view of eternalism by grasping the unbroken continuity of the stream—which proceeds due to the connection of cause and effect—as a single entity.

Avijjādīnaṃ pana yathāsakaṃ lakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ nānattanayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto navanavānaṃ uppādadassanato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto ekasantānapatitassa bhinnasantānasseva nānattaggahaṇato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The distinguishing of the characteristics of ignorance and so forth, each according to its own individual nature, is called the method of diversity. Seeing rightly, one abandons the eternalist view by seeing the arising of new and new states. Seeing wrongly, one grasps the annihilationist view by taking the diversity of a single continuum to be like that of different continuums.

Avijjāya pana “saṅkhārā mayā uppādetabbā, saṅkhārānaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ amhehī”ti evamādibyāpārābhāvo abyāpāranayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passantokārakassa abhāvāvabodhato attadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, micchā passanto yo asatipi byāpāre avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvaniyamasiddho hetubhāvo, tassa aggahaṇato akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

Regarding ignorance, the absence of activity such as, 'Formations should be produced by me, or the consciousness of formations should be produced by us,' is called the method of non-operation. One who sees rightly abandons the view of self by understanding the absence of a maker, while one who sees wrongly clings to the view of non-action by failing to grasp the causal state of ignorance and so on, which is established by their own nature even in the absence of activity.

Avijjādīhi [M 0.0215] pana kāraṇehi saṅkhārādīnaṃyeva sambhavo khīrādīhi dadhiādīnaṃ viya, na aññesanti ayaṃ evaṃdhammatānayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto paccayānurūpato phalāvabodhato ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ, akiriyadiṭṭhiñca pajahati, micchā passanto paccayānurūpaṃ phalappavattiṃ aggahetvā [V 0.0165] yato kutoci yassa kassaci asambhavaggahaṇato ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ ceva niyatavādañca upādiyatīti ayamettha nayabhedoti evaṃ vijānīyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

From ignorance and other causes, only formations and so on arise, just as from milk and so on, only curds and the like arise, not anything else–this is called the method of suchness. One who sees rightly abandons the view of no-cause and the view of non-action by understanding the result in accordance with its conditions. But one who sees wrongly, failing to grasp the arising of the result in accordance with its conditions, clings to the view of no-cause and the doctrine of determinism by assuming that anything arises from anywhere at all or for anyone at all. This is the distinction in method here–thus should the analysis free from mere reliance on the Pāli texts be understood.

Paccayākāravibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the Analysis of Conditional Relations is completed.

Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Mātikā of the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness

Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo, tena na tato heṭṭhā, na uddhanti dīpeti. Satipaṭṭhānāti ettha dve satipaṭṭhānā satigocaropi satipi. “Catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.408) hi satigocaro “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati, tassattho patiṭṭhāti tasminti paṭṭhānaṃ, kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Padhānaṃ ṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ, satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.147) pana sati. Tassattho patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkantitvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho. Satiyeva paṭṭhānatthena satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, sā ca upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānanti satipaṭṭhānaṃ, idamidha adhippetaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā satipaṭṭhānāti bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ? Satiyā bahuttā. Ārammaṇabhedena hi bahukā tā satiyo.

In the Mātikā of the Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness, first, as to the meaning of the terms—'four' denotes the numerical division, thereby indicating that there is nothing less nor more. As for `satipaṭṭhāna`—here, two aspects of `satipaṭṭhāna` are intended: the object of mindfulness and mindfulness itself. In passages such as, 'Monks, I shall teach the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness,' the object of mindfulness is called `satipaṭṭhāna`. Its meaning is 'establishment'—thus, `paṭṭhāna`. What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is `satipaṭṭhāna`. Or, `paṭṭhāna` means 'principal place' or 'basis.' The foundation of mindfulness is `satipaṭṭhāna`. In passages such as, 'When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,' mindfulness itself is meant by `satipaṭṭhāna`. Its meaning is 'establishment'—thus, `paṭṭhāna`, meaning it is present, enters into, and proceeds. Mindfulness itself, in the sense of foundation, is `satipaṭṭhāna`. Alternatively, mindfulness has the characteristic of recollection; and that is called `paṭṭhāna` by the meaning of being present—thus, `satipaṭṭhāna`. This is what is intended here. If so, why is `satipaṭṭhāna` used in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. For due to the diversity of objects, there are many instances of mindfulness.

Idhāti [M 0.0216] imasmiṃ sāsane, tena ajjhattādivasena sabbappakāracatucattālīsavidhasatipaṭṭhānanibbattakassa puggalassa nissayabhūtaṃ sāsanameva, nāññaṃ sāsananti dīpeti. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇehi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214; ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241).

'Here'—in this Dispensation. Thus, it indicates that this Dispensation itself is the basis for the individual who develops the forty-four kinds of satipaṭṭhāna in every way by way of internal, and so forth, and not another Dispensation. For it was said: "Here, monks, is the ascetic... empty are the doctrines of other ascetics."

Bhikkhūti saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhanako. Tena kiñcāpi bhagavato devaloke nisīditvā satipaṭṭhānaṃ desentassa santike devagaṇaṃ muñcitvā ekabhikkhupi nisinno nāma natthi, tathāpi devo vā hotu manusso vā gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā, saṃsāre bhayanti sammā ikkhamāno yathānusiṭṭhaṃ [V 0.0166] paṭipajjamānova bhikkhu nāma hoti, nāññoti dasseti. Yathāha “alaṅkato cepī”ti (dha. pa. 142).

'Monk'—one who sees danger in saṃsāra. Therefore, even if there is not a single monk seated near the Blessed One while he teaches the satipaṭṭhāna from the heavenly realm after dismissing the assembly of gods, still, whether a deva or a human, a householder or a renunciant—whoever rightly sees danger in saṃsāra and practices as instructed is called a monk, and no other is. As it is said, "Even if adorned..."

Ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ. Kāyeti ettha āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyanti? Kucchitā kesādayo, iti kucchitānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Atha vā aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ, kesādīnañca samūhaṭṭhenapi kāyo, rūpakāyo, tasmiṃ attano kāyeti attho. Kāyānupassīti kāyaṃ anupassanasīlo. “Kāye”ti ca vatvā puna “kāyānupassī”ti dutiyakāya-ggahaṇaṃ “evaṃ na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī, na ca bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, atha kho rathasambhāranagarāvayavakadalikkhandhavibhāgānupassako viya yathākkamaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgakesādibhūtupādāyasamūhānupassī evā”ti dassanatthaṃ kataṃ. Tathā hettha yathāvuttadhammasamūhavinimutto itthipurisādiko, añño vā koci dhammo na dissati, yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana bālā tathā tathā subhādito ca micchābhinivesaṃ karonti, ayaṃ [M 0.0217] pana yogī tattha kāyānupassī eva aniccadukkhaanattāsubhānupassī evāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yvāyaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhāne assāsapassāsādiko cuddasavidho kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiṃyeva kāye anupassanato “kāye kāyānupassī”ti evamādināpi attho daṭṭhabbo.

`Ajjhattaṃ` means one's own internal. As for `kāya`, here `āya` means "that from which (things) come." What comes? Impure things such as hairs and so on; thus, `kāya` is that from which impure things come. Alternatively, `kāya` signifies the collection of limbs, parts, hairs and so forth; the physical body. In this context, it means one's own body. `Kāyānupassī` means one who is habitually observing the body. The statement "in the body" (`kāye`) followed again by "contemplating the body" (`kāyānupassī`), the second use of `kāya` is to show this: "Thus, one is not contemplating a single phenomenon separate from the limbs and parts of the body; nor is one contemplating a man or woman separate from hairs, body hair, and so on; nor is one contemplating a single phenomenon separate from the elements and derived elements. But rather, just as one observing the components of a chariot, the sections of a city, or the parts of a banana trunk observes them sequentially, so too one observes the collection of limbs and parts, hairs and so on, elements and derived elements." This is stated to show that here, apart from the collection of elements mentioned, no other phenomenon is seen, such as a man or a woman, or anything else. Fools, however, develop wrong adherence to just such a collection of elements in various ways, perceiving it as beautiful. But this yogi, contemplating the body, is simply observing it as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive. Alternatively, the fourteen kinds of body, including in-and-out breaths, taught in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, are all included in this very body. Hence, the meaning should also be understood through phrases like "contemplating the body in the body."

Viharatīti iriyati, catūsu iriyāpathesu ekenāgataṃ sarīrabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā apatamānaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati, pavattetīti attho. Bahiddhā kāyeti parassa kāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā kāyeti kālena attano, kālena parassa kāye. Kālena hi ajjhattabahiddhākāyesupi ekasmiṃ khaṇe kāyānupassanā uppajjati, paguṇakammaṭṭhānassa pana aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakālo ettha kathito. Ātāpīti kāyapariggāhakavīriyena vīriyavā. So hi yasmā kilesānaṃ ātāpanato ātāpo vuccati vīriyaṃ, so cassa atthi, tasmā ātāpīti vuccati. Sampajānoti kāyapariggāhakena sampajaññena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati, vīriyena ca antarā vosānaṃ nāpajjati, tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ sampajjati, tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī sampajāno satimā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

`Viharati` means to move. When discomfort arises in one posture, one shifts to another, sustaining the body—this is the meaning. `Bahiddhā kāye` refers to another's body. `Ajjhattabahiddhā kāye` means at times one's own body, at times another's body. For at times contemplation of the body arises in the internal and external bodies; for one with a proficient meditation subject, the time of alternating between them is spoken of here. `Ātāpī` means possessing the energy that comprehends the body. Because energy is called 'ardor' due to its burning up of defilements, and one possesses this, one is called 'ardent.' `Sampajāno` means endowed with the clear comprehension that comprehends the body. `Satimā` means endowed with the mindfulness that comprehends the body. And since one observes with wisdom after grasping the object with mindfulness, and with energy does not cease in the interim, it should be understood that 'ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful' is said to show those qualities by whose power this foundation of mindfulness is accomplished.

Iti [V 0.0167] kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, sampayogaṅgañca dassetvā idāni pahānaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ “vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi yvāyaṃ ajjhattādibhedo kāyo vutto, sveva idha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko nāma. Vibhaṅge pana yasmā rūpakāye [M 0.0218] pahīnaabhijjhādayo vedanādīsupi pahīyanti eva, tasmā pañcapi upādānakkhandhā “loko”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassasaṅkhātaṃ kāmacchandabyāpādaṃ vineyyāti sambandho. Imassa ca nīvaraṇesu balavadhammadvayassa pahānadassanena sesanīvaraṇānampi pahānaṃ vuttaṃyevāti veditabbaṃ. Visesena cettha abhijjhādomanassavinayena yathākkamaṃ kāyasampattivipattimūlānaṃ anurodhavirodhānaṃ, attaabhiratitadasubhākārādibhāvanānabhiratīnaṃ, abhūtaguṇapakkhepabhūtadosāpanayanānañca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ, tena yogāvacarassa yogānubhāvanibbattaphalaṃ, yogasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti.

Thus, having shown the contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness along with its associated factors, now to show the factor of abandoning, the phrase, 'having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world' is stated. Herein, `vineyya` means having removed either by substitution or by suppression. `Loke` refers to this very body, which was previously described as internal and so forth, here called 'the world' in the sense of being subject to breaking and dissolution. However, in the Vibhaṅga, because when covetousness and the like are abandoned in the material body, they are also abandoned in feelings and so on, therefore the five aggregates subject to clinging are called 'the world.' In that world, what is termed covetousness and grief—namely, sensual desire and ill will—should be removed; this is the connection. And it should be understood that by showing the abandonment of these two powerful states among the hindrances, the abandonment of the remaining hindrances is also implied. Herein, specifically, through the removal of covetousness and grief, the abandonment is taught of attraction and aversion, the roots of success and failure in the body, respectively; of delight in self and non-delight in developing the aspect of unattractiveness; and of attributing non-existent virtues and removing existing faults. Thereby, the fruit born of the meditator's meditative power and their proficiency in the practice are illuminated.

Ajjhattaṃ vedanāsūtiādīsupi ajjhattādīni vuttanayena veditabbāni. Ettha pana vedanāti tisso vedanā lokiyā, tathā cittaṃ, dhammā ca, tesaṃ vibhāgo vibhaṅganaye āvi bhavissati. Kevalaṃ panettha yathā vedanādayo anupassanto vedanādianupassī nāma hoti, so nayo dassetabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – vedanāsu tāva sukhā vedanā dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, itarā ca aniccato anupassitabbā. Yathāha –

`Ajjhattaṃ vedanāsu` and so forth, the terms 'internal,' and so forth, should be understood in the manner stated above. Here, however, `vedanā` refers to the three worldly feelings, and similarly the mind and phenomena—their classification will become clear in the section on analysis. But here, what should be shown is how one who contemplates feeling, and so forth, is called 'one who contemplates feeling,' and so forth. For example—first, regarding feelings: pleasant feeling should be contemplated as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and the neutral feeling as impermanent. As it is said—

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.253; itivu. 53).

"He who saw pleasure as suffering, saw suffering as a dart; he saw the peaceful state of neither-pleasure-nor-pain as impermanent."

Sabbā eva etā dukkhato anupassitabbā “yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259) vacanato. Evaṃ anupassanto pana aniccādisattānupassanāvasena vā anupassantopi “imaṃ vedanaṃ ko vedayati, kassāyaṃ vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇāyaṃ vedanā”ti upaparikkhitvā “na koci sattādiko vedayati, na kesañci sattādīnaṃ vedanā, vatthārammaṇādikāraṇā [M 0.0219] panāyaṃ vedanā uppajjatī”ti anupassantopi vedanānupassī nāma hoti. Atha vā sukhādīnaṃ uppattikkhaṇe dukkhādīnaṃ asambhavā aniccā addhuvā vipariṇāmadhammāti evaṃ vā anupassanto vedanānupassī nāma hoti. Imināva nayena pāḷinayānusārena [V 0.0168] sesacittadhammānampi anupassanākāro veditabbo. Visesato panettha cittesu aniccatāvasena, dhammesu anattatāvasena ca anupassanto cittānupassī, dhammānupassī ca nāma hotīti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

All these should be contemplated as suffering, for it is said, "Whatever is felt, that I declare as suffering." Yet, one who contemplates thus—whether through the sevenfold contemplation of impermanence and so on, or by examining, "Who feels this feeling? To whom does this feeling belong? What is the cause of this feeling?"—and then realizes, "No being or person feels, nor does this feeling belong to any being or person; rather, this feeling arises due to basis, object, and other conditions"—such a one is called a contemplator of feeling. Alternatively, one who contemplates that pleasant feelings, and so forth, at the moment of their arising are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change because suffering, and so forth, cannot coexist with them—such a one is also called a contemplator of feeling. In this same way, the manner of contemplating the remaining mind and phenomena should be understood according to the method of the Pali texts. Specifically, here, one who contemplates the mind through the aspect of impermanence and phenomena through the aspect of non-self is called a contemplator of mind and a contemplator of phenomena, respectively. The rest is easily understood. This, indeed, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedo panettha natthi, saraṇavasena ca ekāva sati ārammaṇavasena “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti vuttāti.

Here, there is no division in the state of mindfulness itself; for mindfulness is one in its characteristic of remembering, but it is called 'the four foundations of mindfulness' on account of its objects.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīye tāva ajjhattabahiddhātadubhayakāye kesādikoṭṭhāsabhāvanāvasena paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ vitthāritaṃ. Tathā ajjhattādīsu paccekaṃ sāmisanirāmisavasena duvidhānaṃ sukhadukkhaadukkhamasukhavedanānaṃ vasena dutiyaṃ, sarāgavītarāgasadosavītadosasamohavītamohasaṃkhittavikkhittamahaggataamahaggatasauttarānuttarasamāhitāsamāhitavimuttāvimuttabhedato soḷasavidhehi cittapajānanavasena tatiyaṃ, pañcanīvaraṇānaṃ, sattabojjhaṅgānañca sambhavāsambhavauppādapahānapahīnānuppattibhāvanāpāripūrihetujjhānavasena catutthaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ vitthāritaṃ. Ayaṃ suttantabhājanīyanayo.

Here, in the Exposition Method, the first foundation of mindfulness is elaborated in the Suttanta division by way of contemplating the body internally, externally, and both, through the meditation on the parts beginning with the head-hairs. Similarly, the second is detailed in terms of the internal and so forth, individually, through the two kinds of feelings—with material and without material—and by way of pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings. The third is explained by discerning the mind in sixteen ways—whether lustful or free from lust, hateful or free from hate, deluded or free from delusion, contracted or distracted, developed or undeveloped, surpassable or unsurpassable, concentrated or unconcentrated, liberated or unliberated. The fourth foundation of mindfulness is elaborated by way of the arising and non-arising, production and abandoning, non-arising of the abandoned, development, and fulfillment of the five hindrances and the seven factors of enlightenment, as well as by way of their causes and jhānas. This is the method of the Suttanta division.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana tāva “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Idha bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati vedanāsu…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”ti (vibha. 380) evaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ vuttanayassa vitthāresu aṭṭhasu lokuttaracittesu sampayuttasativaseneva vitthārato vibhattā.

In the Abhidhamma division, first, having set forth the matrix thus: “The four foundations of mindfulness. Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, feelings in feelings… phenomena in phenomena” (Vibh. 380), it is extensively analyzed, following the method stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the eight supramundane consciousnesses, specifically through the mindfulness associated with them.

Pañhāpucchakanayepi [M 0.0220] catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ kati kusalā…pe… kati araṇā? Siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā…pe… anupādinnaanupādāniyāva, asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesikāva…pe… anidassanaappaṭighāva. Na hetū ahetukāva…pe… anuttarā araṇāvāti lokuttaravaseneva vibhattā. Sammāsambuddhena hi suttantabhājanīyasmiññeva lokiyalokuttaramissakā satipaṭṭhānā kathitā, abhidhammabhājanīyapañhāpucchakesu pana lokuttarāyeva. Tesu ca lokiyā nānācittesu eva labbhanti. Aññeneva hi cittena kāyaṃ paggaṇhanti, aññena vedanādayoti. Lokuttarā pana cattāropi maggakkhaṇe ekacitteyeva labbhanti. Ekasmiñhi maggacittakkhaṇe ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇā ekāva sati kāyādīsu subhasukhaniccaattavipallāsasamucchedakatāya [V 0.0169] catukiccasādhanaṭṭhena cattāripi nāmāni labhatīti ayamettha vibhaṅganayo.

In the Question-and-Answer Method too, how many of the four foundations of mindfulness are wholesome… how many are stainless? They may be wholesome, they may be indeterminate… ungrasped and ungraspable, undefiled and undefiling… invisible and non-resistant. They are not roots, they are rootless… unsurpassed and stainless—thus they are analyzed only according to the supramundane aspect. For by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, in the Suttanta division alone, the foundations of mindfulness were taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane. But in the Abhidhamma division and Question-and-Answer sections, only the supramundane ones are discussed. Among these, the mundane ones are found only in various minds. Indeed, with one mind they grasp the body, and with another, feelings, and so forth. The supramundane ones, however, are all four attained in a single mind-moment of the path. For in a single mind-moment of the path, with Nibbāna as its object, there is just one mindfulness. Yet because it cuts through the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self, and accomplishes four functions, it obtains all four designations. This is the Exposition Method here.

Kamato satipaṭṭhāne, anūnādhikatopi ca;

Pāḷimuttanayo ñeyyo, tattha kosallamicchatā.

In the foundations of mindfulness by way of sequence, and also in terms of neither less nor more, the method beyond the Pāḷi should be understood by one desiring skill therein.

Tattha kamato tāva ayampi desanākkamova, sopi pākaṭāpākaṭavasena vutto. Imāsu hi rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭanti paṭhamaṃ kāyānupassanā vuttā. Tato arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tatthāpi ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantī uppajjamānā vedanā pākaṭāti anantarā vedanānupassanā, tato ārammaṇaṃ vijānantaṃ viññāṇaṃ pākaṭanti cittānupassanā, citte pākaṭe tannissitā sukhumāpi dhammā pākaṭā hontīti ante dhammānupassanā vuttā. Ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Here, first, this is also the order of teaching, and that too is stated by way of the manifest and the unmanifest. For among these, the form meditation subject is manifest, thus the contemplation of the body is taught first. Then comes the formless meditation subject. Therein, the feeling arising while experiencing the object is manifest, hence the contemplation of feelings is taught immediately after. Next, the consciousness that cognizes the object is manifest, thus the contemplation of consciousness is taught. When the mind is manifest, even the subtle phenomena dependent on it become manifest, thus the contemplation of phenomena is taught last. This, then, is the sequence here.

Anūnādhikatoti ettha pana kasmā bhagavatā cattārova satipaṭṭhānā vuttā, anūnā anadhikāti? Taṇhācaritadiṭṭhicaritasamathayānikavipassanāyānikānaṃ mandatikkhavasena dvidhā pavattānaṃ visuddhimaggavasena. Mandassa hi taṇhācaritassa oḷārikaṃ [M 0.0221] kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa sukhumaṃ vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, diṭṭhicaritassāpi mandassa nātippabhedagataṃ cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, tikkhassa atippabhedagataṃ dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo. Samathayānikassa ca mandassa akicchena adhigantabbanimittaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa dutiyaṃ, vipassanāyānikassāpi mandassa tatiyaṃ, tikkhassa catutthaṃ visuddhimaggoti veneyyajjhāsayato cattāro vuttā. Subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsappahānatthaṃ vā caturoghayogāsavaganthaupādānaagatippahānatthampi catubbidhāhārapariññatthañca cattārova vuttā, anūnā anadhikāti ayamettha anūnādhikatā. Evaṃ pāḷimuttanayo ñeyyo.

Here, regarding 'neither less nor more,' why did the Blessed One declare only four foundations of mindfulness, neither less nor more? It is by way of the path to purification for those with craving-temperament, view-temperament, serenity-vehicle, and insight-vehicle, who proceed in two ways, as dull or sharp. For the dull craving-temperament individual, the coarse contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness is the path to purification. For the sharp one, the subtle contemplation of feelings as a foundation of mindfulness is the path. Similarly, for the dull view-temperament individual, the contemplation of mind, not excessively differentiated, as a foundation of mindfulness is the path to purification. For the sharp one, the highly differentiated contemplation of phenomena as a foundation of mindfulness is the path. For the serenity-vehicle of dull faculties, the first foundation of mindfulness, with a sign easily attainable, is the path to purification. For the sharp one, the second is the path. Likewise, for the insight-vehicle of dull faculties, the third is the path, while for the sharp one, the fourth is the path to purification. Thus, the four were taught according to the dispositions of those to be trained. Alternatively, they were taught as four for the abandoning of the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and selfhood; and also for the abandoning of the four floods, yokes, taints, bonds, clingings, and destinations; and for the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment. Thus, they were taught as neither less nor more. This is the meaning of 'neither less nor more' here. Thus, the method beyond the Pāḷi should be understood.

Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the meaning of the matrix of the Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness is concluded.

Sammappadhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Exposition of the Right Efforts

Sammappadhānavibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0170] pana atthato tāva – sammappadhānāti kāraṇappadhānā upāyappadhānā. Yoniso padahanato paramaṃ dhānaṃ padhānaṃ, padhānavīriyānīti attho. Idha bhikkhūti imasmiṃ sāsane paṭipannako bhikkhu. Anuppannānanti anibbattānaṃ. Pāpakānanti lāmakānaṃ. Akusalānaṃ dhammānanti akosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Anuppādāyāti na uppādanatthāya. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatāsaṅkhātaṃ kusalacchandaṃ janeti uppādeti. Vāyamatīti payogaṃ parakkamaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti kāyikacetasikavīriyaṃ karoti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti teneva sahajātavīriyena cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti padhānavīriyaṃ karoti. Paṭipāṭiyā panetāni cattāripi padāni vīriyasseva āsevanābhāvanābahulīkammasātaccakiriyāhi yojetabbāni.

Now, as to the meaning of the matrix of the Exposition of the Right Efforts, first: 'Right effort' (sammappadhāna) means effort that is the cause and effort that is the means. Because one strives wisely, it is supreme striving; this is the meaning of 'striving-energy' (padhāna-vīriya). Here, 'bhikkhu' means a bhikkhu who has entered upon this Dispensation. 'Unarisen' (anuppanna) means 'not yet come into being' (anibbatta). 'Evil' (pāpaka) means 'base' (lāmaka). 'Unwholesome states' (akusala dhamma) means 'states born of unskillfulness' (akosalla-sambhūta dhamma). 'For the non-arising' (anuppādāya) means 'for the purpose of not bringing into being' (na uppādanatthāya). 'He generates desire' (chandaṃ janeti) means he generates wholesome desire, which is defined as the wish to act. 'He exerts himself' (vāyamati) means he makes an exertion, a striving. 'He arouses energy' (vīriyaṃ ārabhati) means he performs bodily and mental energy. 'He uplifts his mind' (cittaṃ paggaṇhāti) means he uplifts the mind with that very co-arisen energy. 'He strives' (padahati) means he makes an exertion of effort. In sequence, these four terms should be connected with the cultivation, development, frequent repetition, and continuous action of energy itself.

Uppannānanti [M 0.0222] anuppannāti avattabbataṃ āpannānaṃ. Pahānāyāti pajahanatthāya. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānanti anibbattānaṃ kosallasambhūtānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Uppādāyāti uppādanatthāya. Uppannānanti nibbattānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthāya. Asammosāyāti anassanatthaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunaṃ bhavanāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāyāti vaḍḍhiyā. Pāripūriyāti paripūraṇatthāya. Sesaṃ padato uttānameva.

'Arisen' (uppanna) means those that have reached the state of not being called 'unarisen'. 'For abandoning' (pahānāya) means 'for the purpose of abandoning' (pajahanatthāya). 'Of unarisen wholesome states' (anuppanna kusala dhamma) means 'of states born of skillfulness that have not come into being' (anibbatta kosalla-sambhūta dhamma). 'For arising' (uppādāya) means 'for the purpose of bringing into being' (uppādanatthāya). 'Of arisen' (uppanna) means 'of those that have come into being' (nibbatta). 'For maintenance' (ṭhitiyā) means 'for the purpose of maintaining' (ṭhitatthāya). 'For non-confusion' (asammosāya) means 'for the purpose of not perishing' (anassanatthaṃ). 'For further development' (bhiyyobhāvāya) means 'for coming into being again and again' (punappunaṃ bhavanāya). 'For abundance' (vepullāya) means 'for the state of being abundant' (vipulabhāvāya). 'For cultivation' (bhāvanāya) means 'for growth' (vaḍḍhiyā). 'For fulfillment' (pāripūriyā) means 'for the purpose of fulfilling' (paripūraṇatthāya). The rest is clear from the words themselves.

Atthato panettha “anuppannānaṃ pāpakāna”ntiādīsu asamudācāravasena vā ananubhūtārammaṇavasena vā kilesānaṃ anuppatti veditabbā. Aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā akusaladhammā nāma natthi. Kusaladhammesu pana ratanattayappasādavipassanādivivaṭṭūpanissayakusalādivasena anuppannāpi atthi. Tesampi uppannapubbatte sati sabbasattānaṃ ito pubbe ca āsavakkhayappasaṅgato. Ekantappavattasādhakā tesaṃ. Tattha ekaccassa vattaganthadhutaṅgasamādhivipassanānavakammesu aññatarasmiṃ niccappayuttassa, ghaṭato, vāyamato ca brahmalokā āgatattā bhavavasena kilesesu aladdhāsevanassa sattassa kilesā na samudācaranti, aparabhāge panassa vattādīni vissajjetvā kusītassa carato ceva akalyāṇamittādito kilesesu laddhāsevanassa ca ayonisomanasikāraṃ, sativossaggañca āgamma uppajjanti. Evaṃ tāva asamudācāravasena kilesānaṃ anuppatti veditabbā.

Now, as to the meaning here, in phrases such as 'of unarisen evil states,' the non-arising of defilements should be understood either in terms of their non-occurrence or in terms of their not having been experienced as objects. Otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence, there are no unwholesome states that have never arisen. Among wholesome states, however, there are those that have not arisen, such as wholesome states that are a supporting condition for turning away from the cycle of rebirths, like faith in the Triple Gem and insight. For if even these had arisen previously, it would follow that all beings would have attained the destruction of the taints before now, which would establish them as constantly progressing. In this regard, defilements do not occur for a certain individual who is constantly engaged in one of the following—such as the observances, the study of texts, the ascetic practices, concentration, insight, or new works—and who is striving diligently, having come from a Brahma world, and thus having not cultivated defilements due to that existence. But later, if that individual abandons those observances and so on, becomes lazy, and cultivates defilements due to associating with bad friends, they arise through unwise attention and the neglect of mindfulness. Thus, the non-arising of defilements should be understood in terms of their non-occurrence.

Ekaccassa [V 0.0171] pana tasmiṃ attabhāve ananubhūtapubbaṃ dibbādibhedaṃ manāpiyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ labhitvā tattha ayonisomanasikārasativossagge āgamma kilesā uppajjanti, alabhitvā evaṃ ananubhūtārammaṇavasena kilesānaṃ anuppatti veditabbā.

However, for some, when they obtain a delightful object, never before experienced in that existence—such as a divine or other kind of pleasing object—defilements arise for them due to unwise attention and the neglect of mindfulness regarding that object. If they do not obtain such an object, then the non-arising of defilements should be understood in terms of their not having been experienced as objects.

“Uppannānaṃ [M 0.0223] pāpakāna”nti ettha pana catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ vattamānabhūtāpagataokāsakatabhūmiladdhavasena, tesaṃ vibhāgo uppannattike vuttova. Aparampi catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ samudācāraārammaṇādhiggahitaavikkhambhitaasamugghātitavasena. Tattha sampati vattamānaṃyeva samudācāruppannaṃ nāma. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Yasmā panettha imesu uppannesu vattamānabhūtāpagataokāsakatasamudācārasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ na maggādivajjhaṃ, tasmā bhūmiladdhaārammaṇādhiggahitaasamugghātitasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ sandhāyettha “uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ pahānāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, however, in the phrase 'of arisen evil states,' 'arisen' is fourfold: in terms of presently occurring, past, having found an opportunity, and having attained a basis. Their classification is as stated in the 'Arisen Triad.' Furthermore, 'arisen' is also fourfold: in terms of occurrence, having grasped an object, not having been suppressed, and not having been eradicated. Herein, only what is presently occurring is called 'arisen by occurrence.' The rest are evident. But since here, among these arisen states, the fourfold arisen—comprising presently occurring, past, having found an opportunity, and arisen by occurrence—are not liable to be destroyed by the path, etc., therefore, the fourfold arisen—comprising having attained a basis, having grasped an object, not having been suppressed, and not having been eradicated—is intended here by the phrase, 'for the abandoning of arisen evil states'.

Kathaṃ pana maggakkhaṇe anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ uppādāya vāyāmo hoti, kathañca uppannānaṃ ṭhitiyāti? Maggappavattiyā eva. Maggo hi pavattamāno pubbe anuppannapubbattā anuppanno nāma vuccati. Yā cassa pavatti, ayameva ṭhiti nāmāti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

How then, at the moment of the path, is there effort for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and how for the maintenance of arisen ones? It is precisely through the occurrence of the path. For the path, while occurring, is called 'unarisen' because it had not arisen before. And its very occurrence is called 'maintenance.' This is the bare meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedo panetthāpi ekasseva vīriyassa kiccabhedato catudhā vuttāti ayamettha pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

Here too, the division of states is spoken of as fourfold due to the division of functions of a single energy; this is the decision based on non-canonical sources here.

Vibhaṅganayato pana suttantabhājanīye tāva cattāro sammappadhānā lokiyalokuttarakusalacittasampayuttavīriyavasena akusalādipadehi saddhiṃ vitthārato vibhattā. Abhidhammabhājanīyapañhāpucchakesu panete lokuttarakusalacittasampayuttavaseneva vibhattā, phalacittasampayuttā pana na gahitā. Teneva pañhāpucchake “kusalā eva, vipākadhammadhammā eva, apacayagāminova, sekhāvā”tiādinā vuttā. Seso panettha vinicchayo satipaṭṭhāne vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

Now, according to the method of the Vibhaṅga, in the Suttanta division, the four right efforts are analyzed in detail in terms of the energy associated with mundane and supramundane wholesome consciousness, along with terms such as 'unwholesome states.' However, in the Abhidhamma division and in the question-and-answer sections, these are analyzed only in terms of being associated with supramundane wholesome consciousness, while those associated with fruition consciousness are not included. For this reason, in the question-and-answer sections, it is stated: 'Are they only wholesome? Are they only states that are conditions for resultants? Do they only lead to accumulation? Are they only for trainees?' and so on. The remaining decision here should be understood in accordance with the method explained in the Satipaṭṭhāna.

Sammappadhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Exposition of Right Effort is concluded.

Iddhipādavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Exposition of the Bases of Spiritual Power

Iddhipādavibhaṅgamātikāya [M 0.0224][V 0.0172] pana cattāro iddhipādāti ettha ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati nipphajjatīti attho, iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Ijjhanti vā etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontītipi iddhi, pajjanti etenāti pādo, patiṭṭhā adhigamūpāyoti attho, iddhiyā pādo iddhipādo. Chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgatanti ettha chandahetuko, chandādhiko vā samādhi chandasamādhi, kattukamyatāchandaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā, catukiccasādhakassa sammappadhānavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samannāgatanti tena chandasamādhinā, padhānasaṅkhārena ca upetaṃ. Iddhipādanti yathāvuttatthena “iddhī”ti saṅkhyaṃ gatānaṃ upacārajjhānādikusalacittasampayuttānaṃ chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena pādabhūtasesacittacetasikarāsiṃ. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti, attano santāne punappunaṃ janetīti attho. Iminā nayena sesesupi attho veditabbo. Tattha vīmaṃsāti paññā. Sesaṃ padato suviññeyyameva.

In the matrix of the Exposition of the Bases of Spiritual Power, concerning 'the four bases of spiritual power': Here, 'spiritual power' (iddhi) means 'it succeeds' (ijjhati), that is, 'it is accomplished, it is brought to fruition.' Spiritual power itself is the 'basis' (pāda), hence 'basis of spiritual power' (iddhipāda), meaning a component of spiritual power. Or alternatively, beings succeed by means of this, they become spiritually powerful, developed, and exalted—thus it is also spiritual power. 'Basis' (pāda) means 'they proceed by this,' signifying a foundation, a means of attainment. The basis of spiritual power is the foundation for spiritual power. Regarding 'endowed with concentration due to zeal and striving-formations' (chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata): Here, concentration that has zeal as its cause, or is dominated by zeal, is 'concentration due to zeal' (chandasamādhi). This is a designation for concentration attained by making the desire to act (kattukamyatāchanda) the dominant factor. 'Striving-formations' (padhānasaṅkhārā) are formations that constitute striving; this is a designation for right effort (sammappadhānavīriya), which accomplishes the fourfold task. 'Endowed' (samannāgata) means possessed of that concentration due to zeal and striving-formations. 'Basis of spiritual power' (iddhipāda) refers, in the sense explained above, to the remaining mass of consciousness and mental factors that serve as the foundation (pāda) for those states counted as 'spiritual power' (iddhi)—namely, the concentration due to zeal and striving-formations associated with wholesome consciousness of access-jhāna and so on—by virtue of their being a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna). 'Develops' (bhāveti) means 'increases,' generating it repeatedly in one’s own continuity—this is the meaning. The meaning of the remaining terms should be understood in the same way. Here, 'investigation' (vīmaṃsā) is wisdom (paññā). The rest is easily understood from the words themselves.

Atthato panettha tena kiṃ kathitaṃ? Catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ matthakappattaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Yathā hi catūsu amaccaputtesu ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā vicarantesu eko upaṭṭhānena, eko sūrabhāvena, eko jātisampattiyā, eko mantabalenāti evaṃ te paccekakāraṇena rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇanti, evaṃ bhikkhūpi chandavīriyacittavīmaṃsāsu ekekaṃ jeṭṭhaṃ dhuraṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammanibbattakā honti. Ettha ca chando samādhi padhānasaṅkhāroti tayo dhammā iddhīpi honti iddhipādāpi, sesā pana sampayuttā cattāro khandhā iddhipādā eva. Evaṃ sesādhipatiyuttacittesupi iddhipādāti veditabbā.

But what is the meaning taught here? The meditation subject that has reached its culmination, taught for four bhikkhus. Just as, among four ministers' sons roaming about seeking promotion, one pleases the king through attendance, one through heroism, one through excellence of birth, and one through the power of counsel—thus they, by their individual reasons, having pleased the king, attain promotion—so too bhikkhus, having made one of zeal, energy, consciousness, or investigation the chief, the lead, and the forerunner, become producers of the supramundane Dhamma. And here, zeal, concentration, and the striving-formations are three things that are both spiritual power and bases of spiritual power, while the remaining four associated aggregates are solely bases of spiritual power. Thus, it should be understood that even in minds associated with the other dominances, these are the bases of spiritual power.

Apica [M 0.0225] jhānavipassanāsu pubbabhāgo iddhipādo. Yo paṭilābho, sā iddhi. Paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ hi pubbabhāgaparikammāni iddhipādo nāma, paṭhamajjhānādayo iddhi nāma. Paṭhamamaggādīnaṃ pubbabhāgavipassanā iddhipādo nāma, paṭhamamaggādayo iddhi nāma. Paṭilābhavasenāpi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Paṭhamajjhānādayo hi paṭhamamaggādayo ca iddhipādo nāma, dutiyajjhānādayo, dutiyamaggādayo ca iddhi nāmāti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

Moreover, the preliminary part in jhāna and insight is the basis of spiritual power. The attainment is spiritual power. For the preliminary preparations for the first jhāna and so forth are called the basis of spiritual power, while the first jhāna and so forth are called spiritual power. Similarly, the preliminary insight leading to the first path and so forth is called the basis of spiritual power, while the first path and so forth are called spiritual power. It is also fitting to explain this in terms of attainment. For the first jhāna and so forth, as well as the first path and so forth, are called the basis of spiritual power, while the second jhāna and so forth, as well as the second path and so forth, are called spiritual power. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedo [V 0.0173] panettha vibhaṅganayeneva pākaṭo bhavissati. Tattha hi suttantabhājanīye tāva chandādīnaṃ padānaṃ vibhaṅgaṃ vatvā ante “iddhipādoti tathābhūtassa vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho. Iddhipādaṃ bhāvetīti te dhamme āsevati bhāveti bahulīkaroti, tena vuccati iddhipādaṃ bhāvetī”ti (vibha. 434) evaṃ sabbe lokiyalokuttaradhammā iddhipādoti vuttā.

Here, the distinction of states will become clear through the method of the Vibhaṅga. In this regard, in the Suttanta division, after giving the analysis of terms such as 'zeal,' etc., it is stated at the end: 'The basis of spiritual power is the feeling aggregate… the consciousness aggregate of one who has become thus. To develop a basis of spiritual power means to cultivate, develop, and frequently practice those states. Therefore, it is said, “One develops a basis of spiritual power.”' (Vibh. 434) In this way, all mundane and supramundane states are said to be a basis of spiritual power.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana chandādīni padāni vibhajitvā ante “iddhipādoti tathābhūtassa phasso…pe… paggāho avikkhepo”ti (vibha. 447) evaṃ sabbe lokuttarakusaladhammā iddhipādāti vatvā puna “chandiddhipādo vīriyiddhipādo cittiddhipādo vīmaṃsiddhipādo”ti (vibha. 457) mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā “tattha katamo chandiddhipādo? Idha bhikkhu yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti…pe… yo tasmiṃ samaye chando chandikatā…pe… ayaṃ vuccati chandiddhipādo”tiādinā lokuttarakusalacittasampayuttachandavīriyacittavīmaṃsā eva iddhipādāti vuttā. Tathā pañhāpucchakepi kusalā eva, anidassanaappaṭighā eva, vīmaṃsiddhipādo hetu, sesā na hetū…pe… cittiddhipādo na vattabbo, sesā cittasampayuttā…pe… anuttarāva, araṇāvāti. Sesamettha satipaṭṭhāne vuttasadisameva. Pāḷimuttakanayo panetthāpi na uddhaṭoti.

In the Abhidhamma division, however, after analyzing terms such as 'zeal,' etc., it is stated at the end: 'The basis of spiritual power is the contact of one who is thus…pe… exertion and non-distraction.' (Vibh. 447) Thus, all supramundane wholesome dhammas are said to be bases of spiritual power. Further, after setting up the matrix with 'the basis of spiritual power of zeal, the basis of spiritual power of energy, the basis of spiritual power of mind, the basis of spiritual power of investigation' (Vibh. 457), it is explained: 'Herein, what is the basis of spiritual power of zeal? Herein, a bhikkhu, at a time when he develops supramundane jhāna…pe… whatever zeal, desire to act…pe… there is at that time—this is called the basis of spiritual power of zeal,' etc. Thus, only the zeal, energy, mind, and investigation associated with supramundane wholesome consciousness are said to be bases of spiritual power. Similarly, in the question-and-answer section, they are only wholesome, only invisible and non-impinging. The basis of spiritual power of investigation is a root, while the others are not roots…pe… the basis of spiritual power of mind is not designated, the others are associated with consciousness…pe… they are unsurpassed, free from conflict. The rest here is similar to what was stated in the section on the foundations of mindfulness. But here too, the method that goes beyond the Pāḷi text has not been presented.

Iddhipādavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the bases of spiritual power is concluded.

Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment

Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅgamātikāya [M 0.0226] pana atthato tāva – satta bojjhaṅgāti ettha bodhiyā, bodhissa vā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāya eva dhammasāmaggiyā maggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccādianekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayādisattavidhāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhati, kilesaniddāya uṭṭhahati, saccāni vā paṭivijjhati, tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgāni viya. Yo panesa yathāvuttappakārāya etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Apica “bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā”tiādinā [V 0.0174] paṭisambhidānayenāpi bojjhaṅgattho veditabbo. Pasattho, sundaro vā bojjhaṅgo sambojjhaṅgo, satiyeva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgo. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tattha dhamme vicināti aniccādito parivīmaṃsati jānāti, dhamme vā etena sattā vicinantīti dhammavicayo, paññā. Upekkhati samarasānaṃ dhammānaṃ hāpanavaḍḍhane avāvaṭatāya paṭisaṅkhānākārena majjhattā hotīti upekkhā, tatramajjhattatā. Paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇo hi upekkhāsambojjhaṅgoti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho. Dhammabhedopettha suviññeyyova.

Now, as to the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the factors of enlightenment: Herein, “the seven factors of enlightenment” means “limbs of awakening” (bodhi) or “limbs of the awakened one” (bodhi). This is what is meant: The noble disciple awakens, rises from the slumber of defilements, or penetrates the truths by means of that very harmony of states which arises at the moment of the path, which is the antidote to many afflictions such as sluggishness and agitation, and which is a sevenfold harmony of states beginning with mindfulness and investigation of states. The limbs of that awakening, which is designated the harmony of states, are the factors of enlightenment, just like the factors of jhāna or the factors of the path. And because the noble disciple awakens by means of this harmony of states of the kind described, he is called “the awakened one” (bodhī); the limbs of that awakened one are the factors of enlightenment, like the limbs of an army or a chariot, and so on. Moreover, the meaning of “factors of enlightenment” should also be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, as in “They conduce to awakening, hence they are factors of enlightenment,” and so on. A praised or beautiful factor of enlightenment is a factor of full enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga); mindfulness itself is the factor of full enlightenment of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga). The same applies to the others. Herein, “investigation of states” (dhammavicaya) means wisdom (paññā), which investigates, scrutinizes, and knows states from the perspective of impermanence, etc., or by which beings investigate states. “Equanimity” (upekkhā) is neutrality, the state of being balanced by means of reflection, due to not being engaged in the increase or decrease of states that are of a similar nature; it is neutrality in regard to them. For the factor of full enlightenment of equanimity has reflection as its characteristic. The rest is easily understood. This, then, is the meaning of the terms here. The distinctions among the states here are also easily understood.

Vibhaṅganayato panettha suttantabhājanīye tāva lokiyalokuttaravasena sesesu lokuttarakusalavipākavasena vibhattā. Pañhāpucchake pana siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā, pītisambojjhaṅgo sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttova, sesā dvīhi…pe… pītisambojjhaṅgo sukhasahagatova, sesā tidhāpi, anidassanaappaṭighā, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo [M 0.0227] hetu, sesā na hetū…pe… rūpāvacarāva, araṇāvāti. Sesaṃ satipaṭṭhāne vuttanayameva. Ayamettha vibhaṅganayo.

Now, according to the method of analysis here, in the Suttanta division, they are first classified as mundane and supramundane, and in the remaining sections, as supramundane wholesome and resultant. But in the question-and-answer section, they may be wholesome or indeterminate. The factor of full enlightenment of joy is associated only with pleasant feeling; the rest with two... The factor of full enlightenment of joy is accompanied by happiness; the rest in three ways... They are invisible and non-impinging... The factor of full enlightenment of investigation of states is a root; the rest are not roots... They are only of the form sphere... They are free from conflict. The rest is just as stated in the section on the foundations of mindfulness. This is the method of analysis here.

Idāni pana –

Now—

Kamato tāvattato ca, hetubhūmivibhāgato;

Vivekato ca viññeyyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

From sequence and from limitation, from the division of cause and plane, and from seclusion should be known the determination that is beyond the Pāḷi.

Tattha kamato tāva ayampi desanākkamova. Sabbesaṃ hi bojjhaṅgānaṃ upakārattā satisambojjhaṅgo paṭhamaṃ vutto, tato yasmā upaṭṭhitasatiko dhamme paññāya pavicināti, pavicitadhammo vīriyaṃ ārabhati, āraddhavīriyassa pīti uppajjati, pītimanassa kāyopi cittampi passambhati, passaddhakāyassa sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitacitto taṃ cittaṃ sādhukaṃ ajjhupekkhitā hoti, tasmā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo yathākkamaṃ vuttāti ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Herein, first, as to sequence, this is also the sequence of exposition. Indeed, because the factor of full enlightenment of mindfulness is helpful to all the factors of enlightenment, it is mentioned first. Then, because one whose mindfulness is established investigates states with wisdom, one who has investigated states arouses energy, for one who has aroused energy joy arises, for one whose mind is joyful both body and mind become tranquil, for one whose body is tranquil and who is happy the mind becomes concentrated, one whose mind is concentrated becomes one who observes that mind well with equanimity. Therefore, the factors of full enlightenment beginning with investigation of states are mentioned in sequence. This, then, is the sequence here.

Tāvattato pana kasmā te satteva vuttā, anūnā anadhikāti? Līnuddhaccapaṭipakkhato, sabbattikato ca. Ettha hi tayo bojjhaṅgā līnassa paṭipakkhā. Yathāha – “yasmiṃ ca kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo [V 0.0175] vīriya…pe… pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Tayo uddhaccassa paṭipakkhā. Yathāha – “yasmiṃ ca kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhi…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Eko panettha loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu sabbabojjhaṅgesu icchitabbo. Yathāha – “satiñca [M 0.0228] khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Evaṃ līnuddhaccapaṭipakkhato ca sabbatthikato ca satteva vuttāti ayaṃ tāvattato.

Now, as to limitation, why are only these seven mentioned, neither fewer nor more? Because they are the antidote to sluggishness and agitation, and because of their universal applicability. Herein, three factors of full enlightenment are the antidote to sluggishness. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to cultivate the factor of full enlightenment of investigation of states, the time for the factor of full enlightenment of energy…pe… the time for the factor of full enlightenment of joy.” Three are the antidote to agitation. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, when the mind is agitated, that is the time to cultivate the factor of full enlightenment of tranquility, the time for the factor of full enlightenment of concentration…pe… the time for the factor of full enlightenment of equanimity.” Herein, one factor, like salt seasoning in all dishes, is to be desired in all factors of enlightenment. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, I declare mindfulness to be universally applicable.” Thus, because they are the antidote to sluggishness and agitation and because of their universal applicability, only these seven are mentioned. This, then, is the explanation as to limitation.

Hetubhūmivibhāgatoti ettha hetuvibhāgato tāva – cattāro satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti satisampajaññaṃ muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tathā satta dhammā dutiyassa paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ sarīraparikkhārabhūtānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ vatthuvisadakiriyā nāma. Tathā ekādasa dhammā tatiyassa apāyabhayagamanavīthidāyajjamahattasatthumahattajātimahattasabrahmacārimahattānaṃ paccavekkhaṇatā ānisaṃsadassāvitā piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha “buddhādīhi gatamaggo mayā gantabbo”ti paccavekkhaṇā vīthipaccavekkhaṇā nāma. “Dāyakehi dinnapiṇḍapātassa mahapphalataṃ sampādessāmī”ti attānaṃ damanaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma. Tathā ekādasa dhammā catutthassa buddhadhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatopasamānussatiyo satta, lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā siniddhapuggalasevanatā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tathā satta dhammā pañcamassa paṇītabhojanasevanatā, utusukhairiyāpathasukhasevanatā dve majjhattappayogatā sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā santakāyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Ekādasa dhammā chaṭṭhassa vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nimittakusalatā samaye cittassa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanajjhupekkhanā catasso[M 0.0229], asamāhitasamāhitapuggalānaṃ parivajjanasevanatā dve, jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha kasiṇādinimittānaṃ uggahaṇakusalatā nimittakusalatā nāma. Pañca dhammā sattamassa sattasaṅkhārakelāyanamajjhattapuggalānaṃ parivajjanasevanatā [V 0.0176] dve dve, tadadhimuttatāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana sammohavinodaniyā vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya gahetabboti ayamettha hetuvibhāgo.

Here, as to the division of causes and planes, first, as to the division of causes: four things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of forgotten mindfulness, associating with persons whose mindfulness is established, and being inclined towards that. Similarly, seven things conduce to the second factor: thorough questioning, purifying the object, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on profound knowledge and conduct, and being inclined towards that. Therein, “purifying the object” means making clear the internal and external objects that serve as bodily requisites. Likewise, eleven things conduce to the third factor: reflecting on the fear of the lower realms, the journey, the path, the greatness of the heritage, the greatness of the Teacher, the greatness of birth, and the greatness of spiritual companions; showing the benefits, revering almsfood, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and being inclined towards that. Therein, reflecting on “the path gone by the Buddhas and others must be gone by me” is called “reflecting on the path.” Taming oneself with the thought, ‘I shall bring about great fruit for the almsfood given by donors,’ is called ‘revering almsfood.’ Similarly, eleven things conduce to the fourth factor: the seven recollections of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, and peace; avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being inclined towards that. Likewise, seven things conduce to the fifth factor: consuming excellent food, enjoying suitable climate and comfortable postures (two), practicing moderation, avoiding restless persons, associating with calm persons, and being inclined towards that. Eleven things conduce to the sixth factor: purifying the object, balancing the faculties, skill in signs, the fourfold application of the mind at the right time—exerting, restraining, gladdening, and observing with equanimity; avoiding unbalanced persons and associating with balanced persons (two); reflecting on jhāna and liberation, and being inclined towards that. Therein, “skill in signs” means proficiency in grasping kasiṇa and other meditation objects. Five things conduce to the seventh factor: avoiding and associating with persons who delight in worldly activities, and avoiding and associating with moderate persons (four in total); and being inclined towards that. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the Vibhaṅga commentary, the Sammohavinodanī. This is the division of causes here.

Bhūmivibhāgato panete kāmāvacarā, lokuttarā vā honti, kāmāvacaresu balavavipassanādīsu eva bojjhaṅgā labbhanti, na itaresu. Lokuttaresu pana sabbattha labbhanti, rūpāvacarārūpāvacaracittesu sabbathā na labbhanti abodhipakkhikattā. Keci pana therā vipassanāpādakesu kasiṇāsubhabrahmavihārajjhānesupi bojjhaṅge uddharanti, na ca te paṭisiddhā aṭṭhakathācariyehi, tasmā tesaṃ matena rūpāvacarāpi honti, na kenaci pariyāyena arūpāvacarāti ayamettha bhūmivibhāgo.

Now, as to the division by plane, these are either of the sense-sphere or supramundane. In the sense-sphere, the enlightenment factors are found only in strong insight and the like, not in others. In the supramundane, however, they are found everywhere. In the form-sphere and formless-sphere consciousnesses, they are never found because they are not conducive to awakening. Some elders, however, include the enlightenment factors even in the jhānas that serve as a basis for insight, such as the kasiṇas, the foul, and the divine abodes. And they are not refuted by the commentators; therefore, according to their view, they also exist in the form-sphere, but in no way in the formless-sphere. This is the division by plane here.

Vivekatoti ettha vivekoti vivittatā, svāyaṃ pañcavidho tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭipassaddhinissaraṇavivekavasena. Tadaṅgavivekoti vipassanā, vikkhambhanavivekoti aṭṭha samāpattiyo, samucchedavivekoti maggo, paṭipassaddhivivekoti phalaṃ, nissaraṇavivekoti sabbanimittanissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ. Tatrime tadaṅgasamucchedapaṭipassaddhinissaraṇavivekanissitā honti. Tathā hete vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitā, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitā. Maggakāle pana kiccato samucchedavivekanissitā, ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitā, phalakkhaṇe kiccato paṭipassaddhivivekanissitā. Ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitā [M 0.0230] ca honti. Kesañci therānaṃ mate vipassanāpādakarūpāvacarajjhānakkhaṇe vikkhambhanavivekanissitāvāti pañcavivekanissitāpi hontīti ayamettha viveko. Evaṃ viññeyyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

As for seclusion, here 'seclusion' means 'separation.' It is fivefold: temporary seclusion, suppression seclusion, eradication seclusion, tranquilization seclusion, and escape seclusion. Temporary seclusion is insight. Suppression seclusion is the eight attainments. Eradication seclusion is the path. Tranquilization seclusion is the fruit. Escape seclusion is Nibbāna, escaped from all signs. These enlightenment factors depend on temporary, eradication, tranquilization, and escape seclusion. For at the moment of insight, they depend functionally on temporary seclusion and by intention on escape seclusion. At the time of the path, they depend functionally on eradication seclusion and by object on escape seclusion. At the moment of fruition, they depend functionally on tranquilization seclusion and by object on escape seclusion. According to the view of some elders, at the moment of the form-sphere jhāna that serves as a basis for insight, they also depend on suppression seclusion. Thus, they depend on all five kinds of seclusion. This is the seclusion here. The exposition of what is beyond the Pāli should be understood in this way.

Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the enlightenment factors is concluded.

Maggaṅgavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the path factors.

Maggaṅgavibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – ariyoti taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesehi ārakattā[V 0.0177], ariyabhāvakarattā ca ariyo, aṭṭha aṅgāni assāti aṭṭhaṅgiko, nibbānatthikehi maggīyati, nibbānaṃ vā maggati, kilese vā mārento gacchatīti maggo. Seyyathidanti so katamoti ce, idāni svāyaṃ maggo caturaṅginī viya senā aṅgamattameva hoti, aṅgavinimutto natthīti dassento “sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti āha. Tattha sammā passatīti sammādiṭṭhi, paññā. Sammā saṅkappeti takketīti sammāsaṅkappo, vitakko. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Tato dhammabhedopi vibhaṅganayopi bojjhaṅgesu vuttasadiso.

Now, as to the meaning in the matrix of the analysis of the path factors: 'Noble' (ariya) because it is far (āraka) from the defilements to be avoided by each respective path, and because it brings about the noble state. 'Eight-factored' (aṭṭhaṅgiko) because it has eight factors (aṅgāni). 'Path' (magga) because it is sought (maggīyati) by those intent on Nibbāna, or because it seeks (maggati) Nibbāna, or because it goes, killing (mārento gacchati) the defilements. 'That is to say' (seyyathidaṃ)—if it is asked, 'What is that?'—now, this path, like an army with four divisions, is merely factors; there is nothing apart from factors. To show this, he says, 'right view...right concentration.' Herein, 'right view' (sammādiṭṭhi) is seeing rightly (sammā passati)—wisdom (paññā). 'Right intention' (sammāsaṅkappo) is intending rightly, pondering (takketi)—thought (vitakko). The rest is easily understood. Thereafter, the division of states and the method of analysis are similar to what was said for the enlightenment factors.

Abhidhammabhājanīye pana viratittayavajjito pañcaṅgikopi maggo vibhatto, tañca pañcannaṃ aṅgānaṃ kiccādhikataṃ, viratīnañca avuttasiddhataṃ sandhāya, virativajjitassa pana lokuttaramaggassa abhāvā sopi aṭṭhaṅgikovāti veditabbo.

In the Abhidhamma analysis, however, even the five-factored path, excluding the three abstinences, is analyzed, and that analysis is with reference to the prominence of the functions of the five factors, and the implicit inclusion of the abstinences. But since there is no supramundane path without the abstinences, it should be understood that it too is eight-factored.

Pañhāpucchakepi sammāsaṅkappo sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttova, sesā dvīhi. Sammāsaṅkappo avitakkavicāramatto, pītisahagato sukhasahagatova, na upekkhāsahagato, sesā tidhāpi. Sammādiṭṭhi hetu, sesā nahetūti ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ samameva. Idāni pana –

In the question section, too, right intention is associated only with pleasant feeling; the remaining factors are associated with two. Right intention is merely without initial and sustained thought, associated with joy or pleasure, not with equanimity; the remaining factors are associated with all three. Right view is a root, the others are not roots—this is the distinction. The rest is the same. Now—

Kamato [M 0.0231] kiccabhedato, bhūmibhedavivekato;

Maggaṅgesu vijānīyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

By sequence, by functional distinction,

By distinction of planes and seclusion,

The path factors should be understood—

This is the exposition of what is beyond the Pāli.

Tattha kamato tāva ayampi desanākkamova. Bhagavatā hi nibbānādhigamāya paṭipannassa paññāpajjotapaññāsatthatāya avijjandhakāravidhamanato bahūpakārattā paṭhamaṃ sammādiṭṭhi desitā. Tato heraññikassa kahāpaṇaparivattakahattho viya yathāsabhāvadassanassa sammādiṭṭhiyā bahūpakārattā sammāsaṅkappo. Svāyaṃ yathā sammādiṭṭhiyā, evaṃ sammāvācāyapi upakārako. Yathāha “pubbe kho, gahapati, takketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.463), tasmā tadanantaraṃ sammāvācā. Yasmā pana vācāya saṃvidahitvā loke kammante payojenti, tasmā tadanantaraṃ sammākammanto. Kāyavacīduccaritaṃ pahāya ubhayasucaritaṃ pūrentasseva yasmā ājīvaṭṭhamakaṃ sīlaṃ pūrati, na itarassa, tasmā tadubhayānantaraṃ sammāājīvo vutto. Evaṃ “visuddhadiṭṭhisīlenāpi ettāvatā paritosaṃ akatvā idaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhitabba”nti dassetuṃ tadanantaraṃ sammāvāyāmo. Āraddhavīriyenāpi kāyādīsu sati sūpaṭṭhitā kātabbāti dassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ [V 0.0178] sammāsati. Sūpaṭṭhitāya satiyā ekattārammaṇe cittaṃ samādhātuṃ sakkāti tadanantaraṃ sammāsamādhi vuttoti ayaṃ tāvettha kamo.

Here, firstly, this is also the sequence of teaching. For the Blessed One first taught right view because it is most beneficial for one striving to attain Nibbāna, as it dispels the darkness of ignorance, being like a lamp of wisdom and a whetstone of wisdom. Then, just as a money-changer turns over a coin in his hand, right intention follows because it is highly beneficial to right view for seeing things as they truly are. This right intention, just as it is helpful to right view, is also helpful to right speech. As it is said: “Householder, having first reflected and considered, one then breaks forth into speech” (MN 1.463), therefore right speech comes next. And because people engage in worldly activities after deliberating with speech, right action follows next. Since only one who abandons bodily and verbal misconduct and fulfills both kinds of good conduct fulfills the virtue ending in livelihood as the eighth, and not another, therefore right livelihood is stated after both of these. To show that “even with purified view and virtue, one should not be content with just this but should arouse energy,” right effort comes next. To indicate that “even with aroused energy, mindfulness should be well-established regarding the body, etc.,” right mindfulness follows. And because “with well-established mindfulness, the mind can be concentrated on a single object,” right concentration is then taught—this is the sequence here.

Kiccato panesaṃ ekekassa tīṇi tīṇi kiccāni, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi tāva aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, ārammaṇato nirodhasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, asammohato sesasaccāni paṭivijjhati. Evaṃ sammāsaṅkappādīnaṃ micchāsaṅkappapajahanādivasena yathānurūpanti kiccatā veditabbā. Visesato panettha sammāsaṅkappo sahajātadhamme abhiniropeti, sammāvācā pariggaṇhāti[M 0.0232], sammākammanto samuṭṭhāpeti, sammāājīvo vodāpeti, sammāvāyāmo paggaṇhāti, sammāsati upaṭṭhāpeti, sammāsamādhi samādahatīti idamettha kiccaṃ.

Regarding their functions, each one has three functions, namely: Right View, for instance, abandons wrong view along with its other opposing defilements, realizes the truth of cessation as its object, and penetrates the remaining truths without confusion. Similarly, the functions of Right Intention and the others should be understood accordingly in terms of abandoning wrong intention, and so on. Specifically here, Right Intention directs co-arisen states, Right Speech encompasses, Right Action initiates, Right Livelihood purifies, Right Effort upholds, Right Mindfulness establishes, and Right Concentration concentrates—this is the function here.

Bhedato pana pubbabhāge sammādiṭṭhi “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādinā catūsu saccesu ñāṇavasena nānakkhaṇā nānārammaṇā nānānāmā hoti, dutiyo pana nekkhammaabyāpādaavihiṃsāsaṅkappavasena, viratiyo catubbidhavacīduccaritatividhakāyaduccaritamicchājīvaviramaṇasaṅkhātacetanāvasenapi virativasenapi, chaṭṭhasattamā catubbidhasammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasena nānakkhaṇā nānārammaṇā nānānāmā honti. Maggakāle panete sammādiṭṭhiādayo ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Kiccato pana tāni pubbabhāge nānānāmāni labhanti, sammāsamādhi pana pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi catukkapañcakajjhānavasena nānakkhaṇo nānānāmo, maggakkhaṇe pana ekārammaṇo hoti. Ekassa hi paṭhamamaggo pādakajjhānādiniyamato paṭhamajjhānādiko vā dutiyajjhānādīsu aññatarajjhāniko vā, dutiyamaggādayopissa paṭhamamaggasadisajjhānikā vā visadisajjhānikā vāti so maggakālepi nānakkhaṇo nānānāmo vāti ayamettha bhedo.

In terms of distinction, in the preliminary stage, Right View, by way of knowledge in the four truths, such as 'knowledge of suffering,' is of various moments, various objects, and various names. The second factor, Right Intention, is by way of intentions of renunciation, non-ill will, and non-cruelty. The abstinences are defined by way of the volition consisting of refraining from the fourfold verbal misconduct, the threefold bodily misconduct, and wrong livelihood, and also by way of abstinence itself. The sixth and seventh factors, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, are of various moments, various objects, and various names by way of the fourfold right exertions and the foundations of mindfulness. At the path moment, however, these factors—Right View and so on—are of one moment and one object. Functionally, however, they acquire various names in the preliminary stage. But Right Concentration, even in the preliminary stage and at the path moment, is of various moments and various names by way of the fourfold or fivefold jhānas; at the path moment, however, it has one object. For a certain person, the first path is necessarily based on the first jhāna and so on, or on some other jhāna such as the second; and for that person the second path and the others may have a jhāna basis similar or dissimilar to the first path. Thus, even at the path moment, it is of various moments and various names—this is the distinction here.

Bhūmito ca vivekato ca vinicchayo bojjhaṅgesu vuttānusārena veditabboti evaṃ vijānīyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

And the determination by way of plane and by way of seclusion should be understood according to what was said in the section on the enlightenment factors. Thus, the exposition of what is beyond the Pāḷi should be understood.

Maggaṅgavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the analysis of the path factors is concluded.

Jhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of Jhāna

Jhānavibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0179] pana atthato tāva – pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutotiādīsu pātimokkhanti sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Taṃ hi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi [M 0.0233] dukkhehi, tasmā “pātimokkha”nti vuccati. Saṃvaraṇaṃ, saṃvaranti vā tenāti saṃvaro, pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro, kammavācāpariyosāne ijjhanakassa atthato cetanādirūpassa pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tena saṃvuto pihitakāyavacīpayogoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto. Viharatīti iriyati pavatteti. Ācāragocarasampannoti ettha ācaritabbato ācāro, gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, gunnaṃ caraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃsadisatāya pana sabbopi pavattivisayo gocaroti veditabbo. Tesaṃ vibhāgo niddese vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Now, in the matrix of the Analysis of Jhāna, first as to the meaning: in such phrases as 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,' 'Pātimokkha' here means the virtue of the training rules. For it protects one who guards it, and it liberates, it frees one from the sufferings of the woeful states and so on; therefore it is called 'Pātimokkha.' Restraining, or that by which one is restrained, is 'restraint' (saṃvara). The Pātimokkha itself is the restraint, the Pātimokkha-restraint. This is a designation for the virtue of the Pātimokkha-restraint, which in essence is intention and so on for one who succeeds at the conclusion of the formal act. One who is restrained by it, with bodily and verbal application covered, is 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.' 'Dwells' means one moves about, one proceeds. In 'endowed with proper conduct and resort,' here 'conduct' is so called because it should be practiced, and 'resort' is where cattle roam, a grazing ground for cattle.
