By analogy, however, the entire sphere of activity should be understood as 'resort.' Their distinction should be understood in the way stated in the Exposition.

Niddese hi –

For in the Exposition:

“Ācāragocarasampannoti atthi ācāro, atthi anācāro. Tattha katamo anācāro? Kāyiko vītikkamo, vācasiko vītikkamo, kāyikavācasiko vītikkamo, ayaṃ vuccati anācāro, sabbampi dussīlyaṃ anācāro, idhekacco veḷudānena vā patta…pe… pupphaphalasinānadantakaṭṭhadānena vā cāṭukamyatāya vā muggasupyatāya vā pāribhaṭutāya vā jaṅghapesanikena vā aññataraññatarena vā buddhapatikuṭṭhena micchāājīvena jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ vuccati anācāro.

'Endowed with conduct and resort': There is conduct and there is misconduct. Therein, what is misconduct? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, and bodily-verbal transgression—this is called misconduct. All bad morality is misconduct. Here, a certain person makes a living by giving bamboo, or a bowl ...pe... or by giving flowers, fruits, bath powder, and tooth-wood, or by flattery, or by hinting, or by acting as a lackey, or by running messages, or by some other wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddha—this is called misconduct.

“Tattha katamo ācāro? Kāyiko avītikkamo”tiādinā (vibha. 513) –

Therein, what is conduct? It is defined by the passage beginning: 'Bodily non-transgression…' (Vibh 513).

Vuttavipariyāyena ācāro niddiṭṭho.

Conduct is explained by way of the reverse of what has been said.

“Gocaroti [M 0.0234] atthi gocaro, atthi agocaro. Tattha katamo agocaro? Idhekacco vesiyāgocaro vā hoti, vidhavā…pe… thullakumārīpaṇḍakabhikkhunīpānāgāragocaro [V 0.0180] vā, saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena saṃsaggena, yāni vā pana tāni kulāni assaddhāni appasannāni…pe… tathārūpāni kulāni sevati bhajati payirupāsati, ayaṃ vuccati agocaro.

'Resort': There is a resort and a non-resort. Therein, what is the non-resort? Here, a certain person has as his resort prostitutes, or widows ...pe... or mature maidens, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, or taverns; or he dwells associated with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians in unsuitable association; or again, whatever families are faithless, unconvinced ...pe... he serves, frequents, and attends upon such families—this is called the non-resort.

“Tattha katamo gocaro? Idhekacco na vesiyāgocaro hotī”tiādinā (vibha. 514) –

Therein, what is the resort? It is defined by the passage beginning: 'Here, a certain person does not have prostitutes as his resort…' (Vibh 514).

Vuttavipariyāyena gocaro niddiṭṭho.

The resort is explained by way of the reverse of what has been said.

Apicettha therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ purato gamananisīdanacaṅkamanaghaṭṭanābhibhavanādikāyikācittīkārakiriyānañceva there bhikkhū anāpucchā dhammakathanakhuṃsanādivācasikācittīkārakiriyānañca anācārānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena kāyikavācasiko ācāro veditabbo. Apica bhikkhu sagāravo sappatisso hirottappasampanno sunivattho supāruto pāsādikena abhikkantādinā okkhittacakkhu iriyāpathasampanno ābhisamācārikesu sakkaccakārī garucittīkārabahulo viharati, ayaṃ vuccati ācāro. Gocaro pana tividho upanissayagocaro ārakkhagocaro upanibandhagocaroti. Tattha dasakathāvatthuguṇasamannāgato kalyāṇamitto upanissayagocaro nāma. Antaragharādīsu okkhittacakkhutādīhi disā vidisā anoloketvā gamanaṃ ārakkhagocaro nāma. Cattāro pana satipaṭṭhānā upanibandhagocaro nāma. Yattha cittaṃ upanibandhati, ayaṃ tividhopettha [M 0.0235] gocaroti veditabbo. Imināti iminā ācārena, gocarena ca samannāgato ācāragocarasampanno nāma.

Moreover, here bodily and verbal conduct should be understood as the opposite of such misconduct as disrespectful bodily actions—walking, sitting, pacing, jostling, and overpowering in front of elder bhikkhus—and disrespectful verbal actions such as teaching the Dhamma or reviling without asking the elder bhikkhus. Furthermore, a bhikkhu who dwells respectful, deferential, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, properly dressed and robed, graceful in his advancing and so on, with eyes downcast, accomplished in deportment, acting carefully in the rules of proper conduct, and abounding in respect and reverence—this is called conduct. The resort, however, is threefold: the resort as support, the resort as guard, and the resort as binding. Therein, a good friend endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of conversation is called the resort as support. Going into a house, etc., without looking around at the directions and intermediate directions, with eyes downcast, is called the resort as guard. The four establishments of mindfulness are called the resort as binding. That to which the mind is bound—this threefold resort should be understood here. 'By this' means: endowed with this conduct and this resort, one is called 'endowed with conduct and resort'.

Aṇumattesu vajjesūti aṇuppamāṇesu dosesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassanasīlo, aṇumattaṃ reṇuṃ sinerusadisaṃ passanto viya sabbalahukampi dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattaṃ pārājikasadisaṃ katvā vajjato bhayato dassanasīloti attho. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃ kiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ suṭṭhu ādāya gahetvā sikkhati.

'In minute faults' means in faults of tiny measure. 'Seeing danger' means one who is by nature one who sees danger; the meaning is that one is by nature one who sees danger in a fault, like one seeing a minute speck of dust as like Mount Sineru, treating even the slightest offense of wrong-doing or wrong speech as similar to a pārājika offense. 'He trains, having undertaken the training rules' means: whatever is to be trained in among the training rules, he trains having undertaken and grasped it well.

Indriyesu guttadvāroti manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu rūpādiārammaṇanimittādīnaṃ aggahaṇasaṅkhātasatisaṃvarena [V 0.0181] pihitadvāro. Bhojane mattaññūti piṇḍapāte paṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu paccavekkhaṇañāṇavasena ceva appicchatādīhi ca mattajānanako, piṇḍapātavasena cettha catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atha vā bhuñjitabbato bhojananti catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pubbarattāpararattanti ettha aḍḍharattisaṅkhātāya rattiyā pubbe pubbarattaṃ, iminā paṭhamayāmañceva pacchābhattañca gaṇhāti. Rattiyā pacchā apararattaṃ, iminā pacchimayāmañceva purebhattañca gaṇhāti. Pacchimayāmo panassa bhikkhuno niddākilamathavinodanokāsoti na gahito.

'With sense faculties guarded' means one whose doors are closed in the six sense faculties with mind as the sixth, by the restraint of mindfulness, which consists in not grasping the signs of objects such as forms. 'Knowing moderation in eating' means one who knows the measure in receiving and consuming almsfood, both by way of the knowledge of reflection and by way of having few wishes and so on. Here, by way of almsfood, the taking of the four requisites should be understood. Or, since it is to be eaten, 'eating' should be understood as the taking of the four requisites. In 'the early part of the night and the latter part of the night': here, the early part of the night is what is before midnight; by this is included the first watch and the time after the meal. The latter part of the night is what is after midnight; by this is included the last watch and the time before the meal. But the last watch is not included for this bhikkhu, as it is an occasion for dispelling sleepiness and weariness.

Jāgariyānuyogamanuyuttoti asubhabhāvanāsaṅkhātassa bhāvanārāmassa anuyogasaṅkhātaṃ āsevanabhāvanaṃ anuyutto caṅkamananisajjāhi yonisomanasikārena āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaparisodhane yuttappayuttoti attho. Sātaccaṃ nepakkanti satataṃ pavattayitabbato sātaccasaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ, paripākagatattā nepakkasaṅkhātañca paññaṃ anuyuttoti sambandho. Iminā vīriyapaññāhi yuttasseva jāgariyānuyogasiddhīti dasseti.

'Devoted to the practice of wakefulness' means one is devoted to the application—that is, the cultivation and repeated practice—of the delight in development known as the meditation on the unlovely. The meaning is that one is engaged and devoted to purifying the mind of the hindrances by means of walking and sitting with wise attention. 'Persistence and prudence': the connection is that one is devoted to the energy called 'persistence,' because it is to be constantly exerted, and to the wisdom called 'prudence,' because it has reached maturity. By this it is shown that the accomplishment of the practice of wakefulness comes only to one who is endowed with energy and wisdom.

Idāni [M 0.0236] taṃ jāgariyānuyogaṃ sarūpato dassento “bodhipakkhikānaṃ dhammāna”ntiādimāha. Bodhipakkhikānaṃ dhammānanti catusaccāvabodhasaṅkhātassa maggañāṇassa pakkhe bhavānaṃ catusaccasatipaṭṭhānādisattatiṃsadhammānaṃ. Niddese panassa lokiyabhāvanāya visesabodhipakkhiyadhamme ekārammaṇe pavattanasamatthatāya satta bojjhaṅgā eva niddiṭṭhā. Tesaṃ gahaṇena pana sesānampi tattha gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. So abhikkante paṭikkantetiādīsu abhikkantaṃ vuccati purato gamanaṃ, paṭikkantaṃ nivattanaṃ, tadubhayañca ṭhānanisajjāsayanesupi purato, pacchato ca kāyassa abhigamanaapagamanavasena labbhati. Sampajānakārī hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī, sampajaññasseva vā kārī, sampajañña-ggahaṇena cettha avippayogato satipi gahitāva hoti. Tenevassa niddese “sato sampajāno abhikkamatī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, showing that practice of wakefulness in its own nature, he states the passage beginning 'of the things pertaining to enlightenment.' 'Of the things pertaining to enlightenment' means of the thirty-seven things—such as the four establishments of mindfulness and so on—that are on the side of the path knowledge which is the awakening to the four truths. However, in the Exposition of this, only the seven enlightenment factors are pointed out, as they are the special things pertaining to enlightenment in mundane development, because of their ability to proceed on a single object. But by their inclusion, the inclusion of the rest there should also be understood. In 'in going forward, in returning,' etc., 'going forward' is called going ahead; 'returning' is turning back. And both are found in standing, sitting, and lying down, by way of the body's moving towards and moving away, forwards and backwards. 'He acts with clear comprehension' means he is one who does all actions with clear comprehension, or one who is a doer of clear comprehension itself. And here, by the inclusion of clear comprehension, mindfulness too is included because of its inseparability. For that reason, in its Exposition it is said: 'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he goes forward,' and so on.

Ālokitetiādīsu ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhanaṃ. Vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhanaṃ. Imesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ gahaṇena heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhanasaṅkhātāni olokitullokitāpalokitānipi gahitānīti veditabbāni.

In 'in looking at,' etc., 'looking at' (ālokita) means looking forwards. 'Looking around' (vilokita) means looking towards the intermediate directions. But by the inclusion of these two, it should be understood that looking down, looking up, and looking back—called 'olokita,' 'ullokita,' and 'apalokita'—are also included.

Samiñjite [V 0.0182] pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjane, pasāraṇe ca. Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ nivāsanapārupanavasena, pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena ca paribhogo dhāraṇaṃ nāma. Asiteti piṇḍapātādibhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyite. Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya. Sutteti sayane. Jāgariteti jāgaraṇe. Ettha ca bhikkhācāragamanādivasena [M 0.0237] “abhikkante”ti vuttaṃ. Vihāre pana caṅkamanādiiriyāpathavaseneva “gate”tiādi vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Bhāsiteti kathane. Tuṇhībhāveti akathane.

'In bending and stretching' means in the bending and stretching of the limbs. 'In wearing the patchwork outer robe, bowl, and robe': here 'wearing' means the use of the patchwork outer robe and the inner robe by way of dressing and robing, and of the bowl by way of receiving alms and so on. 'In eating' means in eating almsfood and so on. 'In drinking' means in drinking gruel and so on. 'In chewing' means in chewing hard food such as cakes. 'In tasting' means in tasting things like honey and molasses. 'In the act of defecating and urinating' means in the doing of defecation and urination. 'In going' means in movement. 'In standing' means in a standing position. 'In sitting' means in a seated position. 'In being asleep' means in lying down. 'In being awake' means in wakefulness. And here, 'in going forward' was said with reference to going on the almsround and so on. But in the monastery, it should be understood that 'in going' and so on was said with reference to the postures such as walking meditation. 'In speaking' means in talking. 'In being silent' means in not talking.

Sabbesu pana tesu abhikkantādīsu paccekaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññanti catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha abhikkamitukāmatādicitte uppanne cittavaseneva gamanādiṃ akatvā “kiṃ nu me tattha gatena attho”ti pariggaṇhitvā cetiyadassanādino tassa tassa atthassa pariggaṇhanaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ nāma. Sātthakesu panetesu gamanādīsu jīvitabrahmacariyantarāyānañceva sallekhapaṭipattivighātakarānaṃ kāyikacetasikaparikkilesānañca sabbesānaṃ sabbhāvābhāvaṃ pariggahetvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ nāma. Evaṃ pariggahitasātthakasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu, vipassanāya vā attano abhirucitaṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocaraṃ avissajjetvāva abhikkamādīnaṃ karaṇaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ nāma. Abhikkamādīsu pana andhabālaputhujjanā “attā abhikkamādīni karoti, ahaṃ karomī”ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhitvā “abhikkamitukāmatādicittakiriyavāyodhātu vipphārādikāraṇasāmaggiyā ayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāto aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo abhikkamādīni karoti, tato añño abbhantare attā vā satto vā abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā…pe… tuṇhī bhavanto vā natthī”ti evamādinā yāthāvato jānanavasena paññāya pavattanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāma. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 508) gahetabbo.

Furthermore, in all these cases—going forward and so on—clear comprehension should be understood as fourfold in each case: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of the domain, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. Herein, when the thought to go forward and so on arises, without simply acting by the force of that thought, one considers, 'What is the purpose for me in going there?' This discerning of the purpose, such as to see a shrine and so on, is called clear comprehension of purpose. Among these purposeful actions, such as going and so on, one examines the presence or absence of all bodily and mental defilements that obstruct both the life and the holy life, and that are a hindrance to the practice of effacement. This discerning of what is suitable is called clear comprehension of suitability. Having thus discerned the purpose and suitability, the performance of actions like going forward without abandoning one’s chosen meditation subject—whether among the thirty-eight meditation subjects or in insight—is called clear comprehension of the domain. Now, regarding going forward and so on, blind worldlings become deluded, thinking, 'A self performs going forward and so on; I am doing it.' But without such delusion, one understands according to reality through wisdom: 'This aggregate of bones, known as the body, performs going forward and so on due to the combination of conditions such as the intention to go forward and the activity of the air element. Apart from this, there is no inner self or being that is going forward, or going back… or remaining silent.' This is called clear comprehension of non-delusion. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken from the Sammohavinodanī (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 508).

Idāni yasmā yassa abbhantare yathāvuttā ettakā guṇā natthi, tassa araññavāso pana makkaṭādīnaṃ viya anucchaviko [M 0.0238] na hoti, upacāramattampissa jhānaṃ na uppajjati. Yassa pana santi, tassa araññavāso anucchaviko hoti. So hi tattha sabbappakārajjhānaṃ nibbattetuṃ [V 0.0183] sakkoti, araññavāsañceva āraññake ca upasobheti, sakalañca sāsanaṃ pasādeti, tasmā evarūpassa bhikkhuno upāsanaṭṭhānayogapathaṃ sappāyasenāsanaṃ dassento “so vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajatī”tiādimāha. Tattha vivittanti suññaṃ. Seti ceva āsati ca etthāti senāsanaṃ, mañcādi, vihārādi ca. Tenevassa niddese “mañco pīṭha”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, for one who lacks these aforementioned qualities, dwelling in the forest is not suitable, just as it is for monkeys and so on, and not even access jhāna arises for him. But for one who possesses these qualities, dwelling in the forest is suitable. For he is able to produce all kinds of jhāna there; he beautifies both the forest dwelling and the forest-dweller, and inspires confidence in the entire Dispensation. Therefore, to show a suitable lodging for such a bhikkhu, a place conducive to his practice, it is said: 'He resorts to a secluded lodging,' and so on. Herein, 'secluded' means empty. A 'lodging' (senāsana) is where one lies down and sits—that is, a couch, a seat, a monastery, and so on. That is why in the explanation it is said: 'a couch, a seat,' etc.

Idāni aññampissa pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “arañña”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha araññanti vinayapariyāyena tāva ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ, suttantapariyāyena ca āraññakaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchimaṃ araññanti vuttaṃ, abhidhammapariyāyena pana gāmadvārassa indakhīlato bahi sabbaṃ “arañña”nti gahetabbaṃ. “Nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā”ti (vibha. 529) hi vuttaṃ. Kandaranti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena daritaṃ udakena bhinnaṃ pabbatapadesaṃ, yaṃ “nitumba”ntipi “nadīkuñja”ntipi vadanti. Tattha hi rajatapaṭṭasadisavālikāpuline maṇivitānasadise sandacchāye vanagahane nisīditvā maṇikkhandhasadise udake sandamāne sītena vātena bījiyamānassa samaṇadhammaṃ karoto cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti. Giriguhanti dvinnaṃ pabbatānamantaraṃ, ekasmiññeva vā umaṅgasadisaṃ mahāvivaraṃ. Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasanti na vapanti. Tenevassa niddese “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Now, to show another of its divisions, 'forest,' etc., is said. Herein, 'forest,' according to the Vinaya, is all the rest apart from a village and its precincts. According to the Suttanta, with reference to a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, it is said that the forest is the area at least five hundred bow-lengths away. But according to the Abhidhamma, everything outside the village gate-post should be taken as 'forest.' For it is said: 'Having gone out beyond the boundary post.' 'A ravine' (kandara): 'kaṃ' is said to be water; 'daritaṃ' by that is a mountain region split by water, which they also call a 'slope' (nitumba) or a 'river-thicket' (nadīkuñja). There, sitting on sandbanks like silver sheets, in the dense shade of the woods like a jeweled canopy, with water clear as a mass of gems flowing by, fanned by a cool breeze, the mind of one practicing the ascetic's duties becomes concentrated. 'A mountain cave' (giriguhā) is the space between two mountains, or a large tunnel-like opening in a single mountain. 'Wilderness' (vanapattha) is a place beyond the village limits, not frequented by people, where they do not plow or sow. That is why in its explanation it is said: 'Wilderness is a designation for remote lodgings,' and so on.

Abbhokāsanti acchannaṃ. Ākaṅkhamāno panettha cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasati. Palālapuñjanti palālarāsiṃ. Mahāpalālapuñjato [M 0.0239] hi palālaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā pabbhāraleṇasadise ālaye karonti, gacchagumbādīnampi upari palālaṃ pakkhipitvā heṭṭhā nisīdanti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Appasaddantiādīsu vacanasaddena virahitattā appasaddaṃ. Nagaranigghosasaddena ceva migapakkhinigghosena ca rahitattā appanigghosaṃ. Vijanavātanti anusañcarakajanassa sarīravātena virahitattā vijanavātaṃ, “vijanavāda”ntipi pāṭho. Senāsanassa anto janavādasaddena rahitanti attho. Manussānaṃ rahassa kiriyārahattā manussarāhasseyyakaṃ, tato tato paṭinivattitvā sammadeva kammaṭṭhāne cittassa līyanato paṭisallānasaṅkhātassa vivekassa bhāvanārāmassa anurūpattā paṭisallānasāruppaṃ. Bhajatīti sambandho. Araññagatotiādīsu araññaṃ, rukkhamūlañca ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ sabbampi senāsanaṃ suññāgārena saṅgahitaṃ.

'In the open' means unroofed. If he wishes, he can make a hut of robes there and live. 'A heap of straw' means a pile of straw. For they pull straw from a large heap of straw and make shelters like caves in a cliff; or they place straw on top of bushes and shrubs and sit underneath. This is said in reference to that. In 'with little sound,' etc., 'with little sound' means free from the sound of speech. 'With little noise' means free from the clamor of cities and the cries of beasts and birds. 'With breezes of seclusion' means free from the bodily 'wind' of people moving about. There is also the reading 'vijanavāda' (secluded from talk); the meaning is free from the sound of people's talk inside the lodging. 'Fit for the secret life of humans' because it is suitable for secret actions. 'Suitable for seclusion' because it is fit for developing the seclusion called withdrawal, since the mind, having turned back from this and that, settles right down upon the meditation subject. The connection is with 'resorts to.' In 'gone to the forest,' etc., apart from the forest and the root of a tree, all the remaining lodgings are included under 'empty hut'.

Pallaṅkaṃ [V 0.0184] ābhujitvāti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimakāyaṃ ujuṃ ṭhapetvā, aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evaṃ nisinnassa hi cammamaṃsanahārūni na paṇamanti, athassa tesaṃ apaṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā na uppajjanti, tato cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ upagacchati. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ paṭṭhapetvā, mukhasamīpe vā katvā. Tenevassa niddese “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti sūpaṭṭhitā, nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā”ti (vibha. 537) vuttaṃ. Mukhanimittanti cettha uttaroṭṭhassa vemajjhapadeso, yattha nāsikāvāto paṭihaññati. Atha vā “parīti pariggahaṭṭho, mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho, satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho, tena vuccati parimukhaṃ sati”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho “pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvā”ti.

'Having folded his legs crosswise' means having bound the thighs together all around in a seated posture. 'Holding his body erect' means keeping the upper body straight, making the eighteen spinal vertebrae connect end to end. For one sitting thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews are not bent; then, because they are not bent, painful feelings do not arise for him moment after moment. Thereby his mind becomes concentrated, and the meditation subject grows. 'Having established mindfulness in front of him' means having established mindfulness facing the meditation subject, or having made it present at the mouth. That is why in its explanation it is said: 'This mindfulness is established, well-established, at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth.' Herein, 'the sign of the mouth' is the central point of the upper lip where the air from the nose strikes. Alternatively, the meaning here should be seen according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: '“Pari” has the sense of grasping, “mukha” has the sense of outlet, “sati” has the sense of establishment; thus it is called “parimukhaṃ sati.”' The brief meaning there is: 'having made mindfulness a grasped outlet'.

Abhijjhaṃ [M 0.0240] loketiādīsu abhimukhaṃ jhāyati cintetīti abhijjhā, rāgo. Lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko, pañcupādānakkhandhā. Tesu kāmacchandaṃ vikkhambhetvāti attho. Vikkhambhanavaseneva vigatābhijjhena, na cakkhuviññāṇādisadisenāti attho. Cetasāti cittena, itthambhūto viharatīti attho. Abhijjhāyāti abhijjhāto. Cittaṃ parisodhetīti yathā naṃ sā muñcitvā na puna gaṇhāti, evaṃ parimocetīti attho. Byāpajjati iminā cittaṃ pūtikummāsādayo viya pakatiṃ jahātīti byāpādo. Vikārappattiyā padussati, paraṃ vā padūseti vināsetīti padoso, ubhayampetaṃ kodhassevādhivacanaṃ. Yasmā cetaṃ sabbakammaṭṭhānasādhāraṇavasena desīyati, tasmā “sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī”ti evaṃ mettāvasena avatvā “abyāpannacitto”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

In 'covetousness in the world,' etc., 'covetousness' (abhijjhā) is so called because one contemplates or thinks about something with longing; it is lust. 'World' (loko) is so called in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating; it means the five aggregates subject to clinging. The meaning is that one has suppressed sensual desire in regard to them. The meaning of 'with covetousness abandoned' is that it is abandoned by way of suppression, not in the way that eye-consciousness and so on are. 'With a mind' (cetasā) means one dwells with a mind that has become like that. 'From covetousness' (abhijjhāya). 'He purifies his mind' means he fully liberates it so that, having been released from it, it does not take it up again. 'Ill will' (byāpādo) is so called because by it the mind is afflicted, abandoning its natural state like spoiled gruel. 'Malice' (padoso) is so called because it is corrupted by being distorted, or it corrupts and destroys another. Both are synonyms for anger. And since this is taught as common to all meditation subjects, instead of speaking by way of loving-kindness, as 'compassionate for the welfare of all living beings,' just this much was said: 'with a mind free from ill will'.

Thinaṃ cittassa gelaññaṃ, middhaṃ cetasikānaṃ. Ālokasaññīti rattiyampi divāpi diṭṭhaālokasañjānanasaññāya samannāgato, tāya pana ālokasaññāya thinamiddhavinodanassa visesato satisampajaññaṃ icchitabbanti āha “sato sampajāno”ti.

'Sloth' (thina) is the sickness of the mind; 'torpor' (middha) is the sickness of the mental factors. 'Perceiving light' means being endowed with the perception that recognizes light seen by day or by night. But since by means of this perception of light, mindfulness and clear comprehension are especially desired for the dispelling of sloth and torpor, it is said, 'mindful and clearly comprehending'.

Anuddhatoti avikkhitto tathā eva ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto. Tiṇṇavicikicchoti vicikicchaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhito. Akathaṃkathī kusalesu dhammesūti anavajjadhammesu “kathaṃ ime, kathaṃ ime”ti evaṃ pavattanato kathaṃkathīsaṅkhātāya vicikicchāya virahito. Evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇappahānaṃ [V 0.0185] dassetvā idāni yasmā appahīnanīvaraṇassa jhānaṃ na uppajjati, na hi kāmacchandādīhi nānāvisayavikkhittacittaṃ ekattārammaṇe samādhiyati, na kāmadhātusamatikkamanāya vā paṭipajjati, tasmā “so ime pañca nīvaraṇe pahāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha [M 0.0241] soti yo yathāvuttasīlādiguṇe patiṭṭhāya araññādianurūpasenāsanagato attano cariyānukulakammaṭṭhāne līnuddhaccarahitāya sātaccakiriyāya uppāditupacārajjhānena pahīnapañcanīvaraṇo paṭhamajjhānādhigamāya vāyamati, soti attho.

‘Unagitated’ means not agitated, and likewise, with mind inwardly pacified. ‘Having crossed over doubt’ means one who stands having overcome doubt. ‘Not perplexed about wholesome states’ refers to being free from the doubt reckoned as ‘how-and-what-ness,’ which arises from wondering, ‘How are these? How are these?’ regarding blameless states. Having thus shown the abandoning of the five hindrances, now, because jhāna does not arise for one whose hindrances are not abandoned—for a mind distracted by various objects through sensual desire and so on is not concentrated on a single object, nor does it practice for the surmounting of the sense-sphere—therefore, it is said, ‘He, having abandoned these five hindrances…,’ etc. Herein, ‘he’ refers to one who, established in the qualities of virtue as described, having gone to a suitable dwelling such as a forest, with continuous effort free from sloth and restlessness at a meditation subject suitable for one’s temperament, has abandoned the five hindrances by means of access concentration that has been generated and strives for the attainment of the first jhāna—this is the meaning.

Cetaso upakkileseti cittassa appabhassarabhāvakaraṇe. Paññāya dubbalīkaraṇeti yasmā ime nīvaraṇā uppajjamānā anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na denti, uppannāya pana lokiyaaṭṭhasamāpattiyā, abhiññābhūtāya vā mūlaṃ upacchinditvā pātenti, tasmā “paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā”ti vuccanti. Vivicceva kāmehītiādīsu kāmehīti vatthukāmakilesakāmehi. Viviccevāti viviccitvā vinā hutvā, apakkamitvāti attho. Niyamatthena panettha eva-kārena jhānapaṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ kāmānaṃ pariccāgeneva paṭhamajjhānādhigamo, andhakārapariccāgeneva dīpappavatti viyāti dasseti. Uttarapadepi cesa eva-kāro ānetvā “vivicceva akusalehi dhammehī”ti sambandhitabbo. Na hi sakkā kāmato aññehi nīvaraṇasaṅkhātehi akusaladhammehi aviviccāpi jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Padadvayepi pana “viviccā”ti iminā kāyavivekādīsu, tadaṅgavivekādīsu ca tadaṅganissaraṇavivekavajjitā sabbepi vivekā idha adhippetā. Vatthukāmavivekavacanato hi kāyaviveko vutto, kilesakāmehi pana sesākusalehi ca vivekavacanato cittaupadhivivekā, vikkhambhanādivivekā ca vuttā. Lokuttarajjhānampi saṅgahitattā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evametena padadvayena yathākkamaṃ kāmacchandanīvaraṇasesanīvaraṇavikkhambhanādiko vutto. Evaṃ oghādīsupi yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

‘Defilements of the mind,’ because they cause the mind to lose its luminosity. ‘Weakeners of wisdom,’ because when these hindrances arise, they prevent mundane and supramundane wisdom that has not yet arisen from arising; and as for wisdom that has arisen, whether in the eight mundane attainments or as higher knowledge, they cut off its root and make it fall. Therefore, they are called ‘weakeners of wisdom.’ In the phrase ‘secluded from sensual pleasures,’ ‘from sensual pleasures’ (kāmehi) refers to both sensual objects and sensual defilements. ‘Secluded indeed’ (vivicceva) means having separated from, being without, or having withdrawn—this is the meaning. Here, the particle ‘indeed’ (eva) has the sense of a rule, showing that the attainment of the first jhāna comes only through the abandonment of sensual pleasures, which are the opponents of jhāna, just as the appearance of a lamp comes only through the abandonment of darkness. This particle ‘indeed’ should also be brought into the following phrase and connected as ‘secluded indeed from unwholesome states.’ For it is impossible to enter and abide in jhāna without also having become secluded from the other unwholesome states reckoned as hindrances. In the two phrases, by the word ‘secluded,’ all types of seclusion are intended here—such as bodily seclusion, seclusion by substitution of opposites, etc.—except for seclusion by escape. For by the mention of seclusion from sensual objects, bodily seclusion is stated; but by the mention of seclusion from sensual defilements and the other unwholesome states, mental seclusion, seclusion from the substrata, and seclusion by suppression, etc., are stated. Supramundane jhāna should also be understood as included. Thus, by these two phrases, the suppression of the hindrance of sensual desire and of the remaining hindrances is stated in sequence. Similarly, this should be applied as appropriate in the case of the floods, etc.

Ettāvatā ca paṭhamassa jhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”ntiādi vuttaṃ[M 0.0242]. Tattha vitakkena ca vicārena ca saha vattati rukkho viya pupphena, phalena cāti idaṃ jhānaṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti vuccati. Vivekajanti ettha vivitti viveko, nīvaraṇavigamoti attho. Vivittoti vā viveko, nīvaraṇavivitto jhānasampayuttadhammarāsīti attho, tasmā vivekato, tasmiṃ vā viveke jātanti vivekajaṃ. Pītisukhanti ettha pītīti appanāppattā pharaṇāpīti, sukhañca taṃsampayuttaṃ, iti ayañca pīti [V 0.0186] idañca sukhaṃ assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā atthīti idaṃ jhānaṃ “pītisukha”nti vuccati. Atha vā pīti ca sukhañca pītisukhaṃ, vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ assa, asmiṃ vāti vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ, evaṃ ekapadavasena “vivekajapītisukha”nti vattabbe niggahītāgamaṃ katvā “vivekajaṃ pītisukha”ntipi vattuṃ yujjati. Yatheva hi jhānaṃ, evaṃ pītisukhampi vivekajameva hotīti. Paṭhamaṃ jhānanti gaṇanānupubbato paṭhamaṃ, paṭhamaṃ uppattitopi paṭhamaṃ. Ārammaṇūpanijjhānato, paccanīkajhāpanato vā jhānaṃ, iminā nayena upari “dutiyaṃ jhāna”ntiādīsu attho veditabbo. Upasampajja viharatīti evaṃ pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ adhigantvā tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena pavattatīti attho. Ettha ca cittekaggatā kiñcāpi “savitakkasavicāra”nti imasmiṃ pāṭhe na niddiṭṭhā, tathāpi vibhaṅge “jhānanti vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 569) vuttattā aṅgameva.

Having thus shown the abandoning factors of the first jhāna, now to show its associated factors, it is said: ‘accompanied by applied and sustained thought,’ etc. Herein, just as a tree exists along with its flowers and fruits, so this jhāna exists along with applied thought and sustained thought—thus it is called ‘accompanied by applied and sustained thought.’ ‘Born of seclusion’ (vivekajaṃ): Here, seclusion (viveka) means detachment, the removal of hindrances. Or, seclusion is the secluded—the collection of jhāna-associated states that is secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is ‘born of seclusion’ because it arises from seclusion or exists within seclusion. ‘With rapture and happiness’ (pītisukhaṃ): Here, rapture (pīti) refers to the pervading rapture that has reached absorption, and happiness (sukha) is what accompanies it. Thus, this jhāna possesses both rapture and happiness—therefore it is called ‘with rapture and happiness.’ Alternatively, rapture and happiness are ‘rapture-happiness’; it has rapture-happiness born of seclusion, or there is in it rapture-happiness born of seclusion. Thus, though it could be expressed as a single compound (vivekajapītisukhaṃ), by inserting a niggahita it is also correct to say ‘born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness.’ For just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too are the rapture and happiness. ‘The first jhāna’: it is ‘first’ in the sequence of enumeration and also ‘first’ in the order of arising. It is called ‘jhāna’ from its contemplating the object or from its burning up the opposing states. In this way, the meaning should be understood for the subsequent terms like ‘the second jhāna,’ etc. ‘Enters and abides’: having attained the first jhāna—which is free from five factors, endowed with five factors, threefold wholesome, and complete with ten characteristics—one abides, conducting oneself in a posture suitable to it. Here, although one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is not explicitly mentioned in this passage, it is nevertheless a factor, as stated in the Vibhaṅga: ‘Jhāna is applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind’ (Vibh. 569).

Evaṃ paṭhamajjhānādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni tadanantaraṃ adhigatapaṭhamajjhānassa taṃ āvajjanasamāpajjanavuṭṭhānādhiṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇasaṅkhātāhi pañcahi vasīhi vasībhūtaṃ katvā tato vuṭṭhāya tattha āsannanīvaraṇapaccatthikatāya ceva oḷārikavitakkavicārakkhobhasamaṅgitāya ca dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya vitakkādibhedoḷārikaṅgappahānāya, pītiādisantaṅgapaṭilābhāya [M 0.0243] ca tadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ punappunaṃ manasikaroto dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ uppajjati, tappādakañca lokuttarajjhānaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānena dassetuṃ “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”tiādimāha. Tattha vūpasamāti samatikkamā, dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ajjhattanti attani jātaṃ, attasantāne nibbattanti attho. Sampasādananti saddhāsaṅkhātasampasādanayogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Ekodibhāvanti ettha vitakkavicārehi anajjhāruḷhattā eko aggo seṭṭho udetīti ekodi, samādhi. Taṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti dutiyajjhānaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ. So panāyaṃ ekodi yasmā cetaso, na sattassa, na jīvassa, tasmā etaṃ “cetaso ekodibhāva”nti vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown the attainment of the first jhāna, now, after one has attained the first jhāna and brought it to a state of mastery by the five kinds of mastery—namely, adverting, attaining, emerging, resolving, and reviewing—one emerges from it. Then, seeing the fault in it on account of its proximity to the hindrances as its enemy and its possession of the disturbance of gross applied and sustained thought, and having overcome delight in it, one repeatedly gives attention to that same meditation subject in order to abandon the gross factors of applied thought, etc., and to acquire the tranquil factors of rapture, etc. Thereupon the second jhāna arises. To show this, and the supramundane jhāna which is based on it, with reference to the person, it is said: ‘With the stilling of applied and sustained thought…,’ etc. Herein, ‘stilling’ means transcending; it is said to mean their non-manifestation at the moment of the second jhāna. ‘Internal’ means born in oneself, arisen in one’s own continuum. ‘Confidence’: because of its connection with confidence in the sense of faith, the jhāna itself is called ‘confidence,’ like a blue cloth is called ‘blue’ because of its connection with the color blue. ‘Unification of mind’: here, because it is not overridden by applied and sustained thought, it arises as one, foremost, and best; thus it is `ekodi`, which is concentration. One develops and cultivates this; hence the second jhāna is the unification of mind. And since this unification pertains to the mind, not to a being or a soul, it is called ‘unification of mind.’

Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, ayañca ekodināmako samādhi, atha kasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti? Vuccate – imasmiñhi jhāne vitakkavicārakkhobhābhāvena balavatī saddhā, samādhi ca, tasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti. Avitakkaṃ avicāranti bhāvanāya pahīnattā natthi [V 0.0187] etasmiṃ, etassa vā vitakko vicāro, na tatiyajjhānādi viya, cakkhuviññāṇādi viya ca abhāvappattito, tasmā imassa “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti idaṃ kāraṇavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samādhijanti paṭhamajjhānasamādhito, sampayuttasamādhito vā jātaṃ, vitakkādikkhobhābhāvena cetassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ idameva “samādhija”nti vuttaṃ. Upasampajja viharatīti evaṃ duvaṅgavippahīnaṃ tivaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇādiyuttaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ adhigantvā vuttanayena vattatīti attho.

Now, is not this faith present also in the first jhāna, and is not this concentration also called unification? Why, then, is it stated thus only here? It is said: because in this jhāna, faith and concentration are strong due to the absence of the disturbance of applied and sustained thought. Therefore, it is stated thus only here. ‘Without applied thought, without sustained thought’: because they have been abandoned through development, this jhāna is without them, nor does it possess applied thought and sustained thought. This is unlike the third jhāna and so on, or eye-consciousness and so on, where their absence is due to their non-existence. Therefore, the phrase ‘with the stilling of applied and sustained thought’ should be seen as a statement of the reason. ‘Born of concentration’: born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or from its associated concentration. For the purpose of extolling the state of mind due to the absence of disturbance from applied thought and the like, this alone is called ‘born of concentration.’ ‘Enters and abides’: having attained the second jhāna, which is devoid of two factors, endowed with three factors, and connected with the threefold wholesomeness and so on, one abides in the manner described. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ dutiyajjhānādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni tadanantaraṃ adhigatadutiyajjhānassa taṃ vuttanayeneva vasībhūtaṃ katvā tattha [M 0.0244] āsannavitakkavicārapaccatthikatāya ceva oḷārikapītaṅgasamaṅgitāya ca dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya tadoḷārikaṅgappahānāya sesasantaṅgapaṭilābhāya tadevārammaṇaṃ punappunaṃ manasikaroto tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ uppajjati, tappādakañca lokuttaraṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “pītiyā ca virāgā”tiādimāha. Tattha virajjanaṃ virāgo, samatikkamo, tasmā virāgā. Ca-kārena vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamaṃ sampiṇḍeti “pītiyā ca virāgā, vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti. Idañcetassa āgamanamaggaparidīpanatthaṃ, vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañca vuttaṃ. Upekkhako viharatīti ettha upapattito ikkhati apakkhapatitā hutvā passatīti upekkhā, tatramajjhattatā. Tāya visadāya pītivirāgapadaṭṭhānāya thāmagatāya samannāgatattā tatiyajjhānasamaṅgī “upekkhako”ti vuccati, vitakkādikkhobhābhāvena panesā ettheva paribyattakiccā jātā, na paṭhamajjhānādīsūti. Sato ca sampajānoti puggalādhiṭṭhānena sati ca sampajaññañca vuttaṃ, idañca satisampajaññabaleneva ṭhitaṃ taṃpītisahacaritaṃ sukhaṃ, tato apanītaṃ vaccho viya bandhanabalena dhenuṃ pītiṃ na upagacchati, imasmiñca sati atimadhure sukhe yogino na sārajjanti, no aññathāti imampi atthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ idheva vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti ettha kiñcāpi tatiyajjhānasamaṅgino sukhapaṭisaṃvedanābhogo natthi, evaṃ santepi yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ atipaṇītaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhitena tassa atipaṇītena rūpena rūpakāyo phuṭṭho, yassa phuṭṭhattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi kāyikasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya, tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento “sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetī”ti āha. Yaṃ tantiādīsu yanti yasmā, yaṃ [M 0.0245] jhānahetūti attho. Tanti taṃ tatiyajjhānasamaṅgipuggalaṃ buddhādayo ariyā ācikkhanti pasaṃsanti. Kinti? “Upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī”ti. Evaṃ ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ duvaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇādiyuttaṃ [V 0.0188] tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ adhigantvā pavattatīti attho. Yaṃ pana jhānaṃ vibhaṅge “jhānanti upekkhā sati sampajaññaṃ sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 591) vuttaṃ, taṃ saparikkhāraṃ jhānaṃ dassetuṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Upanijjhānalakkhaṇānaṃ pana sukhacittekaggatānaṃ vasena duvaṅgikamevetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hotī”tiādi (vibha. 624).

Having thus shown the attainment of the second jhāna, now, for one who has attained the second jhāna, after he has mastered it in the way described and has seen the fault in it—because applied and sustained thought are its near enemies and because it possesses the gross factor of rapture—and after he has overcome delight in it, for the abandoning of that gross factor and for the attainment of the remaining peaceful factors, as he gives repeated attention to that same object, the third jhāna arises, and the supramundane jhāna based on it. To show this, the text begins, ‘With the fading away of rapture….’ Herein, virāga means fading away, transcending; hence virāgā (with the fading away). The word ‘and’ (ca) includes the stilling of applied and sustained thought, the meaning being: ‘with the fading away of rapture, and with the stilling of applied and sustained thought.’ This is stated to explain its path of approach and to praise it. ‘He dwells equanimous’: Herein, equanimity (upekkhā) means looking on with an attitude of neutrality, seeing without partiality; it is impartiality. Because one who has attained the third jhāna is endowed with this clear, powerful equanimity, which has the fading of rapture as its basis, he is called ‘equanimous.’ Moreover, because there is no disturbance from applied thought and so on, its function becomes fully manifest right here, not in the first jhāna and so on. ‘Mindful and clearly comprehending’: This refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension with the person as the basis. And this happiness, which was accompanied by rapture, is now established by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Being withdrawn from rapture, it does not go back to it, just as a calf, tied up, does not go back to the cow. And when this mindfulness is present, yogis are not infatuated by this exceedingly sweet happiness, as they otherwise would be. This too should be understood as stated here to show this special meaning. ‘And he experiences happiness with the body’: Herein, although one who has attained the third jhāna has no advertence to experiencing happiness, nevertheless, because there is for him an extremely sublime happiness associated with the mental body, and because the physical body is pervaded by the extremely sublime form born of that happiness, one who has emerged from that jhāna might experience bodily happiness due to that pervasion. Therefore, to show this meaning, it is said: ‘and he experiences happiness with the body.’ ‘That which the noble ones describe…’: Here, ‘that which’ (yaṃ) means ‘because of which’ (yasmā), that is, ‘because of this jhāna.’ ‘That’ (taṃ) refers to the person who has attained the third jhāna, whom the noble ones, such as the Buddhas, describe and praise. How? As ‘equanimous, mindful, a happy dweller.’ Thus, having abandoned one factor and possessing two factors, endowed with the threefold excellence, one attains and abides in the third jhāna. This is the meaning. But as to the jhāna which in the Vibhaṅga is described as: ‘Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, happiness, and unification of mind’ (Vibh. 591), that is stated figuratively to show the jhāna with its accessories. However, it should be understood as having two factors in terms of the characteristics of absorption, namely, happiness and unification of mind. As it is said: ‘The jhāna has two factors,’ and so on (Vibh. 624).

Evaṃ tatiyajjhānādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni tadanantaraṃ adhigatatatiyajjhānassa taṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvā tato vuṭṭhāya tattha vuttanayena dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya oḷārikasukhaṅgappahānāya, upekkhekaggatāsaṅkhātasesasantaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva nimittaṃ manasikaroto catutthaṃ jhānaṃ uppajjati, tappādakañca lokuttaraṃ, taṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānena dassetuṃ “sukhassa ca pahānā”tiādimāha. Tattha sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānāti kāyikassa sukhassa, dukkhassa ca pahānā. Pubbevāti tañca kho pubbeva, na catutthajjhānakkhaṇeti attho. Somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cetasikassa sukhassa, dukkhassa ca pubbeva pahānā. Kadā pana tesaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti? Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe. Dukkhadomanassasukhasomanassāni hi yathākkamaṃ paṭhamādicatunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe eva pahīyanti. Yadi evaṃ, kasmā panesa “vivicceva…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, etthuppannaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.510) evaṃ jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti? Atisayanirodhassa [M 0.0246] vuttattā. Upacārakkhaṇesu hi yo nirodho, so nirodho eva, nātisayanirodho, so pana jhānakkhaṇesu eva. Tato eva hi tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ katanti, tattha tattha pana pahīnāpi etā vedanā ettha duviññeyyalakkhaṇāya adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya dukkhādibyatirekena sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ, vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañcassa jhānassa samāhaṭā, paccayadassanatthañcassa. Yathāha – “cattāro kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā, idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.458).

Having thus shown the attainment of the third jhāna, now, for one who has attained the third jhāna, after he has mastered it, emerged from it, seen the fault in it in the way described, and overcome his attachment to it, for the abandoning of the gross factor of pleasure and for the attainment of the remaining peaceful factors called equanimity and one-pointedness, as he gives attention to that same sign, the fourth jhāna arises, and the supramundane jhāna based on it. To show this with the person as the basis, the text begins, ‘With the abandoning of pleasure….’ Herein, ‘with the abandoning of pleasure and with the abandoning of pain’ means with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and pain. ‘Previously’ means indeed before that, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna; this is the meaning. ‘With the disappearance of joy and sorrow’ means with the previous abandoning of mental pleasure and pain. But when does their abandoning occur? In the access moment of the four jhānas. For pain, sorrow, pleasure, and joy are abandoned respectively in the access moments of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas. If so, why then is it said in the suttas, ‘Secluded… he enters and dwells in the first jhāna; herein the faculty of pain that has arisen ceases without remainder… he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; herein the faculty of joy that has arisen ceases without remainder’ (SN 48:40), thus stating that the cessation occurs in the jhānas themselves? Because the ultimate cessation is spoken of. For the cessation in the access moments is just cessation, not ultimate cessation; that occurs only in the jhāna moments. That is why the word ‘without remainder’ is used in each case. Moreover, although these feelings have been abandoned in their respective places, they are brought together here to distinguish the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, which is difficult to discern, from pain and so on; for the sake of grasping what is meant by ‘pleasure’ that is abandoned; for praising this jhāna; and for showing its condition. As it is said: ‘Friend, there are four conditions for the attainment of the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Here, friend, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure…’ and so on (MN 44).

Upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti tatramajjhattatāsaṅkhātāya upekkhāya janitasatiyā pārisuddhi. Nirupaklesatāya hi taṃ parisuddhattaṃ. Na kevalañcettha upekkhāya sati eva parisuddhā, apica kho sabbepi sampayuttadhammā, satisīsena panāyaṃ desanā katāti. Upasampajja viharatīti evaṃ ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ [V 0.0189] duvaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇādiyuttaṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ adhigantvā tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena pavattatīti attho.

‘Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity’: This is the purity of mindfulness that is generated by equanimity, which is defined as neutrality. For its purity is due to the absence of defilements. And not only is mindfulness purified here by equanimity, but so too are all its associated states. However, this teaching is given with mindfulness as the heading. ‘He enters and dwells’: The meaning is that having attained the fourth jhāna—which has one factor abandoned, is endowed with two factors, and is possessed of the threefold excellence—he abides, conducting himself with a posture and mode of living suitable to it.

Evaṃ rūpāvacaralokuttaracatukkajjhānaṃ dassetvā idāni arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ dassento yaṃ tattha paṭhamaṃ, evaṃ adhigatarūpāvacaracatutthajjhānassa karajarūpe daṇḍādānādīnañceva cakkhurogādiābādhānañca vasena diṭṭhādīnavassa karajarūpassa samatikkamāya ākāsakasiṇavirahitesu navasu kasiṇesu aññatarasmiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā tassārammaṇabhūtaṃ kasiṇapaṭibhāgarūpampi karajarūpapaṭibhāgatāya, araññe sappānubandhassa bhayena palāyato rajjutālapaṇṇādiṃ sappapaṭibhāgatāya viya samatikkamitukāmassa pañcahākārehi taṃ jhānaṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvā tato vuṭṭhāya tattha [M 0.0247] nibbejanīyarūpapaṭibhāgārammaṇatāya, āsannasomanassapaccatthikatāya ca dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya aṅgesu samatikkamitabbābhāvena ārammaṇasamatikkamabhūtaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ santato manasikaritvā cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ vā yattakaṃ vā icchati, tattakaṃ kasiṇaṃ pattharitvā vā kasiṇaṃ amanasikaritvā tena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti vā “ananto ākāso”ti vā manasikārena kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā vā taṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsanimittaṃ “ākāso”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ tāva dassetuṃ “sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā”tiādimāha.

Having thus shown the four jhānas of the form sphere and the supramundane, now, to show the formless-sphere jhānas, beginning with the first of them: For one who has attained the fourth form-sphere jhāna and has seen the dangers in the physical body—in terms of taking up sticks and so on, and of afflictions such as eye diseases—and who wishes to transcend the physical body, he first develops the fourth jhāna in one of the nine kasiṇas other than the space kasiṇa. Then, wishing to transcend the kasiṇa’s counterpart sign, which is the object of that jhāna, because it is a counterpart of the physical body—just as one fleeing in fear from a place in the forest haunted by a snake might wish to transcend a rope or a palm leaf that is a counterpart of a snake—he masters that jhāna in the five ways and emerges from it. Then, having seen the fault in that object—namely, that it is a counterpart sign of form, which is a basis for revulsion, and that joy is its near enemy—and having overcome his attachment to it, since there are no factors to be transcended among the jhāna factors, he gives peaceful attention to the base of boundless space, which constitutes the transcending of the object. As he does so—either by extending the kasiṇa as far as the world-sphere or as far as he wishes, and then, not attending to the kasiṇa but to the space touched by it, he removes the kasiṇa by attending to it as ‘space, space’ or ‘boundless space’; or else, by repeatedly attending to the sign of space from which the kasiṇa has been removed as ‘space’—the base of boundless space arises. To show this, the text begins, ‘With the complete transcendence of perceptions of form….’

Tattha sabbasoti sabbākārena, sabbāsaṃ vā anavasesānanti attho. Rūpasaññānanti saññāsīsena vuttānaṃ kusalavipākakiriyavasena pañcadasarūpāvacarajjhānānañceva tadārammaṇānañca. Rūpajjhānampi hi “rūpe saññā rūpasaññā”ti evaṃ saññāsīsena vuccati, tadārammaṇakasiṇampi rūpanti saññā nāmamassāti “rūpasañña”nti vuccati. Samatikkamāti virāgā, nirodhā ca. Vibhaṅge pana saññāsu samatikkantāsu ārammaṇaṃ samatikkantameva hotīti “samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā”tiādinā (vibha. 602) saññānameva samatikkamo vutto, ārammaṇe avirattassa saññāsamatikkamo natthevāti taṃ samatikkamavasenāpi atthavaṇṇanā kātabbāva.

Herein, ‘completely’ (sabbaso) means in every way, or of all without remainder; this is the meaning. ‘Perceptions of form’ refers to the fifteen form-sphere jhānas—spoken of under the heading of perception—in their wholesome, resultant, and functional aspects, and to their objects. For the form jhāna itself is called ‘perception of form’ under the heading of perception thus: ‘perception in relation to form is perception of form.’ And its object, the kasiṇa, is also called ‘perception of form’ because perception has ‘form’ as its designation. ‘Transcendence’ means through fading away and through cessation. In the Vibhaṅga, however, since the object is transcended when the perceptions are transcended, only the transcendence of perceptions is mentioned, as in the passage beginning: ‘For one who has attained, or for one who has been reborn, or for one who is a happy dweller in this very life…’ (Vibh. 602). Since for one who is not dispassionate towards the object there is no transcendence of perception, the explanation of the meaning must be made in terms of the transcendence of the object as well.

Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ, rūpādīnañca ārammaṇānaṃ paṭighātena samuppannā [V 0.0190] dvipañcaviññāṇasaññā paṭighasaññā, tāsaṃ atthaṅgamā. Kiñcāpi tā rūpāvacarajjhānasamāpannassāpi na santi, atha kho na pahīnattā na santi. Na hi rūpavirāgāya rūpāvacarabhāvanā saṃvattati, rūpāyattāva etāsaṃ [M 0.0248] pavatti, ayaṃ pana bhāvanā rūpavirāgāya saṃvattati, tasmā tā ettha pahīnāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārāti nānatte gocare pavattānaṃ, nānattānaṃ vā manoviññāṇadhātuvasena pavattānañca catucattālīsakāmāvacarasaññānaṃ amanasikārā anāvajjanā. Ettha ca rūpapaṭighasaññānaṃ iminā jhānena nibbattabhavepi anuppattito “samatikkamā atthaṅgamā”ti evaṃ abhāvo eva vutto. “Nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā”ti aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalānaṃ navakiriyānaṃ dasākusalānaṃ vasena sattavīsatisaññānaṃ arūpabhavepi manasikārena uppattisambhavato tāsaṃ amanasikārā icceva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

The passing away of perceptions of resistance: Perceptions of resistance are the perceptions of the two sets of fivefold consciousness that have arisen through the impact of the bases such as the eye and the objects such as forms; it is their passing away. Although they are not present for one who has attained a form-sphere jhāna, this is not because they have been abandoned. For the development of the form-sphere jhānas does not lead to dispassion towards form; their occurrence is dependent on form. But this development leads to dispassion towards form; therefore it is proper to say that they are abandoned here. By not attending to perceptions of diversity means the non-attending, the non-adverting to the forty-four sense-sphere perceptions that occur in regard to diverse objects or that occur by way of the mind-consciousness element. Here, since perceptions of resistance to forms do not arise even in an existence produced by this jhāna, their absence is stated thus: 'by transcending... their passing away.' As to 'by not attending to perceptions of diversity,' it should be understood that since twenty-seven perceptions—namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome, nine functional, and ten unwholesome—can possibly arise even in the formless existence through attention, it is just their non-attention that is stated.

Ananto ākāsoti ettha nāssa uppādanto vā vayanto vā paññāyatīti ananto. Ākāsoti kasiṇugghāṭimākāso vuccati, manasikāravasenapettha anantatā veditabbā. Teneva vibhaṅge vuttaṃ “tasmiṃ ākāse cittaṃ ṭhapeti…pe… anantaṃ pharati, tena vuccati ananto ākāso”ti (vibha. 605). Idaṃ panassa bhāvanākāradassanaṃ. Ākāsānañcāyatananti ettha nāssa antoti anantaṃ ākāsameva anantaṃ ākāsānantaṃ, ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ, tadeva ākāsānañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena, sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ, taṃ ārammaṇamassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Taṃ upasampajja vuttanayena viharatīti attho.

'Space is infinite': here, since its arising or passing away is not discerned, it is infinite. 'Space' refers to the space created by the removal of the kasiṇa; its infinity should be understood by way of attention. For that reason it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'He establishes the mind in that space... he pervades it as infinite; therefore it is called "infinite space"' (Vibh 605). This, however, is a demonstration of the method of its development. 'Base of the infinity of space': here, 'it has no end,' thus it is infinite. Infinite space itself is the infinity of space (ākāsānantaṃ). The infinity of space itself is ākāsānañcaṃ. That same ākāsānañcaṃ is a base (āyatana) in the sense of a foundation and in the sense of a meeting place. It is the object for this jhāna with its associated states; thus it is the base of the infinity of space. The meaning is that having entered upon and attained it, one dwells in the way described.

Evaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ tadanantaraṃ adhigatapaṭhamāruppassa taṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvā tattha āsannarūpajjhānapaccatthikatāya, rūpapaṭibhāgākāsārammaṇatāya ca dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya taṃ samatikkamāya ākāsaṃ pharitvā pavattaṃ viññāṇaṃ “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti punappunaṃ [M 0.0249] manasikaroto viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ “sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pubbe vuttanayena jhānampi ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ārammaṇampi. Ārammaṇampi hi purimanayena ākāsānañcañca taṃ paṭhamāruppassa ārammaṇattā vuttanayena āyatanañcāti “ākāsānañcāyatana”nti vuccati. Iti ubhayassāpi appavattikaraṇena, amanasikaraṇena ca ekajjhaṃ katvā “ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Having thus shown the attainment of the base of the infinity of space, now for one who has attained the first formless attainment and brought it to mastery, having seen the fault in its being an adversary close to the form jhānas and in having as its object the space that is the counterpart of form, and having overcome delight in it, in order to transcend it, the base of the infinity of consciousness arises for him as he repeatedly attends to the consciousness that occurred pervading space as 'consciousness is infinite.' To show this, the passage beginning 'by completely transcending the base of the infinity of space...' was stated. Here, in the way stated before, both the jhāna and its object are the base of the infinity of space. For the object, too, is the infinity of space (ākāsānañcaṃ) according to the previous method, and since it is the object of the first formless attainment, it is a base (āyatana) in the way stated; thus it is called 'the base of the infinity of space.' Thus, it should be understood that this was stated, 'by transcending the base of the infinity of space,' having treated both as one by causing them not to occur and by not attending to them.

Anantaṃ [V 0.0191] viññāṇanti taññeva paṭhamāruppaviññāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ anantato pharitvā pavattaṃ “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti evaṃ manasikarototi vuttaṃ hoti, manasikāravasena vā anantaṃ. Vibhaṅgepi hi “anantaṃ pharatī”ti (vibha. 610) vuttaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatananti ettha vuttanayena anantameva ānañcaṃ, viññāṇañca taṃ ānañcañcāti viññāṇānantanti vattabbe ruḷhito “viññāṇañca”nti vuttaṃ, tadeva āyatanamārammaṇamassāti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

'Consciousness is infinite': this means that one attends to that very consciousness of the first formless attainment, which occurred pervading space as infinite, as 'consciousness is infinite'; or it is infinite by way of attention. For in the Vibhaṅga too it is said: 'He pervades it as infinite' (Vibh 610). 'Base of the infinity of consciousness': here, in the way stated, the infinite (ananta) is ānanca. And that is consciousness (viññāṇa) and it is infinite (ānanca); thus, while 'the infinity of consciousness' (viññāṇānantaṃ) should be said, by convention 'viññāṇañca' is said. That itself is the base (āyatana) for this jhāna and is its object; thus it is the base of the infinity of consciousness. The rest is in the way already stated.

Evaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ tadanantaraṃ adhigatadutiyāruppassa taṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvā tattha āsannākāsānañcāyatanapaccatthikatāya, tadārammaṇatāya ca dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya taṃ samatikkamāya paṭhamāruppaviññāṇābhāvaṃ “natthi natthī”ti vā “suññaṃ suñña”nti vā “vivittaṃ vivitta”nti vā punappunaṃ manasikaroto ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ “sabbaso”tiādimāha. Idhāpi vuttanayena jhānassa, tadārammaṇassa ca viññāṇañcāyatanassa samatikkamova veditabbo. Natthi kiñcīti “natthi natthi, suññaṃ suññaṃ, vivittaṃ vivitta”nti evaṃ manasikarototi attho.

Having thus shown the base of the infinity of consciousness, now for one who has attained the second formless attainment and brought it to mastery, having seen the fault in its being an adversary close to the base of the infinity of space and in having that as its object, and having overcome delight in it, in order to transcend it, the base of nothingness arises for him as he repeatedly attends to the absence of the first formless consciousness as 'there is nothing, there is nothing,' or 'it is void, it is void,' or 'it is secluded, it is secluded.' To show this, he stated the passage beginning 'Completely...' Here too, the transcending of the jhāna of the base of the infinity of consciousness and of its object should be understood in the way stated. 'There is nothing whatsoever' means that one attends thus: 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' or 'It is void, it is void,' or 'It is secluded, it is secluded.' This is the meaning.

Ākiñcaññāyatananti [M 0.0250] ettha nāssa kiñcananti akiñcanaṃ, antamaso bhaṅgamattampissa avasiṭṭhaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti, akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇāpagamassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, ākiñcaññaṃ āyatanamārammaṇamassāti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Base of nothingness': Here, 'there is nothing of his,' thus he is one who has nothing; this means that not even a mere fragment remains for him. The state of one who has nothing is nothingness. This is a designation for the departure of the consciousness of the base of the infinity of space. Nothingness is the base for this jhāna and is its object; thus it is the base of nothingness. The rest is easy to understand.

Evaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ tadanantaraṃ adhigatatatiyāruppassa taṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvā tattha āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikatāya dosaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya taṃ samatikkamāya tadeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ “santaṃ santa”nti punappunaṃ manasikaroto nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ “sabbaso”tiādimāha. Tattha nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvato, sukhumāya ca bhāvato nevassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa saññā nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññaṃ, tadeva dhammāyatanamanāyatanapariyāpannattā āyatananti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ.

Having thus shown the attainment of the base of nothingness, now for one who has attained the third formless attainment and brought it to mastery, having seen the fault in its being an adversary close to the base of the infinity of consciousness, and having overcome delight in it, in order to transcend it, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises for him as he repeatedly attends to that very base of nothingness as 'peaceful, peaceful.' To show this, he stated the passage beginning 'Completely...' Here, 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception': because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, the perception of this jhāna with its associated states is 'neither perception' nor 'non-perception'; thus it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That itself is a base because it is included under the mind-object base and not included under the other bases; thus it is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Atha vā yāyamettha saññā, sā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena [V 0.0192] vijjamānattā nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññā, nevasaññānāsaññā ca sā sampayuttadhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanañcāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ. Na kevalañcettha saññāva edisī, api tu phassopi nevaphasso nāphasso, cittampi nevacittaṃ nācittaṃ, evaṃ sesasampayuttadhammāpi, saññāsīsena panāyaṃ desanā katāti veditabbā. Tattha saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvenāti accantasukhumabhāvappattasaṅkhārabhāvena. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Alternatively, the perception here is 'neither perception' because it is incapable of performing the function of keen perception; it is 'not non-perception' because it exists in a subtle state as a residual formation. Thus it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And that neither-perception-nor-non-perception is also a base in the sense of being a foundation for its associated states; thus it is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Not only perception is like this here, but contact too is neither contact nor non-contact, consciousness is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness, and so too are the other associated states. But it should be understood that this exposition is given with perception as the heading. Here, 'in a subtle state as a residual formation' means in the state of a formation that has reached extreme subtlety. The rest is as stated before.

Ayaṃ panettha ādito paṭṭhāya piṇḍatthappakāsanā – “idha bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”tiādinā sāsane lokiyalokuttarajjhānanibbattakapuggalassa [M 0.0251] patiṭṭhābhūtasīlesu pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlavisuddhiṃ upadisati. “Viharatī”ti iminā tadanurūpavihārasamaṅgibhāvaṃ. “Ācāragocarasampanno”ti iminā ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ, tadupakārake ca dhamme. “Aṇumattesū”tiādinā yathāvuttasīlehi acavanaṃ, tesañca anavasesato samādānaṃ. “Indriyesu guttadvāro”ti iminā indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ. “Bhojane mattaññū”ti iminā paccayasannissitasīlaṃ, santosādiguṇañca. “Pubbarattāpararatta”ntiādinā sīladhutaṅgesu patiṭṭhitassa bhāvanārāmassa tadupakārake dhamme. “Bodhipakkhikāna”ntiādinā paṭipattiyā nibbedhabhāgiyataṃ. “So abhikkante”tiādinā yathāvuttaguṇānaṃ aparihānāya, vakkhamānānañca paṭilābhāya satisampayogaṃ. “So vivitta”ntiādinā bhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaṃ. “So araññagato”tiādinā jhānabhāvanārambhappakāraṃ. “So abhijjha”ntiādinā jhānabhāvanābhiyogena pahīnapañcanīvaraṇassa upacārajjhānuppattiṃ. “So ime pañca nīvaraṇe”tiādinā tassa uparūpari vāyamato rūpārūpajjhānuppattikkamaṃ upadisati. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

This is the explanation of the summary meaning here, starting from the beginning: With the words, 'Here, a bhikkhu is restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint,' etc., he points out the purification of virtue consisting in the Pātimokkha restraint among the virtues that are the foundation in the Teaching for a person who generates mundane and supramundane jhānas. By 'he dwells,' he points out the possession of a suitable way of dwelling. By 'endowed with good conduct and resort,' he points out the virtue of purified livelihood and the qualities that support it. By 'in things of the slightest,' etc., he points out non-transgression of the aforesaid virtues and undertaking them completely. By 'with doors guarded in his sense faculties,' he points out the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties. By 'knowing the right measure in eating,' he points out the virtue concerning requisites and the qualities of contentment, etc. By 'in the first and last watches of the night,' etc., he points out the qualities that support one who delights in development and is established in the virtues and ascetic practices. By 'the things partaking of enlightenment,' etc., he points out that the practice is conducive to penetration. By 'when he goes forward,' etc., he points out the application of mindfulness for the non-decline of the aforesaid qualities and for the attainment of those to be spoken of. By 'secluded,' etc., he points out the adoption of a dwelling suitable for development. By 'having gone to the forest,' etc., he points out the way of beginning the development of jhāna. By 'having abandoned covetousness,' etc., he points out the arising of access concentration for one who has abandoned the five hindrances by application to the development of jhāna. By 'having abandoned these five hindrances,' etc., he points out the sequence of the arising of the form and formless jhānas for one who strives ever higher. This, for a start, is the meaning of the words here.

Dhammabhedo panettha vibhaṅganaye pākaṭo bhavissati. Tīsu hi nayesu mahaggatalokuttarā kusalavipākakiriyacittasampayuttā vitakkavicārapītisukhaupekkhāekaggatāsaṅkhātā jhānadhammā nānānayehi vibhattā, jhānasampayuttā pana sesakāmāvacaradhammāva idha saṅgahitā. Kiñcāpi panettha pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlādayopi vuttā, tathāpi te jhānānaṃ pubbabhāgappaṭipattidassanavasena ceva jhānasampayuttadhammavasena ca vuttā, idha pana na saṅgahitāti veditabbā.

The differentiation of phenomena here will become clear in the method of the Analysis. For in the three methods, the jhāna factors—namely, initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, equanimity, and one-pointedness—associated with wholesome, resultant, and functional sublime and supramundane consciousness, are classified in various ways. However, only the remaining sense-sphere phenomena associated with jhāna are included here. Although the Pātimokkha restraint and other kinds of virtue are mentioned here, they are stated for the purpose of showing the preliminary practice for the jhānas and as phenomena associated with the jhānas, but it should be understood that they are not included here.

Pañhāpucchake pana siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā, tīṇi jhānāni sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā, catutthaṃ adukkhamasukhāya [M 0.0252] vedanāya sampayuttaṃ, upekkhā panettha vedanā na vattabbā, siyā [V 0.0193] vipākā, siyā vipākadhammadhammā, paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicāravajjitaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ, vitakko panettha avitakkavicāramatto, vicāro na vattabbo, tīṇi jhānāni avitakkaavicārā, dve jhānāni pītivajjitāni pītisahagatāni, tīṇi sukhavajjitāni sukhasahagatāni, catutthaṃ upekkhāvajjitaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ, tatiyajjhāne sukhaṃ, upekkhā ca idha na vattabbaṃ…pe… siyā mahaggatā, siyā appamāṇā, tīṇi siyā appamāṇārammaṇā, siyā na vattabbā, catutthaṃ tidhāpi na vattabbañca, tīṇi siyā maggahetukā, siyā maggādhipatino, siyā na vattabbā, catutthaṃ tidhāpi na vattabbañca…pe… pīti bahiddhārammaṇāni, catutthaṃ tidhāpi na vattabbañca…pe… anidassanaappaṭighā na hetū…pe… nocittacetasikā araṇāti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pāḷimuttanayo panettha natthi, ito paraṃ pana ettakampi avatvā vijjamānaṭṭhāne eva vakkhāma.

In the Questioning section, however, they may be wholesome or they may be indeterminate. Three jhānas are associated with pleasant feeling; the fourth is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Here, equanimity as feeling is not to be stated. They may be resultant, or they may be states that are causes of results. The first jhāna is devoid of initial and sustained application; it is with initial and sustained application. Here, initial application is only sustained application without initial application; sustained application is not to be stated. Three jhānas are without initial and sustained application. Two jhānas are devoid of joy and accompanied by joy. Three are devoid of happiness and accompanied by happiness. The fourth is devoid of equanimity and accompanied by equanimity. In the third jhāna there is happiness, and equanimity is not to be stated here… They may be sublime, they may be immeasurable. Three may have an immeasurable object, or this is not to be stated; for the fourth, this is not to be stated in any of the three ways. Three may be a cause of the path, may be a dominant condition for the path, or this is not to be stated; for the fourth, this is not to be stated in any of the three ways… Joy has external objects. For the fourth, this is not to be stated in any of the three ways… They are non-manifest and non-resistant, not roots… neither consciousness nor mental factors; they are conflict-free. The rest is easy to understand. Here there is no method apart from the Pāḷi text. Henceforth, without saying even this much, we will speak only on points where it is present.

Jhānavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of Jhāna is finished.

Appamaññāvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Immeasurables

Appamaññāvibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – catasso appamaññāyotiādīsu pharaṇaappamāṇavasena appamaññāyo. Etā hi ārammaṇavasena appamāṇe vā satte pharanti, ekasattamhi vā anavasesapharaṇavasena appamāṇato pharantīti evaṃ pharaṇaappamāṇavasena “appamaññāyo”ti vuccanti, satta appamāṇavasenāpi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Mettāsahagatenāti mettāya samannāgatena. Ekaṃ disanti puratthimādīsu catūsu disāsu yaṃ kiñci ekaṃ disaṃ, taṃdisāpariyāpannasattapharaṇavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pharitvāti phusitvā ārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0253] katvā. Viharatīti pavatteti. Tathā dutiyantiādīsu. Yathā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā, tatheva tadanantaraṃ dutiyaṃ, tatiyaṃ, catutthañcāti attho. Iti uddhamadho tiriyanti eteneva nayena uparimaṃ disaṃ, heṭṭhimaṃ disaṃ, anudisañca anukkamena mettāsahagatena cetasā pharitvā viharatīti attho. Ettāvatā ekamekaṃ disaṃ pariggahetvā odhiso mettāpharaṇataṃ dassitaṃ.

Now, as to the meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Immeasurables: In the passage beginning, “the four immeasurables,” they are called “immeasurables” on account of the immeasurability of their pervasion. For they pervade immeasurable beings by way of their object, or they pervade a single being immeasurably by way of pervading without remainder. Thus they are called “immeasurables” on account of the immeasurability of their pervasion. It is also fit to say this is on account of the immeasurability of beings. “Accompanied by loving-kindness” means endowed with loving-kindness. “One direction” refers to any one of the four directions—east, etc.—and this is said with reference to pervading the beings included in that direction. “Having pervaded” means having touched, having made it an object. “He abides” means he makes it proceed. So too in the passage beginning “the second.” The meaning is that just as he has pervaded one direction, so immediately after he pervades the second, the third, and the fourth. “Thus above, below, across”: by this method, the meaning is that he abides pervading the upper direction, the lower direction, and the intermediate directions in succession with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness. By this much, the pervasion of loving-kindness with specific limitation has been shown by taking up each direction one by one.

Sabbadhītiādi [V 0.0194] pana anodhiso dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbadhīti sabbattha. Sabbattatāyāti sabbesu hīnamajjhimukkaṭṭhamittasapattamajjhattādippabhedesu attatāya, tesu vibhāgaṃ akatvā attasamatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā sabbattatāyāti sabbena cittabhāvena, īsakampi bahi avikkhepamānoti attho. Sabbāvantanti sabbasattavantaṃ, sabbasattayuttanti attho. Lokanti sattalokaṃ. Puna “mettāsahagatenā”ti idaṃ “vipulenā”tiādīhi visesanehi sambandhadassanavasena vā vuttaṃ, nigamanavasena vā. Tattha pharaṇavasena vipulatā veditabbā. Bhūmivasena pana mahaggatatā. Paguṇavasena, appamāṇasattārammaṇavasena ca appamāṇatā. Byāpādapaccatthikappahānena averatā. Domanassappahānena niddukkhatā, saṅkhatatā, abyāpajjatā ca daṭṭhabbā. Evaṃ karuṇāsahagatenātiādīsupi attho veditabboti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

The passage beginning “everywhere” is stated to show the unlimited pervasion. Herein, “everywhere” means in every way. “With a self-like identity towards all” means with an identity equal to one’s own self towards all beings, whether inferior, middling, or superior, friends, enemies, or neutral, without making any distinction among them. Or else, “with a self-like identity towards all” means with one’s entire mental state, without letting it be distracted externally in the least. “Containing all” means containing all beings, that is, endowed with all beings. “The world” means the world of beings. The phrase “accompanied by loving-kindness” is stated again either to show its connection with the qualifiers beginning with “vast,” or as a conclusion. Herein, vastness should be understood by way of pervasion. Sublimity should be understood by way of the plane of existence. Immeasurability should be understood by way of proficiency and by way of having immeasurable beings as object. Freedom from enmity is due to the abandoning of enmity and opposition. Freedom from suffering, freedom from distress, and freedom from affliction should be seen as due to the abandoning of mental pain. The meaning should be understood in the same way in the passages beginning “accompanied by compassion.” This, for now, is the word-by-word meaning.

Dhammabhedo panettha suviññeyyova. Vibhaṅganayena pana tīsu rūpāvacarakusalavipākakiriyācittesu sampayuttā sattesu mettādibrahmavihārabhūtā adoso karuṇā muditā tatramajjhattatāti cattāro dhammā nānānayehi vibhattā, taṃsampayuttā pana kāmāvacarabhūtā ca etā idha na gahitā. Arūpāvacaralokuttaresu panetā appamaññā natthevāti. Pañhāpucchake panetā tāva siyā kusalā, siyā [M 0.0254] abyākatā. Tisso sukhāya, catutthā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā. Vipākattike tidhāpi, upekkhā avitakkaavicārā, sesā tidhāpi, mahaggatāva, parittārammaṇaatītārammaṇattikesu na vattabbāva, bahiddhārammaṇāva, anidassanaappaṭighāva, mettā hetu, sesā na hetū, no cittā, cetasikā, rūpāvacarā, sauttarāva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

The differentiation of phenomena here is easy to understand. By the method of the Analysis, the four phenomena associated with the three kinds of fine-material-sphere consciousness—wholesome, resultant, and functional—which constitute the divine abidings toward beings, namely, non-hatred, compassion, gladness, and neutrality, are classified in various ways. But those associated with them that belong to the sense sphere are not included here. In the immaterial sphere and the supramundane, these immeasurables do not exist at all. In the Questioning section, however, they may be wholesome or they may be indeterminate. Three are associated with pleasant feeling, the fourth with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. In the triad of resultants, they are of three kinds. Equanimity is without initial and sustained application; the others are of three kinds. They are exclusively sublime. In the triads of limited object and past object, they are not to be stated. They have only external objects. They are non-manifest and non-resistant. Non-hatred is a root; the others are not roots.
