They are not consciousness but mental factors. They belong to the fine-material sphere. They are states that have a superior. The rest is easy to understand.

Appamaññāvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Immeasurables is finished.

Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of the Training Rules

Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgamātikāya pana atthato tāva – sikkhāpadānīti sikkhitabbapadāni, sikkhākoṭṭhāsāti attho. Apica sabbepi kusalā dhammā sikkhitabbato sikkhā, tāsaṃ patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena [V 0.0195] padaṃ, pañcasu pana sīlaṅgesu yaṃ kiñci aṅgaṃ. Pāṇātipātādīsu pāṇassa atīva pāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadhoti attho. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ, tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto, tasmā pāṇātipātā. Veramaṇīti virati, sā eva vuttanayena sikkhāpadanti veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ. Adinnanti na dinnaṃ, parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitassa adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ. Parassa haraṇaṃ theyyaṃ corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthato pana parapariggahite tathāsaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Micchācārāti kilesakāmavasena lāmakācārā, purisassa māturakkhitādisaṅkhātāsu, itthiyā attano [M 0.0255] niyamitapurisato parapurisasaṅkhātesu ca agamanīyaṭṭhānesu vītikkamācārāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthato pana agamanīyavatthūsu maggenamaggappaṭipādanopakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā, adhivāsanākārappavattā vā methunacetanā kāmesumicchācāro. Musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu, vādoti tassa abhūtataṃ ñatvāva bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ ñatvā tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa atthabhañjakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. Surāti piṭṭhasurā pūvasurā odanasurā kiṇṇapakkhittā sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañca surā. Merayanti pupphāsavo phalāsavo guḷāsavo madhvāsavo sambhārasaṃyuttoti pañca āsavā. Tadubhayampi madanīyaṭṭhena majjaṃ, yāya cetanāya taṃ majjaṃ pivati, sā pamādakāraṇattā pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

Now, as to the meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Training Rules: first, 'training rules' (sikkhāpadāni) are rules to be trained in; the meaning is 'divisions of training.' Furthermore, all wholesome qualities are to be trained in, hence 'training' (sikkhā), and 'rule' (pada) in the sense of being their foundation; among the five factors of virtue, any one is a 'rule.' 'Destruction of life' (pāṇātipāta) means the excessive striking (pāta) of a living being (pāṇa); the meaning is 'killing a living being.' Here, 'living being' (pāṇa) conventionally refers to a sentient being, but in the ultimate sense to the life faculty. Regarding that living being, when one perceives it as such, the volition to kill—arising from an effort to cut off the life faculty and expressed through the door of either body or speech—is 'destruction of life.' Abstention (veramaṇī) from this is restraint (virati), and this, in the manner explained, is the 'training rule of abstention' (veramaṇisikkhāpada). 'What is not given' (adinnaṃ) means what has not been given, what is possessed by another. Taking what is possessed by another and not given is 'taking what is not given' (adinnādāna). It is said to be stealing (theyya), theft (corikā). In terms of meaning, regarding what is possessed by another, when one perceives it as such, the volition to steal—arising from an effort to take it—is 'taking what is not given.' 'In sensual pleasures' (kāmesu) means in objective sensual pleasures. 'Wrong conduct' (micchācāra) is base conduct (lāmakācāra) driven by defiled sensual desire (kilesakāma); this is said to be transgressive conduct in forbidden unions—for a man, with women protected by their mother, etc., and for a woman, with men other than her designated partner. In terms of meaning, regarding a forbidden partner, the volition for sexual intercourse—arising from an effort to accomplish the path by means of a non-path, or proceeding as a form of consent—is 'wrong conduct in sensual pleasures.' 'False' (musā) refers to an unreal, untrue matter; 'speech' (vāda) is to declare it as real and true while knowing it is unreal. In terms of its characteristic, knowing a matter to be untrue, the volition of one who desires to make another understand it as true—arising from a bodily or verbal effort that misrepresents the facts—is 'false speech' (musāvādo). 'Fermented drink' (surā) includes five types: flour liquor, cake liquor, rice liquor, liquor mixed with yeast, and liquor blended with other ingredients. 'Distilled liquor' (meraya) includes five types: flower-based, fruit-based, molasses-based, honey-based, and blended liquors. Both of these, due to their intoxicating nature, are 'intoxicants' (majja). The volition by which one drinks such an intoxicant, being a cause of heedlessness, is a 'basis for heedlessness' (pamādaṭṭhāna); hence the full term is 'fermented and distilled intoxicants which are a basis for heedlessness.' The rest is easily understood. This, for now, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedo pana vibhaṅganaye pākaṭo bhavissati. Evaṃ uparipi. Vibhaṅganayesu cettha suttantabhājanīyaṃ natthi, abhidhammabhājanīye panetāni pañca sikkhāpadāni kāmāvacarakusalacittasampayuttānaṃ viratīnaṃ vasena nānappakārato paṭhamavāre vibhattāni, tathā dutiyavāre cetanāvasena, viraticetanāsampayuttā panettha dhammā na sikkhāpadāni, sikkhāpadasampayuttā pana honti, tathā tatiyanaye phassādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ vasena nānappakārato vibhattāti.

The classification of states, however, will become clear in the method of analysis. The same applies to what follows. Among these methods of analysis, there is no Suttanta analysis here. However, in the Abhidhamma analysis, these five training rules are analyzed in various ways: in the first section, by way of the abstinences associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness; similarly, in the second section, by way of volition. Here, the states associated with the volition of abstinence are not the training rules themselves, but they are associated with the training rules. Likewise, in the third method, they are analyzed in various ways by way of all the states beginning with contact.

Pañhāpucchake pana cetanāya, phassādīnañca pariyāyasikkhāpadattā nippariyāyasikkhāpadabhūtānaṃ viratīnaṃ vaseneva vibhattāni. Tattha hi pañca sikkhāpadāni kusalā eva, siyā [V 0.0196] sukhāya, siyā adukkhamasukhāya sampayuttā…pe… parittārammaṇāva, paccuppannārammaṇāva, bahiddhārammaṇāva, anidassanaappaṭighāva, na hetū, sahetukā, no cittā, cetasikā, kāmāvacarā[M 0.0256], sauttarāva, araṇāvāti. Ettha ca yāni sikkhāpadāni sattārammaṇāni vuttāni, tāni ca viratisabhāvattā yasmā “satto”ti saṅkhaṃ gate parittadhamme eva paccuppanne eva dhamme ārammaṇaṃ karonti, tasmā parittārammaṇāti ca vuttāti veditabbā. Idāni viramitabbapāṇātipātādīnaṃ –

In the Catechism, however, since volition, contact, and so on are training rules in an indirect sense, the analysis proceeds only by way of the abstinences, which are training rules in a direct sense. There, the five training rules are exclusively wholesome. They may be associated with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling… they have a limited object, a present object, an external object; they are non-manifestive and non-impinging; they are not roots but are accompanied by roots; they are not consciousness but mental factors; they are of the sense sphere; they are surpassable; and they are non-conflicting. Here, it should be understood that those training rules said to have beings as their object are called 'of limited object' because, being of the nature of abstinence, they take as their object only limited states and only present states that have come to be designated as 'a being.' Now, concerning the destruction of life and so on from which one should refrain—

Dhammakammapathālamba-vedanāmūlakammato;

Sāvajjaṅgādito ñeyyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

The analysis apart from the canon should be known by way of: state, path of action, object, feeling, root, and action; and by way of blameworthiness, factors, and so on.

Tattha dhammato tāva – pañcapete pāṇātipātādayo cetanāsabhāvāva honti. Kammapathato pañca kammapathāva. Ārammaṇato pana pāṇātipāto jīvitindriyārammaṇo, adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇaṃ, saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā, tathā musāvādo, micchācāro itthipurisārammaṇo, surāpānaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ. Vedanāto pana pāṇātipāto dukkhavedano, adinnādānaṃ tivedanaṃ, tathā musāvādo, micchācāro pana sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedano, tathā surāpānaṃ. Mūlato pana paṭhamo dosamohamūlo, dutiyaṃ siyā lobhamohamūlaṃ, siyā dosamohamūlaṃ, tathā musāvādo, micchācāro pana lobhamohamūlova, tathā surāpānaṃ. Kammato panettha musāvādo vacīkammaṃ, sesā kāyakammameva.

Here, firstly, by way of state: these five—beginning with the destruction of life—have the nature of volition. By way of path of action: they are the five paths of action. By way of object: destruction of life has the life faculty as its object; taking what is not given has a being or a formation as its object, and similarly false speech; sexual misconduct has a woman or man as its object; drinking intoxicants has a formation as its object. By way of feeling: destruction of life is accompanied by painful feeling; taking what is not given is accompanied by the three kinds of feeling, and similarly false speech; sexual misconduct is accompanied by two kinds of feeling, that is, pleasant or neutral, and similarly drinking intoxicants. By way of root: the first is rooted in hatred and delusion; the second may be rooted in greed and delusion or in hatred and delusion, and similarly false speech; sexual misconduct is rooted only in greed and delusion, and similarly drinking intoxicants. By way of action: here false speech is verbal action; the rest are only bodily action.

Sāvajjato pana pāṇātipāto tāva amanussake pāṇe appasāvajjo, manussake mahāsāvajjo. Tesu ca khuddakasarīre appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Payogasamattepi appaguṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ, upakkamānañca mudutibbatāya appamahāsāvajjo hoti, khīṇāsave pana mahāsāvajjataroti. Adinnādānaṃ vatthuno hīnappaṇītatāya ceva guṇavirahitatabbantasantakatāya [M 0.0257] ca. Tatthāpi taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya ca appamahāsāvajjaṃ, khīṇāsavasantake mahāsāvajjataranti veditabbaṃ. Micchācāro dussīlasīlavantavatthuvītikkamanena. Tatthāpi taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya ca appamahāsāvajjo, khīṇāsavavatthuvītikkamane mahāsāvajjataroti ca veditabbo. Musāvādo yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appamahantataṃ, vatthusāmino guṇavirahitataṃ, tabbantatañca upādāyupādāya appamahāsāvajjo hoti. Apica attano [V 0.0197] santakaṃ adātukāmatāya, hasādhippāyena vā “nattheta”ntiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃ “diṭṭha”ntiādinā kūṭasakkhiādibhāvena vā pavatto mahāsāvajjo, musā vatvā pana saṅghabhedane mahāsāvajjataro. Surāpānaṃ bindumattato paṭṭhāya taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya appasāvajjaṃ, bahuke mahāsāvajjaṃ, kāyavikārajananapahonakapāne pana mahāsāvajjatarameva.

By way of blameworthiness: first, the destruction of life. Killing a non-human being is less blameworthy; killing a human being is highly blameworthy. Among them, killing a small-bodied being is less blameworthy, a large-bodied being more so. Why? Because of the magnitude of the effort. Even with equal effort, killing a being of little virtue is less blameworthy, one of great virtue more so. When bodily qualities and virtues are equal, it is less or more blameworthy according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements and the effort. But against an arahant, it is most blameworthy. Taking what is not given is less or more blameworthy based on the inferior or superior nature of the object and on whether its owner is devoid of or endowed with virtue. Here too, depending on the case, it is less or more blameworthy. But taking what belongs to an arahant is to be understood as most blameworthy. Sexual misconduct varies by transgressing against an immoral person or a virtuous one. Here too, depending on the case, it is less or more blameworthy. But transgression against an arahant is to be understood as most blameworthy. False speech is less or more blameworthy depending on the triviality or importance of the matter it ruins, and on whether the owner of the thing is devoid of or endowed with virtue. Furthermore, speaking from an unwillingness to give what one owns, or with the intention to jest, saying, 'There is nothing here,' and so on, is less blameworthy. But speaking falsely by saying 'I saw' what one did not see, or by acting as a false witness, is highly blameworthy. However, speaking falsely to create a schism in the Sangha is most blameworthy. Drinking intoxicants, from a single drop onwards, is less blameworthy depending on the case; drinking a large quantity is highly blameworthy. But drinking enough to cause bodily derangement is most blameworthy indeed.

Aṅgādito pana pāṇātipātassa pāṇo pāṇasaññitā vadhakacittaṃ upakkamo tena maraṇanti pañca aṅgāni. Sāhatthiko āṇattiko nissaggiko thāvaro vijjāmayo iddhimayoti cha payogā. Adinnādānassa parapariggahitatā tathāsaññitā theyyacittaṃ upakkamo tena haraṇanti pañca aṅgāni. Sāhatthikādayo cha eva payogā. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahārādīnaṃ vasena pavattā. Micchācārassa agamanīyavatthutā sevanacittaṃ maggena maggappaṭipattīti tīṇi aṅgāni. Sāhatthiko ekova payogo. Evaṃ sesānampi payogo veditabbo. Musāvādassa atathaṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti cattāri aṅgāni. Surāpānassa surādīnaṃ aññataratā ajjhoharaṇanti dve aṅgānīti.

Furthermore, beginning with the factors: For the destruction of life there are five factors: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the volition to kill, the effort, and the resulting death. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by missile, by a permanent fixture, by knowledge, and by psychic power. For taking what is not given there are five factors: an object possessed by another, the perception of it as such, the volition to steal, the effort, and the resulting removal. The same six modes of application apply, proceeding appropriately by way of theft, carrying away, and so on. For sexual misconduct there are three factors: an unsuitable partner, the intention to engage, and the act of engaging the path with the path. The mode of application is only one: by one's own hand. The modes of application for the others should be understood similarly. For false speech there are four factors: an untrue matter, the intention to deceive, the effort produced by that, and the other's understanding of that meaning. For consuming intoxicants there are two factors: the substance being one of the intoxicants, and the act of swallowing it.

Evaṃ [M 0.0258] pāṇātipātādīnaṃ dhammādito vinicchayaṃ ñatvā idāni pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādīnaṃ pañcannampi –

Having thus understood the analysis of the destruction of life and so on beginning with the states, now, for the five beginning with abstention from the destruction of life—

Dhammakammapathālamba-samādānapayogato;

Khaṇḍato ca vijānīyo, pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

The analysis apart from the Pāli should be known by way of state, path of action, object, undertaking, and application; and by way of breaking.

Tattha dhammakammapathato vinicchayo vuttanayova. Ārammaṇato panetāni jīvitindriyāditaṃtaṃvītikkamitabbavatthārammaṇāni. Samādānato ekassa santike vā sayameva vā “pañca sīlāni adhiṭṭhahāmī”ti ekato vā pāṭiekkaṃ vā samādiyantena etāni samādinnāneva honti. Payogato pana sabbānipi sāhatthikapayogāneva. Khaṇḍato gahaṭṭhā yaṃ yaṃ vītikkamanti, taṃ tadeva khaṇḍaṃ hoti, netare. Gahaṭṭhā anibaddhasīlā honti, yaṃ yaṃ sakkonti, taṃ tadeva gopenti. Sāmaṇerānaṃ pana ekasmiṃ vītikkamite sabbānipi bhijjantīti evaṃ vijānīyo pāḷimuttavinicchayo.

Herein, the analysis from the perspective of state and path of action is as has been stated. As to their object, these precepts have as their objects the respective things that are to be transgressed, beginning with the life-faculty. As to undertaking, when one undertakes them in the presence of another or by oneself, declaring, “I undertake the five precepts,” either collectively or individually, they are thereby undertaken. As to application, all involve personal application. As to breaking, for householders, whichever precept they transgress, only that one is broken, not the others. Householders have unfixed precepts; they protect whichever they are able to. For novices, however, when one is transgressed, all are broken. Thus should the analysis apart from the Pāli be understood.

Sikkhāpadavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of the Training Rules is finished.

Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of Discernments

Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0198] atthato tāva – catasso paṭisambhidāti cattāro pabhedā. Niddese pana “atthe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā”tiādinā (vibha. 718) ñāṇavasena niddiṭṭhattā ñāṇasseva, na aññassa kassacīti veditabbaṃ. Atthapaṭisambhidāti atthavisayañāṇappabhedā, atthappabhedasallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthatāvasena atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇanti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca atthoti hetuphalaṃ. So hi hetuvasena araṇīyato gantabbato, uppādetabbato ca “attho”ti vuccati. Pabhedato [M 0.0259] panesopi pañcavidho hoti yaṃ kiñci paccayuppannaṃ, nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti.

First, as to the meaning in the matrix of the Analysis of Discernments: 'four discernments' means four divisions. In the exposition, however, since it is indicated by way of knowledge with the words, 'Knowledge of the meaning is the discernment of meaning,' etc. (Vibh 718), it should be understood as being of knowledge alone, not of anything else. 'Discernment of meaning' is a division of knowledge concerning the sphere of meaning; that is, it is knowledge that has attained division in respect to meaning by way of the ability to mark, make clear, and establish the divisions of meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Herein, 'meaning' is the effect of a cause. For it is called 'meaning' because, by means of a cause, it is to be arrived at, gone to, and produced. By way of division, this is also fivefold: whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant, and functional.

Dhammoti paccayo, so hi phalaṃ vidahati pavatteti uppādeti ceva pāpeti cāti “dhammo”ti vuccati. Pabhedato panesopi pañcavidho hoti yo koci phalanibbattako hetu, ariyamaggo, bhāsitaṃ, kusalaṃ, akusalanti.

'Dhamma' is the condition, for it arranges, sets going, generates, and makes one attain the result—thus it is called 'Dhamma.' By way of division, this is also fivefold: any cause that produces a result, the noble path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome.

Niruttīti yathāvuttānaṃ dhammānaṃ, atthānañca vācako sabhāvaniruttisaṅkhāto saddo. Imā dhammatthaniruttiyo ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tattha tattha pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā nāma.

'Expression' (nirutti) is the sound, known as 'natural expression,' which is the verbal expression of the aforesaid dhammas and their meanings. When one reflects upon these expressions of dhammas and meanings as objects, the knowledge that attains division in each case is called the discernment of expression.

Ettha ca niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇā, na paññattārammaṇā, paṭisambhidāpatto hi “phasso vedanā”tiādikaṃ saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, “phassā vedano”tiādikaṃ pana “na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti. Sabhāvaniruttīti (vibha. aṭṭha. 718) ca māgadhikā bhāsā, yāya sammāsambuddhā tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ tantiṃ āropenti, brahmāno ca agāmake araññe kiñci vacanaṃ asutvā vaḍḍhitadārakā ca attano dhammatāya bhāsanti, yā ca apāyesu manusse devaloke ceva māgadhabhāsā ussannā, pacchā ca tato andhakayonakadamiḷādidesabhāsā ceva sakkatādiaṭṭhārasamahābhāsā ca nibbattā, sā hi yasmā itarāsu bhāsāsu parivattantāsupi na parivattati, sabbakālaṃ attano sabhāve eva tiṭṭhati, tasmā “sabhāvaniruttī”ti vuccati. Yā brahmavohāro, ariyavohāroti ca vuccati, tāya pana māgadhabhāsāya tantiṃ āruḷhassa buddhavacanassa paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ sotapathāgamanameva papañco[M 0.0260][V 0.0199]. Sote pana saṅghaṭṭitamatte eva nayasatena nayasahassena attho upaṭṭhāti. Aññāya pana bhāsāya tantiṃ āruḷhaṃ taṃ tesaṃ cittaṃ sahasā nārohati, kicchena uggahetabbaṃ hoti, puthujjanānañca sakalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvāpi paṭisambhidāpatti nāma natthi, ariyasāvako no paṭisambhidāpatto nāma natthi, paṭisambhidāpatto aññaṃ saddaṃ nāmākhyātopasagganipātabhedato jānāti, na jānātīti? Yadaggena saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, tadaggena etampi jānissati, na cetaṃ paṭisambhidākiccanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the discernment of expression has sound as its object, not concepts. For one who has attained the discernments, on hearing sounds such as 'contact, feeling,' understands, 'This is natural expression,' but on hearing an ungrammatical phrase such as 'phassā vedano,' understands, 'This is not natural expression.' Natural expression is the Māgadhan language, in which the Perfectly Enlightened Ones put the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, on the string of the canon. It is the language that Brahmās speak, and that children raised in a forest without a village, having heard no speech, speak by their own nature. It is the language that is prevalent in the woeful states, among humans, and in the deva world. Later, from it arose the languages of the regions of the Andhakas, Yonakas, Damiḷas, etc., and the eighteen great languages such as Sanskrit. Because it does not change even when other languages change, but always remains in its own nature, it is called 'natural expression.' It is also called 'Brahmā speech' and 'noble speech.' For those who have attained the discernments, the coming of the Buddha's word—canonized in the Māgadhan language—to the path of the ear is a simple matter. For as soon as the sound strikes the ear, the meaning presents itself in a hundred, a thousand ways. But if it is canonized in another language, their minds do not readily ascend to it; it must be learned with difficulty. For ordinary people, even if they learn the entire word of the Buddha, there is no attainment of the discernments. There is no noble disciple who has not attained the discernments. Does one who has attained the discernments know another sound by way of its division into noun, verb, prefix, and particle, or not? Insofar as on hearing a sound one knows, 'This is natural expression, this is not natural expression,' to that extent one will know this too. But this should not be understood as the function of the discernments.

Paṭibhānanti dhammatthādivisayaṃ sabbatthakañāṇaṃ, taṃ ñāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā nāma, imā catassopi paṭisambhidā adhigamena pariyattiuggahaṇena sakkaccadhammassavanena atthaparipucchāya pubbayogenāti pañcahi kāraṇehi visadā honti, sekhabhūmiyaṃ, asekhabhūmiyañcāti dvīsu ṭhānesu pabhedaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāvettha padattho.

'Inspired speech' (paṭibhāna) is the all-embracing knowledge concerning subjects such as Dhamma and meaning. The knowledge that attains division for one who reviews that knowledge by taking it as an object is called the discernment of inspired speech. These four discernments become clear through five causes: by attainment, by learning the scriptures, by careful listening to the Dhamma, by inquiry into the meaning, and by prior application. They should be understood as diversifying in two stages: in the stage of a trainee and in the stage of one beyond training. This, for a start, is the meaning of the terms here.

Dhammabhedo panetthāpi vibhaṅganaye pākaṭo bhavissati. Vibhaṅganayesu hi tīsupi dhammaniruttipaṭibhānapaṭisambhidā tissopi kāmāvacarajavanasampayuttañāṇānaṃ vasena tabbisayappabhedena saddhiṃ nānappakārato vibhattā. Atthapaṭisambhidā pana tesaṃ ñāṇānañceva aṭṭhalokuttaracittasampayuttānañca vasena tabbisayappabhedena saddhiṃ. Lokuttarañāṇānipi hi maggappattabbatāya atthabhūtanibbānārammaṇattā “atthapaṭisambhidā”ti vuccati.

Here too, the division of dhammas will become evident according to the method of the Analysis. For in the three methods of analysis, the three discernments—of Dhamma, of expression, and of inspired speech—are distinguished in various ways, together with their diverse objects, based on the knowledges associated with sense-sphere javanas. But the discernment of meaning is distinguished, together with its diverse objects, based on those knowledges and those associated with the eight supramundane consciousnesses. For the supramundane knowledges, too, are called 'discernment of meaning' because they have attained the path and have Nibbāna, which is the essence of meaning, as their object.

Pañhāpucchake pana siyā kusalā, siyā abyākatā, tisso paṭisambhidā siyā vipākadhammadhammā, siyā nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammā, atthapaṭisambhidā tidhāpi, tisso paṭisambhidā parittā, atthapaṭisambhidā siyā parittā, siyā appamāṇā[M 0.0261], niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā, bahiddhārammaṇā ca, sesā tidhāpi, niruttipaṭisambhidā paccuppannārammaṇāva, atthapaṭisambhidā tidhāpi na vattabbā ca, anidassanaappaṭighā, hetū, sahetukā, tisso paṭisambhidā sauttarā, atthapaṭisambhidā dvidhāpi, araṇā cāti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In the Question Section: they may be wholesome or indeterminate. The three analytical knowledges may be resultant dhammas, or dhammas that are neither resultant nor result-producing; the analytical knowledge of meaning can be all three. The three analytical knowledges are limited; the analytical knowledge of meaning may be limited or immeasurable. The analytical knowledge of expression has a limited object and an external object; the others can be all three. The analytical knowledge of expression has only a present object; the analytical knowledge of meaning can have an object of any of the three times and can also be timeless. They are invisible and non-impinging. They are roots and are associated with roots. The three analytical knowledges are surpassable; the analytical knowledge of meaning can be either surpassable or unsurpassable. And they are conflict-free. The rest is easy to understand.

Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the matrix of the Analysis of Discriminations is finished.

Ñāṇavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Matrix of the Analysis of Knowledge.

Ñāṇavibhaṅgamātikāya [V 0.0200] pana atthato tāva – ekavidhenāti ekappakārena, ekakoṭṭhāsena vā. Ñāṇavatthūti ettha pana ñāṇañca taṃ vatthu ca nānappakārānaṃ sampattīnanti ñāṇavatthu. Pañca viññāṇāti cakkhuviññāṇādīni pañca. Na hetū ahetukātiādīsu heṭṭhā hetudukādīsu vuttanayānusārena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Apica hetudukādīsu pañca viññāṇā hetū dhammāti vā sahetukā dhammāti vā na vattabbā, ekantena pana na hetū eva, ahetukā evāti. Evaṃ “yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññā”ti iminā upari ekavidhaparicchedāvasāne vakkhamānena sambandhoti. Iminā nayena sabbattha yathānurūpaṃ attho veditabbo. Tattha ca acetasikāti cittāni eva pañcaviññāṇasampayuttānaṃ idha aparāmaṭṭhattā.

Now, as to the meaning of the matrix of the Analysis of Knowledge—first, 'of one kind' means in one way or in one section. Here, 'the basis for knowledge' means knowledge which is the basis for various kinds of attainments. 'The five consciousnesses' are the five such as eye-consciousness. In such passages as 'not roots' and 'rootless,' the meaning should be understood everywhere according to the method stated previously in the dyads on roots, etc. Moreover, in the dyads on roots, etc., the five consciousnesses cannot be called 'phenomena that are roots' or 'phenomena with roots'; rather, they are exclusively 'not roots' and 'rootless.' Similarly, the connection is with what will be stated later at the end of the section on the onefold division, namely, 'the wisdom that clarifies things as they really are.' In this way, the meaning should be understood appropriately everywhere. And there, 'without mental factors' refers only to the consciousnesses, because the mental factors associated with the five consciousnesses are not dealt with here.

Uppannavatthukā uppannārammaṇāti khaṇapaccuppannavasena anāgatapaṭikkhepo. Na hi tāni anāgatesu pañcasu vatthārammaṇesu uppajjanti. Purejātavatthukā purejātārammaṇāti sahuppattipaṭikkhepo. Na hi tāni sahuppannaṃ vatthārammaṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjanti. Ajjhattikavatthukāti ajjhattajjhattabhūte pañca pasāde vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakā. Ettha ca pañca viññāṇā sayampi ajjhattikā, ajjhattikavatthukā ca, manoviññāṇaṃ [M 0.0262] hadayanissitaṃ ajjhattikaṃ, bāhiravatthukaṃ, pañcaviññāṇasampayuttā tayo khandhā bāhirā, ajjhattikavatthukā, manoviññāṇasampayuttā tayo khandhā bāhirā, bāhiravatthukāti evaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

'Having a presently arisen basis and a presently arisen object' means the rejection of the future, in the sense of the momentarily present. For they do not arise in regard to the five bases and objects that are future. 'Having a pre-arisen basis and a pre-arisen object' means the rejection of co-arising. For they do not arise dependent on a co-arisen basis and object. 'Having an internal basis' means arising by taking as basis the five sense faculties, which are thoroughly internal. Here, the five consciousnesses are themselves internal and have an internal basis; mind-consciousness, being dependent on the heart-base, is internal but has an external basis; the three aggregates associated with the five consciousnesses are external but have an internal basis; the three aggregates associated with mind-consciousness are external and have an external basis. Thus this fourfold scheme should be understood.

Asambhinnavatthukā asambhinnārammaṇāti aniruddhavatthārammaṇā. Na hi tāni niruddhavatthārammaṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjanti. Nānāvatthukā nānārammaṇāti tāni yathākkamaṃ cakkhurūpādiniyatekekavatthārammaṇatāya aññamaññaṃ bhinnavatthukā, bhinnārammaṇā ca. Na hi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ cakkhuṃ muñcitvā sotādīsu aññataraṃ vatthuṃ katvā rūpaṃ muñcitvā saddādīsu aññatarārammaṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjati, na itarāni cetarāni. Na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhontīti iminā ca nesaṃ nānārammaṇataṃyeva vibhāveti. Na asamannāhārā uppajjantīti anāvajjane na uppajjanti, pañcadvārāvajjanena anāvajjite visaye na uppajjantīti attho. Na amanasikārāti tamevettha pariyāyantarena vibhāveti. Na abbokiṇṇāti aññamaññaṃ nirantarā hutvā na uppajjanti. Na apubbaṃ acarimanti ekakkhaṇepi saha na uppajjanti. Na [V 0.0201] kevalañca etāni, aññānipi viññāṇāni dve vā taduttariṃ vā ekato na uppajjanti, ekekameva pana viññāṇaṃ uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhatī”tiādi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.109; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.368; vibha. aṭṭha. 523). Na aññamaññassa samanantarāti iminā anabbokiṇṇatāya eva vibhāvanā.

'Having an un-disintegrated basis and an un-disintegrated object' means having a basis and object that have not ceased. For they do not arise dependent on a basis and object that have ceased. 'Having different bases and different objects' means that because they each have their own fixed basis and object in sequence—such as the eye and forms—they have bases distinct from one another and objects distinct from one another. For eye-consciousness does not arise by abandoning the eye and taking another basis such as the ear, nor by abandoning form and taking another object such as sound; and similarly for the others. By the statement, 'They do not experience one another's range and domain,' this clarifies their having different objects. 'They do not arise without attention' means they do not arise without adverting; that is, they do not arise toward an object that has not been adverted to by the five-door adverting consciousness. 'They do not arise without mental application' clarifies the same point with another term. 'They are not intermingled' means they do not arise immediately one after another. 'Not one before and one after' means they do not arise simultaneously in a single moment. And it is not only these, but other consciousnesses too, two or more, do not arise together; it should be understood that only one consciousness arises at a time. As it is said: 'One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases,' etc. 'They are not immediately consecutive to one another' is a clarification of their non-intermingled nature.

Anābhogāti anāvajjanabhūtā āvajjanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā āvajjanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na samatthāti attho. Na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānātīti “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti (dha. pa. 1-2) evaṃ vuttaṃ ekampi kusalākusalaṃ dhammaṃ kocipi puggalo na paṭivijānāti, tehi viññāṇehi na sādhetīti attho. Aññatra [M 0.0263] abhinipātamattāti ṭhapetvā rūpādiārammaṇānaṃ abhinipātamattaṃ āpāthagamanamattaṃ, byattataropi puggalo pañcaviññāṇehi āpāthagatārammaṇapaṭivijānanamattato aññaṃ kusalākusalapaṭivijānanaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti attho.

'Without effort' (anābhogā) means that being non-adverting, they are incapable of performing the function of adverting, though they stand in the position of adverting. 'It does not discern any phenomenon' means that no person discerns or accomplishes through these consciousnesses even a single wholesome or unwholesome phenomenon of the kind spoken of thus: 'Mind is the forerunner of phenomena….' 'Except for the mere impact' means that, apart from the mere impact, the mere coming into range of objects such as form, even a more intelligent person is unable to accomplish, by means of the five consciousnesses, the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, beyond the mere discernment of an object that has come into range.

Pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ samanantarāpīti manodhātuyāpi. Api-saddo cettha sampiṇḍanattho, tena na kevalaṃ manodhātuyāva, tato parehipi pañcadvārikaviññāṇehi tadārammaṇapariyosānehi na kiñci kusalākusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijānātīti ayamattho dassitoti gahetabbo. Kiñcāpi pañcadvāre kusalākusalādīni javanāni uppajjanti, tathāpi tāni moghapupphāni viya abbohārikānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Na kañci iriyāpathaṃ kappetītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Na hi pañcadvārikaviññāṇehi gamanādīsu kañci iriyāpathaṃ kappeti, na kāyavacīkammaṃ paṭṭhapeti, na viññattiṃ vā samuṭṭhāpeti, na kusalākusalaṃ dhammaṃ samādiyati, na lokiyalokuttaraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjati, na tato vuṭṭhāti, na bhavato cavati, na bhavantare uppajjati, sabbampetaṃ kiccaṃ manodvārikacitteneva hoti. Yathā cetesaṃ etāni kiccāni natthi, evaṃ niyāmokkamanādīnipi. Na hi koci pañcadvārikajavanehi micchattaniyāmaṃ, sammattaniyāmaṃ vā okkamati, na cetāni nāmagottaṃ vā kasiṇādipaññattiṃ vā tilakkhaṇādiṃ vā ārabbha bhavanti. Na supatītiādīsu sabbehi pañcadvārikacittehi na niddaṃ okkamati, na kiñci supinaṃ passati. Niddāyantassa hi indriyesu mahāpadīpaturiyasaddādioḷārikehipi rūpādipañcārammaṇehi ghaṭṭitesu paṭhamaṃ pañcadvārikāni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭetuṃ na sakkonti, manodvārikameva āvajjanaṃ sakkoti, tasmiñca uppanne manodvārikajavanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ [V 0.0202] otarati. Dutiyavāre pana pañcadvārikaāvajjanesu yaṃ kiñci yathārahaṃ [M 0.0264] bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti, tato tadārammaṇapariyosānāni taṃtaṃdvārikavīthicittāni yathākkamaṃ pavattitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otaranti. Tatiyavāre pana manodvārikāvajjanajavanāni pavattanti, tasmiṃ khaṇe rūpādipañcārammaṇavavatthānaṃ hoti, satto ca niddāya paṭibuddhoti, evaṃ manodvārikacitteneva paṭibujjhati.

Immediately after the five consciousnesses, there is also the mind-element. Here the word 'also' has a collective sense. Thus, it should be understood that the meaning shown is that one does not discern any wholesome or unwholesome state, not only by the mind-element, but also by the subsequent five-door consciousnesses that end with registration. Although wholesome and unwholesome impulsion moments arise in the five-door process, they should be seen as ineffectual, like barren flowers. The same principle applies to such statements as 'it does not adopt any posture.' For by means of the five-door consciousnesses one does not adopt any posture such as walking, does not initiate any bodily or verbal action, does not produce any intimation, does not undertake any wholesome or unwholesome state, does not attain any mundane or supramundane concentration, does not emerge from it, does not pass away from an existence, and does not arise in another existence. All these functions are performed only by mind-door consciousness. Just as these functions do not belong to them, so too with such functions as entering upon a fixed course. For no one enters the fixed course of wrongness or the fixed course of rightness through five-door impulsion moments; nor do these arise in connection with name and clan, or concepts such as a kasiṇa, or the three characteristics, etc. In such statements as 'one does not sleep,' one does not fall asleep with any of the five-door consciousnesses, nor does one see any dream. For when a sleeping person's sense faculties are struck by gross objects such as a bright light or the sound of musical instruments, at first the five-door adverting consciousnesses are unable to cause the life-continuum to vibrate; only the mind-door adverting consciousness is able to do so. When that has arisen, the mind-door impulsion runs its course and then subsides into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, whichever of the five-door adverting consciousnesses is appropriate causes the life-continuum to vibrate; then the cognitive-process consciousnesses of the respective doors, ending with registration, proceed in sequence and subside into the life-continuum. On the third occasion, the mind-door adverting and impulsion moments occur; at that moment there is determination of the five sense objects such as form, and the being is awakened from sleep. Thus, one awakens only through mind-door consciousness.

Supinampi hi teneva passati, na pañcadvārikena, tañca panetaṃ supinaṃ passanto catūhi kāraṇehi passati dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vā. Imesaṃ pana saṃsaggasannipātatopi bahudhā papañcenti. Tattha yaṃ vātapittādidhātukkhobhato, anubhūtapubbato ca supinaṃ passati, na taṃ saccaṃ. Yaṃ devatopasaṃhārato passati, taṃ saccaṃ vā hoti alikaṃ vā. Kuddhā hi devatā viparītampi katvā dassenti. Yaṃ pubbanimittato passati, taṃ ekantasaccameva bodhisattakosalarājādīnaṃ pañcasoḷasamahāsupināni viya. Tañca panetaṃ catubbidhaṃ supinaṃ sekhaputhujjanāva passanti, na asekhā pahīnavipallāsattā. Kiṃ panetaṃ passanto sutto passati paṭibuddho vā? Kiñcettha, yadi sutto passati, supinassa kusalādisabhāvato, bhavaṅgassa ca tadabhāvā abhidhammavirodho āpajjati. Atha paṭibuddho, supinaṃ passantena katassa abbohārikassāpi vītikkamassa sabbohārikasseva ekantasāvajjattā anāpatti na siyāti vinayavirodho āpajjati. Pakārantaro ca natthi, yena supinaṃ passeyyāti supinassa abhāvova āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati. Kasmā? Yasmā kapimiddhapareto passati “kapimiddhapareto kho, mahārāja, supinaṃ passatī”ti (mi. pa. 5.3.5) vacanato, yā pana niddā makkaṭaniddā viya punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuparivattā, taṃ kapimiddhaṃ, tena [M 0.0265] sutto supinaṃ passati, tasmā supino kusalopi hoti akusalopi, āvajjanatadārammaṇavasena abyākatopi, supine ca kataṃ kusalākusaladubbalatāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkoti, pavatte vedanīyaṃ pana hoti. “Yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññā”ti ettha yo pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ yathāvutto na hetukaṭṭho, ahetukaṭṭho…pe… na supinaṃ passanaṭṭho, so yāthāvaṭṭho, taṃtaṃyāthāvatthuṃ vibhāvetīti yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā paññā. Evaṃ ekavidhena ñāṇavatthūti evaṃ vuttena ekena pakārena ekena ākārena, ekakoṭṭhāsena ñāṇavatthu hotīti.

Indeed, one sees a dream only with the mind, not through the five sense-doors. One sees that dream for four reasons: due to a disturbance of the elements, or due to previous experience, or due to the influence of deities, or as a portent of the future. From the combination and conjunction of these, they proliferate in many ways. Herein, a dream one sees due to a disturbance of the elements such as wind, bile, etc., or due to previous experience, is not true. A dream one sees due to the influence of deities can be true or false, for angry deities may show things in a distorted way. A dream one sees as a portent of the future is entirely true, like the five great dreams of the Bodhisatta and the sixteen great dreams of King Kosala. And this fourfold dream is seen only by trainees and worldlings, not by non-trainees, because their perversions have been abandoned. Now, does one see this while asleep or while awake? If one sees it while asleep, then since a dream has a wholesome or unwholesome nature, and the life-continuum lacks such a nature, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises. But if one sees it while awake, then for one who sees a dream, even a transgression that is not actionable would be entirely blameworthy just like an actionable one, so there would be no state of non-offense; thus a contradiction with the Vinaya arises. And is there no other way by which one could see a dream, so that the very absence of dreams would result? It does not result. Why? Because one sees it when overcome by 'monkey-sleep,' as it is said: 'Great king, one sees a dream when overcome by monkey-sleep.' That sleep which, like a monkey's sleep, is light and easily disturbed because it is repeatedly interspersed with wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness, is 'monkey-sleep.' One sees a dream while overcome by this. Therefore, a dream can be wholesome, unwholesome, or, by way of adverting and registration, indeterminate. And what is done in a dream, because of the weakness of its wholesome or unwholesome nature, cannot draw forth a rebirth-linking, but it can be experienced in the course of existence. Herein, regarding 'the wisdom that discerns the object in its actual state': that which, among the five consciousnesses, is as stated not the state with roots, the state without roots... and so on... not the state of seeing a dream, that is the actual state. It discerns each respective object in its actual state; thus it is 'the wisdom that discerns the object in its actual state.' Thus, 'the basis of knowledge is of one kind' means that the basis of knowledge is of one kind in the stated way, that is, in one mode, in one aspect, in one division.

Ekakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on singles is finished.

Dukesu [V 0.0203] atthajāpikāti ettha atthapaṭisambhidāvibhaṅge vuttesu pañcasu atthesu yathānurūpaṃ atthaṃ jāpeti janeti pavattetīti atthajāpikā, catubhūmakakusalacittesu ceva asekhānaṃ abhiññāsamāpattīnaṃ parikammādibhūtakāmāvacarakiriyācittesu ca sampayuttā paññā. Tāsu hi yasmā kusalasampayuttāva paññā attano attano bhūmipariyāpannaṃ vipākasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jāpeti janeti. Kāmāvacarakiriyāsampayuttā pana parikammādibhūtā abhiññāsamāpattikiriyā arahattaphalasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jāpeti janeti, tasmā etā atthajāpikāti vuttā. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana pāḷiyaṃ avuttāpi tīsu bhūmīsu kiriyajavanapaññā anantarādipaccayavasena attano anantaraṃ kiriyatthaṃ jāpetīti “atthajāpikā”tveva vuttā. Jāpitatthā paññāti sahajātaṃ vipākatthaṃ jāpetvā ṭhitā, attano vā kāraṇehi jāpitā janitā pavattitā sayampi atthabhūtāti jāpitatthā. Catubhūmakavipākesu ca kiriyābhiññāsamāpattīsu ca sampayuttā paññā. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana pāḷiyaṃ avuttā sesakiriyāsampayuttāpi paññā yathāsakaṃ kāraṇehi jāpitā, sayañca atthabhūtāti [M 0.0266] “jāpitatthā”tveva vuttā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In the pairs, regarding 'result-generative': here, among the five kinds of result mentioned in the analysis of the discrimination of result, it generates, produces, and brings about a result in a corresponding way—thus it is called 'result-generative.' This is the wisdom associated with wholesome consciousness of the four planes and with the sense-sphere functional consciousness that serves as preparation, etc., for the direct knowledges and attainments of non-trainees. For in these cases, the wisdom associated with the wholesome generates and produces the result, designated as 'fruit,' that pertains to its own respective plane. The wisdom associated with sense-sphere functional consciousness, which serves as preparation, etc., for the functional direct knowledges and attainments, generates and produces the result designated as the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, these are called 'result-generative.' In the commentaries, however, though not stated in the Pāli, the wisdom of functional javana in the three planes is also called 'result-generative' because, through conditions such as immediacy, it generates the functional result immediately after itself. 'Wisdom with generated result': it stands having generated the co-nascent resultant fruit; or, having been generated, produced, and set in motion by its own causes, it has itself become a result; thus it is called 'wisdom with generated result.' This is the wisdom associated with the resultants of the four planes and with the functional direct knowledge attainments. In the commentaries, though not stated in the Pāli, the wisdom associated with the remaining functional states is also called 'wisdom with generated result' because it is generated by its respective causes and has itself become a result. The rest is easy to understand.

Dukaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on pairs is finished.

Tikesu pana cintāmayattike parato adisvā asutvāva attano dhammatāya “evaṃ sati evaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ cintāmayaanubuddhiyā uppāditā anavajjakammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānesu paññā ceva kammassakatañāṇaṃ, saccānulomikañāṇañca cintāmayā nāma paññā. Tattha vaḍḍhakikammapupphachaḍḍakakammādi hīnañceva kasivāṇijjādi ukkaṭṭhañca kammameva kammāyatanaṃ. Naḷakārapesakārasippādi hīnañceva muddāgaṇanālekhādi ukkaṭṭhañca sippameva sippāyatanaṃ. Nāgamaṇḍalaparittādi dhammikavijjāva vijjāṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu cintābaleneva uppannā paññā. Bodhisattādayo hi sattahitāya adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ taṃtaṃanavajjakammasippatadupakaraṇakaraṇappakārañca ñāṇabalena cintetvā nipphādenti. Nāgamaṇḍalaparittādivijjampi uppādenti, evaṃ katānipi tāni pubbe uggaṇhitvā karontehi katasippasadisāneva honti. Kammassakatañāṇaṃ nāma kusalakammaṃ sattānaṃ sakaṃ, akusalaṃ no sakanti evaṃ jānanapaññā. Atha vā kusalakammameva sattānaṃ sakaṃ tadāyatthavuttitāya, nāññanti evaṃ jānanapaññāpi. Saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Taṃ hi maggasaccassa paramatthasaccassa anulomanato “saccānulomika”nti vuccati. Idampi hi ñāṇadvayaṃ parato asutvā cintābalena uppāditaṃ cintāmayañāṇameva hoti. Idañca na yesaṃ kesañci sattānaṃ uppajjati, abhiññātānaṃ pana puññavantānaṃ mahāsattānameva uppajjati. Tatthāpi saccānulomikañāṇaṃ pacchimabhavikānaṃ dvinnaññeva bodhisattānaṃ uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Sutamayā paññāti parato sutvā sutavasena uppāditā yathāvuttakammāyatanādipaññāva. Parato asutvā [V 0.0204] pana kammāyatanādi parena kayiramānaṃ, kataṃ vā disvā [M 0.0267] uggahetvā vā paṭiladdhāpi paññā “sutamayā”tveva vuccati. Tadubhayāpi cintāmayā, sutamayā ca kāmāvacarāva. Bhāvanāmayā pana paññā cintāmayavasena, sutamayavasena vā pavattitakāmāvacarapubbabhāgabhāvanānipphattiyā samuppannā mahaggatalokuttarajavanapaññā.

In the threes, in the triad on wisdom consisting of reflection: without having seen or heard from another, by one's own natural inclination, through reflective understanding thinking, 'When this is, that will be,' the wisdom that is produced in the spheres of blameless work, crafts, and sciences, as well as the knowledge of the ownership of kamma and the knowledge in conformity with the truths—this is called wisdom consisting of reflection. Here, lowly work such as carpentry and garland-making, and excellent work such as agriculture and commerce, are the sphere of work. Lowly crafts such as reed-work and weaving, and excellent crafts such as using seals, calculation, and writing, are the sphere of crafts. Righteous sciences such as protective spells like the Nāgamaṇḍala are the sphere of science. In these, wisdom arises solely through the power of reflection. For the welfare of beings, great beings such as the Bodhisatta, without having previously seen or heard, reflect with the power of their knowledge and create various methods for blameless work and crafts and the tools for them. They also originate sciences such as protective spells. Even when these are later learned and practiced by those who do them, they are just like crafts that have been done before. The knowledge of the ownership of kamma is the wisdom of knowing thus: 'Wholesome kamma is beings' own; unwholesome kamma is not their own.' Or it is the wisdom of knowing thus: 'Only wholesome kamma is beings' own, as their existence depends on it; nothing else is.' Knowledge in conformity with the truths is insight knowledge. For because it conforms to the truth of the path, the ultimate truth, it is called 'knowledge in conformity with the truths.' These two kinds of knowledge, too, arising without being heard from another but through the power of reflection, are indeed wisdom consisting of reflection. This does not arise in just any being, but only in distinguished, meritorious great beings. And among them, it should be understood that knowledge in conformity with the truths arises only in the two Bodhisattas in their final existence. Wisdom consisting of learning is the aforesaid wisdom concerning the spheres of work, etc., produced by way of what has been heard from another. But even wisdom acquired without hearing from another, by observing another performing or having performed something in the spheres of work, etc., and grasping it, is still called 'wisdom consisting of learning.' Both wisdom consisting of reflection and wisdom consisting of learning are exclusively of the sense sphere. Wisdom consisting of development, however, is the sublime and supramundane javana-wisdom that has arisen with the accomplishment of the preliminary-part development of the sense sphere, which proceeded by way of reflection or learning.

Dānamayattike deyyadhammapariccāgavasena pavattā dānamayā, sīlapūraṇavasena pavattā sīlamayā, tadubhayāpi kāmāvacarāva. Bhāvanāmayā panettha samathavipassanāvasena pavattā catubhūmakapaññā. Niddese panassa kiñcāpi “samāpannassa paññā”ti (vibha. 768) evaṃ mahaggatalokuttarapaññāva vuttā, tathāpi taṃ ukkaṭṭhavasena vuttaṃ. Kāmāvacarānaṃ pana pubbabhāgabhāvanānaṃ, anussatiupacārabhāvanānañca bhāvanāmaye saṅgahoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimattike panetāsaṃ cintāmaye saṅgahitattā bhāvanāmaye asaṅgaho, tatthāpi bhāvanābalanipphannānameva saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

In the triad on what consists of giving: that which proceeds by way of relinquishing a thing to be given is what consists of giving; that which proceeds by way of fulfilling virtue is what consists of virtue; both of these are exclusively of the sense sphere. Here, what consists of development is the wisdom of the four planes that proceeds by way of serenity and insight. However, in its exposition, although 'the wisdom of one who has attained absorption' (Vibh 768) is stated, and thus only sublime and supramundane wisdom is mentioned, still this is stated with reference to the highest instance. It should be understood, however, that the preliminary-part development of the sense sphere and the development of recollection up to access concentration are included in what consists of development. But in the preceding triad, because these are included in what consists of reflection, they are not included in what consists of development; even there, it should be understood that only what is accomplished by the power of development is included.

Adhisīlattike pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vipassanāhetuttā sesasīlato adhikaṃ sīlanti adhisīlaṃ, tasmiṃ sampayuttā paññā adhisīle paññā. Vipassanāpādikā pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo sesacittehi adhikattā adhicittaṃ, tasmiṃ paññā adhicitte paññā, cittasīsena cettha samādhi niddiṭṭho. Savipassanā pana maggaphalapaññā sesāhi adhikattā adhipaññā nāma. Sā ca adhipaññāya paññāti desanāya samarasatāya vuttā. Sīlādayo “sīlaṃ cittaṃ paññā, adhisīlaṃ adhicittaṃ adhipaññā”ti paccekaṃ duvidhā honti. Tesu purimā pañcasīladasasīlāni, vaṭṭapādikaaṭṭhasamāpattiyo, nibbedhabhāgiyakammassakatapaññā ca yathākkamaṃ honti. Te ca dhammā anuppannepi tathāgate bodhisattānaṃ, tāpasaparibbājakānaṃ, cakkavattirājādīnañca [M 0.0268] kāle pavattanti, pacchimā pana vuttāvasesā uppanne eva tathāgate vitthārikā honti, no anuppanneti veditabbo. Ettha ca ratanattaye dānāpacāyanādivasena, saraṇagamanasaddhammasavanādivasena ca pavattā vivaṭṭūpanissayabhūtā kusaladhammāpi adhisīlaadhipaññāsu gahitā evāti gahetabbā.

In the triad on higher virtue, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha is called 'higher virtue' because it is a cause for insight and surpasses the other virtues. The wisdom associated with it is 'wisdom in higher virtue.' The eight attainments, which are a foundation for insight, are called 'higher mind' because they surpass other states of mind. The wisdom associated with them is 'wisdom in higher mind'; and here concentration is designated by the term 'mind' as its head. The wisdom of the path and fruition, along with insight, is called 'higher wisdom' because it surpasses the rest. And this is spoken of as 'wisdom in higher wisdom' in the teaching because of the uniformity of flavor. Virtue, mind, and wisdom are each twofold: 'virtue and higher virtue, mind and higher mind, wisdom and higher wisdom.' Among these, the first set comprises, respectively, the five and ten precepts; the eight attainments that are a basis for the round of existence; and the wisdom of ownership of kamma that partakes of penetration. These phenomena occur even when a Tathāgata has not arisen, in the time of bodhisattas, ascetics, wanderers, wheel-turning monarchs, and others. The latter set, however, the remainder of what was mentioned, become widespread only when a Tathāgata has arisen, not when one has not arisen. This should be understood. Here, it should be understood that wholesome states that arise through giving and honoring the Triple Gem, and through taking refuge and listening to the good Dhamma—which serve as a supporting condition for turning away from the round—are also included under higher virtue and higher wisdom.

Āyakosallattike [V 0.0205] āyoti vaḍḍhi, sā akusalādianatthahānito, kusalādiatthuppattito ca duvidhā. Apāyoti avaḍḍhi, sāpi kusalādiatthahānito, akusalādianatthuppattito ca duvidhā. Tesu kosallaṃ, kusalasabhāvā paññā. Apāyakosallaṃ paññavato eva “evaṃ manasikārādippavattiyaṃ avaḍḍhi uppajjati, vaḍḍhi parihāyatī”ti ñatvā tadubhayapaṭipattisambhavato. Upāyakosallanti atra upāyo accāyikakiccādīsu ṭhānuppattikaupāyajānanapaññā, tividhāpi cetā kāmāvacarapaññāti veditabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In the triad on skill in gain, 'gain' (āya) is increase. It is twofold: through the decline of what is unbeneficial, such as the unwholesome, and through the arising of what is beneficial, such as the wholesome. 'Loss' (apāya) is decrease. It too is twofold: through the decline of what is beneficial, such as the wholesome, and through the arising of what is unbeneficial, such as the unwholesome. Skill in these is wisdom, which has a wholesome nature. Skill in what leads to loss is possible only for one with wisdom, who knows: 'When such attention, etc., occurs, decrease arises and increase declines,' and is thus able to undertake the practice concerning both. 'Skill in means' is the wisdom that knows the resourceful means in urgent duties and so on. All three should be understood as sense-sphere wisdom. The rest is easily understood.

Tikaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The triad is concluded.

Catukkesu pana paṭhame kammassakatañāṇaṃ saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇañca vuttameva, idha pana ṭhapetvā saccānulomikañāṇaṃ sabbāpi sāsavā kusalā paññā kammassakatañāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Catūsu maggesu, phalesu ca paññāva maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ, phalasamaṅgissa ñāṇañcāti.

Now, in the first of the tetrads, the knowledge of ownership of kamma and the knowledge in conformity with the truths have already been mentioned. But here, setting aside the knowledge in conformity with the truths, all mundane wholesome wisdom should be understood as the knowledge of ownership of kamma. In the four paths and four fruits, wisdom itself is the knowledge of one endowed with the path and the knowledge of one endowed with the fruition.

Saccacatukke ariyamaggaphalapaññāva catūsu saccesu ekapaṭivedhavasena “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādinā catūsu ṭhānesu gahitā. Kiñcāpi hi kāmāvacarañāṇampi catūsu saccesu ārammaṇavasena pavattati, paṭivedhakiccavasena pana idhādhippetattā pāḷiyaṃ taṃ na gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

In the tetrad on the truths, the wisdom of the noble path and fruition itself is taken in four instances, beginning with 'knowledge in suffering,' by way of the single penetration of the four truths. Although sense-sphere knowledge also occurs with the four truths as its object, it should be understood that it is not included in the Pāli text here, because what is intended is the function of penetration.

Dhammacatukke maggaphalesu paññā dhamme ñāṇaṃ nāma. Tesu hi maggañāṇaṃ tāva catusaccadhammānaṃ ekapaṭivedhavasena jānanato “dhamme [M 0.0269] ñāṇa”nti vuccati. Phalañāṇaṃ pana nirodhasaccavasena dhamme ñāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Maggānubhāvanibbattaṃ pana atītānāgatesu saccapaṭivedhanayasaṅgahaṇavasena pavattaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ anvaye ñāṇaṃ nāma. Tassa ca yehi nayehi ariyā atītamaddhānaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ jāniṃsu, tepi imaññeva catusaccaṃ evameva jāniṃsu, anāgatamaddhānampi jānissantīti evaṃ jānanavasena pavatti ākāro veditabbo. Sarāgādivasena paracittaparicchedañāṇaṃ pariye ñāṇaṃ nāma. Dhammanvayapariyañāṇāni pana ṭhapetvā sabbalokiyapaññāñāṇanti sammatattā sammutimhi ñāṇanti sammutiñāṇaṃ nāma.

In the tetrad on the Dhamma, wisdom in the path and fruition is called 'knowledge in the Dhamma.' For path knowledge is called 'knowledge in the Dhamma' because it knows the dhammas of the four truths by way of a single penetration. But fruition knowledge should be understood as 'knowledge in the Dhamma' by way of the truth of cessation. The reviewing knowledge, which is produced by the power of the path and proceeds by way of comprehending the method of penetrating the truths in the past and future, is called 'knowledge of inference.' Its mode of proceeding should be understood as knowing thus: 'By these same methods the noble ones in the past knew the Dhamma of the four truths; they knew just this same fourfold truth in just this way, and so they will know it in the future.' The knowledge that defines the minds of others by way of lust, etc., is called 'knowledge of penetration.' Setting aside knowledge in the Dhamma, knowledge of inference, and knowledge of penetration, because all worldly wisdom is agreed upon as 'knowledge,' it is 'knowledge in convention' and is thus called 'conventional knowledge.'

Ācayacatukke kāmāvacarakusale paññā ācayāya no apacayāya. Sā hi cutipaṭisandhiṃ [V 0.0206] ācinoti eva, no apacinoti. Maggapaññā pana apacayāya no ācayāya. Rūpārūpakusalapaññā ācayāya ceva apacayāya ca. Sā hi vikkhambhanavasena kilese ca tammūlake ca vipākadhamme apacinoti. Sesā abyākatā paññā nevācayāya no apacayāya.

In the tetrad on accumulation, wisdom in the sense-sphere wholesome is for accumulation, not for decline. For it only accumulates death and rebirth-linking; it does not diminish it. Path wisdom, however, is for decline, not for accumulation. Wisdom in the fine-material and immaterial wholesome is for both accumulation and for decline. For by way of suppression, it diminishes the defilements and the resultant states rooted in them. The remaining indeterminate wisdom is neither for accumulation nor for decline.

Nibbidācatukke rūpāvacarapaṭhamajjhānapaññā nibbidāya no paṭivedhāya. Sā hi kāmavivekena pattabbattā kilesanibbidāya pavattati, abhiññāpādakabhāvaṃ pana appattatāya nevābhiññāpaṭivedhāya saṃvattati. Catutthajjhānapaññā paṭivedhāya no nibbidāya. Sā hi abhiññāpādakabhāvenāpi abhiññābhāvappattiyāpi paṭivedhāya saṃvattati. Paṭhamajjhānakkhaṇe eva nīvaraṇanibbindanattā no nibbidāya. Dutiyatatiyajjhānapaññā pana somanassasahagatatāya paṭhamajjhānasannissitā vā avitakkatāya catutthajjhānasannissitā vā kātabbā. Maggapaññā pana nibbidāya ceva paṭivedhāya ca. Ettha hi catusaccapaṭivedhavasena nibbidāya cevetāsaṃ chaḷabhiññāppattiyā paṭivedhāya ca saṃvattanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesā lokiyalokuttarā [M 0.0270] paññā neva nibbidāya no paṭivedhāya.

In the tetrad on disenchantment, the wisdom of the first fine-material jhāna is for disenchantment, not for penetration. Since it is to be attained through seclusion from sensual pleasures, it conduces to disenchantment with the defilements; but because it has not reached the state of being a basis for the direct knowledges, it does not lead to penetration by direct knowledge. The wisdom of the fourth jhāna is for penetration, not for disenchantment. Since it serves as a basis for the direct knowledges and also attains the state of direct knowledge, it conduces to penetration; and because one has already become disenchanted with the hindrances at the moment of the first jhāna, it is not for disenchantment. The wisdom of the second and third jhānas, because it is accompanied by joy, should be classified with the first jhāna; or, because it is without thought-conception, with the fourth jhāna. Path wisdom, however, is for both disenchantment and penetration. Here, it should be understood that it conduces to disenchantment through the penetration of the four truths, and to penetration through the attainment of the six direct knowledges. The remaining worldly and supramundane wisdoms are neither for disenchantment nor for penetration.

Hānabhāgiyacatukke hānaṃ bhajatīti hānabhāginī, evaṃ sesesupi. Nibbedhoti cettha ariyamaggo tannibbattakavipassanāpādakattā. Nibbedhabhāginīti catūsupi ṭhānesu rūpārūpakusalapaññāva vuttā. Tāni hi attano sabhāvā parihāyitvā heṭṭhā orohaṇapaccayabhūtā hānabhāginī. Upanijjhānapaccayabhūtā visesabhāginī, taṃ pana jhānanikantiyā balavatāya visesaṃ, hāniṃ vā anussukkitvā ṭhitikoṭṭhāsikā ṭhitibhāginī, ariyamaggapadaṭṭhānavipassanāpādakabhūtāva nibbedhabhāginī ca hontīti veditabbā.

In the tetrad on what partakes of decline: 'it partakes of decline' (hānaṃ bhajati), thus it is 'partaking of decline' (hānabhāginī); and so for the others. Here, 'penetration' (nibbedha) is the noble path, because it has for its basis the insight that produces it. In all four cases, what is spoken of is the wholesome wisdom of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. For these states of wisdom become 'partaking of decline' when, having fallen away from their own nature, they become a condition for descending to a lower state. They become 'partaking of distinction' when they are a condition for close contemplation. When, through a strong delight in jhāna, one is not eager for distinction or decline, they are 'partaking of stability' as a fixed portion. And they become 'partaking of penetration' when they are a basis for insight, which is the foundation for the noble path. This is how it should be understood.

Catasso paṭisambhidāti atthadhammaniruttipaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāva. Catasso paṭipadāti dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññādayo heṭṭhā vuttāva. Cattāri ārammaṇānīti parittā, parittārammaṇātiādikā heṭṭhā vuttanayāva. Jarāmaraṇādicatukkesupi maggañāṇavaseneva catasso yojanā vuttā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

The four analytical knowledges are the analytical knowledge of meaning, of Dhamma, of language, and of perspicuity. The four modes of practice are the painful practice with slow direct knowledge and so on, as mentioned previously. The four objects are the limited, the object that is limited, and so on, in the way mentioned previously. In the tetrads beginning with aging-and-death, too, the four applications are stated only by way of path knowledge. The rest is easily understood.

Catukkaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The tetrad is concluded.

Pañcakesu [V 0.0207] pana pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhīti pītipharaṇatā sukhapharaṇatā cetopharaṇatā ālokapharaṇatā paccavekkhaṇanimittanti evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttehi pañcahi ñāṇaṅgehi samannāgato samādhi. Tattha pītiṃ pharamānā uppajjatīti dvīsu jhānesu paññā pītipharaṇatā nāma, sukhaṃ pharamānā uppajjatīti tīsu jhānesu paññā sukhapharaṇatā nāma. Paresaṃ cetopharamānā uppajjatīti cetopariyañāṇaṃ cetopharaṇatā nāma. Ālokapharaṇe uppajjatīti dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ ālokapharaṇatā nāma. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ nāma. Ettha ca pītipharaṇatā, sukhapharaṇatā ca dve pādā viya, cetopharaṇatā, ālokapharaṇatā ca dve [M 0.0271] hatthā viya, paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ sīsaṃ viya, abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ majjhimakāyo viya. Iti bhagavā pañcaṅgikaṃ sammāsamādhiṃ aṅgapaccaṅgasampannaṃ purisaṃ viya katvā dasseti. Iminā ca samādhinā aṅgāni pañca ñāṇaṅgāni vuttānīti veditabbāni.

Now, in the pentads, 'five-factored right concentration' is concentration endowed with the five factors of knowledge stated in the Pāli as: pervasion by rapture, pervasion by pleasure, pervasion of mind, pervasion by light, and the sign of reviewing. Therein, 'pervasion by rapture' is the name for the wisdom in the two jhānas that arises while pervading with rapture. 'Pervasion by pleasure' is the name for the wisdom in the three jhānas that arises while pervading with pleasure. 'Pervasion of mind' is the name for the knowledge of others' minds that arises while pervading their minds. 'Pervasion by light' is the name for the knowledge of the divine eye that arises in the pervasion of light. The knowledge of reviewing is called 'the sign of reviewing.' Here, pervasion by rapture and pervasion by pleasure are like the two feet; pervasion of mind and pervasion by light are like the two hands; the sign of reviewing is like the head; and the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges is like the torso. Thus the Blessed One shows the five-factored right concentration by making it like a person complete with major and minor limbs. And it should be understood that by this concentration, five factors—the factors of knowledge—have been stated.

Pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhīti –

The right concentration with five knowledges is this:

“‘Ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko’ti paccattaññeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, ‘ayaṃ samādhi ariyo nirāmiso’ti…pe… ‘mahāpurisasevito’ti…pe… ‘santo paṇīto paṭipassaddhiladdho ekodibhāvādhigato na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato’ti…pe… ‘so kho panāhaṃ imaṃ samādhiṃ satova samāpajjāmi, sato vuṭṭhahāmī’ti paccattaññeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjatī”ti (vibha. 804) –

"'This concentration is pleasant in the present and results in pleasure in the future'—knowledge arises for oneself. 'This concentration is noble and unworldly'… 'resorted to by great persons'… 'peaceful, sublime, attained by serenity, achieved by unification, not obtained by means of forceful suppression and restraint'… 'And I, indeed, mindfully attain this concentration and mindfully emerge from it'—knowledge arises for oneself" (Vibh 804).

Evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttehi pañcahi paccavekkhaṇañāṇehi yutto arahattaphalasaṅkhāto samāpattiphalasamādhi. So evaṃ hi appitappitakkhaṇe sukhattā paccuppannasukho, purimo purimo pacchimassa pacchimassa samādhisukhassa ceva attanā samuṭṭhāpitampi paṇītarūpena phuṭṭhasakalakāyatāya phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhitakāle atipaṇītaṃ kāyaviññāṇasukhassa paccayattā āyatiṃ sukhavipāko uppajjati, imināpi pariyāyena āyatiṃ sukhavipākoti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, kilesehi ārakattā ariyo kāmāmisavaṭṭāmisalokāmisānaṃ abhāvā nirāmisoti ekaṃ, buddhādīhi mahāpurisehi sevitattā akāpurisasevisoti ekaṃ, aṅgārammaṇe santatāya, sabbakilesadarathasantatāya ca santo atappanīyaṭṭhena paṇīto [M 0.0272] kilesapaṭipassaddhibhāvassa laddhattā paṭipassaddhaladdho [V 0.0208] ekodibhāvena ca adhigato appaguṇasāsavasamādhi viya sasaṅkhārena sappayogena paccanīkadhamme niggayha kilese vāretvā anadhigatattā na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Puggalassāyaṃ samādhīti evaṃ khīṇāsavassa sativepullappattiyā yathāparicchinnakālavasena imaṃ samādhiṃ satova samāpajjati, uṭṭhahati cāti ekamaṅganti imehi pañcahi aṅgehi sabbākārato yuttattā “pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhī”ti vuccati.

Thus, endowed with the five reviewing knowledges stated in the Pāḷi, there is the concentration of the fruit of attainment, called the fruit of arahantship. For this is pleasant in the present because of the pleasure at the very moment of absorption. The earlier moments are a condition for the later happiness of concentration; and because the entire body is pervaded by a sublime form produced by it, and because at the time of emerging from the attainment of fruition it is a condition for the extremely sublime pleasure of bodily consciousness, a pleasant result arises in the future. In this way, 'having a pleasant result in the future' is one factor. Being far from the defilements, it is noble; due to the absence of the baits of sensual pleasures, the baits of the round, and the baits of the world, it is 'unworldly'—this is one factor. Because it is resorted to by great persons such as the Buddhas, it is 'not resorted to by inferior persons'—this is one factor. Because of the tranquility of its object and the tranquility of all defilements and distress, it is peaceful; because it does not cause torment, it is sublime; and because the state of pacification of the defilements has been obtained, it is 'obtained through pacification' and attained through unification. Unlike a concentration with taints and of little quality, it is not attained by suppressing opposing states and warding off defilements with effort and exertion; thus it is 'not gone to by suppression and warding off with effort.' This concentration belongs to the person. Thus, for one whose taints are destroyed, who has attained fullness of mindfulness, he mindfully enters and emerges from this concentration for a pre-determined period of time—this is one factor. Because it is endowed in all aspects with these five factors, it is called 'right concentration with five knowledges.'

Pañcakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the fives is finished.

Chakke chasu abhiññāsu paññāti iddhividhe ñāṇaṃ, dibbasotadhātuyā ñāṇaṃ, cetopariye ñāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsānussatiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ, cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ, āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇanti evaṃ vuttāni chaḷabhiññācittasampayuttāni ñāṇāni. Tesu pacchimaṃ lokuttaraṃ, sesāni rūpāvacarapañcamajjhānikānīti.

In the section on the sixes, wisdom in the six direct knowledges is: the knowledge of the kinds of spiritual power, the knowledge of the divine ear element, the knowledge of encompassing mind, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. These are the knowledges associated with the consciousness of the six direct knowledges. Among them, the last is supramundane, while the rest belong to the fifth jhāna of the form sphere.

Chakkaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the sixes is finished.

Sattake sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnīti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ ekaṃ, “asati avijjāya natthi saṅkhārā”ti ekanti dve ñāṇāni, evaṃ atītepi dve, anāgatepi dveti cha, taṃ chabbidhampi ñāṇaṃ “khayadhamma”ntiādinā paccavekkhaṇañāṇena saddhiṃ satta ñāṇāni. Evaṃ sesesupi jātipariyosānesu cāti evaṃ ekādasasu paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu paccekaṃ kālattayepi anvayabyatirekañāṇaṃ tesaṃ vayadassanañāṇassa ca vasena satta satta katvā sattasattati ñāṇāni.

In the section on the sevens, the seventy-seven grounds of knowledge are as follows: The reviewing knowledge 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be' is one. 'When there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations' is one—thus two knowledges. Similarly, there are two for the past and two for the future, making six. These six kinds of knowledge, together with the reviewing knowledge of them as 'subject to destruction,' etc., make seven knowledges. In the same way, for the remaining links ending with birth, for each of the eleven links of dependent origination, by way of the knowledge of positive and negative correlation in the three periods of time and the knowledge of seeing their passing away, there are seven each, making seventy-seven knowledges.

Sattakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the sevens is finished.

Aṭṭhakaṃ suviññeyyameva.

The section on the eights is easy to understand.

Navake navasu anupubbavihārasamāpattīsu paññāti nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjantassa anupaṭipāṭiyā vihātabbato uppādetabbato anupubbavihārasaṅkhātāsu rūpārūpasamāpattīsu [M 0.0273] sampayuttā [V 0.0209] aṭṭha paññā ceva tadanantaraṃ nirodhaṃ phusitvā vuṭṭhitassa nirodhaṃ santato paccavekkhaṇañāṇañcāti nava.

In the section on the nines, wisdom in the nine successive abidings is: the eight wisdoms associated with the form and formless attainments—called the 'successive abidings' because they are to be abided in and generated in sequence by one who is attaining the attainment of cessation—and, immediately after that, for one who has emerged after touching cessation, the reviewing knowledge of cessation as peaceful. These are the nine.

Navakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the nines is finished.

Dasake tathāgatassāti yathā vipassīādayo pubbakā isayo āgatā, tathā āgatassa sammāsambuddhassa. Tathāgatabalānīti aññehi asādhāraṇāni tathāgatasseva balāni, yathā vā pubbabuddhānaṃ balāni puññussayasampattiyā āgatāni, tathā āgatāni balānītipi attho. Tattha duvidhaṃ tathāgatassa balaṃ kāyabalaṃ, ñāṇabalañca. Tesu kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ porāṇehi –

In the section on the tens, 'of the Tathāgata' means: of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One who has 'thus come' (tathā āgata) just as the former seers, Vipassī and others, came. 'The Tathāgata's powers' means the powers of the Tathāgata alone, not shared by others. Or the meaning is: 'powers that have thus come' (tathā āgatāni) just as the powers of past Buddhas came through the accomplishment of an abundance of merit. Herein, the Tathāgata's power is twofold: bodily power and the power of knowledge. Among these, bodily power is to be understood in accordance with the elephant clans. For it has been said by the ancients:

“Kāḷāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti. (vibha. aṭṭha. 760; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.22; a. ni. 10.21; udā. aṭṭha. 75; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 1.39; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.44; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 81);

“Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha and Chaddanta—these are the ten.”

Imāni hi dasa hatthikulāni. Tattha kāḷāvakanti pakatihatthikulaṃ, yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ, taṃ ekassa kāḷāvakahatthino balaṃ, yaṃ tesaṃ dasannaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ tambassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthino, tesaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ hemassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ uposathassa, tesaṃ dasannaṃ balaṃ chaddantassa, yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ balaṃ, taṃ tathāgatassa nārāyaṇabalanti vuccati. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthigaṇanāya hatthīnaṃ koṭisahassaṃ, purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāva tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ. Yāni pana dasabalacatuvesārajjādīni anekāni ñāṇasahassāni, etaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ nāma. Idhāpi ñāṇabalameva adhippetaṃ. Ñāṇañhi akampiyaṭṭhena, upatthambhanaṭṭhena ca balanti vuttaṃ.

These are the ten elephant clans. Among them, the Kāḷāvaka is the ordinary elephant clan. The bodily power of ten men is the power of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The power of ten such elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya. The power of ten of those is that of one Paṇḍara. The power of ten of those is that of one Tamba. The power of ten of those is that of one Piṅgala. The power of ten of those is that of one Gandha elephant. The power of ten of those is that of one Maṅgala. The power of ten of those is that of one Hema. The power of ten of those is that of one Uposatha. The power of ten of those is that of one Chaddanta. The power of ten Chaddanta elephants is called the Nārāyaṇa power of the Tathāgata. This amounts to the power of a thousand koṭis of ordinary elephants, or the power of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, for a start, is the Tathāgata's bodily power. But the many thousands of knowledges—the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, etc.—are called the power of knowledge. Here, too, it is the power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called a power because it is unshakeable and supportive.

Yehi [M 0.0274] balehi samannāgatoti yehi dasahi ñāṇabalehi upeto. Āsabhaṇṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Apica [V 0.0210] gavasatajeṭṭhako usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho. Vajasatajeṭṭhako vā usabho, vajasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho, sabbagavaseṭṭho nisabho, seto pāsādiko mahābhāravaho sabbaparissayasaho asanisatasaddehipi akampanīyo nisabho, so idha usabhoti adhippeto. Idampi hi tassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ. Ṭhānanti tassa nisabhabalasamannāgatassa catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ pana āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yatheva hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho usabhabalena samannāgato catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi hi dasabalasamannāgato catuvesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisapathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci appadhaṃsiyo acalena ṭhānena tiṭṭhati, tañcesa paṭijānāti upagacchati na paccakkhāti attani āropeti, tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti (vibha. 760).

'Endowed with which powers' means endowed with the ten powers of knowledge. 'A bull's position' means the foremost position. Further, the chief of a hundred cattle is a bull (usabha); the chief of a thousand cattle is a great bull (vasabha). Or the chief of a hundred herds is a bull; the chief of a thousand herds is a great bull. The best of all cattle is a lordly bull (nisabha): white, inspiring, a bearer of great loads, an endurer of all hardships, unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts. Such a nisabha is the bull intended here. This is a synonym for it. 'Of the bull' (usabhassa) is āsabhaṃ. 'Position' means the unmoving stance of one endowed with the power of a lordly bull, pressing down on the earth with four feet. This, being like a bull's, is āsabhaṃ. For just as the bull called nisabha, endowed with a bull's power, stands with an unmoving stance, pressing down on the earth with its four feet, so the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers, stands with an unmoving stance, unassailable by anyone in the world with its gods, having pressed down on the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of the fearlessnesses. He acknowledges this, accepts it, does not deny it, and claims it for himself. Therefore it is said: 'He claims the bull's position.'

Parisāsūti aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ, sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadati. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena dīpetabbo. Yathā vā sīho sahanato ca hananato ca “sīho”ti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgatopi lokadhammānaṃ sahanato, parappavādānañca hananato “sīho”ti vuccati, tassa nādaṃ nadati.

'In the assemblies' means in the eight assemblies. 'He roars the lion's roar' means he utters the supreme roar, the fearless roar, or he utters a roar like a lion's roar. This meaning should be illustrated by means of the Sīhanāda Sutta. Or, just as a lion (sīha) is so called because it endures (sahanato) and because it strikes (hananato), so the Tathāgata is called a 'lion' because he endures worldly conditions and demolishes the tenets of others; he utters his roar.

Brahmacakkantiādīsu brahmanti uttamaṃ visuddhaṃ.
