Cakka-saddo panāyaṃ “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.31) sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Pādatalesu cakkāni [M 0.0275] jātānī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.35; 3.204; ma. ni. 2.386) lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti (dha. pa. 1) ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) ettha iriyāpathe. “Cakkaṃ pavattaya sabbapāṇina”nti (jā. 1.7.149) ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti (dī. ni. 3.85) ettha ratanacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti (jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103) ettha uracakke. “Khurapariyantena cepi cakkenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166) ettha paharaṇacakke. “Asanicakka”nti (dī. ni. 3.61; saṃ. ni. 2.162) ettha asanimaṇḍale. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562) ettha dhammacakke. Idha pana dhammacakke pavattati.

In terms like 'brahmacakka,' 'brahma' means supreme, purified. The word 'cakka,' however, is seen in the sense of accomplishment in passages such as, 'Monks, there are these four wheels by which devas and humans are endowed' (A. Ni. 4.31). In phrases like 'wheels appeared on the soles of the feet' (Dī. Ni. 2.35; 3.204; Ma. Ni. 2.386), it is in the sense of a mark. In 'like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox' (Dha. Pa. 1), it is in the sense of a chariot-wheel. In 'four-wheeled, nine-gated' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.29), it is in the sense of deportment. In 'set the wheel rolling for all beings' (Jā. 1.7.149), it is in the sense of giving. In 'the divine wheel-treasure appeared' (Dī. Ni. 3.85), it is in the sense of a jewel-wheel. In 'for a man struck by desire, the wheel spins on his head' (Jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103), it is in the sense of the chest-wheel. In 'even if with a razor-rimmed wheel' (Dī. Ni. 1.166), it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In 'thunderbolt-wheel' (Dī. Ni. 3.61; Saṃ. Ni. 2.162), it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle. In 'the wheel set in motion by me' (Su. Ni. 562), it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. Here, however, it functions as the Dhamma-wheel.

Dhammacakkañca [V 0.0211] duvidhaṃ hoti paṭivedhañāṇañca desanāñāṇañca. Tattha paññāpabhāvitaṃ attano ariyaphalāvahaṃ lokuttaraṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ, karuṇāpabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyaphalāvahaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ desanāñāṇaṃ, ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānaññeva orasañāṇaṃ, taṃ pavatteti uppādeti vibhāveti vitthārikaṃ karotīti attho.

The Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Herein, the knowledge of penetration, developed by wisdom, brings about the noble fruits for oneself and is supramundane. The knowledge of teaching, developed by compassion, brings about the noble fruits for disciples and pertains to the sense-sphere. Both these knowledges are unshared by others and are the genuine, innate knowledge of the Buddhas alone. ‘He sets it in motion’ means that he produces it, clarifies it, and makes it extensive—this is the meaning.

Idāni yāni dasa ñāṇāni ādito “tathāgatabalānī”ti nikkhittāni, tāni vitthāretuṃ “katamāni dasa? Idha tathāgato”tiādimāha. Tattha ṭhānañca ṭhānatoti kāraṇañca kāraṇato. Kāraṇaṃ hi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttitāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati. Aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānatoti akāraṇañca akāraṇato. Yampīti yena ñāṇena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, idampi ṭhānāṭhānañāṇaṃ tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ nāma hotīti attho. Evaṃ uparipi sabbattha yojanā veditabbā. Kathaṃ panettha bhagavā ṭhānañca ṭhānato, aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato [M 0.0276] yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti? Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya…pe… kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, pitaraṃ…pe… arahantaṃ jīvitā voropeyya, paduṭṭhacittena tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbatteyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, puthujjano panetaṃ sabbaṃ kareyyāti ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti pajānāti, tathā yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ, tathā dve rājāno cakkavattī uppajjeyyuṃ, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, eko pana uppajjati, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti pajānāti, tathā yaṃ kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ duccaritānaṃ iṭṭho vipāko, sucaritānañca aniṭṭho vipāko nibbatteyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, tabbiparīto pana nesaṃ vipāko nibbatteyyāti ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti, ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ, itare aṭṭhānanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettha panāyaṃ saṅkhepato aṭṭhakathāvinicchayo. “Sukhato upagaccheyyā”ti idaṃ “ekantasukhī attā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.27) diṭṭhivipallāsavasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, saññācittavipallāsavasena pana ariyasāvakopi kilesapariḷāhābhibhūto mattahatthiparitāsito viya, sucikāmo gūthakūpaṃ viya kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati, attato upagamanavāre kasiṇādipaṇṇattiyā, nibbānassa ca saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “saṅkhāra”nti avatvā “kañci dhamma”nti vuttaṃ.

Now, to elaborate on the ten knowledges that were initially set forth as the ‘Tathāgata’s powers,’ the text states: ‘What are the ten? Here, the Tathāgata…,’ and so on. Herein, ‘what is possible as possible’ means the cause as the cause. For a cause is called a ‘possibility’ (ṭhāna) because the result is established (tiṭṭhati) in it; that is, being dependent on it, the result arises and continues. ‘What is impossible as impossible’ means what is not a cause as not a cause. And that knowledge by which he understands this as it really is—this knowledge of the possible and the impossible is a power of the Tathāgata. The same principle should be applied to all the rest. But how does the Blessed One understand what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, as it truly is? It is impossible, there is no opportunity, that a person accomplished in view would regard any conditioned thing as permanent… or regard any phenomenon as self, would deprive his mother of life, his father… an arahant of life, with a malicious mind shed the blood of the Tathāgata, cause a schism in the Sangha, acknowledge another teacher, or bring about an eighth existence—this is not possible. But that an ordinary person could do all these—this is possible, he understands. Similarly, that two arahants, perfectly enlightened ones, should arise simultaneously in one world-system, or that two wheel-turning monarchs should arise—this is not possible. But that one of each should arise—this is possible, he understands. Further, that the three types of misconduct—bodily misconduct, etc.—should result in a desirable outcome, or that good conduct should result in an undesirable outcome—this is not possible. But that the opposite result should occur for them—this is possible, he understands. He understands as it truly is that whatever phenomena are causes and conditions for the arising of whatever other phenomena—that is possible, while the others are impossible. Here, this is a brief commentary-decision. The phrase ‘would regard it as pleasant’ is said with reference to grasping at pleasantness due to the distortion of view, as in ‘the self is exclusively happy.’ But due to the distortion of perception and mind, even a noble disciple, overwhelmed by the torment of defilements, like one frightened by a rutting elephant, or like one desiring purity approaching a cesspit, may regard some conditioned thing as pleasant. In the case of regarding as self, to include designations like the kasiṇa and also Nibbāna, instead of saying ‘any conditioned thing,’ it is said ‘any phenomenon.’

Mātarantiādīsu [V 0.0212] kiñcāpi ariyasāvako sīsacchedaṃ pāpuṇantopi kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya pāṇātipātaṃ, adinnādānādīsu vā yaṃkiñci duccaritaṃ apāyahetubhūtaṃ kātuṃ bhavantarepi [M 0.0277] na sakkoti, puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjatādassanatthamettha pañcānantariyāneva uddhaṭāni. Sāvajjo hi puthujjanabhāvo, yatra hi nāma ānantariyānipi karissatīti. Ettha ca manussabhūtasseva manussabhūtaṃ janikaṃ mātaraṃ, pitaraṃ vā api parivattaliṅgaṃ jīvitā voropentassa kammaṃ ānantariyaṃ hoti. Tiracchānabhūtaṃ pana mātaraṃ, pitaraṃ vā sayaṃ vā tiracchānabhūto manussabhūtaṃ, tiracchānabhūtaṃ vā jīvitā voropento ānantariyaṃ na phusati, kammaṃ pana bhāriyaṃ, ānantariyaṃ āhacceva tiṭṭhati. Arahantampi manussabhūtameva ghātento ānantariyaṃ phusati. Tassa ca puthujjanakāle pahāraṃ datvā arahattaṃ patvā tasmiṃ teneva rogena matepi arahantaghātako hoti, na yakkhabhūtaṃ arahantaṃ, sesaariyapuggale vā manussabhūtepi ghātento, kammaṃ pana ānantariyasadisaṃ hoti. Yaṃ pana puthujjanakāle dinnaṃ dānaṃ arahattaṃ patvā paribhuñjati, puthujjanasseva taṃ dinnaṃ hoti, sesaariyapuggale mārentassa ānantariyaṃ natthi, kammaṃ pana garukaṃ hoti. Ettha ca eḷakādicatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ – “eḷakaṃ māremī”ti hi abhisandhinā eḷakaṭṭhāne nipannaṃ mātaraṃ, pitaraṃ, arahantaṃ vā mārento ānantariyaṃ phusati, eḷakābhisandhinā vā mātādiabhisandhinā vā eḷakaṃ mārento ānantariyaṃ na phusati, mātādiabhisandhinā te eva mārento phusateva. Esa nayo coracatukkādīsupi.

In regard to matricide and so on, even though a noble disciple, even if facing beheading, would not be capable of intentionally killing a living being, down to a tiny ant, or of committing any other misconduct that is a cause for the plane of misery, even in a future existence, nevertheless, to show how very blameworthy the state of an ordinary person is, the five heinous crimes alone have been singled out here. For the state of an ordinary person is blameworthy, since he might even commit the heinous crimes. Here, the deed becomes a heinous crime only when a human being deprives of life another human being who is his own mother or father, even one who has changed gender. But one who deprives of life an animal mother or father, or who, being an animal, deprives of life a human or an animal, does not commit a heinous crime, though the kamma is weighty; it borders on a heinous crime. One who kills a human being who is an arahant also commits a heinous crime. And if one strikes a person when he is an ordinary person, and that person later attains arahantship and dies from that very injury, the perpetrator is a slayer of an arahant. But one does not commit a heinous crime if one kills an arahant who is a yakkha, or any other noble person who is human; in such cases, however, the kamma is similar to a heinous crime. If a gift given to someone when he was an ordinary person is consumed by him after he attains arahantship, that gift was given to an ordinary person. Killing other noble persons does not constitute a heinous crime, but the kamma is serious. Here, the fourfold case of the goat should be understood: If, with the intention ‘I will kill a goat,’ one kills one’s mother, father, or an arahant lying in the goat’s place, one commits a heinous crime. But if, with the intention to kill a goat, or with the intention to kill one’s mother, one kills a goat, one does not commit a heinous crime. One commits it only when, with the intention to kill one’s mother, etc., one actually kills them. The same principle applies to the fourfold case of the thief and so on.

Lohituppāde tathāgatassa abhejjakāyatāya kuddhacittassa parassa upakkamena cammacchedo, lohitapaggharaṇaṃ vā natthi, devadattena pana paviddhasilāto bhijjitvā gatasakkhalikappahārena viya sarīrassa antoyeva ekasmiṃ ṭhāne yathā khuddikamakkhikāpivanamattampi lohitaṃ visamaṃ samosarati, tathā karontassa ānantariyaṃ hoti, na pana jīvakasseva muducittena duṭṭhalohitaṃ nīharitvā phāsukaṃ karontassa[M 0.0278], puññameva panassa hoti, parinibbute bhagavati cetiyaṃ bhindantassa, bodhiṃ chindantassa, dhātūsu upakkamantassa ca ānantariyaṃ na hoti, kammaṃ pana ānantariyasadisaṃ hoti. Bodhirukkhassa pana thūpaṃ vā sadhātukaṃ paṭimaṃ vā bādhayamānaṃ sākhaṃ, cetiyavatthuṃ bhinditvā gacchantaṃ bodhimūlañca chinditvā harituṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi sākhāya nilīnā sakuṇā cetiye vaccaṃ pātenti, chindituṃ vaṭṭati. Paribhogacetiyato hi sarīracetiyameva mahantataraṃ. Dhātunidhānarahitaṃ paṭimāgharaṃ vā bodhigharaṃ vā bādhentaṃ [V 0.0213] sākhaṃ chindituṃ na vaṭṭati, ojoharaṇasākhaṃ, panassa pūtiṭṭhānaṃ vā chindituṃ vaṭṭati, sarīrapaṭijaggane viya puññameva hoti.

In the case of shedding the Buddha’s blood, because the Tathāgata’s body is invulnerable, there is no cutting of the skin or shedding of blood from an attack by another with an angry mind. However, when Devadatta hurled a rock, a splinter from it struck the Blessed One, and in one spot within his body blood collected unevenly, as much as a tiny fly might sip. One who does such a thing commits a heinous crime. But this is not so for one like Jīvaka, who with a gentle mind removes tainted blood to bring relief; for him, there is only merit. After the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, one who breaks a shrine, cuts down the Bodhi tree, or attacks the relics does not commit a heinous crime, but the kamma is similar to a heinous crime. However, it is permissible to cut a branch of the Bodhi tree that is damaging a stupa or a relic-containing image, and to cut and remove a root of the Bodhi tree that is breaking through the foundation of a shrine. Even if birds perched on a branch defecate on a shrine, it is permissible to cut the branch. For a shrine of bodily relics is more important than a shrine of use. It is not permissible to cut a branch that is damaging a relic-less image hall or a Bodhi-tree shrine. However, it is permissible to cut a branch that draws away the sap or a rotten part; just as in caring for the body, this is only meritorious.

Saṅghabhede samānasaṃvāsasīmāya samānasaṃvāsake saṅghe ekato ṭhite visuṃ vaggasaṅghaṃ gahetvā pañcahi kāraṇehi saṅghaṃ bhindantassa saṅghabhedo hoti ānantariyakammañca. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “pañcahi, upāli, ākārehi saṅgho bhijjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Kammena uddesena voharanto anussāvanena salākaggāhenā”ti (pari. 458). Tattha kammenāti apalokanādīsu catūsu aññatarena kammena. Uddesenāti pātimokkhuddesena. Voharanto kathayanto tāhi tāhi upapattīhi “adhammaṃ dhammo”tiādīni aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni dīpento. Anussāvanenāti “nanu tumhe jānātha mayhaṃ bahussutādibhāvaṃ, kathaṃ hi nāma mādiso uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ gāheyya, kimahaṃ apāyato na bhāyāmī”tiādinā nayena kaṇṇamūle vacībhedaṃ katvā anussāvanena. Salākaggāhenāti evaṃ vohārānussāvanehi tesaṃ cittaṃ upatthambhetvā anivattidhammaṃ katvā “gaṇhatha imaṃ salāka”nti salākaggāhena.

In the case of schism in the Sangha, when the Sangha of common communion is dwelling together within a single boundary, if someone forms a separate, factional group and splits the Sangha by five methods, this constitutes a schism in the Sangha and is a deed of immediate retribution. For it has been said: ‘Upāli, the Sangha is split in five ways. What five? By a formal act, by a recitation, by speaking, by an announcement, and by the taking of voting tickets.’ Here, ‘by a formal act’ means by one of the four kinds of formal acts, such as an act of seeking approval. ‘By a recitation’ means by the recitation of the Pātimokkha. ‘By speaking’ means by speaking and expounding with various arguments the eighteen grounds for schism, such as ‘What is not the Dhamma is the Dhamma.’ ‘By an announcement’ means by making an announcement, causing a division in speech by whispering in the ear with such words as: ‘Surely you know of my great learning and so on. How could a person like me take what is not-Dhamma and not-Vinaya to be the Teacher’s Dispensation? Do I not fear the plane of misery?’ ‘By the taking of voting tickets’ means that after having thus bolstered their minds with speech and announcements and made them irreversible, he has them take voting tickets, saying, ‘Take this voting ticket.’

Ettha [M 0.0279] ca kammameva uddeso vā pamāṇaṃ, vohārānussāvanasalākaggāhā pana pubbabhāgā. Tesu nipphannesupi abhinnova hoti saṅgho. Yadā pana vohārānussāvanehi cattāro vā atireke vā bhikkhū salākaṃ gāhetvā vaggaṃ saṅghaṃ gahetvā visuṃ kammaṃ vā uddesaṃ vā karoti, tadā saṅgho bhinno nāma hoti. Abhedapurekkhārassa pana samaggasaññāya vaṭṭati. Samaggasaññāya hi karontassa neva bhedo hoti, na ānantariyaṃ, tathā tato ūnaparisāya karontassa. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “ekato, upāli, cattāro honti ekato cattāro, navamo anussāvetī”tiādi (cūḷava. 351).

Here, the formal act or the recitation is the standard, while the speaking, announcement, and taking of voting tickets are preliminary parts. Even when these are completed, the Sangha is not yet divided. However, when four or more bhikkhus, having been persuaded by speaking and announcements to take voting tickets, form a faction and perform a separate formal act or recitation, then the Sangha is said to be divided. But for one whose aim is non-division, it is permissible if done with the perception of unity. For one acting with the perception of unity, there is neither schism nor a deed of immediate retribution, and similarly for one acting with an incomplete assembly. For it has been said: 'On one side, Upāli, there are four; on another side, four; the ninth makes the announcement,' and so on (Cūḷavagga 351).

Imesu pana pañcasu ānantariyesu saṅghabhedo vacīkammaṃ, sesāni kāyakammāni, sabbāneva kho tāni kāyadvāratopi vacīdvāratopi samuṭṭhahanti. Saṅghabhedopi hi hatthamuddāya bhedaṃ karontassa kāyadvāratopi samuṭṭhāti, saṅghabhedo cettha kappaṭṭhitiyo. Kappavināse eva hi saṅghabhedato muccati, sesānaṃ pana tathā niyamo natthi. Yena ca pañcapetāni kammāni katāni honti, tassa saṅghabhedova niraye vipaccati, sesāni “ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko”ti evamādīsu saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti. Saṅghabhedābhāve lohituppādo, tadabhāve arahantaghāto[V 0.0214], tadabhāve mātughāto, pitughāto vā, tasmimpi sīlasampannatare. Purimāni cettha cattāri sabbesaṃ gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇāni, saṅghabhedo pana pakatattassa bhikkhunova, asādhāraṇo aññesaṃ, bhikkhunīpi hi saṅghaṃ na bhindati, pageva itare. Pañcapi cetāni dukkhavedanāsampayuttāni, dosamūlāni cāti veditabbāni.

Among these five deeds of immediate retribution, schism in the Sangha is a verbal deed, while the rest are bodily deeds. However, all of them can arise through either the body-door or the speech-door. For instance, schism in the Sangha also arises through the body-door for one who causes division by a hand-gesture. Here, schism in the Sangha endures for an eon. Indeed, one is freed from the consequence of schism in the Sangha only upon the destruction of the eon, but there is no such fixed rule for the other acts. For one who has committed these five deeds, only the schism in the Sangha ripens in hell, while the rest are reckoned among such categories as 'there was the deed, but there was no result of the deed.' In the absence of schism in the Sangha, shedding the Buddha's blood takes precedence; in its absence, killing an arahant; in its absence, killing one’s mother or father, and between them, the killing of the more virtuous parent takes precedence. Here, the first four are common to both householders and monastics, but schism in the Sangha pertains only to a bhikkhu in good standing—it is not shared by others. Indeed, even a bhikkhunī does not cause schism in the Sangha, let alone others. These five should be understood as associated with painful feeling and rooted in hatred.

Aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nibbatteyyāti ettha ariyasāvakassa aṭṭhamabhavāgahaṇaṃ kena niyāmitanti? Vipassanāya. Yassa hi sā [M 0.0280] tikkhā, so ekaṃ eva bhavaṃ nibbattitvā arahattaṃ patvā ekabījī nāma hoti. Yassa mandā, so dutiye…pe… chaṭṭhe vā bhave arahattaṃ patvā kolaṃkolo nāma hoti. Yassa pana atimandā, so sattamaṃ bhavaṃ nātikkamati, tattha niyamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā sattakkhattuparamo nāma hoti. Sacepi hissa sattame bhave niddaṃ okkantassa matthake asani vā pabbatakūṭo vā pateyya, tasmimpi kāle arahattaṃ patvāva parinibbāti. Uttamakoṭiyā hi sattamabhavānatikkamanaññeva sandhāyeva “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.66; 2.169; saṃ. ni. 5.998) vuttoti.

In the phrase 'would an eighth existence arise?', by what is the noble disciple's non-acceptance of an eighth existence determined? By insight. For one whose insight is keen, having generated only one more existence and attained arahantship, is called a 'one-seeder.' For one whose insight is moderate, having attained arahantship in the second... or up to the sixth existence, is called a 'kolaṅkola.' But for one whose insight is very dull, they do not exceed a seventh existence; there, by necessity, attaining arahantship, they are called a 'seven-times-at-most.' Even if, in their seventh existence, a thunderbolt or a mountain peak were to fall on their head while they were asleep, at that very moment, having attained arahantship, they would attain final nibbāna. Indeed, it is with reference to not exceeding a seventh existence as the highest limit that it is said, 'one destined for supreme enlightenment' (MN 1.66; 2.169; SN 5.998).

Ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhātiādīsu dasasahassacakkavāḷasaṅkhātaṃ jātikhettaṃ ekā lokadhātu nāma āṇāvisayakhettesu buddhuppattisaṅkāya evābhāvato. Tattha dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ uppattipaṭisedhaṃ akatvā jātikhette eva kato. Ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā na uppajjanti buddhattahetūnaṃ anādibuddhaparamparādīnaṃ tathābhāvā. Tato eva hi sattā niravasesato nibbutiṃ na pāpuṇanti. Yadi hi sabbacakkavāḷesu buddhā uppajjeyyuṃ, sabbe sattā ito pubbe niravasesato nibbutiṃ pāpuṇeyyuṃ, na ca taṃ atthi, tasmā anādibuddhaparamparāya vivaṭṭūpanissayasampannānaṃ nivāsabhūte imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe eva uppajjantīti veditabbā. Te cetthāpi dullabhā, tesaṃ dullabhattā evettha kappānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyampi buddhuppādarahitaṃ hoti. Yadi ca te sulabhā bhaveyyuṃ, ekasmiṃ vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyiasaṅkhyeyye catusaṭṭhibuddhānampi uppajjituṃ sakkā bhaveyya antarakappassa buddhantarattā. Bhaddakappesu cettha pañca buddhā eva uppajjanti. Kathaṃ panetthāpi dullabhatarā cakkavāḷantaresu uppajjeyyuṃ, buddhānañca dullabhatā kāraṇadullabhatāya, tasmā imasmiññeva [M 0.0281] cakkavāḷe buddhā uppajjanti? Etthāpi na devabrahmalokesu, manussaloke eva pana uppajjanti ettheva sabbaso tividhasaddhammādhārassa saṅgharatanassa pātubhāvato, itaralokesu niravasesato pakārāsambhavato ca.

In phrases like 'two Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones, do not arise in a single world-system,' a single world-system (lokadhātu) here means the birth-field, reckoned as ten thousand world-systems; for in the spheres of authority, there is no possibility of a Buddha arising. There, the prohibition on the arising of two Buddhas is made only with respect to the birth-field. Excluding this world-system, Buddhas do not arise in other world-systems because the causes for Buddhahood—such as the beginningless succession of Buddhas—are not present there. For that very reason, beings do not attain nibbāna without remainder. Indeed, if Buddhas were to arise in all world-systems, all beings would have already attained nibbāna without remainder, but that is not the case. Therefore, it should be understood that Buddhas arise only in this world-system, which is the abode of those endowed with the supporting conditions for the evolving eon, due to the beginningless succession of Buddhas. Even here, they are rare, and because of their rarity, countless eons pass without the appearance of a Buddha. If they were common, it would be possible for even sixty-four Buddhas to arise in a single incalculable eon of evolution, since an intermediate eon is the interval between Buddhas. In fortunate eons, only five Buddhas arise here. Since they are so rare here, how could they arise in other world-systems? The rarity of Buddhas is due to the rarity of their causes. Therefore, Buddhas arise only in this world-system. Moreover, even here, they do not arise in the realms of devas or brahmās, but only in the human world. This is because it is here alone that the jewel of the Sangha, the repository of the threefold true Dhamma, appears in its entirety, and because in other realms this is completely impossible.

Yadi [V 0.0215] hi buddhā devalokādīsu uppajjeyyuṃ, manussā bhayena upasaṅkamitumeva na sakkonti, pageva dhammasavanapabbajjādiṃ kātuṃ, teneva amhākaṃ bodhisatto attano rūpakāyānubhāvādisampattiyā uppannaamanussasaṅkākutūhalaṃ janaṃ nijjhāpetuṃ uttānaseyyakādiniyāmena vaḍḍhitvā dārapariggahādiṃ akāsi, evaṃ katvā pabbajitampi naṃ rājagahe piṇḍāya pavisitvā paṇḍavapabbatapasse nisīditvā piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjantaṃ bimbisāro nānappakārato manussabhāvaṃ vicinitvāva upasaṅkamituṃ visahi, no aññathā. Lokanitthāraṇatthāya hi buddhā uppajjanti, na attano sakkārādiatthāya, tasmā manussesu eva uppajjantīti veditabbo. Tatthāpi imasmiṃ jambudīpe eva, tatthāpi imasmiṃ majjhimapadese eva. Na kevalañca buddhāva, paccekabuddhā, aggasāvakamahāsāvakā ca cakkavattiādayo ca aññepi puññavantasattā ettheva uppajjanti.

Indeed, if Buddhas were to arise in the deva-worlds and so forth, humans would not even be able to approach them out of fear, let alone listen to the Dhamma or undertake ordination and so on. Therefore, our Bodhisatta, to dispel the curiosity and the idea that he was not a human being—which arose due to the splendor of his physical body and so on—grew up in the usual manner, lying on his back and so forth, and then took a wife and so on. Having done so, even after he had gone forth, when he entered Rājagaha for alms and sat on the slopes of Paṇḍava Mountain to eat his alms-food, Bimbisāra dared to approach him only after thoroughly investigating his human nature in various ways—not otherwise. Indeed, Buddhas arise for the deliverance of the world, not for their own honor and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that they arise only among humans. And even there, specifically in this Jambudīpa, and even there, specifically in this Middle Country. Not only Buddhas, but also Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, great disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and other meritorious beings arise here.

Apubbaṃ acarimanti ettha mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇato pure pubbaṃ nāma, dhātuantaradhānato pacchā carimaṃ nāma, ubhinnamantarā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ nāma. Etthantare aññassa buddhassa uppatti nivāritā, dhātuantaradhāne pana jāte aññassa uppatti na nivāritā. Kiñcāpi na nivāritā, antarakappaṃ pana khepetvāva uppajjantīti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, regarding the phrase 'unprecedented and unrepeated,' 'before' refers to the time prior to taking rebirth-linking in a mother's womb, and 'after' refers to the time following the disappearance of the relics. The interval between these two is called 'unprecedented and unrepeated.' During this interval, the arising of another Buddha is prevented, but once the disappearance of the relics has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is not prevented. Although it is not prevented, it should be understood that they arise only after an intermediate eon has elapsed.

Pañca hi antaradhānāni nāma adhigamaantaradhānaṃ paṭipattiantaradhānaṃ pariyattiantaradhānaṃ liṅgaantaradhānaṃ dhātuantaradhānanti. Tattha adhigamoti maggaphalābhiññāpaṭisambhidāyo, so [M 0.0282] parihāyamāno paṭisambhidāto paṭṭhāya parihāyati. Parinibbānato hi vassasahassameva paṭisambhidā nibbattetuṃ sakkonti, tato paraṃ abhiññā, tāpi nibbattetuṃ asakkontā sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavā honti, tato anāgāmino, tato sakadāgāmino, sotāpannā ca honti, tesu dharantesupi adhigamo anantarahitova hoti, pacchimakassa pana sotāpannassa jīvitakkhayena adhigamo antarahito nāma hoti. Idaṃ adhigamaantaradhānaṃ.

Indeed, there are five kinds of disappearances: the disappearance of attainment, the disappearance of practice, the disappearance of learning, the disappearance of the outward signs, and the disappearance of the relics. Herein, 'attainment' refers to the paths, fruits, higher knowledges, and analytical knowledges. When this declines, it declines starting with the analytical knowledges. For a thousand years after the Parinibbāna, analytical knowledges can be produced. After that, the higher knowledges. Unable to produce even these, they become dry-insight arahants; then non-returners, then once-returners, and stream-enterers. Even while these remain, the attainment has not yet disappeared. But with the exhaustion of the life of the last stream-enterer, the attainment is said to have disappeared. This is the disappearance of attainment.

Tato maggaphalāni nibbattetuṃ asakkontā “natthi dāni no ariyadhammapaṭivedho”ti jhānavipassanāsu vosānaṃ āpajjitvā kosajjabahulā catupārisuddhisīlamattaṃ rakkhanto aññamaññaṃ na codenti, na sārenti, akukkuccakā honti, tato paṭṭhāya khuddānukhuddakāni maddanti, tato garukāpattiṃ āpajjanti, pārājikamattameva rakkhanti, tesu dharantesupi paṭipatti [V 0.0216] anantarahitāva hoti, pacchimakassa pana bhikkhuno sīlabhedena vā jīvitakkhayena vā paṭipatti antarahitā nāma hoti. Idaṃ paṭipattiantaradhānaṃ nāma.

Then, unable to produce the paths and their fruits, they conclude, 'Now there is no penetration of the noble Dhamma for us,' and, ceasing to strive in jhāna and insight, they become prone to laziness. They merely maintain the fourfold purity of moral discipline, they neither reprove nor admonish one another, and become free from compunction. From then on, they transgress the minor and lesser precepts, then fall into grave offenses, preserving only the pārājika precepts. Even while they remain, the practice has not yet disappeared. But when the moral discipline of the last monk is broken or his life is exhausted, then the practice is said to have disappeared. This is called the disappearance of the practice.

Pariyattīti sāṭṭhakathaṃ tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, gacchante gacchante kāle adhammikehi kaliyugarājādīhi vipannasassādisampattitāya paccayadāyakā duggatā honti, bhikkhū ca paccayehi kilamantā antevāsike gahetuṃ na sakkonti. Tato aṭṭhakathā parihāyati, pāḷivaseneva pariyattiṃ dhārenti, tato pāḷiṃ sakalaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkonti, paṭhamaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ parihāyati, tañcassa parihāyanaṃ matthakato paṭhāya. Paṭhamameva hi mahāpakaraṇaṃ parihāyati, tato yamakaṃ kathāvatthu puggalapaññatti dhātukathā vibhaṅgo dhammasaṅgaho ca anukkamena parihāyanti, tato matthakato paṭṭhāya suttantapiṭakaṃ parihāyati, paṭhamaṃ hi aṅguttaranikāyo [M 0.0283] ekādasakanipātato paṭṭhāya yāvaekakanipātā parihāyati, tato matthakato paṭṭhāya saṃyuttanikāyo, paṭhamaṃ hi mahāvaggo parihāyati, tato saḷāyatanavaggo khandhakavaggo nidānavaggo sagāthāvaggoti, evaṃ majjhimanikāyadīghanikāyādayo ca matthakato paṭṭhāya parihāyanti, tato vinayapiṭakameva tiṭṭhati, tampi parivārato paṭṭhāya yāva mahāvibhaṅgā parihāyati, tato uposathakkhandhakato mātikāmattameva dhārenti, tadāpi yāva catuppadikāpi gāthā manussesu pavattati, tāva pariyatti anantarahitāva hoti, tāya antarahitāya pariyatti antarahitā nāma hoti. Idaṃ pariyattiantaradhānaṃ nāma.

The textual learning is the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, along with its commentaries. As time goes on, because of unrighteous kings of the degenerate age and so on, harvests and other resources fail, and the donors of requisites become poor. The bhikkhus, afflicted by the lack of requisites, are unable to accept pupils. Then the commentaries disappear, and they maintain the textual learning only by way of the Pāḷi text. Then they are unable to retain the entire Pāḷi. First the Abhidhamma Piṭaka disappears, and its disappearance begins from the top. For first the Mahāpakaraṇa disappears, then in sequence the Yamaka, Kathāvatthu, Puggalapaññatti, Dhātukathā, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaha disappear. Then the Suttanta Piṭaka disappears, starting from the top. First the Aṅguttara Nikāya disappears, starting from the Book of Elevens down to the Book of Ones. Then the Saṃyutta Nikāya disappears, starting from the top: first the Mahāvagga disappears, then the Saḷāyatanavagga, the Khandhavagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Sagāthāvagga. Similarly, the Majjhima Nikāya, Dīgha Nikāya, and others also disappear, starting from the top. Then only the Vinaya Piṭaka remains. That too disappears, starting from the Parivāra down to the Mahāvibhaṅga. Then they retain only the matrix of the Uposathakkhandhaka. Even then, as long as a four-lined stanza is current among human beings, the textual learning has not yet disappeared. When that has disappeared, the textual learning is said to have disappeared. This is called the disappearance of the textual learning.

Gacchante gacchante kāle pattacīvaraggahaṇādiākappaṃ na pāsādikaṃ hoti, nigaṇṭhādayo viya alābupattādiṃ aggabāhāya pakkhipitvāpi olambitvāpi sikkāya olaggetvāpi vicaranti, cīvararajanampi na sāruppaṃ, oṭṭhaṭṭhikavaṇṇaṃ katvā dhārenti, tato rajanampi ovaṭṭikavijjhanampi na hoti, dasā chetvā paribbājakā viya kāsāvamattameva dhārenti, tato parikkhīṇe kāle khuddakakāsāvakhaṇḍaṃ hatthe vā gīvāya vā bandhitvā kasikammādīni katvā dārabharaṇādiṃ karonti, tadā dakkhiṇaṃ dento jano saṅghaṃ uddissa etesaṃ deti, idaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā vuttaṃ “bhavissanti kho panānanda, anāgatamaddhānaṃ gotrabhuno kāsāvakaṇṭhā dussīlā pāpadhammā, tesu dussīlesu saṅghaṃ uddissa dānaṃ dassanti, tadāpahaṃ, ānanda, saṅghagataṃ dakkhiṇaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ appameyyaṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 3.380). Tato “papañco esa, kiṃ iminā amhāka”nti [V 0.0217] taṃ kāsāvakhaṇḍaṃ chinditvā araññe khipanti, etasmiṃ [M 0.0284] kāle liṅgaṃ antarahitaṃ nāma hoti. Idaṃ liṅgaantaradhānaṃ nāma.

As time goes on, their deportment in handling the bowl and robe is not inspiring. Like the Nigaṇṭhas and others, they carry their gourd-bowls and so on, sometimes tucked under their arm, sometimes dangling, sometimes hanging from a net-bag. Even the dyeing of robes is not suitable; they dye them the color of a camel's bone. Then there is neither proper dyeing nor even patching. Like wanderers, they cut off the fringes and wear only a mere yellow cloth. When even that wears out, they tie a small scrap of yellow cloth to their hand or neck and engage in farming and other work to support their families. At that time, when people give alms, they dedicate them to the Saṅgha but give them to these individuals. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: 'But in the future, Ānanda, there will be those who are bhikkhus only in name, with the yellow cloth around their necks, immoral, of evil character. People will give gifts to these immoral ones on behalf of the Saṅgha. Even then, Ānanda, I say that a gift to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable.' Then, thinking, 'This is a proliferation, what use is this to us?' they cut off that piece of yellow cloth and throw it away in the forest. At that time, the outward sign is said to have disappeared. This is called the disappearance of the outward sign.

Tato tattha tattha sakkārasammānaṃ alabhamānā dhātuyo buddhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabalena sakkārasammānalabbhamānakaṭṭhānaṃ gamissanti, tato sabbattha alabhamānā sabbadhātuyo mahābodhimaṇḍameva gamissanti. Sāsapamattāpi hi dhātu na antarā nassissati, tā pana bodhimaṇḍe pallaṅkena nisinnabuddhasarīrasiriṃ, yamakapāṭihāriyañca dassessanti, tato dhātusarīrato tejo samuṭṭhāya taṃ sarīraṃ apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gameti, tadā dasasahassacakkavāḷe devatā parinibbānadivase viya paridevitvā pūjāsakkāraṃ katvā pakkamanti. Idaṃ dhātuantaradhānaṃ nāma.

Then, not receiving honor and veneration in various places, the relics, by the power of the Buddha's determination, will go to places where they are honored and venerated. Then, not receiving honor anywhere, all the relics will go to the site of the great awakening. For not even a relic the size of a mustard seed will be lost on the way. But at the site of awakening, they will display the splendor of the Buddha's body seated cross-legged and the twin miracle. Then, fire will arise from the relic-body and bring that body to a state where it cannot be designated. At that time, the devas in the ten-thousand-world-system, lamenting as on the day of the Parinibbāna, will make offerings and pay homage, and then depart. This is called the disappearance of the relics.

Imassa pañcavidhassa antaradhānassa pariyattiantaradhānameva mūlaṃ. Pariyattiyaṃ hi sati paṭivedhādayopi naṭṭhā nāma na honti, asati naṭṭhāti. Yathā ca nidhikumbhiyā jānanatthāya pāsāṇapiṭṭhe upanibaddhaakkharesu dharantesu nidhikumbhi naṭṭhā nāma na hoti, akkharesu pana naṭṭhesu naṭṭhā, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathāha –

The root of this fivefold disappearance is indeed the disappearance of the textual learning. For when the textual learning exists, penetration and the other aspects are not said to be lost; when it does not exist, they are lost. Just as, when the letters inscribed on a stone slab for the purpose of knowing the location of a buried treasure are preserved, the treasure is not said to be lost, but when the letters are lost, the treasure is lost—so too should this be understood. As it is said:

“Yāva tiṭṭhanti suttantā,

Vinayo yāva dippati;

Tāva dakkhanti ālokaṃ,

Sūriye abbhuṭṭhite yathā.

“As long as the discourses stand, as long as the Vinaya shines, so long will they see the light, just as when the sun has risen.

“Suttantesu asantesu,

Pamuṭṭhe vinayamhi ca;

Tamo bhavissati loke,

Sūriye atthaṅgate yathā.

“When the discourses are no more, and the discipline is forgotten; there will be darkness in the world, just as when the sun has set.

“Suttante [M 0.0285] rakkhite sante,

Paṭipatti hoti rakkhitā;

Paṭipattiyaṃ [V 0.0218] ṭhito dhīro,

Yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatī”ti; (A. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.130; sārattha. ṭī. pācittiya 3.438);

“When the discourses are protected, the practice is also protected. The wise one, established in the practice, does not fall away from the security from bondage.”

Evamimesu pañcasu antaradhānesu dhātuantaradhānato pacchā carimaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, among these five disappearances, it should be understood that 'the last' refers to the time after the disappearance of the relics.

Kasmā pana dve sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ na uppajjantīti? Niratthakatova. Ekova hi sammāsambuddho anantesu cakkavāḷesu sabbasattānampi yadi upanissayo bhaveyya, ekakkhaṇe sapāṭihāriyaṃ sabbānukūlaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā te vinetuṃ sakkoti, kimaṅgaṃ pana nānakkhaṇesu, tasmā ekasmiṃ kāle anekesaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ uppatti niratthikāva. Anatthakatā pana anacchariyaagāravavivādādidosato ceva mahāpathaviyā dvinnaṃ buddhānaṃ dhāraṇe asamatthatāya vikiraṇādidosato ca veditabbā. Cakkavattino pana ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe dve ekato na uppajjanti, ekova uppajjati. Nānācakkavāḷesu pana bahūpi ekato uppajjantīti veditabbā. Ettha hi “ekissā lokadhātuyā”ti etassa ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷeti attho gahetabbo. Apubbaṃ acarimañcettha cakkaratanapātubhāvaantaradhānānaṃ vemajjhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Antaradhānañcassa cakkavattino kālakiriyato, pabbajjāto vā sattame divase hoti, tassa ca ānubhāvena dvinnaṃ ekattha sahaanuppatti ca veditabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Ṭhānāṭhānañāṇabalaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Why, then, do two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas not arise simultaneously? Because it would be pointless. For a single Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, if there were the supporting condition for all beings in the infinite world-systems, could discipline them by teaching the Dhamma with its marvels, in a way suitable for all, in a single moment—what to say of at different moments? Therefore, the arising of many Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas at one time is pointless. And it should be understood that it is disadvantageous due to faults such as it not being marvelous, lack of reverence, and disputes, and because the great earth is unable to bear two Buddhas, which would cause it to shatter and other such faults. As for wheel-turning monarchs, two do not arise together in a single world-system; only one arises. But it should be understood that in different world-systems, many can arise together. Here, the meaning of 'in one world-element' should be taken as 'in one world-system.' And here, 'not before and not after' should be understood as the period between the appearance and disappearance of the wheel-treasure. Its disappearance occurs on the seventh day after the wheel-turning monarch's death or his going forth; and it should be understood that through its power, two cannot arise together in one place. The rest is easy to understand. This is the first power, the knowledge of the possible and the impossible.

Dutiye kammasamādānānanti samādiyitvā katānaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ, kammameva vā kammasamādānaṃ. Ṭhānaso hetusoti paccayato ceva hetusaṅkhātakāraṇato ca[M 0.0286]. Tattha gatiupadhikālapayogā vipākassa paccayā, kammaṃ hetu. Tadubhayato kammavipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Kathaṃ? Bhagavā hi “ekaccassa bahūni pāpakammāni gatiupadhikālapayogānaṃ sampattiyā paṭibāhitāni na vipaccanti, tesaṃ vipattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti, ekaccassa bahūni kalyāṇakammāni tesaṃ vipattiyā paṭibāhitāni na vipaccanti, tesaṃ sampattiṃ āgamma vipaccantī”ti pajānāti.

In the second case, 'of undertakings of kamma' refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma that has been undertaken and performed, or 'undertaking of kamma' is simply kamma itself. 'By way of location and cause' means by way of condition and by way of the reason designated as cause. Here, destination, substrate, time, and endeavor are conditions for the result, while kamma is the cause. From both of these he understands kamma and its result as they really are. How? The Blessed One understands thus: 'For some, many evil kammas, though obstructed by the attainment of a favorable destination, substrate, time, and endeavor, do not ripen; they ripen when these fail. For some, many good kammas, though obstructed by the failure of these, do not ripen; they ripen when these are attained.'

Tattha gativipattīti cattāro apāyā. Gatisampattīti manussadevagatiyo. Upadhīti attabhāvo[V 0.0219]. Tassa samiddhi sampatti nāma, asamiddhi vipatti nāma. Kālasampattīti surājasumanussakālasaṅkhāto sampannakālo, tappaṭipakkho kālavipatti nāma. Tassa tassa pana kammassa sammāpayogo payogasampatti, micchāpayogo payogavipatti nāma. Tattha hi ekaccassa kusalakammena devagatiādīsu gatiyaṃ nibbattassa taṃ gatisampattiṃ āgamma kusalāni eva vipaccanti. Tāya pana gatisampattiyā paṭibāhitāni akusalāni tattha vipaccituṃ na sakkonti. Tāni puna nirayādīsu apāyesu nibbattassa taṃ gativipattiṃ āgamma yathāsukhaṃ vipaccanti. Tāya pana gativipattiyā paṭibāhitāni kusalāni tattha vipaccituṃ na sakkonti. Ekaccassa dassanīyenābhirūpena kāyena samannāgatassa yadipi so dāso vā hoti hīnajacco vā, taṃ upadhisampattiṃ āgamma kusalāni evassa vipaccanti. Tādisaṃ hi surūpaṃ “ayaṃ kiliṭṭhakammassa nānucchaviko”ti uccesu amaccādiṭṭhānesu ṭhapenti, caṇḍālimpi surūpaṃ aggamahesiādiṭṭhānesu ṭhapenti. Tāya pana upadhisampattiyā paṭibāhitāni akusalānassa vipaccituṃ na sakkonti. Tāni pana upadhivipattiyaṃ ca ṭhitassa yathāsukhaṃ vipaccanti. Rājakulādīsu hi uppannampi durūpaṃ hīnesu ṭhapenti. Ekaccassa pana paṭhamakappikānaṃ vā cakkavattirañño vā buddhānaṃ vā surājasumanussānaṃ [M 0.0287] sampanne kāle nibbattassa taṃ kālasampattiṃ āgamma kusalāni eva vipaccanti, na akusalāni. Tāni puna durājadumanussānaṃ vipanne kāle taṃ kālavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti, na pana kusalāni tāya kālavipattiyā paṭibāhitattā. Ekaccassa pana sīlasaṃyamādianavajjapayogena ceva sāvajjena vā anavajjena vā desakālānusārena āyudhasippādipayogasāmatthiyena ca samannāgatassa taṃ payogasampattiṃ āgamma kusalāni eva vipaccanti, na akusalāni. Tāni puna yathāvuttaviparītapayogavipattiṃ āgamma vipaccanti, na pana kusalāni tāya paṭibāhitattā. Yuddhādīsu hi pāṇātipātādiakusalaṃ karontāpi taṃtaṃāyudhasippādipayogasampattiṃ nissāyeva senāpatiṭṭhānādimahāsampattiṃ labhanti, na pana taṃ akusalaṃ nissāya. Yathā dānaveyyāvaccādīsu kusalaṃ karontāpi adhimattavāyāmādipayogavipattiṃ nissāya anayabyasanampi pāpuṇanti, na pana taṃ kusalaṃ nissāya. Evametāhi catūhi sampattīhi, vipattīhi ca kusalākusalānaṃ vipaccanāvipaccanavibhāgaṃ bhagavā yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ tāvettha vibhaṅganayena dutiyabalassa vibhāvanā.

Herein, 'failure of destination' refers to the four states of woe. 'Success of destination' refers to the human and divine destinations. 'Substrate' means individual existence. Its flourishing is called success, its lack is called failure. 'Success of time' refers to a fortunate time, reckoned as the time of good kings and good people; its opposite is called 'failure of time'. For each particular kamma, right application is called 'success of application', while wrong application is called 'failure of application'. Herein, for some, when rebirth occurs in destinations like the divine realm due to wholesome kamma, only wholesome kammas ripen due to that success of destination. Unwholesome kammas, being obstructed by that success of destination, cannot ripen there. Those same unwholesome kammas, however, ripen as they please when one is reborn in miserable destinations like hell, due to that failure of destination. But there, wholesome kammas, being obstructed by that failure of destination, cannot ripen. For some, possessing a pleasing and beautiful body, even if they are slaves or of low birth—this is success of substrate—wholesome kammas ripen for them. For such a handsome person, those in high positions think, "This one is not suited for defiled kamma," and place them in high positions such as among ministers. Even a beautiful outcaste woman may be placed in the position of chief queen. Due to this success of substrate, their unwholesome kammas cannot ripen. But those same unwholesome kammas ripen as they please for one who is in a state of failure of substrate. Even if born in royal families, an ugly person is placed in lowly positions. For some, being born in a time of success—such as during the era of the first cosmic aeon, or of a wheel-turning monarch, or of the Buddhas, the time of good kings and good people—wholesome kammas ripen due to that success of time, not unwholesome ones. But those same unwholesome kammas ripen in times of failure, such as during the time of bad kings and bad people. Wholesome kammas do not ripen, being obstructed by that failure of time. For some, possessing skill in right application—such as through blameless application like moral discipline and restraint, and proficiency in the use of weapons and crafts according to place and time, whether such actions are blameworthy or blameless—wholesome kammas ripen due to that success of application, not unwholesome ones. But those same unwholesome kammas ripen due to the opposite, failure of application, while wholesome kammas do not ripen, being obstructed by that failure of application. For instance, even those who commit unwholesome kammas like killing in battle may attain great prosperity, such as the rank of general, due to their skill in the use of weapons and crafts—not because of those unwholesome kammas. Similarly, even those who perform wholesome kammas like giving and service may meet with unhappiness and ruin due to excessive exertion or wrong application—not because of those wholesome kammas. Thus, the Blessed One truly knows the division of ripening and non-ripening of wholesome and unwholesome kammas in accordance with these four kinds of success and failure. This, then, is the explanation of the second power by way of analysis.

Aparena cassa –

And further, for him –

“Ahosi [V 0.0220] kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko, ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko, atthi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko, bhavissati kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko[M 0.0288], bhavissati kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.234) –

"There was kamma, there was kamma-result; there was kamma, there was no kamma-result; there was kamma, there is kamma-result; there was kamma, there is no kamma-result; there was kamma, there will be kamma-result; there was kamma, there will be no kamma-result; there is kamma, there is no kamma-result; there is kamma, there is no kamma-result; there is kamma, there will be kamma-result; there is kamma, there will be no kamma-result; there will be kamma, there will be kamma-result; there will be kamma, there will be no kamma-result." (Patisambhidamagga 1.234)

Iminā paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttenāpi nayena vibhāvanā veditabbā. Tattha yaṃ atītattabhāve āyūhitaṃ kammaṃ vuttaṃ, hetupaccayaṃ āgamma tattheva vipākaṃ adāsi. Idaṃ sandhāya “ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko”ti paṭhamaṃ padaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ atītesu pana diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīsu bahūsu ekaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ laddhapaccayaṃ vipākaṃ deti, sesāni avipākāni. Ekaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ pana paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati, ekaṃ ānantariyaṃ nirayapaṭisandhiṃ deti, sesāni avipākāni. Aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ekāya brahmaloke nibbattati, sesā avipākā. Idaṃ sandhāya “ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko”ti dutiyaṃ padaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ atītaṃ kammaṃ etarahi vipākaṃ deti, idaṃ sandhāya tatiyaṃ. Yaṃ purimanayena na vipaccati, idaṃ sandhāya catutthaṃ. Yaṃ anāgate vipākaṃ dassati, idaṃ sandhāya pañcamaṃ. Yaṃ na vipaccati, idaṃ sandhāya chaṭṭhaṃ. Yaṃ etarahi āyūhitaṃ kammaṃ etaraheva vipākaṃ deti, idaṃ sandhāya sattamaṃ. Yaṃ na vipaccati, idaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhamaṃ. Iminā nayena sesapadānampi attho daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ tathāgatassāti idaṃ sabbehi etehi pakārehi atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammantaravipākantarānaṃ yathābhūtato jānanañāṇanti attho. Dutiyabalaṃ.

The explanation should also be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidā. Therein, the kamma that was accumulated in a past existence, which is mentioned, gave its result right there, based on a cause as condition. With reference to this, the first phrase was stated: 'There was kamma, there was kamma-result.' However, among many past kammas, such as those to be experienced in this very life, one kamma to be experienced in this very life that has obtained its conditions gives its result, while the rest are without result. One kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life draws one to rebirth; one kamma with immediate result gives rebirth in hell, while the rest are without result. Through one of the eight attainments, one is reborn in the Brahma world, while the rest are without result. With reference to this, the second phrase was stated: 'There was kamma, there was no kamma-result.' That past kamma which gives its result now—with reference to this, the third phrase. That which does not ripen according to the previous method—with reference to this, the fourth. That which will give its result in the future—with reference to this, the fifth. That which does not ripen—with reference to this, the sixth. That kamma which is accumulated now and gives its result right now—with reference to this, the seventh. That which does not ripen—with reference to this, the eighth. In this way, the meaning of the remaining phrases should also be understood. 'This belongs to the Tathāgata' means the knowledge of knowing as it really is, in all these ways, the variety of kamma and the variety of its results in the past, future, and present. The second power.

Tatiye sabbatthagāmininti sabbagatigāminiñca agatigāminiñca. Paṭipadanti maggaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti bahūsupi manussesu pāṇātipātādīsu ekameva akusalaṃ ekato karontesu imassa cetanā nirayagāminī bhavissati, imassa tiracchānayonigāminī, imassa pettivisayagāminī, nirayādīsupi panesā evarūpe evarūpe ṭhāne evañcevañca vipākaṃ dassati, imassa paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkoti, aññena kammena [M 0.0289] dinnapaṭisandhikassa dubbalaṃ upadhivepakkaṃ bhavissati. Bahūsu vā ekato dānādikusalaṃ, vipassanaṃ vā paṭṭhapentesu imassa [V 0.0221] cetanā manussagatigāminī bhavissati, imassa devagatigāminī, tatthāpi evañcevañca vipākaṃ dassati, imassa vā vipassanā ekaṃ maggaṃ dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā paṭisambhidādisahite vā rahite vā nipphādessati, imassa na kañci paṭivedhaṃ sādhessatītiādinā anantehi ākārehi ekavatthusmimpi uppannaṃ kusalākusalasaṅkhātaṃ sabbatthagāminipaṭipadaṃ aviparītato pajānātīti. Tatiyabalaṃ.

In the third, 'going to all destinations' refers to that which leads to all destinations and that which does not lead to any destination. 'The path' means the way. 'He understands as it really is' means that even among many people together committing the same unwholesome act, such as killing living beings, this one's volition will lead to hell, that one's to the animal realm, another's to the realm of ghosts. And even within hell and other realms, this volition will produce such and such results in such and such places. For one person, it may not be able to bring about rebirth, but for one whose rebirth is given by another kamma, it will become a weak result ripening in the substratum of existence. Or, among many together performing wholesome acts like giving, or establishing insight, this one's volition will lead to the human realm, that one's to the deva realm, and there too it will produce such and such results. For one person, insight will accomplish one, two, three, or four paths, either with or without the analytical knowledges, while for another it will not accomplish any penetration. Thus, in infinite ways, he understands without error the path that goes to all destinations, reckoned as wholesome or unwholesome, arisen from a single basis. This is the third power.

Catutthe anekadhātunti cakkhudhātuādīhi, kāmadhātuādīhi vā bahudhātuṃ. Nānādhātunti tāsaññeva dhātūnaṃ vilakkhaṇattā nānappakāraṃ dhātuṃ. Lokanti khandhāyatanadhātulokaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti tāsaṃ tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ khandhāyatanadhātuvibhaṅgādīsu vuttanayena anantappabhedaṃ nānattaṃ aviparītato pajānāti. Na kevalañca tathāgato upādinnakasaṅkhāralokasseva nānattaṃ pajānāti, atha kho anupādinnakasaṅkhāralokassāpi paccekabuddhādīhi paṭivijjhituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ nānattaṃ pajānātiyeva. Tehi upādinnakalokassāpi nānattaṃ ekadesatova jānanti, anupādinnassa pana neva jānanti, sabbaññubuddhassevetaṃ visayo. Evaṃ hi imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannāya imesaṃ rukkhagacchalatādīnaṃ, khandhadaṇḍavallitacapattapupphaphalādino saṇṭhānavaṇṇagandharasaojāhi, desakālehi ca anantappabhedaṃ nānattaṃ, pathavīpabbatādīnañca nānattaṃ hotīti anantehi ākārehi jānituṃ sakkoti, nāññeti. Catutthabalaṃ.

In the fourth, 'manifold elements' means many elements, such as the eye element and so on, or the sensual-realm element and so on. 'Diverse elements' means those same elements are diverse due to their distinct characteristics. 'The world' refers to the world of aggregates, sense bases, and elements. 'He understands as it really is' means he comprehends without error the infinite diversity of those elements in the manner explained in the analysis of aggregates, sense bases, and elements, and so on. Not only does the Tathāgata understand the diversity of the world of formations subject to clinging, but he also understands the diversity of the world of formations not subject to clinging, a diversity which even Paccekabuddhas and others are unable to penetrate. They know the diversity of the world subject to clinging only partially, and do not know at all the one not subject to clinging—this is the domain of the omniscient Buddha alone. For when a certain element is predominant, he is able to know in endless ways that trees, shrubs, and creepers, as well as their trunks, stalks, vines, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits, exhibit infinite diversity with respect to configuration, color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence, depending on the place and time, as do earth and mountains, and so on; no one else can. This is the fourth power.

Pañcame nānādhimuttikanti hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti tīsupi kālesu hīnādhimuttikā hīnādhimuttike eva sevanti, paṇītādhimuttikā ca paṇītādhimuttike. Tatthāpi assaddhā assaddhe, dussīlā [M 0.0290] dussīle, micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhike, saddhā saddhe, sīlasutacāgapaññādisampannā ca te te eva sevantīti nānappakārato jānāti. Saddhāsīlādisampannā hi tabbirahite attano ācariyupajjhāyepi na sevanti, tepi itare, attanā attanā pana sadise eva sevantīti. Pañcamabalaṃ.

In the fifth, 'diverse inclinations' means the state of having diverse inclinations by way of inferior inclinations and so on. 'He understands as it really is' means that in all three times, those with inferior inclinations associate with those of inferior inclinations, and those with superior inclinations with those of superior inclinations. Even there, the faithless associate with the faithless, the immoral with the immoral, those with wrong view with those with wrong view, the faithful with the faithful, and those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so on associate with those like themselves—thus he knows in various ways. For those endowed with faith, virtue, and so on do not associate even with their own teachers and preceptors if the latter lack these qualities, and vice versa. Rather, each associates with those like themselves. This is the fifth power.

Chaṭṭhe parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ hīnasattānaṃ. Ekatthameva vā etaṃ padadvayaṃ veneyyavasena dvidhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattanti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvañca aparabhāvañca, vuddhiñca hāniñcāti attho. Yathābhūtanti sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiādīhi saddhādi tikkhindriyamudindriyataṃ sabbākārato jānāti. Tattha āsayoti [V 0.0222] nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ, yattha sattānaṃ cittasantānaṃ niccaṃ nivasati. So duvidho vaṭṭāsayo vivaṭṭāsayo ca. Tattha sassatucchedavasena pavattaṃ sabbaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ vaṭṭāsayo nāma. Sappaccayanāmarūpapariggahato paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ, maggañāṇañca vivaṭṭāsayo nāma. Maggañāṇampi hi “dasayime, bhikkhave, ariyāvāsā, yadariyā āvasiṃsū”tiādivacanato (a. ni. 10.19) āsayova. Imaṃ pana bhagavā sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānanto ubhinnaṃ diṭṭhiñāṇānaṃ appavattikkhaṇepi jānāti eva. Kāmarāgādikilesādhimuttaññeva hi puggalaṃ bhagavā tatheva jānāti. “Ayaṃ nekkhammādiabhirato vivaṭṭāsayo”ti nekkhammādiṃ sevantaññeva jānāti, “ayaṃ kāmādiabhirato vaṭṭāsayo”ti anusayacaritādijānanepi eseva nayo. Tattha anusayo kāmarāgānusayādito sattavidho. Caritanti tīhi dvārehi abhisaṅkhatalokiyakusalākusalaṃ. Adhimuttīti ajjhāsayo. Evamettha āsayānusayañāṇaṃ, indriyaparopariyattañāṇañcāti dve ñāṇāni ekato hutvā ekaṃ balañāṇaṃ nāma jātanti. Chaṭṭhabalaṃ.

In the sixth, 'other beings' refers to beings with superior faculties. 'Other persons' refers to those other than them, beings with inferior faculties. Alternatively, these two terms have the same meaning but are stated in two ways according to those to be trained. 'The superiority and inferiority of the faculties of others' means the superiority and inferiority, the growth and decline, of faculties such as faith. 'As it really is' means he knows in every way the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all beings, based on their underlying tendency, latent tendency, conduct, inclination, and so on. Here, 'underlying tendency' (āsaya) is the abode where the mental continuum of beings constantly dwells. It is twofold: the tendency toward the round of existence and the tendency toward liberation. Therein, all speculative views that proceed by way of eternalism and annihilationism are called the tendency toward the round. All insight knowledge and path knowledge, starting from the comprehension of name-and-form together with its conditions, are called the tendency toward liberation. For even path knowledge is an 'abode' (āvāsa), according to the statement: 'Monks, these ten are the noble abodes in which the noble ones have dwelt,' and so on. The Blessed One, however, knows this underlying tendency of beings even at a moment when neither the view nor the knowledge is occurring. For the Blessed One knows a person inclined toward sensual desire and other defilements just as they are. He knows one who delights in renunciation and so on as having a tendency toward liberation, and one who delights in sensual pleasures and so on as having a tendency toward the round of existence; the same method applies to knowing latent tendencies, conduct, and so on. Therein, 'latent tendency' (anusaya) is sevenfold, beginning with the latent tendency of sensual desire. 'Conduct' (carita) is worldly wholesome and unwholesome kamma constructed through the three doors. 'Inclination' (adhimutti) is one's disposition (ajjhāsaya). Thus, here, the knowledge of underlying and latent tendencies and the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of others' faculties, having come together, become one knowledge-power. This is the sixth power.

Sattame [M 0.0291] jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ, “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ, savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ, paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnaṃ navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyaṃ dhammaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti yena kāraṇena jhānādīhi vuṭṭhahanti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ vodānampi bhavaṅgampi. Heṭṭhimaṃ hi paguṇaṃ jhānaṃ attano vodānavasena uparimassa jhānassa padaṭṭhānato “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuccati, tamhā tamhā pana samādhimhā bhavaṅgavaseneva vuṭṭhānato bhavaṅgampi. Nirodhato pana phalasamāpattiyāva vuṭṭhahanti. Idaṃ pāḷimuttakavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma, taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā yathābhūtaṃ sabbākārena pajānāti. Sattamabalaṃ.

In the seventh, the knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence concerning the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments: that is, the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations such as 'one with form sees forms'; the three concentrations such as that with initial and sustained thought; and the nine successive attainments starting with the first jhāna attainment. 'Defilement' is a state associated with decline. 'Purification' is a state associated with distinction. 'Emergence' is the reason by which one emerges from jhāna and the like. This is twofold: purification and the life-continuum. For the lower jhāna, when mastered, is called 'emergence,' as it serves as the basis for the higher jhāna through its own purification; however, emergence from each of those concentrations occurs by way of the life-continuum. But from cessation, one emerges by way of the fruition attainment. This is called the emergence not found in the texts, and the Blessed One understands all of it as it really is, in every way. This is the seventh power.

Aṭṭhame pubbenivāsānussatīti pubbenivutthakkhandhānussaraṇaṃ, taṃ nāmagottavaṇṇāhārasukhadukkhādīhi tattha tattha bhave vijjamānehi anantehi ākārehi yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti. Aṭṭhamabalaṃ.

The eighth is the recollection of past abodes: the recollection of aggregates formerly dwelt in. He understands it as it actually is with its infinite aspects such as name, clan, complexion, food, and the experience of pleasure and pain that existed in various existences. The eighth power.

Navame cutūpapātanti cutiñca upapātañca, taṃ cavamānaupapajjamānahīnapaṇītasuvaṇṇadubbaṇṇādito anantapabhede yathākammūpage satte dibbacakkhuñāṇena vaṇṇāyatanaggahaṇamukhena disvā sabbākārato pajānātīti. Navamabalaṃ.

The ninth is the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings: it is the passing away and rebirth. By means of the divine eye, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly—in endless varieties according to their kamma, and understands them in all aspects through the modality of apprehending the visual form base. This is the ninth power.

Dasame [V 0.0223] āsavānaṃ khayanti āsavanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ, taṃ arahattamaggañāṇena catusaccapaṭivedhato pajānātīti. Dasamabalaṃ.

The tenth is the destruction of the taints: the cessation of the taints, which is Nibbāna; this he understands through the penetration of the four truths by the knowledge of the path of arahantship. This is the tenth power.

Imānīti yāni heṭṭhā “tathāgatassa dasa tathāgatabalānī”ti avoca, imāni tānīti appanaṃ karoti. Yasmā cetopariyañāṇādīni sāvakādīnampi yathārahaṃ vijjamānānipi savisayaṃ kiñcideva jānanti, na ca sabbākārato. Buddhānaṃ [M 0.0292] pana sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya sabbadhammesu yathāsakaṃ visaye sabbattha sabbākārato ekakkhaṇe appaṭihataṃ pavattati, tasmā “tathāgatabalānī”ti vuccanti. Yadi evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedo hoti, kasmā pana “dasabalañāṇānī”ti visuṃ vibhattānīti? Visayakiccabhūmibhedato nesaṃ aññattā. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti, dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva jānāti, tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva, catutthaṃ nānattakāraṇameva, pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva, chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva, sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva, aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakkhandhasantatimeva, navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva, dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva, nāññaṃ.

"These" refers to what was previously stated as "the ten powers of the Tathāgata," thus specifying them. Although the knowledge of others' minds and similar abilities exist to some extent in disciples and others according to their capacity, they know only a limited scope, not in all aspects. But the omniscient knowledge of the Buddhas operates unimpeded in a single moment, comprehending all phenomena in every aspect within their respective domains, everywhere. Therefore, they are called "the powers of the Tathāgata." If this is merely a subdivision of omniscient knowledge, why are they separately classified as "the ten powers of knowledge"? It is due to the differences in their objects, functions, and planes. For in the ten powers of knowledge: the first knows only causes and non-causes; the second knows only the diversity of kamma and its results; the third knows only the destination of actions; the fourth knows only the cause of diversity; the fifth knows only the inclinations and dispositions of beings; the sixth knows only the keenness or dullness of faculties; the seventh knows only their defilements, purifications, and so on, along with the jhānas and so on; the eighth knows only the continuity of aggregates formerly dwelt in; the ninth knows only the death and rebirth-linking of beings; the tenth knows only the delimitation of the truths, and nothing else.

Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca sabbaṃ atītādibhedaṃ ekakkhaṇe sabbākārato jānāti, etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Taṃ hi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Dasabalañāṇāni pana taṃ sabbaṃ yathārahaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti. Tesu ca paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇāni kāmāvacarāni, tato dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ lokuttaraṃ. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana kāmāvacaramevāti evaṃ visayakiccabhūmibhedato aññameva dasabalañāṇaṃ. Aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇanti. Ayaṃ tāva padatthānusārato vinicchayo. Dhammabhedādito pana sabbopi vinicchayo ekavidhakoṭṭhāsato paṭṭhāya ettha vuttānusāratova ñātabbo, suttantabhājanīyādayo hi vibhaṅganayabhedā ettha, ito paresu ca vibhaṅgesu natthīti.

The omniscient knowledge, however, knows all that is to be known by these and beyond that, everything classified as past, present, and future, in a single moment, in all aspects. Yet, it does not perform all the functions of these powers. For it cannot, being a jhāna, enter into absorption; being a psychic power, perform transformations; or, being a path, eradicate defilements. The ten powers of knowledge, however, can perform all these appropriately. Among them, in sequence, seven knowledges pertain to the sense-sphere, then two to the form-sphere, and finally one is supramundane. The omniscient knowledge, however, pertains only to the sense-sphere. Thus, in terms of object, function, and plane, the ten powers of knowledge are distinct. The omniscient knowledge is another matter. This, indeed, is the analysis following the wording. As for the analysis based on different kinds of dhammas, the entire discussion should be understood as stated here, starting from the section on single items. The classifications such as the Suttanta method of analysis, etc., are not found here or in the subsequent analyses.

Ñāṇavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Matrix of the Analysis of Knowledge is finished.

Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of the Analysis of Minor Items

Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgamātikāya [M 0.0293][V 0.0224] panāyaṃ nikkhepaparicchedena saddhiṃ atthato vinicchayo. Mātikāya hi ādito tāva – jātimadotiādayo tesattati ekakā nikkhittā, tato kodho ca upanāho cātiādayo aṭṭhārasa dukā, akusalamūlādayo pañcatiṃsa tikā, āsavacatukkādayo cuddasa catukkā, orambhāgiyasaṃyojanādayo pannarasa pañcakā, vivādamūlādayo cuddasa chakkā, anusayādayo satta sattakā, kilesavatthuādayo aṭṭha aṭṭhakā, āghātavatthuādayo nava navakā, kilesavatthuādayo satta dasakā, channaṃ aṭṭhārasakānaṃ vasena aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni ca yathākkamaṃ nikkhipitvā ante dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni brahmajālasutte atidassitānīti sabbānipi tesaṭṭhiadhikāni aṭṭhakilesasatāni nikkhittānīti veditabbāni. Ayaṃ tāva nikkhepaparicchedo.

Now, this is the determination of the meaning of the matrix for the Analysis of Minor Items, together with the section on classification. For in the matrix, to begin with, seventy-three single items such as 'conceit of birth' are set down. Then, eighteen dyads such as 'anger and hostility'; thirty-five triads such as 'the unwholesome roots'; fourteen tetrads such as 'the tetrad of taints'; fifteen pentads such as 'the lower fetters'; fourteen hexads such as 'the roots of dispute'; seven heptads such as 'the underlying tendencies'; eight octads such as 'the grounds for defilements'; nine nonads such as 'the grounds for resentment'; and seven decads such as 'the grounds for defilements'. Then, having set down in sequence the one hundred and eight discursions of craving by way of six sets of eighteen, at the end are the sixty-two kinds of views shown in detail in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Thus it should be understood that altogether eight hundred and sixty-three defilements are set down. This, to begin with, is the section on classification.

Atthato pana “jātimado”tiādīsu jātiuccākulīnataṃ nissāya “khattiyādīnaṃ catunnampi vaṇṇānaṃ ahaṃ uttamajātiko, ime na uttamajātikā”ti evaṃ attukkaṃsanaparavambhanavasena uppanno majjanākārappavatto māno jātimado nāma. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha ādiccagottakassapagottādiuttamagottaṃ nissāya gottamado. Nirābādhataṃ, yobbaññaṃ, “ciraṃ sukhaṃ jīviṃ jīvāmi jīvissāmī”ti evaṃ jīvitaṃ, bahulābhañca nissāya yathākkamaṃ ārogyamadādayo vuttā. Sukatapaṇītapaccayalābhaṃ, mānanavandanādigarukāraṃ maññeva pamukhaṃ katvā pañhaṃ pucchanti, parivāretvā gacchantīti evaṃ purekkhāraṃ, mahāparivāraṃ, suciparivārañca nissāya yathākkamaṃ sakkāramadādayo ca veditabbā. Bhogo pana kiñcāpi lābhaggahaṇeneva gahito, nihitadhanavasena panettha [M 0.0294] lābho veditabbo, “annapānavatthābharaṇamālāgandhādiupabhogasamiddhivasenāpi vattuṃ vaṭṭatī”tipi vadanti. Sarīravaṇṇaṃ, guṇavaṇṇañca nissāya vaṇṇamado. Bāhusaccaṃ, paṭibhānaṃ, “vaṇṇaṃ buddhavaṃsaṃ rājavaṃsaṃ janapadavaṃsaṃ gāmavaṃsaṃ rattindivaparicchedaṃ nakkhattamuhuttayogaṃ jānāmī”ti evaṃ rattaññutaṃ vā nissāya yathākkamaṃ sutamadādayo ca veditabbā. Jātipiṇḍapātikataṃ, anavaññātataṃ, iriyāpathapāsādikataṃ, mahiddhikatañca nissāya yathākkamaṃ piṇḍapātikamadādayo. Kiñcāpi parivāra-ggahaṇena yaso gahito. Parivārassa pana savasavattakabhāvena patthaṭataṃ kittiyasaññeva vā nissāya yasamado. Parisuddhasīlaṃ[V 0.0225], upacārappanājhānaṃ, sippakosallaṃ, sarīrassa ārohasampadaṃ, pariṇāhasampadaṃ, anūnaniddosaaṅgapaccaṅgatāya sarīrapāripūriñca nissāya sīlamadādayo veditabbā.

As to the meaning, however, in the case of 'conceit of birth' and so on, the conceit that arises in the manner of intoxication—by way of exalting oneself and disparaging others based on high birth, thinking, 'Among the four castes such as the khattiyas, I am of the highest birth, these others are not of the highest birth'—is called conceit of birth. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Therein, based on a superior clan such as the Ādicca or Kassapa clan, there is conceit of clan. Based respectively on freedom from disease, on youthfulness, on longevity—thinking 'I have lived, am living, and will live long and happily'—and on abundant gain, conceit of health and so on are spoken of. Based respectively on the gain of well-made and fine requisites; on being honored—thinking, 'They ask questions considering me as the foremost; they accompany me in procession'; on having a large retinue; and on having a pure retinue, conceit of honor and so on should be understood. Although wealth is included by the mention of gain, here it should be understood as gain in the sense of deposited treasure; but some say it is also fit to be spoken of in the sense of an abundance of consumables such as food, drink, clothing, ornaments, garlands, and perfumes. Based on beauty of body and beauty of virtue, there is conceit of appearance. Based respectively on great learning, on ready wit, or on seniority—thinking 'I know the lineages of Buddhas, royal lineages, district lineages, village lineages, the divisions of day and night, the constellations, and auspicious moments'—conceit of learning and so on should be understood. Based respectively on being a natural alms-food-eater, on being beyond contempt, on dignified deportment, and on great psychic power, there is conceit of being an alms-food-eater and so on. Although fame is included by the mention of retinue, conceit of fame is based on the pervasiveness of one's retinue being under one's own control, or on the very notion of renown. Based on perfectly pure virtue, on access and absorption jhāna, on skill in crafts, on perfection of bodily height, on perfection of girth, and on the completeness of the body through having limbs and members that are not deficient and are flawless, conceit of virtue and so on should be understood.

Iminā ettakena ṭhānena savatthukaṃ mānaṃ dassetvā idāni avatthukameva sāmaññato mānaṃ dassento “mado”ti āha. Pamādotiādīsu pañcakāmaguṇesu cittavossaggasaṅkhāto sucaritāsevanāya, duccaritasevanāya ca hetubhūto pamajjanākārappavatto akusalacittuppādo pamādo nāma, svāyaṃ sativossaggalakkhaṇo. Vātabharitabhattā viya mātāpitūsupi anoṇatabhāvasaṅkhāto kakkhaḷamāno thambho nāma, svāyaṃ cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇo. Aññesaṃ gehādiupakaraṇasampadaṃ, vijjāsampadaṃ vā disvā taddiguṇasamārambhanavasappavatto akusalacittuppādo sārambho nāma. Ganthopi hi sārambhavasena uggahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, akusalameva hoti. Svāyaṃ karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo.

Having thus far shown conceit with a basis, now, showing conceit in general without a basis, he says 'mada.' In 'heedlessness' (pamādo) and so on: heedlessness is the unwholesome thought-arising that proceeds in the manner of negligence, which is the cause for cultivating both good and bad conduct and is defined as the release of the mind upon the five strands of sensual pleasure. It has the characteristic of the release of mindfulness. Like a pot filled with wind, the harsh conceit defined as an unbending nature even towards one's parents is called 'obstinacy' (thambho). It has the characteristic of the mind's inflation. Having seen the accomplishment of others in household equipment or in knowledge, the unwholesome thought-arising that proceeds by way of an undertaking to equal their qualities is called 'contention' (sārambho). For even a text should not be learned with contention, as it would be simply unwholesome. This has the characteristic of over-exertion.

Atra [M 0.0295] atra visaye icchā assāti atriccho, puggalo, tassa bhāvo atricchatā. Evaṃ mahicchatādīsupi attho veditabbo. Tattha yaṃ yaṃ laddhaṃ, tena tena asantussitvā aparassa aparassa patthanāvasena pavatto lobho atricchatā. Yāya attanā laddhaṃ paṇītampi lāmakaṃ viya khāyati, parena laddhaṃ lāmakampi paṇītaṃ viya khāyati. Sāyaṃ aparāparalābhapatthanālakkhaṇā. Santaguṇavibhāvanāvasappavatto ceva taduppannehi atimahantehipi vatthūhi asantussanākārappavatto ca lobho mahicchatā. Yāya samannāgato puggalo paccayehi duppūro aggi viya upādānena, samuddo viya ca udakena. Yā cāyaṃ santaguṇasambhāvanatā, paṭiggahaṇe ca paribhoge ca amattaññutā, etaṃ mahicchatālakkhaṇaṃ.

One who has desire for this and that object is a person with excessive desire (atriccho); his state is excessive desire (atricchatā). The meaning should be understood similarly in cases like 'great desire' (mahicchatā) and so on. Therein, being discontent with whatever has been gained, the greed that proceeds by way of longing for more and more is excessive desire. Through this, what one has gained oneself, though it may be fine, seems poor, while what another has gained, though it may be poor, seems fine. It has the characteristic of longing for one gain after another. The greed that proceeds by way of proclaiming one's existing virtues and also proceeds in the manner of discontent even with extremely great things produced by them is 'great desire' (mahicchatā). A person endowed with this is hard to fill with requisites, like a fire with fuel or the ocean with water. And this overestimation of one's existing virtues, and immoderation in accepting and using, is the characteristic of great desire.

Asantānaṃ pana saddhāsīlānaṃ, maggaphalādīnañca lokiyalokuttarānaṃ guṇānaṃ vibhāvanāvasappavatto ceva taduppannehi atimahantehipi paccayehi asantussanākārappavatto ca lobho pāpicchatā. Yā cāyaṃ asantaguṇasambhāvanatā, paṭiggahaṇe ca paribhoge ca amattaññutā etaṃ pāpicchatālakkhaṇaṃ.

But the greed that proceeds by way of making a display of non-existent mundane and supramundane qualities—such as faith, virtue, path, and fruition—and that also proceeds in the manner of discontent even with extremely great requisites produced thereby, is 'evil desire' (pāpicchatā). And this pretension to non-existent qualities, and immoderation in accepting and using, is the characteristic of evil desire.

Siṅganti vijjhanaṭṭhena siṅgaṃ, nāgarikabhāvasaṅkhātassa kilesasiṅgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ atthato siṅgārakaraṇavasappavatto lobhova. Tintiṇanti khīyanaṃ, taṃ atthato nivāsaṭṭhāne sunakhānaṃ [V 0.0226] viya aññamaññaṃ sattānaṃ “tava santakaṃ, mama santaka”nti khiyyanākārappavatto dosova. Cāpalyanti capalatā, taṃ pattacīvarādiparikkhārānaṃ, attabhāvassa ca maṇḍanavibhūsanakeḷāyanavasappavatto rāgova, yena samannāgato jiṇṇopi daharo viya hoti. Asabhāgavuttīti visabhāgavutti visabhāgakiriyā, sā garuṭṭhāniyesupi anādaravasena vipaccanīkaggāhitāvasappavatto dosova[M 0.0296], yāya samannāgato gilānepi mātāpituācariyupajjhāyādike na oloketi, tehi saddhiṃ lābhasakkārakāraṇā kalahaṃ karoti, tesu hirottappaṃ, cetiyādīsu cittīkārañca na paccupaṭṭhapeti. Aratīti pantesu senāsanesu, samathavipassanāsu ca anabhiramaṇā ukkaṇṭhitatā, sā tathāpavatto akusalacittuppādo. Tandīti ālasyaṃ. Vijambhitāti kāyassa ānamanādiākārena phandanā vijambhanā. Bhattasammadoti bhattamucchāya kāyassa akammaññatā. Cetaso ca līnattanti cittasaṅkoco. Atthato panetāni sabbānipi thinamiddhavasena cittassa gilānākārova.

`Siṅga` is so called in the sense of piercing. It is a designation for the 'horn of defilements,' which is defined as the state of a townsman. In meaning, it is just the greed that proceeds by way of coquetry. `Tintiṇa` is wrangling. In meaning, it is just the hate that proceeds in the manner of beings wrangling with one another like dogs in their living place, saying, 'This is yours, this is mine.' `Cāpalya` is fickleness. It is just the lust that proceeds by way of adorning, beautifying, and playing with one's requisites such as bowl and robes, and with one's own person. Endowed with this, even an old person acts like a youth. `Asabhāgavutti` is unseemly conduct, improper action. It is just the hate that proceeds by way of disrespect even toward those worthy of reverence and by way of adopting a contrary position. Endowed with this, one does not look after one's parents, teachers, preceptors, and so on, even when they are sick; one quarrels with them for the sake of gain and honor; and one does not establish shame and fear of wrongdoing toward them, or reverence toward shrines. `Arati` is discontent, a state of dissatisfaction and non-delight in remote lodgings and in serenity and insight; it is an unwholesome thought-arising that proceeds in that way. `Tandī` is laziness. `Vijambhitā` is stretching, the movement of the body in the form of bending and so on. `Bhattasammado` is drowsiness after a meal, the unwieldiness of the body due to torpor from food. And `cetaso līnattā` is sluggishness of mind, a contraction of the mind. In meaning, however, all these are just the sickened state of the mind due to sloth and torpor.
