Kuhanātiādīsu lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa tena tena upāyena vimhāpanā kuhanā nāma. Sā tividhā paccayapaṭisevanasāmantajappanairiyāpathasaṇṭhāpanavasena. Tattha cīvarādīhi nimantitassa tadatthikasseva sato pāpicchataṃ nissāya paṭikkhipanena, te ca gahapatike attani suppatiṭṭhitasaddhe ñatvā puna tesaṃ “aho ayyo appiccho na kiñci paṭiggaṇhituṃ icchati, suladdhaṃ vata no assa, sace appamattakaṃ kiñci paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti nānāvidhehi upāyehi paṇītāni cīvarādīni upanāmentānaṃ tadanuggahakāmataññeva āvikatvā paṭiggahaṇena ca tato pabhuti api sakaṭabhārehi upanāmanahetubhūtaṃ vimhāpanaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātā kuhanā nāma. Pāpicchasseva pana sato “yo evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, so samaṇo mahesakkho”tiādinā uttarimanussadhammādhigamaparidīpanavācāya tathā tathā vimhāpanaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātā kuhanā nāma. Pāpicchasseva pana sato samāhitasseva sambhāvanādhippāyakatena paṇidhāya saṇṭhapitena gamanādiiriyāpathena vimhāpanaṃ iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanasaṅkhātā kuhanā nāma.

In 'deceit' (kuhanā) and so on: deceit is the deluding by various means on the part of one with evil desires who is dependent on gain, honor, and fame. It is threefold: by way of using requisites, by way of suggestive talk, and by way of arranging one's deportment. Therein, when one with evil desires, though wanting them, refuses robes and so on with which he has been invited, and then, knowing that those householders have well-established faith in him, he accepts when they bring fine robes and so on by various means—thinking, 'Ah, the venerable one has few wishes and does not want to accept anything! It would be a great gain for us if he would accept just a little!'—revealing only his wish to favor them. This delusion, which from then on becomes a cause for them to bring offerings even by the cartload, is called deceit by way of using requisites. Again, the delusion by one with evil desires, by means of speech that points to the attainment of superhuman states, such as by saying, 'Whoever wears such a robe is an eminent ascetic,' is called deceit by way of suggestive talk. Again, the delusion by one with evil desires, by means of deportment such as walking that is deliberately arranged with the intention of being esteemed as one who is concentrated, is called deceit by way of arranging one's deportment.

Ālapanātiādinā [M 0.0297] pana vuttapaccayapaṭisaṃyuttā vācāyeva dassitā. Anuppiyabhāṇitā, cāṭukamyatā, muggasūpyatā, pāribhaṭayatā ca ālapanā nāma. Tattha ālapanātiāditova lapanā. Anuppiyabhāṇitāti saccānurūpaṃ, dhammānurūpaṃ vā anapaloketvā punappunaṃ piyabhaṇanaṃ. Cāṭukamyatāti [V 0.0227] nīcavuttitā, attānaṃ heṭṭhato ṭhapetvā pavattanaṃ. Muggasūpyatāti muggasūpasadisatā, apakkamuggasadisena appasaccena samannāgatavacanatā. Pāribhaṭayatāti kuladārakānaṃ aṅkena pariharaṇādikaṃ paribhaṭassa kiccaṃ. Evamayaṃ sabbopi kiriyābhedo “lapanā”tveva vuccati. Paresaṃ pana paccayadānasaññājanakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ nemittikatā nāma, yā “parikathobhāsanimittakamma”nti vuccati. Akkosanavambhanagarahaṇādīhi yathā dāyako avaṇṇaṃ bhāyati, evaṃ taṃ nippīḷanaṃ nippesikatā nāma. Ayaṃ hi yasmā veḷupesikāya viya abbhaṅgaṃ imāya parassa guṇaṃ nippeseti nipuñchati, yasmā vā gandhajātaṃ pisitvā gandhamagganā viya paraguṇe nippisitvā vicuṇṇetvā esā lābhamagganā hoti, tasmā “nippesikatā”ti vuccati. Ekasmiṃ pana kule laddhāmisaṃ aññattha dānavasena lābhena lābhassa patthanā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā nāma. Ime ca kuhanādayo pañcapi tathā tathā pavattā lobhādiakusalacittuppādāti veditabbā. “Seyyohamasmī”tiādayo dvādasa mānā heṭṭhā saṃyojanagocchake vuttānusārena suviññeyyāva. Tattha ca ādito tayo mānā puggalaṃ anissāya jātigottarūpabhogasippasutādimānavatthuvaseneva kathitā, tato paraṃ pana nava mānā seyyasadisahīnapuggale nissāya kathitā.

By 'flattery' (`ālapanā`) and so on, speech connected with the aforesaid requisites is shown. Flattering speech, ingratiation, insincerity, and servility are called 'flattery.' Herein, 'flattery' (`ālapanā`) is simply talking (`lapanā`). 'Speaking what is pleasing' (`anuppiyabhāṇitā`) means repeatedly speaking pleasing words without regard for truth or the Dhamma. 'Ingratiation' (`cāṭukamyatā`) means behaving in a lowly manner, placing oneself in an inferior position. 'Insincerity' (`muggasūpyatā`) means being like lentil soup—speech endowed with little truth, like half-cooked lentils. 'Servility' (`pāribhaṭayatā`) means performing tasks such as carrying children on the hip, which is the work of a servant. Thus, all these types of actions are simply called 'talking.' Moreover, bodily and verbal actions that generate in others the idea of giving requisites are called 'hinting' (`nemittikatā`), which is referred to as 'allusive talk, showing signs, and making hints.' Through abuse, insult, and reproach, oppressing a donor so that he fears disrepute is called 'grinding down' (`nippesikatā`). For just as one scrapes off ointment with a strip of bamboo, so with this one scrapes and wipes away another's virtue; or, just as seeking for scents is done by grinding fragrant substances, so this is a seeking for gain by grinding down and pulverizing the virtues of others; therefore, it is called 'grinding down.' Furthermore, having obtained a material gain from one family, desiring a greater gain from another by means of giving it away is called 'pursuing gain with gain' (`lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā`). These five—deceit and so on—should be understood as arising from unwholesome states of mind such as greed. The twelve kinds of conceit, such as 'I am better,' are easily understood according to the explanation given in the section on the fetters. Among them, the first three kinds of conceit are spoken of based on the grounds of birth, clan, form, wealth, skills, learning, and so on, without reference to a person. The remaining nine are spoken of in reference to someone who is better, equal, or inferior.

Evametehi dvādasahi padehi savatthuke māne kathetvā idāni avatthukaṃ dassetuṃ “māno”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tato [M 0.0298] paraṃ atimānotiādīsu “jātiādīhi mayā sadiso natthī”ti atikkamitvā maññanāvasena pavatto māno atimāno nāma. “Ime mayā pubbe sadisā, idāni ahaṃ seṭṭho, ime hīnatarā”ti uppanno māno bhārātibhāro viya mānātimāno nāma. Attānaṃ pana avamaññanāvasena pavatto māno omāno nāma, so “hīnohamasmī”ti pavattahīnamānasadisova. Anadhigatesu ariyadhammesu “adhigatā mayā”ti uppanno māno adhikamānattā adhimāno nāma, ayaṃ pana sotāpannādiariyasāvakānaṃ “ahaṃ sakadāgāmī”tiādinā na uppajjati tesaṃ maggaphalanibbānapahīnakilesāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇena ariyaguṇapaṭivedhe nikkaṅkhattā. Dussīlassa pana na uppajjateva, sīlavatopi pariccattakammaṭṭhānassa na uppajjati, parisuddhasīlasseva pana suddhasamathalābhino, suddhavipassanālābhino, tadubhayalābhino vā uppajjati. Tesu tadubhayalābhī arahatte eva adhimaññitvā patiṭṭhāti suvikkhambhitakilesattā, parimadditasaṅkhārattā ca, itare sotāpannādīsupīti veditabbā. Pañcasu pana khandhesu “ahamasmī”tiādinā pavatto māno asmimāno [V 0.0228] nāma. Pāpakena pana parūpaghātakena kammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānādinā attānaṃ seyyādito jappanavasena pavatto māno micchāmāno nāma.

Having thus explained conceit with its twelve bases, now to illustrate baseless conceit, the term 'conceit' and so on is introduced. Next, regarding 'conceit of superiority' (`atimāna`) and so on: the conceit that arises by way of conceiving that one has surpassed others, thinking, 'There is no one like me in birth, etc.,' is called 'conceit of superiority.' The conceit that arises with the thought, 'These were once my equals, but now I am superior, and they are inferior,' is called 'excessive conceit' (`mānātimāna`), like an overloaded burden. The conceit that arises by way of belittling oneself is called 'inferiority conceit' (`omāna`); it is similar to the conceit of inferiority that proceeds as 'I am inferior.' The conceit that arises regarding unattained noble qualities with the thought, 'I have attained them,' is called 'overestimation conceit' (`adhimāna`) because of overestimating. However, this does not arise in noble disciples such as stream-enterers with thoughts like, 'I am a once-returner,' because they have no doubt about their realization of noble qualities, having reflected on the defilements abandoned through the path, fruition, and Nibbāna, and the remaining defilements. In an immoral person, it does not arise at all. Even in a virtuous person who has relinquished their meditation subject, it does not arise. But it does arise in one of purified virtue who has attained pure serenity, pure insight, or both. Among them, one who has attained both may become established in the overestimation of arahantship due to the thorough suppression of defilements and the crushing of formations. It should be understood that the others may do so even regarding the stages of stream-entry and so on. The conceit that arises in relation to the five aggregates with thoughts like 'I am' is called 'ego-conceit' (`asmimāna`). The conceit that arises by way of boasting about oneself as superior and so on due to evil, harmful actions, occupations, skills, sciences, etc., is called 'wrong conceit' (`micchāmāna`).

Ñātivitakkotiādīsu “mayhaṃ ñātakā sukhajīvino sampattiyuttā”ti evaṃ gehasitapemena ñātake uddissa uppanno vitakko ñātivitakko nāma, “ñātakā khayaṃ gatā vayaṃ gatā saddhā pasannā”tiādinā pana nekkhammasito ñātivitakko nāma na hoti. Evaṃ janapadavitakkepi, tassa pana “amhākaṃ janapado subhikkho sundaro”tiādinā pavattiākāro veditabbo. Amaratthāya vitakko, amaro [M 0.0299] vā vitakkoti amaravitakko. Tattha yo ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi dukkhe nijjiṇṇe samparāye attā sukhī amaro hotīti evaṃ pavatto, so amaratthāya vitakko nāma. Yo pana diṭṭhigatikassa ekasmiṃ pakkhe asaṇṭhahitvā “evampi me no, tathāpi me no, aññathāpi me no”tiādinā amaramaccho viya gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya pavatto, so amaro vitakko nāma. Taṃ duvidhampi ekato katvā idha “amaravitakko”ti vutto.

In the case of 'thoughts about relatives' and so on: a thought that arises concerning one's relatives with household-bound affection, such as 'My relatives live happily and are prosperous,' is called a 'thought about relatives.' However, a thought concerning relatives that is connected with renunciation, such as 'My relatives, who were faithful and devoted, have perished and passed away,' is not considered a 'thought about relatives.' The same applies to 'thoughts about one's country,' the mode of which should be understood as, for example, 'Our country is prosperous and beautiful.' A 'thought for the sake of immortality' or an 'immortal thought' is called a 'thought about immortality.' Therein, a thought that proceeds thus, 'Through austerities such as the squatting exertion, when suffering is worn away, in the future life the self will be happy and immortal,' is called a 'thought for the sake of immortality.' On the other hand, the thought of one holding a speculative view that, not settling on any one side, proceeds from an inability to be grasped, like an eel (lit. 'immortal fish'), thinking, 'It is not so for me, it is not thus for me, it is not otherwise for me,' is called an 'immortal' (i.e., evasive) thought. Both these types are combined here and referred to as 'a thought about immortality.'

Anuddayatā patirūpakena pana gihīhi sahasokisahananditādivasena gehasitapemena yutto parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nāma. Lābhena ceva sakkārena ca kittisaddena ca saddhiṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena yutto gehasito vitakko lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nāma, tassa pana “aho vata me lābhādayo uppajjeyyu”ntiādinā pavattiākāro veditabbo. “Aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyu”nti uppanno gehasito vitakko anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nāma. Ekakaṃ.

A thought connected with counterfeit compassion for others is one that is joined with household-based affection by way of sharing sorrow and joy with householders. A thought rooted in household life, connected with gain, honor, and renown by way of making them an object, is called a thought associated with gain, honor, and renown. Its mode of occurrence should be understood as: 'Oh, may gains and so on arise for me!' A thought rooted in household life that arises as: 'Oh, may others not despise me,' is called a thought associated with non-contempt. The Singles.

Dukādīsu kodhādayo heṭṭhā vuttatthe vajjetvā avasesānaññeva vaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha dukesu tāva upanāhotiādīsu pubbabhāge kodho “akkocchima”ntiādinā āsevanena aparakāle veracitte daḷhataraṃ ābaddho upanāho nāma, yena samannāgato veraṃ nissajjituṃ na sakkoti vasātelamakkhitapilotikā viya, sodhiyamānampissa cittaṃ na parisujjhati, svāyaṃ verupanibandhanalakkhaṇo.

In the sections on the dyads and so forth, anger and the like, having been mentioned earlier, are to be set aside, and only the remaining terms will be described. There, in the dyads, first among 'resentment' and so on: in the preliminary stage, anger, through repetition of 'he insulted me' and so on, later, with a mind of hostility, becomes very firmly bound as 'resentment,' by which one endowed with it cannot give up enmity, like a rag smeared with fat and oil; even when cleaned, their mind is not purified. This has the characteristic of being bound by enmity.

Paraguṇaṃ pana vināsetvā tattha dosamakkhanavasena pavatto kodho makkho nāma. Ayaṃ hi paṭhamataraṃ [V 0.0229] attano cittaṃ gūtho viya gūthaggāhakaṃ hatthaṃ makkheti, pacchā [M 0.0300] paranti “makkho”ti vutto, svāyaṃ paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo. Paḷāsetīti paḷāso, parassa guṇe dassetvā attano guṇehi same karotīti attho. Tathāpavatto lobho, svāyaṃ yugaggāhalakkhaṇo.

But anger that proceeds by way of effacing another's virtue and smearing it with fault is called 'denigration' (makkha). For this first smears one's own mind, just as filth smears the hand that grasps it; afterwards, it is said to be 'denigration' towards another. This has the characteristic of besmirching another's virtue. 'Rivalry' (paḷāsa) is so called because one vies with others; the meaning is that one makes oneself equal with the virtues of another. Greed that proceeds in such a way has the characteristic of taking up a yoke with another.

Dvārattayepi vijjamānasseva dosassa paṭicchādanato cakkhumohanamāyā viyāti māyā, sā katadosapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā. Saṭhassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā sāṭheyyaṃ, kerāṭiyaṃ, taṃ avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ.

Because of the concealment of a fault that indeed exists in the three doors, it is called 'deceit' (māyā), like the illusion that deludes the eye. Its characteristic is the concealment of a committed fault. The state of a cheat, or their action, is 'fraud' (sāṭheyya), or 'trickery' (kerāṭiyaṃ). Its characteristic is the display of non-existent qualities.

Anajjavādayo heṭṭhā vuttaajjavādipaṭipakkhaakusalavasena veditabbā. Ajjhattasaṃyojanantiādīsu ajjhattanti kāmabhavo, tattha satte bandhanavasena pavattāni pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Bahiddhāti rūpārūpabhavo. Tattha bandhanavasena pavattāni pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni bahiddhāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma. Kāmabhave hi sattānaṃ ālayo bahuko, na itaresu, tasmā so ajjhattaṃ itare ca bahiddhāti veditabbā. Dukaṃ.

Dishonesty and so on should be understood as the unwholesome states that are the counterparts of honesty and so on, mentioned earlier. In the terms 'internal fetter' and so on, 'internal' refers to the realm of sensual existence, where the five lower fetters that bind beings there are called the 'internal fetter.' 'External' refers to the realms of form and formless existence; there, the five higher fetters that bind are called the 'external fetter.' For beings in the realm of sensual existence, attachment is abundant, not so in the others. Therefore, that should be understood as 'internal,' and the others as 'external.' The dyad.

Tikesu pana lobhādīni tīṇi akusalamūlāni nāma. Kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāsampayuttā vitakkā tayo akusalavitakkā nāma. Te eva saññāsīsena tisso akusalasaññā. Sabhāvaṭṭhena tisso akusaladhātuyoti ca vuccanti. Kāyavacīmanoduccaritāni tīṇi duccaritāni nāma, tāni dvārattayappavattānaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ, sabbākusalānaṃ vā vasena yojetabbāni. Suttantapariyāyena pana diṭṭhāsavavajjitā kāmāsavādayo tayo āsavā nāma. Sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsā tīṇi saṃyojanāni nāma.

In the triads, the three unwholesome roots are called greed and so forth. The three thoughts associated with sensual desire, ill-will, and violence are called unwholesome thoughts. These same, when considered under the heading of perception, are the three unwholesome perceptions. By their intrinsic nature, they are also called the three unwholesome elements. The three evil conducts are called misconduct of body, speech, and mind. These, arising through the three doors, should be connected with killing living beings and so forth, or with all unwholesome states. According to the Suttanta method, the three taints, excluding the taint of views, are called the taint of sensual desire and so forth. The three fetters are called personality belief, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals.

Kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā ca tisso taṇhā nāma. Tattha sassatadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo bhavataṇhā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato [M 0.0301] rāgo vibhavataṇhā, avasesā pana sabbāpi taṇhā kāmataṇhā. Kāmadhātupaṭisaṃyutto vā rāgo kāmataṇhā, rūpārūpadhātupaṭisaṃyutto bhavataṇhā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato vibhavataṇhāti veditabbā. Kāmataṇhā rūpataṇhā arūpataṇhā ca aparāpi tisso taṇhā nāma. Rūpataṇhā arūpataṇhā nirodhataṇhā ca puna aparāpi tisso taṇhā nāma. Tattha nirodhataṇhāti ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato. Kāmesanā bhavesanā brahmacariyesanā ca tisso esanā nāma. Tattha brahmacariyesanāti sassatucchedadiṭṭhisaṅkhātabrahmacariyassa gavesanā. “Seyyohamasmīti [V 0.0230] vidhā, sadisohamasmīti vidhā, hīnohamasmīti vidhā”ti evaṃ vuttamānavidhā tisso vidhā nāma. Māno hi seyyādivasena vidahanato maññanato “vidhā”ti vuccati. Jātijarāmaraṇāni paṭicca uppannāni bhayāni tīṇi bhayāni nāma. “Atītaṃ vā addhānaṃ ārabbhā”tiādinā vuttāni tīṇi, buddhādīsu kaṅkhanavicikicchanavasena pavattā tisso avijjā tīṇi tamāni nāma. Vicikicchāsīsena tassa vibhaṅge taṃsampayuttā avijjāva vuttā, tassā eva paṭicchādakattenapi tamabhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—these are called the three cravings. Herein, lust associated with the eternalist view is craving for existence; lust associated with the annihilationist view is craving for non-existence; and all remaining craving is craving for sensual pleasures. Alternatively, lust connected with the sense-sphere realm is craving for sensual pleasures; lust connected with the fine-material and immaterial realms is craving for existence; and lust associated with the annihilationist view is to be understood as craving for non-existence. Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless—these are another set of three cravings. Craving for form, craving for the formless, and craving for cessation—these are yet another set of three cravings. Herein, craving for cessation is that associated with the annihilationist view. The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life—these are called the three searches. Herein, the search for the holy life is the quest for a holy life reckoned in terms of eternalist or annihilationist views. ‘I am superior,’ ‘I am equal,’ ‘I am inferior’—these ways of conceiving are called the three conceits (vidhā). For conceit (māno), because it sets up and fancies oneself as superior and so on, is called vidhā. The fears that have arisen in dependence on birth, aging, and death are called the three fears. Those three mentioned beginning with ‘concerning the past period,’ and the three ignorances operating as doubt and uncertainty regarding the Buddha and so on, are called the three darknesses. In the analysis of doubt, it is the ignorance associated with it that is mentioned; it should be understood that this very ignorance, by its nature of concealing, also constitutes darkness.

Yaṃ kiñci pana sattassa sukhādikaṃ uppajjati, taṃ sabbaṃ pubbekatahetūti ekaṃ titthāyatanaṃ, issaranimmānahetūti dutiyaṃ, ahetuappaccayāti tatiyanti imāni tīṇi titthāyatanāni nāma. Tattha paṭhamavādī kusalākusalakiriyautucittāhārādikaṃ, gatiupadhiādikaṃ, sappurisūpanissayasaddhammassavanādikañca sabbaṃ paccayapaccayuppannaṃ paṭikkhipitvā ekaṃ kammavipākameva sampaṭicchati, itare pana dvepi sabbaṃ hetuṃ paṭikkhipitvā issarahetukaṃ, ahetukañca sampaṭicchanti, tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vādānaṃ vaseneva payojanābhāvādito yathānurūpaṃ doso ñātabbo. Ganthavitthārabhayena panettha na vitthārayimha.

Whatever pleasure and so forth arises for a being, it is all caused by past deeds—this is one sectarian tenet. It is caused by the creation of a Lord—this is the second. It is without cause or condition—this is the third. These are called the three sectarian tenets. Here, the proponent of the first view rejects all causes and causally arisen phenomena—such as wholesome and unwholesome actions, physical functions, climate, mind, and nutriment; destiny and substratum of rebirth; and association with superior persons and hearing the good Dhamma—and accepts only the result of kamma. The other two, however, reject all causes and accept either a Lord as cause or no cause at all. The fault of these three views should be known appropriately from their lack of purpose and so on. We have not elaborated on this here for fear of expanding the text.

Rāgadosamohā [M 0.0302] pana tayo palibodhaṭṭhena kiñcanā nāma. Te eva hi kilesaṭṭhena aṅgaṇāni, malīnabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena malāni, pakkhalanapātahetuto visamāni ca honti. Pāṇātipātādīni kāyavacīmanovisamāni aparānipi tīṇi visamāni nāma. Rāgadosamohā anudahanaṭṭhena tayo aggī, kasaṭanirojaṭṭhena kasāvā ca honti. Pāṇātipātādīni kāyakasāvādayo pana aparepi tayo kasāvā nāma. Assādadiṭṭhittike kāmaparibhoge “natthi kāmesu doso”ti evaṃ pavattā sassatadiṭṭhi assādadiṭṭhi nāma. Vīsativatthukā pana attadiṭṭhi attānaṃ anugatattā attānudiṭṭhi nāma. Tassā pana “rūpaṃ attato samanupassati, rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ, attani vā rūpaṃ, rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ samanupassatī”ti evaṃ rūpakkhandhe catasso diṭṭhiyo. Evaṃ sesakkhandhesupīti vīsativatthukatā veditabbā.

Lust, hatred, and delusion are called impediments (kiñcana) in the sense of being obstructions. Indeed, they are stains (aṅgaṇa) in the sense of being defilements, taints (mala) in the sense of causing defilement, and inequalities (visama) because they are a cause for stumbling and falling. The destruction of life and so on, which are bodily, verbal, and mental inequalities—these are another three inequalities. Lust, hatred, and delusion are the three fires in the sense of burning up, and they are blemishes (kasāva) in the sense of producing what is worthless. The destruction of life and so on, which are bodily blemishes, etc.—these are another three blemishes. In the triad of the view of gratification, the eternalist view that occurs in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures with the thought, ‘There is no danger in sensual pleasures,’ is called the view of gratification. The twenty-grounded identity view, because it follows after the self, is called the view attached to self. Regarding this: ‘One regards form as self, or the self as possessing form, or form as in the self, or the self as in form’—thus there are four views concerning the form aggregate. In the same way, its twenty-grounded nature should be understood in regard to the remaining aggregates.

Tattha ca rūpaṃ attatodiādinā pañcakkhandhe attato gahaṇavasena pavattā pañca ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā pana sassatadiṭṭhiyoti veditabbā. “Natthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattā pana natthikadiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhi nāma, lāmakadiṭṭhīti attho. Aratittike pāṇileḍḍudaṇḍādīhi sattānaṃ [V 0.0231] vihiṃsanā vihesā nāma. Dvārattayappavattaakusaladhammassa cariyā adhammacariyā nāma. Dovacassatātike sāva kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāsaññā nānārammaṇesu pavattito, nānābhūtattā ca nānattasaññā nāma. Uddhaccattike kusītassa bhāvo kosajjaṃ, pamādova. Anādariyattike ovādassa anādiyanavasappavatto kodho anādariyaṃ nāma. Assaddhiyattike ratanattayakammaphalānaṃ asaddahanavasappavattā akusaladhammā assaddhiyaṃ nāma. Pañcavidhamacchariyavasena “dehī”ti vacanassa ajānanā avadaññutā nāma.

Herein, the five views that occur by way of grasping the five aggregates as self, beginning with ‘form as self,’ are annihilationist views; the remaining ones should be understood as eternalist views. The nihilistic view that proceeds in the manner of ‘There is nothing given,’ etc., is called wrong view, meaning a base view. In the triad of discontent, the harming of beings with hand, clods of earth, sticks, and so on, is called vexation. The practice of unwholesome states occurring through the three doors is called unrighteous conduct. In the triad of being difficult to correct, those same perceptions of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness, because they occur in regard to diverse objects and because they are of diverse kinds, are called perceptions of diversity. In the triad of restlessness, the state of an indolent person is indolence, which is just negligence. In the triad of disrespect, the anger that occurs by way of not heeding advice is called disrespect. In the triad of faithlessness, the unwholesome states that occur by way of not having faith in the Three Jewels and the fruit of kamma are called faithlessness. Not knowing the words ‘Please give’ on account of the five kinds of stinginess is called ungenerosity.

Uddhaccattike [M 0.0303] manacchaṭṭhesu indriyesu aguttadvāratā asaṃvaro nāma. Kāyikavācasikavītikkamo dussīlyaṃ nāma. Ariyattike buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ dassanopāsanādīsu anicchā ariyānaṃ adassanakamyatā nāma. Bodhipakkhikasaddhammassa savanadhāraṇādīsu anicchā saddhammaṃ asotukamyatā nāma. Parassa dosāropane randhagavesitāsaṅkhāto upārambhova upārambhacittatā nāma. Muṭṭhassaccattike uddhaccaṃ cetaso vikkhepo nāma. Ayonisomanasikārattike “anicce nicca”ntiādinā, saccapaṭipakkhavasena vā anupāyamanasikārasaṅkhātaṃ āvajjanacittaṃ ayonisomanasikāro nāma. Micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappādayo aṭṭha micchāmaggā kummaggo nāma, micchāmaggassa āsevanā kummaggasevanā nāma. Thinamiddhaṃ cetaso ca līnattaṃ nāma. Tikaṃ.

In the triad of restlessness, unguardedness of the doors in regard to the six faculties with the mind as the sixth is called lack of restraint. Bodily and verbal transgression is called immoral conduct. In the triad concerning the noble ones, the lack of desire to see, attend upon, and so on, the Buddha, paccekabuddhas, and disciples is called unwillingness to see the noble ones. The lack of desire to hear, remember, and so on, the good Dhamma that is on the side of enlightenment is called unwillingness to hear the good Dhamma. Censoriousness, reckoned as fault-finding when imputing faults to another, is called a censorious mind. In the triad of muddle-headedness, restlessness is mental distraction. In the triad of unwise attention, the advertence of the mind reckoned as an improper means of attention—such as ‘permanent in the impermanent,’ etc., or in a way contrary to the truths—is called unwise attention. The eight factors of the wrong path—wrong view, wrong intention, and so on—are called the wrong path. The cultivation of the wrong path is called frequenting the wrong path. Sloth and torpor is mental sluggishness. The Triads.

Catukkesu cīvarādīsu catūsu paccayesu “kattha manāpaṃ labhissāmī”ti taṇhāya uppādo cattāro taṇhuppādā nāma. Na gacchanti etāhi ariyāti agatiyo, chandadosamohabhayā. Tā hi agantabbamaggagamanāni akattabbakaraṇāni cattāri agatigamanāni nāma. Tattha chandoti pakkhapātarāgo. Bhayanti tathāpavatto doso. Aniccādīsu “niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā subha”nti evaṃ pavattā cattāro vipariyāsā viparītato dhamme esanato. Tesu vā āsanato pavisanato cattāro vipariyāsā nāma. Te saññācittadiṭṭhivipariyāsavasena paccekaṃ tayo tayo hutvā dvādasa honti. Tesu anicce niccaṃ, anattani attāti saññācittadiṭṭhivipariyāsā cha, dukkhe sukhaṃ, asubhe subhanti diṭṭhivipariyāsā dve cāti aṭṭha sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti, asubhe subhanti saññācittavipariyāsā dve anāgāmimaggena, dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipariyāsā dve arahattamaggenāti veditabbā.

In the tetrads: In regard to the four requisites—robes, and so on—the arising of craving with the thought, ‘Where will I get a pleasing one?’ is called the four arisings of craving. The noble ones do not go by these, thus they are wrong courses: desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. For these are goings on a course that should not be gone upon and doings of what should not be done; thus they are called the four goings on a wrong course. Herein, desire is lustful partiality. Fear is aversion occurring in that way. The four perversions that occur in regard to the impermanent, etc., as ‘permanent, happiness, self, beautiful,’ arise from seeking things in a contrary way. Or, because one sits on them and enters into them, they are called the four perversions. By way of the perversions of perception, of thought, and of view, they each become three, making twelve in total. Among these, the six perversions of perception, thought, and view that perceive the impermanent as permanent and what is not-self as self, and the two perversions of view that perceive suffering as happiness and the foul as beautiful, are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The two perversions of perception and thought that perceive the foul as beautiful are abandoned by the path of the non-returner. The two perversions of perception and thought that perceive suffering as happiness are to be understood as abandoned by the path of arahantship.

Adiṭṭhe [M 0.0304][V 0.0232] diṭṭhaṃ, asute sutaṃ, amute mutaṃ, aviññāte viññātanti evaṃ pavattā cattāro anariyavohārā nāma. Diṭṭhādīsu pana adiṭṭhaṃ asutaṃ amutaṃ aviññātanti evaṃ pavattā aparepi cattāro anariyavohārā nāma. Ime ca purimehi saddhiṃ aṭṭha anariyavohārātipi vuccanti. Pāṇātipātaadinnādānakāmesumicchācāramusāvādā cattāri duccaritāni nāma. Musāvādādivacīduccaritāni aparānipi cattāri vacīduccaritāni nāma. Jātijarābyādhimaraṇabhayāni cattāri bhayāni nāma. Rājacoraaggiudakabhayāni cattāri, samuddaṃ orohantassa pana uppajjanakāni ūmikumbhīlaāvaṭṭasusukābhayāni ca cattāri, attānuvādaparānuvādadaṇḍaduggatibhayāni cattāri cāti imāni vā aparāni tīṇi catukkāni cattāri bhayāni nāma. Tattha susukāti caṇḍamacchā. Sabbānipi cetāni bhayāni paṭighacittānīti veditabbāni. Sabbaṃ sukhadukkhādikaṃ sayaṃkataṃ paraṃkataṃ ubhayakataṃ adhiccasamuppannanti evaṃ uppajjamānā imā catasso diṭṭhiyo nāma. Catukkaṃ.

‘In the unseen, seen’; ‘in the unheard, heard’; ‘in the unsensed, sensed’; ‘in the uncognized, cognized’—these are called the four ignoble usages. Conversely, in the seen, etc., ‘unseen,’ ‘unheard,’ ‘unsensed,’ ‘uncognized’—these are another four ignoble usages. These, together with the former, are also called the eight ignoble usages. Destruction of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech are called the four kinds of misconduct. The four kinds of verbal misconduct, beginning with false speech, are another four kinds of verbal misconduct. The fears of birth, aging, sickness, and death are called the four fears. The fears of kings, thieves, fire, and water are four; for one descending into the ocean, the fears that arise of waves, crocodiles, whirlpools, and sharks are another four; the fears of self-reproach, others’ reproach, punishment, and a bad destination are another four. These or the other three tetrads are called the four fears. Herein, susukā are fierce fish. All these fears should be understood as states of mind associated with aversion. That all pleasure, pain, and so on, is self-made, other-made, both-made, or arisen fortuitously—these are called the four views. The Tetrads.

Pañcakesu pañcorambhāgiyātiādīsu oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu heṭṭhābhāvato, tattha upapattinipphādanato taṃ oraṃ bhajantīti sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsakāmarāgapaṭighā pañca orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma. Uddhanti rūpārūpadhātu uparibhāvato, taṃ vuttanayena bhajantīti rūparāgaarūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjā pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma. Rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhiyo pañca lagganaṭṭhena saṅgā nāma. Te eva pañca anupavisanaṭṭhena, tudanaṭṭhena ca pañca sallā nāma. Satthudhammasaṅghasikkhāsu kaṅkhanāni cattāri, sabrahmacārīsu kupitacittatā cāti ime pañca cittassa thaddhakacavarakhāṇukabhāvakaraṇattā cetokhilā nāma. Kāmesu avītarāgo. Kāye…pe… rūpe…pe… yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ [M 0.0305] passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ caratīti evaṃ pavattā pañca dhammā cittaṃ bandhitvā muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā viya gahaṇato cetasovinibandhā nāma. Tattha kāyeti ajjhattike kāye, rūpeti bahiddhārūpe. Saññī attā, asaññī attā, nevasaññīnāsaññī attā, saṃvijjamāno pana attā ucchijjati, diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā pāpuṇātīti evaṃ pavattā pañca diṭṭhiyo nāma.

In the pentads, concerning the five lower fetters, etc.: ‘ora’ (lower) refers to the sense-sphere realm because it is below. Because they bring about rebirth there, they partake of that lower realm; these five lower fetters are: identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. ‘Uddha’ (higher) refers to the form and formless realms as being above; in the same way, they partake of that higher realm; these five higher fetters are: lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views are called the five attachments because of their characteristic of clinging. These same five are called the five darts because of their characteristic of penetrating and tormenting. Four doubts—about the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training—along with a mind of anger toward fellow practitioners: these five are called the barrennesses of mind because they make the mind rigid, fallow, and like a stump. Not being free from lust for sensual pleasures; not being free from lust for the body; not being free from lust for forms; having eaten one's fill, one dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of lying on one's side, and the pleasure of torpor; one practices the holy life aspiring to a certain group of deities: these five things bind the mind, grasping it as if in a fist, hence they are called the bonds of the mind. Here, ‘body’ refers to the internal body, and ‘form’ refers to external form. The five views are: the self is percipient; the self is non-percipient; the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient; an existing self is annihilated; or one attains Nibbāna in this very life.

Pāṇātipātādimajjapānapariyosānā pañca verakaraṇaṭṭhena verā nāma. Ñātibhogarogasīladiṭṭhibyasanāni pañca byasanā nāma. Tattha byasanāti vināsasahajātā, tato uppannā akusalā[V 0.0233]. Bahujanassa appiyatā, verabahulatā, vajjabahulatā, sammūḷhamaraṇaṃ, apāyagamananti ime pañca akkhantiyā ādīnavā, anadhivāsanāya dosāti attho. Ājīvakabhayaṃ asilokabhayaṃ parisasārajjabhayaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ duggatibhayanti imāni pañca bhayāni nāma. Yāvadatthaṃ pañcakāmaguṇaparibhogena ceva paṭhamajjhānādīhi catūhi jhānehi cāti pañcahi kāraṇehi attā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto hotīti pavattā vādā pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā nāma. Pañcakaṃ.

The five precepts, beginning with the destruction of life and ending with intoxicating drinks, are called enmities because they are causes of enmity. The five misfortunes are the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, and right view. Here, ‘misfortunes’ are those born together with destruction, unwholesome states arising from that. The five dangers of impatience are: being disliked by many people, abundance of enmity, abundance of faults, a confused death, and going to the lower realms; the meaning is that these are the drawbacks, the faults of not enduring. The five fears are: fear of livelihood, fear of ill-repute, fear of timidity in assemblies, fear of death, and fear of a bad destination. The five theories of Nibbāna in this very life are the views that one attains the highest Nibbāna visible in this life through five causes: indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure, and the four jhānas beginning with the first jhāna. The Pentads.

Chakkesu pana kodho makkho issā sāṭheyyaṃ pāpicchatā sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitāti imāni cha vivādamūlāni. Manāpiyesu rūpādīsu chasu ārammaṇesu chandarāgoti ime cha chandarāgā gehasitā dhammā nāma. Amanāpiyesu chasu ārammaṇesu paṭigho cha virodhavatthūni nāma. Virodho eva vatthu virodhavatthu. Chasu ārammaṇesu taṇhāva cha taṇhākāyā nāma. Satthudhammasaṅghasikkhāsu, appamāde, paṭisanthāre ca agāravā cha agāravā nāma. Kammārāmatā, bhassaniddāsaṅgaṇikasaṃsaggapapañcārāmatā ca cha parihāniyā dhammā nāma, parihānikarāti attho. Tattha savanadassanasamullapanaparibhogakāyasaṃsaggesu [M 0.0306] pañcasu yuttapayuttatā saṃsaggārāmatā. Taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcesu yuttapayuttatā papañcārāmatāti veditabbaṃ. Kammabhassaniddāsaṅgaṇikārāmatā cattāro, dovacassatā, pāpamittatā dve cāti ime aparepi cha parihāniyā dhammā nāma.

In the hexads: anger, contempt, envy, hypocrisy, evil desire, and clinging to one's own views—these six are the roots of dispute. Desire and lust in regard to the six pleasing objects, such as forms, etc.—these six are called states connected with the household. Resentment in regard to the six unpleasing objects—these six are called the grounds of opposition. Opposition itself is the ground, thus it is called the ground of opposition. Craving in regard to the six sense objects—these six are called the six bodies of craving. Disrespect towards the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, heedfulness, and hospitality—these six are called the six kinds of disrespect. Delight in activity, talk, sleep, socializing, association, and mental proliferation—these six are called states of decline, meaning they cause decline. Here, delight in association is being unduly engaged in the five: listening, seeing, conversing, enjoying, and bodily contact. Delight in mental proliferation should be understood as being unduly engaged in craving, conceit, views, and proliferation. Delight in activity, talk, sleep, and socializing—these four, along with being difficult to admonish and having bad friends—these two, are another set of six states of decline.

Somanassaṭṭhāniyesu rūpādīsu chasu ārammaṇesu uppannā gehasitasomanassasampayuttā vicārā somanassupavicārā nāma, vitakkādayo dhammā, taṃsampayuttā cāti gahetabbā. Esa nayo itaradvayepi. Aññāṇasahitā panettha vedanupekkhā upekkhāti veditabbā, yā “aññāṇupekkhā”tipi vuccati. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattesu chasu ārammaṇesu yathākkamaṃ uppannā vedanā “cha gehasitāni somanassānī”tiādinā chakkattayena vuttā. “Atthi me attā”ti vā, “natthi me attā”ti vā, “attanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā, “attanā vā anattānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā, “attanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmī”ti vā, “so me ayaṃ attā kārako vedako nicco dhuvo”ti evaṃ uppajjamānā imā cha diṭṭhiyo nāma. Tattha atthīti sassatadiṭṭhi. Natthīti ucchedadiṭṭhi. Pañcapi khandhe “attā”ti gahetvā saññākkhandhena sesānaṃ jānanavasena attanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmīti diṭṭhi, saññākkhandhaṃ pana “attā”ti, itare ca “anattā”ti gahetvā attanā vā anattānaṃ sañjānāmīti diṭṭhi, saññākkhandhaṃ [V 0.0234] pana “anattā”ti, itare ca “attā”ti gahetvā anattanā vā attānaṃ sañjānāmīti diṭṭhi ca veditabbā. Chakkaṃ.

In the six objects such as forms that are grounds for joy, the sustained thoughts associated with household joy that have arisen are called 'joyous sustained thoughts' (somanassupavicārā). The mental factors like initial thought (vitakka) and others, and those associated with them, are to be understood. This same method applies to the other two. Here, the feeling of equanimity accompanied by ignorance is to be understood as equanimity, which is also called 'equanimity due to ignorance' (aññāṇupekkhā). In the six objects—desirable, undesirable, and neutral—the feelings that arise respectively are spoken of in the three sets of six, beginning with 'six household joys' (cha gehasitāni somanassāni). The six views that arise thus: 'I have a self,' or 'I have no self,' or 'I perceive a self by means of a self,' or 'I perceive a non-self by means of a self,' or 'I perceive a self by means of a self,' or 'This self of mine is the doer, the experiencer, permanent, and stable'—these are called the six views. Therein, 'there is' is the eternalist view. 'There is not' is the annihilationist view. Taking all five aggregates as 'self,' the view 'I perceive a self by means of a self' is due to the perception aggregate knowing the remaining ones. Taking the perception aggregate as 'self' and the others as 'non-self,' the view is 'I perceive a non-self by means of a self.' And taking the perception aggregate as 'non-self' and the others as 'self,' the view 'I perceive a self by means of a non-self' should be understood. The set of six.

Sattakesu pana kāmarāgapaṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchābhavarāgaavijjā satta thāmagataṭṭhena, appahīnaṭṭhena ca cittasantāne anu anu sayanato anusayā nāma. Te eva satte vaṭṭasmiṃ saṃyojanato saṃyojanāni. Samudācāravasena pariyuṭṭhānato pariyuṭṭhānāti veditabbā. Assaddhiyaṃ [M 0.0307] ahirikaṃ anottappaṃ appassutatā kosajjaṃ muṭṭhassaccaṃ duppaññatāti ime satta asataṃ asappurisānaṃ, asantā vā lāmakā dhammāti asaddhammā nāma. Pāṇātipātādayo kāyavacīduccaritāni satta duccaritāni nāma. Māno atimāno mānātimāno omāno adhimāno asmimāno micchāmānoti ime satta mānā nāma. “Manussaloke mātāpettikasambhavo attā ucchijjati, tathā chasu devalokesu dibbo kabaḷīkārabhakkho attā, rūpaloke rūpī manomayo attā, catūsu arūpabhavesu catubbidho arūpī attā tattha tattha ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā”ti evaṃ pavattā satta ucchedadiṭṭhiyo satta diṭṭhiyo nāma. Ettha ca ādito tisso diṭṭhiyo rūpakkhandhaṃ attato gahetvā pavattā ucchedadiṭṭhiyo, sesā catasso arūpakkhandheti ñātabbā. Sattakaṃ.

In the sevenfold group, sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, craving for existence, and ignorance are called latent tendencies because they lie dormant again and again in the mental continuum due to their strength and their not being abandoned. These same seven are called fetters because they bind to the round of rebirth, and they are to be understood as obsessions because they obsess the mind by way of manifestation. Lack of faith, shamelessness, lack of fear of wrongdoing, little learning, laziness, forgetfulness, and poor wisdom—these seven are called bad qualities because they belong to the wicked, to unworthy persons, or because they are inferior, unwholesome states. The seven misdeeds of body and speech, beginning with killing living beings, are called the seven wrong conducts. Conceit, excessive conceit, conceit beyond conceit, inferiority conceit, arrogance, the conceit 'I am,' and wrong conceit—these seven are called the conceits. 'In the human world, the self that arises from mother and father is annihilated; similarly, in the six heavenly realms, the divine self that consumes solid food; in the realm of form, the self that has form and is mind-made; in the four formless realms, the fourfold formless self—in each case, it is annihilated, perishes, and does not exist after death.' Thus occurring, these seven annihilationist views are called the seven views. Herein, the first three views are annihilationist views that proceed by taking the form aggregate as self; the remaining four are to be known as pertaining to the formless aggregates. The sevenfold.

Aṭṭhakesu pana lobho doso moho māno diṭṭhi vicikicchā thinaṃ uddhaccañcāti aṭṭha kilesavatthūni nāma. “Yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ kattabbaṃ me”ti ekaṃ, tathā “kataṃ me”ti, “maggo me gantabbo”ti, “gato”ti, “appakaṃ me bhutta”nti, “subhutta”nti, “ābādho me uppanno”ti, “aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā”ti ekanti imāni aṭṭha kusītavatthūni nāma, kusītassa kosajjakāraṇānīti attho. Lābhe alābhe ca yase ayase ca pasaṃsāya nindāya ca sukhe dukkhe ca yathākkamaṃ rāgadosehi cittassa paṭihananaṃ aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu cittassa paṭighāto nāma. Heṭṭhā dvīhi catukkehi vuttā aṭṭha anariyavohārā nāma. Micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappādayo aṭṭha micchattā nāma. Bhikkhūhi vijjamānāya āpattiyā codiyamānassa “na sarāmī”ti nibbeṭhanaṃ ekaṃ, “tvaṃ bālo”tiādinā [M 0.0308] codakapaṭippharaṇaṃ ekaṃ, tathā “tuvaṃ cetamāpanno”ti codakassa paccāropanaṃ, aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ, saṅghe bāhāvikkhepabhaṇanaṃ, tuṇhībhāvena viheṭhanaṃ, saṅghaṃ, codakañca anādiyitvā pakkamanaṃ, codanābhayā sikkhāpaccakkhānanti ime aṭṭha purisadosā nāma. Asaññī attā rūpī, arūpī[V 0.0235], rūpī ca arūpī ca, nevarūpīnārūpī, antavā, anantavā, antavā ca anantavā ca, nevantavānānantavāti evaṃ pavattā aṭṭha asaññīvādā nāma. Nevasaññīnāsaññī attā rūpī arūpītiādinā pavattā aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā nāma. Aṭṭhakaṃ.

In the eightfold group, greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, and restlessness—these are called the eight bases of defilement. 'Whatever work is to be done by me' is one; likewise 'it has been done by me,' 'the path is to be trodden by me,' 'it has been trodden,' 'little has been eaten by me,' 'well eaten,' 'sickness has arisen in me,' 'recently recovered from illness'—these are called the eight bases of laziness, meaning the causes of idleness for a lazy person. In gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain—the striking of the mind by lust and hatred respectively regarding these eight worldly conditions is called the mind's aversion to the eight worldly conditions. The eight ignoble modes of expression spoken of below in two sets of four are so called. Wrong view, wrong intention, and so on—these eight are called wrongnesses. When a monk, being accused of an existing offense, evades by saying, 'I do not remember,' that is one; retorting to the accuser with 'You are a fool,' etc., is another; likewise, turning the accusation back on the accuser, saying, 'You yourself have committed this offense'; evading by changing the subject; speaking while gesticulating with one's arms in the Saṅgha; harassing by means of silence; departing without regard for the Saṅgha and the accuser; renouncing the training out of fear of accusation—these are called the eight faults of a person. 'The self is unconscious and has form,' 'is formless,' 'is both with form and formless,' 'is neither with form nor formless'; 'is finite,' 'is infinite,' 'is both finite and infinite,' 'is neither finite nor infinite'—thus occurring are the eight doctrines of an unconscious self. 'The self is neither percipient nor non-percipient and has form,' 'is formless,' etc.—thus occurring are the eight doctrines of a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self. The eightfold.

Navakesu pana “anatthaṃ me acari, carati, carissati, piyassa me anatthaṃ acari, carati, carissati, appiyassa me atthaṃ acari, carati, carissatī”ti evaṃ pavattā nava āghātā eva āghātavatthūni nāma. Kodho makkho issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyaṃ musāvādo pāpicchatā micchādiṭṭhīti imāni nava purisamalāni nāma. “Seyyassa seyyohamasmī”tiādayo navavidhā mānā nāma. “Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, taṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, taṃ paṭicca chandarāgo, taṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, tathā pariggaho, macchariyaṃ, ārakkho, ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādādianeke pāpakā dhammā”ti evaṃ vuttā ime nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā nāma. Tattha vinicchayoti ñāṇataṇhādiṭṭhivitakkavasena catūsu vinicchayesu vitakkavinicchayo idha adhippeto. Lābhaṃ hi labhitvā “idaṃ rūpārammaṇatthāya, idaṃ saddārammaṇādiatthāyā”ti evaṃ vitakkeneva vinicchayo. Chandarāgo dubbalarāgo, ajjhosānanti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ. Pariggahoti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena pariggahakaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. “Asmī”ti, “ahamasmī”ti, “ayamahamasmī”ti, “bhavissa”nti, “rūpī bhavissa”nti, “arūpī bhavissa”nti, “saññī bhavissa”nti, “asaññī [M 0.0309] bhavissa”nti, “nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa”nti evaṃ vuttāni imāni nava calanaṭṭhena iñjitāni nāma. Imāneva maññanaṭṭhena maññitāni, vipphandanato vipphanditāni, papañcanato papañcitāni, tāneva tehi tehi kāraṇehi saṅkhatattā saṅkhatāni ca nāma honti. Sabbehi tehi pañcahi navakehi māno eva kathito. Sopi hi “asmī”tiādīhi saññīhi ca ākārehi diṭṭhi viya pavattatīti. Navakaṃ.

Further, in the nines: 'Harm was done to me, is being done, will be done; harm was done to one dear to me, is being done, will be done; a benefit was done to one not dear to me, is being done, will be done'—thus occurring, these nine resentments themselves are called the grounds for resentment. Anger, contempt, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, false speech, evil wishes, and wrong view—these are called the nine stains of a person. 'I am better than the better,' and so on—these are called the nine kinds of conceit. 'Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is acquisition; dependent on that, there is decision; dependent on that, there is desire and lust; dependent on that, there is attachment; likewise possessiveness, avarice, guarding; and on account of guarding, there arise the taking up of rods and weapons, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, and many other evil, unwholesome states'—these, so stated, are called the nine things rooted in craving. Herein, 'decision,' among the four kinds of decision—by way of knowledge, craving, view, and thought—refers to the decision by thought intended here. For having acquired a gain, the decision is made just by thought thus: 'This is for the sake of a form-object, this is for the sake of a sound-object,' and so on. 'Desire and lust' is weak lust; 'attachment' is strong resolve. 'Possessiveness' should be understood as the act of taking possession by way of craving and view. 'I am,' 'I am this,' 'This I am,' 'I will be,' 'I will be with form,' 'I will be formless,' 'I will be percipient,' 'I will be non-percipient,' 'I will be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient'—these, so stated, are called the nine 'tremblings' because of their nature of agitation. These same things are called 'conceivings' because of conceiving, 'quiverings' because of quivering, 'proliferations' because of proliferating; and those same things are also called 'conditioned things' because they are conditioned by these and those causes. By all those five nines, it is conceit alone that is spoken of. For that too proceeds like a view through such perceptions and modes as 'I am,' and so on. The ninefold.

Dasakesu pana lobho doso moho māno diṭṭhi vicikicchā thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime dasa kilesā eva kilesavatthūni nāma. “Anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādayo nava khāṇukaṇṭakādīsu aṭṭhānaāghātena saddhiṃ dasa āghātavatthūni nāma. Pāṇātipātādayo dasa akusalakammapathā nāma. Kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsabhavarāgaissāmacchariyaavijjāsaṃyojananti imāni dasa saṃyojanāni nāma. Micchādiṭṭhimicchāsaṅkappādayo [V 0.0236] aṭṭha, micchāñāṇamicchāvimuttīhi saddhiṃ dasa micchattā nāma. Tattha micchāñāṇanti pāpakiriyāsu upāyacintāvasena ceva pāpakaṃ katvā “sukataṃ mayā”ti paccavekkhaṇavasena ca pavatto moho. Micchāvimuttīti avimuttasseva sato vimuttasaññitā. “Natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭha”ntiādīhi dasahi ākārehi pavattaṃ natthikadassanaṃ dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi nāma. “Sassato loko, tathā asassato, antavā, anantavā, taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti vā, “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti vā, “hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā, “na hoti…pe… hoti ca na hoti ca, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā”ti vā evaṃ pavattā dasavatthukā antaggāhikā diṭṭhi nāma. Tattha lokoti khandhādayo, “antavā”ti idaṃ parittaṃ kasiṇajjhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Anantavā”ti idaṃ vipulanti gahetabbaṃ. Tathāgatoti satto. Dasakaṃ.

Further, in the tens: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of moral dread—these ten defilements themselves are called the grounds of defilement. The nine grounds for resentment beginning with “He did me harm,” together with groundless resentment in such cases as over stumps and thorns, are called the ten grounds for resentment. The ten unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life are so called. The ten fetters are: the fetter of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, view, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, craving for existence, envy, avarice, and the fetter of ignorance. The eight wrongnesses beginning with wrong view and wrong intention, together with wrong knowledge and wrong liberation, are called the ten wrongnesses. Here, wrong knowledge is the delusion that arises by way of contemplating the means for evil actions and by way of reflecting after having done an evil deed, “I have done well.” Wrong liberation is the perception of being liberated on the part of one who is not liberated. The nihilistic view that proceeds in ten modes, beginning with “There is nothing given, there is no offering,” is called the ten-factored wrong view. A view that proceeds in ten ways, such as “The world is eternal,” “The world is not eternal,” “The world is finite,” “The world is infinite,” “The soul and the body are the same,” “The soul and the body are different,” “A Tathāgata exists after death,” “A Tathāgata does not exist after death,” “…exists and does not exist…,” or “A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death”—this is called the ten-factored view that grasps at extremes. Here, ‘world’ means the aggregates, and so on. ‘Finite’ is said with reference to a limited kasiṇa meditation. ‘Infinite’ should be taken as extensive. ‘Tathāgata’ means a being. The Tens.

Aṭṭhārasakesu [M 0.0310] taṇhāvicaritānīti taṇhāsamudācārā taṇhāpavattiyo. Ajjhattikassupādāyāti ajjhattikaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Idaṃ hi upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tattha “asmīti hoti, itthasmīti hoti, evasmīti hoti, aññathāsmīti hoti, tathā bhavissanti, itthaṃ bhavissanti, evaṃ bhavissanti, aññathā bhavissanti hoti, tathā asmīti, sātasmīti hoti, tathā siyanti, itthaṃ siyanti, evaṃ siyanti, aññathā siyanti hoti, tathā apāhaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ itthaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ evaṃ siyanti, apāhaṃ aññatā siyanti hotī”ti evaṃ vuttāni imāni ajjhattikassupādāya aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni nāma.

In the eighteens: ‘wanderings of craving’ means the behavior of craving, the occurrences of craving. ‘With reference to the internal’ means with reference to the internal five aggregates. For this is a genitive in the sense of relation. Therein, the following, so stated, are called the eighteen wanderings of craving with reference to the internal: there is ‘I am,’ there is ‘I am of this sort,’ there is ‘I am thus,’ there is ‘I am otherwise,’ there is ‘I am existent,’ there is ‘I am non-existent’; there is ‘I will be,’ there is ‘I will be of this sort,’ there is ‘I will be thus,’ there is ‘I will be otherwise,’ there is ‘I will be existent,’ there is ‘I will be non-existent’; there is ‘may I be,’ there is ‘may I be of this sort,’ there is ‘may I be thus,’ there is ‘may I be otherwise,’ there is ‘may I be existent,’ there is ‘may I be non-existent.’”

Tattha asmīti hotīti ajjhattikesu khandhapañcakesu samūhato “ahamasmī”ti gahaṇe satīti attho. Evaṃ pana gahaṇe sati tato paraṃ anupanidhāya, upanidhāya vāti dvidhā gahaṇaṃ hoti. Tattha anupanidhāyāti aññaṃ ākāraṃ anupanidhāya anupagamma sakabhāvamevārammaṇaṃ katvā itthasmīti hoti. Tassa “khattiyādīsu idaṃpakāro aha”nti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena gahaṇaṃ hotīti attho. Upanidhāya gahaṇaṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti samato ca asamato ca. Tattha samato gahaṇaṃ evasmīti idaṃ, tassa yathā ayaṃ khattiyo, brāhmaṇādayo vā devamanussarūpīarūpiādayo vā, evamahamasmīti attho. Aññathāsmīti idaṃ pana asamato gahaṇaṃ, tassa yathā ime khattiyādayo, tato aññathā ahaṃ hīno vā adhiko vāti attho. Imāni tāva paccuppannavasena cattāri taṇhāvicaritāni, bhavissantiādīni pana cattāri anāgatavasena [V 0.0237] vuttāni. Tesaṃ purimacatukke vuttanayavasena attho veditabbo. Tattha asmītiādidvayaṃ sassatucchedaggāhavasena vuttaṃ. Tattha hi asmīti sassataṃ, sīdatīti sātaṃ, asassataṃ, ito parāni [M 0.0311] siyantiādīni cattāri saṃsayaparivitakkavasena vuttāni. Apāhaṃ siyantiādīni cattāri “api nāmāhaṃ bhaveyya”nti evaṃ pavattapatthanākappanavasena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhārasakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

Here, ‘the thought “I am” occurs’ means when there is the grasping ‘I am’ with regard to the internal five aggregates taken as a whole. When such grasping occurs, it proceeds in two ways: without comparing and by comparing. Here, ‘without comparing’ means without comparing or approaching another mode, but taking one’s own state as the object, the thought ‘I am of this sort’ occurs. This means the grasping occurs by way of craving, conceit, and view, as in: ‘Among khattiyas and others, I am of this type.’ But grasping by comparing is twofold: as equal and as unequal. Grasping as equal is this: ‘I am thus.’ This means: ‘Just as this khattiya, brahmin, or other, or this deva, human, being with form, or being without form is, so too am I.’ But ‘I am otherwise’ is grasping as unequal. This means: ‘I am otherwise than these khattiyas and others, that is, I am inferior or superior.’ These first four are wanderings of craving by way of the present. The next four beginning with ‘I will be’ are stated by way of the future. Their meaning should be understood in the way stated for the first tetrad. Therein, the first two, beginning with 'I am,' are stated by way of grasping at eternalism and annihilationism. For here ‘I am’ is eternalism; and what perishes is annihilationism. The next four beginning with ‘may I be’ are stated by way of doubt and speculation. The four beginning with ‘may I indeed be’ should be seen as stated by way of longing and imagining that proceed as ‘Oh, that I might be!’ The first eighteen.

Dutiye bāhirassupādāyāti bāhiraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya. Tattha “iminā asmīti hoti, iminā itthasmīti hoti, iminā evasmīti hoti, iminā aññathāsmīti hotī”tiādinā anantare vuttanayena bāhirassupādāya aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritānīti veditabbāni. “Iminā”ti padamattameva hettha purimehi viseso. Tattha imināti iminā bāhirena rūpena vā…pe… viññāṇena vāti attho. Tattha ca chattakhaggabījaniannapānadhanadhaññādiupakaraṇavasena bāhiraṃ rūpaṃ veditabbaṃ. Dāsadāsiñātiparijanahatthiassādiupakaraṇavasena vedanādayo veditabbā. Imehi bāhirehi rūpādīhi “itthasmīti evasmī”tiādinā sabbattha yojanā veditabbā. Aṭṭhārasakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

In the second case, ‘with reference to the external’ means with reference to the external five aggregates. Here, the eighteen wanderings of craving with reference to the external should be understood according to the method stated immediately before, beginning: ‘By this, the thought “I am” occurs; by this, the thought “I am of this sort” occurs; by this, the thought “I am thus” occurs; by this, the thought “I am otherwise” occurs,’ and so on. Here, only the word ‘by this’ is the difference from the previous case. ‘By this’ means by this external form, or… by this external consciousness. Here, external form should be understood by way of equipment such as an umbrella, a sword, seeds, food and drink, wealth, grain, and so on. Feeling and the rest should be understood by way of equipment such as male and female slaves, relatives, retinue, elephants, horses, and so on. The connection with these external forms and so on should be understood everywhere as ‘I am of this sort,’ ‘I am thus,’ and so on. The second eighteen.

Itaresu pana tadekajjhaṃ abhisaṃyūhitvātiādīsu tadubhayaṃ aṭṭhārasakaṃ ekato yojetvā chattiṃsataṇhāvicaritāni honti, evaṃ ekekassa puggalassa atītakāle dvinnaṃ aṭṭhārasakānaṃ vasena chattiṃsa, tathā anāgate chattiṃsa honti. Paccuppanne pana ekassa yathālābhavasena tānipi labbhanti, sabbasattānaṃ vasena paccuppannepi chattiṃsa labbhanti. Iti evaṃ vuttena pakārena taṃ sabbaṃ ekato katvā sabbasattānaṃ kālattayepi channaṃ aṭṭhārasakānaṃ vasena aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhāvicaritāni hontīti attho. Aṭṭhataṇhāvicaritasataṃ hotīti etthāpi evameva attho daṭṭhabbo.

But in other texts, in such phrases as ‘having heaped them together into one,’ by combining both sets of eighteen together, there are thirty-six wanderings of craving. Thus for each single person, there were thirty-six in the past by way of the two sets of eighteen, and similarly there will be thirty-six in the future. In the present, however, for a single person, these too are obtained according to what is acquired. By way of all beings, thirty-six are obtained even in the present. Thus, in the way so stated, having put all that together, for all beings in the three times, there are one hundred and eight wanderings of craving by way of six sets of eighteen. This is the meaning. Here too, in the statement ‘there are one hundred and eight wanderings of craving,’ the meaning should be seen in the very same way.

Taṇhāvicaritāni niṭṭhitāni.

The Wanderings of Craving are concluded.

Yāni cātiādīsu yāni cettha dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni vattabbāni, tāni brahmajālanāmake dīghanikāyassa paṭhamasuttante [M 0.0312] (dī. ni. 1.29 ādayo) satthārā sayaṃ āhacca bhāsitānīti attho. Brahmajāle hi cattāro sassatavādā, cattāro ekaccasassatikā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā, dve adhiccasamuppannikā, soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā[V 0.0238], aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, satta ucchedavādā, pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti imāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni sanidānāni nānānayato vuttāni, tattha vuttanayeneva nesaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāvettha padatthānusārato vinicchayo, sesopettha vinicchayo padatthe vuttānusāratova suviññeyyoti.

In the passage beginning 'And which...,' the meaning is that the sixty-two speculative views to be spoken of here are those that were spoken by the Teacher himself after having addressed them, in the first sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya, named the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN 1.29ff). For in the Brahmajāla Sutta, there are four eternalist views, four semi-eternalist views, four views on the finite and the infinite, four evasive prevarications, two views of fortuitous origination, sixteen perceptionist views, eight non-perceptionist views, eight neither-perceptionist-nor-non-perceptionist views, seven annihilationist views, and five views of Nibbāna in this very life—these sixty-two speculative views are stated with their sources and in various ways. Their classification should be understood in the way stated there. This, for now, is the determination in accordance with the meaning of the words. The remaining determination here should also be easily understood in accordance with the meaning of the words as stated.

Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mātikā of the Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga is finished.

Dhammahadayavibhaṅgamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Mātikā of the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga

Dhammahadayavibhaṅgamātikāya pana padatthādito vinicchayo pubbe vuttova. Yasmā pana bhagavatā heṭṭhā nānānayato vibhattānaññeva khandhāyatanādīnaṃ dvādasannaṃ dhammakoṭṭhāsānaṃ puna sabbasaṅgāhikacatubhūmuppattitappariyāpannatādīhi dasahi vārehi apubbanayasahassavibhāvakehi sabbadhammādhippāyasaṅkhātehi dhammahadayehi vibhāgadassanatthamevāyaṃ vibhaṅgo vutto, tasmā vibhaṅganayato cettha vinicchayo hoti. Vibhaṅge hi paṭhamaṃ “kati khandhā”tiādinā sapucchakaṃ dvādasapadikaṃ mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā heṭṭhā vuttānusāreneva catubhūmakasāmaññato sabbasaṅgāhikavāro nāma vibhatto, tattha satta phassādayo sattannaṃ viññāṇadhātūnaṃ vasena veditabbā.

Now, for the Mātikā of the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga, the determination beginning with the meaning of the words has already been stated. However, since this analysis was spoken by the Blessed One for the very purpose of showing the classification of the twelve portions of the Dhamma—the aggregates, bases, etc.—which he had previously analyzed in various ways, by means of the 'hearts of the Dhamma,' which are reckoned as the intention of all dhammas and which illuminate a thousand unprecedented methods, through ten sections beginning with the all-inclusive, arising in the four planes, and inclusion therein; therefore, the determination here is by way of the method of analysis. For in the Analysis, having first laid down the twelve-term mātikā with questions, beginning 'How many aggregates?,' the section called 'The All-Inclusive' is analyzed in accordance with what was stated previously, from the standpoint of what is common to the four planes. Therein, the seven factors beginning with contact should be understood by way of the seven consciousness elements.

Dutiyo [M 0.0313] pana vāro tesaṃ catūsu bhūmīsu catūhi koṭṭhāsehi uppattānuppattidassanavasena pavatto. Tattha paṭhamakoṭṭhāse tāva –

The second section, however, proceeds by way of showing the arising and non-arising in those four planes through four divisions. Therein, in the first division:

“Kāmadhātuyā kati khandhā…pe… kati cittāni? Kāmadhātuyā pañcakkhandhā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, tīṇi saccāni, bāvīsatindriyāni, nava hetū, cattāro āhārā, satta phassā, vedanā, saññā, cetanā, cittānī”ti –

"In the desire realm, how many aggregates ... pe ... how many kinds of consciousness? In the desire realm, there are five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, three truths, twenty-two faculties, nine roots, four nutriments, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven perceptions, seven volitions, and seven kinds of consciousness."

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Tattha yasmā catubhūmakāpi dhammā yebhuyyena kāmāvacarasattānaṃ uppajjanti[V 0.0239], na kāmāvacarāva. Tenettha “pañcakkhandhā”tiādinā catubhūmakāpi vuttā. Tatthuppajjanakadhammā hettha adhippetā, na taṃbhūmipariyāpannāva. Rūpadhātuādīsupi eseva nayo.

Having laid down the mātikā, it is analyzed. Herein, since dhammas of the four planes for the most part arise for beings of the desire sphere—not only desire-sphere dhammas—for that reason 'five aggregates,' etc., are stated here as including those of the four planes. Here, dhammas that arise in that sphere are intended, not only those included in that plane. This same method applies to the form realm and so on.

Ettha ca tīṇi saccānīti idaṃ nirodhasaccassa desavinimuttatāya katthaci dese aniddisitabbato taṃ vajjetvā vuttaṃ. Kāraṇasāpekkhā hi dhammā attano nissayakāraṇabhūtaṃ desaṃ samāvasanti akāraṇassa anissayattā, yathā vā kadāci upalabbhamānā dhammā kālaniyatatāya attano saṅkhatattaṃva sūcenti. Aññathā itarakālesupi bhāvassa ca pasaṅgato, etarahipi vā abhāvassa, evaṃ kvaci dese upalabbhamānāpīti gahetabbaṃ. Sabbadesaabyāpitā pana asaṅkhatassa, saṅkhatassa vā asambhavato eva nopapajjati, tasmā desakālavinimuttameva asaṅkhatanti gahetabbaṃ.

Herein, 'three truths' is stated by excluding the truth of cessation because, being free from location, it is not to be specified in any particular place. For phenomena dependent on causes abide in the location that is their supporting cause, since what is causeless is unsupported. Just as phenomena that are found only at certain times thereby indicate their conditioned nature—for otherwise, it would follow that they exist at other times too, or that they do not exist even now—so too it should be understood of phenomena that are found only in certain places. However, being non-pervasive of all locations is not tenable for the unconditioned, and is impossible for the conditioned. Therefore, the unconditioned should be understood as being free from location and time.

Dutiyakoṭṭhāse pana –

In the second division, however:

“Rūpadhātuyā pañcakkhandhā, cha āyatanāni, nava dhātuyo, tīṇi saccāni, cuddasindriyāni, aṭṭha hetū, tayo [M 0.0314] āhārā, cattāro phassā…pe… cattāri cittānī”ti –

"In the form realm, there are five aggregates, six bases, nine elements, three truths, fourteen faculties, eight roots, three nutriments, four contacts ... pe ... four kinds of consciousness."

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Yasmā pana rūpīnaṃ ghānādīnaṃ abhāvena vijjamānānipi gandhāyatanādīni āyatanādikiccaṃ na karonti, tasmā te vajjetvā “cha āyatanāni, nava dhātuyo”tiādi vuttaṃ na tesaṃ abhāvā. Keci pana “rūpaloke gandharasā kabaḷīkāro āhāro ca mahābhūtānañca phoṭṭhabbakiccatā natthi, teneva pāḷiyaṃ na uddhaṭā”ti vatvā taṃ sādhetuṃ bahuṃ hetupaṭirūpakaṃ vatvā papañcenti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattamevāti na gahetabbaṃ. Gandhādīnaṃ avinibbhogattā, phoṭṭhabbattā, dhātusabhāvattā ca ghānādittayabhāvadvayasukhadukkhadomanassindriyāni, pana domanassahetukabaḷīkārāhāraghānādittayasamphassādīni ca vajjetvā cuddasindriyādibhāvo veditabbo.

Having laid down the mātikā, it is analyzed. Since, due to the absence of the physical sense faculties beginning with the nose in form-realm beings, the existing odor base, etc., do not perform the function of a base, they are excluded. Therefore it is said 'six bases, nine elements,' etc., not because of their absence. Some, however, saying, 'In the form world, odors, tastes, physical nutriment, and the function of the tangible for the great elements do not exist; for that reason they are not mentioned in the Pāli,' then elaborate, adducing much specious reasoning to establish this. That is merely their own opinion and should not be accepted. Because of the inseparability of odors, etc., their tangibility, and their nature as elements, the state of there being fourteen faculties, etc., should be understood by excluding the three faculties beginning with the nose, the two sex faculties, the faculties of pleasure, pain, and displeasure, and also physical nutriment which is a condition for displeasure, the contacts of the three senses beginning with the nose, and so on.

Tatiyakoṭṭhāse pana –

In the third division, however:

“Arūpadhātuyā [V 0.0240] cattāro khandhā, dve āyatanāni, dve dhātuyo, tīṇi saccāni, ekādasindriyāni, aṭṭha hetū, tayo āhārā, eko phasso…pe… ekaṃ citta”nti –

"In the formless realm, there are four aggregates, two bases, two elements, three truths, eleven faculties, eight roots, three nutriments, one contact ... pe ... one kind of consciousness."

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Ettha ca cakkhusotaanaññātaññassāmītindriyānampi abhāvā ekādasindriyāni veditabbāni.

Having laid down the mātikā, it is analyzed. And here, eleven faculties are to be understood due to the absence of the eye and ear faculties and also the faculty of 'I shall know the unknown'.

Catutthakoṭṭhāse pana –

In the fourth division, however:

“Apariyāpanne cattāro khandhā, dve āyatanāni, dve dhātuyo, dve saccāni, dvādasindriyāni, cha hetū, tayo āhārā, eko phasso…pe… ekaṃ citta”nti –

"In the supramundane, there are four aggregates, two bases, two elements, two truths, twelve faculties, six roots, three nutriments, one contact ... pe ... one kind of consciousness."

Mātikaṃ [M 0.0315] nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Yasmā ca okāsavasena vā sattuppattivasena vā apariyāpannadhātu nāma natthi, tasmā “apariyāpannadhātuyā”ti avatvā nibbattitalokuttarameva dassetuṃ “apariyāpanne cattāro khandhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ catūhi koṭṭhāsehi dutiyo vāro veditabbo.

Having laid down the mātikā, it is analyzed. And since there is no 'supramundane realm' either in the sense of location or in the sense of the arising of beings, therefore, instead of saying 'in the supramundane realm,' it is said, 'in the supramundane, four aggregates,' etc., in order to show only the arisen supramundane. Thus the second section is to be understood by way of the four divisions.

Tatiyo pana vāro –

The third section, however:

“Rūpakkhandho kāmadhātupariyāpanno, cattāro khandhā siyā kāmadhātupariyāpannā, siyā na kāmadhātupariyāpannā”tiādinā –

"'The form aggregate is included in the desire realm; the four aggregates may be included in the desire realm or may not be included in the desire realm,' and so on.

Catūsu bhūmīsu catūhi koṭṭhāsehi taṃtaṃbhūmipariyāpannadhammadassanavasena pavatto, so ca heṭṭhā vuttānusārena sakkā ñātunti na vitthārito. Tattha ca kāmadhātupariyāpannoti kāmāvacarabhāvena tattha antogadho kāmāvacaroti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

It proceeds by way of showing the dhammas included in the respective planes in the four planes through four divisions. And since that can be known in accordance with what was stated previously, it is not elaborated. Herein, 'included in the desire realm' means it is of the desire sphere, being comprised therein because it is of the desire sphere. This same method applies to the remaining cases.

Catuttho pana vāro tīsu bhūmīsu catūhi koṭṭhāsehi paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjanakānuppajjanakadhammadassanavasena pavatto. Tattha paṭhamakoṭṭhāse tāva –

The fourth section, however, proceeds by way of showing the dhammas that arise and do not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking in the three planes, through four divisions. Therein, in the first division:

“Kāmadhātuyā [V 0.0241] upapattikkhaṇe sabbesaṃ pañcakkhandhā pātubhavanti, kassaci ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavanti, kassaci dasāyatanāni pātubhavanti, kassaci aparāni dasa, kassaci nava, kassaci satta, kassaci ekādasa dhātuyo…pe… satta dhātuyo. Sabbesaṃ ekaṃ saccaṃ pātubhavati. Kassaci cuddasindriyāni, kassaci terasa, kassaci aparāni terasa, kassaci dvādasa, kassaci dasa, kassaci nava, kassaci aparāni nava, kassaci aṭṭha, kassaci aparāni aṭṭha, kassaci satta[M 0.0316], kassaci pañca, kassaci cattārindriyāni pātubhavanti, kassaci tayo hetū pātubhavanti, kassaci dve, kassaci ahetukā pātubhavanti. Sabbesaṃ cattāro āhārā, eko phasso…pe… ekaṃ cittaṃ pātubhavatī”ti –

"At the moment of rebirth in the desire realm, for all beings the five aggregates appear. For some, eleven bases appear; for some, ten bases appear; for some, another ten; for some, nine; for some, seven. For some, eleven elements ... pe ... seven elements appear. For all, one truth appears. For some, fourteen faculties appear; for some, thirteen; for some, another thirteen; for some, twelve; for some, ten; for some, nine; for some, another nine; for some, eight; for some, another eight; for some, seven; for some, five; for some, four faculties appear. For some, three roots appear; for some, two; for some, the rootless appear. For all, four nutriments, one contact ... pe ... one kind of consciousness appears."

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Tattha paṭisandhikkhaṇe kāmāvacarānaṃ opapātikānaṃ, āpāyikānaṃ, devamanussānaṃ paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ saddāyatanavajjitāni ekādasāyatanāni pātubhavanti, tāneva ekādasa dhātuyo honti. Saddo hi ekantena paṭisandhiyaṃ na uppajjati, tesaññeva pana jaccandhānaṃ dasa, jaccabadhirānaṃ aparāni dasa, jaccandhabadhirānaṃ nava, gabbhaseyyakānaṃ rūpagandharasakāyaphoṭṭhabbamanodhammavasena satta āyatanadhātuyo pātubhavanti. Opapātikānaṃ tihetukānaṃ manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni, bhāvadvaye ekaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ, somanassupekkhindriyesu ekaṃ, saddhādīni pañcāti cuddasindriyāni, tesaṃ dvihetukānaṃ paññindriyaṃ vajjetvā terasa, paṭhamakappikānaṃ manussānaṃ tihetukānaṃ bhāvindriyaṃ vajjetvā aparānipi terasa, tesaññeva duhetukānaṃ dvādasa, gabbhaseyyakānaṃ pana tihetukānaṃ purimesu cuddasasu cakkhādīni cattāri vajjetvā dasa, tesaṃ duhetukānaṃ nava, opapātikānaṃ ahetukānaṃ paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ purimesu cuddasasu saddādīni vajjetvā aparāni nava, tesaññeva jaccandhānaṃ aṭṭha, tathā badhirānaṃ, andhabadhirānaṃ pana satta, gabbhaseyyakānaṃ pana ahetukānaṃ kāyamanobhāvajīvitaupekkhindriyāni pañca, tesaññeva napuṃsakānaṃ cattāri pātubhavanti. Ahetukacittesu hi vijjamānāpi ekaggatā samādhindriyataṃ na gacchati, manoviññāṇadhātuvasena pana “eko phasso”tiādayo veditabbā.

Having laid down the matrix, it is analyzed. At the moment of rebirth-linking, for spontaneously born beings in the sense-sphere—whether in the woeful planes, or among devas and humans with complete sense bases—eleven sense bases arise, excluding the sound base. These same eleven become the elements. Sound does not arise at all during rebirth-linking. For those born blind, ten arise; for those born deaf, another ten; for those born blind and deaf, nine. For womb-born beings, seven sense bases and elements arise: form, odor, taste, body, tangibles, mind, and phenomena. For spontaneously born beings with three roots, fourteen faculties arise: the six faculties ending with the mind faculty, one of either sex, the life faculty, one of the faculties of joy or equanimity, and the five beginning with faith. For those with two roots, thirteen arise, excluding the faculty of wisdom. For humans in the first aeon with three roots, another thirteen arise, excluding the sex faculty. For those with two roots, twelve arise. For womb-born beings with three roots, ten arise, excluding the four beginning with the eye faculty from the aforementioned fourteen. For those with two roots, nine arise. For spontaneously born rootless beings with complete sense bases, another nine arise from the aforementioned fourteen, excluding those beginning with faith. For those born blind among them, eight arise; similarly for those born deaf. For those born blind and deaf, seven arise. For rootless womb-born beings, five faculties arise: body, mind, sex, life, and equanimity. For neuter beings among them, four arise. Though one-pointedness exists in rootless consciousnesses, it does not attain the status of the faculty of concentration. However, by way of the mind-consciousness element, 'one contact,' and so on, should be understood.

Dutiyakoṭṭhāse [M 0.0317] pana –

In the second section, however—

“Rūpadhātuyā [V 0.0242] upapattikkhaṇe ṭhapetvā asaññasattānaṃ devānaṃ pañcakkhandhā pātubhavanti. Pañcāyatanāni, pañca dhātuyo, ekaṃ saccaṃ, dasindriyāni, tayo hetū, tayo āhārā, eko phasso…pe… ekaṃ citta”nti –

"At the moment of arising in the form realm, for the devas except for the non-percipient beings, the five aggregates arise. Five sense bases, five elements, one truth, ten faculties, three roots, three nutriments, one contact...pe...one consciousness."

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā vibhattā. Tattha cakkhurūpasotamanodhammānaṃ vasena pañcāyatanadhātuyo veditabbā. Etthāpi gandharasaphoṭṭhabbānaṃ aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ pubbe vuttameva. Cakkhusotamanojīvitindriyāni, somanassupekkhānaṃ aññataraṃ, saddhādīni pañcāti dasindriyāni veditabbāni.

Having laid down the matrix, it is analyzed. Herein, the five sense bases and elements should be understood by way of eye, form, ear, mind, and phenomena. Here too, the reason for not including odor, taste, and tangibles is as stated before. The ten faculties should be understood as: the eye faculty, ear faculty, mind faculty, life faculty; one of either joy or equanimity; and the five beginning with faith.

Tatiyakoṭṭhāse pana –

In the third section, however—

“Asaññasattānaṃ devānaṃ upapattikkhaṇe eko khandho pātubhavati rūpakkhandho, dve āyatanāni rūpāyatanaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ, dve dhātuyo rūpadhātu dhammadhātu, ekaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, ekaṃ rūpajīvitindriyaṃ, asaññasattā devā ahetukā, anāhārā, aphassakā…pe… acittakā”ti –

"At the moment of arising for the non-percipient devas, one aggregate arises—the form aggregate; two sense bases—the form base and the phenomena base; two elements—the form element and the phenomena element; one truth of suffering; one material life faculty. The non-percipient devas are without roots, without nutriment, without contact…pe…without consciousness."

Saniddesamātikā nikkhittā. Ettha ca rūpampi kiñcāpi tesaṃ āyatanādikiccaṃ na karoti, saviññāṇakarūpīsu pana gahitattā idhāpi gahitaṃ. Gandhādayo pana tattha na gahitattā idhāpi na gahitā, no avijjamānatāya. Ekatalavāsikānaṃ vā sesabrahmānaṃ cakkhuvisayattā idhāpi rūpāyatanaṃ uddhaṭaṃ, asaññīnaṃ pana pañcāyatanāni, eko āhāro uppajjatīti veditabbaṃ.

The matrix with its explanation has been laid down. Here, although form does not perform the function of a sense base and so on for them, because it is included among forms associated with consciousness, it is also included here. However, odors and so on are not included there, so they are also not included here—not because they are non-existent. Or, because the form base is an object of the eye for those dwelling on one plane and the remaining brahmās, it is extracted here; but for the non-percipient beings, it should be understood that five sense bases and one nutriment arise.

Catutthakoṭṭhāse –

In the fourth section—

“Arūpadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe cattāro khandhā, dve āyatanāni, dve dhātuyo, ekaṃ saccaṃ, aṭṭhindriyāni[M 0.0318], tayo hetū, tayo āhārā, eko phasso…pe… ekaṃ citta”nti –

"At the moment of arising in the formless realm, four aggregates, two sense bases, two elements, one truth, eight faculties, three roots, three nutriments, one contact...pe...one consciousness."
