Ayaṃ vippayuttenasaṅgahitāsaṅgahitapade nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepato vibhaṅganayena saddhiṃ atthanicchayo, vitthāro pana dhātukathāpāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu (dhātu. 12; dhātu. aṭṭha. 1-2) gahetabboti.

Herein, this is the method: Phenomena dissociated from the form aggregate are included by four aggregates, two sense bases, and eight elements; they are not included by one aggregate and ten sense bases and elements. Phenomena dissociated from the truth of suffering are included by four aggregates, two sense bases, and two elements. Herein, 'dissociated from the truth of suffering' means supramundane consciousness and mental factors, and these phenomena are included by the four aggregates headed by the feeling aggregate, and by two elements, namely, the mind-consciousness element and the mental-object element. The rest is easy to understand. This is the method in the section on what is included and not included by the dissociated. This is the brief determination of meaning here, in accordance with the method of the Vibhaṅga; the detailed explanation, however, should be sought in the Pāḷi text of the Dhātukathā and its commentary (Dhātu. 12; Dhātu. Aṭṭha. 1–2).

Mohavicchedaniyā abhidhammamātikatthavaṇṇanāya

In the Mohavicchedanī, the Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix,

Dhātukathāmātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the meaning of the matrix of the Dhātukathā is finished.

4. Puggalapaññattimātikā

4. The Matrix of the Designation of Persons

Ekakamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Meaning of the Onefold Matrix

Idāni [M 0.0342][V 0.0262] puggalapaññattimātikāsaṃvaṇṇanānayo hoti. Tattha anuttānatthato tāva cha paññattiyoti ettha “ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) āgataṭṭhāne sandassanā pakāsanā paññatti nāma. “Supaññattaṃ mañcapīṭha”nti (pārā. 269) āgataṭṭhāne ṭhapanā nikkhipanā paññatti nāma, idha ubhayampi vaṭṭati. Cha paññattiyoti hi cha paññāpanā cha sandassanā pakāsanātipi, cha ṭhapanā nikkhipanātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Nāmapaññattiyeva hi te te vijjamānāvijjamāne dhamme sandassetītipi. Tena tena koṭṭhāsena ṭhapetītipi. Khandhapaññattītiādi pana saṅkhepato tāsaṃ paññattīnaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ. Tattha khandhānaṃ “khandhā”ti paññāpanā sandassanā pakāsanā ca ṭhapanā nikkhipanā ca khandhapaññatti nāma…pe… puggalānaṃ “puggalā”ti paññāpanā sandassanā pakāsanā ca ṭhapanā nikkhipanā ca puggalapaññatti nāma. Imā eva cha paññattiyo vijjanti. Aññāsampi sammutiparamatthakathānaṃ paññattīnaṃ anantattā, upalakkhaṇavasena pana padhānabhāvato ca etāva vuttā. Pāḷimuttakanayena pana sabbasaṅgāhikā vijjamānapaññattiādayo cha nāmapaññattiyo aṭṭhakathāsu (pu. pa. aṭṭha. mātikāvaṇṇanā 1) āgatā, tā ca heṭṭhā vuttāti idha na vuttā. Tāsu idha puggalapaññattipadena avijjamānapaññatti, sesehi vijjamānapaññatti cāti dve eva labbhanti.

Now begins the method for the explanation of the matrix of the Designation of Persons. First, regarding the six designations in terms of their meaning that is not obvious: where it says, 'He points out, teaches, makes known, establishes' (SN 2.20), 'designation' means showing and clarifying. Where it says, 'a well-designated bed and seat' (Pārā 269), 'designation' means placing and setting down. Here, both are applicable. For 'six designations' means six ways of designating—that is, six ways of showing and clarifying, and also six ways of placing and setting down. For it is name-designation that both points out those various existent and non-existent phenomena and establishes them in various categories. 'Aggregate-designation,' etc., is a brief presentation of the nature of these designations. Therein, the designating, showing, clarifying, placing, and setting down of aggregates as 'aggregates' is called 'aggregate-designation.' … The designating, showing, clarifying, placing, and setting down of persons as 'persons' is called 'person-designation.' Only these six designations exist. Although other designations concerning conventional and ultimate truth are endless, only these are mentioned because they are primary and serve as examples. However, according to the method independent of the canon, six all-encompassing name-designations, such as designation of the existent, are found in the commentaries (Pug-a, Mātika-vaṇṇanā 1); and since they have been mentioned previously, they are not stated here. Among these, here the term 'person-designation' yields the designation of the non-existent, while the remaining terms yield the designation of the existent. Thus only two are obtained.

Aṭṭhakathāmuttakena pana ācariyanayena aparāpi cha paññattiyo – upādāpaññatti upanidhāpaññatti samodhānapaññatti upanikkhittapaññatti tajjāpaññatti santatipaññattīti, yā “atthapaññattī”ti [V 0.0263] vuccati. Tattha yā khandhapañcakaṃ upādāya nissāya sammatā [M 0.0343] sattādikā, aṅgāni upādāya rathādikā, candādiparivattādayo upādāya kāladisādikā, taṃtaṃbhūtanimittaṃ, bhāvanāvisesañca upādāya kasiṇādiuggahapaṭibhāganimittādikāti ayaṃ evarūpā sabhāvadhammehi ekattena vā sacchikaṭṭhaparamatthena anupalabbhasabhāvā upādāpaññatti nāma. Paññāpetabbaṭṭhena cesā paññatti vuttā, na pana paññāpanaṭṭhena. Yā tassa tassatthassa paññāpanā, sā avijjamānapaññattiyeva.

However, according to the teachers' method, which is independent of the commentary, there are another six designations: derivative designation, designation by reference, designation by combination, designation by juxtaposition, designation based on that, and designation by continuity, which are called 'meaning-designations.' Herein, that which is conceptually constructed by relying on the five aggregates, such as 'a being'; by relying on the parts, such as 'a chariot'; by relying on the revolutions of the moon and so on, such as 'time' and 'direction'; and by relying on this or that elemental sign and on a special meditative development, such as the kasiṇa learning sign and counterpart sign—this kind of thing, whose nature is not discoverable in the sense of ultimate reality, either as identical with real phenomena or as a reality to be realized in its own right, is called derivative designation. This is called a 'designation' in the sense of what is to be designated, not in the sense of the act of designating. The act of designating that particular meaning is simply a designation of the non-existent.

Yā pana aññaṃ paṭhamādiṃ upanidhāya apekkhitvā dutiyaṃ rassaṃ dīghaṃ dūraṃ santikantiādikā tadaññāpekkhūpanidhā, chattapāṇītiādikā hatthagatūpanidhā, kuṇḍalītiādikā sampayuttūpanidhā, dhaññasakaṭanti ādikā samāropitūpanidhā, indasālaguhātiādikā avidūragatūpanidhā, suvaṇṇavaṇṇotiādikā paṭibhāgūpanidhā, brāhmaṇagāmotiādikā tabbahulūpanidhā, maṇikaṭakantiādikā tabbisiṭṭhūpanidhāti evamādi anekappakārā paññāpanā, ayaṃ upanidhāpaññatti nāma.

Furthermore, the designation of a second thing as 'short,' 'long,' 'far,' 'near,' etc., by referring to and considering another, primary thing, is designation by reference to another. Designations such as 'one with an umbrella in hand' are designations by reference to what is held in the hand. Designations such as 'one with earrings' are designations by reference to what is associated. Designations such as 'a cart of grain' are designations by reference to what is loaded on. Designations such as 'the Indasāla cave' are designations by reference to what is nearby. Designations such as 'golden-colored' are designations by reference to a counterpart. Designations such as 'a brahmin village' are designations by reference to its prevalence. Designations such as 'a jeweled bracelet' are designations by reference to its distinction. Designating in these and many other various ways is called designation by reference.

Dhaññarāsītiādikā pana samodhānapaññatti nāma. Purimassa purimassa upanikkhipitvā dve tīṇītiādikā upanikkhittapaññatti nāma. Taṃtaṃsabhāvanissitā pathavīādikā tajjāpaññatti nāma. Āsītikotiādikā pana santatipaññatti nāma.

'A heap of grain,' etc., is called designation by combination. Designating 'two,' 'three,' etc., by placing one upon another is called designation by juxtaposition. 'Earth,' etc., which depends on its respective intrinsic nature, is called designation based on that. 'Eighty crores,' etc., is called designation by continuity.

Aṭṭhakathāmuttakeneva ācariyanayena aparāpi dhammakathikādikā kiccapaññatti, kisathūlādikā saṇṭhānapaññatti, itthipurisādikā liṅgapaññatti, kāmāvacarādikā, kosalakādikā ca bhūmipaññatti, tisso nāgotiādikā paccattapaññatti, nirodhādikā asaṅkhatapaññatti cāti cha paññattiyo.

Again, according to the teachers' method, which is independent of the commentary, there are another six designations: designation by function, such as 'a Dhamma preacher'; designation by shape, such as 'thin' and 'thick'; designation by gender, such as 'female' and 'male'; designation by plane, such as 'belonging to the sense sphere' and 'belonging to Kosala'; designation of individuals, such as 'Tissa' and 'Nāga'; and designation of the unconditioned, such as 'cessation.'

Etāsu [M 0.0344] pana dvādasasu tajjāpaññatti, ekaccā bhūmipaññatti, asaṅkhatapaññatti ca vijjamānapaññattisaṅkhātā nāmapaññatti, tadaññā paramatthāvasesā, pana atthapaññattīti dīpitā avijjamānādipaññattiyo cāti. Ayaṃ tāvettha anuttānatthato saṃvaṇṇanā.

Now, among these twelve, designation based on that, a certain kind of designation by plane, and designation of the unconditioned are name-designations, reckoned as designations of the existent. The others, the remaining ones, are shown to be meaning-designations, that is, designations of the non-existent, etc. This, for now, is the explanation of what is not obvious in meaning.

Atthanicchayo panetthāpi pāḷinayeneva saddhiṃ hoti, na vinā pāḷiṃ tassa vattumasakkuṇeyyattā[V 0.0264]. Pāḷiyañca yasmā ādito pañca paññattiyo, tadatthabhūtā khandhādayo ca heṭṭhā vibhaṅgappakaraṇe nippadesato kathitāti tā idha “kittāvatā khandhānaṃ khandhapaññatti, yāvatā pañcakkhandhā rūpakkhandho”tiādinā saṅkhepeneva niddiṭṭhā, tā cetthāpi vuttatthā. Puggalapaññatti pana heṭṭhā na vuttāti “kittāvatā puggalānaṃ puggalapaññatti? Samayavimutto, asamayavimutto”tiādinā ekakādibhedena yāva dasakā dasadhā mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthāreneva vibhattā, sā ca ñātabbapabhedato avuccamānā dubbiññeyyā, tasmā puggalapaññattiyā eva cettha pāḷinayānusārena saṅkhepato atthanicchayo hoti, so cettha mātikāyaṃ vutte sabbapuggale anuddharitvā ñātabbānaṃ dubbiññeyyānaṃ puggalānaṃ ekakādibhedatova mātikaṃ uddharitvā vibhajanavasena saṅkhepatova hoti. Kathaṃ? “Samayavimutto asamayavimutto, kuppadhammo akuppadhammo, cetanābhabbo anurakkhaṇābhabbo, bhayūparato abhayūparato, bhabbāgamano abhabbāgamano, niyato aniyato, paṭipannako phale ṭhito, samasīsī ṭhitakappī, sotāpanno sattakkhattuparamo kolaṃkolo ekabījī, sakadāgāmī, anāgāmī antarāparinibbāyī upahaccaparinibbāyī asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī, arahā”ti ekakamātikā.

Here too, however, the determination of meaning occurs together with the method of the Pāḷi, for without the Pāḷi it would be impossible to state it. And since in the Pāḷi the first five designations and the aggregates, etc., which are their meaning, have been discussed exhaustively in the book of the Vibhaṅga, they are indicated here only briefly, as: 'To what extent is there designation of aggregates? As far as the five aggregates: the form aggregate…' etc.; and their meaning has also been stated here. But since the designation of persons was not stated previously, it is analyzed in detail, from the onefold division up to the tenfold, by setting up a matrix beginning: 'To what extent is there designation of persons? The one liberated at a time, the one liberated timelessly…' etc. And since its divisions, which should be known, would be difficult to understand if not stated, the determination of meaning for the designation of persons occurs here briefly in accordance with the method of the Pāḷi. This occurs briefly by way of analysis, extracting the matrix only according to the onefold division, etc., for those persons who should be known and are difficult to understand, without extracting all the persons mentioned in the matrix. How? 'One liberated at a time, one liberated timelessly; one liable to fall away, one not liable to fall away; one capable through volition, one capable through guarding; one restrained by fear, one not restrained by fear; one capable of progress, one incapable of progress; one who is certain, one who is not certain; one on the path, one established in the fruit; one of equal heads, one who stands for the aeon; a stream-enterer, a seven-times-at-most returner, a family-to-family returner, a one-seeder; a once-returner; a non-returner—one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval, one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing, one who attains final Nibbāna without exertion, one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion, one who is bound upstream for the Akaniṭṭha realm; an Arahant'—this is the onefold matrix.

Tattha [M 0.0345] yo appanaṃ nibbattetuṃ yuttapattakāle rūpārūpasamāpattisaṅkhātehi aṭṭhahi vimokkhehi paccanīkadhammato vimuccitvā tīsu maggesu yena kenaci yathāsakaṃ āsave khepetvā vuṭṭhito, ayaṃ samayavimutto nāma. “Ekacce āsavā parikkhīṇā”tiādivacanato (pu. pa. 1) hi aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī puthujjano vā khīṇāsavo vā idha na gahito, samāpattilābhino pana phalaṭṭhasekhāva gahitāti veditabbā. Sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavo, sabbepi ca ariyā maggavimokkhaṃ sandhāya asamayavimuttā nāma. Bāhirānañhi aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ samāpajjantassa pavivekaṭṭhānalābhādisamayopi atthi, vattakaraṇakālādiasamayopi atthi. Maggavimokkhena vimuccanassa pana tādiso samayo vā asamayo vā natthi, yassa saddhā balavatī, vipassanā ca āraddhā, tassa gacchantassa vā bhuñjantassa vā maggaphalapaṭivedho nāma na hotīti natthi, tasmā sabbe ariyā ariyavimokkhe asamayavimuttāti veditabbā. Purimapadepi lokiyasamāpattiññeva sandhāya sekhā samayavimuttā nāma jātā.

Herein, one who, at the appropriate time for generating absorption, having been liberated from opposing states by means of the eight liberations—that is, the form and formless attainments—emerges after having destroyed the taints by any of the three paths according to his own capacity, is called one 'liberated at a time.' For, based on the statement, 'In some, the taints are destroyed,' etc. (Pug. 1), an ordinary person who has obtained the eight attainments or an arahant is not included here. Rather, it should be understood that only trainees established in the fruit who have obtained the attainments are included. A dry-insight arahant, and indeed all noble ones with reference to liberation by the path, are called 'liberated not at a time.' For one outside who is entering the eight attainments, there is a suitable time, such as for gaining a place of seclusion, and there is an unsuitable time, such as the time for performing one's duties. But for liberation by means of the path, there is no such time or non-time. For one whose faith is strong and whose insight has been initiated, there is nothing to prevent the penetration of the path and fruit whether one is walking or eating. Therefore, all noble ones should be understood as 'liberated not at a time' in respect to the noble liberation. In the first case, too, it is with reference to the mundane attainments that trainees come to be called 'liberated at a time.'

Avasibhāvā aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī pana puthujjano, sotāpannasakadāgāmino dve sekhā aṭṭhasamāpattiṃ [V 0.0265] sandhāya kuppadhammo nāma. Parihānadhammotipi duvidhā eva. Anāgāmiādayo suppahīnasamādhipāripanthikattā vasibhāvā samāpattilābhī puthujjano, ariyā ca lokuttaradhammepi sandhāya akuppadhammo nāma. Aparihānadhammoti te eva. Cetanābhabboti cetanāsaṅkhātena jhānasamāpattivaḷañjanena aparihāniṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbo. Yo hi rūpārūpajjhānesu āciṇṇavasitāya cetanāsaṅkhātāya jhānasamāpattiyā nirantaraṃ vaḷañjamāno tehi na parihāyati, avaḷañjamāno ca parihāyati, ayaṃ vaḷañjamāno cetanābhabbo [M 0.0346] nāma. Anurakkhaṇābhabboti jhānassa upakārānupakāradhamme jānitvā anurakkhaṇāya avaḷañjamānopi aparihāniṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbo, eso ca purimato balavataro, āciṇṇavasino paññāsampadāya upakārānupakāradhamme jānitvā tadanurūpaṃ paṭipajjanatoti veditabbo.

An ordinary person who has obtained the eight attainments but lacks mastery over them, and the two trainees—the stream-enterer and the once-returner—are, with reference to the eight attainments, called 'liable to fall away.' These same two types are also called 'liable to decline.' A non-returner and an arahant; an ordinary person who has obtained the attainments with mastery; and noble ones are called 'unshakable' with reference to the supramundane states as well, because the obstacles to concentration are completely abandoned. They are also the ones called 'not liable to decline.' 'Capable through volition' means one who is capable of not declining through the practice of the jhāna-attainments, which is known as volition. For one who, due to long practice and mastery in the form and formless jhānas, continuously practices the jhāna-attainments called 'volition,' does not decline from them, but declines when not practicing them—this one who practices them is called 'capable through volition.' 'Capable through guarding' means one who is capable of not declining even without practicing, by knowing the helpful and unhelpful qualities for jhāna and guarding accordingly. This one is stronger than the former. It should be understood that this is because one who has long-practiced mastery, through the accomplishment of wisdom, knows the helpful and unhelpful qualities and practices accordingly.

Bhayūparatoti bhayena pāpato uparato virato sekho, kalyāṇaputhujjano ca. Tesu pacchimo duggativaṭṭakilesaupavādasaṅkhātehi catūhi bhayehi pāpato oramati, sekho duggativajjehi, apāyehi muttattā. Khīṇāsavo pana abhayūparato nāma samucchinnabhayattā, upavādato pana oramitabbo.

'One restrained out of fear' is a trainee, and a virtuous ordinary person, who is restrained and abstains from evil out of fear. Among them, the latter—the virtuous ordinary person—desists from evil due to the four fears, namely, fear of a bad destination, fear of the round, fear of defilements, and fear of blame. The trainee, being freed from the lower realms, desists from evil due to the other fears, excluding the fear of a bad destination. The one whose taints are destroyed, however, is called 'one restrained without fear' because his fears have been eradicated. He should, however, still desist from what is blameworthy.

Abhabbāgamanoti sammattaniyāmāgamanassa abhabbo, ye ānantariyasaṅkhātena kammāvaraṇena, niyatamicchādiṭṭhisaṅkhātena kilesāvaraṇena, ahetukaduhetukapaṭisandhisaṅkhātena vipākāvaraṇena ca samannāgatā, buddhādīsu ca saddhārahitā, maggabhāvanāya ca uttarakurukādayo viya acchandikā, pubbūpanissayarahitā ca, sabbete abhabbāgamanā nāma. Viparītā bhabbāgamanā nāma. Pañcānantariyaniyatamicchādiṭṭhikā nirayagamane, aṭṭha ariyapuggalā anupādāparinibbānādīsu niyatā nāma. Avasesapuggalā anibaddhagatikatāya aniyatā nāma, uttarakurukā pana sugatiniyatāpi micchattasammattaniyāmasseva idhādhippetattā “niyatā”ti na vuttā. Maggasamaṅgī puggalo maggakkhaṇe phalatthāya paṭipannako nāma, phalasamaṅgī phalānuppattiyampi phale ṭhito nāma.

'Incapable of attainment' means one who is incapable of entering the fixed path of rightness. Those who are endowed with the karmic obstruction consisting of the deeds with immediate result, with the defilement-obstruction consisting of fixed wrong view, and with the resultant-obstruction consisting of rebirth with no root-causes or with two root-causes; and who lack faith in the Buddha and so on; and who, like the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, lack the desire for cultivating the path; and who are devoid of a previous supporting condition—all these are called 'incapable of attainment.' The opposite are called 'capable of attainment.' Those who commit the five deeds with immediate result and those with fixed wrong view are fixed for going to hell. The eight noble individuals are fixed for final Nibbāna without residue and so on. The remaining individuals, due to their unfixed destiny, are called 'unfixed.' However, since what is intended here is the fixedness of wrongness and rightness, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, although fixed for a good destination, are not called 'fixed.' A person endowed with the path, at the moment of the path, is called 'one practicing for the attainment of the fruit.' A person endowed with the fruit, at the very arising of the fruit, is called 'one established in the fruit.'

Yassa pana apubbācarimaṃ āsavapariyādānañca hoti jīvitapariyādānañca, ayaṃ samasīsī nāma. So ca tividho hoti iriyāpathasamasīsī rogasamasīsī jīvitasamasīsīti. Tattha yo catūsu iriyāpathesu ekasmiṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā [M 0.0347] arahattaṃ patvā tasmiññeva iriyāpathe parinibbāti, ayaṃ iriyāpathasamasīsī nāma. Yo pana ekaṃ rogaṃ patvā antoroge eva [V 0.0266] vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ patvā teneva rogena parinibbāti, ayaṃ rogasamasīsī nāma. Yassa pana kilesasīsasaṅkhātā avijjā, arahattamaggena pavattasīsasaṅkhātaṃ jīvitindriyañca cuticittena samaṃ pariyādānaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ jīvitasamasīsī nāma. Kathamidaṃ samaṃ hotīti? Vārasamatāya. Yasmiṃ hi vāre maggena kilese khepite paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni pavattanti, tassānantarameva parinibbāyato imāya vārasamatāya idaṃ ubhayasīsapariyādānampi samaṃ hoti nāma, ayameva jīvitasamasīsī idhādhippeto.

But one for whom the exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur simultaneously, not one before the other, is called 'equal-headed.' This person is of three kinds: equal-headed as to posture, equal-headed as to disease, and equal-headed as to life. Herein, one who establishes insight in one of the four postures, attains arahantship, and attains final Nibbāna in that very posture—this one is called 'equal-headed as to posture.' One who, having contracted a disease, establishes insight while in the midst of that disease, attains arahantship, and attains final Nibbāna on account of that very disease—this one is called 'equal-headed as to disease.' One for whom ignorance, reckoned as the head of the defilements, and the life faculty, reckoned as the head of the ongoing process, both come to exhaustion simultaneously with the death-consciousness—this one is called 'equal-headed as to life.' How is this simultaneous? By simultaneity of the cognitive series. For in the very cognitive series in which the taints are destroyed by the path, the reviewing knowledges arise, and immediately after that one attains final Nibbāna. By this simultaneity of the cognitive series, this exhaustion of both heads is called simultaneous. It is this 'equal-headed as to life' that is intended here.

Ṭhitakappīti ṭhito kappo ṭhitakappo, svāssa atthīti ṭhitakappī, kappamhi vinassamānamhi kappaṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthoti attho.

'One who can remain for the aeon': a standing aeon is a 'ṭhitakappa.' One who possesses this is a 'ṭhitakappī.' The meaning is that when the aeon is being destroyed, one is capable of making the aeon stand.

Sace hi yesaṃ maggasamaṅgikkhaṇe kappavināso bhaveyya, neva tāva kappo vinasseyya, yāvāyaṃ yathāsakaṃ phalaṃ na sacchikarotīti te vinassamānampi kappaṃ ṭhapentīti ṭhitakappino nāma jātāti. Kiñcāpi kappavināsanakāle sāsanaṃ natthi, gatakoṭike hi kāle kappavināso hoti, evaṃ santepi maggānantaraphalassa anantarāyaṃ dīpetuṃ idaṃ abhūtampi kāraṇaṃ āhaṭaṃ.

For if the destruction of the aeon were to occur at the moment they are endowed with the path, the aeon would not be destroyed until they realize their respective fruit. Thus, they make the aeon stand even while it is being destroyed, and so they come to be called 'those who can remain for the aeon.' Although at the time of an aeon's destruction the Dispensation does not exist—for the destruction of an aeon occurs when its limit has been reached—even so, to illustrate that there is no obstruction to the fruit that immediately follows the path, this reason, though it does not actually occur, has been adduced.

Sotāpannoti nibbānasamuddaninnatāya sotasaṅkhātassa maggassa paṭhamasamaṅgī vuccati, idha pana phalaṭṭho adhippeto. Tasseva ca pabhedadassanatthaṃ “sattakkhattuparamo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sattavārā paramā assa bhavūpapattīti sattakkhattuparamo, tato paraṃ aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nādiyatīti attho. Sotāpanno hi yo sattakkhattuṃ devesu, manussesu ca paṭisandhiṃ [M 0.0348] gahetvā sattame bhave dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo nāma. Kulato kulaṃ bhavato bhavaṃ gacchatīti kolaṃkolo. So hi devamanussavasena dve gatiyo bhave saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo nāma. Kammapaṭisandhiyā ekaṃ kammaṃ kilesabījaṃ assāti ekabījī. So hi ekasmiññeva bhave khīṇāsavo hoti. Kiṃ panassa bhedassa niyāmakanti? Vipassanābhiññābhedā. Sotāpannesu hi yo vipassanāya pamatto, so sattakkhattuparamo hoti. Yo kiñci appamatto, so kolaṃkolo. Yo pana vipassanāya ativiya appamatto, so ekabījī hoti. Ye pana abhiviya pamattā vaṭṭajjhāsayā anāthapiṇḍikavisākhāsakkādayo, te punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva vicarantā ādito paṭṭhāya cha devaloke osāpetvā brahmalokesupi yathākkamaṃ nibbattitvā akaniṭṭhe ṭhatvā parinibbanti, na te idha gahitā. Te hi manussagatiṃ punappunaṃ [V 0.0267] ādiyanti. Ye pana manussagatiyampi bhavaṃ ādiyanti, tesaṃ vasena sattakkhattuparamo kolaṃkolo mānusikabhavanibbattako eva ekabījī gahito. Te pana saddhādhurena āgatā tayo, paññādhurena āgatā tayoti sotāpanno chabbidho hotīti veditabbo.

A 'stream-enterer' is so called because he is the first to be endowed with the path, known as the 'stream' because it is inclined to the ocean of Nibbāna. Here, however, one established in the fruit is intended. To show the distinctions among them, it is said, 'one with at most seven more lives,' and so on. 'One with at most seven more lives' means that his rebirths in a state of existence are at most seven; he does not take up an eighth state of existence. For a stream-enterer who takes rebirth among gods and humans seven times and in the seventh state of existence makes an end of suffering is called a 'one with at most seven more lives.' 'One who goes from clan to clan' is one who goes from clan to clan, from one state of existence to another. For he, having wandered through becomings in the two destinies of gods and humans, makes an end of suffering. This one is called a 'one who goes from clan to clan.' 'One-seeder' means one for whom there is a single kamma that is the seed of defilements for rebirth. For he becomes one whose taints are destroyed in just one more state of existence. What determines this distinction? The difference in insight and direct knowledge. Among stream-enterers, one who is negligent in insight becomes a 'one with at most seven more lives.' One who is somewhat diligent becomes a 'one who goes from clan to clan.' But one who is exceedingly diligent in insight becomes a 'one-seeder.' However, those who are extremely negligent, with a disposition for the round of rebirths—such as Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and Sakka—wander repeatedly in the round. Having completed the six celestial worlds, they are reborn in due order in the Brahmā worlds and attain final Nibbāna while abiding in the Akaniṭṭha realm; they are not included here, for they repeatedly take up a human destiny. But with respect to those who take up a state of existence in the human destiny, the 'one with at most seven more lives,' the 'one who goes from clan to clan,' and the 'one-seeder' are taken as only those who bring about a human becoming. Moreover, the stream-enterer should be understood as being sixfold: three who proceed by the vehicle of faith and three who proceed by the vehicle of wisdom.

Paṭisandhivasena pana sakiṃ imaṃ manussagatiṃ āgacchatīti sakadāgāmī, dutiyamaggaphalasamaṅgī. Iminā pañcasu sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekova gahito. Ekacco hi sakadāgāmiphale ṭhatvā puna dutiyabhave idheva parinibbāti, ekacco idha patvā devaloke parinibbāti, ekacco devaloke patvā dutiyabhave tattheva parinibbāti, ekacco devaloke patvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāti, ime cattāropi idha na gahitā. Yo pana idha patvā devaloke [M 0.0349] nibbattitvā puna idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāti, ayamekova idha gahito. Imassa ca dve paṭisandhiyo, ekabījissa pana ekāvāti idaṃ tesaṃ nānākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

However, by way of rebirth-linking, one who comes to this human destination only once is a once-returner, one endowed with the fruit of the second path. By this, among the five kinds of once-returners, four are excluded and only one is included. For one person, having become established in the fruit of a once-returner, attains final Nibbāna right here in a second existence; another, having attained it here, attains final Nibbāna in the deva world; another, having attained it in the deva world, attains final Nibbāna right there in a second existence; another, having attained it in the deva world, is reborn here and then attains final Nibbāna. These four are not included here. But the one who, having attained it here, is reborn in the deva world and then, being reborn here again, attains final Nibbāna—this one alone is included here. For this one there are two rebirth-linkings, but for the one-seeder there is only one. This should be understood as what distinguishes them.

Paṭisandhivasena kāmabhavaṃ nāgacchatīti anāgāmī, tatiyamaggaphalasamaṅgī. Tasseva pana pabhedadassanatthaṃ “antarāparinibbāyī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha antarāparinibbāyīti āyuvemajjhassa antarā eva arahattamaggaṃ uppādetvā kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyanasīlo eko anāgāmī. So ca uppannasamanantaraṃ parinibbāyī, āyuvemajjhaṃ appatvā parinibbāyī, āyuvemajjhaṃ patvā parinibbāyīti tividho hoti. Upahaccaparinibbāyīti āyuvemajjhaṃ upahacca atikkamitvā, maraṇasamayaṃ vā upahacca upagantvā parinibbāyī, āyuvemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā yāva maraṇasamayā parinibbāyīti attho. Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti asaṅkhārena appadukkhena adhimattappayogaṃ akatvā parinibbāyanasīlo. Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti sasaṅkhārena dukkhena kasirena adhimattappayogena parinibbāyanasīlo. Uddhaṃsototi uddhaṃvāhibhāvena uddhamassa taṇhāsotaṃ vaṭṭasotañca, uddhaṃ vā gantvā paṭilabhitabbato uddhaṃ maggasotamassātipi uddhaṃsoto. Akaniṭṭhaṃ gacchatīti akaniṭṭhagāmī. Imesaṃ pana anāgāmīnaṃ pabhedadassanatthampettha uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmītiādi catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

By way of rebirth-linking, one who does not come to the sense-sphere existence is a non-returner, one endowed with the fruit of the third path. To show the subdivisions of this, it is said: 'one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval,' etc. Here, an antarāparinibbāyī is a type of non-returner who has the nature of attaining final Nibbāna by the final Nibbāna of the defilements, having generated the path to arahantship within the first half of the lifespan. This one is of three kinds: one who attains final Nibbāna immediately after arising, one who attains final Nibbāna without reaching the lifespan's midpoint, and one who attains final Nibbāna after reaching the lifespan's midpoint. An upahaccaparinibbāyī is one who attains final Nibbāna having surpassed the lifespan's midpoint, or having approached the time of death; that is, one who attains final Nibbāna after surpassing the lifespan's midpoint up to the time of death. An asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī is one who has the nature of attaining final Nibbāna without prompting, with little difficulty, without making excessive effort. A sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī is one who has the nature of attaining final Nibbāna with prompting, with difficulty, with toil, through excessive effort. An uddhaṃsoto is an 'upward-streamer' because the stream of craving and the stream of the round for one who is 'upward' flows upward; or, because the stream of the path is 'upward' as it is to be attained by going upward. One who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm is an akaniṭṭhagāmī. To show the subdivisions of these non-returners, the fourfold classification beginning with uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī should be understood here.

Tattha yo avihato paṭṭhāya catūsu yathākkamaṃ uppajjitvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā cuto akaniṭṭhe uppajjitvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana akaniṭṭhaṃ appatvā antarā parinibbāti, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo manussaloko akaniṭṭhameva [V 0.0268] gantvā parinibbāti, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana heṭṭhā catūsu suddhāvāsesu aññatarasmiṃ uppajjitvā tattheva parinibbāti, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma[M 0.0350]. Evamete anāgāmino aṭṭhacattālīsavidhā honti. Kathaṃ? Avihesu tāva tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsototi pañca, te asaṅkhāraparinibbāyisasaṅkhāraparinibbāyivasena dasa honti, evaṃ atappasudassasudassīsūti cattālīsaṃ, akaniṭṭhe pana uddhaṃsoto natthi, tasmā tattha taṃ sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhāravasena duvidhaṃ uddhaṃsotaṃ vajjetvā aṭṭha cāti aṭṭhacattālīsa honti.

Here, one who, starting from the Aviha realm, is reborn sequentially in the four Pure Abodes, remains for the full lifespan, passes away, is reborn in the Akaniṭṭha realm, and attains final Nibbāna—this one is called an 'upward-streamer who goes to Akaniṭṭha.' But one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval without reaching Akaniṭṭha—this one is called an 'upward-streamer who does not go to Akaniṭṭha.' One who goes from the human world directly to Akaniṭṭha and attains final Nibbāna—this one is called a 'non-upward-streamer who goes to Akaniṭṭha.' And one who is reborn in one of the four lower Pure Abodes and attains final Nibbāna right there—this one is called a 'non-upward-streamer who does not go to Akaniṭṭha.' Thus these non-returners are of forty-eight kinds. How so? In the Aviha realm, there are three who attain Nibbāna in the interval, one who attains Nibbāna upon impact, and one upward-streamer—making five. These become ten when divided into those who attain Nibbāna without prompting and with prompting. It is the same in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms, making forty. But in the Akaniṭṭha realm there is no upward-streamer. Therefore, excluding the twofold upward-streamer—with and without prompting—there are eight. Thus there are forty-eight.

Arahāti kilesārīnaṃ hatattādinā khīṇāsavo arahā nāma. So suññatādivimokkhattayavasena tividho hutvā puna paccekaṃ paṭipadācatukkavasena dvādasavidhā honti. Yathā ca arahā dvādasavidho, evaṃ dvādaseva sakadāgāmino, catuvīsati sotāpannā aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāminova paccekanti veditabbaṃ. Ime ca sabbe ariyā imasmiṃ sāsane eva uppajjanti, no bahiddhāti. Ekakanayo.

An arahant is so called because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements, and so on; he is one whose taints are destroyed. He is threefold by way of the three liberations—emptiness, etc.—and then becomes twelvefold, each by way of the fourfold mode of practice. And just as the arahant is twelvefold, so too it should be understood that there are twelve once-returners, twenty-four stream-enterers, and forty-eight non-returners, each individually. All these noble ones arise only within this Dispensation, not outside it. End of the section on singles.

Dukādimātikatthavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Meaning of the Matrix of Dyads, etc.

Dukādīsu “dve puggalā – kodhano ca upanāhī ca makkhī ca paḷāsī cā”tiādinā dukañca, “tayo puggalā – nirāso āsaṃso vigatāso”tiādinā tikañca, “cattāro puggalā – asappuriso, asappurisenaasappurisataro, sappuriso, sappurisenasappurisataro”tiādinā catukkañca, “pañca puggalā – atthekacco puggalo ārabhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hoti, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti, atthekacco puggalo ārabhati na vippaṭisārī ca hoti…pe… aparisesā nirujjhanti, atthekacco puggalo nārabhati vippaṭisārī ca hoti…pe… aparisesā nirujjhanti. Atthekacco [M 0.0351] puggalo nārabhati na vippaṭisārī hoti…pe… aparisesā nirujjhantī”tiādinā pañcakañca vitthārato mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā sabbepi te puggalā niddiṭṭhā, idha pana te ganthavitthārabhayena sabbe na uddiṭṭhā, pāḷiyā eva ñātabbāti.

In the sections on dyads, etc., the dyads are laid out, beginning with: 'Two persons: the angry and the resentful; the denigrator and the domineering.' The triads are laid out, beginning with: 'Three persons: one without hope, one with hope, one whose hope is gone.' The tetrads are laid out, beginning with: 'Four persons: an inferior person; one more inferior than an inferior person; a superior person; one more superior than a superior person.' The pentads are laid out in detail in the matrix, beginning with: 'Five persons: there is a person who begins but is remorseful, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind, that liberation by wisdom, wherein his arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder. There is a person who begins but is not remorseful … cease without remainder. There is a person who does not begin but is remorseful … cease without remainder. There is a person who does not begin and is not remorseful … cease without remainder.' All these persons have been indicated, but here, for fear of expanding the text, they are not all listed; they should be known from the Pāli itself.

Tattha [V 0.0269] tike nirāsoti arahattāsāya virahito dussīlo. Tassa hi attano abhabbatāya bhabbasahāyakassa sīlavato arahattappattiṃ sutvā, caṇḍālaputtassa viya kassaci rājaputtassa rajjābhisekaṃ sutvā abhisekappattiyaṃ, “kudāssu nāmāhampi arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti arahattappattiyaṃ patthanāpi na uppajjati. Āsaṃsoti arahattaṃ āsīsamāno patthayamāno sīlavā. Tassa hi arahattapatthanāya sīlasampattiyā ṭhitattā kassaci arahattappattiṃ sutvā, ubhatosujātassa rājakumārassa viya tādisassa kassaci rajjābhisekaṃ sutvā abhisekappattiyaṃ, arahattappattiyaṃ patthanā uppajjati. Vigatāsoti arahā. So hi pattaarahattatāya tattha vigatāso hoti pattābhiseko viya khattiyo abhisekappattiyanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, in the triad, 'one without hope' refers to an immoral person devoid of hope for arahantship. For such a person, because of his own unsuitability, on hearing that a virtuous companion who is suitable has attained arahantship—like a son of an outcaste hearing of some prince's consecration to kingship—not even the wish for the attainment of arahantship arises, the thought: 'When, indeed, will I too attain arahantship?' 'One with hope' refers to a virtuous person who hopes and longs for arahantship. For such a person, being established in virtue with a desire for arahantship, on hearing of someone's attainment of arahantship—like a prince of pure lineage on both sides hearing of the consecration of such a one to kingship—the wish for the attainment of arahantship arises. 'One whose hope is gone' refers to an arahant. For him, having attained arahantship, hope in regard to it is gone, just as for a khattiya who has received the consecration, hope for the consecration is gone. This is how it should be understood.

Catukke pana pāṇātipātādiakusalakammapathasamannāgato asappuriso nāma. Yo pana sayampi pāṇātipātādīni katvā parañca tattha samādapeti, ayaṃ asappurisenaasappurisataro, asappurisatopi asappurisataroti attho. Vuttapaṭipakkhakusalavasena sappuriso, sappurisenasappurisataro ca veditabbo.

In the tetrad, one who is endowed with the unwholesome courses of action beginning with the destruction of life is called an inferior person. But one who, having himself done acts such as the destruction of life, also instigates another in them, this one is more inferior than an inferior person; this is the meaning of 'more inferior than an inferior person.' A superior person and one who is more superior than a superior person are to be understood by way of the wholesome qualities opposite to what has been stated.

Pañcake ārabhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotīti ettha ārambha-saddo āpattivītikkame vattati, tasmā āpattivītikkamavasena ārabhati ceva tappaccayā ca vippaṭisārī hotīti attho. Cetovimuttinti phalasampayuttasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti phalasampayuttañāṇaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti anadhigatattā [M 0.0352] yathāsabhāvato nappajānāti. Yatthassāti yasmiṃ arahattaphalasaṅkhāte jhāne adhigate assa puggalassa sabbe pāpakā akusalā dhammā niravasesā nirujjhanti, te nappajānātīti sambandho. Kiñcāpi te maggakkhaṇe eva nirujjhanti nāma, phalakkhaṇe pana niruddhā nāma honti, idha pana maggakiccavasena “phalakkhaṇe nirujjhantī”ti vuttāti veditabbā.

In the pentad, regarding 'he begins and is remorseful,' the word 'beginning' here pertains to the transgression of an offense. Therefore, the meaning is that he transgresses an offense and, on account of that, is remorseful. 'Liberation of mind' means the concentration associated with the fruit. 'Liberation by wisdom' means the knowledge associated with the fruit. 'He does not understand it as it really is' means that because he has not attained it, he does not know it according to its real nature. 'Wherein for him': when that jhāna designated as the fruit of arahantship has been attained, all evil, unwholesome states of this person cease without remainder. 'He does not understand them'—this is the connection. Although they are in fact extinguished at the moment of the path, they are said to be extinguished at the moment of the fruit. Here, however, it should be understood that it is said 'they cease at the moment of the fruit' on account of the function of the path.

Ārabhati na vippaṭisārī ca hotīti āpattiṃ āpajjati, taṃ pana desetuṃ sabhāgapuggalaṃ pariyesati, vuṭṭhāpeti vā, tasmā na vippaṭisārī hoti. Nārabhati vippaṭisārī ca hotīti āpattiṃ nāpajjati, vinayapaññattiyaṃ pana akovidattā anāpattiyā āpattisaññitāya vuṭṭhitāyapi taṃ āpattiyā vippaṭisāraṃ vinodetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya vippaṭisārī hoti. Nārabhati na vippaṭisārī hotīti nārabhati neva āpattiṃ āpajjati, na vippaṭisārī hoti. Arahattañca [V 0.0270] na pāpuṇāti. Kataro panesa puggaloti? Sīlavā ossaṭṭhavīriyo puggalo. So hi “kiṃ me imasmiṃ buddhakāle parinibbānena, anāgate metteyyasammāsambuddhakāle parinibbāyissāmī”ti visuddhasīlopi paṭipattiṃ na pūreti. Ime cattāropi puggalā tathā tathā ovaditvā āsavakkhaye patiṭṭhāpetabbā. Evaṃ hi tepi yvāyaṃ pañcamo puggalo nārabhati na vippaṭisārī āraddhavīriyo arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tena samasamāva bhavissantīti.

He undertakes and is not remorseful—thus he commits an offense. But to confess it, he seeks a suitable person, or he rehabilitates himself; therefore, he is not remorseful. He does not undertake but is remorseful—thus he does not commit an offense. However, due to being unskilled in the Vinaya regulations, even after having rehabilitated himself from what was perceived as an offense when it was not, he is unable to dispel his remorse concerning that 'offense'—thus he is remorseful. He does not undertake and is not remorseful—thus he neither commits an offense, nor is he remorseful. But he does not attain arahantship. Who, then, is this person? It is a virtuous person who has relaxed his energy. For he thinks: 'What is the use for me of attaining final Nibbāna in this Buddha's era? In the future, during the time of Metteyya, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, I will attain final Nibbāna.' Though pure in virtue, he does not fulfill the practice. These four types of persons should be advised accordingly and established in the destruction of the taints. For in this way, they too will become equal to the fifth person—the one who does not undertake, is not remorseful, is energetic, and attains arahantship.

Chakkādīsu –

In the sections on the sixes, etc.:

“Cha puggalā – atthekacco puggalo pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhati, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇāti balesu ca vasībhāvaṃ. Atthekacco puggalo…pe… abhisambujjhati, na ca tattha sabbaññutaṃ [M 0.0353] pāpuṇāti, na ca balesu vasibhāvaṃ. Atthekacco puggalo…pe… anabhisambujjhati, diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti, sāvakapāramiñca pāpuṇāti. Atthekacco puggalo…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti, na ca sāvakapāramiṃ pāpuṇāti. Atthekacco puggalo…pe… anabhisambujjhati, na ca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti, anāgāmī hoti anāgantā itthattaṃ. Atthekacco puggalo…pe… anabhisambujjhati, na ca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti, āgāmī hoti āgantā itthatta”nti –

‘Six persons: There is a certain person who, by himself, awakens to the truths concerning things unheard of before, and therein he attains omniscience and mastery over the powers. There is a certain person who … awakens … but does not therein attain omniscience nor mastery over the powers. There is a certain person who … does not awaken … but in this very life makes an end of suffering and attains the perfection of a disciple. There is a certain person who … makes an end of suffering but does not attain the perfection of a disciple. There is a certain person who … does not awaken … nor in this very life does he make an end of suffering; he is a non-returner, not coming back to this state of being. There is a certain person who … does not awaken … nor in this very life does he make an end of suffering; he is a returner, coming back to this state of being.’

Chakkaṃ, “satta puggalā – satta udakūpamā puggalā sakiṃ nimuggo nimuggova hoti, ummujjitvā nimujjati, ummujjitvā ṭhito hoti, ummujjitvā vipassati viloketi, ummujjitvā patarati, ummujjitvā paṭigādhappatto hoti, ummujjitvā tiṇṇo hoti pāraṅgato, thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”tiādinā sattakaṃ, “aṭṭha puggalā – cattāro maggasamaṅgino, cattāro phalasamaṅgino puggalā”ti aṭṭhakaṃ, “nava puggalā – sammāsambuddho paccekasambuddho ubhatobhāgavimutto paññāvimutto kāyasakkhī diṭṭhippatto saddhāvimutto dhammānusārī saddhānusārī”ti navakaṃ, “dasa puggalā – pañcannaṃ idha niṭṭhā, pañcannaṃ idha vihāya niṭṭhā”ti dasakañca mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā pāḷiyaṃ niddeso kato. Tattha chakke paṭhamena padena sammāsambuddho daṭṭhabbo. So hi anācariyako attanā uppāditena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānena arahattamaggañāṇena sabbākārato saccāni abhisambujjhitvā sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇi, dasañāṇabalesu [V 0.0271] ca vasibhāvanti. Dutiyena pana paccekasambuddho daṭṭhabbo. Tatiyena aggasāvako, catutthena avasesā arahanto[M 0.0354], pañcamena anāgāmī, chaṭṭhena sotāpannasakadāgāmino daṭṭhabbā. Te hi “āgantā itthatta”nti vuttāti.

The sixfold section. The sevenfold section begins: ‘Seven persons—seven persons comparable to those in water: one who, having sunk once, remains sunk; one who emerges and then sinks; one who emerges and stays put; one who emerges, looks around, and surveys; one who emerges and swims across; one who emerges and reaches a footing; one who emerges, has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on high ground as a brahmin.’ The eightfold section: ‘Eight persons—four persons endowed with a path, and four persons endowed with its fruit.’ The ninefold section: ‘Nine persons—the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Individually Enlightened One, one liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a bodily witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, a faith-follower.’ The tenfold section: ‘Ten persons—for five there is accomplishment here, and for five there is accomplishment after departing from here.’ Having thus laid down the matrix, the exposition is given in the Pāḷi. Therein, in the sixfold section, by the first term the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is to be understood. For he, being without a teacher, by means of the knowledge of the path of arahantship, which is the basis for the self-produced knowledge of omniscience, fully understood the truths in all their aspects, attained omniscience, and mastery over the ten powers. By the second, the Individually Enlightened One is to be understood. By the third, the chief disciple; by the fourth, the remaining arahants; by the fifth, the non-returner; by the sixth, the stream-enterer and the once-returner are to be understood. For they are the ones spoken of as ‘coming back to this state of being.’

Sattake paṭhamena padena sāsane aniviṭṭhasaddho niyatamicchādiṭṭhidhammehi ekantakāḷakehi samannāgato gahito. So hi samudde udakabhīrukapuriso viya saṃsāre apāye nimuggo nimuggova hoti, na puna bhavato vuṭṭhāti, anantampi kālaṃ bhave eva vicarati sāsanasamāyogābhāvā. Dutiyena padena sāsane paṭiladdhasaddhopi devadattādayo viya saddhādiparihāniyaṃ ṭhito dussīlo gahito. So hi samudde kenaci kāraṇena ummujjitvā puna nimuggo viya sāsanasaddhāya ummujjitvāpi apāye nimujjati eva, ayaṃ pana cirakālātikkamena buddhādīhi, attanā eva vā paccekabodhiñāṇena bhavato uddharaṇīyo hoti sāsane sakiṃ uppannāyapi saddhāya mokkhabhāvena niyamena nibbānāvahattā. Ayameva hissa purimapuggalato viseso, itarathā tassa visuṃ gahaṇe payojanameva na siyāti gahetabbaṃ. Tatiyena sāsane uppannasaddho ṭhitibhāgiyehi sīlādiguṇehi samannāgato gahito. So hi ummujjitvā tīraṃ adisvāva samuddamajjhe nāvādiāgamanaṃ olokento puna animujjitvā uṇṇatappadese ṭhito viya sāsanasaddhāya ummujjitvā nibbānaṃ adisvāva buddhādiṃ olokayamāno sagge, sīlādimhi ṭhito hoti. Catutthena pana sotāpanno gahito. So hi ummujjitvā ṭhito tīraṃ disvā uttaraṇūpāyaṃ vilokayamāno viya lokuttarasaddhāya ummujjitvā nibbānatīraṃ disvā uttaraṇopāyaṃ viloketi. Pañcamena sakadāgāmī gahito. So hi samudde tīraṃ disvā tadabhimukhaṃ [M 0.0355] pataramāno viya paṭhamamaggena nibbānatīraṃ disvā tadabhimukhaṃ dutiyamaggena patarati nāma. Chaṭṭhena anāgāmī gahito. So hi pataritvā tīraṃ upaggamma kaṭippamāṇe udake ṭhito viya arahattasamīpe satikavāṭapatitthe anāvattidhammatāya tatiyamaggena tiṭṭhati. Sattamena pana arahā gahito, so hi taritvā pāraṃ patvā ṭhitapuriso viya cattāro oghe taritvā nibbānatthale ṭhito khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo nāma hotīti.

In the sevenfold section, by the first term is meant one whose faith in the Dispensation is unsettled, who is endowed with the entirely dark qualities of fixed wrong view. For he, like a man in the ocean who is afraid of water, is sunk in saṃsāra, in the plane of misery; having sunk, he remains sunk. He does not rise up again from existence but wanders on in existence for an endless time for lack of a connection with the Dispensation. By the second term is meant an immoral person who, though he has gained faith in the Dispensation, stands in a state of decline in faith and other good qualities, like Devadatta and others. For he, like one who for some reason emerges from the ocean only to sink again, having emerged through faith in the Dispensation, sinks back into the plane of misery. This one, however, can be uplifted from existence after a long time by the Buddhas and others, or by himself through the knowledge of individual enlightenment, because faith, even if it has arisen only once in the Dispensation, by its nature as a share in liberation, is certain to lead to Nibbāna. This is his distinction from the first person; otherwise, there would be no point in mentioning him separately. By the third term is meant one in whom faith in the Dispensation has arisen, who is endowed with qualities such as virtue that partake of stability. For he, like one who, having emerged in the middle of the ocean and not seeing the shore, looks for the arrival of a boat and stays on a high spot without sinking again, is one who, having emerged through faith in the Dispensation and not seeing Nibbāna, looks for a Buddha or others while standing firm in a heavenly world, in virtue, and the like. By the fourth term, a stream-enterer is meant. For he, like one who has emerged, stays put, sees the shore, and looks for a means of crossing, has emerged through supramundane faith, sees the shore of Nibbāna, and looks for the means to cross. By the fifth term, a once-returner is meant. For he, like one in the ocean who sees the shore and swims towards it, having seen the shore of Nibbāna with the first path, is said to swim towards it with the second path. By the sixth term, a non-returner is meant. For he, like one who has swum across, approached the shore, and stands in waist-deep water, stands by means of the third path near to arahantship, established at the threshold of mindfulness due to his nature of non-returning. By the seventh term, an arahant is meant. For he, like a man who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on high ground, has crossed the four floods and stands on the ground of Nibbāna, a brahmin whose taints are destroyed.

Navake ubhatobhāgavimuttoti rūpārūpasamāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena, ariyamaggena samucchedavimokkhena kilesato vimutto, arūpasamāpattiyā vā rūpakāyato, maggena ca nāmakāyatoti imehi ubhatobhāgehi vimuttotipi ubhatobhāgavimutto, so catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ [V 0.0272] ekekato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattappattānaṃ catunnaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya arahattappattaanāgāmino ca vasena pañcavidho, tesu pacchimova nippariyāyato ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma, sesā pariyāyena. Ettha ca rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ kilesakāyato vimuttampi rūpakāyato avimuttaṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ pana tadabhayatopi vimuttaṃ, tasmā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā arahattappattova ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti, na rūpāvacaranti veditabbaṃ. Paññāvimuttoti arahattamaggapaññāya āsavehi vimutto. So hi sukkhavipassako, catūhi rūpāvacarajjhānehi vuṭṭhāya arahattappattā cattāro cāti pañcavidho. Arūpāvacarajjhānesu hi ekasmimpi sati ubhatobhāgavimuttova nāma hoti.

In the ninefold section, one liberated in both ways is liberated from the defilements by the liberation-by-suppression through a form or formless attainment, and by the liberation-by-cutting-off through the noble path. Or, he is liberated from the form-body by a formless attainment and from the mentality-body by the path; being liberated in these two portions, he is one liberated in both ways. He is of five kinds: the four who attain arahantship by emerging from each of the four formless attainments and contemplating formations, and the non-returner who attains arahantship by emerging from the attainment of cessation. Among these, only the last is called one liberated in both ways in the primary sense; the others are so in a secondary sense. Here, the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, though liberated from the body of defilements, is not liberated from the form-body. But a formless attainment is liberated from both. Therefore, it should be understood that only one who has attained arahantship by making a formless attainment his basis is one liberated in both ways, not one who makes a form-sphere jhāna his basis. One liberated by wisdom is liberated from the taints by the wisdom of the path of arahantship. He is a dry-insight meditator; along with the four who attain arahantship by emerging from the four form-sphere jhānas, he is of five kinds. For if there is even one of the formless-sphere jhānas, one is called 'liberated in both ways.'

Kāyasakkhīti rūpārūpajjhānalābhī ariyo. So hi sotāpattimaggaṭṭhavajjitānaṃ channaṃ sekhānaṃ vasena chabbidho. Teneva [M 0.0356] hissa “ekacce āsavā parikkhīṇā”ti niddese vuttaṃ. Sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassa ca na kecipi āsavā parikkhīṇāti vattabbā, parikkhīyissantīti pana vattabbā, arahato pana sabbepi āsavā parikkhīṇā, na ekacceti. So hi phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhī, phuṭṭhānaṃ paṭiladdhānaṃ jhānānaṃ anantaraṃ nāmakāyena nirodhaṃ sacchikarotītipi kāyasakkhī, kāyenāti cettha “nāmakāyena ceva paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca ativijjha passatī”ti vacanato arahattaphalaṃ ṭhapetvā sesamaggaphalānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tena kāyena paṭhamajjhānānantaraṃ nibbānassa sacchikaraṇatopi kāyasakkhīti keci. Diṭṭhippattoti sukkhavipassako, rūpajjhānalābhī ca yathāvutto chabbidho sekho ca, ayaṃ diṭṭhantappattoti diṭṭhippatto. Dassanaṃ diṭṭhi, paṭhamamaggo, tassa anantaraṃ nirodhappattoti attho. Diṭṭhappattotipi pāṭho, tassa paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ puna pattoti attho.

A 'bodily witness' is a noble one who has attained the form and formless jhānas. He is sixfold by way of the six trainees, excluding the one established in the stream-entry path. For this reason, it is stated in the exposition: 'Some taints are destroyed.' But for one established in the stream-entry path, it should not be said that any taints are destroyed; rather, it should be said that they will be destroyed. For the Arahant, however, all taints are destroyed, not just some. He is called a bodily witness because he directly realizes what is touched. He is also a bodily witness because, immediately after the jhānas that have been obtained, he realizes cessation with the mentality-body. Here, 'with the body' means that 'he realizes the ultimate truth both with the mentality-body and by penetrating it with wisdom'; by this statement, this is a designation for the remaining paths and fruits, excluding the fruit of arahantship. Some say he is a bodily witness because he realizes Nibbāna with the body immediately after the first jhāna. A 'one attained to view' is a dry-insight meditator, and also a trainee who has attained the form jhānas, being one of the six kinds described above. This one is called 'attained to view' because he has attained the state of having vision. Vision is view, which is the first path; the meaning is that he attains cessation immediately after it. There is also the reading 'one who has attained what was seen'; the meaning is that having seen Nibbāna with the first path, he attains it again.

Saddhāvimuttoti sukkhavipassako, rūpajjhānalābhī ca yathāvutto chabbidho sekho ca. Ayaṃ hi saddahanto vimuttoti saddhāvimutto. Kathaṃ panetassa diṭṭhippattato nānattanti? Āgamanīyapaṭipadāya. Diṭṭhippatto hi paññāsampadāya pubbabhāge vipassanāya kilese appadukkhena vikkhambhento āgato, saddhāvimutto pana saddhābahulatāya kilese dukkhena vikkhambhento āgato. Etameva hi bhedaṃ sandhāya niddese “ekacce āsavā parikkhīṇā honti, no ca kho yathādiṭṭhippattassā”ti vuttaṃ.

A 'faith-liberated one' is a dry-insight meditator, and also the sixfold trainee who has attained the form jhānas, as previously described. Indeed, this one is 'faith-liberated' because he is liberated by believing. But how is there a difference between this one and the one attained to view? By the path of approach. Indeed, the one attained to view arrives having suppressed the defilements with little difficulty through insight in the preliminary stage of wisdom. The faith-liberated one, however, arrives having suppressed the defilements with difficulty through the predominance of faith. It is precisely this distinction that is referred to in the exposition when it is said, 'Some taints are destroyed, but not as in the case of the one attained to view.'

Dhammānusārīti [V 0.0273] yassa sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, ayaṃ paññāsaṅkhātena dhammena sarati anussaratīti dhammānusārī, sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Phale pana patte diṭṭhippatto nāma hoti. Saddhānusārīti yassa [M 0.0357] sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, ayaṃ saddhāya sarati anussaratīti saddhānusārī, sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Phale pana patte saddhāvimutto nāma hoti.

A 'Dhamma-follower' is one for whom the faculty of wisdom is predominant at the moment of the stream-entry path. This one follows and recollects by means of the Dhamma, which is characterized as wisdom—thus he is called a 'Dhamma-follower.' This is the name for one established in the stream-entry path. Upon attaining the fruit, however, he is called 'one attained to view.' A 'faith-follower' is one for whom the faculty of faith is predominant at the moment of the stream-entry path. This one follows and recollects through faith—thus he is called a 'faith-follower.' This is the name for one established in the stream-entry path. Upon attaining the fruit, however, he is called 'faith-liberated.'

Lokuttaradhammaṃ hi nibbattentānaṃ dve dhurāni nāma, dve abhinivesā nāma, dve sīsāni nāma. Tattha saddhādhuraṃ paññādhuranti dve dhurāni nāma. Eko pana samathābhiniveso, eko vipassanābhinivesoti dve abhinivesā. Eko ca arahattaṃ matthakaṃ pāpuṇanto ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti, eko paññāvimuttoti imāni dve sīsāni nāma. Ye hi keci lokuttaraṃ dhammaṃ nibbattenti, sabbe te dve ime dhamme dhuraṃ katvā imesu dvīsu ṭhānesu abhinivisitvā imehi dvīhi ṭhānehi vimuccanti. Tesu yo bhikkhu aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā samathavasena abhiniviṭṭho aññataraṃ arūpasamāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī nāma. Parato pana chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhī nāma. Arahattaphalaṃ patte ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma.

For those who bring forth the supramundane Dhamma, there are indeed two vehicles, two inclinations, and two culminations. Herein, the vehicle of faith and the vehicle of wisdom are the two vehicles. One is the inclination to serenity, the other the inclination to insight—these are the two inclinations. One, reaching arahantship as the culmination, becomes liberated in both ways, while the other becomes liberated by wisdom—these are the two culminations. All who bring forth the supramundane Dhamma take these two qualities as a vehicle, are inclined to these two positions, and are liberated by means of these two positions. Among them, a monk who has attained the eight attainments, taking wisdom as his vehicle, inclined by way of serenity, making one of the formless attainments his basis, establishes insight and attains arahantship—he is called a 'Dhamma-follower' at the moment of the stream-entry path. Thereafter, in the six instances, he is called a 'body-witness.' Upon attaining the fruit of arahantship, he is called 'liberated in both ways.'

Aparo paññameva dhuraṃ katvā vipassanāvasena abhiniviṭṭho suddhasaṅkhāre vā rūpāvacarajjhānesu vā aññataraṃ sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayampi sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī nāma. Parato pana chasu ṭhānesu diṭṭhippatto nāma, arahattaṃ patte paññāvimutto nāma.

Another, taking wisdom as his vehicle, inclined by way of insight, contemplates either the bare formations or one of the form-sphere jhānas, and attains arahantship. He too is called a 'Dhamma-follower' at the moment of the stream-entry path. Thereafter, in the six instances, he is called 'one attained to view.' Upon attaining arahantship, he is called 'liberated by wisdom.'

Aparo pana aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī saddhaṃ dhuraṃ katvā samādhivasena abhiniviṭṭho aññataraṃ arūpasamāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī nāma, parato chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhīyeva [M 0.0358] nāma. Arahattaṃ patte ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma. Aparo saddhameva dhuraṃ katvā vipassanāvasena abhiniviṭṭho suddhasaṅkhāre vā rūpāvacarajjhānesu vā aññataraṃ sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayampi sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī nāma, parato chasu ṭhānesu saddhāvimutto nāma. Arahattappatte paññāvimutto nāma. Ime satta puggalā sammāsambuddhapaccekasambuddhehi saddhiṃ nava loke aggadakkhiṇeyyā nāmāti.

Another, who has attained the eight attainments, taking faith as his vehicle, inclined by way of concentration, making one of the formless attainments his basis, establishes insight and attains arahantship. He is called a 'faith-follower' at the moment of the stream-entry path. Thereafter, in the six instances, he is called a 'body-witness.' Upon attaining arahantship, he is called 'liberated in both ways.' Another, taking faith as his vehicle, inclined by way of insight, contemplates either the bare formations or one of the form-sphere jhānas, and attains arahantship. He too is called a 'faith-follower' at the moment of the stream-entry path. Thereafter, in the six instances, he is called 'liberated by faith.' Upon attaining arahantship, he is called 'liberated by wisdom.' These seven persons, together with the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas, are called the nine in the world worthy of the highest offerings.

Dasake [V 0.0274] pañcannaṃ idha niṭṭhāti sattakkhattuparamo, kolaṃkolo, ekabījī, sakadāgāmī kāmāvacarapaṭisandhiko, arahā cāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ idha kāmāvacarabhūmiyaññeva anupādisesanibbānasaṅkhātā niṭṭhāti attho. Kāmāvacarattabhāve eva hi ete parinibbāyanti, nāññasmiṃ. Pañcannaṃ idha vihāya niṭṭhāti antarāparinibbāyī upahaccaparinibbāyī asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī cāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ idha kāmāvacare attabhāvaṃ vihāya vijahitvā brahmattabhāve ṭhitānaññeva niṭṭhāti attho. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepato pāḷinayena saddhiṃ atthanicchayo, vitthāro pana puggalapaññattipāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu (pu. pa. mātikā 1 ādayo; pu. pa. aṭṭha. mātikāvaṇṇanā 1) gahetabboti.

In the section on the tens, the consummation of five occurs in this very realm: the one who goes at most seven times, the one who goes from family to family, the one-seeder, the once-returner who takes rebirth in the sensual sphere, and the Arahant. The meaning is that the consummation for these five, known as Nibbāna without residue, occurs right here in the sensual sphere itself. Indeed, they attain final Nibbāna only in a sensual-sphere existence, not in another. The consummation of five occurs after abandoning this realm: the one who attains Nibbāna in the interval, the one who attains Nibbāna upon landing, the one who attains Nibbāna without exertion, the one who attains Nibbāna with exertion, and the one who is bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. The meaning is that the consummation for these five occurs only while they are established in a Brahma existence, having abandoned and relinquished their existence in the sensual sphere. The rest here is of obvious meaning. This is the brief determination of meaning here, in accordance with the Pāli text. For the detailed explanation, however, one should refer to the Pāli text and commentaries on the Puggalapaññatti (Pp. mātikā 1 onwards; Pp. aṭṭha. mātikāvaṇṇanā 1).

Mohavicchedaniyā abhidhammamātikatthavaṇṇanāya

Of the Mohavicchedanī, an Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix

Puggalapaññattimātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Puggalapaññatti Matrix is Completed.

5. Kathāvatthumātikā

5. The Matrix of the Kathāvatthu

Puggalakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on Persons

Idāni [M 0.0359][V 0.0275] kathāvatthumātikāya atthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo hoti. Tattha anuttānatthato tāva “puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti ayaṃ pucchā, “āmantā”ti ayaṃ paṭijānanā. Kassa panāyaṃ pucchā, kassa paṭijānanāti? “Asukassā”ti na vattabbā. Na hi bhagavā paravādīhi saddhiṃ viggāhikakathaṃ kathento imaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapesi, puggalapaññattidesanādiṃ pana nissāya “paramatthato attā nāma atthī”tiādinā anāgate vipallāsagāhibhikkhūnaṃ, paravādīnañca nānappakāradiṭṭhiṭṭhānavisodhanatthaṃ moggaliputtatissattherassa vādanayadassanavasena puggalavādametaṃ ārabbha tantivasena mātikaṃ ṭhapento sakavādiparavādīnaṃ pucchāvisajjanadosāropananiggahapāpanādivacanapaṭivacanavaseneva ṭhapesi, tasmā tadatthassa sukhāvadhāraṇatthaṃ sakavādīpucchā paravādīpucchā sakavādīpaṭiññā paravādīpaṭiññāti evaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetvā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

Now begins the method of explaining the meaning of the Kathāvatthu Matrix. Here, first, regarding the meaning that is not readily apparent, the question is: 'Is a person apprehended in the real and ultimate sense?' The acknowledgment is: 'Yes.' But whose question is this, and whose acknowledgment? It should not be said, 'It is so-and-so's.' For the Blessed One did not establish this matrix while engaging in disputatious talk with those of other doctrines. Rather, relying on the teaching of the designation of persons and so forth, and for the purpose of purifying the various standpoints of wrong views held by monks in the future who would grasp at perversions—thinking, 'In the ultimate sense, a self exists'—and also by those of other doctrines, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa established this matrix. Demonstrating the method of debate, he established it based on the doctrine of the person as its central theme, setting it forth entirely by way of statements and counter-statements between his own school and other schools, consisting of questions, answers, imputation of faults, refutation, leading to a conclusion, and so on. Therefore, for the easy ascertainment of that meaning, we will provide an explanation of the meaning by showing the division as follows: the question of one's own school, the question of another school, the acknowledgment of one's own school, and the acknowledgment of another school.

“Puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti ayaṃ sakavādīpucchā, tāya ca “ye ‘atthi puggalo’ti evaṃladdhikā puggalavādino, te evaṃ pucchitabbā”ti dīpeti. Ke pana te puggalavādinoti? Sāsane vajjiputtakā ceva sammitiyā ca bahiddhā bahū aññatitthiyā ca. Kadā panete sāsane uppannāti? Parinibbānato dutiye vassasate. Bhagavati kira parinibbute mahākassapattherena samussāhitehi tappamukhehi vasigaṇehi subhaddavuḍḍhapabbajitādīnaṃ pāpabhikkhūnaṃ pavesokāsanisedhanatthaṃ ajātasatturājānaṃ sahāyaṃ labhitvā dhammavinayasarīraṃ saṅgahaṃ āropetvā sāsane acale pavattāpite tato vassasatassa accayena vesāliyaṃ vajjiputtakehi dīpitāni [V 0.0276] dasa vatthūni madditvā te ca bhikkhū [M 0.0360] niggahetvā yasattherasamussāhitehi vasigaṇehi puna dhammavinayasaṅgahe kate tehi niggahitā dasasahassā vajjiputtakā kañci dubbalarājānaṃ balaṃ labhitvā mūlasaṅgahaṃ bhinditvā attano anācārānukūlavacanaṃ pakkhipitvā buddhavacanañca chaḍḍetvā mahāsaṅgītīhi visuṃ dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ katvā mahāsaṅghikācariyakulaṃ nāma akaṃsu. Parisuddhasāsanaṃ pana therehi paripālitattā “theravādo”ti paññāyi, imesu pana dvīsu vādesu mahāsaṅghikato bhijjitvā ekabyohārikā, gokulikā ca, tato paṇṇattivādā, bahuliyā, cetiyavādā cāti pañca vādā, mahāsaṅghikehi pana saddhiṃ cha ācariyakulāni nāma jātāni. Tathā theravādato bhijjitvā mahisāsakā, vajjiputtakā ca, tato dhammuttariyā, bhadrayānikā, channāgārikā, sammitiyā ca, mahisāsakato dhammaguttikā, sabbatthikā ca, tato kassapikā, tato saṅkantikā, tato suttavādā cāti ime ekādasa vādā jātā. Te purimehi chahi saddhiṃ sattarasa bhinnavādā dutiye vassasate uppannā, theravādo pana ekova asambhinnako, tena saddhiṃ sāsane aṭṭhārasa nikāyā jātāti veditabbā, ye “aṭṭhārasācariyakulānī”ti pavuccanti. Imesaṃ pana aṭṭhārasannaṃ ācariyavādānaṃ vasena āyatiṃ sāsanassa āluḷanaṃ ñatvā sammāsambuddho dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ accayena sāsane paṭiladdhasaddhena asokena dhammaraññā bāhirake anoloketvā sāsane eva lābhasakkāre pavattante lābhasakkāratthāya sāsanavesaṃ gahetvā sakāni sakāni diṭṭhigatāni tathato dīpentesu dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatikesu yathāvuttasattarasācariyakulesu ca samayakusalatāya vicinitvā setakāni datvā uppabbājitesu parisuddhe mahābhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā moggaliputtatissattherassa yāni tadā uppannāni vatthūni, yāni ca āyatiṃ uppajjissanti, sabbānipi [M 0.0361] tāni attano satthārā dinnamātikāmukhamattena paṭibāhitvā suttasahassapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ parappavādamathanaṃ āyatilakkhaṇaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ mātikāvibhajanavasena bhāsitvā taṃ tatiyasaṅgītiyaṃ saṅgahaṃ āropetvā āluḷitaṃ sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ samatthabhāvaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pakāsanatthaṃ āyativādappaṭibāhananayadassanavasena imaṃ kathāvatthumātikaṃ vatvā therassa okāsaṃ ṭhapento tassā vibhaṅgaṃ na avocāti veditabbaṃ.

“A person is found in the true and ultimate sense”—this is the question of the proponent of his own thesis, and by it, it is shown that those who hold the view “a person exists,” the personalists, should be questioned thus. But who are these personalists? Within the Dispensation, they are the Vajjiputtakas and the Sammitiyas, and outside it, many other sectarians. When did they arise in the Dispensation? In the second century after the Parinibbāna. It is said that after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, having rallied the assembly of masters with him as their chief, with the support of King Ajātasattu, prevented the entry of wicked monks like the aged Subhadda and others, and having established the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya in a compilation, set the Dispensation in motion, unshaken. Then, after a hundred years had passed, the ten points put forth by the Vajjiputtakas in Vesālī were crushed and those monks were censured. Then the Elder Yasa, having rallied the assembly of masters with him as their chief, again made a compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. Those ten thousand Vajjiputtakas who had been expelled, having gained the support of some weak king, broke the original compilation, inserted words agreeable to their own misconduct, discarded the Buddha’s words, and, having made a separate compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya at a great council, formed what is called the Mahāsaṅghika school. The pure Dispensation, however, having been preserved by the Elders, came to be known as the Theravāda. From these two schools, the Mahāsaṅghikas split into the Ekabyohārikas and the Gokulikas; and from them, the Paṇṇattivādins, the Bahuliyas, and the Cetiyavādins—thus five schools. Together with the Mahāsaṅghikas, six schools of teachers arose. Similarly, from the Theravāda split the Mahīsāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas; from the latter, the Dhammuttariyas, the Bhadrayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Sammitiyas; and from the Mahīsāsakas, the Dhammaguttikas and the Sabbatthivādins; from the latter, the Kassapikas; from them, the Saṅkantikas; and from them, the Suttavādins—thus these eleven schools arose. These, together with the previous six, were seventeen divergent schools that arose in the second century. The Theravāda, however, remained one and undivided. Thus, it should be understood that eighteen schools arose in the Dispensation, which are called the “eighteen schools of teachers.” The Perfectly Enlightened One had foreseen the future turmoil of the Dispensation on account of these eighteen schools of teachers. After two hundred years had passed, faith having been restored in the Dispensation by King Asoka, the Righteous King, and when those who, for the sake of gain and honor that arose within the Dispensation itself without regard for outsiders, had taken up the guise of the Dispensation and were proclaiming their own views as true—those among the holders of the sixty-two views and the aforementioned seventeen schools of teachers—had been skillfully investigated, given white robes, and expelled, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, sitting amidst the purified great Saṅgha of monks, refuted all the issues that had arisen then and that would arise in the future by means of the outline given by his Teacher. He spoke the Kathāvatthu—adorned with a thousand suttas, a crusher of opposing views, characterized by its relevance for the future—by way of classifying the outline. Having had it included in the Third Council, and to demonstrate to the Saṅgha of monks his ability to uplift the agitated Dispensation and to show the method for refuting future views, he spoke this outline of the Kathāvatthu, leaving the opportunity for its analysis to himself as the Elder. Thus it should be understood that he did not speak its detailed explanation.

Tattha puggaloti attā jīvo satto. Upalabbhatīti paññāya upagantvā labbhati, ñāyatīti attho. Saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti ettha saccikaṭṭhoti māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtākārena aggahetabbo bhūtaṭṭho. Paramatthoti anussavādivasena aggahetabbo uttamattho. Ubhayenāpi yathā rūpavedanādayo [V 0.0277] dhammā bhūtena sabhāvena upalabbhanti, evaṃ tāva “puggalo upalabbhatī”ti pucchati. Paravādī “āmantā”ti paṭijānāti. Paṭijānanañhi katthaci “āma bhante”ti āgacchati, katthaci “āmo”ti āgacchati, idha pana “āmantā”ti āgataṃ. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – paravādī hi yasmā bhagavatā “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”tiādinā (a. ni. 4.95-96) puggalo pakāsito, bhagavā ca avitathavādī, tasmā so “saccikaṭṭhaparamattheneva atthī”ti laddhiṃ gahetvā “āmantā”ti paṭijānāti.

Here, ‘person’ (puggala) refers to the self, the living being, the creature. ‘Is found’ (upalabbhati) means it is obtained by approaching through wisdom; it is known—this is the meaning. ‘In the true and ultimate sense’ (saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena)—here, ‘true’ (saccikaṭṭha) means the real state, not to be grasped in an unreal form like illusions or mirages. ‘Ultimate’ (paramattha) refers to the supreme meaning, not to be grasped through tradition or hearsay. By means of both, just as phenomena like form and feeling are found by their real, intrinsic nature, so too he asks, ‘Is a person found thus?’ The opponent agrees, saying, ‘Indeed.’ For agreement comes in some cases as ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ in others as ‘Yes,’ but here it comes as ‘Indeed.’ The implication here is this: The opponent, because the Blessed One has declared in passages like ‘There is a person striving for their own welfare’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.95-96), and because the Blessed One speaks truth, holds the view that ‘a person exists in the true and ultimate sense’ and thus agrees, saying, ‘Indeed.’

Athassa tādisassa lesavacanassa chalavādassa okāsaṃ adadamāno sakavādī “yo saccikaṭṭho”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yvāyaṃ heṭṭhā rūpavedanādiko dhammappabhedo āgato, na sammutisaccavasena, nāpi anussavādivasena gahetabbo, attano pana bhūtatāya eva saccikaṭṭho, attapaccakkhatāya ca paramattho, so [M 0.0362] tathāpaṭiññāto puggalo tato tena saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena ākārena upalabbhati, yathā ruppanānubhavanādinā sakiyenākārena puna saccikaṭṭhaparamattho upalabbhati, kiṃ tava puggalopi evaṃ upalabbhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na hevaṃ vattabbeti avajānanā paravādissa. So hi tathārūpaṃ puggalaṃ anicchanto avajānāti. Na hi attā nāma khandhādivimutto koci dissati aññatra byāmohamattā. Tatrāyaṃ padacchedo – na hi evaṃ vattabbeti. “Na ha eva”ntipi paṭhanti, dvinnampi evaṃ na vattabboti attho.

Then, not allowing any room for such prevarication or evasive speech, the proponent of his own thesis says, “That which is the true…” Here, the meaning is this: That classification of phenomena, such as form, feeling, etc., which was mentioned before, is not to be grasped based on conventional truth, nor based on tradition, etc., but is true by its own being-so, and ultimate by its own direct experience. That person, acknowledged in this way, is found by that mode of the true and ultimate sense, just as that which is true and ultimate is again found by its own characteristic, such as being subject to affliction and experiencing. Thus, it is said, ‘Is your person also found in this way?’ ‘It should not be said thus’ is the opponent's rejection. For the opponent, not wanting such a person, rejects it. Indeed, no self is seen apart from the aggregates, except as mere delusion. Here, the word division is: ‘It should not be said thus.’ Some read it as ‘Indeed not,’ but for both, the meaning is: it should not be said thus.

Ājānāhi niggahanti sakavādivacanaṃ. Yasmā te purimāya vattabbapaṭiññāya pacchimā navattabbapaṭiññā, pacchimāya ca purimā na sandhīyati, tasmā niggahaṃ patto, taṃ niggahaṃ dosaṃ aparādhaṃ ājānāhi, sampaṭicchāhīti attho. Evaṃ niggahaṃ ājānāpetvā idāni taṃ ṭhapanāya ceva anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanānañca vasena pākaṭaṃ karonto “hañci puggalo”tiādimāha. Tattha hañcīti yadi, sace puggalo upalabbhatīti attho. Ayaṃ tāva paravādīpakkhassa anuvadanena ṭhapanato niggahapatiṭṭhāpanato niggahapāpanāropanānaṃ lakkhaṇabhūtā anulomaṭṭhapanā nāma. Tena vata retiādi anulomapakkhe niggahassa pāpikattā anulomapāpanā nāma. Tattha tenāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Vatāti okappanavacanaṃ niyamavacanaṃ. Reti āmantanavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tena vata re vattabbe vata re hambho bhadramukha tena kāraṇena vattabbo evāti attho. Yaṃ tattha vadesītiādi anulomapakkhe niggahassa āropitattā anulomaropanā nāma. Yañcassa pariyosāne “micchā”ti padaṃ, tassa purato “idaṃ [V 0.0278] te”ti āharitabbaṃ. Idaṃ te micchāti ayañhettha attho. Evaṃ uparipi[M 0.0363]. Parato pāḷiyampi etaṃ āgatameva. No ce pana vattabbetiādi “na hevaṃ vattabbe”ti paṭikkhittapakkhassa anuvadanena ṭhapitattā paṭilomato niggahapāpanāropanānaṃ lakkhaṇabhūtā paṭilomaṭṭhapanā nāma. No ca vata retiādi paṭilomapakkhe niggahassa pāpitattā paṭilomapāpanā nāma. Puna yaṃ tattha vadesītiādi paṭilomapakkhe niggahassa āropitattā paṭilomaropanā nāma.

“Know the refutation!”—this is the proponent’s statement. Since your earlier assertion, ‘it should be said,’ and your later assertion, ‘it should not be said,’ do not reconcile—and the later with the earlier—therefore you have incurred a refutation. Acknowledge that refutation, that fault, that offense; accept it—this is the meaning.
