Having thus made him acknowledge the refutation, now, to establish it and to make it evident by way of forward and reverse application and imposition, he says, ‘If, indeed, a person…’ Here, ‘if indeed’ (hañci) means ‘if a person is found’—this is the meaning. This, first, is called ‘forward establishment’ because it is an establishment by way of repeating the opponent’s position, thereby establishing the refutation, and it has the characteristics of applying and imposing the refutation. Then, ‘therefore, indeed, reverend…’ and so on is called ‘forward application’ because it applies the refutation to the forward position. Here, ‘therefore’ (tena) is a word of reason; ‘indeed’ (vata) is a word of conviction or determination; ‘reverend’ (re) is a term of address. This means: ‘Therefore, indeed, O reverend one, it must be said; O worthy one, O good sir, for that reason it must be said’—this is the meaning. ‘And what you say there…’ and so on is called ‘forward imposition’ because the refutation is imposed on the forward position. At the end of this, where the word ‘wrong’ appears, before it, the phrase ‘this of yours’ should be supplied. ‘This of yours is wrong,’ this is the meaning here. The same applies above. Later, this also appears in the Pāli text itself. ‘But if it should not be said…’ and so on is called ‘reverse establishment’ because it is established by repeating the rejected position, and it has the characteristics of applying and imposing the refutation in reverse. ‘Indeed, it should not…’ and so on is called ‘reverse application’ because it applies the refutation to the reverse position. Again, ‘and what you say there…’ and so on is called ‘reverse imposition’ because the refutation is imposed on the reverse position.

Tatrāyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṅkhepattho – yadi puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena, tena vata bho so upalabbhatīti vattabbo. Yaṃ pana tattha vadesi “vattabbo kho purimapañhe ‘saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhatī’ti no ca vattabbo dutiyapañhe ‘tato so puggalo upalabbhatī’”ti, idaṃ te micchāti evaṃ tāva anulomato ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā honti.

Here, the concise meaning from the beginning is as follows: If a person is found in the truly real, ultimate sense, then indeed, sir, it must be said that he is found. But what you say there—‘It must be said in the first question, “He is found in the truly real, ultimate sense,” but it must not be said in the second question, “therefore, that person is found”’—this of yours is wrong. Thus far, the establishment, application, and imposition proceed in the forward order.

Atha na vattabbo dutiyapañhe “tato so puggalo upalabbhatī”ti, purimapañhepi na vattabbova. Yaṃ pana tattha vadesi “vattabbo kho purimapañhe ‘saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhatī’ti, no ca vattabbo dutiyapañhe ‘tato so puggalo upalabbhatī’”ti, idaṃ te micchāti evaṃ paṭilomato ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā honti. Evametaṃ niggahassa ca anulomato dvinnaṃ, paṭilomato dvinnanti catunnaṃ pāpanāropanānañca vuttattā upalabbhatītiādikaṃ anulomapañcakaṃ nāma. Ettha ca kiñcāpi anulomato pāpanāropanāhi eko, paṭilomato pāpanāropanāhi ekoti dve niggahā katā, ājānāhi niggahanti etasseva pana paṭhamassa niggahassa dvīhākārehi āropitattā ekovāyaṃ niggahoti gahetabbo. Paṭhamo niggaho.

Then, if in the second question it should not be said, 'Therefore, that person is found,' then in the first question also it should not be said. But what you say there—'In the first question, it should be said, “He is found in the truly real, ultimate sense,” but in the second question, it should not be said, “Therefore, that person is found”'—this of yours is wrong. Thus, in the reverse order, there are establishment, application, and imposition. In this way, because two applications and impositions of the refutation have been stated in the forward manner and two in the reverse manner, making four, this section beginning with ‘is found’ is called the ‘forward pentad’. Here, although one refutation is made by way of forward application and imposition, and one by way of reverse application and imposition—thus two refutations are made—the phrase ‘Know the refutation!’ refers to this very first refutation, which, being imposed in two ways, should be understood as a single refutation. The first refutation.

Idāni [M 0.0364] paccanīkanayo hoti. Tattha puggalo nupalabbhatīti pucchā paravādissa. Sakavādī yathā rūpavedanādayo dhammā upalabbhanti, evaṃ anupalabbhanīyato “āmantā”ti paṭijānāti. Puna itaro attanā adhippetaṃ saccikaṭṭhaṃyeva sandhāya “yo saccikaṭṭho”tiādimāha. Sammutisaccaparamatthasaccāni vā ekato katvāpi paravādī evamāha. Sakavādī puggalo hi upādāyapaññattisabbhāvatopi dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ ekato katvā pucchitattāpi “na heva”nti paṭikkhipati. Idāni kiñcāpi tena paṭhamaṃ paramatthasaccavasena nupalabbhanīyatā sampaṭicchitā, pacchā pana sammutisaccavasena vā vomissakavasena vā paṭikkhittā. Paravādī pana [V 0.0279] “nupalabbhatī”ti vacanasāmaññamattaṃ chalavādaṃ nissāya “yaṃ tayā paṭhamaṃ paṭiññātaṃ, taṃ pacchā paṭikkhitta”nti bhaṇḍanassa paṭibhaṇḍanaṃ viya attano katassa niggahakammassa paṭikammaṃ karonto “ājānāhi paṭikamma”nti āha. Idāni yathāssa anulomapañcake sakavādinā vādaṭṭhapanaṃ katvā anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanāhi paravādiniggaho pākaṭo kato, evaṃ paṭikammaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto “hañci puggalo”tiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva atthato veditabbaṃ. Yasmā panettha ṭhapanā nāma paravādipakkhassa ṭhapanato “ayaṃ tava doso”ti dassetuṃ ṭhapanamattameva hoti, na niggahassa vā paṭikammassa vā pākaṭībhāvakaraṇaṃ, pāpanāropanāhi panassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ hoti, tasmā idaṃ anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanānaṃ vasena catūhākārehi paṭikammassa katattā paṭikammacatukkaṃ nāmāti ekaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now comes the method of counter-argument. Here, the opponent’s question is, ‘Is a person not found?’ The proponent acknowledges with ‘Yes’ that the person is not found in the same way that phenomena such as form and feeling are found. Then the other, referring to what he himself intends as the truly real sense, says, ‘That which is the truly real sense,’ and so on. The opponent speaks thus even when combining conventional truth and ultimate truth. The proponent, however, rejects this with ‘Not so,’ because the person, although existing as a concept dependent on grasping, is being questioned by combining both truths. Now, although he initially accepted the person’s non-apprehensibility from the standpoint of ultimate truth, he later rejected it from the standpoint of conventional truth or a mixed standpoint. The opponent, however, relying on the mere verbal similarity in the statement ‘is not found’ as a deceptive argument, makes a counter-argument to the dispute, as if performing a counter-action to the act of refutation done to him, saying, ‘Know the counter-action!’ Now, just as in the forward pentad the proponent established the argument and made the opponent’s refutation clear through forward and reverse application and imposition, so too here, making the counter-action clear, he says, ‘If indeed a person,’ and so on. Its meaning should be understood in the way explained above. For here, the ‘establishment’ is merely an establishment to point out the opponent's fault by saying, ‘This is your error,’ and does not make the refutation or the counter-action evident; it is through application and imposition that it becomes evident. Therefore, because this counter-action is made in four ways through forward and reverse application and imposition, it should be understood as the ‘counter-action quartet,’ which is one quartet.

Evaṃ paṭikammaṃ katvā idāni yvāssa anulomapañcake sakavādinā niggaho kato, tassa tameva chalavādaṃ nissāya dukkaṭabhāvaṃ dassento “tvaṃ ce pana maññasī”tiādimāha. Tattha tvaṃ ce pana maññasīti yadi tvaṃ maññasi. “Vattabbe [M 0.0365] kho”ti idaṃ paccanīke “āmantā”ti paṭijānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, “no ca vattabbe”ti idaṃ pana “na hevā”ti avajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tena tava tatthāti tena kāraṇena tvaṃyeva tasmiṃ “yo nupalabbhatī”ti pakkhe hevaṃ paṭijānanti “āmantā”ti evaṃ paṭijānanto. Hevaṃ niggahetabbeti puna “na hevā”ti avajānanto evaṃ niggahetabbo. Atha taṃ niggaṇhāmāti athevaṃ niggaṇhanārahaṃ taṃ niggaṇhāma, suniggahito ca hosīti sakena matena niggahitattā suniggahito ca bhavasi. Evamassa niggahetabbabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ niggaṇhanto “hañcī”tiādimāha. Tattha ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Pariyosāne pana idaṃ te micchāti idaṃ tava vacanaṃ micchā hotīti attho. Idaṃ chalavādena catūhi ākārehi niggahassa katattā niggahacatukkaṃ nāma.

Having made this counter-action, he now shows the wrongness of the refutation made by the proponent in the forward pentad, relying on that same deceptive argument, and says, ‘But if you think…’ and so on. Here, ‘But if you think’ means ‘if you think.’ ‘It should be said’ is said with reference to the acknowledgment with ‘Yes’ in the counter-argument section. ‘But it should not be said’ is said with reference to the rejection with ‘Not so.’ The phrase ‘Therefore, in that case, for you’ means: for that reason, you yourself, in that position of ‘who is not found,’ acknowledging by saying ‘Yes’… The phrase ‘should be refuted thus’ means: one who rejects again by saying ‘Not so’ should be refuted in this way. Then, ‘we refute you’ means: we refute you who are thus worthy of refutation. And ‘you will be well-refuted’ means: you will be well-refuted because you are refuted by your own opinion. Having thus shown that he is to be refuted, now, refuting him, he says, ‘If indeed…’ and so on. Here, the establishment, application, and imposition should be understood in the way explained above. At the conclusion, however, ‘this of yours is wrong’ means ‘this statement of yours is wrong.’ This is called the ‘refutation quartet’ because the refutation is made in four ways through a deceptive argument.

Evaṃ niggahaṃ katvāpi idāni “yadi ayaṃ mayā tava matena kato niggaho dunniggaho, yopi mama tayā heṭṭhā anulomapañcake kato niggaho, sopi dunniggaho”ti dassento “ese ce dunniggahite”tiādimāha. Tattha ese ce dunniggahiteti eso ce tava vādo mayā dunniggahito, atha vā eso ce tava mayā kato niggaho dunniggaho. Hevamevaṃ tattha dakkhāti tatthāpi tayā mama heṭṭhā kate niggahe evamevaṃ passa. Idāni yvāssa heṭṭhā sakavādinā niggaho [V 0.0280] kato, taṃ “vattabbe kho”tiādivacanena dassetvā puna taṃ niggahaṃ aniggahabhāvaṃ upanento “no ca mayaṃ tayā”tiādimāha. Tattha no ca mayaṃ tayā tattha hetāya paṭiññāyātiādīsu ayamattho – yasmā so tayā mama kato niggaho dunniggaho, tasmā mayaṃ tayā tattha anulomapañcake “āmantā”ti etāya paṭiññāya evaṃ paṭijānantā puna “na hevā”ti paṭikkhepe katepi [M 0.0366] “ājānāhi niggaha”nti evaṃ niggahetabbāyeva, evaṃ aniggahetabbampi maṃ niggaṇhāsi, īdisena pana niggahena dunniggahitā mayaṃ homa. Idāni yaṃ niggahaṃ sandhāya dunniggahitā ca homāti avoca, taṃ dassetuṃ “hañci puggalo…pe… idaṃ te micchā”ti āha. Evamidaṃ anulomapaṭilomato catūhi pāpanāropanāhi niggahassa upanītattā upanayanacatukkaṃ nāma hoti.

Having thus made a refutation, now, showing, 'If this refutation made by me according to your view is a bad refutation, then that refutation made of me by you previously in the fivefold direct implication is also a bad refutation,' he says, 'If this is badly refuted,' and so on. Here, 'If this is badly refuted' means: if this statement of yours is badly refuted by me, or if this refutation of yours made by me is a bad refutation. In the same way, 'see it thus there' means: in that refutation made of me by you previously, see it in the same way. Now, having shown the refutation made previously by the proponent with the words, 'It should be said,' etc., and then bringing that refutation to the state of not being a refutation, he says, 'But we are not by you,' and so on. Herein, in 'But we are not by you there for that reason, by that admission,' and so on, the meaning is this: because that refutation made of me by you is a bad refutation, therefore we, who in the fivefold direct implication acknowledged with 'Yes,' thus admitting, are then, when a rejection is made with 'Not so,' still to be refuted by you with 'Acknowledge the refutation.' But you refute me who should not be refuted in this way. Thus, by such a refutation, we are badly refuted. Now, to show which refutation he meant when he said, 'We are badly refuted,' he says, 'If a person... this is wrong for you.' Thus, because this refutation is presented through four applications and imputations by way of direct and inverse implication, it is called the 'fourfold application'.

Idāni na hevaṃ niggahetabbetiādikaṃ niggamanacatukkaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha na hevaṃ niggahetabbeti yathāhaṃ tayā niggahito, na hi evaṃ niggahetabbo, etassa hi niggahassa dunniggahabhāvo mayā sādhito. Tena hīti tena kāraṇena. Yasmā esa niggaho dunniggaho, tasmā yaṃ maṃ niggaṇhāsi. Hañci puggalo…pe… idaṃ te micchāti idaṃ niggaṇhanaṃ tava micchāti attho. Tena hi ye kate niggaheti yena kāraṇena idaṃ micchā, tena kāraṇena yo tayā niggaho kato, so dukkaṭo. Yaṃ mayā paṭikammaṃ kataṃ, tadeva sukataṃ. Yāpi cesā paṭikammacatukkādivasena kathāmaggasampaṭipādanā katā, sāpi sukatāti. Tadeva puggalo upalabbhatītiādikassa anulomapañcakassa nupalabbhatītiādikānaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānañca vasena anulomapaccanīkaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā sakavādino pubbapakkhe sati paravādino vacanasāmaññamattena chalavādena jayo hoti.

Now, what begins with 'one should not be refuted thus' is called the concluding tetrad. Here, 'one should not be refuted thus' means: just as I was refuted by you, one should not be refuted thus, for the flawed nature of this refutation has been demonstrated by me. 'Therefore' means for that reason. Since this refutation is a bad refutation, therefore your refutation of me—'If a person... this is wrong for you'—means this refutation of yours is wrong. Therefore, 'regarding the refutation made' means: for the reason that this is wrong, the refutation made by you is ill-done. What rejoinder was made by me, that alone was well done. And that presentation of the path of discussion conducted by means of the rejoinder tetrad, etc., was also well done. Thus, it should be understood that the direct and counter-argument is explained by means of the fivefold direct implication beginning with 'a person is found,' and the rejoinder, refutation, application, and concluding tetrads beginning with 'is not found,' and so on. Thus far, when the proponent's initial position exists, the opponent's victory is achieved through mere verbal similarity by means of a deceptive argument.

Idāni yathā paravādino pubbapakkhe sati sakavādino dhammeneva tathena jayo hoti, tathā vāduppattiṃ dassetuṃ “puggalo nupalabbhatī”ti paccanīkānulomapañcakaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha paccanīke pucchā paravādissa, rūpādibhedaṃ saccikaṭṭhaparamatthaṃ [M 0.0367] sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa, suddhasammutisaccaṃ vā paramatthamissakaṃ vā sammutisaccaṃ sandhāya “yo saccikaṭṭho”ti puna anuyogo paravādissa, sammutivasena “puggalo nupalabbhatī”ti navattabbattā missakavasena vā anuyogassa saṃkiṇṇattā “na heva”nti paṭikkhepo sakavādissa, paṭiññātaṃ paṭikkhipatīti vacanasāmaññamattena “ājānāhi niggaha”ntiādivacanaṃ paravādissa. Evamayaṃ puggalo nupalabbhatīti [V 0.0281] dutiyavādaṃ nissāya dutiyo niggaho hotīti veditabbo. Evaṃ tena chalena niggaho āropito.

Now, to show how, when the opponent's initial position exists, the proponent's victory is achieved rightfully and truthfully, the fivefold negative-affirmative method beginning with 'a person is not found' is commenced. Here, in the negative argument, the question is posed by the opponent; the admission by the proponent refers to the ultimate reality, which is distinguished by form, etc.; the opponent's repeated questioning, 'that which is real?' refers to either purely conventional truth or conventional truth mixed with ultimate truth; the proponent's rejection with 'Not so' is because 'a person is not found' cannot be stated conventionally, or because the questioning is mixed; and the opponent's statement, 'Acknowledge the refutation,' etc., is based merely on verbal similarity, implying that 'what was admitted is being rejected.' Thus, it should be understood that this second refutation is based on the second argument, 'a person is not found.' In this way, the refutation is imposed through that deception.

Idāni dhammena samena paravādipaṭiññāya attano vāde jayaṃ dassetuṃ anulomanaye pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhiṃ nissāya paṭiññā paravādissa, laddhiyā okāsaṃ adatvā paramatthavasena puna anuyogo sakavādissa, paramatthavasena puggalassa anupalabbhanato paṭikkhepo paravādissa, tato paraṃ dhammena samena attano jayadassanatthaṃ “ājānāhi paṭikamma”ntiādi sabbaṃ sakavādivacanameva hoti. Tattha sabbesaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Evamidaṃ “puggalo nupalabbhatī”tiādikassa paccanīkapañcakassa “upalabbhatī”tiādīnaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānañca vasena paccanīkānulomapañcakaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti. Evametāni paṭhamasaccikaṭṭhe dve pañcakāni niddiṭṭhāni, tatthetaṃ vuccati –

Now, to demonstrate victory in one's own argument over the opponent's admission by righteous and impartial means: in the affirmative method, the question is from the proponent; the admission is from the opponent, based on their own tenet; without granting scope to their tenet, the proponent again questions in terms of ultimate reality; the rejection is from the opponent, due to the non-apprehension of a person in an ultimate sense. Thereafter, for the purpose of demonstrating one's own victory righteously and impartially, all statements such as 'Acknowledge the rejoinder' belong solely to the proponent. Here, the meaning of all the tetrads—rejoinder, refutation, application, and conclusion—should be understood in the manner stated above. Thus, this is designated as the fivefold negative-affirmative method, by way of the negative pentad beginning with 'a person is not apprehended,' and the tetrads of rejoinder, refutation, application, and conclusion concerning the affirmative statement 'is apprehended,' and so on. In this way, these two fivefold methods have been designated in the first ultimate truth. In this regard, it is said:

“Niggaho paravādissa, suddho paṭhamapañcake;

Asuddho pana tasseva, paṭikammajayo tahiṃ.

Refutation of the opponent is pure in the first fivefold method; but his victory by rejoinder therein is impure.

“Niggaho sakavādissa, asuddho dutiyapañcake;

Visuddho pana tasseva, paṭikammajayo tahiṃ.

Refutation of the proponent is impure in the second fivefold method; but his victory by rejoinder therein is pure.

“Tasmā dvīsupi ṭhānesu, jayova sakavādino;

Dhammena hi jayo nāma, adhammena kuto jayo.

Therefore, in both instances, victory belongs to the proponent; for victory is indeed by the Dhamma; how can there be victory by what is not the Dhamma?

“Saccikaṭṭhe [M 0.0368] yathā cettha, pañcakadvayamaṇḍite;

Dhammādhammavaseneva, vutto jayaparājayo.

Just as here in the ultimate truth, adorned with the two fivefold methods, victory and defeat are declared by way of the Dhamma and what is not the Dhamma.

“Ito paresu sabbesu, saccikaṭṭhesu paṇḍito;

Evameva vibhāveyya, ubho jayaparājaye”ti. (kathā. aṭṭha. 7-10);

In all other ultimate truths from this one, the wise one should discern both victory and defeat in just this way.

Paṭhamo suddhikasaccikaṭṭho niṭṭhito.

The first simple ultimate truth is concluded.

Evaṃ [V 0.0282] suddhikasaccikaṭṭhaṃ vitthāretvā idāni tameva aparehipi okāsādīhi nayehi vitthāretuṃ puna “puggalo upalabbhatī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna sabbatthāti sarīraṃ sandhāya anuyogo sakavādissa, rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassanādosañca “aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra”nti āpajjanadosañca disvā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesamettha anulomapaccanīkapañcake heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Pāṭho pana saṃkhitto. Tattha yasmā sarīraṃ sandhāya “sabbattha nupalabbhatī”ti vutte sarīrato bahi upalabbhatīti āpajjati, tasmā paccanīke paṭikkhepo sakavādissa, paṭhamaṃ anujānitvā pacchā avajānātīti chalavādassa vasena paṭikammaṃ paravādissa, sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

Having explained the simple ultimate truth in detail, now, to elaborate on it further by other methods such as 'scope,' etc., the section beginning with 'a person is apprehended' is commenced. Herein, the question belongs to the proponent, and the admission to the opponent. Again, the proponent's inquiry, 'everywhere?' refers to the body. Seeing the fault of perceiving a self in form and the fault of incurring the view 'the soul is one thing, the body another,' the rejection belongs to the opponent. The rest here in the fivefold affirmative-negative method should be understood in the same way as stated above. The text, however, is concise. Here, because when it is said 'is not apprehended everywhere' with reference to the body, the implication arises that it is apprehended outside the body, therefore, in the negative argument, the rejection belongs to the proponent. The rejoinder belongs to the opponent by way of a deceptive argument, as they first admit and then reject. The rest is evident.

Dutiyanaye sabbadāti purimapacchimajātikālañca dharamānaparinibbutakālañca sandhāya anuyogo sakavādissa, sveva khattiyo so brāhmaṇotiādīnaṃ āpattidosañca dharamānaparinibbutānaṃ visesābhāvadosañca disvā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesaṃ paṭhamanaye vuttasadisameva.

In the second method, the proponent's inquiry concerns 'always' with reference to the time of past and future births, and the time of those who are living and those who have attained final Nibbāna. Seeing the fault of incurring statements like 'that very khattiya is that brahmin,' etc., and the fault of the absence of distinction between those who are living and those who have attained final Nibbāna, the opponent makes a rejection. The remainder is similar to what was stated in the first method.

Tatiyanaye sabbesūti khandhāyatanādīni sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, rūpasmiṃ attā, cakkhusmiṃ attātiādidosabhayena paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

In the third method, the proponent's question concerning 'in all' is with reference to the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. The opponent's rejection is due to the fear of faults such as 'self in form,' 'self in the eye,' and so on. The rest is just the same.

Evamimāni [M 0.0369] tīṇi mukhāni anulomapaccanīkapañcake anulomamattavaseneva tāva paṭipāṭiyā bhājetvā puna paccanīkānulomapañcake paccanīkamattavaseneva bhājetuṃ “puggalo nupalabbhatī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha heṭṭhā vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Ettāvatā suddhikassa ceva imesañca tiṇṇanti catunnaṃ saccikaṭṭhānaṃ ekekasmiṃ saccikaṭṭhe anulomapaccanīkassa, paccanīkānulomassa cāti dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ paccanīkānaṃ vasena ayaṃ aṭṭhamukhā nāma vādayutti niddiṭṭhā hotīti veditabbā. Yā ekekasmiṃ mukhe ekekassa niggahassa vasena vuccati. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

Thus, having first divided these three modes in order by way of the affirmative method alone in the fivefold affirmative-negative method, then, to divide them by way of the negative method alone in the fivefold negative-affirmative method, the section beginning with 'a person is not apprehended' is commenced. Herein, the meaning should be understood in the manner stated previously. Thus far, for the four ultimate truths—the pure method and these three—in each ultimate truth, by way of two counter-arguments for each, namely, the affirmative-negative and the negative-affirmative, this method of debate called the eight-fold approach is designated. It is spoken of in each mode by way of each refutation. In this regard, it is said:

“Evaṃ catubbidhe pañhe, pañcakadvayabhedato;

Esā aṭṭhamukhā nāma, vādayutti pakāsitā.

"Thus, in the fourfold question, by way of the division into two fivefold methods, this method of debate called the eight-fold approach is explained."

“Aṭṭheva [V 0.0283] niggahā tattha, cattāro tesu dhammikā;

Adhammikā ca cattāro, sabbattha sakavādino;

Jayo parājayo ceva, sabbattha paravādino”ti. (kathā. aṭṭha. 14);

"There are indeed eight refutations therein: four of them are righteous, and four are unrighteous. In every case, victory belongs to the proponent, and defeat belongs to the opponent."

Ayaṃ tāvettha anuttānatthato saṃvaṇṇanā.

This, so far, is the exposition here of the profound meaning.

Atthavinicchayo panetthāpi moggaliputtatissattherena kataniddesassa nayamukhamattadassanavaseneva hoti. Therena hi bhagavatā ṭhapitāya etissā mātikāya paduddhāravasena niddesaṃ akatvā bhagavatā dinnaaṭṭhamukhavādayuttinaye ṭhatvā aparehi pariyāyehi puggalavādaṃ, tadaññaṃ nānappakāraṃ micchāgāhañca nirākaronteneva puggalakathaṃ ādiṃ katvā sādhikadvisatakathāhi niddeso kato.

However, the determination of meaning here too is merely by way of showing the outline of the method of the exposition made by the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa. For the Elder, without making an exposition by extracting words from this matrix established by the Blessed One, but rather standing firm on the eight-fold method of debate given by the Blessed One and, by other approaches, refuting the personalist doctrine and other various kinds of wrong views, made an exposition with over two hundred topics, beginning with the discussion on the person.

Tattha puggalavādanirākaraṇatthaṃ tāva khandhāyatanadhātuindriyavasena sattapaññāsāya dhammesu ekekena saddhiṃ “puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena, rūpañca upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena…pe… puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena, vedanāpi [M 0.0370] upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”tiādinā nayena puggalasaṃsandanavasappavattaṃ suddhikasaṃsandanaṃ, yathā rūpavedanādayo sattapaññāsa dhammā aññamaññā visadisā upalabbhanti, evaṃ rūpādīhi visadiso puggalo upalabbhatīti pucchanavasappavattaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ, “rūpaṃ puggalo, rūpasmiṃ puggalo, aññatra rūpā puggalo, puggalasmiṃ rūpa”nti evaṃ catukkanayena sattapaññāsāya dhammehi pucchanavasappavattaṃ catukkanayasaṃsandananti tividhā saṃsandananayā vuttā. Tattha puggalassa rūpādisabhāvatte niccasassatucchedādippasaṅgato yathānurūpaṃ nirākaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, ativitthārabhayenettha upari cetaṃ na vitthārīyati.

Here, to refute the doctrine of a person, first, regarding the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and faculties, among the fifty-seven phenomena, each is examined in conjunction with the statement: 'Is a person apprehended in the ultimate sense and as an ultimate reality? And is form apprehended in the ultimate sense and as an ultimate reality? ... Is a person apprehended in the ultimate sense and as an ultimate reality? And is feeling apprehended in the ultimate sense and as an ultimate reality?' and so on. This is the pure comparison, proceeding by way of juxtaposing the person. Just as the fifty-seven phenomena—such as form, feeling, and the rest—are apprehended as distinct from one another, so too is a person apprehended as distinct from form and the others. This is the analogical comparison, proceeding by way of questioning. Then, 'Is form the person? Is the person in form? Is the person apart from form? Is form in the person?' This is the fourfold method of comparison, proceeding by way of questioning with the fifty-seven phenomena in a fourfold manner. Thus, three types of comparison methods are stated. Here, if the person were of the nature of form and the like, then due to the implication of eternalism, annihilationism, etc., the refutation should be understood accordingly. Due to the fear of excessive elaboration, this is not expanded upon further here.

Tato “yathā rūpādayo sappaccayā, appaccayādayo vā honti, evaṃ tava puggalopi sappaccayatādilakkhaṇayutto”ti pucchanavasappavattā lakkhaṇayuttikathā, “puggalo”ti, “upalabbhatī”ti ca padadvayādisodhanatthaṃ “yo puggalo, so upalabbhati. Yo vā upalabbhati, so puggalo”tiādipucchanavasappavattaṃ vacanasodhanaṃ, “rūpadhātuyā rūpī”tiādi nāmapaññattisodhanavasappavatto paññattānuyogo ca, “sova puggalo sandhāvati asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ, añño vā, na añño vā, neva añño nānañño vā”tiādinā gatiparivattanamukhena cutipaṭisandhānuyogo[V 0.0284], “rukkhaṃ upādāya chāyādīnaṃ viya khandhādiṃ upādāya paramatthato puggalapaññattī”ti vāde tassa aniccasaṅkhatatādippasaṅgadīpako upādāpaññattānuyogo, “kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ kārako puggalo”ti vāde tassa vaṭṭadukkhānupacchedādippasaṅgadīpako purisakārānuyogo ca, “yo iddhivikubbako, so puggalo”tiādivādabhedako abhiññānuyogo, “mātāpitādayo nāma atthi, tena puggalo atthī”ti vādabhedako ñātakānuyogo[M 0.0371], “evaṃ khattiyo”tiādi jātyānuyogo, “gahaṭṭho pabbajito”tiādi paṭipattānuyogo, “devo manusso”tiādi upapattānuyogo, “sotāpanno”tiādi paṭivedhānuyogo, “aṭṭha purisapuggalā”tiādi saṅghānuyogo, “puggalo saṅkhato”tiādivasappavatto saccikaṭṭhasabhāgānuyogo, “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno”tiādi vedakānuyogo, “kāye kāyānupassī”tiādi kiccānuyogo, “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”tiādinā puggalasabhāvasādhakasuttesu sannissitesu –

Then there is the discussion on characteristics, which proceeds by way of questioning: “Just as form and so on are conditioned or unconditioned, so too is your person endowed with the characteristic of being conditioned, etc.” There is the purification of statements, to clarify the two terms “person” and “is apprehended,” by way of questions like, “Is it that the person is apprehended? Or that what is apprehended is the person?” and so on. There is the inquiry into designation, to purify name-and-concept, such as “one who has form in the form element,” and so on. There is the inquiry into passing away and relinking, through the mode of change of destination: “Does that very person transmigrate from this world to the next, or another, or not another, or neither another nor not-another?” and so on. There is the inquiry into dependent designation, which, in the case of the view that “just as shadows and such depend on a tree, so the designation of a person depends on aggregates and such,” reveals the implication of impermanence, conditioned nature, and so on. There is the inquiry into personal action, which, in the case of the view that “the person is the doer of good and bad deeds,” points to the implication of the non-interruption of the suffering of the round of rebirth, and so on. There is the inquiry into higher knowledge, which refutes views such as “the one who performs supernormal feats is the person.” There is the inquiry into relatives, which refutes the view that “parents and such exist, therefore the person exists.” There is the inquiry into birth, such as “Thus, a Khattiya.” There is the inquiry into practice, such as “A householder, a renunciant.” There is the inquiry into rebirth, such as “A god, a human.” There is the inquiry into penetration, such as “A stream-enterer.” There is the inquiry into the Sangha, such as “The eight kinds of noble persons.” There is the inquiry into what partakes of the ultimate truth, which proceeds by way of “The person is conditioned,” and so on. There is the inquiry into the feeler, such as “Feeling a pleasant feeling.” There is the inquiry into function, such as “Contemplating the body in the body.” When they rely on suttas that establish the existence of a person, such as “There is a person practicing for their own welfare”—

Sabbe dhammā anattā (ma. ni. 1.353, 356; dha. pa. 279), dukkhameva uppajjamānaṃ uppajjati (saṃ. ni. 2.15).

All phenomena are not-self (MN 1.353, 356; Dhp 279); only suffering arises when it arises (SN 2.15).

Kinnu sattoti paccesi, māra diṭṭhigataṃ nu te;

Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjoyaṃ, nayidha sattūpalabbhati.

“What ‘being’ do you believe in, Māra? Is that your speculative view? This is a heap of pure formations; no being is found here.”

Dukkhameva hi sambhoti, dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti ca;

Nāññatra dukkhā sambhoti, nāññaṃ dukkhā nirujjhati. (saṃ. ni. 1.171);

For only suffering comes to be; suffering persists and passes away. Nothing other than suffering comes to be; nothing other than suffering ceases (SN 1.171).

Yasmā ca kho, ānanda, suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā…pe… tasmā suñño lokoti vuccati (saṃ. ni. 4.85).

And because, Ānanda, it is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self… therefore it is said, ‘The world is empty’ (SN 35.85).

“Attani vā, bhikkhave, sati attaniyaṃ meti assāti…pe… attani ca bhikkhave attaniye ca saccato thetato anupalabbhaniyamāne yampi taṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, so loko, so attā, so pecca bhavissāmi, nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo, sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmīti[V 0.0285], nanāyaṃ, bhikkhave, kevalo paripūro bāladhammo”ti (ma. ni. 1.244), “tatra, seniya, yvāyaṃ satthā diṭṭhe ceva dhamme attānaṃ saccato thetato na paññāpeti, abhisamparāye ca…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, seniya, satthā [M 0.0372] sammāsambuddho”tiādinā puggalābhāvadīpakasuttasandassanavasappavatto suttasandassanānuyogo cāti ettakena kathāmaggena vitthārato paṭhamā puggalakathā vibhattā. Tattha “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”tiādīsu yathā rūpādayo dhammā paccattalakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena labbhanti, na evaṃ puggalo, rūpādīsu pana sati lokavohāramattena “atthi puggalo”ti vuccatīti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā – “imā kho, citta…pe… lokavohārā lokapaññattiyo”ti (dī. ni. 1.440). Dvidhāpi buddhānaṃ kathā sammutikathā, paramatthakathā ca. Tattha “satto puggalo gāmo pabbato”tiādikā sammutikathā nāma, “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā khandhā āyatanānī”tiādikā paramatthakathā nāma. Buddhā hi ye ye sattā yathā yathā bujjhitvā catusaccapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ sakkonti, tesaṃ tesaṃ tathā tathā sammutivasena vā paramatthavasena vā vomissakavasena vā desetvā nāmarūpaparicchedadassanavaseneva amataṃ maggaṃ pakāsenti. Ayañhi –

“Monks, if there were a self, would there be what belongs to the self? … Monks, when neither a self nor what belongs to a self can truly and firmly be found, then this speculative view—‘This is the world, this is the self, this I shall be after death, permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I shall endure as long as eternity’—is this not, monks, entirely the doctrine of fools?” (MN 1.244). “Here, Seniya, that teacher who does not proclaim a self as truly and firmly existing either in this visible life or in the hereafter… such a one, Seniya, is called a teacher who is a perfectly enlightened one.” Thus, by showing suttas that demonstrate the non-existence of a person, the first discussion on the person is elaborated in detail by this path of discussion. Here, in statements like “There is a person striving for their own welfare,” etc., a person is not found in the way that phenomena like form, etc., are found through their specific and general characteristics. Rather, when form, etc., exist, it is merely by way of worldly convention that it is said, “There is a person.” This has also been stated by the Blessed One: “These, Citta… are worldly usages, worldly designations” (DN 1.440). The teachings of the Buddhas are twofold: conventional discourse and ultimate discourse. Here, expressions like “a being, a person, a village, a mountain,” etc., are called conventional discourse, while statements like “impermanent, suffering, non-self, aggregates, sense bases,” etc., are called ultimate discourse. For the Buddhas, discerning how various beings are able to awaken and penetrate the Four Noble Truths, teach them accordingly—whether by way of convention, ultimate truth, or a mixture of both—and they reveal the deathless path solely by means of the vision of the delimitation of name-and-form. For this—

Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nupalabbhati.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, best of speakers, proclaimed two truths: conventional and ultimate; a third is not found.

Tattha –

Here—

Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇaṃ;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ.

Conventional speech is true, being a cause of worldly convention; ultimate speech is true, being the true characteristic of phenomena.

Tasmā viññū akatvāna, byañjanebhinivesanaṃ;

Paramatthe patiṭṭhāya, puggalādiṃ vivajjaye.

Therefore, a wise person, not adhering to the mere letter, should be established in the ultimate meaning and avoid such things as ‘person’.

Paññattiṃ anatikkamma, paramattho pakāsito;

Vināyakena so yasmā, tasmā aññopi paṇḍito;

Paramatthaṃ pakāsento, samaññaṃ nātidhāvayeti. (kathā. aṭṭha. 237);

Since the ultimate meaning was revealed by the Guide without transgressing designation, therefore another wise person too, while revealing the ultimate meaning, should not overstep convention (Kathā-aṭṭha. 237).

Ayaṃ puggalakathānayo.

This is the method of the discussion on the person.

Parihānikathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on Decline, Etc.

Puggalakathāto [M 0.0373][V 0.0286] paraṃ “parihāyati arahā arahattā”tiādinā asekhā, sotāpannavajjitasekhā ca aggamaggaphalato parihāyantīti pavattā parihānikathā. Pabbajjā viya paṭivedhasaṅkhāto brahmacariyavāsopi manussesu eva bhavati, natthi devesu brahmacariyavāsoti pavattā brahmacariyakathā. Dukkhadassanena ekadesato kilesā pahīyanti, tathā samudayadassanādīhīti evaṃ nānābhisamayavasena odhiso kilesā pahīyantīti pavattā odhisokathā. Jhānalābhī puthujjano kāmarāgabyāpāde samucchedavasena jahati, so catusaccābhisamayā paṭhamameva anāgāmī hotīti pavattā jahatikathā. Atītādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ khandhādikaṃ kālattayepi khandhādisabhāvena atthīti pavattā sabbamatthītikathā. Atītaṃ, anāgatañca khandhādikaṃ atthīti pavattā atītakkhandhādikathā. Atītesu vipākadhammadhammesu ekaccaṃ avipakkavipākameva atthi, na itaranti pavattā ekaccamatthītikathā. Sabbe dhammā satipaṭṭhānāti pavattā satipaṭṭhānakathā. Atītānāgatādivasena natthi, sakabhāvena vā atthi, parabhāvena natthīti pavattā hevatthikathā. Tattha hevatthīti evaṃ iminā pakārena atthīti attho.

After the discussion on the person, the discussion on decline proceeds from the statement, “An arahant declines from arahantship,” and so on, meaning that those beyond training and those in training—except for stream-enterers—decline from the highest path and fruit. The discussion on the holy life proceeds from the statement that, like the going forth, the dwelling in the holy life, designated as penetration, exists only among humans; there is no dwelling in the holy life among the gods. The discussion on gradual abandonment proceeds from the statement that through seeing suffering, defilements are abandoned in part, and similarly through seeing the origin, etc.; thus, by way of various realizations, defilements are abandoned gradually. The discussion on abandoning proceeds from the statement that an ordinary person who is a jhāna-attainer abandons sensual desire and ill will by way of eradication, and that upon the first realization of the four truths, he becomes a non-returner. The discussion that “all exists” proceeds from the statement that all phenomena, such as the aggregates, differentiated as past, etc., exist in the three periods of time with the nature of aggregates, etc. The discussion on past aggregates, etc., proceeds from the statement that past and future aggregates, etc., exist. The discussion that “a certain one exists” proceeds from the statement that among past phenomena that are of the nature of ripening, a certain one exists that is an unripened result, but not another. The discussion on the foundations of mindfulness proceeds from the statement that all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness. The discussion that “it exists thus” proceeds from the statement that in terms of past, future, etc., it does not exist; or it exists by its own nature but not by the nature of another. Here, “it exists thus” means it exists in this manner; this is the meaning.

Adhimānikānaṃ, kuhakānaṃ vā arahattapaṭiññānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ disvā mārakāyikā devatā upasaṃharantīti pavattā parūpahārakathā. Arahato paresaṃ nāmagottādīsu atthi aññāṇaṃ, atthi kaṅkhā, parehi ñāpanīyato atthi paravitaraṇāti tisso kathā. Sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dukkhanti vācā bhijjatīti pavattā vacībhedakathā. Dukkhanti vācaṃ bhāsanto dukkhe ñāṇaṃ āharati, tañca lokuttaranti pavattā dukkhāhārakathā. Samāpattiyaṃ, bhavaṅge ca cittaṃ ciraṃ tiṭṭhatīti [M 0.0374] pavattā cittaṭṭhitikathā. Sabbe saṅkhārā nippariyāyena ādittā kukkuḷanirayasadisāti pavattā kukkuḷakathā. Paccekaṃ catusaccadassanavasena ekekassa maggassa catukkhattuṃ uppattivasena soḷasahi koṭṭhāsehi arahattappattīti pavattā anupubbābhisamayakathā. Buddhānaṃ vohāravacanaṃ lokuttaranti pavattā vohārakathā. Suddhasattānaṃ appaṭisaṅkhāya maggena vinā kilesanirodhasaṅkhāto appaṭisaṅkhānirodho, paṭisaṅkhāya tena maggena kilesanirodhoti dve nirodhāti pavattā nirodhakathā.

The discussion on being instigated by others proceeds from the statement that on seeing the seminal emission of those who are conceited, fraudulent, or who claim arahantship, deities of Māra’s host instigate them. Then there are three discussions: that for an arahant there is ignorance regarding the names and clans of others; that there is doubt; and that there is being led by others, since he has to be informed by others. The discussion on the breaking forth of speech proceeds from the statement that at the moment of the path of stream-entry, the utterance “Suffering!” breaks forth. The discussion on bringing suffering to bear proceeds from the statement that in uttering the word “Suffering,” one brings knowledge to bear on suffering, and that knowledge is supramundane. The discussion on the stability of mind proceeds from the statement that in meditative attainment and in the life-continuum, the mind remains for a long time. The discussion on hot embers proceeds from the statement that all conditioned formations are, without qualification, ablaze like the hell of hot embers. The discussion on gradual realization proceeds from the statement that by way of seeing the four truths individually, through the arising of each path four times, arahantship is attained in sixteen parts. The discussion on conventional speech proceeds from the statement that the conventional speech of the Buddhas is supramundane. The discussion on cessation proceeds from the statement that for pure beings there are two kinds of cessation: the cessation of defilements without the path, called cessation without deliberation, and the cessation of defilements with deliberation by means of that path.

Tathāgatabalaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇanti pavattā balakathā. Āsavakkhayañāṇavirahitaṃ navabalaṃ lokuttaranti [V 0.0287] pavattā ariyantikathā. Sarāgaṃ cittaṃ nibbānaṃ ārabbha rāgato vimuccatīti pavattā vimuttikathā. Jhānena vikkhambhanavimuttiyā paṭhamaṃ vimuttaṃ cittaṃ maggakkhaṇe samucchedavimuttiyā vimuccamānaṃ nāma hotīti pavattā vimuccamānakathā. Aṭṭhamakasaṅkhātassa sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassa anulomagotrabhukkhaṇe diṭṭhivicikicchā pahīyanti nāma, maggakkhaṇe pahīnā nāmāti pavattā aṭṭhamakakathā. Aṭṭhamakassa maggakkhaṇe saddhindriyādīni paṭilabhanti, na paṭiladdhānīti pavattā aṭṭhamakassa indriyakathā. Catutthajjhānadhammupatthaddhaṃ maṃsacakkhumeva dibbacakkhu nāmāti pavattā dibbacakkhukathā. Tathā maṃsasote dibbasotakathā. Yathākammūpagatañāṇameva dibbacakkhūti pavattā yathākammūpagatañāṇakathā. Devabrahmānaṃ pāṇātipātādiasaṃvarābhāvamattena sampattaviratiyā abhāvepi saṃvaro atthīti pavattā saṃvarakathā. Asaññīnampi cutipaṭisandhikkhaṇe saññā atthīti pavattā asaññakathā. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabhūmiyaṃ saññā nappavattatīti pavattā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathā.

The discussion on powers proceeds from the statement that the Tathāgata's powers are common to his disciples. The discussion on what pertains to the noble ones proceeds from the statement that the nine powers, when devoid of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, are supramundane. The discussion on liberation proceeds from the statement that a mind with lust, by taking Nibbāna as its object, is liberated from lust. The discussion on being liberated proceeds from the statement that a mind first liberated by the liberation of suppression through jhāna is called 'being liberated' at the moment of the path by the liberation of eradication. The discussion on the eighth person proceeds from the statement that for one designated as the eighth, who stands on the path of stream-entry, wrong view and doubt are said to be abandoned at the moment of conformity and change-of-lineage, and are said to be abandoned at the moment of the path. The discussion on the faculties of the eighth person proceeds from the statement that at the moment of the path, he acquires the faculties of faith, etc.; they had not been acquired before. The discussion on the divine eye proceeds from the statement that the divine eye is simply the fleshly eye supported by the phenomena of the fourth jhāna. Similarly, there is the discussion on the divine ear in relation to the fleshly ear. The discussion on the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma proceeds from the statement that this knowledge itself is the divine eye. The discussion on restraint proceeds from the statement that for devas and brahmās, even in the absence of undertaken abstinence, there is restraint merely through the absence of non-restraint regarding killing living beings, etc. The discussion on non-percipient beings proceeds from the statement that even for non-percipient beings, perception exists at the moment of death and rebirth-linking. The discussion on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception proceeds from the statement that in the plane of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, perception does not occur.

Arahā [M 0.0375] gihī assāti pavattā gihissa arahātikathā. Anāgāmino suddhāvāsesu paṭisandhicittena upapattikkhaṇe arahanto hontīti pavattā upapattikathā. Arahato lokiyadhammāpi anāsavāti pavattā anāsavakathā. Paccuppannakkhaṇe samaṅgibhāvasamannāgamo ca rūpāvacarādibhūmantarapaṭilābhasamannāgamo cāti dve samannāgamā, yesaṃ pana ime dve samannāgame ṭhapetvā aññopi hettha upapattidhammavasena eko samannāgamo nāma atthi, tena arahā catūhi phalehi samannāgatoti pavattā samannāgatakathā. Imināva nayena arahā chahi upekkhāhi samannāgatoti pavattā upekkhāsamannāgatakathā. Maggañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhātabodhiyā sadā sannihitabhāvena buddhoti pavattā bodhiyā buddhotikathā. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇayuttāva bodhisattāti pavattā lakkhaṇakathā. Bodhisattānampi magganiyāmo atthīti pavattā niyāmokkantikathā. Catutthamaggaṭṭho tīhi phalehi samannāgatotiādinā pavattā aparāpi samannāgatakathā. Paṭhamamaggādīhi pahīnehi saddhiṃ nippariyāyato arahattaṃ sabbasaṃyojanappahānanti pavattā sabbasaṃyojanapahānakathā.

The discussion on a layperson being an arahant proceeds from the statement that an arahant may be a layperson. The discussion on arising proceeds from the statement that non-returners in the Pure Abodes become arahants at the moment of arising with their rebirth-linking consciousness. The discussion on being taintless proceeds from the statement that even the mundane phenomena of an arahant are taintless. The discussion on being endowed proceeds from the statement that in the present moment there are two kinds of endowment: endowment by way of possession and endowment by way of attaining an intermediate plane such as the fine-material sphere. But for those for whom, apart from these two endowments, there is another kind of endowment by way of the nature of rebirth, an arahant is endowed with the four fruits. In the same way, the discussion on being endowed with equanimity proceeds from the statement that an arahant is endowed with six kinds of equanimity. The discussion on being a Buddha by enlightenment proceeds from the statement that one is called a Buddha due to the constant presence of enlightenment, which is designated as path-knowledge and omniscience. The discussion on the marks proceeds from the statement that Bodhisattas are endowed with the marks of a great person. The discussion on entry into the fixed course proceeds from the statement that for Bodhisattas too there is the fixed course of the path. Another discussion on being endowed proceeds from the statement that one standing on the fourth path is endowed with the three fruits, and so on. The discussion on the abandoning of all fetters proceeds from the statement that arahantship is, without qualification, the abandoning of all fetters, together with those abandoned by the first path and so on.

Nippariyāyato phalaṃ vimutti nāma, vipassanāmaggapaccavekkhaṇañāṇāni pana pariyāyato. Evaṃ pana aggahetvā yaṃ kiñci kilesavippayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ vimuttīti pavattā vimuttikathā. Buddhādiasekhārammaṇaṃ asekhañāṇanti pavattā asekhañāṇakathā. Pathavīkasiṇādisamāpattiyo [V 0.0288] paramatthato avijjamāne paññattārammaṇe pavattattā viparītañāṇanti pavattā viparītakathā. Tattha anicce niccantiādinā catubbidho vipallāso veditabbo. Sabbesaṃ puthujjanānaṃ niyāmagamanāya ñāṇaṃ atthīti pavattā niyāmakathā. Sabbaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisambhidāti [M 0.0376] pavattā paṭisambhidākathā. Sammutivisayampi ñāṇaṃ bhūtārammaṇamevāti pavattā sammutiñāṇakathā. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ cittārammaṇameva, na taṃsampayuttarāgādicetasikārammaṇanti pavattā cittārammaṇakathā. Sabbasmiṃ anāgatadhamme sabbesaṃ ñāṇaṃ atthīti pavattā anāgatañāṇakathā. Paccuppanne attano ñāṇepi ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti pavattā paṭuppannañāṇakathā. Buddhā viya sāvakāpi tena tena veneyyajanena pattabbaphalaṃ ñatvāva tadatthāya dhammaṃ desentīti pavattā phalañāṇakathā.

The discussion on liberation proceeds from the statement that, without qualification, the fruit is called liberation, but the knowledges of insight, path, and reviewing are so called with qualification; however, not accepting this, some hold that any knowledge dissociated from the defilements is liberation. The discussion on the knowledge of one beyond training proceeds from the statement that the knowledge of one beyond training has as its object a Buddha or another one beyond training. The discussion on perverted knowledge proceeds from the statement that the attainments of the earth-kasiṇa, etc., are perverted knowledge because they occur with a conceptual object that is ultimately non-existent. Here, the fourfold perversion should be understood as perceiving the impermanent as permanent, and so on. The discussion on the fixed course proceeds from the statement that all worldlings possess the knowledge for entering the fixed course. The discussion on the analytical knowledges proceeds from the statement that all knowledge is analytical knowledge. The discussion on conventional knowledge proceeds from the statement that even knowledge that has a conventional object has a real object. The discussion on the mind as object proceeds from the statement that the knowledge of others' minds has only the mind as its object, not the mental factors associated with it, such as lust. The discussion on future knowledge proceeds from the statement that all beings have knowledge regarding all future phenomena. The discussion on present knowledge proceeds from the statement that in the present, knowledge occurs even regarding one's own knowledge. The discussion on knowledge of the fruit proceeds from the statement that, like the Buddhas, the disciples too, having known the fruit to be attained by this or that person to be trained, teach the Dhamma for that purpose.

Sammattaniyāmo niyamato niccaṭṭhena asaṅkhatoti pavattā niyāmakathā. “Dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā”tiādivacanato paṭiccasamuppādo asaṅkhatoti pavattā paṭiccasamuppādakathā. “Saccāni tathāni avitathānī”tiādivacanato catusaccāni asaṅkhatānīti pavattā saccakathā. “Cattāro āruppā āneñjā”ti vacanato asaṅkhatāti pavattā āruppakathā. Nirodhasamāpatti asaṅkhatāti pavattā nirodhasamāpattikathā. Asaṅkhato ākāsoti ākāsakathā. Ākāso sanidassanotikathā. Pathavīdhātu sanidassanātiādiṃ katvā kāyakammaṃ sanidassananti pariyosānakathā.

The discussion on the fixed course proceeds from the statement that the fixed course of rightness is unconditioned because of its fixedness, in the sense of being constant. The discussion on dependent origination proceeds from such statements as “the stability of phenomena, the lawfulness of phenomena,” to argue that dependent origination is unconditioned. The discussion on the truths proceeds from such statements as “the truths are so, not otherwise,” to argue that the four truths are unconditioned. The discussion on the formless attainments proceeds from the statement “the four formless attainments are imperturbable,” to argue that they are unconditioned. The discussion on the attainment of cessation proceeds from the statement that the attainment of cessation is unconditioned. The discussion on space proceeds from the statement that space is unconditioned. There is a discussion that space is visible. The concluding discussion takes as its starting point that the earth element is visible and so on, and concludes that bodily action is visible.

Natthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi saṅgahitā, tena ekavidhena rūpasaṅgahotiādi niratthakanti pavattā saṅgahitakathā. Vedanādayo arūpadhammā aññamaññaṃ na sampayuttāti pavattā sampayuttakathā. Cetasikaṃ natthīti pavattā cetasikakathā. Cetanādhammova dānaṃ, na deyyadhammoti pavattā dānakathā. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ paribhogamayaṃ puññaṃ atthīti pavattā paribhogakathā. Petā ito dinnacīvarādīheva yāpentīti pavattā itodinnakathā. Pathavīkammavipākotikathā[M 0.0377]. Jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākotikathā. Kilesappahānamattameva sāmaññaphalaṃ, na cittacetasikā dhammāti pavattā ariyadhammavipākakathā. Aññamaññādipaccayatāya vipāko vipākadhammadhammotikathā.

The discussion on inclusion arose from the view that no phenomena are included by any other phenomena, and therefore the inclusion of form in one way, etc., is meaningless. The discussion on association arose from the view that immaterial phenomena such as feeling, etc., are not associated with each other. The discussion on mental factors arose from the view that there are no mental factors. The discussion on giving arose from the view that giving is merely the phenomenon of volition, not the object given. The discussion on use arose from the view that merit exists as the recipients' act of using. The discussion on things given from here arose from the view that departed spirits subsist only on robes, etc., given from here. The discussion on earth being the result of kamma. The discussion on old age and death being the result. The discussion on the result of noble phenomena arose from the view that the mere abandonment of defilements is the fruit of asceticism, and not mental phenomena and mental factors. The discussion on phenomena that are the result of phenomena arose from the view that due to conditionality among each other, etc., the result is a phenomenon that is the result of phenomena.

Asurakāyena saddhiṃ cha gatiyoti pavattā gatikathā. Matasatto mātuutusamayañca mātāpitusaṃyogañca olokayamāno sattāhaṃ, atirekasattāhaṃ vā yasmiṃ bhave tiṭṭhati, so antarābhavo [V 0.0289] nāma atthīti pavattā antarābhavakathā. Rūpādipañcakāmaguṇāva kāmadhātu nāma, na tu vatthukāmakilesakāmāti pavattā kāmaguṇakathā. Pañcevāyatanāni kāmātikathā. Rūpadhammāva rūpadhātūtikathā. Arūpadhammāva arūpadhātūtikathā. Rūpadhātuyā sattā ghānādīhi saddhiṃ saḷāyatanikāti pavattā rūpadhātuyāāyatanakathā. Āruppepi atthi sukhumarūpantikathā. Kāyavacīviññattivasena rūpaṃ kammantikathā. Cittavippayutto arūpadhammova jīvitindriyaṃ, rūpajīvitindriyaṃ natthīti pavattā jīvitindriyakathā. Ariyupavādakammena arahattā parihāyatīti pavattā kammahetukathā.

The discussion on destinies arose from the view that there are six destinies, including the host of asuras. The discussion on the intermediate existence arose from the view that a deceased being, observing the time of the mother’s womb and the union of parents, remains for seven days or more than seven days in a certain existence, and this is called the intermediate existence. The discussion on the strands of sensual pleasure arose from the view that only the five strands of sensual pleasure—forms and so on—are called the sensual realm, not sensual objects or sensual defilements. The discussion on sensual desires arose from the view that only the five sense bases are sensual desires. The discussion on the realm of form arose from the view that only material phenomena are the realm of form. The discussion on the formless realm arose from the view that only immaterial phenomena are the formless realm. The discussion on the sense bases in the realm of form arose from the view that beings in the realm of form possess the six sense bases, including the nose, etc. The discussion on subtle form arose from the view that even in the formless attainments, there is subtle form. The discussion on kamma arose from the view that bodily and verbal intimation constitute kamma as form. The discussion on the life faculty arose from the view that the life faculty is an immaterial phenomenon disconnected from the mind, and there is no material life faculty. The discussion on the cause of kamma arose from the view that through the kamma of reviling the noble ones, one falls from arahantship.

Aniccādivasena saṅkhāre ādīnavato apassitvā nibbānaṃ ānisaṃsato passantassa saṃyojanappahānaṃ hotīti pavattā ānisaṃsadassāvikathā. Nibbānārammaṇampi saṃyojanaṃ atthīti pavattā amatārammaṇakathā. Rūpaṃ sārammaṇantikathā. Anusayā anārammaṇātikathā. Ñāṇaṃ anārammaṇantikathā. Atītārammaṇañca anāgatārammaṇañca cittaṃ anārammaṇantikathādvayaṃ. Sabbaṃ cittaṃ vitakkānupatitantikathā. Vitakkavipphārova saddo, so ca na sotaviññeyyoti pavattā vitakkavipphārasaddakathā. Vināpi cittena vācā pavattatīti pavattā nayathācittassavācātikathā. Vināpi [M 0.0378] cittena kāyakammaṃ pavattatīti pavattā nayathācittassakāyakammantikathā. Atītehipi jhānehi, anāgatehipi yogino samannāgatāti pavattā atītānāgatasamannāgatakathā.

The discussion on the exposition of seeing benefit proceeds from the statement that the abandoning of fetters occurs for one who, not seeing the danger in formations by way of impermanence and so on, sees the benefit in Nibbāna. The discussion on the deathless object proceeds from the statement that a fetter exists even with Nibbāna as an object. The discussion on having an object proceeds from the statement that form has an object. The discussion on being without an object proceeds from the statement that latent tendencies are without an object. The discussion on being without an object proceeds from the statement that knowledge is without an object. The two discussions on being without an object proceed from the statements that the mind with a past object is without an object, and the mind with a future object is without an object. The discussion on being accompanied by thinking proceeds from the statement that all mind is accompanied by thinking. The discussion on the sound of thought-diffusion proceeds from the statement that the diffusion of thinking is sound, and that it is not to be known by the ear. The discussion on speech not according to mind proceeds from the statement that speech occurs even without mind. The discussion on bodily action not according to mind proceeds from the statement that bodily action occurs even without mind. The discussion on being endowed with past and future proceeds from the statement that a meditator is endowed with past and future jhānas.

Bhavaṅgacitte aniruddhe eva kusalākusalacittāni uppajjanti, tadabhāve ca santatinirodho siyāti pavattā nirodhakathā. Saha vācāhi viññattirūpaṃ maggotikathā. Pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissāpi maggabhāvanā atthīti pavattā pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissamaggakathā. Pañcaviññāṇā kusalāpi akusalāpītikathā. Pañcaviññāṇā sābhogātikathā. Maggakkhaṇe lokiyena, lokuttarena cāti dvīhi sīlehi yuttātikathā. Sīlaṃ acetasikantikathā. Sīlaṃ na cittānuparivattītikathā. Samādānahetucittavippayutto puññopacayo hotīti pavattā samādānahetukakathā. Viññatti sīlantikathā. Pāṇātipātādayo vināpi viññattiṃ hontīti pavattā aviññattidussīlyakathā.

When the life-continuum consciousness has not ceased, wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses arise; in its absence, there would be a cessation of continuity—thus is the discourse on cessation. Together with speech, the form of intimation is the path—thus is the discourse on the path. Even for one endowed with the five sense consciousnesses, there is development of the path—thus is the discourse on the path for one endowed with the five sense consciousnesses. The five sense consciousnesses are both wholesome and unwholesome—thus is the discourse on that. The five sense consciousnesses are with deliberation—thus is the discourse on that. At the moment of the path, one is endowed with two kinds of virtue: mundane and supramundane—thus is the discourse on that. Virtue is not a mental factor—thus is the discourse on that. Virtue does not follow consciousness—thus is the discourse on that. An accumulation of merit occurs dissociated from the consciousness that is the cause of undertaking—thus is the discourse on the cause of undertaking. Intimation is virtue—thus is the discourse on that. Killing living beings and other such acts occur even without intimation—thus is the discourse on immorality without intimation.

Anusayā abyākatā, ahetukā, cittavippayuttāti tissopi anusayakathā. Asekhassa ñāṇavippayuttappavattiyā so ñāṇīti navattabboti pavattā ñāṇakathā. Ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttantikathā[V 0.0290]. Maggakkhaṇe idaṃ dukkhanti ñāṇaṃ pavattanti pavattā idaṃ dukkhantikathā. Buddhā iddhibalena āyukappaṃ vināpi mahākappaṃ tiṭṭhantīti pavattā iddhibalakathā. Cittasantati samādhi, na ekacittakkhaṇikoti pavattā samādhikathā. Avijjādipaṭiccasamuppādaṅgehi aññā dhammaṭṭhitatāti pavattā dhammaṭṭhitatākathā. Rūpādīhi aññā aniccatāti pavattā aniccatākathā.

The latent tendencies are indeterminate, without roots, and dissociated from consciousness—thus are the three discourses on latent tendencies. Because one beyond training has occurrences of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, he should not be called 'one with knowledge'—thus is the discourse on knowledge. Knowledge is dissociated from consciousness—thus is the discourse on that. At the moment of the path, the knowledge 'This is suffering' arises—thus is the discourse on 'This is suffering.' Buddhas, through psychic power, can remain for a life-span or even for a great aeon—thus is the discourse on psychic power. The continuity of consciousness is concentration, not a single moment of consciousness—thus is the discourse on concentration. The fixed nature of phenomena is different from the factors of dependent origination, beginning with ignorance—thus is the discourse on the fixed nature of phenomena. Impermanence is different from form and so on—thus is the discourse on impermanence.

Viññattiyo vināpi indriyasaṃvaro kāyavacīkammanti pavattā kathā. Sabbaṃ kammaṃ vipākajanakanti pavattā kammakathā. Saddo vipākoti pavattā kathā. Saḷāyatanaṃ vipākoti pavattā [M 0.0379] kathā. Maggaṃ vināpi sattakkhattuparamotikathā. Tathā kolaṃkolaekabījikathāsupi. Diṭṭhisampanno jīvitā voropetītikathā. Diṭṭhisampannassa apāyaduggatiyā saddhiṃ rūpāditaṇhāsaṅkhātaduggatipahīnāti pavattā duggatikathā. Sattamabhavikassa taṇhāsambhavato duggati appahīnāti pavattā sattamabhavikakathā.

Restraint of the faculties is bodily and verbal action, even without intimations—thus is the discourse. All kamma produces a result—thus is the discourse on kamma. Sound is a result—thus is the discourse. The six sense bases are a result—thus is the discourse. Even without the path, one is one who is reborn at most seven times—thus is the discourse. Likewise, in the discourses on the 'family-to-family' and 'single-seed' attainers. One accomplished in view takes life—thus is the discourse. For one accomplished in view, bad destinations are abandoned, along with the bad destination designated as craving for form and so on—thus is the discourse on bad destinations. For one in their seventh existence, the bad destination is not abandoned because of the arising of craving—thus is the discourse on one in their seventh existence.

Saṅghabhedādikappaṭṭhaṃ kammaṃ katvā tena mahākappaṃ asītibhāgaṃ katvā tato ekabhāgamattaṃ kālaṃ āyukappaṃ niraye paccantīti aggahetvā sakalaṃ mahākappaṃ paccanti, vinassamānepi kappe cakkavāḷantaresu paccantīti pavattā kappaṭṭhakathā. Saṅghabhedako appanākusalāni viya kāmāvacarakusalampi na paṭilabhatīti pavattā kusalapaṭilābhakathā. Aṅgasampannāya āṇattiyā abhāvepi mātughātādiānantariyakammapayojako micchattaniyato evāti pavattā anantarāpayuttakathā. Aniyatadhammesupi keci kusalasampayuttāniyatā atthīti pavattā niyatassa niyāmakathā. Nīvaraṇehi nivutena paṭicchanneneva cittena nīvaraṇaṃ pajahantīti pavattā nivutakathā. Sammukhībhūtaṃ saṃyojanameva jahatīti pavattā sammukhībhūtakathā. Samāpanno ca jhānārammaṇanikantiyā jhānaṃ assādetīti pavattā samāpanno assādetītikathā. Dukkhavedanāyapi rāgassādavedanā hotīti pavattā assātarāgakathā. Dhammataṇhā abyākatātikathā. Dhammataṇhā na dukkhasamudayotikathā.

Disregarding the view that after committing an act that lasts for an aeon, such as schism in the Sangha, one suffers in hell for a life-span, a period equal to one-eightieth of a great aeon, the correct view is that they suffer for the entire great aeon, and even when the aeon is being destroyed, they suffer in other world-systems—thus is the discourse on what lasts for an aeon. A schismatic in the Sangha does not attain wholesome states of the sense-sphere, just as they do not attain wholesome states of absorption—thus is the discourse on the attainment of the wholesome. Even in the absence of a command fulfilled with all its factors, one who instigates an act with immediate retribution, such as matricide, is one fixed in wrongness—thus is the discourse on one who instigates an act with immediate retribution. Even among indeterminate phenomena, some are fixed and associated with the wholesome—thus is the discourse on the determination of the fixed. One abandons the hindrances with a mind that is covered and veiled by the very hindrances—thus is the discourse on being covered. One abandons only the fetter that has come face-to-face—thus is the discourse on what is face-to-face. One who has attained an absorption savors the jhāna through desire for the object of jhāna—thus is the discourse on one in absorption savoring it. Even in painful feeling, there can be a feeling of the savor of lust—thus is the discourse on the savor of lust. Craving for phenomena is indeterminate—thus is the discourse on that. Craving for phenomena is not the origin of suffering—thus is the discourse on that.

Kusalaṃ vā akusalassa, akusalaṃ vā kusalassa anantarā uppajjantīti pavattā kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathā. Gabbhaseyyakānampi bījamattaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjatīti pavattā saḷāyatanuppattikathā. Pañcaviññāṇāni aññamaññassa anantarā uppajjantīti [V 0.0291] pavattā anantarapaccayakathā. Sammāvācākammantaviññattiyo ariyarūpantikathā. Kāmarāgādito [M 0.0380] añño anusayotikathā. Kilesapariyuṭṭhānaṃ cittavippayuttantikathā. Yathā kāmarāgo kāmadhātuyaṃ pariyāpanno, evaṃ rūparāgaarūparāgā rūpārūpabhūmiyaṃ pariyāpannāti pavattā pariyāpannakathā. Dvayaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ abyākatantikathā. Diṭṭhigataṃ apariyāpannantikathā. Yo yesaṃ hetupaccayo, so puna tesaṃ sahajātādipaccayo na hoti, ekadhāva ekassa paccayo hotīti pavattā paccayatākathā. Avijjāva saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo, na pana saṅkhārā avijjāyāti pavattā aññamaññapaccayakathā. Kāladdhānā ime parinipphannena paññattimattāti pavattā addhākathā. Evaṃ khaṇalayamuhuttakathā. Aññassa āsavassa abhāvā āsavā anāsavāti pavattā āsavakathā. Lokuttarānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ lokuttaranti pavattā jarāmaraṇakathā. Nirodhasamāpatti lokuttarāti pavattā saññāvedayitakathā. Sā lokiyāti pavattā dutiyasaññāvedayitakathā. Nirodhasamāpannopi kālaṃ kareyyāti pavattā tatiyasaññāvedayitakathā. Nirodhasamāpatti asaññasattupikātikathā. Kammato añño cittavippayutto kammūpacayotikathā.

A wholesome state arises immediately after an unwholesome one, or an unwholesome state immediately after a wholesome one—thus is the discourse on the linking of wholesome and unwholesome states. For those lying in the womb, the six sense bases, as small as a seed, arise at the moment of rebirth-linking—thus is the discourse on the arising of the six sense bases. The five sense consciousnesses arise immediately after one another—thus is the discourse on the immediate condition. The intimations of right speech and right action are noble matter—thus is the discourse on that. There is another latent tendency apart from sensual desire and so on—thus is the discourse on latent tendencies. The outburst of defilements is dissociated from consciousness—thus is the discourse on that. Just as sensual desire is included in the sense-sphere realm, so too are desire for form and desire for the formless included in the form and formless realms—thus is the discourse on inclusion. The pair of views is indeterminate—thus is the discourse on that. What is held by view is not included—thus is the discourse on that. That which is a root condition for certain things is not, in turn, a conascence condition or other condition for them; a condition is a condition for something in only one way—thus is the discourse on conditionality. Ignorance is a condition for formations, but formations are not a condition for ignorance—thus is the discourse on mutual conditions. These temporal durations are mere concepts by way of what is accomplished—thus is the discourse on time. Likewise, the discourse on moments, instants, and short periods. Because there is no other canker, the cankers are without cankers—thus is the discourse on cankers. The aging and death of supramundane phenomena are supramundane—thus is the discourse on aging and death. The attainment of cessation is supramundane—thus is the discourse on the cessation of perception and feeling. It is mundane—thus is the second discourse on the cessation of perception and feeling. One who has attained cessation may also die—thus is the third discourse on the cessation of perception and feeling. The attainment of cessation is like that of non-percipient beings—thus is the discourse on that. The accumulation of kamma, dissociated from consciousness, is different from kamma—thus is the discourse on the accumulation of kamma.

Balappattā buddhādayo iddhibalena sattānaṃ cittaṃ rāgādianuppattiyā niggaṇhantīti pavattā niggahakathā. Evaṃ kusaluppattiyā paracittapaggahanakathā. Buddhā iddhiyā paresaṃ sukhaṃ dentīti pavattā sukhānuppadānakathā. “Saṅkhārā aniccā”ti manasikaroto atītādibhedabhinne sabbe saṅkhāre ārammaṇavasena ekato adhigaṇhātīti pavattā adhigayhamanasikārakathā. Rūpaṃ hetukantikathā. Evaṃ rūpaṃ sahetukantikathā. Rūpaṃ kusalākusalantikathā. Rūpaṃ vipākotikathā, yathā kāmāvacarakammena jātaṃ rūpaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, evaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammehi jātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarantikathā[M 0.0381]. Rūparāgo rūpadhātuyā, arūparāgo ca arūpadhātuyā pariyāpannotikathā.

The Buddhas and others, having attained the powers, restrain the minds of beings by means of psychic power so that lust and so on do not arise—thus is the discourse on restraint. Likewise, the discourse on uplifting the minds of others for the arising of the wholesome. The Buddhas, through psychic power, give happiness to others—thus is the discourse on bestowing happiness. For one who attends, 'Formations are impermanent,' all formations, distinguished as past and so on, are comprehended as one by way of object—thus is the discourse on comprehensive attention. Form has a cause—thus is the discourse on that. Likewise, form is with a cause—thus is the discourse on that. Form is wholesome and unwholesome—thus is the discourse on that. Form is a result—thus is the discourse on that; just as form born from sense-sphere kamma is of the sense-sphere, so too form born from form-sphere and formless-sphere kamma is of the form-sphere and formless-sphere—thus is the discourse on that. Lust for form is included in the form realm, and lust for the formless is included in the formless realm—thus is the discourse on that.

Atthi arahato puññūpacayotikathā. Natthi arahato akālamaccūtikathā. Yaṃ kiñci uppajjati, sabbamidaṃ kammatotikathā. Indriyabaddhameva dukkhaṃ, na sabbe saṅkhārāti pavattā indriyabaddhakathā. Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā ṭhapetvā ariyamaggantikathā. Maggaphalāneva saṅgho nāma, na ca tāni dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhātītikathā. Tathā na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetītikathā. Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho bhuñjatītikathā. Na vattabbaṃ saṅghassa [V 0.0292] dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathā. Buddhā na kiñci bhuñjanti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ buddhassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathā. Dāyakato dānaṃ visujjhati, na paṭiggāhakatoti pavattā dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā.

There is accumulation of merit for the Arahant—thus is the discourse. There is no untimely death for the Arahant—thus is the discourse. Whatever arises, all of this is from kamma—thus is the discourse. Suffering is bound to the faculties, not all formations—thus is the discourse on being bound to the faculties. All formations are suffering, except for the Noble Path—thus is the discourse. The Sangha is only the path and fruit; they do not accept offerings, therefore it should not be said that the Sangha accepts offerings—thus is the discourse. Likewise, it should not be said that the Sangha purifies offerings—thus is the discourse. It should not be said that the Sangha eats—thus is the discourse. It should not be said that what is given to the Sangha is of great fruit—thus is the discourse. The Buddhas do not eat anything, therefore it should not be said that what is given to the Buddha is of great fruit—thus is the discourse. The gift is purified by the giver, not by the recipient—thus is the discourse on the purification of the offering.

Buddhā tusitaloke eva nibbattanti, na manussaloke. Ettha hi nimmitarūpamattaṃ dassentīti pavattā manussalokakathā. Nimmitarūpaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, na buddhoti pavattā dhammadesanākathā. Rāgova karuṇā nāma, tato natthi buddhānaṃ karuṇātikathā. Buddhānaṃ uccārapassāvo aññe gandhajāte ativiya adhigaṇhātīti pavattā gandhajātakathā. Buddhā ekena maggena cattāri sāmaññaphalāni sacchikarontīti pavattā ekamaggakathā. Parikammādiṃ vināva paṭhamādijjhānā dutiyādijjhānaṃ saṅkamatīti pavattā jhānasaṅkantikathā. Pañcakanaye avitakkavicāramattaṃ jhānaṃ visuṃ jhānaṃ nāma na hoti, jhānantarikaṃ nāma hotīti pavattā jhānantarikakathā. Samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātītikathā. Viññāṇaṃ vinā pasādacakkhunā rūpaṃ passatītikathā.

The Buddhas are born only in the Tusita heaven, not in the human world; here they merely display an emanation body—thus is the discourse on the human world. The emanation body teaches the Dhamma, not the Buddha—thus is the discourse on the teaching of the Dhamma. Compassion is merely a kind of desire; hence, the Buddhas have no compassion—thus is the discourse. The excrement and urine of the Buddhas far surpasses all other fragrances—thus is the discourse on fragrances. The Buddhas realize the four fruits of recluseship through a single path—thus is the discourse on the one path. Without preliminary practice, one transitions from the first jhāna to the second jhāna—thus is the discourse on the transition of jhānas. In the fivefold system, a jhāna that has only sustained thought without initial thought is not called a separate jhāna, but an intermediate jhāna—thus is the discourse on the intermediate jhāna. One in absorption hears sounds—thus is the discourse. One sees forms with the eye faculty without consciousness—thus is the discourse.

Tekālike kilese pajahatīti pavattā kilesappajahanakathā. Nibbānasaṅkhātāpi suññatā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannāti pavattā suññatakathā. Asaṅkhatameva sāmaññaphalantikathā[M 0.0382]. Yesaṃ kesañci dhammānaṃ paṭilābhā asaṅkhatāti pavattā pattikathā. Sabbadhammānaṃ sabhāvasaṅkhātā tathatā asaṅkhatāti pavattā tathatākathā. Anavajjaṭṭhena nibbānampi kusalantikathā. Ānantariyādiṃ vināpi atthi puthujjanassa accantaniyāmatātikathā. Lokiyasaddhādayo na indriyānīti pavattā indriyakathā.

One abandons defilements pertaining to the three periods of time—thus is the discourse on the abandoning of defilements. Even emptiness, designated as Nibbāna, is included in the aggregate of formations—thus is the discourse on emptiness. The unconditioned alone is the fruit of recluseship—thus is the discourse. The attainment of any dhammas whatsoever is unconditioned—thus is the discourse on attainment. The suchness, designated as the intrinsic nature of all dhammas, is unconditioned—thus is the discourse on suchness. Nibbāna is also wholesome in the sense of being blameless—thus is the discourse. Even without an act with immediate consequence, there is ultimate certainty for the worldling—thus is the discourse. Worldly faith and so on are not faculties—thus is the discourse on faculties.

Asañciccāpi ānantariko hotīti pavattā asañciccakathā. Natthi puthujjanassa ñāṇanti pavattā ñāṇakathā. Nerayikānaṃ kammāneva nirayapālarūpena vadhenti, na nirayapālāti pavattā nirayapālakathā. Atthi devesu tiracchānātikathā. Viratittayaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ, pañcaṅgikova maggoti pavattā maggakathā. Paṭiccasamuppādesu ñāṇaṃ lokuttaranti pavattā ñāṇakathā.

One can commit an act with immediate consequence even unintentionally—thus is the discourse on the unintentional. The worldling has no knowledge—thus is the discourse on knowledge. For those in hell, their own kamma torments them in the form of hell-wardens; there are no actual hell-wardens—thus is the discourse on hell-wardens. There are animals among the gods—thus is the discourse. The three abstinences are dissociated from mind, and the path consists of five factors—thus is the discourse on the path. Knowledge of dependent origination is supramundane—thus is the discourse on knowledge.

Tisso saṅgītiyo ārabbha sāsanaṃ navaṃ katanti pavattā sāsanakathā. Puthujjano ekakkhaṇe tedhātukehi dhammehi avivittoti pavattā avivittakathā. Ñeyyāvaraṇahetukaṃ kiñci saṃyojanaṃ [V 0.0293] appahāyapi arahā hotīti pavattā saṃyojanakathā. “Saṅkhārā niccā hontu, rukkhā niccapupphaphalādiyuttā khemino hontū”tiādinā yathādhippāyaṃ iddhi pavattatīti pavattā iddhikathā. Buddhānaṃ sarīraāyupabhāvemattato aññāpi vemattatā atthīti pavattā buddhakathā. Ekasmiṃ khaṇe sabbalokadhātūsu aneke buddhā santīti pavattā sabbadisākathā. Sabbe dhammā niyatāti pavattā dhammakathā. Sabbakammāni phaladāne niyatānīti pavattā kammakathā.

The teaching was renewed by means of three councils—thus is the discourse on the teaching. An ordinary person is not dissociated from the dhammas of the three realms in a single moment—thus is the discourse on non-dissociation. Without abandoning some fetter connected with the hindrance to knowledge, one can become an arahant—thus is the discourse on the fetter. "May formations be permanent, may trees be perpetually endowed with flowers and fruits, may they be secure"—such powers arise according to one's wish—thus is the discourse on psychic power. In respect of the Buddhas, there are differences other than in their bodies, lifespan, and radiance—thus is the discourse on the Buddhas. In a single moment, many Buddhas exist in all world-systems—thus is the discourse on all directions. All phenomena are fixed—thus is the discourse on phenomena. All actions are fixed in giving results—thus is the discourse on actions.

Arahā asabbaññubhāvena sabbaññuvisaye kiñci saṃyojanaṃ appahāya parinibbātīti pavattā parinibbānakathā. Arahā kusalacitto parinibbāyatīti pavattā kusalacittakathā. Arahā āneñje saṇṭhito parinibbāyatīti pavattā āneñjakathā[M 0.0383]. Atthi gabbhaseyyāya dhammābhisamayo, atthi gabbhaseyyāya arahattappatti, supinante dhammābhisamayo, arahattappatti cāti pavattā tissopi kathā. Sabbaṃ supinacittaṃ abyākatantikathā. Khaṇikatāya cittānaṃ natthi āsevanapaccayatātikathā. Sabbe saṅkhatā ekacittakkhaṇikāti pavattā khaṇikakathā.

An arahant, due to not being omniscient, attains final Nibbāna without abandoning some fetter related to the sphere of omniscience—thus is the discourse on final Nibbāna. An arahant with a wholesome mind attains final Nibbāna—thus is the discourse on the wholesome mind. An arahant established in the imperturbable attains final Nibbāna—thus is the discourse on the imperturbable.
