The intention is that this question is unprecedented. In the chapter on person and occasion, 'of four' means of ordinary persons, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. In the converse, 'of two' is stated with reference to non-returners and arahants—this is the method in the chapter on underlying tendencies.

Sānusayavāre pana “yo kāmarāgānusayena sānusayo, so paṭighānusayena sānusayoti? Āmantā…pe… mānānusayena [M 0.0423] sānusayoti? Āmantā. Yo vā pana mānānusayena sānusayo, so kāmarāgānusayena sānusayoti? Anāgāmī mānānusayeneva, na kāmarāgānusayena, tayo pana puggalā tadubhayenāpi anusayenā”ti iminā nayena sesesu dukamūlādīsu pucchāvissajjananayo ñātabbo, ayaṃ puggalavāre nayo.

In the Chapter on (Persons) with Underlying Tendencies, however: 'One who has the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does he have the underlying tendency of aversion? Yes… and so on… Does he have the underlying tendency of conceit? Yes. Or, one who has the underlying tendency of conceit, does he have the underlying tendency of sensual desire? A non-returner has only the underlying tendency of conceit, not the underlying tendency of sensual desire, but the three persons have both underlying tendencies.' By this method, the way of questions and answers should be known for the remaining root-pairs, etc. This is the method in the Chapter on Persons.

“Yato kāmarāgānusayena sānusayo, tato paṭighānusayena sānusayoti? No…pe… mānānusayena sānusayoti? Āmantā. Yato vā pana mānānusayena sānusayo, tato kāmarāgānusayena sānusayoti? Rūpārūpadhātuyā mānānusayeneva, netarena, kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu tadubhayenāpī”tiādinā okāsavāre ca,

'Where one has the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does one there have the underlying tendency of aversion? No… and so on… does one there have the underlying tendency of conceit? Yes. Or, where one has the underlying tendency of conceit, does one there have the underlying tendency of sensual desire? In the form and formless realms, it is only by the underlying tendency of conceit, not by the other; in the sensual realm, in two feelings, it is by both.' And so on, in the Chapter on Occasion,

“Yo yato kāmarāgānusayena sānusayo, so tato paṭighānusayena sānusayoti? No”tiādinā puggalokāsavāre cāti evaṃ anulomanaye ca, “yo kāmarāgānusayena niranusayo, so paṭighānusayena niranusayoti? Āmantā”tiādinā paṭilomanayepi sabbattha anusayavāre vuttānusārato pucchāvissajjananayo ñātabbo.

'One who, where he has the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does he there have the underlying tendency of aversion? No,' and so on in the Chapter on Person and Occasion; and thus in the direct method. 'One who is without the underlying tendency of sensual desire, is he without the underlying tendency of aversion? Yes,' and so on also in the converse method. Everywhere in the Chapter on Underlying Tendencies, the way of questions and answers should be known in accordance with what has been stated.

Tattha yato kāmarāgānusayena sānusayoti yato kāraṇato uppannena kāmarāgānusayena sānusayo, kiṃ so tato kāraṇato uppannapaṭighānusayenapi sānusayoti vuccati. Yasmā panete dve ekasmā ṭhānā na uppajjanti, tasmā “no”ti paṭisedho kato sesaṃ tādisamevāti ayaṃ sānusayavāre nayo.

Here, 'where one has the underlying tendency of sensual desire' means: having the underlying tendency of sensual desire arisen from a certain cause, is one said to also have the underlying tendency of aversion arisen from that same cause? Since these two do not arise from a single basis, the negation 'No' is made. The rest is similar. This is the method in the Chapter on (Persons) with Underlying Tendencies.

Pajahanavāre [M 0.0424] pana “yo kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati, so paṭighānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Āmantā…pe… mānānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahati. Yo vā pana mānānusayaṃ pajahati, so kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti? No…pe… so diṭṭhānusayaṃ vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahatīti? No. Yo vā pana vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahati, so kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti[V 0.0324]? Tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahati. Yo…pe… bhavarāgānusayaṃ avijjānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahati…pe… yo kāmarāgānusayañca paṭighānusayañca mānānusayañca…pe… pajahatīti? Natthī”tiādinā puggalavāre,

In the Chapter on Abandoning, however: 'Does one who abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire also abandon the underlying tendency of aversion? Yes… and so on… the underlying tendency of conceit? He abandons it at the same time. Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency of conceit also abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire? No… and so on… does he abandon the underlying tendency of views and the underlying tendency of doubt? No. Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency of doubt also abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire? He abandons it at the same time. Does one… and so on… abandon the underlying tendency of craving for existence and the underlying tendency of ignorance? He abandons it at the same time… and so on… Does one abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire and the underlying tendency of aversion and the underlying tendency of conceit… and so on…? There is not.' And so on, in the Chapter on Persons,

“Yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati, tato paṭighānusayaṃ pajahatīti? No…pe… yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati, tato mānānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Āmantā. Yato vā pana mānānusayaṃ pajahati, tato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Rūpārūpadhātuyā tato mānānusayameva, kāmadhātuyā pana dvīsu vedanāsu tato mānānusayaṃ pajahatī”tiādinā okāsavāre ca,

'Where one abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does one there abandon the underlying tendency of aversion? No… and so on… Where one abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does one there abandon the underlying tendency of conceit? Yes. Or, where one abandons the underlying tendency of conceit, does one there abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire? In the form and formless realms, from that basis one abandons only the underlying tendency of conceit; but in the sensual realm, in two feelings, from that basis one abandons the underlying tendency of conceit.' And so on, in the Chapter on Occasion,

“Yo yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati, so tato paṭighānusayaṃ pajahatīti? No…pe… mānānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahati…pe… vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahatīti? No. Yo vā pana yato vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahati, so tato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti? Aṭṭhamako dukkhāya vedanāya rūpārūpadhātuyā so tato vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahati, no ca so tato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati, sveva puggalo kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu so tato vicikicchānusayaṃ pajahati, kāmarāgānusayaṃ tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahatī”tiādinā puggalokāsavāre cāti evaṃ anulomanaye ca, “yo kāmarāgānusayaṃ na pajahati, so paṭighānusayaṃ na pajahatīti? Āmantā…pe… vicikicchānusayaṃ na pajahatīti[M 0.0425]? Aṭṭhamako kāmarāgānusayaṃ na pajahati, netaraṃ, anāgāmimaggasamaṅgiṃ, aṭṭhamakañca ṭhapetvā avasesā puggalā tadubhayaṃ na pajahantī”tiādinā paṭilomanaye ca sabbattha pucchāvissajjananayo ñātabbo.

'One who, where he abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does he there abandon the underlying tendency of aversion? No… and so on… does he there abandon the underlying tendency of conceit? He abandons it at the same time… and so on… does he there abandon the underlying tendency of doubt? No. Or, one who, where he abandons the underlying tendency of doubt, does he there abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire? The eighth person, in relation to painful feeling in the form and formless realms, there abandons the underlying tendency of doubt, but he does not there abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire. That same person, in relation to two feelings in the sensual realm, there abandons the underlying tendency of doubt, and abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire at the same time.' And so on, in the Chapter on Person and Occasion; and thus in the direct method. 'One who does not abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire, does he not abandon the underlying tendency of aversion? Yes… and so on… does he not abandon the underlying tendency of doubt? The eighth person does not abandon the underlying tendency of sensual desire, but not the other; setting aside the one endowed with the non-returner's path and the eighth person, the remaining persons do not abandon both.' And so on, also in the converse method; and everywhere the way of questions and answers should be known.

Tattha pajahatīti tena tena maggena pahānapariññāvasena pajahati. Tadekaṭṭhanti pahānekaṭṭhataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paṭhamamaggādinā hi na kevalaṃ diṭṭhādikā eva dhammā pahīyanti, atha kho apāyagamaniyā tena kāmarāgapaṭighamānādayopi pahīyanti eva. Paṭhamamaggavajjhā hi kāmarāgā, apāyagamaniyā ca mānāvijjādayopi, tatiyamaggavajjhāti pahānekaṭṭhā hutvā pahīyanti evāti “no”ti arahattamaggaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi kāmarāgānusayaṃyeva pahīnattā na pajahatīti. Yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti yato uppajjanakaṃ kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti attho, aṭṭhamakoti sotāpattimaggaṭṭho. So hi dakkhiṇeyyakkamena arahattaphalaṭṭhato paṭṭhāya gaṇiyamāno aṭṭhamako nāma. Paṭilomanaye anāgāmimaggasamaṅgiñca aṭṭhamakañca ṭhapetvā avasesāti [V 0.0325] puthujjanasesasekhāsekhā. Tesu hi puthujjanā pahānapariññāya abhāvena na pajahanti, sesā tesaṃ pahīnattāti iminā nayena sabbattha vinicchayo veditabboti ayaṃ pajahanavāre nayo.

Therein, 'abandons' means one abandons through that respective path by way of the full understanding that is abandonment. 'That single state' is said with reference to the singleness of abandonment. For by the first path and so on, not only are things such as wrong views abandoned, but also sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and so on, which lead to the lower realms, are indeed abandoned. For sensual lusts are to be abandoned by the first path, and also conceit, ignorance, and so on, which lead to the lower realms, are to be abandoned by the third path; thus, being of a single state of abandonment, they are indeed abandoned. But 'no' is said with reference to one at the stage of the Arahant path, for he does not abandon it, as the latent tendency to sensual lust has already been abandoned. 'From when he abandons the latent tendency to sensual lust' means from when he abandons the latent tendency to sensual lust that is about to arise. 'An eighth person' refers to one at the stage of the stream-entry path. For when counted in the order of those worthy of offerings, beginning from one at the stage of the fruit of Arahantship, he is called the eighth. In the reverse order, excluding one endowed with the path of non-returning and the eighth person, the rest are ordinary persons, the remaining trainees, and non-trainees. Among them, ordinary persons do not abandon due to the absence of the full understanding that is abandonment; the rest do not abandon because for them these have been abandoned. Thus, the discrimination should be understood everywhere in this way. This is the method in the section on abandoning.

Pariññāvāro pana “yo kāmarāgānusayaṃ parijānāti, so paṭighānusayaṃ parijānātī”tiādinā pajahanavārasadisova. Ayampi hi pajahanavāro viya maggaṭṭhānaññeva vasena vissajjito. Tattha parijānātīti tīhi pariññāhi parijānātīti attho. Ayaṃ pariññāvāre nayo.

The section on full understanding, however, is similar to the section on abandoning, as in: "One who fully understands the latent tendency to sensual lust, fully understands the latent tendency to aversion," and so on. This too, like the section on abandoning, is explained only in terms of those at the path stage. Here, "fully understands" means that one fully understands through the three kinds of full understanding. This is the method in the section on full understanding.

Pahīnavāre pana “yassa kāmarāgānusayo pahīno, tassa paṭighānusayo pahīnoti? Āmantā…pe… mānānusayo pahīnoti? Anāgāmissa kāmarāgānusayova, arahato [M 0.0426] pana mānānusayopi pahīno”tiādinā puggalavāre, “yattha kāmarāgānusayo pahīno, tattha paṭighānusayo pahīnoti? Na vattabbo pahīnoti vā appahīnoti vā. Yattha vā pana…pe… na vattabbo…pe… tattha mānānusayo pahīnoti? Āmantā. Yattha vā pana…pe… pahīnoti? Rūpārūpadhātuyā ettha mānānusayo pahīno, kāmarāgānusayo na vattabbo, kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu ettha tadubhayaṃ pahīna”ntiādinā okāsavāre, puggalokāsavāreti evaṃ anulomanaye, “yassa kāmarāgānusayo appahīno, tassa paṭighānusayo appahīnoti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā…pe… yassa vā pana mānānusayo appahīno, tassa kāmarāgānusayo appahīnoti? Anāgāmissa mānānusayova, tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ tadubhayaṃ appahīna”ntiādinā paṭilomanaye ca vuttanayeneva pucchāvissajjananayo ñātabbo.

In the section on what is abandoned, however: "For one whose latent tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, is the latent tendency to aversion also abandoned? Yes... Is the latent tendency to conceit abandoned? For the non-returner, the latent tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, but for the Arahant, the latent tendency to conceit is also abandoned." Thus, in the section on individuals. "Where the latent tendency to sensual lust is abandoned, is the latent tendency to aversion also abandoned? It cannot be said that it is abandoned or not abandoned. Where, however... it cannot be said... is the latent tendency to conceit abandoned there? Yes. Where, however... is it abandoned? In the form and formless realms, the latent tendency to conceit is abandoned there, but regarding the latent tendency to sensual lust, it cannot be stated; in the sensual realm, in regard to two feelings, both are abandoned there." Thus, in the section on occasions, and in the section on individuals and occasions, in the forward order. "For one whose latent tendency to sensual lust is not abandoned, is the latent tendency to aversion also not abandoned? Yes. For one whose... yes... For one whose latent tendency to conceit is not abandoned, is the latent tendency to sensual lust also not abandoned? For the non-returner, only the latent tendency to conceit is not abandoned, but for three individuals, both are not abandoned." Thus, in the reverse order, the method of questioning and answering should be understood according to the method stated.

Ettha ca phalaṭṭhavaseneva attho gahetabbo maggaṭṭhānaṃ pahīnakilesattābhāvā. Tesaṃ hi anusayā pahīyanti eva, na pana pahīnāti anāgāmiādayo phalaṭṭhāva gahetabbā, okāsavāre pana “na vattabbo”ti idaṃ ubhinnaṃ uppattiṭṭhānassa asādhāraṇattā vuttaṃ. Aññaṃ hi kāmarāgānusayassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ, aññaṃ paṭighānusayassa. Abhāvitamaggassa ca yattha anusayo uppajjati, magge bhāvite tattheva so pahīno nāma hoti, tasmā so tattha pahīnoti vā, appahīnoti vā na vattabbo, sabbatthāpi pana sayaṃ abhāvena tattha appahīnoti na vattabbo. Ubhinnaṃ pana sādhāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya [V 0.0326] “āmantā”ti vuttaṃ. Mānānusayo hi kāmadhātuyā vedanādvayasaṅkhāte sādhāraṇaṭṭhāne kāmarāgena saddhiṃ pahīno nāma hoti[M 0.0427]. Yassa kāmarāgānusayo appahīnoti puthujjanassa, sotāpattisakadāgāmiphalaṭṭhānañca vasena attho gahetabbo. “Tiṇṇaṃ puggalāna”nti hi vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti ayaṃ pahīnavāre nayo.

Here, the meaning should be taken solely in terms of those at the stage of fruition, because those at the path stage do not have the state of having abandoned defilements. For their latent tendencies are being abandoned, but are not yet abandoned; thus, the non-returners and others should be taken as those at the stage of fruition. However, in the section on occasion, 'it cannot be stated' is said because the ground of arising for the two is not common. For the ground of arising for the latent tendency to sensual lust is one thing, and that for the latent tendency to aversion is another. Moreover, for one who has not developed the path, wherever a latent tendency arises, it is called 'abandoned' right there when the path has been developed. Therefore, it cannot be stated that it is abandoned or not abandoned there. But in all cases, due to its own absence there, it cannot be said that it is 'not abandoned' there. However, regarding a shared ground for both, it is said, 'Yes.' For the latent tendency to conceit is called 'abandoned' along with the latent tendency to sensual lust in the shared ground, which is designated as the two feelings in the sensual realm. Regarding 'for one whose latent tendency to sensual lust is not abandoned,' the meaning should be taken by way of the worldling, and those at the stage of the fruit of stream-entry and once-returning. For it is said, 'For three persons.' The rest is easily understood. This is the method in the section on what is abandoned.

Uppajjanavāre pana “yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati, tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatī”tiādinā sabbattha anusayavārasadisovāti ayaṃ uppajjanavāre nayo.

In the section on arising, however, the method is similar to the section on latent tendencies everywhere, as in: "For whom the latent tendency to sensual lust arises, for him does the latent tendency to aversion arise," and so on. This is the method in the section on arising.

Dhātuvāre pana “kāmadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kati anusayā anusenti, kati anusayā nānusenti, kati anusayā bhaṅgā? Kāmadhātuyā cutassa rūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa…pe… kati bhaṅgā? Kāmadhātuyā cutassa arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa…pe… rūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa na arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa…pe… kati bhaṅgaṃ? Kāmadhātuyā cutassa na kāmadhātuṃ, na arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa…pe… na rūpadhātuṃ na arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa. Na kāmadhātuṃ na rūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kati bhaṅgā”ti evaṃ kāmadhātumūlakā nava pucchā, tathā “rūpadhātuyā cutassā”tiādinā rūpadhātumūlakā nava, arūpadhātuyā nava cāti sattavīsati anulomapucchā, tathā “na kāmadhātuyā cutassā”tiādinā sattavīsati paṭilomapucchā ca, tathā “na kāmadhātuyā na arūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassā”tiādinā sattavīsati dukamūlakā pucchā cāti evaṃ pucchāvāre ekāsīti pucchā veditabbā.

In the section on elements, however: "For one who has passed away from the sensual realm and is reborn in the sensual realm, how many latent tendencies persist, how many do not persist, and how many are subject to distribution? For one who has passed away from the sensual realm and is reborn in the form realm... how many are subject to distribution? For one who has passed away from the sensual realm and is reborn in the formless realm... for one reborn in the form realm but not reborn in the formless realm... how many are subject to distribution? For one who has passed away from the sensual realm and is reborn neither in the sensual realm nor the formless realm... nor in the form realm nor the formless realm... nor in the sensual realm nor the form realm, how many are subject to distribution?" Thus, there are nine questions rooted in the sensual realm. Similarly, there are nine questions rooted in the form realm, such as 'For one who has passed away from the form realm...,' and nine rooted in the formless realm, making twenty-seven forward questions. Likewise, there are twenty-seven reverse questions, such as 'For one who has not passed away from the sensual realm...,' and twenty-seven questions rooted in pairs, such as 'For one who has passed away neither from the sensual realm nor the formless realm and is reborn in the sensual realm....' In this way, the section on questions should be understood as comprising eighty-one questions.

Tattha anusentīti cittasantāne anugatā hutvā kati anusenti, bhaṅgāti anusenti ca nānusenti cāti evaṃ kati vibhajitabbāti attho. Na kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassāti kāmadhātuvirahitā dve rūpārūpadhātuyo upapajjantassa. Na kāmadhātuṃ na rūpadhātunti arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa. Na kāmadhātuyāti rūpārūpadhātūhi cutassa, evaṃ sesesupi sabbattha [M 0.0428] paṭisandhivasena, dhātuvasena ca attho veditabboti ayaṃ uddesavāre nayo.

Here, 'persist' means how many latent tendencies, having followed along, continue in the mental continuum; while 'subject to distribution' refers to how many are to be divided into those that persist and those that do not persist—this is the meaning. 'Not reborn in the sensual realm' refers to being reborn in the two realms of form and formlessness, which are devoid of the sensual realm. 'Neither in the sensual realm nor the form realm' means being reborn in the formless realm. 'Not from the sensual realm' means having passed away from the form and formless realms. Similarly, in all other cases, the meaning should be understood by way of rebirth-linking and by way of the realms. This is the method in the summary section.

Niddesavāre panassa “kāmadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci satta anusayā anusenti, kassaci pañca anusayā anusenti, anusayā bhaṅgā natthi, kāmadhātuyā cutassa rūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci satta anusayā anusenti, kassaci pañca, kassaci tayo [V 0.0327] …pe… bhaṅgā natthī”ti iminā nayena sabbattha vissajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ, ayaṃ panettha viseso – rūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa satteva anusayā anusenti, tathā “arūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassā”tiādīsupi, arūpadhātuyā pana cutassa rūpadhātuyā upapatti natthi, heṭṭhā upapajjamāno kāmadhātuṃ eva upapajjati, satteva anusayā anusentīti evaṃ aññesupi evarūpesu vissajjananayo veditabboti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti ayamettha pāḷinayo.

In the section on exposition, it should be understood that for one who has passed away from the sense-sphere and is reborn in the sense-sphere, for some, seven latent tendencies persist; for some, five latent tendencies persist; there is no cessation of latent tendencies. For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere and is reborn in the form-sphere, for some, seven latent tendencies persist; for some, five; for some, three… there is no cessation. In this way, the explanation should be understood everywhere. Here, however, there is a distinction: for one who has passed away from the form-sphere and is reborn in the sense-sphere, only seven latent tendencies persist, as also in cases like “for one who has passed away from the formless sphere and is reborn in the sense-sphere,” etc. But there is no rebirth in the form-sphere for one who has passed away from the formless sphere; one who is reborn below is reborn only in the sense-sphere, and only seven latent tendencies persist. Thus, the method of explanation should be understood in other similar cases. This is the distinction here; the rest is as previously stated. This is the method of the Pāli text here.

Tattha kassaci sattāti puthujjanavasena vuttaṃ, pañcāti sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ vasena. Tesaṃ hi diṭṭhivicikicchānusayā pahīnāti, kāmadhātuyā pana anāgāmīnaṃ upapattiabhāvato paṭhamavāre “kassaci tayo”ti na vuttaṃ, rūpārūpadhātūsu uppajjanavāresu eva vuttaṃ…pe… anāgāmīnaṃ hi kāmarāgapaṭighānampi pahīnattā tayova anusayā anusenti, idha ca anusayānaṃ uppattivasena nayo, anusayānaṃ anusayanaṃ aggahetvā appahīnabhāvena paṭisandhikkhaṇe api anusayanaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sattevāti ariyasāvakassa rūpārūpadhātuyā cutassa heṭṭhā kāmabhavādīsu upapatti nāma natthi, puthujjanasseva hoti, tasmā “sattevā”ti niyametvā vuttaṃ, arūpadhātuyā cutassa rūpadhātuyā upapatti natthīti. Kasmā natthi? Arūpīnaṃ rūpajjhānassa abhāvā. Te [M 0.0429] hi sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamanarūpadhātuṃ upapannāti. Sesaṃ nayato suviññeyyamevāti ayaṃ dhātuvāre nayo. Ayaṃ anusayayamakamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

Here, 'for some, seven' is stated with reference to ordinary persons; 'five' refers to stream-enterers and once-returners, for whom the latent tendencies of wrong view and doubt are abandoned. However, 'for some, three' is not stated in the first instance, because non-returners are not reborn in the sense-sphere. It is stated only in the instances of arising in the form and formless spheres. For non-returners, since the latent tendencies of sensual desire and aversion are also abandoned, only three latent tendencies persist. Here, the method is in terms of the arising of latent tendencies; their persistence should be understood not as their active manifestation, but as their unabandoned state, which is present even at the moment of rebirth-linking. As for 'only seven': for a noble disciple who has passed away from the form or formless sphere, there is no such thing as rebirth below in the sense-existence and so on; that occurs only for an ordinary person. Therefore, it is stated with the restriction 'only seven.' There is no rebirth in the form-sphere for one who has passed away from the formless sphere. Why is there none? Because those in the formless sphere lack the form jhānas. They are reborn in the formless sphere by completely transcending perceptions of form. The rest should be easily understood from the method. This is the method in the section on elements. This is the method of explaining the meaning of the Anusaya Yamaka Mātikā.

Cittayamakamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The explanation of the meaning of the Cittayamaka Mātikā.

Cittayamakamātikāyaṃ pana pāḷivavatthānaṃ tāva evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imissaṃ hi mātikāyaṃ puggalavāro dhammavāro puggaladhammavāroti āditova tayo suddhikamahāvārā honti, tattha “yassa cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ puggalavasena cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ dīpento gato puggalavāro nāma. “Yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ dhammavaseneva cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ dīpento gato dhammavāro nāma. “Yassa yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ ubhayavaseneva cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ dīpento gato puggaladhammavāro nāma.

In the Cittayamaka Mātikā, the Pāli arrangement should first be understood as follows. In this Mātikā, there are initially three pure great sections: the section on individuals, the section on phenomena, and the section on individuals and phenomena. Here, the section on individuals is so called because it explains the distinctions of the arising and ceasing of consciousness, etc., from the perspective of an individual, as in: “Whose consciousness arises but does not cease.” The section on phenomena is so called because it explains the distinctions of the arising and ceasing of consciousness, etc., from the perspective of phenomena, as in: “Which consciousness arises but does not cease.” The section on individuals and phenomena is so called because it explains the distinctions of the arising and ceasing of consciousness, etc., from both perspectives, as in: “For whom, which consciousness arises but does not cease.”

Tato [V 0.0328] “yassa sarāgaṃ citta”ntiādīnaṃ soḷasannaṃ padānaṃ vasena apare sarāgādipadavisesitā soḷasa puggalavārā, soḷasa dhammavārā, soḷasa puggaladhammavārāti aṭṭhacattālīsa missakavārā honti, te sarāgādipadamattaṃ dassetvā saṃkhittā. Tato “yassa kusalaṃ citta”ntiādinā nayena chasaṭṭhidvisatasaṅkhātānaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadānaṃ vasena apare kusalādipadavisesitā chasaṭṭhidvisatapuggalavārā, chasaṭṭhidvisatadhammavārā, chasaṭṭhidvisatapuggaladhammavārāti aṭṭhanavutisattasatā missakavārā honti, tepi kusalādipadamattaṃ dassetvā saṃkhittāyeva, yānipettha sanidassanādīni padāni cittena saddhiṃ na yujjanti, tāni moghapucchāvasena gahitānīti.

Then, based on the sixteen phrases beginning with “whose consciousness is with lust,” there are sixteen sections on individuals qualified by terms like “with lust,” sixteen sections on phenomena, and sixteen sections on individuals and phenomena—totaling forty-eight mixed sections. These are summarized by showing merely the terms like “with lust.” Next, following the method of the phrases beginning with “whose consciousness is wholesome,” based on the two hundred sixty-six Abhidhamma matrix terms, there are two hundred sixty-six sections on individuals qualified by terms like “wholesome,” two hundred sixty-six sections on phenomena, and two hundred sixty-six sections on individuals and phenomena—totaling seven hundred ninety-eight mixed sections. These too are summarized by showing merely the terms like “wholesome.” Here, the terms like “with visible manifestation,” which do not accord with consciousness, are taken up in the manner of futile questions.

Tesu pana tīsu vāresu sabbapaṭhame suddhikapuggalamahāvāre tāva uppādanirodhakālasambhedavāro uppāduppannavāro nirodhuppannavāro [M 0.0430] uppādavāro nirodhavāro uppādanirodhavāro uppajjamānananirodhavāro uppajjamānuppannavāro nirujjhamānuppannavāro uppannuppādavāro atītānāgatavāro uppannuppajjamānavāro niruddhanirujjhamānavāro atikkantakālavāro cāti cuddasa antaravārā, tesu uppādavāro nirodhavāro uppādanirodhavāroti imesu tīsu vāresu paccekaṃ vattamānātītassa, vattamānānāgatassa, atītānāgatassa cāti tiṇṇaṃ kālabhedānaṃ vasena anulomapaṭilomato cha cha katvā aṭṭhārasa yamakāni, uppannuppādavāre atītānāgatakālavasena anulomato dve, paṭilomato dveti cattāri yamakāni, sesesu ādito niddiṭṭhesu tīsu, antare niddiṭṭhesu tīsu, avasāne niddiṭṭhesu catūsūti dasasu vāresu anulomato ekaṃ, paṭilomato ekanti dve dve katvā vīsati yamakāni, evaṃ sabbesupi cuddasasu antaravāresu dvācattālīsa yamakāni, caturāsīti pucchā, aṭṭhasaṭṭhiatthasataṃ hoti. Yathā ca ekasmiṃ suddhikapuggalamahāvāre, tathā suddhikadhammamahāvāre, suddhikapuggaladhammamahāvārepīti tīsu mahāvāresu chabbīsatiyamakasataṃ, tato diguṇā pucchā, diguṇā atthā ca veditabbā, idaṃ pana vārattayaṃ sarāgādivasena soḷasaguṇaṃ, kusalādivasena chasaṭṭhidvisataguṇaṃ katvā imissā cittayamakamātikāya anekāni yamakasahassāni, taddiguṇā pucchā, taddiguṇā atthā ca honti, pāṭho pana saṃkhitto. Evamettha pāḷivavatthānaṃ viditvā idāni anuttānapadatthānusārena vibhaṅganayasahito saṅkhepatthavaṇṇanānayo evaṃ veditabbo.

Now, in these three sections, first in the Suddhika Puggala Mahāvāra, there are fourteen intermediate sections: the section on the combination of the time of arising and cessation, the section on arising and arisen, the section on cessation and arisen, the section on arising, the section on cessation, the section on arising and cessation, the section on the cessation of what is arising, the section on the arising and the arisen, the section on the ceasing and the arisen, the section on the arisen and arising, the section on past and future, the section on the arisen and the arising, the section on the ceased and the ceasing, and the section on elapsed time. Among these, in the three sections on arising, cessation, and arising and cessation, for each of the three time-divisions—present and past, present and future, and past and future—there are six pairs in forward and reverse order, making eighteen pairs. In the section on the arisen and arising, considering past and future time, there are two pairs in forward order and two in reverse, totaling four pairs. In the remaining ten sections—the first three mentioned, the middle three, and the last four—there is one pair in forward order and one in reverse for each, making twenty pairs. Thus, in all fourteen intermediate sections, there are forty-two pairs, eighty-four questions, and one hundred and sixty-eight cases. Just as in the one Suddhika Puggala Mahāvāra, so too in the Suddhika Dhamma Mahāvāra and the Suddhika Puggala Dhamma Mahāvāra. In these three great sections, there are one hundred and twenty-six pairs, twice that number of questions, and twice that number of cases. Furthermore, this triad of sections, when multiplied by the sixteen factors such as 'with lust,' etc., and by the two hundred and sixty-six factors such as 'wholesome,' etc., results in many thousands of pairs in this Cittayamaka Mātikā, with twice that number of questions, and twice that number of cases. The text, however, is concise. Having thus understood the arrangement of the Pāli, the method of brief explanation of the meaning, which includes the method of analysis according to the detailed meaning of the terms, should now be understood as follows.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjatīti yassa puggalassa cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇasamaṅgitāya uppajjati. Na nirujjhatīti [V 0.0329] nirodhakkhaṇaṃ appattatāya na nirujjhati. Tassa cittanti kiṃ tassa puggalassa tato paṭṭhāya [M 0.0431] cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti pucchā, tassā ca, “pacchimacittassa uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhati, nirujjhissati nuppajjissati, itaresaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhati, nirujjhissati ceva uppajjissati cā”ti vissajjanaṃ. Tattha tesaṃ cittanti yesaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ pacchimacittasaṅkhātassa cuticittassa uppādakkhaṇe vattati, tesaṃ tadeva cuticittaṃ uppādappattatāya uppajjati nāma, bhaṅgaṃ appattatāya na nirujjhati nāma, idāni pana bhaṅgaṃ patvā taṃ tesaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissati, tato appaṭisandhikattā aññaṃ nuppajjissati. Itaresanti pacchimacittasamaṅgiṃ khīṇāsavaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesānaṃ sekhāsekhaputhujjanānaṃ nirujjhissati ceva aññaṃ pana tasmiṃ vā attabhāve uppajjissati cāti attho.

“For whom consciousness arises”—for that person, consciousness arises, being endowed with the moment of arising. “It does not cease”—because it has not reached the moment of cessation. “That person’s consciousness”—the question is, “Will that person’s consciousness cease from that point onward?” And the answer to that is: “At the moment of the arising of the final consciousness, for those, consciousness arises but does not cease; it will cease and will not arise again. For others, at the moment of the arising of consciousness, consciousness arises but does not cease; it will cease and will arise.” Here, “their consciousness” refers to those whose taints are destroyed—at the moment of the arising of their death-consciousness, which is termed their final consciousness. That very death-consciousness arises because it has reached the moment of arising, and it does not cease because it has not reached the moment of dissolution. But now, having reached dissolution, that consciousness of theirs will cease, and because there is no further rebirth-linking, another will not arise. “Others” means, excluding the one whose taints are destroyed and who possesses the final consciousness—the remaining trainees, non-trainees, and ordinary people. For them, consciousness will cease, and another will arise in that same existence. This is the meaning.

“Yassa vā pana cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissati, tassa cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatī”ti imissā dutiyapucchāya pacchimacittasamaṅgino khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ sandhāya “āmantā”ti vissajjanaṃ. “Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati nirujjhati, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhissati uppajjissatī”ti pucchāya “no”ti paṭisedhova vissajjanaṃ. Na uppajjati nirujjhatīti hi bhaṅgakkhaṇe arahato pacchimacittampi sesānaṃ bhijjamānacittampi pucchati, tato paṭṭhāya pana arahato tāva cittaṃ na nirujjhissatīti sakkā vattuṃ, uppajjissatīti pana na sakkā, tasmā “no”ti ettha paṭisedho kato, “yassa vā pana cittaṃ na nirujjhissati uppajjissati, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjati nirujjhatī”ti pucchāya “natthī”ti paṭikkhepova vissajjanaṃ. Yassa hi cittaṃ na nirujjhissati uppajjissati, so ca puggalo natthīti.

“Or for one whose consciousness will cease and not arise, does their consciousness arise and not cease?” To this second question, the answer is “Yes,” referring to the consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed, endowed with the final consciousness. “For one whose consciousness does not arise and ceases, will their consciousness not cease and arise?” To this question, the answer is “No,” a denial. For the question concerns the final consciousness of the Arahant at the moment of dissolution and the dissolving consciousnesses of others. From that point onward, it can be said that the Arahant’s consciousness will not cease, but it cannot be said that it will arise. Therefore, the denial is made with “No.” “And for one whose consciousness will not cease and will arise, does their consciousness not arise and cease?” To this question, the answer is “There is none,” a rejection. For there is no such person whose consciousness will not cease and will arise.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā, yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe taṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, no ca uppajjati, sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ cittaṃ uppannañceva uppajjati ca, yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati[M 0.0432], tassa cittaṃ nuppannanti? Cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ nuppajjati, no ca nuppannaṃ, nirodhasamāpannānaṃ asaññasattānaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati ceva nuppannañca. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjatīti? Āmantā. Ettha ca uppannanti uppādasamaṅginopetaṃ nāmaṃ, uppajjatīti ca uppādasamaṅginova.

For whom a mind arises, for them has a mind arisen? Yes. Or for whom has a mind arisen, for them does a mind arise? For all, at the moment of the mind’s dissolution, that mind has arisen but does not arise; for all, at the moment of the mind’s arising, for them the mind has both arisen and arises. For whom a mind does not arise, for them has a mind not arisen? At the moment of the mind’s dissolution, the mind does not arise, but it is not un-arisen; for those in the attainment of cessation and for non-percipient beings, mind does not arise and has not arisen. Or for whom has a mind not arisen, for them does a mind not arise? Yes. Here, 'arisen' is a term also for that which is endowed with the moment of arising, and 'arises' is a term only for that which is endowed with the moment of arising.

Yassa [V 0.0330] cittaṃ nirujjhati, tassa cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… nirujjhatīti? Bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ na nirujjhati, tassa cittaṃ nuppannanti? Nirodhasamāpannādīnaṃ cittaṃ. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā.

For whom a mind ceases, for them has a mind arisen? Yes. Or for whom has a mind arisen, for them does a mind cease? At the moment of dissolution, it is so. For whom a mind does not cease, for them has a mind not arisen? This refers to the mind of those in the attainment of cessation and the like. Or for whom has a mind not arisen, for them does a mind not cease? Yes.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ uppajjitthāti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Ettha ca uppādappattattā uppajjittha, taṃ anatītattā uppajjati nāmāti atthoti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ khaṇapaccuppannavasena attho vutto. Uppajjitthāti pana imassa atītacittakkhaṇavasena atthe gayhamāne eva uparipāḷiyā na virujjhati, na aññathāti paññāyati, tasmā pubbāparaṃ oloketvā pāḷiavirodhena attho gahetabbo.

For whom a mind arises, for them did a mind arise? Yes. Or for whom did a mind arise, for them does a mind arise? For all, at the moment of the mind's arising, it is so. Here, because it has attained arising, it is called "did arise," but because it is not past, it is called "arises"—this is the meaning stated in the commentary, explained in terms of the momentary present. However, if the meaning of "did arise" is taken in terms of the past mind-moment, it does not contradict the preceding text; it is not understood otherwise. Therefore, having considered what comes before and after, the meaning should be taken in a way that does not contradict the Pāli text.

Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjitthāti? Uppajjittha. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjatīti? Natthi. Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? Pacchimacittasamaṅgikhīṇāsavavirahitānaṃ cittaṃ tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ…pe… nuppajjissatīti? Asekhānaṃ pacchimacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjatīti? Pacchimacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ uppajjittha, tassa cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? Pacchimacittasamaṅgiṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjittha, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Natthi. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjitthāti? Uppajjittha.

For whom a mind does not arise, for them did a mind not arise? It did arise. Or for whom did a mind not arise, for them does a mind not arise? There is none. For whom a mind arises, for them will a mind arise? This is so for those apart from the taint-destroyed one endowed with the final consciousness. Or for whom will a mind arise, for them does a mind arise? At the moment of arising, it is so. For whom a mind does not arise, for them will a mind not arise? For the Asekhas, at the dissolution-moment of the final mind, it is so. Or for whom will a mind not arise, for them does a mind not arise? At the dissolution-moment of the final mind, it is so. For whom a mind did arise, for them will a mind arise? Except for one possessing the final mind-moment, for the remaining, it is so. Or for whom will a mind arise, for them did a mind arise? Yes. For whom a mind did not arise, for them will a mind not arise? There is none. Or for whom will a mind not arise, for them did a mind not arise? It did arise.

Yassa [M 0.0433] cittaṃ nirujjhati, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhitthāti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… nirujjhatīti? Bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ…pe… na nirujjhitthāti? Nirujjhittha. Yassa vā pana…pe… natthi. Yassa cittaṃ nirujjhati, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti? Pacchimacittasamaṅgiṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… sesānaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ…pe… nirujjhissati. Yassa vā pana…pe… nirujjhati.

For whom a mind ceases, for them did a mind cease? Yes. Or for whom did a mind cease, for them does a mind cease? At the moment of dissolution, it is so. For whom a mind does not cease, for them did a mind not cease? It did cease. Or for whom did a mind not cease, for them does a mind not cease? There is none. For whom a mind ceases, for them will a mind cease? Except for one possessing the final mind-moment, for the remaining minds at the moment of dissolution, it is so. Or for whom will a mind cease, for them does a mind cease? For the remaining at the moment of dissolution, it is so. For whom a mind does not cease, for them will a mind not cease? It will cease. Or for whom will a mind not cease, for them does a mind not cease? It ceases.

Yassa cittaṃ nirujjhittha, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti? Pacchimacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapetvā [V 0.0331] sesānaṃ cittaṃ tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā. Yassa cittaṃ na nirujjhittha, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhissatīti? Natthi. Yassa vā pana…pe… na nirujjhitthāti? Nirujjhittha.

For whom a mind did cease, for them will a mind cease? Except at the dissolution-moment of the final mind, for the remaining minds, it is so. Or for whom will a mind cease, for them did a mind cease? Yes. For whom a mind did not cease, for them will a mind not cease? There is none. Or for whom will a mind not cease, for them did a mind not cease? It did cease.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhitthāti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhitthāti? Nirujjhittha. Yassa vā pana…pe… natthi, yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhissatīti? Pacchimacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā. Yassa cittaṃ uppajjittha, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti? Nirujjhamānaṃ pacchimacittaṃ ṭhapetvā tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjittha, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhissatīti? Natthi. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjitthāti? Uppajjittha.

For whom a mind arises, for them did a mind cease? Yes. Or for whom did a mind cease, for them does a mind arise? For all, at the moment of the mind's arising, it is so. For whom a mind does not arise, for them did a mind not cease? It did cease. Or for whom did a mind not cease, for them does a mind not arise? There is none. For whom a mind arises, for them will a mind cease? Yes. Or for whom will a mind cease, for them does a mind arise? For all, at the moment of the mind's arising, it is so. For whom a mind does not arise, for them will a mind not cease? At the final mind's dissolution-moment, it is so. Or for whom will a mind not cease, for them does a mind not arise? Yes. For whom a mind did arise, for them will a mind cease? Except for the final mind while ceasing, it is so. Or for whom will a mind cease, for them did a mind arise? Yes. For whom a mind did not arise, for them will a mind not cease? There is none. Or for whom will a mind not cease, for them did a mind not arise? It did arise.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, tassa cittaṃ na nirujjhatīti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjati, tassa cittaṃ nirujjhatīti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppajjatīti? Āmantā.

For whom does a mind arise, for them does a mind not cease? Yes. Or for whom does a mind not cease, for them does a mind arise? For all, at the moment of the mind's arising, it is so. For whom does a mind not arise, for them does a mind cease? For all, at the moment of the mind's dissolution, it is so. Or for whom does a mind cease, for them does a mind not arise? Yes.

Yassa [M 0.0434] cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ, tassa cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppajjamānanti? Sabbesaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjamānaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppannanti? Nirodhasamāpannādīnaṃ cittaṃ tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā.

For whom is a mind arising, for them has a mind arisen? Yes. Or for whom has a mind arisen, for them is a mind arising? For all, at the moment of the mind's arising, it is so. For whom is a mind not arising, for them has a mind not arisen? For those who have attained cessation and so forth, the mind is so. Or for whom has a mind not arisen, for them is a mind not arising? Yes.

Yassa cittaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ, tassa cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… bhaṅgakkhaṇe tathā. Yassa cittaṃ na nirujjhamānaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppannanti? Nirodhasamāpannādīnaṃ cittaṃ tathā. Yassa vā pana…pe… āmantā.

For whom is a mind ceasing, for them has a mind arisen? Yes. Or for whom has a mind arisen, for them is a mind ceasing? At the moment of dissolution, it is so. For whom is a mind not ceasing, for them has a mind not arisen? For those who have attained cessation and so forth, the mind is so. Or for whom has a mind not arisen, for them is a mind not ceasing? Yes.

Yassa cittaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ uppajjitthāti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana…pe… uppannanti[V 0.0332]? Cittasamaṅgīnaṃ tathā. Yassa cittaṃ nuppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjitthāti? Uppajjittha. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppannanti? Natthi…pe… yassa cittaṃ nuppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Uppajjissati. Yassa vā pana…pe… nuppannanti? Uppannaṃ.

For whom has a mind arisen, for them did a mind arise? Yes. Or for whom did a mind arise, for them has a mind arisen? For those endowed with mind, it is so. For whom has a mind not arisen, for them did a mind not arise? It arose. Or for whom did a mind not arise, for them has a mind not arisen? There is none. For whom has a mind not arisen, for them will a mind arise? It will arise. Or for whom will a mind arise, for them has a mind not arisen? It has arisen.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjittha no ca tassa cittaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? Āmantā. Yassa vā pana cittaṃ uppajjissati no ca tassa cittaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ uppajjitthāti? Āmantā. Ettha “no ca tassa cittaṃ nuppanna”nti idaṃ asaññādiacittake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ niyamena cittuppattiyā abhāvato “āmantā”ti ubhayattha vissajjanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañca vāro kālattaye gahetvā samatthitoti gahetabbo.

For whom a mind did arise but for whom a mind has not arisen, for them will a mind arise? Yes. Or for whom a mind will arise but for whom a mind has not arisen, for them did a mind arise? Yes. Here, “and for whom a mind has not arisen” is said with reference to non-percipient beings and so forth, who are without mind. Because for them there is an invariable absence of the arising of mind, the answer “Yes” is given in both cases. And this section should be understood as being established by considering the three periods of time.

“Yassa cittaṃ nuppajjittha no ca tassa cittaṃ nuppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Natthi. Yassa vā pana cittaṃ nuppajjissati no ca tassa cittaṃ nuppannaṃ, tassa cittaṃ nuppajjitthāti? Uppajjittha.

For whom a mind did not arise and for whom a mind has not arisen, for them will a mind not arise? There is none. Or for whom a mind will not arise and for whom a mind has not arisen, for them did a mind not arise? It arose.

Uppannaṃ uppajjamānanti? Uppādakkhaṇe cittaṃ tathā. Uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Nuppannaṃ nuppajjamānanti? Āmantā. Nuppajjamānaṃ nuppannanti? Atītānāgatacittaṃ tathā.

Is the arisen arising? At the moment of arising, the mind is so. Is the arising arisen? Yes. Is the not-arisen not arising? Yes. Is the not-arising not arisen? The past and future mind are so.

Niruddhaṃ [M 0.0435] nirujjhamānanti? No, nirujjhamānaṃ niruddhanti? No, naniruddhaṃ nanirujjhamānanti? Uppādakkhaṇe anāgatañca cittaṃ tathā. Nanirujjhamānaṃ naniruddhantipi tatheva.

Is the ceased ceasing? No. Is the ceasing ceased? No. Is the not-ceased not ceasing? The mind at the moment of arising and the future mind are so. Is the not-ceasing not ceased? Likewise.

Yassa cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, tassa cittanti? No ca bhaṅgakkhaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ, atītaṃ cittaṃ tadubhayaṃ vītikkantaṃ, yassa vā pana cittaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, uppajjamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, tassa cittanti? Atītaṃ citta”nti iminā nayena puggalavāre sabbattha vissajjananayo veditabbo.

“For whom a mind's arising moment has passed and is past time, and its ceasing moment has passed and is past time, for them is there a mind? No. The moment of dissolution has passed; for a past mind, both have passed. Or for whom a mind's ceasing moment has passed and is past time, and its arising moment has passed and is past time, for them is there a mind? It is the past mind.” By this method, the way of answering should be understood in all instances in the section on individuals.

Tattha uppajjamānaṃ khaṇanti uppajjamānassa khaṇaṃ, uppādakkhaṇanti attho. Khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ [V 0.0333] atikkantakālanti na ciraṃ vītikkantaṃ, tameva pana uppādakkhaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālanti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇanti nirujjhamānassa khaṇaṃ, bhaṅgakkhaṇanti attho. Khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālanti kiṃ tassa cittaṃ evaṃ nirodhakkhaṇampi vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hotīti pucchati. Yassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hoti, nirodhakkhaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hoti, atītaṃ pana cittaṃ ubhopi khaṇe khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hotīti atītacittavasena vissajjanaṃ kataṃ. Imināva upāyena uparimesu atthadhammavārādīsu ca sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ atikkantakālavāre nayo.

Therein, ‘the moment of arising’ means the moment of that which is arising; the meaning is ‘the moment of origination.’ ‘A moment that has passed is past time’ means not long passed, but that very moment of origination, having passed, is counted as ‘past time.’ ‘The moment of ceasing’ means the moment of that which is ceasing; the meaning is ‘the moment of dissolution.’ ‘A moment that has passed is past time’—it asks: ‘Is it that for that mind, the moment of cessation also, having passed, is called past time?’ The answer is given by way of the past mind thus: ‘For a mind at the moment of dissolution, the moment of origination, having passed, is called past time; the moment of cessation, having passed, is called past time. But for a past mind, both moments, having passed, are called past time.’ By this very method, the meaning should be understood in the subsequent sections on meaning, phenomena, etc., and in all answers. This is the method in the section on past time.

Yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati nanirujjhati, taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissatīti? Āmantā. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… āmantā. Yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati nirujjhati, taṃ cittaṃ nanirujjhissati uppajjissatīti? No. Yaṃ vā pana cittaṃ nanirujjhissati uppajjissati, taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati nirujjhatīti? Natthi.

A mind that arises and does not cease—will that mind cease and not arise? Yes. Or a mind that will cease and not arise—does that mind arise and not cease? Yes. A mind that does not arise and ceases—will that mind not cease and arise? No. Or a mind that will not cease and will arise—does that mind not arise and cease? There is none.

Yaṃ [M 0.0436] cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… uppajjatīti? Uppādakkhaṇe cittaṃ tathā, evaṃ paṭilomapucchāsupi tato sesāsupi. “Yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ nuppannanti? Atītānāgataṃ cittaṃ tathā. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… āmantā…pe… bhaṅgakkhaṇe citta”ntiādinā, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ uppajjitthāti? No. Yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjitthāti? Bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ anāgatañcā”tiādinā, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? No. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… no, yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Anāgataṃ cittaṃ nuppajjati, no ca taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjissati, bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ atītaṃ citta”ntiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjittha, taṃ cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? No. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… no, yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjittha, taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Anāgataṃ citta”ntiādinā ca,

‘Is a mind that arises, an arisen mind? Yes. Or again, is an arisen mind, a mind that arises? At the moment of arising, the mind is so.’ And likewise in the reverse questions and the rest: ‘Is a mind that does not arise, an unarisen mind? Past and future mind are so. Or again, is an unarisen mind, a mind that does not arise? Yes... the mind at the moment of dissolution,’ and so on. ‘Is a mind that arises, a mind that did arise? No. Is a mind that does not arise, a mind that did not arise? The mind at the moment of dissolution and the future mind,’ and so on. ‘Is a mind that arises, a mind that will arise? No. Or again... No. Is a mind that does not arise, a mind that will not arise? A future mind does not arise, and it is not that that mind will not arise; the mind at the moment of dissolution and the past mind,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that did arise, a mind that will arise? No. Or again... No. Is a mind that did not arise, a mind that will not arise? Future mind,’ and so on.

“Yaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati, taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhitthāti? No”tiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhitthāti? No”tiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti[V 0.0334]? Āmantā”tiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjittha, taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissatīti? No”tiādinā ca,

‘Is a mind that is ceasing, a mind that did cease? No,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that is arising, a mind that did cease? No,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that is arising, a mind that will cease? Yes,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that did arise, a mind that will cease? No,’ and so on.

“Yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ, taṃ cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… uppajjamānanti…pe… uppādakkhaṇe citta”ntiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhamānaṃ, taṃ cittaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā”tiādinā ca, “yaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ cittaṃ uppajjitthāti? No. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… no”tiādinā ca,

‘Is a mind that is arising, an arisen mind? Yes. Or again... is it arising?... the mind at the moment of arising,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that is ceasing, an arisen mind? Yes,’ and so on. And ‘Is a mind that has arisen, a mind that did arise? No. Or again... No,’ and so on.

“Yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjittha no ca taṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ cittaṃ uppajjissatīti? No. Yaṃ vā pana…pe… no. Yaṃ cittaṃ nuppajjittha no ca taṃ cittaṃ nuppannaṃ, taṃ cittaṃ nuppajjissatīti? Āmantā”tiādinā ca, “uppannaṃ uppajjamānanti…pe… uppādakkhaṇe uppannañceva uppajjamānañca. Uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti? Āmantā”tiādinā ca, “niruddhaṃ nirujjhamānanti? No”tiādinā ca,

‘That mind which arose but is not arisen—will it arise? No. Or again... No. That mind which did not arise and is not unarisen—will it not arise? Yes,’ and so on. And, ‘Is the arisen arising?... At the moment of arising, it is both arisen and arising. Is the arising arisen? Yes,’ and so on. And, ‘Is the ceased ceasing? No,’ and so on.

“Yaṃ [M 0.0437] cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālaṃ, taṃ cittanti…pe… atītaṃ citta”ntiādinā ca dhammavāre,

‘That mind which, arising, moment by moment has passed, is past time; ceasing, moment by moment has passed, is past time’... ‘Past mind,’ and so on, in the section on phenomena.

“Yassa yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhati, tassa taṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissatīti? Āmantā”tiādinā ca puggaladhammavāre ca, sarāgādipadehi, kusalādipadehi ca missesu sabbavāresu ca pucchāsu heṭṭhā vuttānusārena vissajjananayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ cittayamakamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

‘For one whose mind arises but does not cease, will that mind cease and not arise? Yes,’ and so on. And in the section on individuals and phenomena, and in all the mixed sections with terms like ‘with lust,’ ‘wholesome,’ etc., the method of answering the questions should be understood in accordance with what has been stated above. This is the method of explaining the meaning of the Citta-yamaka matrix.

Dhammayamakamātikatthavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Meaning of the Dhamma Yamaka Matrix

Dhammayamakamātikāya pana khandhayamake vuttanayeneva pāḷivavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Yo kusalaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveti, so akusalaṃ dhammaṃ pajahatī”ti āgatattā panettha pariññāvāro bhāvanāvāro nāma. Tattha yasmā abyākato dhammo neva bhāvetabbo na pahātabbo, tasmā padameva na uddhaṭanti veditabbaṃ[V 0.0335]. Pucchāvissajjane panettha “kusalākusalā dhammāti? Āmantā”tiādinā, “dhammā akusalā dhammāti? Akusalā dhammā dhammā ceva akusalā dhammā ca, avasesā dhammā na akusalā dhammā”tiādinā ca paṇṇattivāre vissajjananayo ñātabbo.

In the Matrix of the Dhamma Yamaka, the arrangement of the Pāḷi text should be understood in the same way as stated in the Khandha Yamaka. Here, since it is stated: “One who develops a wholesome quality abandons an unwholesome quality,” this is called the section on full understanding and the section on development. Here, since an indeterminate quality is neither to be developed nor abandoned, it should be understood that the term itself is not brought up. In the question-and-answer section here, the method of answering in the section on designations should be understood, as in: “Are these qualities wholesome and unwholesome? Yes,” and similarly, “Are these qualities unwholesome qualities? Unwholesome qualities are both qualities and unwholesome qualities; the remaining qualities are not unwholesome qualities.”

“Yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa akusalā dhammā uppajjantīti? No. Yassa vā pana…pe… yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa abyākatā dhammā uppajjantīti? Pañcavokāre kusalānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe…pe… uppajjantī”tiādinā ca, “yattha kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tattha akusalā dhammā uppajjantīti? Āmantā…pe… tattha abyākatā dhammā uppajjantīti? Āmantā. Yattha vā pana abyākatā dhammā uppajjanti, tattha kusalā dhammā uppajjantīti [M 0.0438] …pe… catuvokāre…pe… uppajjantī”tiādinā ca, “yassa yattha kusalā dhammā…pe… uppajjantīti? No”tiādinā ca,

“For whom do wholesome states arise, for them do unwholesome states arise? No. Or for whom… For whom do wholesome states arise, for them do indeterminate states arise? In the five-constituent existence, at the moment of the arising of wholesome states… they arise.” And so on, as in: “Where wholesome states arise, do unwholesome states arise there? Yes… do indeterminate states arise there? Yes. Or where indeterminate states arise, do wholesome states arise there?… In the four-constituent existence… they arise.” And so on, as in: “For whom, where, do wholesome states… arise? No.”

“Yassa kusalā dhammā nuppajjanti, tassa akusalā dhammā nuppajjantīti…pe… sabbesaṃ cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe abyākatacittassa uppādakkhaṇe nirodhasamāpannānaṃ asaññasattānaṃ tesaṃ kusalā ca dhammā nuppajjanti, akusalā ca dhammā nuppajjantī”tiādinā ca, “yassa kusalā dhammā nuppajjanti, tassa abyākatā dhammā nuppajjantīti…pe… sabbesaṃ cavantānaṃ pavatte cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe āruppe akusalānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe ca nuppajjantī”tiādinā ca, “yattha kusalā dhammā nuppajjanti, tattha akusalā dhammā nuppajjantīti? Āmantā…pe… tattha abyākatā dhammā nuppajjantīti? Uppajjanti. Yattha vā pana abyākatā dhammā nuppajjanti, tattha akusalā dhammā nuppajjantīti? Natthī”tiādinā ca uppādavāre,

“For whom wholesome states do not arise, for them do unwholesome states not arise?… And so on, as in: “For all at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness, at the moment of the arising of indeterminate consciousness, for those attained to cessation, and for the non-percipient beings—for them, wholesome states do not arise, and unwholesome states also do not arise.” And so on, as in: “For whom wholesome states do not arise, for them do indeterminate states not arise?… And so on, as in: “For all who are passing away, at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness in the course of existence, and at the moment of the arising of unwholesome states in the formless realms, they do not arise.” And so on, as in: “Where wholesome states do not arise, do unwholesome states not arise there? Yes.… Do indeterminate states not arise there? They arise. But where indeterminate states do not arise, do unwholesome states not arise there? There is not.” And so on, in the section on arising.

“Yassa kusalā dhammā nirujjhanti, tassa akusalā dhammā nirujjhantīti? No”tiādinā nirodhavāre ca,

“For whom wholesome states cease, for them do unwholesome states cease? No.” And so on, in the section on cessation.

“Yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa akusalā dhammā nirujjhantīti? No”tiādinā uppādanirodhavāre ca,

“For whom wholesome states arise, for them do unwholesome states cease? No.” And so on, in the section on arising and cessation.

“Yo kusalaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveti, so akusalaṃ dhammaṃ pajahitthāti? No…pe… yo kusalaṃ dhammaṃ [V 0.0336] na bhāveti, so akusalaṃ dhammaṃ nappajahitthāti? Aggamaggasamaṅgiñca arahantañca ṭhapetvā avasesā puggalā”tiādinā bhāvanāvāre ca pucchāvissajjananayo heṭṭhā vuttānusārena ñātabbo.

“Has one who develops a wholesome quality abandoned an unwholesome quality? No.… Has one who does not develop a wholesome quality not abandoned an unwholesome quality? All individuals except for one possessed of the highest path and the Arahant.” And so on, in the section on development, the method of questioning and answering should be understood according to what was stated above.

Atthavinicchaye panettha idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Imassa hi dhammayamakassa pavattimahāvāre uppajjanti nirujjhantīti imesu uppādanirodhesu kusalākusaladhammā tāva ekantena pavattiyaṃyeva labbhanti, na cutipaṭisandhīsu, abyākatadhammā pana pavatte [M 0.0439] ca cutipaṭisandhīsu cāti tīsupi kālesu labbhanti, evamettha yaṃ yattha yattha labbhati, tassa vasena tattha tattha vinicchayo veditabbo.

Here, in the analysis of meaning, this is the characteristic. For this Dhamma Yamaka, in the great section on occurrence, in these instances of arising and ceasing—wholesome and unwholesome states are found exclusively in the course of existence, not at death or rebirth-linking. But indeterminate states are found in the course of existence, and also at death and rebirth-linking, that is, in all three times. Thus, here, the analysis should be understood in accordance with where each is found.

Tatridaṃ nayamukhaṃ – kusalākusalānaṃ tāva ekakkhaṇe anuppajjanato “no”ti paṭisedho kato. Abyākatā cāti idaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yattha kusalā dhammā nuppajjantīti asaññabhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, abyākatānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattiṭṭhānassābhāvā “natthī”ti paṭikkhepo kato, nirodhavāre kusalākusalānaṃ ekato anirujjhanato “no”ti vuttanti imināva nayamukhena sabbattha vinicchayo veditabbo. Ayaṃ dhammayamakamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

Here is the guiding principle: First, regarding wholesome and unwholesome states, since they do not arise in a single moment, the negation “no” is made. And the term “indeterminate” is said with reference to mind-originated materiality. “Where wholesome states do not arise” is said with reference to the non-percipient existence. Since there is no place of non-arising for indeterminate states, the rejection “there is not” is made. In the section on cessation, since wholesome and unwholesome states do not cease simultaneously, “no” is stated. By this very guiding principle, the analysis should be understood everywhere. This is the method of the exposition of the meaning of the Dhamma Yamaka Matrix.

Indriyayamakamātikatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Indriya Yamaka Matrix

Indriyayamakamātikāyaṃ pana khandhayamakamātikādīsu vuttanayeneva pāḷivavatthānādiko sabbo atthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo veditabbo. Manindriyaṃ panettha yathā cakkhundriyādimūlakehi, tatheva itthindriyādimūlakehi saddhiṃ sampayogaṃ gacchati, tasmā nikkhittapaṭipāṭiyā ayojetvā sabbehipi cakkhundriyamūlādīhi saddhiṃ pariyosāne yojitaṃ, cakkhundriyena ca saddhiṃ sukhindriyadukkhindriyadomanassindriyāni, lokuttarindriyāni ca paṭisandhiyaṃ natthīti na gahitāni. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sesindriyamūlakesupi yathānurūpaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Indriyānaṃ pana bahukatāya dhātuyamakatopi bahutarāni yamakāni honti ayaṃ viseso, sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttānusārena ñātabbanti. Ayaṃ indriyayamakamātikatthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo.

Now, in the matrix of the Indriya Yamaka, the entire method of explaining the meaning, beginning with the arrangement of the Pāḷi text, should be understood in the very same way as stated in the matrix of the Khandha Yamaka and others. Here, the mind faculty associates with the bases beginning with the eye faculty, just as it does with the bases beginning with the femininity faculty. Therefore, without connecting them in the established order, it is connected at the end with all the bases beginning with the eye faculty. And the faculties of pleasure, pain, and displeasure, and the supramundane faculties are not included with the eye faculty because they do not exist at rebirth-linking. Just as here, so too should it be understood appropriately in the remaining instances based on other faculties. But because the faculties are numerous, there are more pairs in the Indriya Yamaka than even in the Dhātu Yamaka—this is the difference. The rest should be understood according to what was stated earlier. This is the method of explaining the meaning of the Indriya Yamaka Matrix.

Mohavicchedaniyā abhidhammamātikatthavaṇṇanāya

In the Dispelling of Delusion: An Explanation of the Meaning of the Abhidhamma Matrix

Yamakamātikatthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Yamaka Matrix is concluded.

7. Paṭṭhānamātikatthavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Meaning of the Paṭṭhāna Matrix

Idāni [M 0.0440][V 0.0337] paṭṭhānamātikāya atthasaṃvaṇṇanānayo hoti. Kenaṭṭhena paṭṭhānanti? Nānappakārapaccayaṭṭhena. Pa-saddo hi nānappakāratthaṃ dīpeti, ṭhāna-saddo paccayatthaṃ. Atha vā vibhajanaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā hi paññāpanā paṭṭhapanā vivaraṇā vibhajanā uttānīkammanti āgataṭṭhāne vibhajanaṭṭho paṭṭhānasaddasamānattho paṭṭhapanā-saddo dissati, evamidhāpi kusalādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ hetupaccayādīhi vibhajanato vibhajanaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Atha vā paṭṭhitaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ, gamanaṭṭhenāti attho. Sabbadhammesu hi asaṅgagamanassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa hetupaccayādibhedabhinnesu kusalādīsu vitthāritanayalābhato nissaṅgavasena pavattagamanattā gamanaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ nāma, iti nānappakārapaccayaṭṭhena, vibhajanaṭṭhena, gamanaṭṭhena ca tikapaṭṭhānādīsu catuvīsatiyā paṭṭhānesu ekekampi paṭṭhānaṃ nāma, tesaṃ pana samūhato pakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāma, tesaṃ paṭṭhānānaṃ mātikā. Sayampi vā paṭṭhānabhūtā mātikā, sabbampetaṃ paṭṭhānamātikā. Yā sā “hetupaccayo, ārammaṇapaccayo…pe… avigatapaccayo”ti evaṃ tikapaṭṭhānādicatuvīsatippabhedasamantapaṭṭhānadesanāya mūlabhūtapaccayabhedassa vasena bhagavatā pakaraṇassa ādimhi ṭhapitā, ayaṃ idha paṭṭhānamātikā nāma.

Now is the method of explaining the meaning of the Paṭṭhāna Matrix. By what meaning is it Paṭṭhāna? By the meaning of various kinds of conditions. For the prefix 'pa-' signifies the meaning of various kinds, and the word 'ṭhāna' signifies the meaning of condition. Or alternatively, Paṭṭhāna is so called by the meaning of analysis. Just as in the passage where 'designation, setting forth, revealing, analysis, and making clear' occurs, the word 'setting forth' is seen to have the meaning of analysis and a meaning similar to the word Paṭṭhāna, so too here, because of the analysis of wholesome and other states by way of root condition and so on, it is called Paṭṭhāna by the meaning of analysis. Or alternatively, Paṭṭhāna is so called by the meaning of establishing, which means by the meaning of going. For in all phenomena, due to the attainment of an expanded method in wholesome and other states, which are differentiated by distinctions such as root condition, the all-knowing knowledge proceeds unhindered by way of non-attachment; hence, it is called Paṭṭhāna by the meaning of going. Thus, by the meaning of various kinds of conditions, by the meaning of analysis, and by the meaning of going, each of the twenty-four Paṭṭhānas in the Triplet Paṭṭhāna and so on is called a Paṭṭhāna. Their collection, however, is called the treatise Paṭṭhāna, and the matrix of those Paṭṭhānas is the Paṭṭhānamātikā. Or the matrix itself is the foundation, the Paṭṭhāna; all of this is the Paṭṭhāna Matrix. That which—'root condition, object condition… up to… non-disappearance condition'—was established by the Blessed One at the beginning of the treatise by way of the distinction of conditions, which is the foundation for the teaching on the Universal Paṭṭhāna with its twenty-four divisions, such as the Triplet Paṭṭhāna, this here is called the Paṭṭhāna Matrix.

Tattha anuttānatthādisahito saṅkhepatthavinicchayo tāva evaṃ veditabbo – hetupaccayotiādīsu hi hetu ca so paccayo cāti hetupaccayo, hetu hutvā paccayo hetupaccayo, hetubhāvena paccayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha hetūti vacanāvayavakāraṇamūlānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Paṭiññāhetū”tiādīsu hi loke vacanāvayavo “hetū”ti vuccati, sāsane pana “ye dhammā hetuppabhavā”tiādīsu [M 0.0441] (mahāva. 60; apa. thera 1.1.286) kāraṇaṃ, “tayo kusalā hetū, tayo akusalā hetū”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1059) mūlaṃ, idaṃ idha adhippetaṃ[V 0.0338], taṃ paṭicca etasmā etīti paccayo, apaccakkhāya naṃ vattatīti attho. Yo hi dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca apaccakkhāya tiṭṭhati vā uppajjati vā, so tassa upakārakalakkhaṇena paccayo nāma. Iti mūlaṭṭhena hetu, upakārakaṭṭhena paccayoti saṅkhepato mūlaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayo, kusalādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhakoti keci, evaṃ sante pana taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpesu hetupaccayatā na sampajjati, ahetukacittānañca vinā etehi abyākatabhāvo siddho, sahetukānampi ca yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, na sampayuttahetupaṭibaddho. Yadi ca siyā, hetūsupi kusalādibhāvasādhakena aññena bhavitabbaṃ, kusalādibhāvasādhanavasena pana hetūnaṃ mūlaṭṭhaṃ aggahetvā suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanavasena gayhamāne na kiñci virujjhati. Laddhahetupaccayā hi dhammā viruḷhamūlā viya pādapā thirā honti suppatiṭṭhitā, itare pana tilabījakādisevālā viya na suppatiṭṭhitā, iti mūlaṭṭhena upakārakoti suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayoti veditabbo.

Here, the concise determination of meanings, including those that are not obvious, should first be understood thus: In the case of "hetupaccayo" (root condition), etc., it is called "hetupaccayo" because it is both a root (hetu) and a condition (paccayo); it is a root condition by being a root and becoming a condition; it is said to be a condition by way of being a root. In this context, the term "hetu" is a designation for verbal components, causes, and roots. For in the world, in phrases like 'Paṭiññāhetū' (reason for a statement), etc., 'hetu' is said to be a verbal component. But in the Dispensation, in phrases like 'ye dhammā hetuppabhavā' (those phenomena that arise from a cause), etc., it refers to a cause, and in phrases like 'tayo kusalā hetū, tayo akusalā hetū' (three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots), etc., it refers to a root. This is what is intended here. That which depends on this and comes from it is a condition (paccayo). The meaning is that it proceeds without rejecting it. For any phenomenon that depends on another phenomenon and exists or arises without rejecting it is called a "condition" by virtue of its supportive characteristic. Thus, a root (hetu) is so by its nature as a basis, and a condition (paccayo) is so by its supportive nature. Therefore, in brief, a phenomenon that is supportive by way of being a root is a root condition. Some say it is what accomplishes the wholesome, etc., nature of wholesome states, etc. However, if this were the case, the root condition would not apply to the material forms arisen from them, and the indeterminate nature of rootless consciousness would be established without these. Moreover, the wholesome, etc., nature of rooted consciousness is connected with wise attention, etc., not with the associated roots. And if it were so, there would have to be another factor besides the roots that accomplishes the wholesome, etc., nature even in the roots themselves. But when the root's nature as a basis is understood not in terms of accomplishing the wholesome, etc., nature, but in terms of establishing well-establishedness, there is no contradiction. For phenomena that have obtained the root condition become firm and well-established like trees with well-grown roots, whereas others are not well-established, like sesame seeds and water weeds, etc. Thus, a phenomenon that is supportive by way of being a root—by establishing well-establishedness—should be understood as the root condition.

Niddese “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti vuttaṃ, tattha “cittasamuṭṭhānāna”nti avatvā “taṃsamuṭṭhānāna”nti idaṃ acittasamuṭṭhānānampi saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ. Pañhāvārasmiṃ hi “paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākābyākatā hetū sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti āgataṃ, kasmā panāyaṃ hetu paṭisandhiyameva kaṭattārūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo hoti[M 0.0442], na pavatteti? Paṭisandhiyaṃ kammajarūpānaṃ cittapaṭibaddhavuttitāya, bhavapaṭhamanipātato cittajāti. Itararūpasantatiuppatthambhābhāvena eva dubbalavatthuṃ cittameva nissāya uppajjati ceva tiṭṭhati ca. Taṃ cittampi hi paṭisandhikkhaṇe kammavegakkhittatāya ceva apurejātavatthukatāya ca appatiṭṭhitaṃ, papāte patitamattako puriso na kiñci sippaṃ kātuṃ viya cittajarūpaṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti, tameva kaṭattārūpaṃ nissāya patiṭṭhāti. Paṭisandhicittāni hi rūpaṃ na janenti, kammajarūpameva pana tesaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, pavattiyaṃ pana paṭiladdhupatthambhatāya taṃ rūpaṃ vināpi kammapaṭibaddhāva pavatti, hetupaccayassa panettha kusalādibhedato, bhūmibhedato ca vibhāgo heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabboti ayaṃ hetupaccaye nayo.

In the Niddesa, it is said: "The root is a condition by way of root condition for the states associated with the root and for the material forms arisen from them." Here, instead of saying 'arisen from consciousness,' the phrase 'arisen from them' is used to include even those not arisen from consciousness. For in the Pañhāvāra, it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, the indeterminate resultant roots are a condition by way of root condition for the associated aggregates and for the material form produced by karma." But why is this root a condition by way of root condition for the material form produced by karma only at rebirth-linking, and not during the course of existence? At rebirth-linking, this is because the occurrence of karma-produced matter is bound to consciousness, and consciousness arises from the very first moment of existence. Due to the absence of support from other material continuities, consciousness itself, relying on the weak basis, arises and persists. That consciousness, at the moment of rebirth-linking, is unsettled because it is propelled by the force of karma and lacks a pre-arisen physical basis—just as a man who has just fallen from a cliff cannot perform any skill, so too the consciousness cannot generate consciousness-produced material form; instead, it depends on that very karma-produced material form to become established. For rebirth-linking consciousnesses do not produce material form; rather, the karma-produced material form stands in place of consciousness-originated material form for them. During the course of existence, however, because support has been gained, its continuation is bound to karma even without that material form. The classification of the root condition here, by way of wholesome, etc., and by way of plane, should be understood in the same way as will be explained below. This is the method regarding the root condition.

Tato paresu ārammaṇabhāvena upakārako dhammo ārammaṇapaccayo, so niddese “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā…pe… phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ kāyaviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca [V 0.0339] dhammānaṃ…pe… rūpāyatanaṃ saddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ manodhātuyā…pe… sabbe dhammā manoviññāṇadhātuyā…pe… yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbha ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti evaṃ niddiṭṭhattā na koci dhammo na hoti. Yathā hi dubbalapuriso daṇḍaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā ālambitvā uṭṭhahati ceva tiṭṭhati ca, evaṃ cittacetasikā dhammā rūpādīsu chasu yaṃ kiñci ālambitvā uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca, tasmā lokiyalokuttarādibhedā sabbepi dhammā yathāyogaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayoti veditabboti ayaṃ ārammaṇapaccaye nayo.

Then, a phenomenon that is supportive by way of being an object is the object condition. In the Niddesa, it is stated thus: 'The visible form base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element… the tangible base is a condition for the body-consciousness element and for the states associated with it… the visible form base, sound, odour, taste, and tangible bases are conditions for the mind element… all phenomena are conditions for the mind-consciousness element… whatever phenomena, when taken as an object, give rise to whatever consciousness and mental factors, those phenomena are conditions for those phenomena by way of the object condition.' Because it is stated thus, no phenomenon is excluded. Just as a weak person, relying on a stick or a rope, both rises and stands, so too do consciousness and mental factors, relying on any of the six objects—forms, etc.—both arise and persist. Therefore, all phenomena, whether distinguished as mundane or supramundane, should be understood as the object condition for consciousness and mental factors, as is fitting. This is the method regarding the object condition.

Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo adhipatipaccayo, so niddese “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca [M 0.0443] rūpānaṃ…pe… vīriyacittavīmaṃsādhipati…pe… adhipatipaccayena paccayo, yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”ti evaṃ dvidhā niddiṭṭho. Tattha chandādayo sahajātādhipatibhāvena vuttā, garukātabbaṃ ārammaṇādhipatibhāvena. Tattha ca lokiyakusalabhūto ārammaṇādhipati lokiyakusalānañceva lobhasahagatacittānañca ārammaṇādhipati hoti, nāññassa, akusalabhūto pana lobhasahagatacittuppādoti vuccati itaresu garukātabbatāya abhāvato, so dvihetukāhetukādilokiyavipākarūpakkhandhabhūto ca lobhasahagatasseva, nāññassa, tathā kiriyabhūtopīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgataṃ, taṃ ñāṇasampayuttakiriyānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇābhiññādipubbavasappavattānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalehi garukātabbabhāvassāvirodhabhāvassa dassanato vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Lokuttarakusalāni pana kāmāvacarañāṇasampayuttajavanānameva ārammaṇādhipatipaccayā honti, nibbānaṃ pana tesaññeva lokuttarakusalavipākānañcāti veditabbanti ayaṃ adhipatipaccaye nayo.

The condition that assists by way of being foremost is the dominance condition. It is explained in two ways: "Desire as dominance is a condition for states associated with desire and for the material forms originating therefrom... energy, mind, and investigation as dominance... by way of the dominance condition. Whatever state is made weighty, whatever consciousness and mental factors arise, those preceding states are a condition for those subsequent states by way of the dominance condition." Herein, desire and the like are mentioned as conascent dominance, while what is to be made weighty is mentioned as object-dominance.
